body.text_en:
All praise is due to Allah, we have gathered once again for these sessions. I am very happy and excited for this opportunity to speak with all of you in these sessions. I have held these sessions once before as well, with a small group. It is their love that, all praise to Allah, they are all present in this session too. And, as God has willed, there are many new people — children and adults alike. I began this series with three or four people. I never even imagined that Allah would grant such blessing. All praise to Allah! God willing, these sessions are for everyone, and I hope that everyone will gain something or other from them. But the purpose of these sessions of mine — the people I want to speak to in them — are the young.

You young people are the primary focus of my sessions, because the true wealth of any nation is always its young generation. As we studied in Chahal Sabaq, Allah created you not just for these times, but for the times to come. God willing, you are the ones who will lead Sulemaniat into the future. You are the ones who will, God willing, uphold the teachings of Rasul Allah, Maulana Ali, and the Imams in the times to come. And this is why, when you attend these sessions, I want you to gain this knowledge first for yourself, and, if you find it useful, then to help the people around you: your younger brothers and sisters, your jamaat brothers and sisters, your children, your family's children. Because this is the whole purpose of knowledge! Criticism has never ever changed a thing. The only way we can bring about a change is by acquiring knowledge, perfecting it within ourselves, and then leading by example.

And for this reason, the very first thing I want to say to all of you is this: in religion, the thing that stops us from moving forward, the thing that stops us from acquiring knowledge, is the search for perfection. The desire to find perfection, or zero tolerance for errors or mistakes, whether that exists in the knowledge or in the teacher. So whoever you acquire knowledge from, whether worldly or religious, do not try to search for perfection in those people. Otherwise you will always be disappointed. Perfect is Allah alone. No servant apart from Him can ever be perfect. And this is by design. Anyone can make a mistake. My intention is to tell you exactly what is correct, but I can make a mistake — whether by intent, by oversight, or by error. It may be that I fail to explain something to you properly. It may be that you do not understand what I say properly. I wanted to say one thing to you, could not explain it well, and you understood something else. All these things can certainly happen.

The second point is this: today you may hold a certain opinion about me. Tomorrow you may come to learn something about me that changes your opinion of me. At that time, forget who I am; simply remember what I said. For Maulana Ali has said: لا تنظر الی ’من‘ قال! أنظر الی ’ما‘ قال۔ Do not look at the one who is speaking, at who he is! Look at what he is saying. Do not focus on who is saying it, focus on what is being said. So from whomever you learn, do not look at who he is or what he does. Look at what he says — whether there is something in it for you to learn or not. The one who tells you has the standing of a postman who has come to hand you your letter. When the postman gives you a letter, what do you do? You look at your name and your address on the letter. If they are correct, you take the letter from him. You do not say to him: you drink wine, you gamble, you commit adultery — I will not take the letter from your hands.

Is that not so? You see that the letter is yours, and you take it from him. This same principle holds for acquiring knowledge. If what I say seems right to you, then take it; if it does not seem right, then leave it. Never reject someone's knowledge simply because you do not like the person. If a person says one thing and does something else, that is on him. That is his weakness. It does not invalidate the knowledge he gave you. You accept the knowledge, and you try to make the best of it! I have always followed this principle, and, Hamdulillah, it has always done wonders for me.

The second thing I want to say is this. When I first held these sessions, I held them with a very small group, one I was very comfortable with. I had no fear at all that anything I said would upset someone, or that anyone would take offense at something of mine, because I knew them, and all of them knew me, very well. But now this group has many people in it — some older, some younger — whom I do not know, and who do not know me personally. To those who do not know me, my manner of speaking may seem very straightforward, very direct. I do not sugarcoat things. I say them just as I see them. For that reason, I am really concerned that something I say might offend someone. My aim is not in the least to criticize anyone. I only wish to place a few things before you, to discuss a few things with you.

There is absolutely no compulsion in religion. لا اکراہ فی الدین۔ قد تبین الرشد من الغی I have clearly separated out the path of guidance from the path of deception for you. I have made the true path so clear for you that if, after that, you are not following it, then that is nothing but your own arrogance and obstinacy. It is not because of any flaw in my religion. Allah is claiming this! And we testify to this verse after every obligatory prayer, in the Verse of the Throne.

So Islam, in the end, really is a personal choice! A choice each and every one of us has to make individually, independently.

So, God willing, this is the purpose of my sessions. This is my intention. May Allah, glorified and exalted, "by the truth of Ta Ha and Ya Sin," grant me success in my purpose. Amen, O Lord of the worlds!

Now let us talk briefly about the format of the sessions.

1. First of all, you will have noticed that I call these sessions, not lessons or gatherings. Because what I have to say does not match the format of a lesson or a gathering. I look at it more as a presentation of Islam than as lessons.

2. In these sessions I do not teach from any book. I will simply take a topic and discuss it. I feel that this kind of impromptu conversation is more powerful than reading from a book. I am able to connect so much better with these sessions that way. A friend really helped me understand what I am actually doing in these sessions. To me these sessions are not just about teaching you or talking about Islam. I feel these sessions are also a medium for me to connect with Allah. So these sessions are as much for me as they are for you. If nothing else, I just want to talk about, and remember, Allah, my prophet, and Maulana Ali, peace be upon them, and glorify them.

3. Today, as you will have noticed, I spoke in both English and Urdu. Some are more comfortable with English, some are more comfortable in Urdu. I will try to use both. However, personally I find it more comfortable to express myself in Urdu. So if that becomes a problem, I was thinking that at the end of each session I can just get online with the kids and give them the gist of the session in ten minutes in English. But, God willing, we will try different things. I will do some sessions in English, some in Urdu. In some I will mix it up. And then we will choose the one that works best for everyone.

4. Last time I finished all my topics in twelve sessions. This time I will not do that. I will do what I can in an hour, and leave the rest for the next session, however many sessions it may take. The real purpose is that the children understand. Let us do a little, but do it well. So I would suggest that you take notes. If we break one topic across multiple sessions, then it is essential that you revise the previous session before coming to the next one, otherwise you will not gain the benefit that I wish to convey.

5. Since these are the sciences within the sphere of Islam, there will be no esoteric interpretation or inner realities discussed in them. The things I will tell you come from my fourteen or fifteen years of research. These sciences come from the books of our own daawat as well as from the books of the Muslims. Maulana Ali has said: الحق ضال المومن۔ Truth is the lost she-camel of a believer. If you own a camel, and you lose it, and later you find it in someone else's possession, what will you do?

You will go and take it from him. You will not concern yourself with that person's character, his religion, or his race. It is your camel, and you will take it back. Knowledge is such a camel. Take it from whoever you receive it from. If you follow this, you will be able to learn a great deal in life, God willing. The one thing that is essential here is that you have that piece of knowledge notarized by our elders. Have it verified. If they say it is true, then take it; otherwise, reject it. God willing, whatever I share with you, I have verified with my teachers and elders.

6. I strongly encourage you to ask questions. You may send them to me on WhatsApp while the session is under way, or I can answer them during the question-and-answer portion of our session. You may also ask questions during the week, and I will answer them in the next session.

8. I do not have permission to record these sessions. For that reason, please do not record them either. Whatever is done without permission becomes corrupted and brings harm.

9. And finally, one of the challenges I face is that ours is an audio conversation. After a while, I begin to feel as though I am talking to my monitor. That is why I am going to use a more interactive method. I have asked some of the children, and they have bravely agreed to come forward and let me hold a conversation with them. I will discuss matters with them, or put rhetorical questions to them, and in this way it will be more interactive than mere passive listening.

Yasmeen, Hussain, Imran Saleem, and Nadia have agreed. But I would ask all the children to volunteer for this. I will not compel anyone. So if you would like to take part, please let me know, and God willing we will have a great deal of fun.

Finally, which topics will we cover? God willing, whatever I tell you, I will tell you from the Quran, the hadith, and the sayings of Maulana Ali.

Nadia, let us imagine that you have been elected the next president of your country. You have an agenda of what you wish to do, what changes you wish to bring about, what kind of support you will need from the people of your country, and so on. Who would be the best person to explain that? If I introduced you at your inauguration ceremony as the next president, would you prefer that I explain your plans, or would you prefer to explain them yourself? Why?

So then, if we wished to understand Allah — who He is, what He wants, why He created us — who is the best being to explain that to us? It is Allah. And where does He explain it? In His book, the Holy Quran. So first, let us establish the importance of this book. Let us begin with this: why is this book a miracle? What is a miracle? How do we know that this book is the word of Allah? We need to establish this first in our hearts — not in our minds, but in our hearts — for only then can we give honest attention to what the book says. So that is where I am going to begin.

Once we have done that, we will see from the Quran what Allah says, and what it is that He wants from us. Does He truly love us? What is love? Who is Rasool Allah? Does Rasool Allah love us? How much does he love us? Is there any proof of that? So we will discuss all these topics, and I will show you how much Allah loves us, and how much His prophet loved us. You will see that love so clearly that it will make it impossible for you not to love them back. If you were to ask me to summarize the entire goal of my sessions in a single word!

It's LOVE! Such immense love that Allah has for us, and I will prove to you that Allah has asked nothing from us in return except that love. Everything we do—prayer, fasting, zakat, the pilgrimage—is an expression of that love.

You are always welcome to disagree or argue with me. In fact, I would appreciate that. I may end up learning from your point of view. So what I am saying is that my intentions are good, but I am not sure about my method or my technique, because I am really not a teacher; I have no training in teaching. I can only share things with you the way I learned them myself. But I do want to challenge your existing concepts, the way I challenged mine. And that can certainly be uncomfortable at times. Yet the purpose of it is not to criticize, not to prove you wrong, but to see whether there is a solution out there, whether there is a different perspective out there. So all I want to do is present a different perspective to you — not as something you must accept and follow, but only as a possibility. Just something to think about, something to try on for size.

I am not a learned man, I am not an orator, I am not a scholar. Allah has been very gracious to me, for He gave me the finest elders and teachers, granted me the honor of acquiring knowledge from them, and the little I have learned from them I wish to share with you. So I make no claim whatsoever to being a learned man of any kind. If something I say seems good to you, seems right, then that is the grace of my elders, and all praise for it belongs to them. And if something seems wrong to you, then I alone am responsible for it; the knowledge of my elders is free from all error.

For anything good that you learn in these sessions, the credit goes to my elders and my teachers. And if you find something wrong in what I said, then I alone am responsible for that error, because of my own incapacity, for the knowledge of my elders is free from all faults. So, as I said earlier, do not reject the knowledge because of the person. If you do not find the answers from me, then strive to find someone better than me to get the answers. But you never stop; you never quit.

Because there is not a single question that we do not have an answer for! So these are just a few things I wanted to say before beginning: today I want to speak with you only about the problems that led me to start these sessions, and in answer to which I began them. We first need to understand the problem before we try to talk about a solution!

Sayyiduna Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in his *Kitab al-'Alim wa'l-Ghulam*, says:

فجعلَ لِکُلِّ أَوَّلِ مِنہُ آخَر۔ وَلِکُلِّ آخِر مِنہُ غاَیَۃ۔ وَلِکُلِّ غَایۃٌ نِّھَایَۃ ۔ لا یَبلُغُ أمْدَھاَ

So for each beginning He has placed in it an end, and for each end a goal; and each goal has a limit whose full extent cannot be attained.

The purpose of any journey is its destination. So in today's session I want to explain: what is the destination of this journey of ours? But even more important than that is this—what is our need to set out on this journey at all? Why do we even want to take this journey?

Today we live in a world surrounded by nudity, violence, shamelessness, bad language, tyranny, and terrorism. And we are told that Islam is supposedly the solution to these problems. However, what we see in reality is the inverse of it! We see Islam to be the cause of these problems in most cases. Today Islam is seen, at the very best, as a major inconvenience in our day-to-day life, and at the very worst as terrorism—a radical religion. And the question we are asked is: if every Muslim is not a terrorist, then how come every terrorist today turns out to be a Muslim?

Today a very bad picture of Islam stands before us. Those who claim to understand Islam present it badly, and so do those who do not understand it. We see that in the name of Islam oppression is being carried out on every side. Terror and fear are being spread. Islam, which is a religion of peace and safety, has among its own followers Muslims who kill people in the name of Islam—and what reason do they give? That by doing so, what will happen? That in exchange God will marry him in Paradise to seventy houris (70 virgins). So is Paradise really a place where things of this kind exist?

And we, as intelligent individuals, ask ourselves: does this even make sense? Is Islam really so messed up? Is it so illogical? I cannot even handle one single wife; what am I going to do with seventy? But these are questions that, if we openly ask, we are a disbeliever. If we do not, then we simply do not know what to believe.

Now the example I just gave you is a very extreme example. But you can find so many logical disconnects between what is being asked of us on a day-to-day basis as well. And in the absence of any real logical answers, we are forced to accept whatever weak rationale is presented to us. For example, learning to read the Qur'an is one of them.

I invite any of you living in the US or England to go and tell one of your American or English friends that you can read this book in Arabic, perfectly, but you do not understand a single word of it. And then I want you to observe the expression on his face. He will look at you as if you are from a different planet. His first response will be—why? That does not make any sense! Because, for your friend, it is absolutely illogical, completely irrational, to take a book in a completely different language, be able to read it, and recite it with no comprehension at all.

But that somehow makes perfect sense to us!! And then tell your friend that this Arabic book you're talking about is in fact the Quran. The book of spiritual guidance that Allah gave to our prophet so that we can be guided by it. And then, to top it off, tell him... oh, by the way, this book of guidance, that I have no understanding of, is actually Allah's greatest miracle for all mankind!! Really! I'm not kidding. I've done this experiment several times. You'll be amazed at their reaction. So how come something that seems so illogical, so irrational, to our friends is perfectly acceptable to you and I?? And this is just one of so many examples. With such amazing and incredible disconnects, how are we supposed to make sense of, and glorify, Islam for ourselves? Forget others!

Look, I completely understand the rationale that we need to learn and memorize the Arabic duas for namaaz so that we can pray. Even reciting the words of the Quran, without understanding, brings us sawaab, so there is value in that as well. I'm not denying that, or disagreeing with that. That is all true... All I'm saying is, why do we choose to stop there? Why do we settle for a drop, when Allah wants to give us the ocean?

So the deeper question is, what is it about religion that forces us to switch our brains off? Is that what faith means? To just believe anything? Is Islam about blind faith?

See, because what happens is that, as a result of these disconnects, we, the intelligent, independent people of this time, are forced to believe that times have changed... This is no longer the times of the prophet, Islam is too restrictive for today's day and age, and therefore it is not applicable in our times. We do it because our parents did it this way, and their parents before them did it this way...

That was about Islam; now let us speak about Allah. Look today: Allah, who has described Himself as الرحمن الرحیم, what has He become in our eyes? Does it not seem to you that His role — نعوذ باللہ — has been reduced to that of a tyrant king? From childhood we hear: do this and it is hell, do that and it is hell. Heaven and hell have basically become the carrot and stick of religion. If someone does not know the carrot and stick philosophy, this is how work was got out of a donkey in the old days. Because a donkey is a very obstinate and stubborn animal. So, to make it work, a carrot would be held up before it: if you work, this is your reward. And if not, a stick would be shown to it, so that, out of fear of the pain, it would work. So today, for Muslims too, heaven has become the carrot and hell the stick.

So the question is: does Allah want to burn us in hell? Is Allah — نعوذ باللہ — a tyrant?? And if that is not so, and He wants to give us heaven, then why did He not simply create us in heaven in the first place? And if that is not it either, then what, in the end, does Allah want from us?? What is this thing called worship? What need does He have of our worship?

I remember this conversation I once had with my friend's dad in Pakistan, who was a maulvi of the local masjid and an aalim. Now granted, I used to be very arrogant in those days, and I deliberately used to get into these arguments with them just to set them off... because I knew they didn't have any answers. So one day he was telling us about the importance of worship... So I asked him... Why does Allah so desperately want us to worship Him? 5 times a day? Fasting? Zakat, Hajj??

Why does He need our worship and prayers so much? Isn't He supposed to be الصمد (The Self-Sufficient)? So he said... Oh no, no no! It's not Allah that needs to be worshiped, you are the one who is in need of worshiping Him! Because He provides for you, takes care of you. So I said... Really? I don't really think I need Him for all that stuff... I have my dad for that... He makes my life awesome. He makes the money that we live off, I have my school, I have my sports practice, I've got good food, servants in the house, I'm all set!! What do I need to pray for? Oh but Allah gave you your dad... and all this money and the comforts you're enjoying... So you need to pray to Allah so that He continues to bless you with these things. So I said... so what you're telling me is that because of all these things Allah has given me, I need to worship Him, and if I worship, I will continue to have these things. Is that correct? He goes, Yes! So I asked, then why did Allah not give all this to my poor friend's dad? He worships more than my dad! Isn't Allah just? Isn't He loving! What's so special about my dad? Why did He give all this to my dad and not my friend's dad? And we would go back and forth, and this conversation eventually always ended in the same way... Badtameez! Kaafir! You're going to hell! So this is what always eventually happens. Try the carrot philosophy; if that doesn't work, resort to the stick. Preach by force. And even if you don't understand, just accept what is being told. Either blindly follow the shareeat, or burn in hell.

So does Islam really have no answers to our questions? What is Allah? Who is He? What is Islam? What is this Qur'an? What is its purpose? In our eyes, what value does this book have, and what value should it have? Is this book only for swearing oaths upon? Is it only to be recited without any understanding?

This amazing book was supposed to be the ultimate guide, the ultimate miracle of Allah to His prophet and to His mankind. We've changed it into nothing more than a paperweight. It just sits on our shelves, or if we recite it, we do so without understanding anything, and we are totally content with that. I'm speaking very generally, of course. But you see, in our day-to-day life, we never act this way. If you're in school and you don't understand a concept, you get after your teacher, you do whatever it takes to understand it. Why? Because if you don't, it will affect your grade. You won't be able to pass your exam. So how come this book, the Quran, which is the solution key for the exam of this life, we don't make the effort to understand?? How come we're not worried about our overall grade in the afterlife? Why did we choose to condition ourselves this way?

My Prophet said: إني تاركُ فيكم الثقلين : كتاب الله ، وعترتي أهل بيتي ، ما إن تَمَسَّكتُم بِهِمَا لَن تَضِلُّوا بعدي أبدا — I am leaving among you two precious things. One is the Book of Allah (the Qur'an), and the other is my household (the line of the Imams). As long as you hold to both of them together, you will never go astray.

We speak ill of the Muslims, we say they are wrong for having grasped only the Qur'an and abandoned the Imams. For this we call them wrongdoers. But if you think honestly, we too have grasped only the Imams and abandoned the Qur'an. So how are we any different from them? For the Messenger of Allah said: ما إن تَمَسَّكتُم بِهِمَا.

Whoever holds to both will not go astray. So if they have abandoned one, we too have abandoned one. How are we any different? We know only as much of the Qur'an as we are told and taught in the gatherings and the lessons. Why can we not understand the Qur'an ourselves? And if learning Arabic is necessary for that, why is that such a problem? We learn other languages too, after all. We can learn French, German, Italian, all these other languages, so why not Arabic?

My next question is about certainty. Do we truly hold the conviction of God's existence that we ought to hold? Because before anything else, we must be certain that God exists. His Messenger, His Book, His religion, these all come afterward. So does God exist? And if He does, what is the proof of it?

Consider this. In our minds we have a notion of God, a concept. But the question is this: is God a concept, or is God a reality? Is he a concept, or is he a reality?

Let me ask it another way. If you were to ask me whether fire burns, and whether this is my concept or a reality, I would tell you it is both! Fire burns, it is a concept, and it is also a reality. You would ask, are you certain? I would say, absolutely certain! Why? Because if you were to light a fire in front of me and say, put your hand into this fire, and then swear to me by God and by the Qur'an that nothing at all would happen to your hand, that your hand would not burn in the least, would I put my hand into the fire? Never would I put it in! Why? Because I am certain that if I put my hand into the fire, my hand would surely burn. There is absolutely no doubt about that. Because I am certain that fire burns.

So now I ask you. We say that we are certain of God's existence, certain of His reward and punishment, that paradise is real, that hell is real. We are certain that there is fire in hell, and that fire burns, and that we will go into hell on account of our sins. If I am fully certain of all these things, then why do I sin? Because I am certain that the fire will burn. The very fire into which, just a moment ago, I was unwilling even to put my hand, if I am certain that on account of my sins my whole being will be burned in that same fire, then why do I sin? All of these things deserve deep thought. Am I truly certain of God, of His paradise and His hell? Or is all of this, to my mind, merely a concept that I have taken to be a reality?

And if it is only a concept, is there any way to change that concept into a reality? And if there is, what is it?

This is the true purpose of my sessions: that God should change, for us, from a concept into a reality. That He should change from a notion into a reality. And I want to take all of you along with me on this beautiful journey. Because these were all my own questions, the questions in search of which I had set out.

Let me tell you a little about myself, about how I changed my 'concept' of God into 'certainty.' From childhood I had no particular interest in religion. That was because my case too was one of blind faith. But when I came to America and the events of 9/11 took place, at that time my religion, my faith, was utterly destroyed. My faith was completely shattered. At that time a doubt arose in me as to whether Islam was even the right religion or not. I asked myself why I was a Muslim. Only because my parents were Muslims? What if Islam is not the right religion? Perhaps Christianity was the right path? So from that time the focus of my life changed. One after another, I began to read all the other religions. I read the Vedas of the Hindus, I read the Ramayana and the Bhagavad Gita, I read the Old Testament and the New Testament, I read about Buddhism, I read a translation of the Qur'an.

I met with them all — pundit, priest, rabbi, and mullah. For nearly three years I researched this, and in the end I became certain that Islam alone is the true religion. And that Islam is not some new religion. Islam says all the very things that the religions before it said, just as God Most High Himself declares: ان الدین عند اللہ الاسلام. With God, the religion has always been Islam. I came to understand that all religions are like versions. All religions are like the OS versions on your phone. We keep getting notifications to upgrade to the latest version. Your computer notifies you of all the latest patches for all the vulnerabilities in your operating system. And given the choice, you always upgrade! Why? Because you want to use the latest, more advanced, more sophisticated features. So Islam is the latest version of this operating system called life! It is a patch for all the deficiencies and weaknesses in previous religions. So after three years of research, I finally concluded that. I basically came full circle.

Then God's grace descended upon me, and He granted me the finest teachers. I studied all these sciences — taawil, mabda and maad, the realities and the fine points, and the rest — and I became completely certain that Islam, and within Islam the Sulaymani path, is the true religion. This was because I had a great deal of material to compare. The sciences of our daawa — these sciences are found in no other religion. And I am certain of this precisely because I have studied the religion of others. So I found the answers to all my questions. Indeed, as my master, Hazrat Zia Ali Sahib the sanctified, once said: we possess the answers to questions that have not yet even arisen. We have the answers, for which questions have not yet been imagined. I received answers far surpassing all the questions I had. الحمد للہ!

Having shared this background with you, I now turn to the purpose of these sessions — what I had in mind when I began them. A few years ago, certain incidents happened to me that brought about a very powerful realization. I caught myself doing a great many wrong things, small and large. And I was greatly astonished: how is it possible that after so many years of study, after acquiring so much knowledge, I am still doing such wrong things? Having read and understood everything, I am still telling pointless little lies, backbiting, deceiving, committing dishonesties both small and large. I am not praying my prayers in full, and when I do pray them, I am not praying them at their earliest appointed time. Why, in the end, is my knowledge not restraining me from these evils? The very purpose of knowledge is to remove the corruptions of the self! So if, even after learning knowledge, the evils within me remain exactly as they were, then what's missing? What have I failed to understand?

And then — حمد للہ — I realized that I had acquired a great deal of knowledge, yet I had not understood the fundamental precepts and principles of Islam at all. The logistics of Islam and faith had settled into my mind: if anyone were to ask me, I could tell them at once where we came from and how we will return, what the Intellects are, what the Worlds are, what the Imam is, and so on. I had grasped all these sciences theoretically, but their correct application simply was not in me. Even today I act upon the same old pattern, without thought or reflection. Even today, God, the Messenger, and religion are for me only a concept, not a reality. You see, we all know about health and diet. Ask any overweight person, and he can tell you more about weight loss than anyone else. I know this because I myself am overweight.

But does all this knowing make me thin? It cannot. All this knowledge sitting in the mind is of no use. It becomes useful only when the motivation for it is present in the heart. Only then can a person put the information in his mind to work and reduce his weight. If there is no motivation in the heart, no solid reason, then weight loss is only a concept, not a reality.

And this is exactly what I came to understand: my mind holds a great deal of information about religion, but there is no real motivation in my heart to act upon it. This is because religion is still a concept in my mind; it has not become a reality that sinks into my heart.

So I set out once more in search of Islam, to find out what the Islam of the heart is. What is its purpose? And how do I bring it down into my own heart? Then I began to read with a new frame of mind. I literally went back to the basics. I had been learning Arabic for eleven years, but now I learned Qur'anic Arabic, understood the Qur'an, and understood the teachings of the Qur'an. I understood what God is, and what He wants from us. And when these things became clear to me, only then did Islam settle into my heart. And when Islam settled into my heart, my whole life changed. My acts of worship changed, my thinking changed, my priorities changed. All the time my thinking had been, what will people say about me? That thinking changed and became, what will God and His Messenger think about me? Acts of worship were no longer difficult, rising in the night was no longer difficult. I began to feel joy in giving charity. It literally felt as though someone had turned on a light in the dark room of my heart!! everything started becoming so clear to me. But all of this happened only when Islam settled into my heart. As long as it was in my mind, it produced no change in my conduct.

So in these sessions of mine I want to take you along with me on that same journey. So this is the journey, I want to have with you. It's my wish that we take a step back and look at Islam from a distance. Not our Islam, the one we see around us, but Rasool Allah's (SW) Islam. The Islam that was revealed to the people of Arabia. Let's study what that Islam was all about. What does Islam wants from us? Is it even beneficial to us. What does it have to offer? Is it applicable in these times? Will it help me in my day to day life? Is there a bigger picture here, or is Islam just for this life? Let's analyze these questions one by one, slowly, carefully. Let's ask the questions we really want to ask, but never dared to ask, and see if Islam has the answers for us? So my goal in these sessions is basically to show off! Not my knowledge or myself, but I wish to show off our Lord Allah, His beloved messanger Muhammd (PBUH), His wasi Maulana Ali, his Ahlul Bait (علیھم السلام)! Because that is what you do with something that is beautiful and something you're proud of. We have the most beautiful religion, based on a love that transcends imagination! I want to show you how beautiful this book Quran is, and how it is a miracle. And how it is the solution to all our problems in not just this life, but also the hereafter. How it is the solution to all our emotional grief, our depressions, or worries, our anxieties. It is the most beautiful book you will ever read InshaAllah! And then, at the end of it, if Islam seems the PERFECT solution, the ONLY solution... not just for this life, but also the after life, ONLY then let's CHOOSE islam for ourselves.

Before the miracle can be discussed, I want us to understand the setting into which the revelation came. Content without its context is a disaster. To grasp any content clearly, you must study it within its proper setting. There are countless examples that show this, but I will give you one simple one.

First, let us count to ten: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten.

Now I will count to ten again, but this time I will place one of the numbers out of context, and you tell me which number is out of place: one, two, three, five, six, four, seven, eight, nine, and ten.

It is easy to see that the number four is out of place. What told you that it was out of place? The numbers around it, was it not? The sequence, the surroundings, revealed to you that the four did not belong. For if I had counted one, three, five, seven, nine, two, four, six, eight, ten, then the four would not be out of place at all, because it falls in line with the numbers around it.

So, in order to understand the miracle of the Qur'an, we must understand it within the context of Arabia, where it was being revealed. One of the greatest reasons we are unable to experience the miracle of the Qur'an is that we try to experience it in the context of 2016. The Qur'an is a timeless miracle, but what we must understand is that it was one kind of miracle for the people in the time of the Prophet, and it is a different kind of miracle for us. There are wonderful things about the Qur'an that the ancient Arabs could see and experience which are completely lost on us. And there are wonderful things about the Qur'an that you and I would find absolutely miraculous which the ancient Arabs could not experience at all. This is what makes the Qur'an a timeless miracle. It continually adapts to the changing times.

As I said in our last session, the best introduction is the one a person gives of himself. For us to know what Allah wants, the best source of that knowledge would be Allah himself. He gives that knowledge in his book, the Holy Qur'an, the ultimate miracle he bestowed upon his beloved Prophet. When you favor someone, you give them more than you give the rest of the world. So, by that reasoning, the Qur'an must be the best of all miracles, the most powerful of all miracles, the most wonderful of all miracles.

Yet we, as Muslims, fail entirely to see that. That is why I wanted to begin with why this book is a miracle, because this revelation is what the Messenger of Allah used as his proof of prophethood. We already believe this book to be a miracle by faith, which is a matter of the heart. But let us see whether we can find a way to believe it with the intellect as well.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
And as I said before, there are only two things that matter: the heart, which is the source of all emotion, and the intellect, which is the source of all reasoning. If you have only information in the mind, it does not naturally turn into action. You must use integrity to force the action. And if you have only faith, then although it will result in action, the action will be weak, and you will not be able to sustain it for long. Faith that stands on the ground of doubt cannot stand for long. Therefore, only when we establish a balance between the heart and the intellect can actions become perfect.

They become everlasting, and they become exceedingly powerful. The miracle of the Qur'an is a vast subject. God willing, I intend to cover it across three sessions. I will show you the actual miracle in the third session, but I must lay the groundwork in these first two so that we are truly able to see the miracle in the third. What I wish to show you requires a complete shift in the way we think. So please do not miss the next two sessions. I promise you it will be truly remarkable, God willing. I especially want you children to see this, and that is why I am going to attempt all three sessions in English, because I do not want any one of you to miss a single thing. This is also why I asked you to take notes if you are able to. Unfortunately, there is a gap of seven days between the two sessions, and for that reason it is very important that when you come to the next session, you remember everything I say today as though you had just heard it from me, because I will pick up exactly where I left off in the previous session.

So let us begin by asking ourselves a couple of basic questions.

My first question is this: Is the Qur'an the word of Allah, or is it the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him)? Did Allah give His Messenger the actual Arabic words, or was it the Prophet's own composition?

My second question: Is the Qur'an for the heart or for the intellect?

What do you think? Simply call it out. Anyone.

As I said in my previous session, the way I want to do this is to pretend that I am speaking to only a couple of people, so that we can make this interactive.

Let us hear from Yasmeen Hussain.

Well, let us look at what the Qur'an itself says:

وَإِنَّهُۥ لَتَنزِيلُ رَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ۔ نَزَلَ بِهِ ٱلرُّوحُ ٱلْأَمِينُ۔ عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ لِتَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُنذِرِينَ۔ بِلِسَانٍ عَرَبِىٍّۢ مُّبِينٍۢ

This Qur'an has been sent down to you by the Lord of the worlds. It was brought down by the trustworthy spirit (Jibra'il), upon your heart, so that you may warn mankind, in a clear Arabic tongue.

So the verse says (عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ), that it was revealed upon the heart. How interesting! Not upon the intellect, but upon the heart. Is that not strange? The intellect is the actual instrument of reasoning, yet Allah says that He revealed it upon your heart, which is the source of the emotions. Why is that?
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
Let me try to explain what was so extraordinary about their poetry. They spoke in riddles. They spoke in images. When an Arab looked out of his window, what did he see? Nothing. He saw only the empty, dry desert. When you see nothing, you develop a most vivid imagination. Today we have little imagination. Do you know why? Because everything we might conceive of has already been pictured for us in science-fiction films. So when we are asked to imagine, we merely recount some variation of what we have already seen. But a fine imagination is the power to imagine what one has never seen before. And this was the imagination of the Arab. They would paint pictures with their words. They used words that were richly pictorial. Their words were full of imagery.

There is a certain poet. He is composing verses about how generous he is and how much he gives away in charity. So his wife comes to him and says: Have you lost your mind? We do not even have food to eat. What are you talking about?

We're bankrupt, and you compose poetry about how generous you are? He turns to her and answers her in poetry. He says:

السَّیلُ حَربٌ عَلی مَکانِ العَالِی

Heavy rain does not get along with a house on top of a hill!

What does that have to do with charity, with being generous? But do you know what he was really saying?

Picture a house on top of a hill. And what is happening? Heavy rain! When it rains, does the water stay on top of the hill, or does it run down to the bottom? So he says: provision comes from the sky. And there are two kinds of people in the world. The lofty and the lowly. Those who are near to God, and those who are of the world. If your house is on top of the hill, are you not near to the sky? Near to God? So the water does not stay with me, meaning the provision does not stay with me. I keep passing it down to the lowly people. And where does the water gather? Where does it collect into a puddle? So the rich are in truth the lowly ones, and I am the lofty one.

And he says all of this by saying what?

السَّیلُ حَربٌ عَلی مَکانِ العَالِی

Five words. Heavy rain does not get along with a house on top of a hill!

So they spoke in these riddles. They wanted you to imagine what was being said. They would not simply state it. And if you did not grasp it, they would say ... hah! Ajam — mute!!! So this was the kind of sensitivity to language that they took pleasure in.

Now think about this. Imagine you are about to fight an opponent with naked swords. You are facing death this very moment. Can you imagine what your state of mind would be? I know that I would not even remember my own name if you asked me! But these Arabs, they would recite poetry! And their poetry was so powerful that their words would shake their opponents to the core!

المَوتُ أَھْلاَ عِندَناَ مِنَ العَصَلِ
نَحنُ بَنُو ضَبَّۃَ أَصحَابُ الجَمَلِ
نحن بَنُو المَوتِ اِذَا المَوتُ نَزَلِ
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
This is the poem that the people of the tribe Banu Dabba would recite when facing their opponent. Death to us is sweeter than the taste of honey. We are the people of Banu Dabbah. We are the sons of death, and where we arrive, count your own death as having arrived!

At the battle of Khyber, Maulana Ali faces Amr Ibn Abd Wud. This man was a monster! It is said that he alone was equal to a thousand soldiers. He challenged the Prophet, saying, "Have you no men left among you to face me? Are you not the ones eager to go to heaven? Face me in battle, and I will send you to the destination you desire!" No one answers his call. Maulana Ali, with the permission of Rasul Allah (PBUH), goes against him, reciting:

أنا الَّذِی سَمَّتْنِی أُمِّی حَیدَرَا
کَلَی صِغَابَاطِلْ کَرِیہِ المَنظَرَا
وَفِیھِمِی بِصَّاعِ کَیلِ سَّندَرَا

I am the one whose mother named him Hyder! Evil trembles when it sees me standing before it. My sword breaks open skulls with a single strike!

یاَ حَبَّ ذَالَجنَّۃُ وَقْتِرَابُھَا ، طَیِّبَۃٌ وَ بَارِدٌ شَرَابُھَا
وَ الرُّومُ رَومُ قَدَّنیٰ عَذَابُھَا ، عَلَیَّ اِلاَّ قَیطُھَا ضَرَابُھا

These are the verses of Hazrat Jaffar Al-Tayyar when he was fighting in the battle of Moota.

أقْسَمتُ یَا نَفسُ لَتَنْزِلِنَّا ، کارِھَۃً أَولیٰ تُطَابِعِنَّا

These are the verses of Hazrat Abdullah ibn Rawaha when he was fighting in the battle of Moota.

طلع البد علینا

A man comes to Naseeruddin Tusi ... who was a scholar, and asks him: Will the love of Ali matter on the Day of Judgment? Now, if someone were to ask you or me this question.

What would we say? Sure! Absolutely! Of course! Right? That is the best we would come up with.... This is what he replies. I am going to recite the poem first, and then I will explain what it says, all right?

لو أن عـبداً أتى بالصـالحـات غداًوود كـــلّ نـّــبي مـرســـــل ووليوصام مـا صام صـوّاماً بلا ضجرِوقام ما قـام قـــوّامـاً بـــــلا مـــللوحجَ ما حجَ من فـرضٍ ومن سننِوطاف ما طاف حـافٍ غير منتعلِیلبسو اليتــامى من الديباج كلهّمُويُطعم الجائعين البـّــر بالعســـــلِوعاش في النــاس آلافــاً مـــؤلفـةًعارٍ من الذنب معصوماً من الزللِما كان يوم الحشـر عند الله منتفعاًإلَّا بحـــب أميــر المـــؤمنين عليّ

The Quran comes to these people through the messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) in this environment. It is a place where they take a word and tear it apart. When you speak a sentence, they will tear it apart and criticize each word to the last degree. They will shred it to pieces. They were extremely critical. They would try to outdo one another. And of course the best way to defeat a poet is to attack what? Not to attack his character, but to attack what? His poetry. You attack his poetry, and now you truly have something. The Quran is revealed, and what are some of the things the disbelievers say about it? It is the word of a poet. The word of magic. The word of a fortune teller.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
So they said he was a شاعر. But when their best poets went to challenge the messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), they came back swearing, by Allah, this is not what? It is not poetry. Then they said he was a mind reader, a کاہن. In those days, when fortune tellers spoke, they talked in gibberish. They uttered this nonsense, and it was supposed to carry some sort of magical effect. Words nobody could understand. And they would say this man is casting a spell. But did the words of the Quran make sense? They did. So it was clearly not the words of a fortune teller.

Then they called him insane. They said these were the words of madness, that he was possessed, and that these were magical words. First of all, the moment you say this is magic, you are acknowledging that it is not normal, that it is paranormal. Even by alleging that the Quran is magic, they accepted its power.

And to say that he was insane was basically to admit that they could not come up with any charge against the Quran itself. If you cannot defeat the Quran, you might as well accuse whom? The messenger. When you lose a debate of ideas, you then begin attacking the person. Is that not so? It is very common. If there is a debate on an issue, and your opponent cannot beat you on the issue, what does he do? He begins to attack your person. Your mother. It is called character assassination. This is what they tried. But in all their criticisms, they acknowledged its victory. Glory be to Allah.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
It is because, you see, the heart is the wellspring and the source of all emotions and feelings, and it is the intellect that turns those emotions into words. Suppose you feel thirsty while you are sitting in someone else's house. What do you do? You ask for water. So you are converting your feeling into what? Into words. That feeling, that desire to ask for water, arises first in your heart, and then the brain turns it into language, into words: "Please, may I have a glass of water?" Do you understand?

So the verse says that We revealed this Qur'an upon your heart. What does the heart deal with, meaning or words? Meaning. But then the next verse says (بِلِسَانٍ عَرَبِىٍّۢ مُّبِينٍۢ), in a clear Arabic tongue. What converts meaning into language? The heart or the intellect? The intellect. So what this verse is telling us is that We revealed the essence of the Qur'an upon your heart, and now it is your task to render it into the Arabic language in order to warn mankind. So the words of the Qur'an are in fact the words of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), not of Allah Himself. Allah revealed the meaning upon his heart, and the Messenger of Allah formulated the words.

So the words of the Qur'an are in truth the words of the Messenger of Allah, and this is the first thing we must understand if we are to begin to appreciate this miracle. Consider it logically. If Allah had merely handed the words to the Messenger of Allah, and the Messenger had done nothing more than repeat them, where would his honor lie in that? In such a case Allah would be using him only as a channel, and He could have chosen anyone else in his place. But no. Allah Himself testifies:

لَوْ أَنزَلْنَا هَذَا ٱلْقُرْآنَ عَلَىٰ جَبَلٍۢ لَّرَأَيْتَهُۥ خَشِعًۭا مُّتَصَدِّعًۭا مِّنْ خَشْيَةِ ٱللَّهِ

Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and shattered to dust out of the fear of Allah.

Fear of what? Fear of its own inability to turn this revelation into perfect words. It was the Messenger of Allah alone, in that age, whose heart had the strength to bear this revelation and then to render it so faithfully into words.

Now it is said that the Messenger of Allah did not know how to read or write. That is a separate discussion, and I will not enter into it here. But our belief is that this notion is entirely incorrect. He most certainly knew how to read and write, and there is an entire majlis of Hazrat Zia Ali Sahab devoted to this.

Now I want you to keep these verses in mind, for we will return to them shortly. Thank you, children.

Let us now speak of why the Qur'an is a miracle. In what ways do we hold the Qur'an to be a miracle?

First, its predictions. These may be miracles to us, but could they truly have been a miracle to the Arabs?

Second, it has remained untampered for more than fourteen hundred years.

Third, its excellence of language.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
All of this is fine and wonderful. Yet consider each in turn. If the power of the Qur'an lies in its predictions, then these may be miracles to us, but they could not possibly have been a miracle to the Arabs. We can appreciate these predictions, but there was no way that they, in their time, could have appreciated any of it. And the Qur'an was not revealed to us. It was revealed to the Arabs of that age. So what was the miracle in it for them?

If it is a miracle because its contents have never been tampered with, then in my opinion that is rather impressive. I would place it in the category of the impressive rather than the miraculous. It is certainly not as astonishing as watching a dead man return to life, or a staff turning into a serpent.

Now if this is a miracle of language, it could certainly have been a miracle to the Arabs. But then it is not a miracle for us, at least not until we learn Arabic. I would hear people say to me, "The Qur'an is so wonderful. Its Arabic is magnificent. No poet of that time could produce anything to compare with it." And I would grow excited and say, "How wonderful the Qur'an is." Then I would pause. Why is it wonderful? Oh, because its Arabic is wonderful. How marvelous. But wait, I do not know Arabic. Well, too bad for you. It is wonderful all the same, and you will never know how wonderful, because you do not know Arabic.

It is as though I were to show you an opaque glass door and say to you, "Behind this door is something truly amazing. It is so incredible that I cannot even begin to tell you how wonderful it is." And then you ask me, "May I see it?" And I say, "No. You may not. Go and learn Arabic first."

But unfortunately, this is the attitude today. The trouble with that approach is this: who is going to learn Arabic for five years merely so that they can behold the miracle of the Qur'an? Most people will never do such a thing.

Certainly not without enough motivation to drive them in that direction. Consider that all the adults here are professionals. Every one of us chose a certain career path, struggled for it, and worked hard for it. But we did not simply pick our careers out of a hat. Something inspired us to choose that path. So either give me the inspiration to want to learn Arabic, or at least show me something. Do not merely throw up your hands and say that I need to know Arabic in order to appreciate the Qur'an.

Now, of course you need to understand Arabic in order to understand the Qur'an. That is a given, because it is the language of the Qur'an. We cannot deny that. And the more I learn Qur'anic Arabic, the more I understand why this is so important. God willing, in a few sessions, you will understand it too. But that does not mean that if we do not know Arabic we cannot at least get a small taste of this miracle. We may not receive the entire hundred percent of it, but we could at least enjoy two percent of it. That is better than nothing. And then, who knows, perhaps we may become so inspired by this two percent that we decide to strive toward understanding the remaining ninety-eight percent.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
Every book in the world has an audience and a subject that it addresses. The audience of the Qur'an, the one it speaks to, is man (الانسان). And the subject of the Qur'an, the topic it addresses for man, is piety (التقوی). So this is the first thing to remember. It speaks about how a man can acquire what? Piety.

In the Qur'an, there are only two types of conversation. It is either giving information or expressing emotion. That is all. There is no third kind. When it speaks about the sacred law, the rules of the permitted and the forbidden, paradise, hell, the hereafter, and angels, is that information or emotion? Information. When it speaks about prayers, supplications, love, desires, and the stories and events of the prophets, what is that, information or emotion? Emotion. Do you know why there are only two types of conversation in the Qur'an? Because these are the only two kinds of conversation we humans can have. Think about it. Think about any conversation you have had in the past, or any conversation you will have in the future. Is it not either giving information or expressing emotion?

Let us now return to the verse:

وَإِنَّهُۥ لَتَنزِيلُ رَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ۔ نَزَلَ بِهِ ٱلرُّوحُ ٱلْأَمِينُ۔ عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ لِتَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُنذِرِينَ۔ بِلِسَانٍ عَرَبِىٍّۢ مُّبِينٍۢ

This Qur'an has been revealed to you by the Lord of the universes. Revealed through the trustworthy spirit, Gabriel. Upon your heart, so that you can warn mankind in clear Arabic language.

Where did God reveal this miracle, upon the heart or upon the intellect? The heart. And immediately after that he says, so that you can warn mankind in clear Arabic language. What converts meaning into language or words, the heart or the intellect? The intellect. So you see, the Qur'an is a miracle for the heart as well as a miracle of the intellect, because those are the only two kinds of conversation we humans can have. Glory be to God.

Now here is the most important part. Let me ask the audience: what does the word miracle mean?

In common language — not in the context of religion, but in our everyday life — when do we use the word miracle, or hear it used? Call it out, anyone. Doctors use the word miracle when a patient recovers unexpectedly. It is used in sports — in cricket, for instance, when a batsman hits a six off the last ball. You are sure you have failed an examination, and then you find out you scored a ninety-seven! You see a wonderful dream. So the word miracle is thrown around all the time in ordinary speech.

Now let us look more closely at the word miracle. What does that word mean to us? When I tell you that I am going to show you a miracle, how, in your mind, would you set that apart from a magic trick or an illusion? Take an example: Moses, peace be upon him, turns his staff into a serpent — is that a miracle or a magic trick? And how would you tell the difference? Jesus, peace be upon him, brings a dead man back to life! Miracle, or magic? Ask the audience: what, then, is the difference between magic and a miracle?
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
In ordinary speech, the word miracle is used for something that is highly unlikely, but not impossible. Something that is what? Highly unlikely, but not impossible! Yet it also carries a spiritual sense, and this is much the same across religions in general. In this spiritual sense, a miracle is something you experience. It is something you feel in your heart. It is not something I can hand to you, because it is a deeply personal experience. In other words, it is not something that can be proven by scientific facts, or measured in scientific terms. In the scientific context, a miracle is irrelevant. Why? Because when the scientific community studies a phenomenon, what is it attempting to do? Is it trying to work out whether this is a miracle, or whether there is a scientific explanation behind it? What is it always attempting to do? To find a scientific explanation! So, scientifically speaking, there is no such thing as a miracle. It must have some scientific explanation. That is the postmodern way of thinking.

Therefore, a miracle can be a matter of ordinary language, or it can be a matter of religion. But what it certainly cannot be is a matter of science. Do you understand? Why? Because science is what you can grasp with the five senses! And when you are speaking of a miracle, you are certainly asking people to go beyond the five senses. Is that not so? So whenever science has no answer, its response is that we do not know why this happened. We do not have an answer yet, but we are sure there is a scientific explanation behind it. There is no leap of faith in science. So, science can tell us how the big bang happened. But what science cannot tell us is why it happened! And if you ask them why, they will say that this is not a scientific question, that it is a philosophical question or a religious question.

But if you and I, today, in this day and age, were to believe in a miracle, then we would have to see something beyond science. Something that simply cannot be explained otherwise. Only something like that will make a believer out of you and me. Because we are living in a highly intellectual, deeply scientific age. In truth, we are far greater believers in science than in religion, even when we are religious people. Because we live in an age of questioning, of challenging, of asking questions and seeking answers of the intellect. Are you with me so far? Any questions?

Now let us agree on a common definition of what a miracle is supposed to be. Religiously, for something to be a miracle, it must meet certain criteria:

1.

A miracle should be impossible for human beings to perform. It is not something that can be produced. It is not a skill. It is not a trick, and it is not technology. It cannot come from a human being. If, for example, you see a person floating in the air, that is not something a human being can do without a device. Or think of a newborn child speaking — and not merely speaking, but speaking with eloquence. That is not something human beings can do. Throughout history, from the beginning of time, there is no record of such a thing happening, except through a miracle. Yet we have Eisa (AS) addressing the people in the most eloquent language when he is one day old.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
2. It breaks the laws of nature. There are certain patterns and laws of nature that we observe every day and take for granted. Fire burns, for example. We know this from all of history. Yet here we have Ibrahim (AS) cast into the middle of a fire, and it does not burn him. Why? Fire is supposed to burn! So that is the second one. It breaks the laws of nature.

3. It cannot be duplicated. Why are magic, or an astonishing trick, or the most remarkable illusions performed by Houdini or David Copperfield not considered a miracle in the Islamic sense? Because they can be duplicated. Someone else can perform the same illusion, the same magic, the same trick. And more than one person can do it.

4. It can ONLY be done by someone claiming to be the messenger of Allah. Musailima (al-Kazzab) saw that the Messenger of Allah (PBUH) had gained so much popularity by claiming to be a prophet, so he thought that if he did the same, he too could become quite popular. So he too declared that he was a messenger of Allah. Now, he lived in a town separate from the Prophet. One day the Prophet was brought to a well that had completely dried up. He was asked to pray to Allah for the well to recover, because the town was suffering on account of it. The Messenger of Allah (PBUH) prayed and spat into the well, and, as the narration goes, it began to overflow with water. In Musailima al-Kazzab's town there was also a well that was half dry. Its supply had grown short. So the people of his town said to him, "You do the same thing. You are Allah's prophet too — don't worry, you have got this!" So he prayed and spat into the well, and it dried up completely. So a miracle can only be done by a true prophet. If anyone else tries to do it, he will fail.

5. The last criterion, and the greatest of all, is that the entire purpose of a miracle is to challenge mankind three times. From the beginning of time, the point of giving a miracle to any prophet has always been to challenge the people of their age. It is a challenge that says: if you think I am lying, if you think I am mad, if you think I am insane, then you do what I am showing you. And if you cannot do it, and no one among you can do it — if you as an individual cannot do it, and if you collectively as a group cannot do it — then what I have been given can only be from Allah. Therefore, when I tell you that I am the prophet, I speak the truth. Nooh (AS) challenged his ummah with the flood. Ibrahim (AS) challenged his ummah with the fire. Moosa (AS) challenged Firaon with the staff turning into a snake, and by parting the water. Eisa (AS) challenged his ummah by bringing the dead back to life, and by curing the leper. So the purpose of a miracle is always to challenge mankind. Suleman (AS) could speak with jinn and animals, could he not? But that is not considered his miracle. Why?

Because he did not use it to challenge the people of his time. What, then, was his miracle? It was the throne of Queen Bilqis (بلقیس کا تخت). He transported it from her kingdom to his own. That was his miracle, because with it he challenged someone.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
Let us now consider what the word "miracle" means. The Arabic word for a miracle is معجزۃ. It is derived from the word أعجاز, which in turn comes from the root عجز. What it means is to bring someone to his knees so that he cannot rise again. It means to incapacitate or overpower an opponent, to render him incapable of any kind of response.

So imagine that I am lost in thought, about to cross a street. A truck is speeding toward me, and I do not see it. As I step into the road, I catch sight of the truck when it is one foot away from me. In that single second, there is the feeling of being completely incapacitated, the feeling of helplessness, the feeling of being brought to my knees, the feeling of being overpowered so utterly that I will not even attempt to save myself, the feeling in which the truck driver will not even attempt to touch the brake, because at this moment it is entirely pointless. So in that one second, just before I am flattened into a pancake, what I have experienced is أعجاز.

In the Qur'an, however, the word معجزۃ is not used. In place of the word معجزۃ, the word used is "Ayah." Ayah in Arabic means two things. It means a miracle, and it also means a sign. So a good translation that would point to both meanings would be a miraculous sign. What, then, is an ayah? It is a miraculous sign.

Now let us begin to speak about why this book is a miracle. One of the reasons we find it so difficult to appreciate the Qur'an as a miracle is that we try to do so in our own present time. Do you know why? Because the Qur'an was not revealed in 2015. Its teachings may certainly apply in our time period, but it was not revealed in our time.

The same holds true for Islam. The Islam we see around us today is not the Islam that existed in the time of the Prophet. That is why we find Islam so confusing today.

That is why we must begin by first understanding why the Qur'an was a miracle in the Prophet's time, and what Islam was in the Prophet's time. So what we must do is travel back in time, more than fourteen hundred years, to this piece of land called Arabia. But before we take this journey, we must prepare for it. Just as, when we plan a vacation to a country, we first try to gain some basic knowledge about that place, do we not? Its culture, its language, and so on. So let us understand a few things about that time before we make this trip.

Let us do an energy-level check. A volunteer.

For our discussion today, the first thing you need to know is that there are three types of Arabic. How many types? And you need to remember them in the order I give them to you.

Spoken Arabic. Another name for spoken Arabic is busted Arabic, ugly Arabic, slang, or twisted, demented, mutated Arabic. It is also called عمِّیَّۃ, which means dialectical Arabic. That is, the Egyptians have their own dialect, the Algerians have their own dialect, the Kuwaitis have their own dialect, and the Saudis have their own dialects. The Arabic is similar, but the dialect varies from country to country.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
Proper Arabic. Any Arabic newspaper you read, or any Arabic news program you watch on television, is all in proper Arabic. It is also called الفصحۃ. Also, if you ever take an Arabic course in college, they call it Modern Standard Arabic.

What they mean by that is فصحۃ. It is correct Arabic, enunciated correctly, and it uses the grammatical rules of Arabic correctly. So when you are learning proper Arabic, you are learning correct Arabic. There is nothing wrong with it. But what we really need to understand for our purpose is the third type of Arabic, which is ancient Arabic.

Ancient Arabic is the original, pure Arabic spoken in the land of Arabia. It was far more sophisticated, far more eloquent, far more complex, far more advanced, far more involved, far more intricate, and far more powerful than proper modern standard Arabic. This is something you truly need to understand in order to appreciate the Quran. If you go to Egypt today, study Arabic for five years, and return speaking the most perfect Arabic, you are still speaking proper Arabic. That still does not mean you have an understanding of ancient Arabic. They are two completely different things. The subtleties and the minute details that the ancient Arabs could detect in a sentence, the proper Arabs cannot. That is why, even today, when the proper Arabs hear the Quran, they do not hear what the ancient Arabs heard when they heard the exact same ayat. So first let us understand how these Arabs reached such linguistic heights.

Every country in this world today has something called nationalism, or patriotism. You take something and say that you are the best at it. For example, one country makes the best baseball bats, or cricket bats. That is their national pride. They unite as a nation in the production of that one particular thing. Today we even have something called state pride. Every state has something it is very proud of. I am from New Jersey; we have the highest murder rate in the country, or something like that.

Very well. So let us go back in time. The year is 610 BC. Rasool Allah (PBUH) has been born, and he is forty years old. And since we come from the future, we know that any day now the Quran is going to be revealed to him. But we are not going to meet Rasool Allah (PBUH) on this trip. The people we really want to meet are the Arabs of this time. So what do we see?

We see a group of Arabs living out in the desert. There are no buildings, no agriculture, not even much of a farming community. They have not even discovered oil yet. One neighbor is the Persian empire, and another is the Roman empire. Now, if you know anything about empires, they are always trying to increase the size of their backyards. They always want to expand. But we see something very strange. Do we see them marching into Arabia? No. Why? Because they are thinking: why should we send our soldiers to be barbequed in the heat of the deserts? What are we going to get out of them anyway? They are useless to us. They have nothing. There is nothing we can take over. They have no monuments, no resources, no buildings; they have absolutely nothing. So there is no point in going after them. And so they simply leave them alone.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
So now we see these Arabs living by themselves in isolation, and we see that they actually enjoy this isolation. And when a group of people live in isolation with no external influence, what happens to their language? It becomes refined. It becomes more and more pure. It becomes perfect. Because they are speaking only among one another, there is no external influence on their language.

Are you with me? So in what did these Arabs take pride? Was it their beautiful architecture, the remarkable structures they raised? The lovely gardens they kept? The formidable armies they commanded? None of these. What, then, was the one thing they possessed in which they could possibly take pride? Their language. That was the only thing they had. And when a people take pride in the one thing they possess, they tend it with the utmost care. So Arabic became their national identity. To be devoted to language became a matter of Arab identity — to excel in it, to set everything else aside and attend to this one thing alone. So much so that, for them, language was the greatest of all things a person could know.

Do you know what the opposite of "Arab" is? العرب وال ؟۔ Ajam. And do you know what ajam means? Dumb. Mute. One who cannot speak. So if a person could not converse with these Arabs at the same level of sophistication with which they spoke their Arabic, this was the name they gave him: mute. As if to say, you might as well have been born dumb and speechless, for you are not even worthy of speaking with us. Such was the extremity of their passion for eloquence.

And what is the summit of any language? Poetry. So the Arabs of this age could recite poems as naturally as you and I hold a conversation. They would speak to one another in the most eloquent verse. It went so far that their very sports were built around poetry. They held an ancient form of contest in mutual disparagement. Just as there is freestyle rap today, they had their own version of it — except that theirs was not slang, but poetry in its highest and purest form. Two tribes would each select one man, the finest man of the tribe, and the two would then do battle in verse before an enormous crowd. The one who won had disgraced the rival tribe for generations to come. The one who lost would, in all likelihood, lose his head — for he had lost not merely the contest but the honor of his tribe, and not for a few days, or a month, or a year, but for generations to come. So these men took their poetry and their literature with the greatest seriousness. It was, to them, a matter of the gravest weight.

Why do I tell you all this? What is its relevance? I tell you all this because you must truly understand how important language was to these Arabs, and to what linguistic heights they had perfected it — for these, remember, are the very people upon whom the Qur'an is about to be revealed.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: A Study in Arabic Linguistics

body.text_en:
All praise belongs to God. We are studying the miracle of the Qur'an. In the previous session we spoke about some of the ways in which we ordinarily take the Qur'an to be a miracle, and about how badly we have underrated the majesty of this revelation. At best we rest its miraculous character on the various predictions it makes, or on its having come down through the centuries untampered with, and so on. All of that is true, but it is very single-dimensional.

We spoke about how the Qur'an is a miracle of the heart as well as of the intellect.

I showed you from the verses of the Qur'an that the language of the Qur'an is in fact the Messenger of God's own words. God did not hand the Messenger of God the words. The words are his own creation, and that is why this Arabic of the Qur'an is the miracle of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him.

Then we discussed in detail the difference between a miracle and magic, and how we miss the miracle of the Qur'an entirely because we are looking for the wrong thing. If we picture a miracle as pulling a rabbit out of a hat, then we will certainly never be able to experience the miracle of the Qur'an.

Then I defined the word "miracle" for you. The word in Arabic is mojiza, which comes from the word Ejaaz, meaning to incapacitate, to render someone incapable of response, or to bring someone down on his knees so that he cannot rise again.

Then I explained five primary characteristics of a miracle:

1. A miracle should be impossible for human beings to perform.
2. It breaks the laws of nature.
3. It cannot be duplicated.
4. It can ONLY be done by someone claiming to be the messenger of God.
5. And most important of all: the entire purpose of a miracle is to challenge mankind. If the prophet does not use it to challenge mankind, then it is not really a miracle. It then falls into a different category — Khurafaat, Tasarrufaat, Karamaat — but not into the category of Ejaaz.

In the Qur'an the word معجزۃ is not used. Instead the word used is "Ayah." In Arabic, Ayah means two things. It means a miracle, and it also means a sign. So an Ayah means a miraculous sign.

Then we looked at three different kinds of Arabic and the differences among them: 1. Spoken Arabic, 2. Proper Arabic, 3. Ancient Arabic.

And then, finally, we went back in time to ancient Arabia to understand what level of sophistication the Arabs enjoyed when it came to language. Why Arabic had developed to such heights, and how it meant EVERYTHING to them. I gave you a couple of examples of how their language was full of imagery, how powerful their imagination was, how they used very picturesque words, and how they painted their imagination with words. Poetry came to them as naturally as conversation comes to us.

In Pakistan, children prepare.

After the people of Mecca rejected the Messenger of God, the news of his coming reached Medina. Everyone came out to the outskirts of Medina to welcome him. All the little girls of ten and eleven years of age gathered right at the front. I swear to you that nobody prepared these little girls in advance. As soon as they saw the face of the Messenger of God rising on the distant horizon, they all began to sing together:

طلع البدر علینا من ثنیات الوداع
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
Here rises the moon from the valley of Wada.

They had not rehearsed this poem beforehand. They composed it as they went along. Have you ever been so in tune with a friend that you can complete each other's thoughts, finish each other's sentences, say the same things at the same moment? That is how in tune they were with Arabic. They were creating and singing this song all together, completing one another's verses.

and these are ten- and eleven-year-old little girls. SubhanAllah!

وجب الشکر علینا ما دعا لی اللہ دعا

Gratitude has become incumbent upon us, for the beautiful call by which you have called us to Allah.

أیھا المبعوث فینا جئتا بی الامر المطاعۃ

O Messenger of Allah, this is not Mecca, where the people rejected you! This is Medina, and every child, every soul here will be obedient to you.

جئتا شرفتا المدینۃ مرحباً بک یا خیر داع

You have honored Medina with your presence! We welcome you with open arms, O Messenger of Allah.

So, with all these examples, if I have been able to give you even a small idea of their eloquence, their sophistication, and the precision of the words they used, then today I would like to move forward and speak about the frame of mind the Arabs were in when the message of Allah was revealed to them by the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him).

Volunteer

I want you to imagine something with me. Imagine that you are sitting in your living room, going about your business, and there is a knock at the door. You open the door and see your neighbor standing outside. After you exchange greetings, he says to you: Last night an angel came to me and told me that Allah has chosen me as His messenger. And Allah has commanded me to deliver His message to mankind. I have already invited my family, but they have all rejected me. Since you are my neighbor, and you have a right over me as my neighbor, I am now delivering the message to you. I am Allah's messenger, and everything I say is not from me but from Allah Himself. So obeying what I say is obeying Allah, and disobeying me is in fact disobeying Allah.

So this is what your neighbor has just hit you with. What is going through your mind right now? What are you going to say to him? Are you all right? What did you have for dinner last night? Is that not so? You have been my neighbor for so many years, I have seen you all my life, and now, all of a sudden, you want me to believe that an angel comes to you and that Allah speaks to you through the angel? And then, on top of that, you are telling me that your own family has rejected you, that they are calling you insane, but you want me to listen to you? To follow you? To obey you?
