To change my life on the basis of what you are saying? Everybody already thinks you are insane! What is going to happen if I follow you? What will they call me?

Ah... I will think about it! Thank you! And you shut the door.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
Think about this for a minute. We condemn the disbelievers so easily: oh, these kuffar! They rejected the Prophet, they called him insane! They are going to hell! Is that not how we speak? But put yourself in their shoes for a moment. What the Messenger of Allah was asking of them was not an easy thing to believe. This bridge from disbelief to faith was not an easy bridge to cross. You see, today it is very easy for us to talk about Islam and to preach Islam, because it has been going on for thousands of years.

I said I was going to begin these sessions on Islam, and you all simply came. I did not have to make any effort to invite you to these sessions. Why? Because you have already accepted the concepts of Islam. But it was not so for the Arabs of that time! This was the first time it was happening. What was being asked of them was a very difficult task. Do you understand?

If your neighbor came to your doorstep and claimed to be a prophet, of course you would think he was insane! Why would you not believe him? Do you know why? Statistics! Because you have never seen such a thing happen before in your life.

Believing in one God is not so far-fetched. Believing in a hereafter is possible. But what is absolutely impossible to believe? What is it that you simply cannot picture happening? You cannot picture a man you have known your whole life suddenly being addressed by an angel. That goes beyond your wildest imagination. Is that not so? Why you? Why not me? What is so special about you?

So I want you to appreciate the state of mind the Arabs were in at that time, when the Messenger of Allah came to them with the message. They were not bad people. They were not evil people. What was being asked of them was extremely difficult. When you are the only person in the whole city holding a particular idea, a particular faith, one that differs from everyone else's faith, what does that make you? Crazy! It makes you insane! And what does it make the next person in line who believes you? Just as insane! So before we write these people off as evil, as unbelievers, put yourself in their shoes for a moment. How easy is it to accept something when no one around you believes it? The message of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) was a very, very, very difficult thing for the people of the city to believe. It was not easy. Faith was an extremely expensive, extremely dangerous commodity at that time. Do you understand?

Very well. If you can appreciate that, I now want you to imagine that the person to whom the angel brought the message of prophethood is none other than you. Now it is you who must go and knock on your neighbor's door and deliver the message to him. What is the state of your heart now? If you tell this to your own parents, they will drag you to a psychiatrist. Imagine having to stand before a group of strangers and promote this strange new idea, one that runs not only against all their existing beliefs but against the beliefs of their forefathers before them. How would you feel about delivering this message? What are some of the things you would be afraid of?
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
Would you be afraid of ridicule? Of being called insane? Would you accept this task? Of course not! It is simply too difficult. But the Messenger of Allah did it. He accepted the responsibility. Why? Was this his ticket to Paradise? No! He was already of Paradise! Paradise was created for him! He already owned it! Then why would he accept such a difficult and painful responsibility? Do you know why? He did it for me! He did it for you! So that you and I could be rescued from the slavery of our own souls. So that you and I could have a real chance at entering Paradise. He said: if I do not take this step, how will the people of my community be free? How will they be guided? He did this for me! He did this for you! He did this for all of us. Now that is love! That is mercy! That is a true blessing!

So, having appreciated how difficult this task was for the prophets, understand that Allah gave His prophets certain miracles. This was in order to make the decision easier for the people they were calling. The purpose was this: if you think I am crazy, then let me show you, let me challenge you with what Allah has given me, and then you tell me whether anyone besides Allah could have given this to me. If no one could, then this miracle is my proof that I am speaking the truth. And if you still will not believe me, it is only because you are arrogant and obstinate; but you can no longer deny that I am Allah's messenger.

When they saw the water part, the staff turn into a serpent, the dead man come back to life, and birds of clay come alive and fly away, they were left powerless. Every argument they had was defeated. It brought them to their knees. And once you are on your knees, you have two choices. Either you surrender and fall into prostration, or you grow arrogant, stand back up, and disbelieve. At that point it becomes a personal choice.

Any questions so far?

Now that we have understood all this, let us begin speaking about the Qur'an itself as a miracle. First, let us understand what it means to feel a miracle. Remember: a miracle is something you experience. It is not merely something you see. You see a magic trick, but you never experience a magic trick. A miracle you can only experience.

We have badly underestimated this word "miracle." We have no idea what a miracle feels like. The best we know of it, as I said last time, is when someone recovers from an unexpected illness, or hits an impossible home run, or passes an examination, or survives a very serious accident. We call these things miracles. So when we hear the Qur'an, we have no true point of reference to compare it to. In order to experience a miracle, we first need some idea of what it feels like. Correct?

So let us once again take a journey back in time, this time to two thousand years before the age of the Prophet.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
Imagine that we are among a group of people who are all running for their lives. We learn that the army of Pharaoh is chasing them. And because we come from the future, we know that if he catches us it means certain death. So we run along with the group until we reach the bank of an enormous river, and there we find ourselves completely trapped. We see Moosa (AS) standing at the bank of the river, holding his staff. We see some of the people blaming him for the situation they are in. They are saying, "Moosa! We are trapped now because of you! You led us to our doom!"

But then we see Musa (AS) raise his staff and strike the water with it, and before our very eyes we see the water splitting. We see the water rising on both sides, standing like huge walls, and leaving a pathway between them for everyone to walk through. As the Qur'an states:

فَأَوْحَيْنَآ إِلَىٰ مُوسَىٰٓ أَنِ ٱضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ ٱلْبَحْرَ ۖ فَٱنفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍۢ كَٱلطَّوْدِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ

Imagine walking through this river, watching the walls made of water on either side. You can touch it, you can feel it, you can hear it. It is still water, and you are experiencing this miracle firsthand. What is the state of your heart at that moment? Would there be the slightest doubt in your heart that Musa (AS) truly is Allah's messenger? You see, what you are feeling right now is the feeling of experiencing a miracle. Could you ever put it into words, even if you tried?

Now think about this. Is this the state of your heart when you recite the Qur'an, or when you hear it recited to you? It is not. Because at best we see the Qur'an as a religious text, and not as a miracle. But do you know what the ancient Arabs felt when they heard these verses recited to them? They felt what you have just experienced standing beside Musa (AS). The Qur'an was without doubt a religious text to them as well, but beyond that, they experienced the miracle every time they heard the verses recited to them.

That is why it struck their hearts with such force.

There is another thing about the Qur'an that I want you to appreciate. Are all the earlier miracles alive today? Is the water still parted, or has it closed back over itself? Are dead men still returning to life? Does fire still turn into a bed of flowers? No. Each happened in a particular moment, and then it was over. But is the Qur'an still alive? If we were able to experience the miracle of the Qur'an, could that experience be repeated as many times as we wished? Could we experience its miracle over and over and over again?
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
When the people standing on the bank of the river saw it split in two, they experienced a miracle. Then they told the event to their children: look, this is what happened! I was standing right there. I saw it with my own eyes. Then the child tells it to his own child: my father was there when it happened. Then that child tells it to his children: my grandfather was right there. And so it goes on until the account reaches us. When we tell the story of Musa (AS) to our children, it comes out more like a yawn: yes, there was something about Musa and the river parting, or something of the sort. Why? Because to us it is only a story, a story we have accepted on faith. But for the man who told it the first time, was it only a story? No, to him it was a miracle. Do you understand?

What created this difference? Why is it a miracle to that man and a story to us? Because the miracle is finished. It happened once in the history of time and never again. The river never split a second time. The bird made of clay never came to life again and flew off. Anything seen with the eye has a short life. You see it, and then it is over, and it becomes a story. So all these miracles that took place in the times of the earlier prophets could well have been miracles to them. But for us they are only stories that we accept on faith.

This is why, when an atheist comes to Jews or Christians and asks, "Is it true that Jesus brought the dead back to life?" they say, "Of course!" He asks, "How do you know that?" The Christian says, "Because it is in the Bible." He asks, "Did you actually see that miracle with your own eyes? Were you there?" No. "Then how do you know it happened? Did anyone record it? Is it on YouTube?" The Christian says, "Because I believe in it." So the atheist says, "Then do not tell me that story, because it is merely your belief." And anybody can believe anything.

Now when the same atheist comes to us Muslims and asks, "Is the Qur'an the message of Allah?" we say, "Of course!" He asks, "Did you see Jibraeel (AS) descend from the heavens with the message?" We say, "No." "Then how do you know this is the message of Allah?" We say, "Let me show you. Let us study this book, and let me show you why this cannot come from a human being." Do you see?

What we have just said to the atheist — "Let me show you" — is the part we all need to understand truly and take seriously. Because if we do not see the miracle ourselves, how are we ever going to show it to someone else? This is why the Qur'an is not changing our lives. Because it is only a book of religious text to us, we are not able to experience it as a miracle. We are not held spellbound by it. And yet every single one of us has access to this book. If we so desired, we could experience this miracle at any minute of the day. We can experience it five times a day in namaaz. Would that not be simply amazing?

Would it not be an extraordinary experience to feel this miracle every single day?
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
Now let us see whether there is a difference between what was given to the earlier prophets and what was given to our Rasul Allah (peace be upon him). Their miracles addressed which sense? Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is thrown into the fire and the fire turns into a bed of flowers. With which sense do people experience that? Which sense is involved? Moosa (peace be upon him) throws his staff on the ground and it turns into a serpent. Which sense is involved? Eisa (peace be upon him) brings the dead back to life. Which sense is involved? All of these miracles are for the eyes to see. Is that not so?

But what is the Qur'an for? Was it revealed as something to see, or as something to hear? It was something to hear, not something to see. It was for the ears, not for the eyes.

قُلْ أُوحِىَ إِلَىَّ أَنَّهُ ٱسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَقَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا سَمِعْنَا قُرْآنًا عَجَبًۭا

وَأَنَّا لَمَّا سَمِعْنَا ٱلْهُدَىٰٓ آمَنَّا بِهِ

قَالُوا۟ يَقَوْمَنَآ إِنَّا سَمِعْنَا كِتَبًا أُنزِلَ مِنۢ بَعْدِ مُوسَىٰ

وَإِذَا تُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَتُنَا قَالُوا۟ قَدْ سَمِعْنَا

What is Allah saying?

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ضُرِبَ مَثَلٌۭ فَٱسْتَمِعُوا۟ لَهُ

Listen! Listen! Listen! O people, I am giving you examples so that you may listen. Why did Allah suddenly change His format? Why did He switch from video to audio? Does that not sound like a step down?

When my daughter Erum was six years old, I was reading her the stories of the prophets. I went through all of them, and when I reached Rasul Allah and told her about the miracle of the Qur'an, she became so upset. She said, "That is not fair, Babu! Everyone else got such a cool miracle, and all our prophet got was a book!" Now, that sounds blasphemous, but she has a point. How is it that every other prophet received such striking miracles? Do you know why she thought they were cool? Because they were for the eyes to see. But the Qur'an was not for the eyes to see; it was for listening. And what happens when you cannot see something? You imagine it. Is imagination more powerful, or is sight more powerful? Is this not why movies are such a disappointment when you have read the book first? Because the movie cannot match what you imagined.

I read the wonderful book Divergent, and later I saw the movie. I swore I would never read a book again, because reading ruins the movies.

So the question is this: why did Allah change the format?

Do you know why He changed the format? Because when you cannot see something, what are you forced to do? You are forced to imagine. What were the Arabs so accomplished at? What did they take such pride in? Their ability to imagine, and to paint that imagination in words. The Qur'an, with its mesmerizing words, created for them the ultimate imagination — an imagination so far superior to the Arab imagination, using words so precise, so perfect, so eloquent, so mesmerizing, that it brought them down on their knees. It rendered them helpless. It was therefore a miracle to them.

This book is so powerful!
body.topic_title_en: The Miracle of the Quran: Its Challenges

body.text_en:
All praise belongs to God. We continue our journey to experience the Qur'an as a miracle. First, a brief review of what we have covered so far.

The Arabic word for a miracle is *mu'jiza*. What does it mean? What is the chief purpose of any miracle given to any prophet in any age? To whom do the words of the Qur'an belong? To whom does the message of the Qur'an belong? Whom does the Qur'an address; who is its audience? What is the subject of the Qur'an? What two kinds of conversation does the Qur'an hold, and why? Is the Qur'an a miracle for the intellect or for the heart? How many kinds of Arabic are there, and what are they? In Arabia, in the time of the Prophet, what mattered most to the Arabs? In what did they take pride? With what did they identify themselves?

In the last session we spoke of how hard it was for the people of Arabia to accept Islam. Once we grasped that, we spoke of how hard it was for the Messenger of God to take up this responsibility, illustrated by the example of changing the place of a dinner, and so of changing gods. Why did he do it? Why did he accept this responsibility? What emotion moved him to accept it? Were the earlier miracles for the eyes or for the ears? What is the Qur'an for? Why did God change the form?

So, praise be to God, we now understand the context, the environment, the circumstances, and the people to whom the Qur'an was revealed. These were people of extraordinary imagination, people of supreme eloquence, people who painted pictures with words. When they went to war, they intimidated their enemies with words. For them the ultimate defeat was not death but defeat in a contest of poetry. If an opponent used a single word wrongly, or failed to set each word in its proper place, they would catch it, seize upon it to attack his poetry, and tear it to shreds. They would criticize it to the utmost degree. And all of this, mind you, they did on the spot, without any preparation beforehand. In short, what we today would call remarkable poetry was, for them, simply ordinary conversation.

Yasmeen, Hussain, you are both very talented tennis players, God has blessed you. Tell me, what kind of opponent do you enjoy playing against: one at your own level, or one far below you? Why? Would it not be easy to win against a weak opponent? Now, what if you faced a player who utterly destroyed you in the match, who beat you fifteen to nothing, who left you running home in tears? Would you play against him again? And if you did, and he beat you the same way, again and again and again, would you want to keep playing against him?

And since language was the one thing they cared about, more than life itself, and since language is something you hear and not something you see, this is why the ultimate miracle, the living miracle, the miracle of all miracles, the Qur'an, was revealed to them chiefly as a miracle of language.

In the end, the Qur'an is a conversation. It is a conversation for all mankind, not only for believers or for disbelievers, but for all mankind in general. God says:

هَذَا بَلَغٌۭ لِّلنَّاسِ وَلِيُنذَرُوا۟ بِهِ وَلِيَعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّمَا هُوَ إِلَهٌۭ وَحِدٌۭ وَلِيَذَّكَّرَ أُو۟لُوا۟ ٱلْأَلْبَبِ
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
This single verse explains everything. What is the Qur'an? هَذَا بَلَغٌۭ — it is a message. For whom is it? لِّلنَّاسِ — for people. Why? وَلِيُنذَرُوا۟ بِهِ — so that they may be warned. Warned of what? وَلِيَعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّمَا هُوَ إِلَهٌۭ وَحِدٌۭ — so that they may come to know that their Lord is only one.

And so what should they do? وَلِيَذَّكَّرَ — remember Him constantly!

But then, in the final part, He changes His tone. Everything He had said until now was general, addressed to all mankind — لِّلنَّاسِ — yet here He singles out one group from among mankind and names them أُو۟لُوا۟ ٱلْأَلْبَبِ, the people of intellect! So although this message is meant for everyone, only the people of intellect will truly believe and accept it.

Today, then, I want to speak to you about the Qur'an in light of its being a message, a conversation. When we communicate, there are three components we must always keep in mind. There are three aspects to communication:

First is the speaker — who is saying it.
Second is the speech — what is being said.
Third is the style — how it is being said.

Have the children repeat this.

Now let us take these components one by one.

The speaker. The first is the speaker. When we see someone speaking, before the person even opens his mouth, we have already formed a judgment about him — from the way he is dressed, the way he looks, his age, his body language. We have already formed an opinion. Consider it this way. Suppose you have an important question about the shariat, and you are seeking religious guidance for it. You walk into the jamaat khana. You see the hazratain seated, the mulla sahibaan seated, and some other people of knowledge present, and you also notice your friend, who is not very religious and not very learned, sitting in a corner. After the musafaha, you sit down and put your question to the elders. The moment you finish, your friend begins to answer it. Would you take his answer seriously? Or would you rather that Hazrat sahab answer your question? Why? Now, what if both of them gave you the exact same answer? Would you still prefer the answer from Hazrat sahab? Why, when they are both giving you the same answer?

The reason is not that your friend's answer is wrong, but that it comes from a source you do not truly acknowledge for that subject. When Hazrat sahab gives you the very same answer, it holds far more value for you. So whom did you take into account there? The speaker!

Here is another example. You are not feeling well. You go to your friend's house, and you see a relative of his who is a doctor. You tell him about your illness. Would you rather that his uncle prescribed a medicine for you, or that your friend suggested something? Why? Again, whom did you take into account there? The speaker! The speaker is a great matter.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
And it is lost to such a degree that people can actually criticize the Qur'an. Why does it say this, why does it say that. They are not overpowered. Any form of communication or literature is subjective. You like a book, I do not. You like a conversation, I do not. It rests on personal opinion. So then how do we judge a good conversation? What is the measuring stick? What influence does it have on the people? What impact does it have on the world? What change does it bring? How does it change people? How does it influence behavior? How does it command over people? That would be the judge. That is a practical judge—of the power of any speech, any literature. You could say it is wonderful, but I could say it is merely fiction. Or you could say it is wonderful and it completely changed my life.

If you study this fact historically, no society ever underwent such a transformation on the basis of a single text the way the Muslims did—with what? The Qur'an. No other society in history. And in how many years was that society transformed? Twenty-three years. Even the orientalists agree to this. The first verse is revealed at the age of forty, and it ceases at the age of sixty-three.

Just 23 years. Has there ever been a change in the world—one that came about in the span of twenty-three, thirty-three, fifty-three, sixty-three years? I do not care; let us speak of five hundred years. A change that changed the way people think, what people love, what people hate, how people dress, how a government is run, how they manage their economy, how they marry and how they divorce, what they eat and what they do not eat, what they say and what they do not say, how they do business, how a loan is taken. It changed every aspect of their life in twenty-three years.

Those of you who are in high school take global history, and you learn about revolutions. You learn about the French Revolution in Europe. These revolutions were either political or economic. They did not change the ethics of the people. They did not change how people eat, sleep, and drink. They did not change what people love and hate. They did not change how people dress. Nothing else changed. There was just one big change over the top, and that was all. And even those changes were brought about by people who read the works of philosophers, and those philosophers had died decades before.

I will give you an example: the Russian Revolution, the communist revolution. Do you know who the author of the communist revolution is? It is Karl Marx. Do you know where Karl Marx is from? He is from Germany, and he died sixty years before the Russian Revolution. The man was a librarian. He was a writer, a philosopher. Sixty years earlier he was sitting in a room writing about all of this, and it was not even in his wildest dreams that people would be killing one another over it. And sixty years after his death, there were people revolutionizing a country on the basis of his works. Right?
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
You see, there is this historical formula: the philosopher of an idea is never on the battlefield. Never. And the philosopher of an idea is not himself a revolutionary; he is simply a philosopher. He does not go out to convince people to make a change; he merely writes. In the case of Muhammad (may the blessings of Allah be upon him and his family and peace), who is delivering the message, and who is on the battlefield? And not only on the battlefield—who is at the front of the battlefield? Who is delivering the message, and who is being boycotted and forced to live in a cave? Who is being expelled from his house? He is not merely standing behind some podium telling the people to march forward. He is the first to march forward when there is no one standing behind him. This has never before happened in history. Ever. Ask your political science professor. Ask your history professor.

In twenty-three years, this man begins—single-handedly, mind you—and by the end of these twenty-three years, what change have these words, and this speaker, and this speech, and this style of speech influenced? You see...

The world has seen many revolutions meant to bring about change. But whenever there is a so-called revolution, the changes it produces are political or economic, or the army in power is exchanged for another. The way people live from one day to the next does not change. When a new government comes to power, it does not change how children speak with their parents, or how a husband speaks with his wife. That remains exactly as it was. But consider the change the Qur'an brought—unparalleled in all of human history.

Did the way people eat change? Did the way people sleep change? Did the way people deal with their families change? Did the way husbands treat their wives change? Did the way people order their day change? Did the way people speak to one another change? Did the way they greet one another change? Did the way they conduct their business change? Did the way they dress change? Did the way they relieve themselves change?

The question is not what changed. Do you know what the right question is? It is: what did not change? Everything changed. Everything changed.

And what changed was not merely social, not merely at the broad level. It also changed the way people think. It changed everything—everything—from the level of the single individual to the level of the whole community, and every degree that lies between the two. This itself is the proof of the unparalleled power of the Qur'an. The unparalleled power of the Qur'an. Subhan Allah.

Now set this beside the definition of a miracle: this is the first miracle. In sha Allah, in the next session, we will select seven out of three hundred and fifty miracles. Screen share.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
The speech. The next component is the speech — the content that is being delivered. You come to a khutba, a sermon. You go to the masjid to hear the khutba. You arrive a little late, so you do not get a chance to enter the main hall, and you simply sit outside. You do not get a chance to see the khateeb, the one delivering the sermon. The khateeb is a young boy. Let us say it is Saleem here — Shadia's son Saleem. He is the khateeb. He comes to the minbar wearing jeans and a T-shirt, with a baseball cap turned backward. Now remember, you cannot see him. And he delivers the most striking khutba you have ever heard! Now, not having seen the speaker, what are you thinking? You are thinking: with whom did this Sheikh, this Maulana sahab, study? So what did you take into account this time? Not the speaker, but the what? The speech! So the speaker is important, but the speech, the content, is just as important.

Do you follow? Style.

The third thing that matters is style. It is time for prayer, and you are busy playing outside the mosque. A mulla sahab, on his way to the mosque, walks past and begins to shout at you. Why are you playing out here? Why are you not inside, praying? Is this how you thank Allah for all His blessings? Shame on you! Stop this nonsense at once and go to the mosque this instant! And then he walks off. What do you do? You wait a few seconds, glance at one another, share a laugh, and go back to your game. A little while later a second mulla sahab walks past, and very gently, very kindly, he reminds you that it is time for prayer. He says something like this: Children! Perhaps you had not noticed that it is time for prayer. I know you are enjoying yourselves, but our Lord, our Creator, is calling us! Let us show Him our gratitude for all His blessings by hurrying toward His call. I am on my way to the mosque now. Would you care to keep me company? Would you like to walk along with me? At once you stop playing and set off walking beside him.

Now, both men are saying the very same thing! Both are asking you to leave off playing and go to prayer. Yet one man's words inspire you, while the other's turn you away. Both are mullas, so the speaker is the same; both are calling you to prayer, so the content is the same. What, then, is different this time? The style! So style — the manner in which a thing is said — is exceedingly important as well. Both mullas were telling you the same thing. But the manner in which they delivered that content either made it effective or made it useless. So it is not only the speaker and the speech that matter; the way in which you present the content must be effective, or else the communication is lost.

In the end, the point of communication is to influence the audience. I will say it three times! The purpose of communication is not merely for someone to hear certain things or see certain things, but to influence them! To move a change within them. And you cannot do that unless you speak effectively, even when you have something good to say.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
Let me give you another example. You attend a majlis with remarkable content, but the manner in which it is delivered is utterly monotone. Utterly monotone! Picture this. You are sitting in a majlis, and the speaker begins: When Allah the Most High resolved to create the earth, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the galaxies, He commanded them, "Be!" and they were. Almighty Allah said: Verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be!" and it is.

He has just recited to you the translation of an ayah. Now, this content is profound! A verse of the Qur'an is being quoted. A truly momentous statement is being made about the creation of the universes, yet the manner in which it is stated is so dull that it will knock you flat! It is verbal anesthesia! It will put you to sleep! And you see, there is nothing wrong with the content, for the content is divine! And there may be nothing wrong with the speaker either. He may be a very learned man. But what is the trouble this time? The mode of speech! The style of speech! The way in which a thing is presented! Do you follow?

So these are the three dimensions of communication.

And the Qur'an is powerful in all three dimensions of communication. It is powerful because its speaker is extraordinary. It is powerful because its content is extraordinary. It is powerful because its style is extraordinary. When all three components are extraordinary, what does that make the discourse? Extraordinary.

But what I wish to dwell upon with you today is not the first dimension, the speaker, nor the second, the content, but the third. Not that Allah speaks, nor what Allah says, but how Allah says it. This is where the Qur'an is so unique in the manner of its communication. The way in which Allah says a thing is so powerful and so extraordinary.

Consider this. When the Qur'an is translated, you already know from whom the message comes. Perhaps, perhaps, you also grasp the content of what is said. Perhaps. But what is it that you will certainly not receive? How it was said. That is entirely, wholly lost in translation. What was said, you may recover from a translation, perhaps. But how it was said is altogether gone, because how it was said exists in which language? In Arabic. Even if you explain it to another person in Arabic, in your own Arabic, it will still not be how it was said. So the creative beauty, the singular beauty, the unparalleled majesty of the words of Allah cannot be translated. Something of the meaning can be translated, but the impact that the original words carry, nothing else can carry.

This is what I want us to understand and to appreciate today: that to translate the words of Allah into our own words, first of all, cannot capture the content as it was originally intended, and it most certainly destroys the manner of the communication. It opens a gap. And in order to understand the width of this gap, consider the distance between Allah and His creation. That should give you some sense of the distance between the words of Allah and the translations of men, for the Qur'an is from Allah, and the translation is from His creation. The translation of a man can never be a substitute for the words of Allah. It simply cannot be.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
This is not a discussion about what is lost in the content. We could certainly speak of that as well, and I could give you many examples of it. But what I wish to speak with you about today is what is lost in the beauty, in the style.

So now I want you to consider this. We, as Muslims, whom do we hold to be the ultimate speaker of this communication? From whom is this message? Allah. This we, as Muslims, believe. But when a non-Muslim, an unbeliever, hears this communication, whom does he see delivering the message? Whom does he hold to be the speaker? The Messenger of Allah. This is very important to understand. To you and to me, this is the message of Allah, but to the unbeliever it is not the message of Allah, because he does not believe in Allah. Were he to believe, that would make him what? A Muslim. So the unbeliever holds this to be the message of the Messenger of Allah.

What are the three components of communication? Speaking logically, then, this Qur'an, on the basis of the components of speaker and content, could be a miracle to a Muslim, but could never be a miracle to the unbeliever. Do you understand? Because they do not believe in the speaker. And when you do not believe in the speaker, you have no wish even to listen to the content.

So then the question we must ask is this: what was it that made this communication a miracle to the unbelievers? What was it that held these people spellbound?

What was it that every time the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, opened his mouth, they were left dumbfounded, not knowing what to say? It was the sheer wonder of its style. It was the style, the beautiful manner in which the words were spoken, that was the miracle for the disbelievers. SubhanAllah! I will share with you three stories that show the power of the Quran's style, and then I am finished, insha'Allah ta'ala.

Tufail ibn Amir al-Dausi. He was the chief of his tribe. The finest man among them would be chosen as their leader. And what was the measure of excellence among the Arabs of that age? Language. So if Tufail ibn Amir was their leader, it follows that he stood above the rest in what? Language. He was the greatest poet of his tribe. Now picture a man in such a position. Is this someone who would be easily impressed by another poet?
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
He came to Makka to perform the tawaf of the Ka'aba. The chiefs of the Quraysh learned that he was on his way. They grew anxious that he might hear the Prophet reciting the Quran, and that, if he did, he might fall under its spell. So they met him as he entered the city and warned him about the Prophet. They said to him: There is a man here who speaks these words and casts a spell upon people. He turns sons against their fathers, brother against brother, husband against wife. He is sowing division within our tribe. When he speaks to people, they seem possessed by demons. We regard you as a man of standing among your people, and we fear your good name will be undone if he is able to work his spell upon you. And as they spoke, they handed him plugs for his ears. They said: To keep yourself safe, simply stop up your ears so that you do not hear a word he says. Now why did they do this? Because when a chief becomes a Muslim, what happens? The members of his tribe follow. So they had to see to the matter.

Tufail ibn Amir went to the Ka'aba and performed his tawaf. The Messenger of Allah was seated there, reciting the Quran. He caught the sweetness of the words and understood that this was the man of whom they had spoken. So what did he do? He stopped up his ears and began to hurry away. Halfway through his flight he stopped and reasoned with himself. I am the chief of my tribe. I am the pride of my people. There is not a single poet who can stand against me in eloquence. I am among the most accomplished poets in all of Arabia. Are mere words going to overpower me? I can withstand this. He took the plugs from his ears, returned to the Messenger of Allah, sat down beside him, and asked: یا محمد! ما عندک؟ O Muhammad, show me what you have.

Now this is where I want you to listen closely. I am going to recite what the Messenger of Allah said to him. You know who the speaker is. You will not understand the content, but what I want you to fix your attention upon is the beauty of the words. I want you to attend to how the words sound. I want you to feel how each word is set like a jewel in a ring. The Messenger of Allah turned to him and said: أِنَّ الحَمدَ لِی اللہَ أحمَدَہُ وَ أستَعِینَہُ وَ أُومِنُ بِہِ وَ أتَوَکَّلُ عَلَیہِ ۔ مَن یَّھدِہِ اللہُ فَلاَ مُضِلَّ لَہ وَ مَن یَّضِلَّ لَہُ فَلاَ ھَادِیَ لَہ. He said: All praise belongs to Allah. I praise Him, and I seek His help, and I believe in Him, and I place my trust in Him, for the one He guides can never go astray, and the one He leaves astray can never be guided.

Tufail ibn Amir heard this single sentence and he was stunned. He was spellbound. He said: أُعِد أُعِد! فقد بلغنا قاموس البحر. Repeat it! Repeat it!

Truly, your single sentence has drawn up the seven seas! Now, this time, you know all three parts of this communication. See whether you can feel its power now. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) says once more:

أِنَّ الحَمدَ لِی اللہَ أحمَدَہُ وَ أستَعِینَہُ وَ أُومِنُ بِہِ وَ أتَوَکَّلُ عَلَیہِ ۔ مَن یَّھدِہِ اللہُ فَلاَ مُضِلَّ لَہ وَ مَن یَّضِلَّ لَہُ فَلاَ ھَادِیَ لَہ
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
Tufail ibn Amir, with tears in his eyes, placed his hand in the hand of the Prophet and said: I submit. Make me a Muslim. He pronounced the testimony of faith, لا الہ الا اللہ, then and there. One verse! One verse! SubhanAllah! He took the testimony of faith, and afterward he told his story. This is how we come to know of it.

The three deniers. Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan, and Akhnas ibn Shurayq were the three chiefs of the Quraysh, the bitterest of those who hated the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him). They were the seniors, the elders of the Quraysh. They were its think tank. In the dead of night they would steal up to the walls of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) house, press their ears against them, and listen to the recitation of the Qur'an, and then slip away again before morning. What happened the first night was that they ran into one another, each unaware that the others were there. So the first of them said, What are you doing here? And the second answered, And what are you doing here? They knew perfectly well what each was doing there. So they swore they would never return. Yet the very next night they caught one another again. Again they swore they would not come back. And they caught one another a third night. This time they swore by their mothers, by their fathers, by their gods, and by their own lives that they would never come again. And so they did not return.

But Akhnas was curious. He went to Abu Sufyan and said to him: We have been listening for three nights. What do you make of it? Is this the truth? Abu Sufyan said to him, "Of course it is the truth. What else could it be?" Very well. Then let us speak to Abu Jahl; he too has been listening. So the two of them went to Abu Jahl and asked him: What do you make of it? Of course it is the truth, he said.

Abu Jahl says, Of course it is the truth? The greatest enemy of Islam, the fiercest hater of the Messenger of Allah, says it is the truth? But then he explains himself. You see, we are the Banu Abd Manaf, and Muhammad is of the Banu Hashim. There it is. Before I say anything further, consider: what did he weigh? The speech, or the speaker? The denier's rejection rested not on the words themselves, for all their power, for all their truth, for all the flawlessness of their content, for all the spell of their style, but on this: we are not willing to accept this man at any cost. For when the Banu Hashim give in charity, we match them. When the Banu Hashim recite poetry, we match them. When the Banu Hashim show valor, we match them. But when one of them comes forth with these words, we can never match them! So they have won for all time, and we cannot allow that to happen. That was the reason.

SubhanAllah! It is an entirely different reading of history. Even those who hated the Qur'an were held spellbound by the Qur'an. Even they were held spellbound by it.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
The last story. عتبہ بن ربیعہ. Uthbah ibn Rabi'ah. Think of him as the master of language, the chief of it. An expert debater, cutting toward those who opposed him in public discourse. He was a negotiator on behalf of feuding tribes; you may think of him as a consultant, hired for tasks of this kind. When someone had to be destroyed through language, Uthbah was the man they turned to.

He would enter, state his terms, and accomplish what he had been sent to do. The Quraish came to him and said that they were losing this war of words, for the other side had a man truly gifted with language — gifted in debate, in discussion, and in negotiation. So they engaged Uthbah. They said to him: Uthbah, go to Muhammad, peace be upon him. He is sitting there. Speak with him. Put demands to him, and find out what he wants. Humble him. Defeat him. We will watch from a distance. Today people watch a match of cricket or basketball; this was their sport. They took pleasure in such contests, and so they were eager for the bout about to unfold.

Uthbah went to the Messenger of Allah, exceedingly rude and exceedingly condescending. "O Muhammad!"

فرقت ديننا، و شتنت آلهتنا، و عبت ديننا، و فرقت أخواننا

You have torn our religion apart, cast our gods as devils, disgraced our faith, and set brother against brother.

By an Arab's measure, his tone amounted to this: What in the world is the matter with you (نعوذ بالله)? What is it that you want from us?

أِنَّما أِن کُنتَ تُرِیدُ بِہِ مُلکاً، مَلَّکناَ عَلی رُؤُسِنَا

Is it authority that you desire? Very well — we will make you our leader and give you complete command over all we possess.

أِن کُنتَ تُرِیدُ بِہِ الشَّرَف، لا نَقطَعُ أَمراً دُونَک

Is it honor that you seek? Very well — we will take no decision without your leave.

أِن کُنتَ تُرِیدُ بِہِ البآءَ، جَمَعنَا لَکَ نِساَءَ قُرَیشٍ فَخُطَّ أَیُّ نِساَءَ قُرَیشٍ فَنُزَوِّجْکَ عَشَرا

Is it women you desire? Very well — we will set before you all the women of the Quraish, and whichever of them you point to, we will give to you in marriage.

أِن کُنتَ تُرِیدُ بِہِ المال، جمعنا لک أَموَالَناَ حَتّٰی تَکُونَ أَغنٰی قُرَیشٍ مالا

Is it wealth you desire? Very well — we will gather all our riches and lay them before you. We will make you the richest man of the Quraish.

Tell us what you want. State your demands.

He barked at the Messenger like a dog, while the Messenger of Allah listened quietly and patiently. And when he had finished, in a very soft tone the Messenger said to him:

أَفَرَغْتَ یا ابا الولید؟

Are you finished?

Uthbah said: Yes. Now it is your turn. The Messenger of Allah said nothing to him but recited the Qur'an. He began to recite the verses of Surah Fussilat. He said:

بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم
حمٓ ۚ تَنزِيلٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ

The first thing he said — a rough rendering, for of course I cannot match what Allah says — is this: It is something sent down from the One who is exceedingly merciful, the One who is constantly merciful.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
Consider: when the attack came from Uthbah, the charge was that this was your message, carried for a hidden purpose, and that you were merely trying to gain something from it. And what is the first thing the Qur'an says in reply? This is not the Prophet's message. Where do these words come from? They come from Allah. You are not negotiating with my Prophet. With whom are you now debating? You are debating Allah. You are not contending with the Prophet; you are contending with Allah. I have sent this message down to my Prophet.

كِتَبٌۭ فُصِّلَتْ آيَتُهُۥ قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّۭا لِّقَوْمٍۢ يَعْلَمُونَ

It is a message whose demands have been made entirely clear, in the Arabic language — your language.

Remember that he asked for the demands to be named? Allah is answering his demands. Allah says: I will tell you what those demands are, and I will tell you in plain Arabic, so that all of you may understand clearly. You wish to know what my demands are? Here they are.

بَشِيرًۭا وَنَذِيرًۭا فَأَعْرَضَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ فَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ

This Qur'an has two functions.

Give good news and a warning—a threat! But most of you deliberately turn away. To turn away is to ignore on purpose. You are refusing, of your own will, to listen to what I am telling you.

So Allah is presenting his demands to Utbah through the verses of the Qur'an. And as the verses are being recited, the people watch from a distance.

The Prophet continues:

وَقَالُوا۟ قُلُوبُنَا فِىٓ أَكِنَّةٍۢ مِّمَّا تَدْعُونَآ إِلَيْهِ وَفِىٓ آذَانِنَا وَقْرٌۭ ۔ وَمِنۢ بَيْنِنَا وَبَيْنِكَ حِجَابٌۭ ۔ فَٱعْمَلْ إِنَّنَا عَمِلُونَ۔ قُلْ إِنَّمَآ أَنَا۠ بَشَرٌۭ مِّثْلُكُمْ ۔ يُوحَىٰٓ إِلَىَّ أَنَّمَآ إِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌۭ وَحِدٌۭ ۔ فَٱسْتَقِيمُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِ وَٱسْتَغْفِرُوهُ ۗوَيْلٌۭ لِّلْمُشْرِكِينَ ۔ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَهُم بِٱلْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كَفِرُونَ۔ إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّلِحَتِ لَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍۢ۔ قُلْ أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَكْفُرُونَ بِٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلْأَرْضَ فِى يَوْمَيْنِ وَتَجْعَلُونَ لَهُ أَندَادًۭا ۚ۔ ذَلِكَ رَبُّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ۔

Now, as these verses are being recited, the people see Utbah's expression begin to change. He had been sitting comfortably and proudly, and now his face is shifting as Allah lays out his demands.

Then they notice something else: he is weeping. Utbah has begun to weep. Their expert negotiator, the disbeliever, the hater of Islam, the man who insulted the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him)—لعنۃ اللہ علیہ—is listening to the Qur'an, and he has begun to weep. As the verses go on, his feeling grows stronger and stronger, and his weeping grows louder.

وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا رَوَسِىَ مِن فَوْقِهَا وَبَرَكَ فِيهَا وَقَدَّرَ فِيهَآ أَقْوَتَهَا فِىٓ أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍۢ سَوَآءًۭ لِّلسَّآئِلِينَ۔ ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰٓ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَهِىَ دُخَانٌۭ فَقَالَ لَهَا وَلِلْأَرْضِ ٱئْتِيَا طَوْعًا أَوْ كَرْهًۭا قَالَتَآ أَتَيْنَا طَآئِعِينَ۔ فَقَضَىٰهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَوَاتٍۢ فِى يَوْمَيْنِ وَأَوْحَىٰ فِى كُلِّ سَمَآءٍ أَمْرَهَا ۚ وَزَيَّنَّا ٱلسَّمَآءَ ٱلدُّنْيَا بِمَصَبِيحَ وَحِفْظًۭا ۚ ذَلِكَ تَقْدِيرُ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْعَلِيمِ۔ أَعْرَضُوا۟ فَقُلْ أَنذَرْتُكُمْ صَعِقَةًۭ مِّثْلَ صَعِقَةِ عَادٍۢ وَثَمُودَ

Let me translate just this last verse for you. Allah says, after listing his demands: If you still turn away from what I am telling you, then I warn you of a punishment like the one that destroyed the tribes of 'Ad and Thamud.

The moment Utbah hears this, he lunges forward and places both his hands over the mouth of the Prophet, and cries out: Stop! Please stop! Please do not recite another word!

The Messenger of Allah continues until he reaches the verses of prostration, and then he falls into prostration.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
Utbah rises and returns to the people who had sent him—this expert debater they had hired to silence the Messenger of Allah, the man in whom all their hopes rested. When they see his face, they say: the Utbah who returns is not the one who left from here. This is not the face you set out with. Utbah says: whatever this man says will one day become an enormous event.

I do not wish to go into each of these verses, but I will speak a little about the last one:

أَعْرَضُوا۟ فَقُلْ أَنذَرْتُكُمْ صَعِقَةًۭ مِّثْلَ صَعِقَةِ عَادٍۢ وَثَمُودَ

And if they continue to turn away deliberately, then you tell them. And who is "you"? Muhammad (peace be upon him). By these words he understands that he is not being addressed as the Messenger of Allah; he is in conversation with Allah at this very moment. Allah does not dignify Utbah by addressing him; Allah tells the Messenger to tell him. Allah does not speak to him directly. Allah could have said أَنذَرْتُكُمْ—I warn you! But instead he said فَقُلْ أَنذَرْتُكُمْ—you warn them! Warn them of what?

Explosions! صَعِقَةًۭ مِّثْلَ صَعِقَةِ عَادٍۢ وَثَمُودَ—a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt that struck the tribes of Aad and Thamud. This was something the Arabs knew. They knew it had happened in the past. And now Utbah, sitting there, realizes that he has been issued a direct threat from Allah himself. He was completely overpowered. He could not hear another word. He tries to stop the Messenger by putting his hands over his mouth. He goes back and tells his people that this is what the Messenger said. I suggest you take him seriously, he says, because you all know that Muhammad has never once lied. سیکون نبأ عظیما—his words, he tells them, are going to become a tremendous event. They say to him, سحَّرَک—he has worked his magic on you too! Utbah answers, say what you will, it is not magic, but I am no longer speaking to him. I am finished. And he sank to his knees.

I wanted to share these stories with you because I wanted to show you a tragedy. The tragedy is that the disbelievers in the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the believers shared one thing. They had one thing in common. They were both overpowered by what? The Qur'an. They were both overpowered by the Qur'an. But we—the believers, the Muslims and the faithful of our own time, not to mention the disbelievers—I am speaking about the believers, we do not appreciate the power of the Qur'an. We are not stunned, mesmerized, or overwhelmed by the words of Allah, not even in the measure that the disbelievers of that age were mesmerized. And that is a shame. That is a real tragedy. That effect of the Qur'an is something that has been lost.
body.topic_title_en: The Speaker's Style: The Miracle of the Qur'an

body.text_en:
A monumental task lies before me today. God willing, I shall begin today to show you the miracles of the Qur'an. I am nervous as much as I am eager. I am nervous because I feel this is a very difficult task for an amateur such as myself. But I am eager, because through the blessings of my elders, Allah has granted me this opportunity to share this extraordinary material with you.

God willing, I will try my utmost to explain these things to you as clearly as I can. But if you do not understand, please stop me and ask me to explain again. For if you do not, the whole purpose will be defeated, and everything we have learned so far will be of no use. This is the goal toward which we have been working in the previous sessions.

Now, before we begin to experience these miracles, you must keep in mind everything I have stated so far. As I said before, we cannot experience these miracles in our own times. We have to think of the Arabs of the time of the Messenger of Allah, who spoke Ancient Arabic. In fact, it is not enough to think of them: we need to BECOME them, we need to BE the Arabs of that time, in order to appreciate these miracles truly.

A quick recap. How many kinds of Arabic did we discuss earlier? What are they? Spoken, Proper, and Ancient.

So when the Qur'an was revealed, it created a category of its own. It was not merely one step ahead of Ancient Arabic; it was miles ahead. Qur'anic Arabic reached where Ancient Arabic never reached. The summit of Ancient Arabic, then, is Qur'anic Arabic. This is why even today the ultimate standard of Arabic is the Qur'an. To judge whether the Arabic of some piece of writing is good or bad, the standard is Qur'anic Arabic. This is understood and appreciated even by non-Arab men of letters.

Rather than giving a full recap of all the previous sessions, I will simply go into the details as and when they apply to a particular miracle. As I mentioned before, the Qur'an is not a miracle in a single dimension. It is a miracle in many dimensions. So, God willing, I will show you a miracle or two from each dimension. I am in no hurry over this. We will move at whatever pace we need. So once again: if you do not understand, please let me know, and I will explain it as many times as you need me to. Agreed?

Now, you may experience a miracle in each and every example I show you, or you may experience it in one particular dimension. But I am confident that, God willing, you will get a taste of it. And that is all we are after. I want you to remember the feeling you had when you stood beside the bank of the river as Moosa (peace be upon him) parted the water with his staff. If you get that same feeling today, in your heart, then you will know that you have experienced a miracle.
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
Let us become aware of what a miracle is, while remembering what it is not. It is not a magic trick. It is not something for the eyes to see. Remember, a miracle is something you experience in your heart, not something you grasp with your intellect. It has to do first and last with the heart. Merely having information about the miracle is not enough. And I will support that statement from the Qur'an.

In the Qur'an, when we think of ایمان, one of the prophets who stands out is Ibrahim (peace be upon him). In the Qur'an we see his prayer:

وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَهِیمُ رَبِّ أَرِنِى كَيْفَ تُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ

And Ibrahim says: O my Lord, show me how you bring the dead back to life.

Allah says: قَالَ أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِن؟ Why, Ibrahim? Do you not believe? Do you not have faith? Why does Allah ask this? Because if a person has faith, why would that person ask for proof? Ibrahim (peace be upon him) says: قَالَ بَلَىٰ وَلَكِن لِّيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِى Of course I have faith! There is no doubt about it. But I ask you to show me so that my heart may be set at ease. Notice that he did not say لِّيَطْمَئِنَّ عقلى, so that my intellect may be set at ease. He said لِّيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِى, so that my heart may be set at ease. Through this incident Allah teaches us that even when a person has faith, the heart can still be unsettled. And the purpose of miracles is not to set the intellect at ease; it is to set the heart at ease, even though both are affected. See, we usually think that we must understand a miracle with the intellect, but the Qur'an is teaching us that we must experience the miracle of the Qur'an with our feeling, from the heart.

This is why I began these sessions with the miracle of the Qur'an, so that it would put your heart at ease. Once your heart is at ease, the message will sink in of its own accord, God willing.

That was the greatest roadblock on my own journey as well. That is why I felt that gaining all this knowledge was not helping me at all. It was because it did not enter my heart. For the longest time it was as though I sat beside a swimming pool and tried to read and study about swimming. Only when I jumped into the water was I able to learn how to swim.

We discussed a few miracles in the previous session. I showed you the miracle of "style," did I not? How that style affected the disbelievers of that time. How Tufail Ibn Amar al-Dausi, an eloquent poet and the leader of his tribe, became a Muslim simply by listening to a single verse of the Qur'an. It took this poet only one single verse to be spellbound. Then I told you about Utba Ibn Rabeeah, the most eloquent debater of that time. How he challenged the Messenger of Allah, and when the Prophet (peace be upon him) recited the verses of Surah Fussilat, how he was overpowered, began to weep, and physically tried to stop the Prophet by placing both hands over his mouth.
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
Then we discussed how the purpose of any communication is to influence the audience, and how the success of any communication rests on how far it changed lives. And how this Qur'an, as a communication, as بلاغ المبین, influenced the people of that time. How it brought about an unprecedented change at the very smallest level. No other message and no other messenger brought about such a change in the whole history of time.

So today, let us actually begin to look at some of these miracles. I told you that the Arabic word for a "miraculous sign" is "ayah." Every ayah is a miracle of the Qur'an. But it is not only the verses. The book itself, its structure, its capacity to be memorized as no other book can be, its eloquence, the imagination it portrays, its literary perfection, its linguistic excellence, the perfection of its choice of words — there are so many dimensions in which this book is a miracle.

So let us take an outside-in approach to this Qur'an. Let us look at the Qur'an from the outside and then reach into its verses. I have selected two miracles that we can experience while looking at the Qur'an from the outside.

Miracle of Remembrance

The first miracle I am going to begin with is what I call the miracle of remembrance.

Volunteer

Is the Qur'an an oral tradition or a written tradition? Oral! This is the first thing about this content that fascinates me. It is a spoken text.

Now tell me this: is it harder to preserve an oral tradition or a written one? Oral! It is extremely difficult to preserve an oral tradition. Let me give you an example. Do you know what Chinese whispers is? Suppose we as a group play this game of Chinese whispers. I begin with you and whisper in your ear, "Aslam bumped into Faisal." All right? Now you whisper it to Yasmeen, she whispers it to Hussain, he whispers it to Nadia, she whispers it to Saleem, and on it goes. What was the original sentence? By the time it reaches the last member of the group, it has turned into "Aslam burned Faisal's house down, destroyed his car, and killed his whole family." This is the sort of thing that happens in an oral tradition. Nobody intended to change the original message. Somebody simply decided to say the same sentence in his own way, and added or removed one percent of it. Somebody else another half percent. Somebody else another two percent. Now, one or two percent is not a major change, is it? But when it passes through many people, the original message becomes completely unrecognizable. Experiments of this kind are carried out in communication psychology all the time. Any oral tradition is impossible to preserve. The farther it travels and the more people it passes through, the more it changes, the more it varies. That is only logical.

By comparison, a written tradition is safe. But it is not entirely safe. In the time of the Prophet (AS), it is not as though they had image scans or backup hard drives. So even if you have a written book, a line could get smudged, a paragraph could become illegible, the page could get torn. And if such a text comes down through the generations, that could raise doubts about the integrity of the original content, could it not?
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
Now, the Qur'an is an oral expression. And when it was compiled in the form of a book, it was not compiled in the order of revelation. What was the manner of recording the Qur'an in those days? The Messenger of God would recite a passage as the divine inspiration (wahi) came to him. The people would memorize it. Now, we ordinarily think — and this is the argument raised against the Qur'an — how could they memorize it so accurately? Let me say a sentence to you, and I want you to recite it back to me word for word. All right? "In my last session, I explained how the Qur'an as a conversation was a miracle of speaker, speech, and style." Now repeat it. You see, you were able to repeat it back to me accurately. Was it hard? No! Do you know why? Because I said it in a language you are very familiar with, a language you have command over. Now, the Qur'an was not revealed to us desis. It was revealed to the Arabs, who were masters of what? Of the Arabic language! So memorizing the Qur'an may be a very difficult task for us, but for them it was a piece of cake. Do you understand?

So as the Qur'an was being revealed, the people around the Messenger of God were listening to it and committing it to memory down to the syllable. Then they would travel far and wide and recite the Qur'an to the Arabs of other cities, who would listen to it, memorize it, and then teach others.

Now add to this the challenge of the change in the order of the Qur'an. Maulana Ali, in the time of Hazrat Usman, compiled the Qur'an in the form it has today. The Qur'an is not compiled in the order of its revelation; it is compiled in a different order.

The first verse to be revealed was ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ, and the last verse to be revealed was ٱلْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِى وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلْإِسْلَمَ دِينًۭا. Yet this is not the order we find in the Qur'an. The first verse there is بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم of Surah Fatiha, and the last verse is من الجنۃ و الناس of Surah al-Nas.

So these Arabs of the time of the Messenger of God memorized the Qur'an, left Arabia, traveled to other countries, and began to spread the Qur'an. Now consider this: once they left their land, they were cut off from it. They had no telephones and no email. They could not call one another to confirm a verse — was it AlHamdu Lillahi or AlHamda Lillahi? Once a man was cut off, he was cut off.

So these people were memorizing the Qur'an and spreading it. The logical assumption, then, is that within a single year there should have been a hundred versions of the Qur'an. Countless variations of the original text. That is what ought to have happened.

Now move forward to 2015.

Today almost every mosque in the world has a program for memorizing the Qur'an. Hundreds of thousands of children memorize the Qur'an every year. All of us have memorized something of it as well — at least a few surahs.
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
Have you ever been to Indonesia? Do you speak Indonesian? Very well. Suppose you travel to Indonesia, which is a Muslim country. You are among a group of local girls who speak neither English nor Urdu, and you do not speak Indonesian. You begin to recite Surah al-Fatiha. You pronounce one syllable wrongly — only one syllable. You say AlHamda Lillahi. Three girls will stop you at once. They will say, "No, it is AlHamdu Lillahi!" Is that not remarkable? You do not know their language, they do not know yours, you have never met before — yet the moment you recite the Qur'an, you are united in a single language.

Suppose I am at the airport and the time for prayer arrives. A man stands up and begins to pray. Other Muslims join him. He begins to recite the Qur'an. They are complete strangers who have never met one another. If he recites one word, one letter, one syllable of a word wrongly, everyone will correct him with the right syllable. Syllable by syllable — SubhanAllah!

Which city do you live in — Karachi? Very well, let us suppose for a moment that every Qur'an in the world has been destroyed. Every book, every digital copy, every form of it is destroyed. It is no longer available anywhere — not on the internet, not on computers, not on your phone, not on any bookshelf. Completely gone. Not only in your city but everywhere in the world. Understood?

The only copy left is the original text, preserved in some library in Russia, let us say. There is no other form of the Qur'an available anywhere in the entire world. Do you understand?

I can guarantee you that within twenty-four hours you will have the original Qur'an back in your city. Not even in another city — in your own city. How? Because of the children in your city who have memorized it. You give each child a few pages to write out, and within twenty-four hours the whole book is back. And when they set it down in writing and you compare it with the copy in that library, what do you find? It matches down to the last syllable! SubhanAllah! Name me one other book in the entire world with which such a thing is possible. SubhanAllah! This is how deeply the Qur'an is rooted in the hearts of the Muslims. And this book is more than six hundred pages long. It is astonishing.

This material fascinates me. How can the whole world be so united when it comes to this one book? So many people are memorizing the Qur'an that, by ordinary reasoning, we ought to have any number of differing versions of it. Yet AllahuAkbar! With the passing of time documents grow less reliable, less sound. This is the one text that grows more and more sound as time goes on. Consider biblical studies. Most Bible scholars who take their doctorates at universities here — Bible scholars themselves — no longer believe that the Bible is historically accurate. They themselves do not believe it. Listen to the remarks of Professor Gerald Derks. Listen to his interview. He holds a Master's degree in divinity, and he does not believe in the Bible. Our message, by contrast, you could not get rid of even if you tried.
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
This is incredible material. When I learned it for the first time, I was overwhelmed. How is such a thing possible? The first time I read the Qur'an, I read it in translation. Then something took hold of my mind, and I became determined to learn Arabic. My goal was to learn enough Arabic to be able to read and understand this book without a translation. I did not want to speak Arabic; I did not want to order a falafel in Arabic; I did not want to make Arab friends. I only wanted to understand this content without the filter of translation. Alhamdulillah, I have been studying Arabic ever since. And the more I study, the more I realize that this book is truly amazing. It is unique in every respect. To this day this book holds me spellbound. The more I sit with it and study it, the more I am enchanted by it. And when I learned this, I simply felt that people need to know about it. It is far too amazing to go unrecognized.

My intention is not to force this on anyone. I do it out of my own fascination. Islam is a vast subject. It has many branches, both in its zaahir and its baatin, in its exoteric form as well as its esoteric form. There is shariah, there is seerah, there is fiqh, there is hadith, there are theological studies. But for me personally, the only thing I wish to study is this book, because to me this book contains Islam in its most complete form.

In any case, let us move on.

Structural Miracle

The next miracle I want to speak about is the Qur'an's unique structure. For this I would like to speak with someone who is aware of the structure of the Qur'an.

First of all, what is the Qur'an? It is a message, and it comes in what form? The form of a book. Even the Qur'an calls itself a kitaab.

ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًۭى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ

ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ نَزَّلَ ٱلْكِتَبَ بِٱلْحَقِّ

آمَنَ ٱلرَّسُولُ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْهِ مِن رَّبِّهِۦ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ ۚ كُلٌّ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَمَلَٓئِكَتِهِۦ وَكُتُبِهِۦ وَرُسُلِهِ

Let us look at the structure of this book. You have read books, have you not? So you know something about how a book is organized. What does a book normally have? It has a table of contents, chapters, paragraphs, lines, and an index at the end. Is that not so?

Now let us look at the structure of the Qur'an.

How many surahs make up the Qur'an? One hundred and fourteen surahs. And what is the word "surah" translated as in English? Chapter. Now tell me: Chapter 1, Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 4.

In any book, is Chapter 4 built upon Chapter 3? Yes, it is.

Now, is what is stated in Chapter 3 repeated again in Chapter 4, and then again in Chapter 5, and then again in Chapter 6? No, it is not. There is no repetition.

Across all the chapters there is some kind of logical and sequential progression. But does the Qur'an repeat itself across several chapters? Yes, it does. It has already told the story of Moosa (AS); it tells it again in chapter 2, and again in 3, and in 4, and in 5. There are seventy passages concerning Moosa (AS) alone, and they are scattered everywhere, in almost every single chapter. Nor do they follow chronological order. They come in every possible order. So then these are not really chapters at all, are they?
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
And if you examine the individual chapters of the Qur'an, you find that many topics are covered, with sudden shifts from one topic to another and then back again. This is because what we call a chapter is something else. A storybook also has chapters, but there the chronology moves forward. So you cannot compare the surah to a chapter. Surah is the Qur'an's own proprietary term. There is no such thing as a surah in any other book.

Now what does a surah contain? Ayaats. And how is the word "ayah" translated? As "verse." Where have you heard the word "verse" before? Not in religion, but outside of Islam, where have you heard the word "verse"? What comes to mind when you hear it? Poetry, songs, or biblical contexts. So when you hear the word "verse," you are thinking of a song, a poem, or the Bible. Now the Qur'an is emphatic in telling us that this content is not poetry:

وما علمنہ الشعر و ما ھو بقول شاعر

We did not teach you poetry. This Qur'an is not poetry. The last thing we should be thinking as Muslims is that this is poetry. And the last thing we should be thinking is that the content of the Qur'an has been plagiarized from the Bible. Yet the two things that come to mind when you hear the word "verse" are a poem and the Bible. Perhaps not to our minds, because we are so conditioned to the word, but to the average non-Muslim, that is the first thing that comes to mind. The word "ayat" is unique. No other book has ayats. It is unique. It is a proprietary term of the Qur'an. Both surah and ayat are proprietary. They are the copyrights of Allah.

You cannot even think of an ayah as a sentence. What is the definition of a sentence? A grammatical unit of one or more words that expresses an independent statement, and that typically has a subject as well as a predicate. Now, in the Qur'an, can you think of a single word that is a complete ayah? Al-Rehman. Just one word, and it is a complete ayah. Have you ever read a sentence that said only "The Magnificent," "The Benevolent"? But in the Qur'an, a single word can be an ayah.

Then again, I can think of three ayats that go together to make one whole sentence:

الحمد للہ رب العالمین، الرحمن الرحیم مالک یوم الدین

These are three ayats, but grammatically they are one sentence. The earlier example was one word yet a complete ayah. Here are three ayats that are grammatically a single sentence. You do not have this in any other language.

Then there are entire passages, entire paragraphs given over to the exposition of an entire subject, and yet they are a single ayah: مُّحَمَّدٌۭ رَّسُولُ ٱللَّهِ ۚ وَٱلَّذِينَ مَعَهُۥٓ أَشِدَّآءُ عَلَى ٱلْكُفَّارِ رُحَمَآءُ بَيْنَهُمْ ۖ تَرَىٰهُمْ رُكَّعًۭا سُجَّدًۭا يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًۭا مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضْوَنًۭا ۖ سِيمَاهُمْ فِى وُجُوهِهِم مِّنْ أَثَرِ ٱلسُّجُودِ ۚ ذَلِكَ مَثَلُهُمْ فِى ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ ۚ وَمَثَلُهُمْ فِى ٱلْإِنجِيلِ كَزَرْعٍ أَخْرَجَ شَطْـَٔهُۥ فَـَٔازَرَهُۥ فَٱسْتَغْلَظَ فَٱسْتَوَىٰ عَلَىٰ سُوقِهِۦ يُعْجِبُ ٱلزُّرَّاعَ لِيَغِيظَ بِهِمُ ٱلْكُفَّارَ ۗ وَعَدَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّلِحَتِ مِنْهُم مَّغْفِرَةًۭ وَأَجْرًا عَظِيمًۢا A whole paragraph in Surah al-Fath! And yet a single ayah! You cannot fit it into any literary category. There is only one word that can describe an ayah, and that word is ayah. This is what makes the structure of the Quran unique, unlike any other book in the world.
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
Then, too, you cannot arrange the contents of the Quran in any chronological order. Do the Meccan surahs come first and the Madani surahs after? No. They are all mixed together. Does the shortest surah come first and the longest last? Or the longest first and the shortest last? No. It does not proceed by size, it does not proceed by subject, it does not proceed by chronology. Every other book in the world has an order, a sequence, a progression — but not the Quran. It has its own unique order, unlike every other book.

Even the Bibles, the Old and New Testaments, have an order. The Old Testament is a compilation of many books. The first seventeen are historical books. They give the history of civilization from creation down to the time of the Persian Empire. They record the history of the Jewish nation from its beginning, through its days of glory and its deportation, and finally through its days of survival as a small, insignificant nation surrounded by enemies bent on destroying it.

Then comes a different set of books, known as the poetic books of the Bible: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon. These books do not relate historical experiences. Rather, they relate the experiences of the human heart through poetry, much like our munajaat. They enter into the questions of suffering, wisdom, life, love, and, most important of all, the character and nature of God.

The next seventeen books of the Bible make up the last division of the Old Testament — the Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi.

But the Quran has no such order. This is so plain that the orientalists who criticize the Quran have concluded that the Quran has no order at all — that it is chaotic (نعوذ باللہ).

There is absolutely nothing comparable to the Quran. SubhanAllah!

If I gave you time, would you be able to find me a book of a similar structure? Does this not leave you incapable of a response? So you see, even the structure of this book is a miracle.
body.topic_title_en: The Quran: The Beginning of Miracles

body.text_en:
Happy Mother's Day to all mothers! All praise belongs to Allah! We have reached this final dimension of the miracles of the Qur'an. It is amazing how time flies — today is our tenth session, MashaAllah!

One of the first miracles I began with was the structural miracle of the Qur'an. We understood a miracle, or the Arabic word اعجاز, as an act that renders someone incapable of a response. And I discussed at length how, and why, a miracle is something you experience, and not necessarily something you see. A magic trick, by contrast, is something you see, but a miracle is an experience that comes to you THROUGH something you see or hear.

I also said that the ultimate purpose of a miracle has always been to challenge mankind. In fact, Allah Himself challenges mankind: if you think this Qur'an is not the word of Allah, then produce a surah similar to it.

وَإِن كُنتُمْ فِى رَيْبٍۢ مِّمَّا نَزَّلْنَا عَلَىٰ عَبْدِنَا فَأْتُوا۟ بِسُورَةٍۢ مِّن مِّثْلِهِۦ

But what is truly incredible is what Allah says after that:

وَٱدْعُوا۟ شُهَدَآءَكُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَدِقِينَ

Once you have come up with something that YOU think is similar to what my messenger has produced, then invite your OWN people to be the judge of it. Now think about that for a moment. I am a software developer by profession. If I challenged you to write better software than mine, would I not want to be the final judge of what you came up with? And if I could not be the judge, would I not at least want a panel of unbiased judges who know neither me nor my opponent? That sounds logical, does it not?

But Allah does not say: once you have produced something similar to what my messenger is telling you, bring it back to me so that I may judge it — nor even, bring it to Rasul Allah so that HE may judge it. Instead Allah says:

وَٱدْعُوا۟ شُهَدَآءَكُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَدِقِينَ

He says: call your OWN people to be the judge of it. Now, whom is Allah addressing in this verse? Whom is He challenging? The disbelievers, is that not so? So whom would these people invite to judge? Disbelievers like themselves. They will invite people who are already biased against Allah and His messenger. And Allah says: call them, call those disbelievers, and let them be the judge. You will see that even they will judge against you! SubhanAllah. Now that is confidence.

But Allah does not stop there. He goes a step further and says:

فَإِن لَّمْ تَفْعَلُوا۟

If you are not able to do it —

وَلَن تَفْعَلُوا۟

and you will CERTAINLY not be able to do it —

فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ ٱلَّتِى وَقُودُهَا ٱلنَّاسُ وَٱلْحِجَارَةُ ۖ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَفِرِينَ

Then be ready for the fire of hell, fueled by disbelievers and stones, prepared especially for the disbelievers.

Allah did not simply say: believe in this book because I am telling you it is a miracle. He said: try to come up with something better, something more perfect. But if you cannot — and I am telling you that you cannot, because I am the One who created you — I know what you are able to do and what you are not able to do. I know that you will never be able to create any text, any prose, any poetry that can match the Qur'an, in any of its dimensions: not in its linguistic excellence, not in its structure, and not in its scientific reasoning.

I am telling you that the finest human speech ever composed cannot compare to the Qur'an in its precision, its perfection, its eloquence, its imagery, or its brevity. So trust me. And if you do not trust me, then try your utmost. Have your attempt judged by your own people. But if even after all of this you still do not believe, then I will fuel my hellfire with you. Subhan Allah!

What is striking is that Allah compares such disbelievers with stones. He says ٱلنَّاسُ وَٱلْحِجَارَةُ — the disbelievers and the stones. Why the comparison with stones?
