Because nothing can penetrate a stone. Allah says that if, after all the evidence I have laid before you, you still do not believe, then you are nothing more than a dead stone. Indeed, in another place Allah says that your hearts are worse than stones: ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكُم مِّنۢ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ فَهِىَ كَٱلْحِجَارَةِ أَوْ أَشَدُّ قَسْوَةًۭ — even harder than stones.

We have now seen many examples drawn from all these different dimensions, and every one of them is astonishing. But what I am going to show you today is, in my personal opinion, simply the most incredible miracle of all. For me personally, this particular dimension was like standing beside Musa (peace be upon him) and watching him split the sea before my own two eyes. This is the structural miracle of the Qur'an.

The nature of a miracle is such that I cannot tell you that this particular dimension is the ultimate miracle of the Qur'an. I may experience the miracle through one dimension while you experience it through another. The Qur'an is not a miracle because of my understanding; it is a miracle because it lies beyond my understanding. But this was certainly the one that made a believer out of me.

When I experienced this miracle, I remember, I was in a public library in New York, studying and researching the Qur'an, and I was so overwhelmed by Allah's majesty and His glory that I needed to fall into sajda. I am not someone who likes to stand out in a crowd or to draw attention to myself. I am always the one hiding in the shadows. But I remember that when I experienced this miracle I was so overwhelmed that I simply had to place my head on the ground in sajda. I could not control myself. That feeling had overpowered me completely. So I rose from my chair, fell into sajda, and began to weep. It was such an incredible feeling. In that moment I did not care who was around me, who was looking at me, whether it was proper or improper. I simply had to submit myself to Allah. And for the first time I understood what Namaz is meant to feel like.

I hope and pray that Allah blesses us all with this same feeling and experience, insha Allah ta'ala, because I have never felt that emotion again, neither before nor after that day, and I long for it deeply.

So today's miracle concerns the structure of the Qur'an. If you remember, I began with the structure of the Qur'an as a miracle. We spoke earlier about the apparent structure of the Qur'an, or rather about its apparent lack of structure.

But I will repeat it very quickly, for the benefit of those who were not present in that session, because you cannot really appreciate what I have to show you today without first appreciating how unique the Qur'an is: even in its outward appearance, it does not fit any existing literary structure. So we know that the Qur'an is the message of Allah delivered in the words of Rasul Allah. In its final form, the Qur'an is a book, a kitaab, as Allah says:

ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًۭى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ

ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ نَزَّلَ ٱلْكِتَبَ بِٱلْحَقِّ

Now, the last time we compared the structure of the Qur'an, as a book, with any other book in the world, we found some remarkable distinctions. Every book we know normally has a table of contents, chapters, paragraphs, lines, and an index at the end, right?

But when we look at the structure of the Qur'an, we see that the way the Qur'an organizes and categorizes its content is very unique. We see that it has something called Surahs. It has a total of 114 surahs. Now, the word Surah is translated into English as what? Chapter! So we have Chapter 1 (Fateha), Chapter 2 (Baqara), Chapter 3 (Aale Imran), Chapter 4 (Nisaa), and so on.

Now you tell me! In every other book that we know, is Chapter 4 usually based on Chapter 3? Is it not? Once you have read Chapter 3, do you find the exact same thing repeated again in Chapter 4, and then again in Chapter 5, and then again in Chapter 6? No, you do not! There is no repetition. When reading any book, we normally find that there is some sort of logical and sequential progression across all the chapters.

But does the Qur'an repeat itself across multiple chapters? Yes, it absolutely does! Even though it has told the story of Moosa (AS) in chapter 2, it tells it again in Chapter 3, again in Chapter 4, and again in Chapter 5. There are over 70 passages in the Qur'an relating to Moosa (AS) alone, and they are scattered everywhere, in almost every single chapter.

Not only that. We also find that these stories are not in any chronological order. The Qur'an does not speak about the birth of Moosa (AS) in chapter 2, then his childhood in Chapter 3, then his adulthood in Chapter 4. No! It begins with his adulthood, then his prophethood, then his birth. It comes in all kinds of order, scattered everywhere!

Then we also see that in the Qur'an numerous topics are covered with sudden switches from one topic to another and then back to the original subject again. But that does not happen in the books we read. Imagine reading a bedtime storybook to your child that goes like this:

The fairy godmother waves her magic wand over Cinderella and her clothes turn into a magnificent gown. And the fox says to the three little pigs, "If you do not open the door, I will huff and puff and I will blow your house down." So Red Riding Hood says, "Wow, Grandma, such big eyes you have." And so the fairy godmother warns Cinderella that the magic will end at midnight!

I seriously doubt this storybook will make it to the best sellers list, right? Because it would not make sense. We do not have different stories, within the same chapter, organized this way. So then, even though we call these surahs "chapters," they are not really "chapters," are they? Because what we call a chapter in a storybook is one thing, and what the Qur'an calls a Surah is something else.

In a chapter of a storybook, what always happens is that the chronology moves forward in a particular order. That is not what happens in a Surah. So you cannot compare a Surah to a chapter. SURAH is the Qur'an's own proprietary term. There is no such thing as a Surah in any other book. Now let us dig deeper. What does a Surah contain? Ayaats! And how is the word "Ayah" translated into English? Verse! Now, where do we hear the word verse outside of Islam? What comes to mind when we hear the word verse? Poetry, songs, even the Bible. Yet the Qur'an is very adamant in letting us know that this content is definitely not poetry: وما علمنہ الشعر و ما ھو بقول شاعروما علمنہ الشعر و ما ینبغیلۃ۔ ان ھو الا ذکر و قرآن مبین We did not teach you poetry! This Qur'an is not poetry. So the last thing we as Muslims should be thinking when we hear the word "verse" is that this is poetry. And the last thing we should be thinking is that the content of the Qur'an has been plagiarized from the Bible. But the two things that come to mind when you hear the word verse are poem and Bible.

So, can we think of an ayah as a sentence? No! Because a sentence is defined as a grammatical unit of one or more words that expresses an independent statement, and that typically has a subject as well as a predicate. Now, in the Qur'an we find that a single word can be a complete ayah. Al-Rehman! YaSeen! Just one word, and it is a complete Ayah! Have you ever read a sentence that said only "Magnificent" or only "Beneficent"? No! That can be a title or a heading, but it cannot be considered a sentence. Yet in the Qur'an, a single word can be a complete ayah.

Then we also find that several ayats can join together to form one complete sentence. الحمد للہ رب العالمین، الرحمن الرحیم مالک یوم الدین Technically, these are three ayats, but grammatically they are just one sentence. In the earlier example, an ayah was a single word. Here we see three separate ayats that are grammatically one single sentence. You do not have this in any other language. And then there are entire passages, entire paragraphs devoted to explaining a whole subject, and all of it is just one single ayah. Nine different sentences, but one single ayah.

So you cannot confine an ayah to any existing literary form. It is completely unique. No other book in the world has anything similar to an ayah. Just like the word Surah, the word Ayah is a proprietary term as well. Copyrights of Allah (AWJ)! There is ONLY one word you can use to describe an ayah, and that word is "Ayah."

So do you see how unique the structure of the Qur'an is? It is unlike any other book in the world.

Then let us take a look at how the Qur'an's content is categorized. Is there any order in the way its content is arranged? Is there any chronological order? Do the Meccan surahs come first and the Madani Surahs after? No! They are all mixed in together. Is the shortest Surah first and the longest Surah last? Or is the longest Surah first and the shortest Surah last? No! So we see that it does not go by size order, it does not go by subject order, it does not go by chronological order, and the stories do not run in any sequence. Every other book in the world has some order, some sequence, some progression — but not the Qur'an.

This led the orientalist to conclude, after researching the Qur'an in every possible way, that the Qur'an has no order at all — that it is chaos. But we know that cannot be true, because we see that there is nothing chaotic about the Qur'an. So there has to be a structure. The reason the orientalist could not identify an order for the Qur'an is that the Qur'an, like the surah and like the ayah, has its own unique order, unlike the order we find in any other book. And it is an order that can never be replicated with this kind of perfection.

So let us begin looking at that order now.

Before I get into it, I want to remind you all that the Qur'an was originally delivered to its audience in the form of speech, through recitation. There was absolutely no editorial process in place. Many of the verses were even revealed on the spot, sometimes as a response to unexpected questions and challenges that were brought forward to Rasul Allah by believers and non-believers alike. I want you to remember also that the Qur'an is made up of 6,236 ayaats, revealed gradually over a period of 23 years, sometimes as complete surahs and sometimes in large passages. So for a completely spontaneous, spoken text of more than 6,000 ayaats, spread over a period of 23 years, you would expect the structure to be extremely incoherent. Would you not? But what we will soon see, InshaAllah, is that the Qur'an, and the surahs within the Qur'an, have a miraculously coherent structure — a structure that is completely and entirely beyond any human possibility.

I also want to say that this is not something very easy to understand, because we are not conditioned to think in this way. I am going to try my best to make it as simple and clear as possible, but it will require some reflection on your part as well. So when I pause and ask whether you have any questions, please do not hesitate. You should not feel bad if you do not understand; this is not an easy topic. I will be happy to repeat it as many times as you need me to. I have also created many diagrams for you to make it easy. I hope and pray to Allah (AWJ) that He makes it easy for all of us to understand this today.

So then, what is this remarkable structure of the Qur'an?

The Qur'an's structure is in fact symmetrical. It has a circular composition, also called a "Ring Composition." What that means is that there is a very clear correspondence, a very clear correlation, between the beginning of a surah and the end of that surah.

So imagine that you cut out a perfect circle from a sheet of paper, and then you fold it in half at its center. You will see that every single point on the right side meets the exact same point on the left side. In other words, point A on one side mirrors point A on the opposite side, point B mirrors point B, and so on.

I will give you a very simple example to make this clear. In the English language, or in any language for that matter, we have a structure that fits this formula. It is called a palindrome. A palindrome is a word that reads the same whether you read it forward or backward — like BOB, MADAM, RACECAR, or my khala AFIFA. A palindrome has this same symmetrical structure. You can see that the word RACECAR spells the same whether you spell it forward or backward.

And this is the structure of the Quran. The entire Quran is built as a palindrome. So if you take any surah and split it in half, you will see that the first half mirrors the second half exactly. This is how every single surah in the Quran is organized. SubhanAllah!

Now, in certain surahs this mirroring is literal; in others it is by meaning. But they are all structured the same way, in a ring composition. Is that not amazing?

Let us assume a surah has 7 ayaats. Now let us assign a letter to each individual ayah. So the first ayah is "A," the second is "B," the third is "C," the fourth is "D." Now, in this case, which letter will be the middle ayah, the center of this circle? It would be "D," would it not? Because you have 3 ayaats before D and 3 ayaats after D. So what we will find is that the ayaats before D in any surah will always mirror the ayaats after D in perfect symmetry.

Now we can replace these variables with ayats, or we can replace them with topics. If we replace them with ayaats, then ayah A on the left will mirror ayah A on the right, ayah B on the left will mirror ayah B on the right, and so on. If we replace these variables with topics, then topic A on the left will mirror topic A on the right, topic B on the left will mirror topic B on the right, and so on.

So now let us take a look at one of the surahs of the Quran. We will start from the outermost level, which is the TOPIC level. I have selected Surah Al-Baqarah for our case study. The reason I chose this surah is that it has a large surface area, which makes it easy to analyze. Hassan.

We know Surah Baqarah is made up of 286 verses. When you study this surah, you will find that the entire content of the surah can be divided into 9 distinct topics. I am not going to go into the details of each of these topics, because that would become a very long discussion. All I want to do for our discussion today is show you this circular pattern.

I have listed the ayats for you in parentheses, and I encourage everyone to check it out when you get the time. But if you look at this image: what is the first topic? What is the last topic? What is the second topic? What is the second to last topic? So do you see what I am talking about? The structure of the Quran is circular. If I rearranged this list to fit into a ring composition, it would look something like this.

Do you see how the first half aligns perfectly with the second half? SubhanAllah! How amazing is that?

So let us discuss for a bit why Allah chose this circular structure. A circle is a very special geometric shape in our religion, especially in the creation of this universe. We all know that a circle exists because of its center. If there is no center, there is no circle. All of Allah's creation is based on this one shape. You see how everything in nature is circular. The earth is circular; its rotation is circular. All processes within nature are cyclic. The seasons repeat in a cycle. All planets are circular, the orbits in which they revolve are circular, and as they revolve, they turn on their axis, which is also circular. Day and night repeat constantly in a cycle. Namaaz is cyclic. Fasts repeat in a cycle. The tawaaf around the Kaaba is circular.

Is that not so? Behind all of these geometric shapes there are in fact taveel and haqaiq. But I do not have permission to enter into that, so I will try to explain the matter only from its outward form.

Why, then, did Allah choose this shape? One reason is that among the attributes of a circle is that it never ends. It is a loop. It begins at a point, arrives at its end, and then begins all over again.

Now listen to this carefully. Consider the four seasons. If you think of all four seasons as a single entity, then I may say that the season begins as an infant with spring, becomes young with summer, begins to grow old with fall, and at last dies in winter. Then a new spring begins and passes through the same cycle again. Among us human beings, a child is born, becomes young, grows old, and dies, and then another generation takes its place. The legacy of the previous generation continues on in the generations to come. So each period may be regarded as an independent circle. A child completes the circle of childhood. Once that circle ends, the circle of youth begins, and that culminates in the beginning of manhood, and then comes the cycle of old age. The advantage of this circular structure is that it produces growth. It carries one from weakness to strength, and then back again from strength to weakness, so that a next cycle may begin.

Continuity, then, is one of the attributes of a circle.

The word Quran means, literally, that which is read over and over again. So the Quran too follows this cyclic pattern. Why? Because the Quran does not stop once it has been recited a single time. Once you have completed its recitation, it begins all over again. Its recitation is constant. Why? Because each cycle is meant to produce growth, and at its end to evolve into something better.

In the first iteration of the Quran we are meant to understand its language; in the next iteration we are meant to understand its taveel; in the next, its haqaiq; in the next, its daqaiq. That is how it is meant to proceed. That is how our deeni system of knowledge works as well. All of it is circular.

That is why the word daira is used, which means circle. Is that not so? Momineen ka daira, mafaseeh ka daira, manaseeb ka daira, taveel ka daira, haqaiq ka daira.

So, as I said, the entire existence of a circle rests upon its center. And now comes the most interesting part.

What did I tell you in the example of the child? What is the center point of a human life? His or her youth. That is when a child is at its peak. Every child's potential is actualized in youth. Ideally speaking, that is when he is strongest, that is when he is healthiest, that is when he is most active. Everything he accomplishes at that point he will now put to use in the remainder of his life. He will carry it with him and refine it through the remaining stages of his life. So man and woman were in fact created for their youth: not for their childhood, not for their old age, but for their youth. Why? So that they may marry and begin the next generation, and give birth to a new circle, a new cycle of life. Does that make sense?

So when we study this Surah, and indeed every other Surah, it is almost as though Allah placed the protractor upon the central topic and then drew the circle. We see that the central idea of the Surah is the declaration of the new Qibla, which is ayats 142 to 152.

In these ten ayats Allah declares, in essence, that the Ka'aba is now the new Qibla for Muslims — and you can see that every remaining topic in the Surah is tied to this central theme. Take the topic of the Ka'aba out of this Surah. Take out the center, and everything around it falls apart. Why? Because everything before the center leads up to the establishment of the Ka'aba, and everything after the center rests upon the existence of the Ka'aba. And there is a systematic progression in this that is astonishing. The Surah begins by speaking of faith and disbelief, and it ends by speaking of faith and disbelief. But the first time it speaks of faith and disbelief, it does so in the abstract sense, as a concept:

ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًۭى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ
ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ وَيُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ
وَٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكَ وَمَآ أُنزِلَ مِن قَبْلِكَ وَبِٱلْآخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ
أُو۟لَٓئِكَ عَلَىٰ هُدًۭى مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ ۖ وَأُو۟لَٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُفْلِحُونَ

These ayats speak of faith in the present tense. Allah says ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ — "Those who believe" — present tense. Who are these people of the present moment, the moment when the Qur'an is being revealed, before the establishment of the Ka'aba? The Bani Israeel. But when the Surah closes with faith and disbelief, after the establishment of the Ka'aba, the tense shifts to the past. It is no longer ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ, no longer وَٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكَ. Instead it now says:

آمَنَ ٱلرَّسُولُ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْهِ مِن رَّبِّهِۦ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ كُلٌّ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَمَلَٓئِكَتِهِۦ وَكُتُبِهِۦ وَرُسُلِهِ

The prophets have believed. Because the Ka'aba has now been established, and the establishment of the Ka'aba means that the people have accepted faith. So the tense changes to the past tense. Before, it was "Those who believe." After the establishment of the Ka'aba, it is now "the prophets who believed," آمَنَ ٱلرَّسُولُ. He no longer says یؤمن ٱلرَّسُولُ. It is now آمَنَ ٱلرَّسُولُ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْهِ مِن رَّبِّهِ. He no longer says ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ. He now says ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ كُلٌّ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَمَلَٓئِكَتِهِۦ وَكُتُبِهِۦ وَرُسُلِهِ.

Before, it is the delivery of the Sharia to the Bani Israeel, because the Ka'aba was not yet established. But now, after the establishment of the Ka'aba, it is the delivery of the Sharia to Muslims. And who are the Muslims? The ones who face the Ka'aba, correct? Before the establishment of the Ka'aba, it is Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the builder of the Ka'aba, who is tested. After the establishment of the Ka'aba, it is the Muslims — the very ones for whom the Ka'aba was built, the followers of the Ka'aba — who are tested.

So we see this incredible evolution, this growth, this maturity in religion as the Surah passes its midpoint. SubhanAllah. How do you do this with spoken literature? How do you do this? And Wallahi, today I am sharing with you only the tip of the iceberg. There is so much depth in this one Surah alone. I would need twenty more sessions to work through it. And this is only the little that I have learned. I truly believe there is no end to the depth of this ocean — and this is just one Surah. AllahuAkbar.

Another example.

Those who have read Surah Yusuf and understand it will be able to appreciate this. The Surah opens with Hazrat Yusuf, peace be upon him, seeing a dream in which eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrate to him; the Surah closes with that dream fulfilled. Second topic: his brothers plot against him. Second topic from the end: his brothers learn their lesson. Third topic: the minister's wife tries to seduce him. Third topic from the end: the minister's wife confesses what she did. Fourth topic: the noblewomen of the city try to seduce him. Fourth topic from the end: they confess their crime. Fifth topic: Yusuf, peace be upon him, goes to prison. Fifth topic from the end: Yusuf, peace be upon him, is freed from prison. Sixth topic: the king has a dream. Sixth topic from the end: the king's dream is interpreted.

So this was about Surah Baqarah and Surah Yusuf. But I want, very quickly, to speak about a few short Surahs that everyone knows and has memorized, and I feel you will be able to appreciate this astonishing symmetry far more, InshaAllah.

What does unique mean? One who needs no one — does such a one need a father or a son? What is the history of this Surah? What is this Surah about?

The last one.

The topics of every Surah are arranged in this way, in a circular composition. And this is spoken text.

Now, if you find this incredible, consider this. It is not only the Surahs that stand in a ring composition; within each Surah there are passages that stand in a ring composition. There are these outer rings, and within them various inner rings. Then it is not only the Surahs that stand in a ring composition; various verses stand in a ring composition. It is not only the verses that stand in a ring composition; the sentences within a verse stand in a ring composition. Then it is not only a single Surah that stands in a ring composition; two Surahs come together to form a ring composition. And it is not only two Surahs that come together to form a ring; two consecutive verses come together to form a ring. AllahuAkbar!

فبای آلاء ربکما تکذبان

We are continuing with the miracles of the Qur'an. Several new people have joined us, so I will begin with a brief review of the earlier sessions. And for those joining today: if you have difficulty following these ideas, we can hold a separate session, and I can go through them with you in greater detail.

Faizah.

Whose message is the Qur'an? The words of the Qur'an — to whom do they belong? The message was revealed as light upon the heart of the Messenger of Allah, and he turned it into words for us.

We have discussed that the Qur'an is, in essence, a conversation. It is a conversation that Allah is having through the medium of His beloved Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Who is the audience of the Qur'an? What is the subject of the Qur'an? What are the two forms in which the conversation of the Qur'an takes place? Either it gives information or it expresses emotion. And why is that? Because human beings are capable of only these same two kinds of conversation. Every human conversation can fall only into these two categories: giving information or expressing emotion.

Information is related to which part of the body — the heart or the intellect? Emotion is related to which part of the body — the heart or the intellect? So the Qur'an is a message for both, the heart and the intellect.

To whom was the Qur'an originally revealed? To the Arabs. What was the most important thing for an Arab in the time of the Prophet? Language. What language did they speak?

We discussed that the Arabs had a very powerful imagination — an imagination that you and I are incapable of. We discussed the factors that developed their superior imagination. And on top of that, they possessed this powerful language. So they would draw out their imagination in words, in poetry. And I gave you a few examples of that as well.

So the language they spoke was Arabic. How many types of Arabic did we discuss? Which Arabic did the people of the Prophet's time speak?

When a tribe would choose its leader, what was the criterion for the choice? Who would be chosen to lead a tribe? When they held poetry competitions, what would happen to the one who lost?

That is the setting in which the Qur'an was revealed. Now let us turn to the miracle itself.

What is the Arabic word for a miracle? Ejaaz. What does the word mean literally? To bring someone down to their knees, to incapacitate someone, to make someone incapable of a response. What was the example I gave for experiencing Ejaaz?

We talked about the difference between a miracle and magic. A miracle is not a magic trick. It is not pulling a rabbit out of a hat. What is the essential purpose of a miracle? Is a miracle for the heart or for the intellect? Do you see a miracle, or do you experience a miracle?

Perfect. Then we began discussing the miracles of the Qur'an from the outside in. The Qur'an is not a miracle in a single dimension. It is a miracle in many dimensions. Let us quickly go over some of the dimensions in which we saw the Qur'an as a miracle.

The Qur'an is, in essence, a conversation. What is the measuring stick of a good conversation? How it influences its audience; how it brings about change in the audience. So the first miracle of the Qur'an that we saw was how it changed its audience at the very smallest level. And we discussed how such a change is without precedent in history.

Then we spoke about the three components of a conversation. What are they?

The speaker, the speech, and the style. So the Qur'an is powerful because its speaker is powerful and its speech is powerful — but in which component does the miracle lie? In the style. And I shared three stories with you to illustrate the power of style and the effect it had upon the disbelievers.

Then, in the previous session, we discussed how the Qur'an is a structural miracle. Although it is a book, it conforms to the rules of no book. I also explained how it is a miracle of remembrance, and how and why this book can never be destroyed. If every Qur'an in the world were destroyed, it could be reproduced accurately within twenty-four hours. This is not possible with any other text in the world.

Allah Himself challenges mankind. He says:

وَإِن كُنتُمْ فِى رَيْبٍۢ مِّمَّا نَزَّلْنَا عَلَىٰ عَبْدِنَا فَأْتُوا۟ بِسُورَةٍۢ مِّن مِّثْلِهِۦ وَٱدْعُوا۟ شُهَدَآءَكُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَدِقِينَ

So now that we have looked at the Qur'an from the outside, let us begin to look at the inside. Let us begin to examine the verses. What is the meaning of the Arabic word *ayah*? Sign and miracle — a miraculous sign. So every verse of the Qur'an is a miracle.

Thank you, Faizah!

Before we begin, I want everyone to become aware of what a miracle feels like. Remember the exercise we did in order to experience a miracle? I want you all to remember that feeling. We all know what the heart feels when it experiences a miracle. So become aware of that feeling, so that you recognize it when you experience it.

**Scientific Miracle**

Today I want to speak about the scientific dimension of the Qur'an as a miracle. As we discussed earlier, to science there is no such thing as a miracle. A miracle is an extremely unscientific concept. There is no empirical evidence to prove the existence of heaven, hell, angels, jinn, everlasting life, and all this sort of thing. We believe that in Paradise we may eat anything we like, that we never need to go to the bathroom, and that we sweat perfume. All of this is very unscientific for someone who does not believe. Is it not?

Yet despite this fact, we see that in recent times this subject — science and the Qur'an — is truly gathering momentum. The reason is that the Qur'an speaks of Allah's creation with one specific intention: the intention of inspiring reflection, inspiring reflection upon the beauty of His creation.

أَوَلَمْ يَتَفَكَّرُوا۟ ۗ مَا بِصَاحِبِهِم مِّن جِنَّةٍ ۚ إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا نَذِيرٌۭ مُّبِينٌ

إِنَّ فِى ذَلِكَ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّقَوْمٍۢ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ

Allah invites us to reflect! Reflect upon what? Upon the subtleties, the design of His creation, the technology He used in His creation. The technology behind a single leaf, the symmetry involved, the advanced technology in a single cell, in an atom. Allah wants us to reflect upon it and to see how advanced it is. With science where it stands today, with such spectacular advancements, we cannot even create a fly or a mosquito. Allah wants us to reflect upon the technology used to create man.

And I think that is why, to the general Muslim population, these scientific phenomena are so amazing. But the truth is that we may be realizing these facts after fourteen hundred years, while they have been true all along. Something to truly appreciate about this dimension is that today, when we read certain verses and say, "This does not seem right," or, "How is this possible?" — well, it is possible, because what was said fourteen hundred years ago is being proven today.

Therefore what is being said today, even if it seems impossible today, may well be possible fourteen hundred years from now.

I want, then, to touch briefly upon a few verses from this dimension. One interesting example is Surah al-Hadeed. Hadeed in Arabic means "iron." Allah says:

وَأَنزَلْنَا ٱلْحَدِيدَ فِيهِ بَأْسٌۭ شَدِيدٌۭ وَمَنَفِعُ لِلنَّاسِ

And We have sent down iron, in which there is great power, and many benefits for mankind.

Now, Allah speaks a great deal about His creation in the Qur'an, and when He does so He uses the word خلق:

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُمْ

هُوَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ لَكُم مَّا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًۭا

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

But when He speaks of iron, He does not use the word خلق. What does He say instead? وَأَنزَلْنَا — We sent down!

The scholars of the past struggled with this idea, because the words of the Qur'an are extremely precise. Muslims would argue that by "sent down" He really meant that He created it. And the reply to that was: No! Had He wished to say that He created it, He would have used the word خلق. He deliberately used the word أَنزَلْنَا, "We sent it down."

And so, in the twentieth century, we find geologists reaching agreement about the beginnings of the earth. One point of agreement is that iron is not part of the earth's original substance. It came to the earth in the form of meteor showers, and it was buried very deep in the earth's core. So the word used, أَنزَلْنَا, "We sent down," becomes a very accurate description of the reality of how iron came into this world, because it was literally sent down.

Another example is in Surah al-Furqan, where Allah says:

تَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ بُرُوجًۭا وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا سِرَجًۭا وَقَمَرًۭا مُّنِيرًۭا

Allah speaks here of the things in the heavens that are at His disposal. تَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ بُرُوجًۭا — Blessed is the One who placed stars in the sky. Then He says وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا سِرَجًۭا — and in the sky He placed for us a lamp. In this verse He calls the sun a lamp. Then He says وَقَمَرًۭا مُّنِيرًۭا. The word qamar means moon, but it is the word muneer that is so scientific. Muneer means something that is given light. It has no light of its own; it receives light from an external source. It is something illuminated, something that does not give out light but is lit by something else. For example, the room you are sitting in is muneer, because of the light in it. The bulb itself is siraaj, but the room is muneer.

So when Allah spoke of the sun, He called it a lamp. But when He spoke of the moon, He called it something that reflects light. At a time when this was not a known phenomenon, the Messenger of Allah was speaking of the moon as a body in space that does not give off its own light. Today, of course, this is common knowledge. But imagine yourself fourteen hundred years ago: it is not at all an obvious idea. The moon looks as though it gives off its own light, does it not?

Then there is another astonishing scientific miracle. In Surah al-Anbiya, Allah describes the heavens and the earth, which is the Arabic expression for the universe:

أَوَلَمْ يَرَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ أَنَّ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ كَانَتَا رَتْقًۭا فَفَتَقْنَهُمَا

Do the disbelievers not see that the heavens and the earth were a single fused mass, and We separated them?

The word ratq means something that is fused together and inseparable.

fused and inseparable. The word ratq is used of a mother carrying a child, because mother and child cannot be separated. And when she begins to deliver, the word used is fataqa. Fataqa is the moment at which she begins to come apart. Her body is literally parting, and she is parting from her child. So the verse says that the heavens and the earth were once fused into a single body, inseparable, and then We caused them to come apart. That is, the universe in its origin was a fused, united body, a single matter, and then it parted and spread out far and wide. The big bang theory is, interestingly, very close to this verse.

Another is where Allah says: وَجَعَلْنَا مِنَ ٱلْمَآءِ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ حَىٍّ We made water the source of life for every living thing. Again, something stated far ahead of its time.

We have been speaking about the Qur'an as a miracle. A brief review is in order. What is the Qur'an? It is a conversation, as Allah says: ھذا بلاغ لی الناس. The message is from Allah, but the words are the creation of Rasul Allah (SA). The words of the Qur'an are not from Allah, as the common Muslims believe. So it is a conversation that Allah holds with His creation through the words of Rasul Allah (SA). Every conversation requires an audience. The audience of the Qur'an is Al-Insaan (Man). And the subject the Qur'an addresses to that audience is Taqwa (Piety).

The word for miracle, معجزۃ, comes from the Arabic word أعجاز, which literally means to bring someone down on his knees. It also means to incapacitate someone, or to leave someone unable to answer. A miracle is something we experience with the heart, unlike a magic trick or magic, which we see with the eyes.

When we hear people speak about the miracles of the Qur'an, at best we hear of its miracles in the single dimension of "predictions." The Qur'an speaks of future events that are coming true today. But as I said earlier, the predictions may be a miracle for us, yet they could not possibly have been a miracle for the Arabs of that time, upon whom the Qur'an was being revealed.

The Qur'an is a miracle in several dimensions, not in one alone. Some of the dimensions in which we have seen the Qur'an as a miracle so far are these.

As a conversation, بلاغ مبین. We learned that every conversation has three components: the Speaker, the Speech (or the content), and the Style. We saw that the Qur'an is powerful in all three dimensions: its Speaker is powerful, and its speech, the content, is powerful. But the true miracle lies in its style, in the manner in which the content is delivered. That in itself was the true miracle. For we know that the disbelievers did not believe in Allah. And when you do not believe the Speaker, his speech, whatever he wishes to say, holds no importance either. Then why, when they heard Rasul Allah (SA) recite a verse, did they immediately accept Islam? Because of its mesmerizing style. So the style in itself became the miracle.

Then we saw how the Qur'an is a miracle in terms of its influence. The measuring stick of any conversation, of any communication, is the influence it has upon its audience. And we saw how the Qur'an influenced so violent and barbaric a community, and transformed it completely at the smallest level. Everything about them changed.

Then we looked at how, in the dimension of remembrance, the Qur'an is a miracle, and how and why this message can never be destroyed for as long as man exists.

We also looked at it as a structural miracle. It is a book, because the Qur'an calls it kitaab. And it has the outward appearance of a book, yet in no way, shape, or form does it conform to the format of any book. Its surahs are called chapters, but they are not really chapters. Its ayats are called verses, but they are not really verses. There is no apparent order in the way the surahs are arranged. It is not in chronological order, it is not in order of size, it is not in the order of revelation, and it is not even in the order of the places where it was revealed.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
Then I showed you how Surah Fateha is the complete index of the Qur'an. A book that spans more than six hundred pages is fully indexed in seven beautiful Ayats, something impossible with any other book.

Then I also showed you how its first Ayat, BismillahAlRehmanAlRaheem, is itself the index of Surah Fateha. SubhanAllah! A book whose index is seven Ayats, and that index has its own index in the form of BismillahAlRehmanAlRaheem. So in essence the whole Qur'an is indexed in its very first Ayat: BismillahAlRehmanAlRaheem. Then, in the last session, we looked at the scientific dimension of the Qur'an, in which Allah speaks of scientific realities far ahead of their time.

So we see that the Qur'an is a miracle in more than one dimension, and it is a living miracle. For over fourteen hundred years it has remained a miracle for its audience, no matter which period they were born into.

There are certain dimensions in which the Qur'an is a miracle for us alone, and not for the Arabs.

There are certain dimensions in which the Qur'an is a miracle for the Arabs alone, and not for us.

And then there are certain dimensions in which the Qur'an is a miracle for both, for us and for the Arabs alike.

For example, in the scientific dimension the Qur'an is a miracle for us alone.

In the dimensions of style and influence, the Qur'an is a miracle for us and for the Arabs alike.

In the linguistic dimension, the Qur'an is a miracle for the Arabs alone and not for us, unless we study ancient Arabic.

Today I want us to experience another dimension of the Qur'an's miracle, the dimension that truly fascinates me. This is the linguistic dimension of the Qur'an. Remember, the Qur'an was revealed to a people who excelled in language.

What always fascinated me, and what drove me to learn ancient Arabic, was to understand exactly this: what was it that these Arabs saw in these Ayats, such that a disbeliever would hear the Prophet recite one single Ayat, or say one single sentence, and would recite the shahadah on the spot?

I remembered this incident while I was doing the session yesterday. A Christian priest comes to Rasul Allah with the intention of debating, with the intention of arguing. He wanted to show Rasul Allah (SA) how wrong he was about Islam.

Now when the intention is to debate, or simply to argue, a person never really listens to what is being said. The intention is never to understand or to learn, is it? The only reason such a person listens is to come up with a response against it. If you say, "The sky is blue," I will say, "Well, not at sunset! Not at midnight! Therefore you are wrong!" Because my entire goal is not to agree with you.

So this Christian priest approaches Rasul Allah (SA) and opens the conversation by saying: یا محمد! ما الاسلام؟ Oh Muhammad! What is Islam?

Rasul Allah looks at him and replies in a very gentle tone:

طيب الكلام وَأَفْشُوا السَّلامَ و إطعام الطعام، وَصَلُّوا بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّاسُ نِيَامٌ

That is all he says. Tears begin to flow from the priest's eyes. He starts to weep. He recites the shahadah right there.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
Now this is amazing to me. This representative of his religion goes to Rasul Allah not to learn but to argue. Rasul Allah says these few words, and he accepts Islam on the spot. I want you to pause for a moment and imagine how powerful these words must have been for that priest. And Rasul Allah did not even say something extremely profound or earth shattering. He simply gave a very simple answer.

When asked what Islam is, all he said was...

طيب الكلام — Islam is saying kind words; وَأَفْشُوا السَّلامَ — and spreading peace; و إطعام الطعام — feeding the hungry; and وَصَلُّوا بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّاسُ نِيَامٌ — and praying in the night while the world sleeps. He summarized the whole essence, the whole beauty of Islam in four things. He did not give the priest an hour-long lecture on Islam. Look, we are holding these weekly sessions on this very subject of "Islam," and they will probably continue for months, InshaAllah. But Rasul Allah did not say that to the priest. He did not schedule a weekly or a daily class with him. He simply answered with four simple things, and the priest accepted Islam. On the strength of that single sentence, the man gave up his religion and changed his entire way of life. Can you imagine the power of Rasul Allah's words, and the power of this message? SubhanAllah!

I also told you the story of Tufail Ibn Amar al-Dausi. I keep returning to it, because it is simply so remarkable, and so closely connected to the linguistic miracle of the Qur'an. Every time I tell you this story I get goosebumps. This man, Tufail Ibn Amar, was no ordinary man. He was an excellent, excellent poet, the leader of his tribe, and already prejudiced by what the mushrikeen and kuffar had told him about Rasul Allah. He challenged Rasul Allah: یا محمد! ما عندک؟ What do you have? Show me what you have. And Rasul Allah (SA) responded with a single verse. Not a long speech. Just one verse:

أِنَّ الحَمدَ لِی اللہَ أحمَدَہُ وَ أستَعِینَہُ وَ أُومِنُ بِہِ وَ أتَوَکَّلُ عَلَیہِ ۔ مَن یَّھدِہِ اللہُ فَلاَ مُضِلَّ لَہ وَ مَن یَّضِلَّ لَہُ فَلاَ ھَادِیَ لَہ

And Tufail Ibn Amar began to weep, and begged Rasul Allah to bring him into Islam. He did not go home to think it over. He did not say, "Wait, wait, wait! You know what, this is rather heavy material. Let me take it home, let me think about it, let me speak with my wife, discuss it with the members of my tribe, let me weigh the pros and cons, let me get back to you on this." No! He accepted Islam on the spot.

If someone hands me a million dollars with no strings attached, I am not going to deliberate over it. I will say, "Thank you! See you!" before he has a chance to change his mind. Right? Or will I say, "Oh, you know what, let me think about it, let me discuss it with my wife"? Absolutely not. I will take the money and go, because the man has just made me an offer I cannot refuse.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
So the million dollar question is this: what was in these verses that was so miraculous to the Arabs, that brought these disbelievers to their knees instantly? What was in these verses that made them an offer they simply could not refuse? That is the linguistic dimension of these miracles. And that is why we spent so much time building up to this point, understanding the mindset of the ancient Arab, so that we can truly understand what they saw and heard when Rasul Allah recited these verses to them.

So this dimension, the linguistic dimension of the Qur'an, rests on several things. I will speak about only two of them today, InshaAllah Ta'ala.

1. The first is the precision in the order of the words.
2. The second is the precision in the choice of the words.

First the order of the words, second the choice of the words. Arabic is a very rich language. Can someone tell me what we mean when we say that a certain language is very rich, or poor?

What does that mean?

5/6/15, 11:08:46 AM: Nabila Lateef: The Arabic dictionary has many names for the lion, as follows — the lion, when he sits in his den with his legs folded, is called Asad; and that same Asad, when he comes out of his den and walks about, is called Zargham; and when Zargham, while walking about, fixes his attention on some place, he is called Ghazanfar; and when Ghazanfar, roaring, walks away from his den, he is called Zaigham; and when Zaigham pounces on his prey, he is called Hamza; and when Hamza holds the prey in his grip so tightly that it cannot breathe properly, he is called Abbas; and when Abbas tears his prey into pieces, he is called Haider...

5/6/15, 11:14:24 AM: Salma Shafique: Very interesting.. thank you Nabila

In Arabic, for any given word there are dozens of synonyms. Dozens of synonyms. Each one carries a slight difference, like a gradient. Suppose you are planning to paint your room and you go to Home Depot for a color swatch. For the color red there are so many gradients, each with a slight difference in shade, and each with its own unique name, correct? Every word in Arabic works the same way.

For example, there are eight words for falling asleep.

نوم، سُبات، سکون، رقاد، کری، ھجوع، ضجع

And the differences between them are these: one is deep sleep; one is being almost asleep; one is for when your eyes are open but your mind is asleep; one is for when you are asleep but can still hear people; another is sleep when you are not lying down flat; one is sleep with a dream in it; one is sleep without a dream in it.

Notice that I needed a whole phrase to describe some of these words, while Arabic has just one word for each of them. This is what I mean when I say that... when the Arabs contended with one another in competition, they would notice a wrong word placed in a given context, and then they would use that against their opponent. Even we do this to some extent. When you listen to a friend speak, if you notice the wrong word used in a sentence, you will correct him. But they would do this to the highest degree, because in Arabic there is a word for every emotion, and for every intensity of that emotion.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
They have so many words simply to describe a farmer. A word for when he is planting the seed, a word for when he has planted the seed, a word for when he is taking the seed out, a word for when he is watering the plant. And all these words are used just to say "farmer."

مزارع، کافر، فلاح، ملتزم

All these words mean farmer... Yes, a farmer is called "Kaafir" in Arabic, because he hides the seed in the ground. The seed was apparent, visible to the eye, but the farmer hides it in the ground... just as a disbeliever hides the truth even though it is apparent... So the word for disbeliever, Kaafir, is in fact the word used for "farmer."

So we shall see that the miracle of Islam lies in the choice of the words used to describe things that are merely uttered in passing. These words are recited casually, like a flow, without any deliberate planning of where each word is placed. Yet the surgical precision they contain cannot be duplicated, even when you sit down and try to write them, let alone in speech. Even ordinary sentences are delivered with words that turn them into a miracle. The very manner in which he speaks of the matter becomes, in itself, uniquely miraculous.

And another thing that is so remarkable is how consistent the Qur'an is in the choice, and in the order, of these words. It is not as though this order exists in only some of the verses...

The more you study this book, the more consistently you will find this precision. So let us set the stage for this discussion before we speak of the miracle itself.

Has anyone here ever given a speech? A speech you had to deliver at school or in your profession, where you had to stand before an audience and convey an important point. Tell me very quickly about that speech — what was it about? Tell me about the preparation you had to go through to put that speech together. Did you write it down? Did you go back and edit what you had first written? Why did you edit it — for eloquence, for a better choice of words? Did you read it again and again, and each time you read it, did you make changes to it? When did you feel satisfied? When you read it through and could think of nothing more to change. And if you looked at that material again today, do you think you would still make changes to it?

Now, you said you wrote this speech down and edited it several times, correct? If you had been made to give this speech on the spot, without preparation and without editing, would it have been the very same speech you delivered after preparation? Would it have carried the same force? Of course not. Why is that?

It is because when you and I speak, we organize our thoughts. When I came to this session, I organized my thoughts beforehand. I said to myself: first I will speak about this, then about that, and then about the other. I even have these points written out in front of me. But you and I are incapable of organizing our words on the basis of what we are going to say later.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
We cannot arrange our words according to what is still to come. We can organize our thoughts, but not our words, when we are speaking without preparation. In writing we can do it. If I am preparing a speech on paper, I can set down my thoughts first and then organize my words. I can have an entire editorial process in place. I can return to the text again and again and keep rephrasing my sentences. But I cannot do this while I am speaking. Do you understand? Do you agree?

Now, is the Qur'an a written tradition or an oral tradition? An oral tradition. And we know that when the revelation came upon the Messenger of God, he would immediately begin reciting these verses in a flow, one verse after another, until the entire passage had been delivered. It was not that he would wait for the whole revelation to descend upon him, then ask for a sheet of paper, set his thoughts down, then organize his words, and go over the material again and again to make sure it was eloquent and that the right words had been used. When we examine history, we see there was no editorial process whatsoever. As the light of revelation came down upon him, he turned it into words. Is that not so? And there was not even a fixed hour for the revelation. It would simply come at any time of the day. He had no way of preparing in advance for it.

Have you ever heard that he spoke a verse and then changed it? Did he ever say: you know, that did not sound right, let me change it? Or: that is not quite what I meant to say, strike that out? Or: I could have said that better, let me try again? No. We see none of that. Not a single instance in which he ever said such a thing. Twenty-three years of Qur'anic revelation, no editorial process, and never a verse revoked unless God Himself revoked it by another verse. Twenty-three years!

We could not do this for twenty-three days! If I had these sessions written out before me, I would edit, amend, and rearrange the words I use without mercy. Because I want them to land! I want them to move the people listening to me. But notice what happens at the end of a session, when we come to the questions and answers: how many times have I said, "That is not what I meant"? Well, if that is not what you meant, why did you say it? Because I had no editorial process in place. When a person speaks spontaneously, the most he can do is organize his thoughts, not his words. Do you all follow? Any questions?

6:151
وَلَا تَقْتُلُوٓا۟ أَوْلَدَكُم مِّنْ إِمْلَقٍۢ ۖ نَّحْنُ نَرْزُقُكُمْ وَإِيَّاهُمْ

17:31
وَلَا تَقْتُلُوٓا۟ أَوْلَدَكُمْ خَشْيَةَ إِمْلَقٍۢ ۖ نَّحْنُ نَرْزُقُهُمْ وَإِيَّاكُمْ ۚ

In the old days (دور جاھلیۃ) — and in truth even today — parents used to kill their unborn children because of poverty. They did not have enough food for themselves, and so they could not afford to feed one more mouth; poverty drove them to kill their own children. In both of these verses God addresses such parents and commands them not to kill their children out of poverty, yet with a subtle difference between the two.

In the first verse He says: Do not kill your children because of poverty; We provide for you all (the parents) and for them (the children).
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
In the second verse He says: Do not kill your children out of fear of poverty; We provide for them (the children) and for you all (the parents).

In the first verse, whose provision does God mention first? The parents! And after them, whose? The children.

In the second verse, whose provision does God mention first? The children! And after them, whose? The parents.

Now, what difference does that make? Parents first and children after, or children first and parents after — it is the same thing, is it not?

Let us see why it is not.

When God says do not kill your children because of poverty, does the poverty already exist? Yes, it does. They do not have enough food for themselves, and that is why they are killing the children. So God addresses the parents first: do not kill your children because of the state you are in now. I will provide for you first, and then I will provide for your children as well.

In the second verse, God speaks of the fear of poverty. Does fear belong to the present or to the future? To the future! This means the parents have their provision for the present moment; what they are anxious about is the future. And who is going to join the family in the future? The children! So when He speaks of the fear of poverty, of provision in time to come, tied to children yet to come, He mentions the children first and the parents after. He says: do not be afraid, do not worry about the children who are coming in the future; We will provide for them, and not for them alone, but for you as well. SubhanAllah!

Do you see how words that are yet to be said, further on, shape the arrangement of the words at the very beginning, before those later words are ever delivered? We human beings have no such capacity when we speak, because we can organize only our thoughts, not our words.

To us, "I worked really hard" and "I really worked hard" are the same thing. There is no difference. Even when we write, we are not that sensitive.

But the Qur'an was not sent down as a written word. It was sent down as a spoken word. These verses passed through no editorial process, and yet we find this astonishing perfection in the way the words are arranged in relation to what is still to come in the sentence. And this kind of perfection, this kind of precision, is found consistently throughout the whole of the Qur'an.

The Arabs noticed it the moment they heard it. They detected this precision, for they were, after all, masters of this language themselves. They understood that, as human beings, they were simply not capable of such perfection in speech delivered on the spot. So they knew that this could not be the word of a man.

Let us look at another instance.

17:96

قُلْ كَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ شَهِيدًۢا بَيْنِى وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ بِعِبَادِهِ خَبِيرًۢا بَصِيرًۭا

29:52

كَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ بَيْنِى وَبَيْنَكُمْ شَهِيدًۭا ۖ يَعْلَمُ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ بِٱلْبَطِلِ وَكَفَرُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ أُو۟لَٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْخَسِرُونَ

The word شَهِيدًۭا means "witness." It is also one of the ninety-nine attributes of Allah, so keep that in mind.

Now let us first go over the highlighted portion.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
The first verse says: Allah is enough as a witness between me and you. Who is speaking this verse? The Messenger of Allah. So the "me" refers to whom? To the Messenger of Allah, and the "you" refers to us, or to whoever is listening. Correct?

The second verse says: Allah is enough between me and you as a witness. Again the "me" refers to the Messenger of Allah and the "you" refers to us. Correct?

So the placement of which word differs in the two verses? Only in the highlighted portion: the word Shaheedan. If you take this word out, both verses would read the same, correct? In the first verse, then, the Messenger of Allah uses the word Shaheedan first and then says "me and you," while in the second verse he says "me and you" first and then uses the word "Shaheedan." Is that clear to everyone?

Now, what difference does it make? They both mean the same thing, do they not?

The point is that the Qur'an is hypersensitive, supersensitive, to context. When the Messenger of Allah spoke, he arranged the words like a beautiful piece of architecture. You cannot move a single brick out of its place; if you do, its perfection is lost forever.

Now I want you to examine the latter part of these verses, the text that comes after the highlighted portion.

You will see that in the first verse Allah closes the verse speaking about Himself. He says إِنَّهُ كَانَ بِعِبَادِهِ خَبِيرًۢا بَصِيرًۭا. Innahoo refers to Allah Himself; He says that Allah has complete knowledge of His slaves. Who has complete knowledge of His slaves? Allah.

You will see that in the latter part of the second verse He speaks about the people: أُو۟لَٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْخَسِرُونَ. They are the ones who are the losers. Who are the losers? The people.

So the first verse ends speaking about Allah, and the second verse ends speaking about people. In the verse that ends speaking about Allah Himself, the Messenger of Allah uses the attribute "Shaheedan" first and then refers to the people. But in the second verse, which ends speaking about people, the Messenger of Allah refers to the people first and then uses Allah's attribute Shaheedan. Subhan Allah!

Once again, words that are about to be spoken in the future exert an influence on how the words at the beginning of the sentence are arranged. This kind of perfection is simply not possible in spontaneous speech.

And the Qur'an is, without any doubt, a spontaneous address that Allah delivers through His Messenger (peace be upon him) — Allahu Akbar!

Now let us look at the perfection in the CHOICE of words in a different verse. We all know the difference between the past tense and the present tense. The Qur'an uses all three tenses. It uses the past tense, the present tense, and of course the future tense. When I say "KILLED," which tense is that? When I say "KILLS," what tense is that? In Surah al-Nisa, Allah says:

4:92

وَمَن قَتَلَ مُؤْمِنًا خَطَـًۭٔا فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍۢ مُّؤْمِنَةٍۢ وَدِيَةٌۭ مُّسَلَّمَةٌ إِلَىٰٓ أَهْلِهِ

And whoever killed a believer by mistake, then he should free another Muslim as recompense and pay the blood money to the relatives of the deceased.

Is "killed" past tense or present tense? It is past tense. So the past tense is used with mistake.

4:93

وَمَن يَقْتُلْ مُؤْمِنًۭا مُّتَعَمِّدًۭا فَجَزَآؤُهُۥ جَهَنَّمُ خَلِدًۭا فِيهَا

And whoever kills a believer on purpose, his recompense is hellfire. He will live in it forever.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
Is "kills" past tense or present tense? It is present tense. And here we see that the tense is tied to intent, to deliberation. The past tense is associated with mistake, and the present tense is associated with intent.

Now notice that this occurs within the same passage. You would expect Allah to keep to a single tense. After all, what difference does it make?

وَمَن قَتَلَ مُؤْمِنًا خَطَـًۭٔا

وَمَن قَتَلَ مُؤْمِنًا مُّتَعَمِّدًۭا

And whoever killed by mistake; and whoever killed on purpose — the same thing. But no! When He mentions killing by mistake, He uses the past tense, and when He mentions killing on purpose, He uses the present tense. Do you know why? Because the past tense happened only once.

I WENT to the Muslim Conference in New York. What does that mean? One time!

I GO to the Microsoft Conference in New York. What does that mean? I go every year.

So in the first verse, Allah Ta'ala speaks of a man who killed by mistake, and He uses the past tense. How many times do you kill by mistake? Just once! You commit such a killing only once. If a second time you say, "Oh, a mistake again," then... So the one who kills on purpose is a perpetrator, and he deserves punishment, because the chances are what? That he will do it again — hence the present tense. Hence the continuity. The past tense with killing, because it is accidental, and it carries no continuity. The present tense with killing, because it is deliberate, and it carries continuity. Subhan Allah!

Even in the tense. Not merely in the choice of words, but even in the tense of the words there is such fine sensitivity, and it exists in no other literary form. And you see, all of this is completely lost when we do not become students of which language? Qur'anic Arabic and ancient Arabic. Qur'anic Arabic is the perfected form, the very summit of ancient Arabic.
body.topic_title_en: The Linguistic Miracle of Divine Order

body.text_en:
Praise be to Allah. We have at last reached the final session on this subject of the miracles of the Qur'an. In the previous session, I showed you the astonishing symmetry in the structure of the Qur'an, how each surah is built as a palindrome. Today I wish to carry this one step further and show you this perfect symmetry at a still finer level. I am somewhat concerned about the time, because I have a great deal to cover, yet I do not want to rush through this, for I want us all truly to delight in this remarkable beauty of the Qur'an's symmetry.

Allah says in Surah al-Muddaththir, which is the seventy-fourth surah of the Qur'an. He opens the surah by saying:

یا أیھا المدثر — O you who covers himself,
قم فأنذر — Rise and warn the people,
و ربک فکبر — and constantly glorify your Lord.

What I want to draw everyone's attention to today is the sentence و ربک فکبر, which means: constantly glorify your Lord.

You can see that it begins with the letter و. In this context, think of this letter as a capital letter. When you begin a new sentence, you start it with a capital letter, and و in Arabic works in the same way. There are many uses of the letter و — more than twenty-one of them — but here let us simply regard it as a capital letter placed at the beginning of a new sentence. And the remainder of the verse says: ربک فکبر — always declare the glory of your Lord!

Let me tell you something about the Arabic language. In English, you have a singular and you have a plural. What is the plural of house? What is the plural of mouse? In Arabic, you do not merely have a plural; you have a singular, a plural, and then a super-plural. The plural of house in English is houses, but you do not have a super-plural, housessss. You have car, and then cars, but you do not have carsessss. In Arabic, however, you do.

So the word کَبِّر in the verse is a super-plural. It comes from the root word کِبر, or کبیر, which means big, immense, or glorious — also the word اکبر, as in اللہ اکبر. The superlative form of the word کبیر is کَبِّر, which means something that is glorious, or magnificent beyond measure. And here it is used as an imperative verb (فعل أمر), meaning that Allah is in fact commanding His Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) to glorify his Lord constantly.

Now, in the previous session, what was one of the attributes of a circle that I mentioned? What does a circle represent? Continuity, correct? And this sentence, ربک فکبر, commands the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) to glorify your Lord constantly. Is this clear so far?

So now let us break these two words down into their letters:

ر ب ک ف ک ب ر

What do you notice about the structure of this sentence? It is a palindrome! But consider the content: constantly declare the glory of your Lord! Does something not have to be in a loop in order to be constant? And when something reads forward the same way it reads backward, is that not an endless loop?

So the words used to represent the continuous, the never-ending, the constant, the everlasting glory of Allah are stated as a palindrome, in a circular composition. Glory be to Allah! How does one do that with spoken text? Allah is commanding His Prophet to remind us that no matter where we look, no matter in which direction we look — north to south, south to north, east to west, west to east — everywhere we will find that Allah is being constantly glorified by all of His creation!

And He states this never-ending cycle of Allah's glory in a circular form! SubhanAllah! Spoken text... no editorial process in place... revealed in passages over twenty-three years... and such incredible symmetry! SubhanAllah!

Faizah, you know Surah Yaseen, right? Allah ta'ala says in Surah Yaseen:

لَا ٱلشَّمْسُ يَنۢبَغِى لَهَآ أَن تُدْرِكَ ٱلْقَمَرَ وَلَا ٱلَّيْلُ سَابِقُ ٱلنَّهَارِ ۚ وَكُلٌّۭ فِى فَلَكٍۢ يَسْبَحُونَ

In this ayah, Allah speaks of all the heavenly bodies. He says: It is not permissible for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day, but each, in an orbit, is rotating. Each has been assigned an orbit, and they are rotating in their orbits! What is He speaking about? Planets in space? Revolving and rotating? When something rotates or revolves, what geometric shape is it making? Circular. Now, when something is moving in a circle, does it repeat itself? Meaning, will it reach the same spot again during its motion? Yes, it will, and it will continue to do so over and over and over again! That is why we see that the planets are in a loop, right?

The first thing I want to present to you about this ayah is that it is a miracle in the scientific dimension as well. For the longest time it was believed that the sun was the center of the universe. But Allah said, fourteen hundred years ago, that the sun too has an orbit. And if it has an orbit, it cannot be the center, because by definition a center cannot move.

Now, the sentence in which Allah states this circular motion is where He says:

كُلٌّۭ فِى فَلَكٍۢ يَسْبَحُونَ

All the heavenly bodies are rotating in their orbits. فَلَكٍۢ means "orbit," and يَسْبَحُونَ means "rotation." I want you to keep that in mind, all right? It is really important.

Now let us break كُلٌّۭ فِى فَلَكٍۢ into its letters: ک ل ف ی ف ل ک + یسبحون. First of all, do you see that this is a palindrome? Now, a palindrome is a circular composition, which means it must have a center. What is the center letter? So can I say that all the other letters are rotating around the letter Ya? Now check this out: what word did Allah use for rotation? یسبحون. What does that word start with? SubhanAllah! The letters are rotating around the very word that Allah uses to say rotation, یسبحون! SubhanAllah! How do you do that? How can human beings come up with this kind of symmetry in spoken text?

Those of you who read the Quran regularly must have noticed that in most ayats Allah closes the verse by naming two of His names:

غفور الرحیم، عزیزٌ حکیم ، عزیزٌ انْتقام،

You will see that Allah mentions two of His names many, many times in the Quran. It is always a pair of names that is used. But if you look at the first ayah of Surah Al-Jumuah, there is something unique here. Tell me what is unique about this ayah.

يُسَبِّحُ لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ٱلْمَلِكِ ٱلْقُدُّوسِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ

Do you notice something different here? Allah uses four names at the end of this ayah. It is unique, is it not, compared to all the other ayats? First I want to go over the meanings of these names with you. I want you to take notes as I tell them to you. I am going to ask you to repeat them back to me.

The first is Malik. Malik means the king. It means what?

Then comes Al-Quddoos. It means the perfectly pure, and you may also say the source of all purity.

Then Al-Azeez. It means the Ultimate Authority.

Finally there is Al-Hakeem. Al-Hakeem has many meanings. I will share only one here; for our purpose it means the wise.

Repeat.

Now, who is the first ayah speaking about?

يُسَبِّحُ لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ٱلْمَلِكِ ٱلْقُدُّوسِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ

Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah. He is the King, the Pure, the Authority, the Wise.

Who is this ayat speaking about? Allah!

Who is the second ayah speaking about?

هُوَ ٱلَّذِى بَعَثَ فِى ٱلْأُمِّيِّۦنَ رَسُولًۭا مِّنْهُمْ يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ

It is He who has sent among the unlettered a Messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and wisdom.

Who is this ayat speaking about? Rasul Allah.

This too is one of the most beautiful ayats of the Quran, because in this single ayah Allah has summarized the entire Seerah of the Prophet (SA). The entire Seerah. In this ayah Allah speaks of the four steps His beloved Messenger, Rasul Allah (SA), took in order to transform society. He took four steps:

يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَتِهِۦ

وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ

وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ

وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ

Hmmm. Where did we hear four before? How many names of Allah were mentioned? And His Messenger follows how many steps? Now let us take a step back, and let me give you something to think about.

Imagine you live in a time, let us say four thousand years ago. You have just bought your brand new donkey and you are taking it out for a ride, and as you travel you see that you are entering a brand new kingdom. How do you know you are entering a new kingdom? At the border, how would you know this? Through the signs of the kingdom! Flags? Statues! Monuments! Right? You notice soldiers who bear the mark of the king. You might notice a castle. You will see certain signs that this is a kingdom, or that this place has a king. You will notice the signs. Do you understand? A king is known by his signs and symbols. You will not know a king unless he is wearing a crown.

If he is wearing a T-shirt, you will not know he is a king. He has to be wearing his robe and a crown. If a king is living in a third-floor apartment, he is not a king. He can call himself royalty all he wants, but he is not really a king. He has to have a castle, a throne. These are all signs that you are dealing with a — ? A king! So the first point I want to make is that a king is known by his signs. What was the first name of Allah mentioned? Al-Malik! What does it mean? King! Allah says in the next verse that His messenger does four things. What is the first one? The first one is يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَتِهِۦ — he recites to the people the king's signs! How is a king known? By his signs! And the messenger tells the people his — signs! Do you notice his kingdom? You see those mountains over there? They are part of his kingdom! You see that sun over there? It is part of his kingdom! You see that moon in the night? It is part of his kingdom! That is how you know you are dealing with a king. You see the stars at night? That is the kingdom of Allah. He is known by His signs.

What was the second name of Allah in the first verse? Al-Quddoos! What did it mean? I forgot! The source of all purity. And what is the second thing the messenger does? وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ — he purifies them! He recites the king's signs to them, and he does what? Purifies them. Do you see a connection?

Now what was the third name of Allah? Al-Azeez! What did it mean? Ultimate authority! Where do laws come from? Laws come from an authority! In a house, the rules come from the parents; they do not come from the child, because the parents have what? Authority! In a classroom the rules come from the teacher; they do not come from the students, because the teacher has what? Authority! In a country, the rules come from the government! They come from the people who make the laws, they come from the courts, not from the common people, because who has the authority? The courts do! Laws come from the authority. Allah says وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ — He teaches them the book. And the word book in Arabic literature is used for "law," so it is like saying that He teaches them the — law! And law can only be given by the proper authority. Al-Azeez is the only one who can make al-Kitaab. You cannot make kitaab without al-Izza. You cannot have law without an authority. And, by the way, even in English literature we say the judge threw the book at him. That does not mean that the judge grew angry and opened his skull by throwing a fifteen-pound book at the plaintiff; it means that the judge used the full extent of the law against this person. He threw the book at him! Or if someone says I am going to do this by the book, what does that mean? I am going to do this according to the law. That is by the book. So Al-Azeez is the authority, and the messenger teaches the law dictated by the authority. وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ

What was the last name of Allah mentioned in this sequence? Al-Hakeem! The Wise! Allah says وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ — He teaches them wisdom! Where does wisdom come from? It comes from the wise! Four names of Allah in the first verse, four activities of the messenger in the next verse, and they are each correlated perfectly. And it took me twenty minutes to explain this to you, but the Messenger of Allah simply says it. He simply says it. What human being is able to think this way?

Consider this: I have just named four of Allah's attributes, so now I must uphold them with four steps, four verbs that correlate with those names in the very same order. Who is able to do that? It lies beyond human capability, and yet the Messenger of Allah brings forth these miracles spontaneously. SubhanAllah! We as Muslims read straight through these miracles without appreciating them; we read straight through these powerful observations without grasping what we have just read. And wallahee, if you do grasp it, you are left simply mesmerized. AllahuAkbar! You are left overwhelmed.

You see, when we create palindromes, what we have to take into consideration is "spelling." And when we take spelling into consideration, we have to compromise our content! But this ayah, even though it is a palindrome, does not compromise on its content one bit! Not only does Allah tell the Arabs about a reality that is being proven today, fourteen hundred years later; not only is He telling us about heavenly bodies rotating in a circle, in a loop; but He does it using words that are in a loop. He tells us with letters that are themselves in rotation, and they are rotating around the very letter that He uses to say the word rotation. AllahuAkbar!

This kalaam, this conversation, simply cannot get any more miraculous than this! Is the most intelligent, most eloquent human being in the world capable of doing this in speech? Can the smartest man on earth spontaneously spit out palindromes with such perfection, not only without compromising the content, but actually revealing its significance? SubhanAllah!

This content was recited to the people..... We are baffled even in the way it is spelled! Absolutely mesmerizing; absolutely stunning in the perfection of its form.

Yasmeen Hussain. My personal favorite — Ayat Al-Kursi. This single verse is made up of nine sentences. All right? Nine independent sentences coming together to form one single verse: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ. لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌۭ وَلَا نَوْمٌۭ. لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ. مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ. يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُم. وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍۢ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ. وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ. وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا. وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ.

So, nine sentences. Now, of course, you have already guessed it — this too is a palindrome. So we will simply go over the translation of each one of these symmetrically.

So we will compare the first with the last, the second with the second to last, the third with the seventh, and so on. Let us begin with the first and the last. The first one is ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ. This beautiful sentence ends with two of Allah's names. What are those two names? al-Hayy, the Living, and al-Qayyum, the source of all establishment, the source of all maintenance, the ever watchful. Qayyum carries many meanings. In essence, everything stands, exists, and is sustained because of Allah. So He does not only create; He also keeps watch over what He has made. If He only created and did not maintain, His creation would fall to ruin. And, naturally, one first creates and then maintains. So the Living comes first and the source of all maintenance comes second. ٱلْحَىُّ first and ٱلْقَيُّومُ second. Because He is the ultimate creator and He is the ultimate maintainer, what does that make Him? Now join this to the ninth sentence, وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ. And He is the lofty and the mighty. Lofty by virtue of creation, mighty by virtue of maintenance. Perfect symmetry.

********************************************************************************************************

Now let us look at the second sentence and the eighth. لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌۭ وَلَا نَوْمٌۭ. Drowsiness and sleep do not so much as touch Him. You children know what drowsiness means, do you not? It is that strange feeling you have during lectures in your classroom. That is drowsiness. Your eyes begin to close a little.
