You are not truly asleep, but you are just about ready to enter dreamland. That is what is called Sinah in Arabic, and the step that comes after it is Naum, which means deep sleep. First comes Sinah, then comes Naum. These are things that belong to creation. Creation grows tired, begins to feel drowsy, and eventually falls asleep. Before we speak of its paired sentence, I want to tell you something about security. Security guards have the hardest job in the world. Why? Because it is the most tedious job on the planet. What do you always find the security guard doing in the movies? He is either staring at the closed-circuit television monitors, and it is the very same picture for twelve hours. He is staring at the battered, third-hand blue Toyota parked in one spot — not even a Porsche or a Lamborghini, not even a Mercedes-Benz. Or he is sitting on a chair, staring into space for hours upon hours. It is truly the most thrilling work you could ever do in your life, especially if you are a college student. So what tends to happen when you are guarding something? You begin to feel sleepy. You begin to grow tired. That is why, in the end, what you always find every security guard doing is what? Sleeping. But Allah says in the eighth sentence, وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا. Guarding the heavens and the earth does not exhaust Allah. What does guarding bring? Drowsiness and sleep. Sinah and Naum. But Allah says, not Me. I guard all My creation, yet I am never exhausted. Perfect symmetry.

********************************************************************************************************

What is the third verse? لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ. He owns whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth.

Before I can explain this connection to you, you must understand the difference between two Arabic words, مالک and مَلِک, because it will let you appreciate these verses as nothing else can. مالک means an owner. مَلِک means a king. Is there a difference between a king and an owner? Yes. You are the owner of your pen, but you do not say that you are the royal sovereign king of this pen. That would make very little sense. Do you follow? People can be the owners of small things. You can own a car, you can own a pen, you can own a phone, a computer. But you cannot own a kingdom. A king is the one who has a kingdom.

Here is another difference. Ownership is a matter of property, but a kingdom is not specifically a matter of property. You are not a king over a tree, nor the king over a piece of land. You are a king over all the people who live in that land. A kingdom is about governing people; ownership is about controlling objects. There is a great difference between the two. Ownership belongs to the small scale, whereas a kingdom belongs to the large scale.

Allah says, لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ. To Me belongs the ownership of everything that is in the heavens and everything that is in the earth. What is this verse about, ownership or kingship? It is about ownership. So every single thing is owned by Allah.

Now let us look at the third-to-last sentence, وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ. His throne extends over the heavens and the earths. Here Allah speaks of His throne. Who has a throne? A king has a throne. So when He speaks of His throne, is He speaking of ownership or of kingship? He is speaking of His kingdom. You see, then, that the previous sentence was about ownership, and this sentence is about kingship, the two together completing the picture. For if you are only an owner, you are not a king; and if you are only a king, you are not necessarily an owner. You can be the king of an island, but does that mean you own every house on that island? No. You may own your own house, but are you the king of that house? No. Yet Allah is not only the owner of all things; He is also the king of all things. He is مالک, and He is also مَلِک. The attribute of Allah as مالک is stated by لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ, and the attribute of Allah as مَلِک is stated by وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ.

Now the next one, مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ. Who is there who will come and make شفاعۃ with Allah unless He grants permission? Let us begin with what the word شفاعۃ means. The translation I sent you uses a large English word, intercession. Let us make it simple. شفاعۃ means that you have connections; you have people. It means that you are about to lose your job, but your uncle is the manager of the company, and he comes and says, no, no, no, he is with me, he is a good man. That is شفاعۃ. Your father is the chief of staff of a hospital, especially if you are in Pakistan, and so you are taken into the emergency or casualty unit even if you have nothing but a headache. You are called in first. That is شفاعۃ. The man with the broken ribs can wait. After all, they will still be broken half an hour later, will they not?

So Allah says, on the Day of Judgment, who is the one who would dare to make شفاعۃ

Who would dare intercede except by MY permission! That means only those He selects can make شفاعۃ. Not everyone. You understand? Allah is about to throw someone into hell, and I cannot simply step forward and say, "Wait, wait, wait, Allah, he is with me!" No. He will throw me in along with him. So no one will have the right to make شفاعۃ on behalf of anyone else except the one He chooses. And the one He has chosen is His beloved messenger, Muhammad Mustafa (peace be upon him). We beg Allah to let us all qualify for his intercession on that Day, because Allah says no one else will come for you on the Day of Judgment. It is not going to happen. So this verse means that no one has any authority unless Allah grants it to them. The only exception is by Allah's permission. If Allah gives permission, someone may intercede; otherwise, no one can say anything on that Day. Is everyone clear about that?

Now let us look at its pair. وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍۢ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ They know nothing, they have no power, they encompass nothing of His knowledge, إِلَّا, except, بِمَا شَآءَ, of what He wills. Both statements are about the exceptions that belong to Allah alone. In the first, no one can intercede except the one who has Allah's permission. In the second, no one can gain anything from His knowledge except the one He chooses. SubhanAllah!

Now what is left? The center statement. يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُم He says He knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them. He knows that everything coming before this statement is in perfect correlation, perfect symmetry, with everything coming after His statement. AllahuAkbar! Right in the middle He is saying, I know what is before and I know what is coming after. He makes this statement the center of the circle. The radius of one end will be equal to the radius of the other end. SubhanAllah! Who can speak like that? The way in which Rasul Allah delivers this message, who can do that?

Again, remember, we read the Quran as a book, but did Rasul Allah recite it that way? Did he say, look, sentence number one and nine, and two and eight, and three and seven, and four and six are in perfect correlation to the fifth sentence? No! This is spoken word. He was simply speaking the Quran. We are able to see these things only when they were put into writing. The Quran was so perfect even when it was delivered in speech!

When is there a greater chance of a mistake, when you write something or when you say something? When you say something! Once you have said it, it is very hard to take it back, especially if it is on YouTube! AllahuAkbar! But if you are writing a nasty email, before you hit send you can think about it and tone it down, you can rephrase things, and finally you just say Eid Mubarak and send it. You have a chance to take it back. But you cannot do that with the spoken word. When you say something, as soon as you have said it, you are done. There is no room to edit, no room to fix it. Allah did not reveal this Quran in writing; He revealed it in speech!

So this, AlHamdulillah, concludes our topic of the miracles of the Quran. This symmetrical miracle was the last one I wanted to show you. There are so many more verses structured this way, but InshaAllah, I hope I was able to deliver the most relevant ones.

And I greatly enjoyed sharing these miracles with you! AlHamdulillah! There is one thing I want to mention briefly about this symmetry of the Quran. Why did Allah choose a circle for the whole of His creation — the universe, its processes, the cycles of the prophets, the cycle of years, months, and weeks? Why did Allah choose this shape? As I said before, one of the attributes of a circle is continuity, so it was chosen to indicate the immense consistency of His nature. Can you imagine if we had a moody Allah (نعوذ باللہ)? We do not think about these things, but imagine for a moment if your day depended on how Allah was feeling that day. What if He were angry today? You know His powers, do you not? Imagine what He can do in a single instant. These are things we take completely for granted. We will speak about this a great deal more, InshaAllah, but one reason for this shape is to show the consistency of His beautiful nature.

Another reason is to indicate "LOVE," because a circle encompasses. What does a mother do when a child runs into her arms? She wraps her arms around the child, does she not? She encompasses the child in her love. The child feels safe and at peace in the mother's embrace. So safety is another reason for this shape. Notice how the circumference of a circle has no gaps in it. Once inside the circle, the child is completely protected by the love and mercy of Allah. That is why, in my first session, I mentioned that if Islam could be summarized in a single word, it would be LOVE! Everything is designed to reveal Allah's love for His creation. Yet we are made to believe that all He wants is to burn us in the fire.

But the circle also indicates justice. Notice how, no matter where you draw the radius, it is always equal. So even though He is a loving Allah, His love is grounded in justice. He loves with justice, and He is just with love. We do not subscribe to the Christian theology that God is nothing but love. In fact, even this belief of the Christians is a deviation from their own principles. The Bible clearly states that Allah is loving and merciful, but that He is also just. He will never commit injustice. So even we, as Muslims, should never forget this. Yes, He is nothing but Love, but that love includes justice, and so we should not take undue advantage of His love. Just because He is all love does not mean that He will not punish. He most certainly will, in order to establish His justice, but His mercy and love supersede everything. Even when He carries out justice, He does it with love. His love is at the root of every single action.

There are many other attributes of a circle, but for our discussion we will, InshaAllah, focus only on these. Now, we have looked at two consecutive Surahs coming together to form a perfect palindrome; now let us look at two consecutive ayats that come together to form a palindrome. Allah (سبحانہ و تعالی) says in Surah Al-Jumuah...

These are the first two ayats:

يُسَبِّحُ لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ٱلْمَلِكِ ٱلْقُدُّوسِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ

هُوَ ٱلَّذِى بَعَثَ فِى ٱلْأُمِّيِّۦنَ رَسُولًۭا مِّنْهُمْ يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ وَإِن كَانُوا۟ مِن قَبْلُ لَفِى ضَلَلٍۢ مُّبِينٍۢ

Ask Yasmeen to explain to everyone what a miracle is.

Another powerful dimension in the miraculousness of the Qur'an is the dimension of "imagination," in which the Qur'an challenges the powerful imaginations of the ancient Arabs. If you recall, we studied this in considerable detail in one of our early sessions. I showed you how the ancient Arabs possessed a very powerful imagination, far more powerful than the imaginations we have today. Do you remember the reason for this? Why were their imaginations so powerful? Because they had nothing, and so they had to imagine. We have no imagination, because everything we could possibly imagine has already been shown to us in science-fiction films. Our imagination, at best, comes from something we have either seen in a film or read in a book. Is that not so? The media has raised our imaginations visually to great heights, but the cost is that we have lost the power of imaginative creativity.

The Arabs, however, were surrounded by what? Desert. They had no natural resources of any kind: no waterfalls, no rainbows, no skyscrapers, no amusement parks, no games. Nothing. All they had was sand and mountains. Can you imagine what the conversation of two Arab friends spending time together in the desert in those days would have been like? One says, "My friend, have you been to that place in the desert? The sand looks so wonderful there; the dust tastes sweet." And the other replies, "No, the sand in this other place looks far more magnificent." Because that was all they had: sand and dust everywhere, and absolutely nothing else. So when you have nothing to look at, you begin to build things up in your imagination. And because they had the gift of language, because they possessed the immense power of articulation through prose and poetry, they would actually paint the images in their minds using what? Words. Prose and poetry.

Do you remember the story I told you of that poor man who has nothing to eat in his house, and who recites poetry to his wife about how generous he is? What was the image he used to express his immense generosity? Do you remember that image? Something to do with a house and rain?

السَّیلُ حَربٌ عَلی مَکانِ العَالِی

Heavy rain does not get along with a house that stands on top of a hill.

Now, to truly understand this dimension of the miraculous, there is one thing you must understand and keep in mind about Arabic eloquence, and it is this saying that the ancient Arabs had:

الخیر الکلام من قل و دل

The best speech is that which is short and precise, short and to the point. If someone used many words to explain something, that was considered a weakness.

So this extremely poor poet, speaking of his generosity, says:

السَّیلُ حَربٌ عَلی مَکانِ العَالِی

Heavy rain does not get along with a house that stands on top of a hill.

Now, what does a house on top of a hill have to do with heavy rain? And what in the world does that have to do with generosity?

For those of you who were not present at that session: picture in your mind a house on top of a hill. And what is happening? Heavy rain. When it rains, does the water remain on top of the hill, or does it gather in a pool at the bottom of the hill? At the bottom, of course.

So he says that rizq, or provision, comes from the sky. And there are two kinds of people in the world: the lofty and the lowly. Those who are near to God, and those who are worldly. If your house is on top of the hill, are you not near to the sky? Near to God?

So the water does not stay with me — that is, the provision does not remain with me. I receive it first, but I do not keep it for myself. I keep passing it down to the lowly people. So the people who are rich are in truth poor, and I am the lofty one, handing them my provisions. And he says all of this by saying what? السَّیلُ حَربٌ عَلی مَکانِ العَالِی Five words. You see how short and precise his words are. Heavy rain does not get along with a house atop a hill. It is concise, it is short; it is a riddle that challenges the imagination. It is all of these things in five words.

So these Arabs were truly devoted to speech that was precise and to the point. They were not like certain people we know, who will talk and talk and talk to explain the very simplest of things. "Oh, last night, I used this marvelous invention that lets me rise to the top of a building one step at a time. I felt as though I were walking toward the sky, one step at a time." My friend, you just took the stairs. Move on.

So the Arabs spoke in these riddles. They wanted you to imagine what was being said. They would not simply state it outright. And if you did not understand it, they would mock you. They would ridicule you: "Hah, ajam — the mute one." So this was the kind of sensitivity to language and power of imagination that they enjoyed.

In those days there were storytellers who would narrate amazing works of fiction. People would find a pleasant, scenic spot, where they could enjoy the view of the sand — which is to say, more or less anywhere in the desert — and they would gather around such a man, who would then begin telling them a story, stop at a crucial point, and say, "We will continue this next week. Please tune in for another episode of Jahiliyya poetry, next week at the same time." And the people would not only come again, they would bring more people with them, because these storytellers had such astonishing imaginations. And, as you now know, every Arab had a powerful imagination. So they were not easily impressed by anyone. But when someone came along who could challenge their imagination — oh, he would be treated like a god among mortals.

And then, forty years later, someone as ordinary, someone as unknown, someone who was very nearly a nobody among the people of Mecca, someone known to possess no poetic skill, someone known for forty years to have no eloquence, comes forth with these words — words that are prose, not poetry, yet sound like poetry. Words that challenged them with an imagination so far beyond their own imaginations, so powerful in their images, in their analogies, in their comparisons, in their language, in their precision and perfection in the choice of their words, in the placement of their words, that they were left utterly incapacitated. These words of the Messenger of Allah (SA) brought the Arabs to their knees.

So I have two examples for you. We will see if we can manage both today, God willing. Allah says in Surah al-Hajj: حُنَفَآءَ لِلَّهِ غَيْرَ مُشْرِكِينَ بِهِۦ ۚ وَمَن يُشْرِكْ بِٱللَّهِ فَكَأَنَّمَا خَرَّ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَتَخْطَفُهُ ٱلطَّيْرُ أَوْ تَهْوِى بِهِ ٱلرِّيحُ فِى مَكَانٍۢ سَحِيقٍۢ

All right. حُنَفَآءَ لِلَّهِ غَيْرَ مُشْرِكِينَ بِهِ There are those who are devoted solely to Allah, without committing any shirk with Him whatsoever. Shirk, in Arabic, means to ascribe partners to someone.

So, in this context, a partner to Allah. وَمَن يُشْرِكْ بِٱللَّهِ — and whoever commits shirk with Allah, فَكَأَنَّمَا خَرَّ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ — it is then as though he had fallen from the sky. I want you to hold on to these images that Allah uses for His example. فَكَأَنَّمَا خَرَّ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ — it is as though he had fallen from the sky. فَتَخْطَفُهُ ٱلطَّيْرُ — the birds are snatching pieces off of him; the birds are making their meal of this man, they are eating him. أَوْ تَهْوِى بِهِ ٱلرِّيحُ فِى مَكَانٍۢ سَحِيقٍۢ — and then a wind is blowing him away to a distant, unmapped place.

There are three parts to this example. The first part: a man is falling from the sky. The second part: the birds are eating him. The third part: the wind is blowing him off to a far-off place. With this, Allah gives the example of a mushrik, one who commits shirk.

Now, consider that the whole purpose of an example is to make the subject easy — to make it simple, to make it approachable, to make it easy to understand. But the purpose of an example, most of all, is to present something the audience can relate to. If the example is harder to understand than the subject itself, then it rather defeats the whole point, does it not?

And here Allah is saying that the person who commits shirk is like the one who falls from a sky, and then the birds make their meal of him, and then a wind blows him away. What does that have to do with shirk? This is not an example we can relate to. There were no planes in those days; how would one fall out of the sky? And not only that: the birds are feeding off of him, and the winds are blowing him away to some unmapped place. The thing is, the man is dead. Who cares whether he is blown to an unknown place or a familiar one? What difference does it make? The man is still dead.

The reason we have difficulty understanding this example is that we are thinking of it in terms of proper Arabic, not Ancient Arabic. One thing I did not tell you about Ancient Arabic is that it has its own expressions, its own idioms. An idiom in English is, "That is cool." If you said this to an Ancient Arab, he would say, "Really? Do you know where you are? Have you been in the sun too long? This is the desert! What are you talking about? There is no such thing as cool here! This is Arabia! It is not cool — it is scorching!" So he would not think of the words "That is cool" the way you young people do. And you young people are amusing. Two children come back after watching the very same basketball match. One says, "That was so cool!" The other says, "That was so hot!" — and they both mean the same thing, do they not? So expressions change.

The Qur'an, in various places, uses the expressions of the Ancient Arabs. Did these expressions change over time? Yes, of course. You have to understand that if you take these expressions literally, you have lost the meaning. It is not literal. If someone tells you there is no use crying over spilt milk, you do not say, "I did not spill any milk — I lost my job!" If you do, you have missed the point, because that is an expression.

So Allah compares a mushrik to a man falling from the sky. These are most of the Arabs of that time, who were idol worshippers. They did not believe in an afterlife. They believed that the only thing they had to look forward to was death — that there was nothing after that. Game over.

So if death is the only thing that lies before you, what then becomes most important? Your legacy — what you leave behind, how people remember you. That was all they had to hold on to. They did not believe in the resurrection, nor in the sun and the moon colliding. They would say — إِنْ هِىَ إِلَّا حَيَاتُنَا ٱلدُّنْيَا نَمُوتُ وَنَحْيَا وَمَا نَحْنُ بِمَبْعُوثِينَ — there is nothing except this worldly life; we live and we die, and there is nothing more. I do not understand this talk of a hereafter!

Allah addresses this obstinate idolater and seeks to show him how dreadful the idolater is in the sight of Allah, using an image that they themselves understood. Allah is speaking to this particular audience in terms it could grasp. Anyone who has studied the Arabs of that age knows that they were warriors, immensely proud of their tribal warfare. Today we have sports, and we take pride in our teams; their pride was in their battles. The worst thing a man could do, the worst legacy he could leave behind, was to die the death of a coward, the death of a loser. For once a man dies, all that remains of him is his legacy, his reputation.

So the Arabs used this expression, "falling from the sky," even before the Qur'an was revealed. They used it constantly. What they meant by it was this. Imagine two tribes at war: one stands at the top of a cliff, the other at its base. Which of them has the advantage? The one at the top. Yet if, despite standing at the top of the cliff, they still lost the battle, what would the enemy do with their bodies once it was over? Throw them off the cliff. This they called "falling from the sky." The expression was used in two situations: either they were such poor fighters that they lost the battle despite holding the advantage, or they were fleeing from the enemy and, in their retreat, tripped and fell from the cliff to their deaths — the death of a coward. So either they died the death of a loser or the death of a coward. These were the worst legacies the Arabs ever wished to leave behind. The ugliest end they could conceive was captured in those words, "falling from the sky."

Allah speaks to these idolatrous Arabs, who have no concept of the hereafter, no concept of the humiliation of the Day of Judgment, and gives them an image that helps them understand that day from their own point of view. Think of the ugliest thing you can imagine — let me tell you, idolatry is like that. It is like falling from the sky.

When a man dies in battle, in the ancient way of humankind, when two sides clash, corpses are left strewn everywhere. Once the battle is over, what becomes of those corpses? Each side comes, gathers up the bodies of its own dead, and gives them a proper burial. Is that not what happens? Unless you regard your soldier as a traitor, a disgrace, or an embarrassment to your tribe — in which case no one comes for you. And when no one comes for you, guess what does come for you? Birds. الطیر — which in classical Arabic, in classical poetry, was used for vultures. Birds of carrion, that feed on dead flesh. So now the birds are eating away at the corpse of this dead man, the body his own tribesmen left behind. And now these foul birds finish their meal, and even they want nothing more from it. Even they are done with it! Now what comes?

Now the wind comes and blows the remains away, the scum of what is left of these people, into uncharted territory. They have become the decomposed refuse of the earth. The ugliest ending the Arabs could ever have imagined is set before them in such beautiful terms, through a single example, so that they might grasp what association is in the sight of Allah. Do you think association is a small matter? Do you think idol worship is a small matter? Let me put this in perspective for you. Do you see how powerful the Qur'an is in its examples?

Here is one of the arguments that people raise. They say that the Qur'an declares itself clear, and so they ought to be able to understand it on their own. But the truth is that although the Qur'an does say it is clear, and although it does say it is self-evident, it never says it is simple. Clear and simple are two very different things. We should not confuse clear and self-evident with simple. The Qur'an sometimes presents very clear solutions to very complex problems, yet not necessarily in a simple way. Imagine a very difficult calculus problem, and the professor writes out a very clear solution to it. The solution may be clear, but does that mean it is simple? No. The professor must still explain its complexities, however clear the solution may be. So do not oversimplify the Qur'an, for it holds a great deal of complexity. This is precisely why we need the true Imams (AS), and their du'at present in every age, to help us understand these complexities in simple terms. We cannot understand this book without the medium of an Imam or a Da'i. That is why the Qur'an says:

فسألو اھل الذکر ان کنتم لا تعلمون

Ask the people of remembrance — the Imams, the du'at — if you do not understand something.

Now for the second example. Every Surah presents such extraordinary imagery through dialogue. I gave you the example of Utbah Ibn Rabeeah, of how Allah comes to the defense of His beloved prophet (AS) against Utbah's accusations. Do you remember what happens to him at the end of that dialogue? He begins to weep, springs forward, places both his hands over the mouth of the prophet (AS), and begs him to stop. Allah uses images and analogies to challenge the Arab imagination across various Surahs. He portrays the unseen beautifully — in Surah al-Rahman, in Surah al-Waqi'ah. You may be aware of the images of paradise and hell that it portrays, the images of the hereafter, and so on. One such Surah is Surah al-Mursalat, which I want to discuss with you today.

There are a handful of Surahs in which a great deal of repetition is used — very few of them. In Surah al-Rahman, as we all know, the verse فبای آلاء ربکما تکذبان is repeated several times, thirty-one times in fact. Then there is Surah الشعراء, which has a repetition of its own. Likewise, Surah al-Mursalat is one of those Surahs in which the verse وَيْلٌۭ يَوْمَئِذٍۢ لِّلْمُكَذِّبِينَ is repeated several times, which means: there will be immense sorrow for those who lied on that day. What day is Allah speaking of? The Day of Judgment. The purpose of these repetitions, and why Allah repeats Himself so many times in these Surahs, is a discussion for another day, insha'Allah, for it has a very profound purpose. What I want to focus on today is presenting to you the imagery of the Qur'an as a miracle. This is from Surah al-Mursalat.

What I wish to show you are the analogies and parallels the Qur'an offers to explain abstract realities: the Hereafter, Allah's power, and His dominion over all things. The Arabs of the Quraish had argued with the Messenger of Allah, saying: You keep speaking of the sun and the moon colliding. You keep speaking of mountains moving swiftly as though they were tufts of wool. You say that people, out of terror, will appear drunk, and that the oceans will boil over. These enormous things you keep describing will never happen. When is all of this supposed to come? We have never witnessed anything of the kind. None of it makes sense, and none of it is possible. So they argued that the warnings in the Qur'an were too cataclysmic, too vast to be real. They claimed:

1. There is no purpose to creation.
2. We depend upon Allah for nothing.
3. There is no Hereafter and no rising from the dead.
4. There is no reward and no punishment.

All of this, they said, was mere nonsense, the raving of a madman (نعوذ باللہ).

In answer to this, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swears a series of oaths in these few verses of Surah al-Mursalat. As I told you last time, Arabic is an exceedingly rich language. For each word there are dozens of synonyms, and a single word may carry ten distinct meanings. The most remarkable thing about it is that all ten of those meanings can apply within the same context. Ordinarily, when a word has many synonyms, different words are used in different contexts. But Arabic is unique, for not only can each word be used in a separate context, all of its forms can be used within a single context as well. God willing, I will show you many examples of this as we proceed.

Now, the word المرسلۃ is used in Arabic, in its literal sense, for that *which has been released.* So in Surah al-Mursalat, Allah is speaking of the winds. The word is also used to describe a very swift horse, one that moves like the wind. And it is used, moreover, to describe a messenger, one who brings a warning: الرسول. So Allah, Mighty is His Majesty, swears by the winds, and He says:

وَٱلْمُرْسَلَتِ عُرْفًۭا

The word عُرف in Arabic refers to the mane, the hair upon the back of a wild horse's neck. If you have no reins or ropes upon a horse, what is the one thing you can use to slow it? The hair upon the back of its neck. Allah presents the image of the winds as though they were wild horses that have been unleashed because their manes have been let go. What happens when you release the mane of a wild horse? It goes mad. It goes out of control. It charges forward at full speed. So what is being drawn in parallel here is the image of a wild horse with the winds.

That is, Allah is telling the Quraish that the winds are not something that merely blows this way or that at random. The soft breeze you feel upon your face is there because its reins are being held. Held by whom? By Allah, Mighty is His Majesty. But it is entirely possible for that supreme Lord to release that lock of hair. If He lets go, what will happen? They will turn into that wild horse, that stallion that crushes whatever lies in its path. What happens when a hurricane decides to take a stroll through a city? It destroys everything in its path, does it not? So the first thing Allah swears by is the winds, which hold the power to destroy once their reins are let go.

Then He says:

فَٱلْعَصِفَتِ عَصْفًۭا

The word عصف in Arabic means to move in a reckless, heedless manner.

What I mean by an inconsiderate manner is that it does not care what lies in its path. When the brakes of a truck or a bulldozer fail, they simply crush whatever comes before them. They do not care. They only keep moving forward. So the movement of a bulldozer is عصف. It is inconsiderate; it does not care what comes in its way. It only keeps moving forward. From عصف comes the word عاصف. And so Allah continues His oath: فَٱلْعَصِفَتِ عَصْفًۭا These winds, which have just been unleashed, have now become inconsiderate, merciless. They do not care what will come in their way. They will simply destroy as they move along.

So in the first two verses, Allah swears by the destruction of the winds. If you have seen videos of what happened after Hurricane Katrina, of what it did in only forty seconds, of the destruction it caused, then you have some idea of the power of these winds. In another place, Allah speaks of such winds sent upon a rebellious nation for seven consecutive days. Can you imagine the destruction they must have caused? If forty seconds can do so much, what will seven consecutive days do?

سَخَّرَهَا عَلَيْهِمْ سَبْعَ لَيَالٍۢ وَثَمَنِيَةَ أَيَّامٍ حُسُومًۭا فَتَرَى ٱلْقَوْمَ فِيهَا صَرْعَىٰ كَأَنَّهُمْ أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ خَاوِيَةٍۢ

We sent upon them winds for seven nights and eight days without pause (حُسُومًۭا), pounding them continuously. We have seen what forty seconds can do. Seven nights and eight days! It turned their skulls like hollow, seedless date stumps. Allahu Akbar! Such powerful words!

Now, the wind is not some cataclysmic event, like the sun and the moon coming together, or the sun increasing its gravitational pull. It is not a special event that requires preparation. You know how special arrangements are made for weapons of mass destruction. What does Allah use to destroy these people? Only the wind! The Quraysh, who knew of this event, are being told by Allah that to destroy them, He needs to make no special arrangements. All He needs to do is release His hold on the lock of the winds. That is all He needs to do.

And then He turns and shows you the other aspect of the winds. After describing the winds as the source of death and destruction, He says: وَٱلنَّشِرَتِ نَشْرًۭا And the winds that serve to spread. نشر literally means to take a handful of seeds and fling them into the air. What happens when you do that? They fall everywhere, in every direction. So Allah swears by the winds that spread and disperse the clouds across the whole world. Because what do the clouds bring us? Rain! And rain is the source of life on this earth. No rain, no life. Drought means death! So the wind that was the source of death and destruction in the first two verses is now, in this third verse, the source of life. Subhan Allah! And now we understand it even better. The winds do not only carry the clouds about; what else do they carry? The pollen! The source of all vegetation. Through what does pollen travel from one place to another? The winds! Those of you who suffer from bad allergies know this all too well, unfortunately. These winds are truly a mercy from Allah. That is why we are reminded to say Alhamdulillah! For why does one sneeze? Because a foreign particle is irritating the inside of the nose. How did that particle get there? Through breathing. And what does one take in through breathing? Air. And where did the air come from? The winds!

SubhanAllah! So Allah spreads these clouds around. Now, when you think of Allah spreading these clouds by the winds, you may imagine that it is all random, that the winds are in control—what science calls the random acts of mother nature. As Muslims, we know there is no such thing. These are precise, carefully calculated acts of whom? Of Allah, exalted is He. So He says: فَٱلْفَٰرِقَٰتِ فَرْقًۭا. He swears by those that make the most precise distinctions. Water will fall here and not there. This land will stay dry; that land will receive water. فَٱلْفَٰرِقَٰتِ فَرْقًۭا.

Two things have now been told to the Quraish through imagery in words: these winds can bring death, and these same winds can bring life. I am the one who decides which brings which, says Allah. He swears by them and declares that He is the one in control. Then He says: فَٱلْمُلْقِيَٰتِ ذِكْرًۭا. These winds bring people into contact with reminders. The word mulqiyaat comes from the root لقی, which means to come into contact with someone. So Allah says that these winds bring people into contact with what? With reminders, by way of reflection.

What are these reminders that Allah is speaking of? What were the arguments of the Quraish? They said:
1. There is no purpose to creation.
2. We depend on Allah for nothing.
3. There is no hereafter and no rising from the dead.
4. There is no reward and no punishment.

The winds create the cooperation between the heavens and the earth. The clouds move in the heavens, and the rain falls upon the earth. All of it to serve whom? Us, the human beings. So the single thing responsible for this coordination is what? The wind. Allah is showing us that there is a single chain of command, a single leadership, and this reveals the purpose of creation. Think about it. If all of this—this entire creation around us, the winds, the clouds, the rain, the vegetation it grows, the animals that eat the vegetation, the animals we feed upon—if all of this has been created to serve us, mankind, then Allah wants us to think: I created everything with a particular purpose, to serve whom? You, and Me. So do you think you were created without a purpose? See how everything comes together in cooperation, all with the purpose of serving you. If Allah created all this to serve me, then, logically, I could not have been created without a purpose. I too must have a purpose to serve, for I too am a creation. SubhanAllah! All this realization from a single wind. So the wind is in truth a reminder of my purpose in life.

The second reminder that the winds carry—let me give you an example. Suppose I have a pet, and I leave it without water all day. After all, I am "Asif." At night, when I return home, at whose mercy is the animal? At mine. I need to put some water in a dish or a bowl and give it to the animal. The animal is not able to help itself at all; it is completely at my mercy. No matter how this animal behaves—whether it damages my property, makes a mess of my things, breaks things, whether it obeys me or not—in the end, at the end of the day, it is completely at my mercy. Is it not? As wild and rebellious as human beings can become, if Allah does not give us these sips of water to drink, where do we go? We have nowhere to go. We are more pathetic and more powerless than the pets we think we own. Who brings the water? The clouds.

Who scatters the clouds—the winds. Glory be to Allah! The winds are a reminder of the lordship of Allah, that no matter who you imagine yourself to be—a poor farmer or the king of nations—you are wholly dependent upon Allah. He is the one letting you have these sips. This water is not something you produced. Walk as arrogantly as you please upon the earth, but if I do not send down this mercy from the sky, where will you be? Do you understand now why we sit down to drink water? Why we honor the water as we drink it?

Then the winds are a reminder of the resurrection. The winds bring the clouds, water falls from the sky, and what happens to the earth? It comes back to life. The dead becomes the living. Now, every time the rains bring life to the dead earth, we are reminded that we too will die, that we too will be laid in the earth, and that just as the rain brings the dead earth to life through its greenery, we too will one day be raised again. On the Day of Judgment, the earth will give up its human beings.

And then, finally, we see that in the first two verses Allah speaks of death and destruction, and the next two verses speak of life and prosperity, using the very same example: the wind. He reminds us that Allah has established a profound system of punishment and reward—things that draw down His wrath, and other things that draw down His mercy. So we are reminded not to cross certain lines and to pursue other things in life. By the winds alone, we are reminded of Allah's justice; we are reminded of Allah's commandments.

And now, after giving the Arabs the example of the winds and asking them to reflect upon it, the Arabs would take it in. Everything I have just explained to you, the Arabs drew out of these verses at once.

And then Allah says: عُذْرًا أَوْ نُذْرًا. Allah says there are two kinds of people who will feel the wind upon their faces. After being warned by the previous five verses, the first is the one who will believe, who will accept the majesty of Allah and submit to His glory. And the other is the one who will do nothing, even after being warned. So for the people who recognized and accepted the wind, the winds served as a warner, نذرا. And for the people who did not care, these same winds are now going to become a means of punishment for them, عذرا. The winds are now going to become a cause, a means, by which they will be punished: عُذْرًا أَوْ نُذْرًا.

Then, after setting this stage, after all this explanation, after all these promises, Allah finally comes to His point: إِنَّمَا تُوعَدُونَ لَوَقِعٌۭ. What you have been promised will, without a doubt, come to pass. What you have been promised will happen. Just as these winds can be a torment or a favor, you too will one day become the recipient of either Allah's most severe wrath or Allah's most abundant favor. It is bound to happen; it is going to happen.

The oaths in the Qur'an are, each one of them, a profound literary masterpiece in their own right. The surahs that begin with oaths require special study of their own—the study of why Allah swears by these things is incredible in itself. And right now I am speaking only of the outer surface, the ظاہر. I am not even touching the باطن, which is so very much more powerful.

In the last session, I showed you how beautiful and precise the words of the Quran are. The Arabs measured the eloquence and power of a speech by how brief and exact it was. That is why they had the saying:

خیر الکلام من قل و دل

The best of speech is that which is brief and exact.

In Surah Mursalaat, we saw how Allah challenged the Arab imagination and addressed the disbelief of the Arabs by using the winds as an example. You saw how brief and exact those ayats were, and the sea of knowledge that those very few words contained. Allah explained the entire concept of akhirah, of punishment and reward, through the winds alone, all in five or six short and simple ayats.

Today I want to continue along the same path and show you a few more of these amazing miracles. This one has to do with the perfection of the choice of words in the literal sense. In Surah Ehzaab, Allah speaks about matters of marriage. He begins by speaking about men, and then He moves on to women.

33:4

مَّا جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِرَجُلٍۢ مِّن قَلْبَيْنِ فِى جَوْفِهِ

Allah did not put two hearts inside of any man.

After speaking about men, He moves on to speak about women:

وَمَا جَعَلَ أَزْوَجَكُم ألتِّی تُظَهِرُونَ مِنْهُنَّ أُمَّهَتِكُمْ

Let me first go over the meaning of this ayah. The word الِرَجُلٍۢ means "man," and it is gender specific. The word قَلْبَيْنِ means "two hearts." It is the plural form of the word "قَلْب," which means a single heart. So قَلْب is singular and means one heart, and قَلْبَيْنِ is a double plural and means two hearts. In Arabic you do not have only singular and plural, you also have what is called the double plural. So for any word you have the singular, then the double plural, meaning exactly two, and then the general plural, meaning more than two. The word جَوْف in Arabic means a hollow space. That is why a cave in Arabic is called جَوْف.

When you read the English translations of this ayah, you will find that most translations say: Allah did not put two hearts inside any man's chest. And that is the wrong translation of the word جَوْف. The Arabic word for chest is صدر. This is why it is so important to learn Quranic Arabic, because the filter of translation takes away so much of the meaning. English is simply not powerful enough as a language to hold the richness of Arabic.

In any case, Allah says: We did not put two hearts inside of any man. Now of course this ayah is not literal, it is metaphorical. What it means is that faith and disbelief cannot live together in any man. A man will believe or he will disbelieve. He will love or he will hate. He cannot do both at the same time.

But what is truly interesting about this ayah is its literal form. Allah did not say that He did not put two hearts inside any human being. Do men and women not both have a single heart? Then why did Allah single out men in this ayah? For He says specifically لِرَجُلٍۢ, which means man. Allah could simply have said:

مَّا جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لی النَّاسِ مِّن قَلْبَيْنِ فِى جَوْفِهِ

Allah did not put two hearts inside any human being. That would have covered both. But Allah left women out of it. And this is perfection in its LITERAL form, not its LITERARY form, but its LITERAL form. Because, you see, a woman can become pregnant. And when a woman becomes pregnant, how many hearts are inside? There could be two, or more. So Allah says that He did not put two hearts inside any man.

Even in its literal form the Qur'an is so incredibly perfect. Nobody can play devil's advocate and say, "Well, what about women? They can get pregnant!" No, you cannot. Allah said only man, لِرَجُلٍۢ! SubhanAllah! Show me this kind of perfection in any other spoken conversation, or even in a book, anywhere in the world.

Now, this next miracle that I want to show you today is also related to the profound nature of the Qur'an's imagery. As we have seen before, the Qur'an is a very coherent text, a very connected text. One part of a verse describes another. One theme is recited in different words. Words that are going to be said later have an influence on words that come at the beginning. Right?

So, in the same context, I want to present this verse to you from Surah Saba. This miracle has multiple dimensions. It is a miracle in the choice of words, it is also a miracle in the placement of words, and it is a miracle of the Qur'an's imagery, in the way it challenges the imagination. Until now I have shown you verses that were a miracle in one specific dimension of their own. And now this one is among the many, many verses that are a miracle in multiple dimensions all at the same time! SubhanAllah!

So Allah says:

يَعْلَمُ مَا يَلِجُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا وَمَا يَنزِلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَاۚ وَهُوَ ٱلرَّحِيمُ ٱلْغَفُورُ

يَعْلَمُ مَا يَلِجُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
He knows what enters into the earth

وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا
and what comes out of it,

وَمَا يَنزِلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ
and what comes down from the sky,

وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَاۚ
and what rises to it.

وَهُوَ ٱلرَّحِيمُ ٱلْغَفُورُ
And He is the constantly merciful and exceedingly forgiving.

Now this is a very interesting verse. If you look at the highlighted part, what do you see the verse ending in? وَهُوَ ٱلرَّحِيمُ ٱلْغَفُورُ. If you read the Qur'an regularly, you must have noticed that you do not normally see the words ٱلرَّحِيمُ ٱلْغَفُورُ. Instead you always see the words ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ. That is the general pattern in the Qur'an. More than seventy times He uses the words ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ in the Qur'an.

قالَ سَوْفَ أَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكُمْ رَبِّىٓ ۖ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّى ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِى فَٱغْفِرْ لِى فَغَفَرَ لَهُۥٓ ۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

ثُمَّ أَفِيضُوا۟ مِنْ حَيْثُ أَفَاضَ ٱلنَّاسُ وَٱسْتَغْفِرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ

قُلْ إِن كُنتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱللَّهَ فَٱتَّبِعُونِى يُحْبِبْكُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَيَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ ذُنُوبَكُمْ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ

So everywhere else in the Qur'an, Allah says غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ, which again means forgiving, comma, merciful. But this is the only place in the entire Qur'an where Allah says ٱلرَّحِيمُ ٱلْغَفُورُ, merciful, comma, forgiving. So what is going on? This is divine speech, and our belief is that every word has to be in its proper place. So how is it that this is the only place where Allah does not say forgiving, comma, merciful, but instead says merciful, comma, forgiving?

First of all, I want to tell you something about these verses. There is a particular pattern in the Qur'an when it comes to these verses. Every time Allah uses the words غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ at the end of a verse, you will find the beginning of that verse talking about human beings, in one way or another. That is important to note, because when it comes to human beings...

they need to be forgiven first, and only then do they become deserving of Allah's mercy. That is the proper order as far as human beings are concerned. And if you think about it, this applies to us as well in our dealings with one another. There is a saying in Arabic: انَّ الدَّرءَ المَفْسَدَۃ مُقَدَّم عَلیٰ جَلبِ المَسْلَحَۃ If you have a dirty glass and you wish to drink juice, what must you do first? Clean the glass. So the negative element is cleared away before the positive element can be added. Forgiveness clears away the negative element, and mercy is plainly the positive element.

If your friend has offended you and you are angry with him, you will need to forgive him first, before you can sincerely show him any kindness. The principle is the same. In order to gain Allah's mercy, we first need to gain His forgiveness.

Now let us return to our verse:

يَعْلَمُ مَا يَلِجُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا وَمَا يَنزِلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَاۚ وَهُوَ ٱلرَّحِيمُ ٱلْغَفُورُ

He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what comes down from the sky, and what rises to it. And He is the constantly merciful and exceedingly forgiving.

I have just told you that every time in the Qur'an the words غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ are used, Allah is speaking about whom? About human beings. In this verse the words are used again, in a different order, but do you see any mention of human beings in this verse? Not directly.

The literal meaning of this verse concerns the "knowledge" of Allah: that Allah knows what goes into the earth, what comes out of it, what comes down from the sky, and what rises back to it, and He is the merciful, comma, forgiving.

So on the outer surface this verse speaks of Allah's knowledge. And here is another interesting fact for you: wherever in the Qur'an Allah speaks of knowledge, you will find mercy mentioned in that passage. Knowledge is joined with mercy everywhere in the Qur'an, because for us to possess Allah's knowledge is, in the end, the greatest mercy of all. And the greatest proof of this idea from the Qur'an is the astonishing verse:

الرحمن علم القرآن

The intensely merciful taught the Qur'an — and that is knowledge and education.

Now, in the verse we are studying, we can understand the presence of the word ٱلرَّحِيمُ because Allah is speaking of knowledge, and, as I said, mercy is associated with knowledge. But why is Allah speaking of forgiveness? Why did He use the word ٱلْغَفُورُ ? Forgiveness is an attribute that concerns human beings. If there is no mention of human beings, there is no need for forgiveness. Have you ever forgiven your car? Have you ever forgiven your lunch box? You strike your foot against the corner of a door; do you later return to it and say, I forgive you, door! No, because forgiveness is associated only with human beings. You will forgive your friend, your brother, your sister.

So the presence of this word غَفُورٌۭ means that this verse is in fact speaking about human beings. It is simply not literal; it is implied. When a farmer hears these words, that Allah knows what enters into the earth, what does he think of? Seeds! And when he hears the words, what comes out, what does he think of? A plant! But if we look more deeply, we human beings will also enter the earth one day, and we too will come out of the earth one day, on the Day of Judgment. Allah says:

He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it. Now, this could refer to seeds and plants, but it could most certainly refer to human beings as well, because they too will enter the earth one day and come out of it. And if you look at the next part of the verse, He says:

وَمَا يَنزِلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَا

He knows what is coming down from the sky and what rises up to it. From the farmer's perspective, what is that? Rain! But from the perspective of human beings, it is revelation, the word of Allah coming down from the sky. Now, once the revelation comes down and people hear it, they either act according to it or they do not act according to it. So what is going back up to the sky? Their deeds! Their deeds! Their actions, for evaluation.

Let us do that again:

مَا يَلِجُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا

Human beings enter the earth when they die; human beings come out of the earth on the Day of Judgment.

وَمَا يَنزِلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَا

Revelation coming down from the sky, and human deeds and actions rising back up to Allah for evaluation.

Now, at the time of death, people are in need of Allah's mercy, because death is a very difficult time. But when they are raised from the ground, they will be in need of Allah's forgiveness. On the Day of Judgment we will all need Allah's forgiveness. So mercy first and forgiveness second.

What comes down from the sky again? Revelation, and revelation is Allah's mercy. And what goes up to the sky again? Human actions, which need forgiveness. Mercy first, forgiveness second. Subhan Allah! This is the only place in the Qur'an where mercy comes first and forgiveness second. SubhanAllah!

Do you see? A very, very accurate use of words, placed precisely where they belong; each word precisely connected to what has been said before, and precisely connected to what is coming later.

Let me tell you something very interesting. This is a side note, but I found it fascinating: when you look at the study of the Qur'an as it has unfolded through history, you will see that the earliest theme of Qur'anic study was اعجاز القرآن, the miracles of the Qur'an. On the basis of the very facts I have shared with you, the scholars would say that this proves the Qur'an is the message of Allah, because human beings are not capable of this kind of perfect and precise composition. But later we see this theme change from اعجاز القرآن to simply جمال القرآن, the beauty of the Qur'an. The scholars began to say that we no longer need to prove it; let us simply explore its beauty. So the theme today has become جمال القرآن.

In any case, this is one profound example, and it belongs not only to the linguistic dimension of the miracles of the Qur'an, but also to the dimension of imagination.

Now let us look at another one. I showed you the placement of words and the choice of words at a very micro level in the previous sessions. We zoomed in on a single verse and examined the precision and accuracy of the Qur'an's words. The one I want to show you now is perfection at the MACRO level. For this one we zoom out, from the level of the verse to the level of the surah.

Now, you know that the Qur'an was not revealed in the order in which we see it in the Qur'an.

The first verse revealed was ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ‏, and the last verse revealed was ٱلْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِى وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلْإِسْلَمَ دِينًۭا. But this is not the order in which we find them in the Qur'an. The first verse we find in the book is بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم of Surah al-Fatiha, and the last verse is من الجنۃ و الناس of Surah al-Nas.

So the order we see in the Qur'an is not the order in which it was revealed. What happened is this: as these passages of verses were being revealed, the Messenger of God was also instructing and teaching Maulana Ali the order of these passages, the order in which they were to be placed, and which passage of verses belonged in which surah. So imagine that these verses are in fact water, coming out of a hose at different times, and the Messenger of God is holding the hose. Before him stand one hundred and fourteen buckets, which represent the one hundred and fourteen surahs. As each batch of water comes out, he instructs Maulana Ali as to which batch goes into which bucket. Do you understand? So over twenty-three years you can imagine these surahs being filled with verses all at the same time, not one after the other.

Now, Surah al-Baqarah is the second and the longest surah in the Qur'an, and it is a Madani surah, which means that it was revealed to the Prophet while he was in Medina. History shows us that the greater part of al-Baqarah was revealed during the first two years of the Holy Prophet's life at Medina. The smaller part was revealed at a later period of his life. And in between, many other surahs and passages were revealed.

Another thing you have to understand is that when we think of verses, we think in terms of numbers. You know: verse 53 of Surah al-Baqarah, verse 6 of Surah al-Fatiha. We can speak about verses using this system of numbers. But the Arabs of that time did not think in terms of numbers. They did not go up to one another and say, "Brother! Did you hear verses 2:53 to 2:75? Was that something, or what?" "Oh yes, my friend, that was magnificent!" No. All they remembered were the verses themselves. They had no concept of verse numbers, because the verses were documented later on by Maulana Ali during the time of Hazrat Usman. Remember, this conversation is an oral tradition, not a written one. It is the spoken word that was later written down. It is not a written word that was then spoken by the Messenger of God. And because of this fact, what I am about to tell you becomes so very wonderful.

In Surah al-Baqarah, God says: وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنَكُمْ أُمَّةًۭ وَسَطًۭا — We have made you a middle nation. The word وسط in Arabic, like any other word, has several different meanings. One meaning of the word is something that is exactly in the middle, something right at the center. It literally means to be in between: فَوَسَطْنَ بِهِ جَمْعًا‏, as God speaks of the horse that drives right into the middle of the army's legions in Surah al-Aadiyat.

Another meaning of the word وسط is this: when you are weighing something on a scale and both sides of the scale are equally balanced, neither side tipping in any direction, and they meet right in the middle, that is called وسط. And that is why وسط also means "just." So God says: وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنَكُمْ أُمَّةًۭ وَسَطًۭا. Whom is this verse speaking about? It is speaking about our ( ائمۃ علیھم السلام).

For every Imam is the most just man of his age. So one meaning is "middle," and another meaning is "just." But in ancient Arabic the word وسط carries a further meaning as well. It serves as the root of واسطۃ, which means a "link." Whatever joins two things together from exactly the center is called واسطۃ. So the Messenger of God was the link, the واسطۃ, between God's message and us human beings in respect of the words. And Maulana Ali and the Imams are the واسطۃ, the link between the Messenger of God and us in respect of the meaning. Do you understand?

The word أُمَّةًۭ means nation, and the nation here refers to the company of Imams who have come into this world from the beginning of time and will continue to come until the end of time. God says that among all human beings He has made the Imams the most just, because they will always keep the scale right in the middle. They will never tip the scale in any direction. Do you understand?

Does anyone know how many verses Surah Baqarah has? Two hundred and eighty-six. In Surah Baqarah, God says: وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنَكُمْ أُمَّةًۭ وَسَطًۭا. وسط means something that stands right in the middle, right at the center. Do you know which verse number this is? It is verse 143. And how many verses are in Surah Baqarah? Two hundred and eighty-six. What is half of two hundred and eighty-six? One hundred and forty-three. SubhanAllah! In the exact middle verse of Surah Baqarah, God speaks of a middle nation. SubhanAllah!

The next matter I wish to place before you rests on research carried out by a man named Tariq ibn Muhammad al-Suwaidan. He delivered a lecture series in Arabic in Kuwait on the miracle of the Qur'an. It is a most interesting study. He demonstrated more than fifty miracles of the Qur'an on scientific grounds. What I wish to share with you is the word count in the Qur'an that he identified in the course of his research. This was not something he set out to do at the start; but as his research went on, he was noting how many times a given word occurs in the Qur'an, and he began to list them. To his astonishment, he found these correspondences matching one another perfectly.

I have personally verified every one of these. I am a software engineer by profession. So I imported the entire Qur'an into a database, split each verse into its words, and then ran word-count comparisons to see whether his claims were true. And SubhanAllah, I was able to match every one of these counts. So I wish to share some of these miracles with you. Again, keep in mind that the Qur'an is not a written text; it is a spoken text that was revealed piece by piece, passage by passage, in every sort of order, over the course of twenty-three years.

The word used for prayers, صلوات, is used, most interestingly, only five times in the whole Qur'an, which of course corresponds to the five prayers of the day.

The word یوم, which means day, is used exactly three hundred and sixty-five times in the Qur'an.

The word دنیا is mentioned one hundred and fifteen times, and so is the word آخرۃ, which means the hereafter.

Angels are mentioned ninety-nine times in the Qur'an, and the word devil is mentioned ninety-nine times in the Qur'an.

Life and death are mentioned an equal number of times in the Qur'an. Both occur one hundred and forty-five times.

People and messengers are mentioned an equal number of times. Why? Because for whom did the messengers come? For people!

Zakat and barakah are mentioned an equal number of times.

Man and woman are mentioned an equal number of times.

Each occurs twenty-four times. Day and night are mentioned an equal number of times. Intellect and light are mentioned an equal number of times. The name of the Prophet Muhammad is mentioned four times, and the word *shariah* is mentioned four times in the Qur'an.

So there are these terms that are paired in meaning and occur in equal numbers. And again, this is a recited word. This was something spoken aloud by the Messenger of God. To hold a balance of this kind is simply not possible, even in a written text, let alone in spoken words.

Now here is one that I find remarkable. The word Iblis, which is the name of Satan, is mentioned eleven times, and seeking refuge from him is mentioned eleven times. And do you know that there are two surahs recited to seek refuge from Satan? Does anyone know which they are? Nas and Falaq. Do you know how many verses they contain between them? Let us count.

Iblis is mentioned eleven times, seeking refuge from him is mentioned eleven times, and the two surahs devoted specifically to seeking refuge from him have eleven verses between them. Glory be to God!

The next one I want to share with you is amazing beyond words. I chose it today also because of what Hassan asked in the last session: how is it that this text is not poetry, when it does have a rhyme scheme? As I said last time, the Qur'an is prose, not poetry. It is prose that sounds like poetry, because it has a rhyme scheme. But having a rhyme scheme alone does not make something poetry. There are various rules that govern poetry, especially Arabic poetry, and rhyme is only one of them.

There are fifteen different meters, called وزن, in Arabic poetry, and they have to do with the length of syllables. In an Arabic *sher*, each line, called a *bayt*, is divided into two halves, and the pair must satisfy those rules. The halves are built of long and short syllables occurring in a specific pattern. Think of it like the beats of music: there is a rhythm, a pattern. And so there are fifteen different kinds of patterns in Arabic poetry: Tawil, Kamil, Wafir, Rajaz, Hajaz, Basit, Khafif.

It is genuinely fascinating. Any piece of Arabic poetry you come across will follow one of these fifteen syllable patterns. The key is that the syllable pattern must be the same across the pair. It does not matter how many words are used in each half; the syllable pattern in each *bayt*, or verse, must be exactly the same as the syllable pattern in the second verse.

Let me give you an example. Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, who was an evil king and ruler of that time, saw how much respect the Muslims were showing to Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin during the Hajj, and he felt jealous, because he himself never received such respect from the people. So he pretended not to recognize the Imam and asked his men, "Who is this man?" Now, he knew exactly who this man was. He knew he was the Imam, son of the Imam. Yet he pretended not to recognize him. There was a poet with him whose name was Farazdaq, who was in fact one of the callers of Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin at that time. At once, and without preparation, he began to recite poetry glorifying the Imam. Beautiful, beautiful words.

So even though the Qur'an has a rhyme scheme, the syllable patterns vary from verse to verse.

They sound like poetry, like the most eloquent and most beautiful poetry, yet they are not poetry, because they do not match any of the fifteen syllable patterns of Arabic verse. So the next miracle I wish to show you has to do with the syllables of the Qur'an. We notice that each surah has a certain rhyme scheme: the last words of the verses rhyme with one another. Then, suddenly, God changes the rhyme scheme in the middle of the surah, and in some cases returns afterward to the earlier rhyme scheme. The words of the surah follow a certain rhyme scheme:

زَكَرِيَّآ، خَفِیَّا، شَقِیَّا، وَلِیَّا، رَضِيًّۭا، نَبِیَّا، سَمِيًّۭا

This rhyme scheme is from Surah Maryam:

ذِكْرُ رَحْمَتِ رَبِّكَ عَبْدَهُۥ زَكَرِيَّآ‏

إِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥ نِدَآءً خَفِيًّۭا‏

قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّى وَهَنَ ٱلْعَظْمُ مِنِّى وَٱشْتَعَلَ ٱلرَّأْسُ شَيْبًۭا وَلَمْ أَكُنۢ بِدُعَآئِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّۭا

وَإِنِّى خِفْتُ ٱلْمَوَلِىَ مِن وَرَآءِى وَكَانَتِ ٱمْرَأَتِى عَاقِرًۭا فَهَبْ لِى مِن لَّدُنكَ وَلِيًّۭا‏

يَرِثُنِى وَيَرِثُ مِنْ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ ۖ وَٱجْعَلْهُ رَبِّ رَضِيًّۭا‏

يَزَكَرِيَّآ إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَمٍ ٱسْمُهُۥ يَحْيَىٰ لَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُۥ مِن قَبْلُ سَمِيًّۭا

The verses continue on and on, and the words at the end of the verses keep rhyming and rhyming and rhyming, until you reach verse thirty-four:

ذَلِكَ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ ۚ قَوْلَ ٱلْحَقِّ ٱلَّذِى فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ

Everything rhymed perfectly up to this point, and now, from here, the rhyme scheme changes:

‏مَا كَانَ لِلَّهِ أَن يَتَّخِذَ مِن وَلَدٍۢ ۖ سُبْحَنَهُۥٓ ۚ إِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًۭا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ‏

وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّى وَرَبُّكُمْ فَٱعْبُدُوهُ ۚ هَذَا صِرَطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ

فَٱخْتَلَفَ ٱلْأَحْزَابُ مِنۢ بَيْنِهِمْ ۖ فَوَيْلٌۭ لِّلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِن مَّشْهَدِ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ‏

أَسْمِعْ بِهِمْ وَأَبْصِرْ يَوْمَ يَأْتُونَنَا ۖ لَكِنِ ٱلظَّلِمُونَ ٱلْيَوْمَ فِى ضَلَلٍۢ مُّبِينٍۢ‏

وَأَنذِرْهُمْ يَوْمَ ٱلْحَسْرَةِ إِذْ قُضِىَ ٱلْأَمْرُ وَهُمْ فِى غَفْلَةٍۢ وَهُمْ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ‏

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَرِثُ ٱلْأَرْضَ وَمَنْ عَلَيْهَا وَإِلَيْنَا يُرْجَعُونَ

So why is this? Is there some logic behind the change, or is it merely random? As we know, the Qur'an is perfect in its form, and everything stands precisely in its place. Every word, and the position it occupies within a verse, has a specific purpose. So plainly it is not possible for the rhyme scheme to be random.

Now, if you afterward read the translation of the verses that carried the first rhyme scheme, you will notice that God is narrating the stories of the prophets. For that He uses one particular rhyme scheme. As soon as the subject changes, the rhyme scheme changes. You know how, in literature, when you wish to begin a new thought you begin it in a new paragraph, with an indentation. The Qur'an does not have paragraphs within its surahs; its way of expressing a change of subject is a change of rhyme scheme.

So in this Surah Maryam, God speaks of the prophets using the rhyme scheme of

زَكَرِيَّآ، خَفِیَّا، شَقِیَّا، وَلِیَّا، رَضِيًّۭا، نَبِیَّا، سَمِيًّۭا

Then, as soon as the subject changes, and God speaks of Himself as the true Lord and the only One worthy of worship, and of how the disbelievers are in great loss, the rhyme scheme changes with the subject:

يَمْتَرُونَ،  فَيَكُونُ،  مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ،  عَظِيمٍ،  مُّبِينٍۢ،  يُؤْمِنُونَ،  يُرْجَعُونَ

Do you see it? As soon as the subject changes, the rhyme scheme changes.

so that the listener would know that a new subject is now being discussed. But what is so interesting, so amazing, is that when God returns to the earlier subject, when He returns to speaking of the prophets again, He picks up that same old rhyme scheme again. Notice in the next verse:

وَٱذْكُرْ فِى ٱلْكِتَبِ إِبْرَهِيمَ ۚ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ صِدِّيقًۭا نَّبِيًّا

Back to the old rhyme scheme, because He is speaking of the prophets again:

شَيْـًۭٔا ‏, سَوِيًّۭا ‏, عَصِيًّۭا ‏, وَلِيًّۭا ‏

A speech that is not poetry, a speech dealing with very, very serious subjects, and yet the listener who listens carefully knows that the subject is one because the rhyme scheme is one. And as soon as the rhyme scheme changes, the subject has moved on to something else; and when the rhyme returns, it is because that digression was necessary to complete the original subject. Glory be to God! Show me another document that does this, consistently throughout its text. Those of you who know Surah An-Naba:

عَم يَتَسَآءَلُونَ
عَنِ ٱلنَّبَإِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ
ٱلَّذِى هُمْ فِيهِ مُخْتَلِفُونَ
كَلَّا سَيَعْلَمُونَ
ثُمَّ كَلَّا سَيَعْلَمُونَ

The subject changes:

أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ ٱلْأَرْضَ مِهَدًۭا
وَٱلْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًۭا
وَخَلَقْنَكُمْ أَزْوَجًۭا
وَجَعَلْنَا نَوْمَكُمْ سُبَاتًۭا
وَجَعَلْنَا ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًۭا

Glory be to God! One subject is finished, and the next one has its own rhyme scheme.

And sometimes you will find long passages with the very same rhyme scheme, with something interjected in the middle that does not fit that rhyme scheme. Do you know why? Because that digression is necessary for the rest of it, and you have to pay attention. God says:

لَآ أُقْسِمُ بِيَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَمَةِ
وَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِٱلنَّفْسِ ٱللَّوَّامَةِ
أَيَحْسَبُ ٱلْإِنسَنُ أَلَّن نَّجْمَعَ عِظَامَهُۥ
بَلَىٰ قَدِرِينَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن نُّسَوِّىَ بَنَانَهُۥ
بَلْ يُرِيدُ ٱلْإِنسَنُ لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُۥ
يَسْـَٔلُ أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ ٱلْقِيَمَةِ

The subject changes:

فَإِذَا بَرِقَ ٱلْبَصَرُ
وَخَسَفَ ٱلْقَمَرُ
وَجُمِعَ ٱلشَّمْسُ وَٱلْقَمَرُ
يَقُولُ ٱلْإِنسَنُ يَوْمَئِذٍ أَيْنَ ٱلْمَفَرُّ
كَلَّا لَا وَزَرَ
إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ ٱلْمُسْتَقَرُّ
يُنَبَّؤُا۟ ٱلْإِنسَنُ يَوْمَئِذٍۭ بِمَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّر

The subject changes:

بَلِ ٱلْإِنسَنُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٌۭ
وَلَوْ أَلْقَىٰ مَعَاذِيرَهُۥ

Then comes a small digression, because God needs to tell us something that is important for understanding what lies ahead. So He changes the rhyme scheme for just one verse:

لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِۦ لِسَانَكَ لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِۦٓ

And then He returns to the original subject from the beginning of the surah:

إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُۥ وَقُرْآنَهُ
فَإِذَا قَرَأْنَهُ فَٱتَّبِعْ قُرْآنَهُ
ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُۥ

Glory be to God! A rhyme scheme that tracks the subject matter. Explain to me how this is possible in spoken conversation. God is greater!

All praise belongs to God: in the previous session we completed the miracles of the Qur'an. Every single verse of the Qur'an is a miracle, though of course we cannot go through each and every verse. I showed you examples drawn from all of these different dimensions, with the structure of the Qur'an itself being the ultimate miracle of them all. In the very first session I told you that we would be studying the Qur'an, its message and its teachings. But in order to do that, we first needed to be sure that this Qur'an is in fact the message of God and the miracle of the Messenger of God. So we took this detour to verify it, and we have seen — and I hope I have convinced you all, beyond the shadow of a doubt — that this speech, this discourse, could not be the work of a human being.

This knowledge itself, and this new conviction that we have acquired, ought truly to change our attitude whenever we read the Qur'an from this point onward. Because we now know that when we recite the Qur'an, we are in fact in direct conversation with our Master.

Now I want to return to the original intent of my sessions, which is to speak about the actual message of this book. For if the message is from the Creator, and we are His creation, then this message must be the ultimate guidance — because only a Creator knows what is best for His creation. So this book is a source of guidance.

ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًۭى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ

Huda in Arabic means guidance, but it also means a "gift" — the word hadiya comes from the same root word. So this message is not merely guidance; it is also God's (SWT) gift to us. We will speak at length about these words, God willing, in future sessions.

This book is also the mercy of God (AWJ).

تِلْكَ آيَتُ ٱلْكِتَبِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ , هُدًۭى وَرَحْمَةًۭ لِّلْمُحْسِنِينَ

Rehma means "mercy." The word Rehma in Arabic is an extremely profound term. I need a couple of sessions simply to explain the word Rehma, and what mercy means when we speak of the mercy of God, the Exalted. I am holding off on all of these terms until we study Surah al-Fateha. Because the way in which God's majesty and His glory, and His love and His Rehma, come together and are presented in Surah al-Fateha, you cannot find anywhere else. You will see how incredible it is, God willing.

This book is so incredible. The more we study it, the more we will realize that it contains all the solutions to the challenges and problems we face in our day-to-day lives.

But before we begin, I thought it would be best if we went over the purpose of these remaining sessions today. What are the things we will cover, and what will we not cover? My intention for these sessions — my dream, really — is to present Islam to the young minds of my family and my jamaat. But Islam is an extremely vast subject that has many, many branches. There is shareeah, seerat, fiqah, hadeeth, theology, and so many other subjects. What I want to focus on in my sessions is the essence, the spirit of Islam, as stated by God Himself in His book. The "what" and the "why" of things. What is the purpose of life? What goals are we trying to achieve — is there a higher goal? Is Islam a difficult religion? If not, why does it feel so difficult to follow? Do I have to follow it blindly? Is there any intellectual reasoning behind the various acts of shareeah?

Why do we pray? Why must we perform ruku and sajdah? Are these various postures meant to signify something, or is namaaz merely a cardiovascular exercise? I said that aloud, did I not? Forgive me.

I have spoken with a great many young Muslims and teenagers, both within the Jamaat and beyond it, and even some in this very group have put the question to me: why is it that, although we love Allah and His Prophet, and although we genuinely wish to follow Islam and to be good Muslims, we still find it so difficult to do? Why do Islam, and the obligations it lays upon us, feel like such a burden?

These are very open-ended questions, and the answer could lie in any number of causes. Yet I believe there is a single thread woven through the fabric of them all. From my own experience, and from my discussions with my teachers, the reason I find at the root of this difficulty is that so many of us have lost the essence, the very soul, of Islam. All that remains to us is the body, the mechanical motions of Islam: a body without a soul. And we all know what such a thing is called, do we not? It is called a corpse.

I do not know whether you have ever considered this, or reflected upon the power and the importance of a soul. What is a soul? It is simply energy. And what is the body? It is mass, matter. When a person is alive, his soul is, in essence, operating the entire machinery of his heavy body. It moves the body and makes it perform its many tasks, and the person does not even feel that he is pushing this weight about all the while. The soul, then, is a very strong and powerful force. But when that same person dies, when this energy no longer works upon his body, the body can no longer carry itself. Now four or five individuals must bear the weight of his lifeless body upon their shoulders and carry him to his grave. And does this dead body feel heavy to those who carry it? Of course it does, for it is an additional weight upon their shoulders, a burden their own souls must now bear on top of their own weight. Do you understand? While the person was alive, he carried his own weight; now that he is dead, others must carry it for him.

This, then, is what I wish to focus on in these sessions: the intellectual dimension of this problem, so that we may revive the spirit of Islam in our hearts, so that we may approach the call with baseerah! And that is why what I wish to do is to have a very honest and open conversation with everyone—especially the young—and to set before you my understanding of Islam, drawn from the Quran. My intention is not to tell you what to do, or what not to do. I only wish to explain Allah's message from Allah's book, in the light of the knowledge I have received from my elders. And, InshaAllah, as and when it is necessary, I will teach you the Arabic you need to know in order to learn and understand this message. InshaAllah.

But you must understand that honest conversations are never comfortable conversations. I wish to challenge our existing ideas with the ideas the Quran presents. I wish to provoke thought. And on that basis, I want you to make your own decisions about what kind of changes you wish to bring into your daily lives. For knowledge that brings about no change is useless knowledge. Hazrat Zia Ali Sahab used to say: the only purpose of religion is transformation. Change! But change is never easy. So many of us reject the truth only because change is uncomfortable. And to be perfectly clear...

I am not a scholar of religion. I am not learned. I am only a student of the Qur'an. So I need these teachings, this guidance, as much as you do — perhaps even more. There are people in this gathering who are more devout than I will ever be in this life. I am only sharing the little I have gathered from the blessings of my elders, and with their permission. I am not trying to display my learning to anyone. I am only trying to display my religion — this astonishingly beautiful and perfect religion, which balances the heart and the intellect in perfect measure.

So let us step back and explore Islam together, with open minds, and then see what it is truly about: what its central message is, what its purpose is, how it helps us as individuals. What does Allah want from us? What kind of Allah are we dealing with? Is He a loving Allah? Is He a cruel Allah? What does the life of the Messenger of Allah teach us?
