body.text_en:
If we study the Qur'an, what we find is that it tells us to glorify Allah, and also to glorify the name of Allah:

سَبَّحَ لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ

Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah. And we also find:

سَبِّحِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ ٱلْأَعْلَى

We glorify the NAME of Allah.

Then we find the same pattern with تبارک, which means "blessed." This word too is used directly with Allah, and it is also used with the name of Allah:

فَتَبَارَكَ ٱللَّهُ أَحْسَنُ ٱلْخَلِقِينَ

and

تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ ذِى ٱلْجَلَلِ وَٱلْإِكْرَامِ

So the word tabarak is used directly with Allah and also with the name of Allah.

The Qur'an likewise tells us to remember Allah, and to remember the NAME of Allah:

فَٱذْكُرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ

and

وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ بُكْرَةًۭ وَأَصِيلًۭا

وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًۭا

So the Qur'an refers to Allah and to the name of Allah as two separate things. Sometimes we are asked to approach Allah directly; sometimes we are asked to approach Him through His name. The point is this: we know that Allah Himself is glorified, but the Qur'an teaches us that His names are glorified as well. So if the name of Allah is glorified, then how much more glorified must Allah Himself be! If Allah's name is so glorified, then how much more glorified must Allah Himself be! If Allah's name is blessed, then how much more blessed must Allah Himself be! If the name of Allah is so worthy of remembrance, then how much more worthy of remembrance must Allah Himself be!

Now the Qur'an never tells us to worship the name of Allah. It always speaks of worshiping Allah directly:

فَلَآ أَعْبُدُ ٱلَّذِينَ تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَكِنْ أَعْبُدُ ٱللَّهَ ٱلَّذِى يَتَوَفَّىٰكُمْ

The Qur'an did not say:

ِ وَلَكِنْ أَعْبُدُ اسم ٱللَّهَ ٱلَّذِى يَتَوَفَّىٰكُمْ

In the same way, the ultimate praise, الحمد, is never given to the name of Allah. The ultimate praise is always associated directly with Allah Himself. So the Qur'an says:

الحمد للہ رب العلمین

The Qur'an does not say:

الحمد اسمِ اللہ رب العلمین

So worship and ultimate praise belong ONLY to Allah Himself, and not to His name. But تبارک and تسبیح and تذکر — these can belong both to Allah and to the name of Allah. We can say that we glorify and exalt Allah, and the name of Allah. We can say that Allah is blessed, and the name of Allah is blessed. We can say that we remember Allah, and the name of Allah. But we worship Allah alone, AND we praise Allah alone.

So the reason we have بسم اللہ is simply this: to mention Allah's name is itself an act of glorification; to mention Allah's name is itself a way of acquiring His blessings; to mention Allah's name is itself a way of remembering Him. And that is why:

سَبِّحِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ

And therefore also بسم اللہ — with the name of Allah we begin. Because the mere mention of Allah's name is a blessing in and of itself; simply mentioning Allah's name draws His blessings, His barakah, into our lives.

But when it comes to actual worship, it is أَعْبُدُ ٱللَّهَ, and when it comes to actual praise, it is الحمد للہ.

Barakah

أنی اذا اُطِعتُ رَضِیتُ. وأذا رَضِیتُ بَارَکتُ. وَ لَیسَ لِبَرَکَتِی نِھَایَۃ

When you obey Me, it pleases Me; when I am pleased, I bless you; and there is no limit to My blessings.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
Now, what is the purpose of saying the Basmallah before we begin something? In the last verse of Surah al-Rahman, Allah AWJ says:

تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ ذِى ٱلْجَلَلِ وَٱلْإِكْرَامِ

The name of Allah.

the name of your master, who is glorious and benevolent. His name is full of barakah. The name of Allah is full of barakah: تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ. But in this verse Allah does not mention which name is full of barakah. He only says that the name of your master is full of barakah. So with what did this surah begin? With al-Rahman! And what is the first attribute of Allah mentioned in the Basmallah? Bismillahi, AL-RAHMAN, al-Raheem. So Allah is telling us something about the word al-Rahman. In Surah al-Rahman, Allah is saying that this name of Allah with which I began, meaning al-Rahman, is full of barakah.

But we also know that Allah Himself is full of barakah, because He says so in the Qur'an: تبرک اللہ احسن الخالقین — your Allah, who is the best of creators, is full of barakah! In this last verse of Surah al-Rahman, however, He does not say تبرک اللہ; He is not speaking about Himself. He is speaking about His name. He says تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ — the name al-Rahman of your master is full of barakah. So Allah is full of barakah, and His name al-Rahman is full of barakah. Do you understand? Now, when we recite the Basmallah, are these two names present in that verse? Bismi ALLAHI ALRAHMAN al-Raheem. Both Allah and al-Rahman, both names of barakah, are used in the Basmallah.

So the reason we recite the Basmallah, the reason we mention Allah's name before beginning a task, is for barakah. This Basmallah is so full of barakah that the mention of it spills that barakah out into the task we are about to perform. And by reciting the Basmallah before every task we are about to perform, we are intentionally asking Allah to bless the task with the barakah of His names in the Basmallah.

Now, there is no word in the English language that can fully encompass the meaning of the word barakah. So we need to understand this word barakah through certain concepts. In Arabic, barakah is defined thus: البرکۃُ النَّماَءُ وَ الزِّیَادَۃ. The first meaning of barakah is growth: something that rises, something that increases, something that makes progress, something that goes further and further and increases فوق التوقع, beyond expectations. If you plant a seed in the ground, how many trees do you expect? Just one! But if you put one seed in the ground and you get ten trees, with fruits producing hundreds of thousands of seeds, that is barakah. You planted one seed and eventually got thousands of seeds; that is growth beyond expectations, and that is what you call barakah. Barakah means: logic says I should get one tree, but I got a whole forest. How did that happen? That is barakah. And what is the comparison of a tree with a seed? There is no comparison; it is beyond comparison. A seed is tiny, a tree is huge; a seed is delicate, a tree is firm; a seed has no value, a tree bears hundreds upon hundreds of fruits, season after season after season, for years and years and years. If you really think about it, what we get from a tree, compared to a seed, there is no comparison. Yet that entire tree came from that one seed. SubhanAllah! That is barakah: unprecedented growth, unlimited increase.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
The linguistic meaning of the name of Allah is "the [sole] deity that deserves to be worshiped." The word "Allah" comes from the root aliha ya'lahu (bi ma'na "abada ya'budu"). He is the ultimate being who is worthy of being worshiped.

Greatest Name

It is said [2] that "Allah" is His Greatest Name, because it is referred to when describing Allah by the various attributes.

For instance, Allah said:

هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِى لاَ إِلَـهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ عَالِمُ الْغَيْبِ وَالشَّهَـدَةِ هُوَ الرَّحْمَـنُ الرَّحِيمُ

He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِى لاَ إِلَـهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ الْمَلِكُ الْقُدُّوسُ السَّلَـمُ الْمُؤْمِنُ الْمُهَيْمِنُ الْعَزِيزُ الْجَبَّارُ الْمُتَكَبِّرُ سُبْحَـنَ اللَّهِ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ

He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Bestower of Faith, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.

هُوَ اللَّهُ الْخَـلِقُ الْبَارِىءُ الْمُصَوِّرُ لَهُ الاٌّسْمَآءُ الْحُسْنَى يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ مَا فِى السَّمَـوَتِ وَالاٌّرْضِ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ

He is Allah, the Creator, the Inventor, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names. Whatever is in the heavens and earth is exalting Him. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise. [Quran, 59:22-24]

Hence, Allah mentioned several of His Names as Attributes for His Name "Allah." Similarly, Allah said:

وَللَّهِ الأَسْمَآءُ الْحُسْنَى فَادْعُوهُ بِهَا

And (all) the Most Beautiful Names belong to Allah, so call on Him by them. [Quran, 7:180]

How the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Quran

Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), when asked about the recitation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, said: "His recitation would be elongated, then he recited 'بسم الله الرحمان الرحيم,' elongating Bismillah, elongating Ar-Rahman, and elongating Ar-Rahim." [Sahih Al-Bukhari; 6/513, no. 566]

الحَمْدُ للهِ الَّذَي لاَ يَبْلُغُ مِدْحَتَهُ القَائِلُونَ، وَلاِ يُحْصِي نَعْمَاءَهُ العَادُّونَ، ولاَ يُؤَدِّي حَقَّهُ الُمجْتَهِدُونَ۔ الَّذِي لاَ يُدْركُهُ بُعْدُ الهِمَمِ، وَلاَ يَنَالُهُ غَوْصُ الفِطَنِ۔ الَّذِي لَيْسَ لِصِفَتِهِ حَدٌّ مَحْدُودٌ، وَلاَ نَعْتٌ مَوْجُودٌ، وَلا وَقْتٌ مَعْدُودٌ، وَلا أَجَلٌ مَمْدُودٌ۔ فَطَرَ الخَلائِقَ بِقُدْرَتِهَ، وَنَشَرَ الرِّيَاحَ بِرَحْمَتِهِ، وَوَتَّدَ بِالصُّخُورِ مَيَدَانَ أَرْضِهِ.

What did he say? (translation)

لَمْ تَرَكَ الْعُيُونُ؟ فَتُخْبِرَ عَنْكَ! بَلْ كُنْتَ قَبْلَ الْوَاصِفِينَ مِنْ خَلْقِكَ،
How could the eyes possess the strength to behold Your manifestation and carry word of You? Rather, You existed before those of Your creation who describe You.

لَمْ تَخُلُقِ الْخَلْقَ لِوَحْشَة، وَلاَ اسْتَعْمَلْتَهُمْ لِمَنْفَعَة
You did not create this world out of loneliness, nor did You make it for any benefit to Yourself.

وَلاَ يَسْبِقُكَ مَنْ طلَبْتَ، وَلاَ يُفْلِتُكَ مَنْ أَخَذْتَ،
Whomever You choose to seize cannot flee from You, and whomever You take hold of cannot slip from Your grasp.

وَلاَ يَنْقُصُ سُلْطَانَكَ مَنْ عَصَاكَ، وَلاَ يَزِيدُ في مُلْكِكَ مَنْ أَطَاعَكَ،
No one who disobeys You can diminish Your sovereignty, and no one who obeys You can enlarge Your sovereignty.

وَلاَيَرُدُّ أَمْرَكَ مَنْ سَخِطَ قَضَاءَكَ، وَلاَيَسْتَغْنِي عَنْكَ مَنْ تَوَلَّى عَنْ أَمْرِكَ
Whoever opposes Your decree cannot reverse it, and whoever turns his face from Your command cannot do without You.

كُلُّ سِرٍّ عِنْدَكَ عَلاَنِيَةٌ، وَكُلُّ غَيْب عِنْدَكَ شَهَادَةٌ
Before You every secret is plain to see, and before You every hidden thing is present.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
They say أبترکت السمآء, which means the rain keeps on coming and coming; so continuity is another characteristic of the word barakah, something that stays constant. You cook food for two people, and suddenly ten guests show up at your door. You all sit down to eat, and from that same food meant for two people, twelve people eat and they leave completely satisfied. That is barakah. That is not logical.

You cooked for only two people. It should not have been enough to satisfy twelve. Yet it satisfies them completely. How did that happen? That is barakah. This actually happened in the time of Ali ibn Sayyidina Sulayman. QRI started this session with five people. Now I have more people in the group than Skype allows. How did that happen? I did nothing. I did not go out inviting people. Yet I ended up with so many more people in the group. This is barakah. Why? Because we are mentioning the name of Allah. Because we are speaking about Allah, and about al-Rahman and al-Rahim.

So the meaning of barakah is growth or increase beyond expectation. Barakah is also used elsewhere in the Arabic language. For example, the Arabs would say: أِذا أَناَخَ الْجَمَل. When the camel settles onto the ground and does not move or budge, that too is barakah. And this is truly beautiful. Because when you grow something, and you grow it too much—I will give an example so that you can understand. When children play with Legos, they build up a huge tower, just block upon block upon block, correct? Now, as the tower grows tall, does it become more stable, or does it become less stable? It becomes less stable. The taller the tower, the less stable it becomes. Eventually it will fall and break, and there will be no tower anymore. Is that not true?

So when something increases rapidly, and increases too much, it becomes less stable. But when something has barakah, it means that the thing will increase, and keep increasing beyond expectation, yet remain as stable as a camel sunk into the sand. Subhan Allah! In other words, do not think this increase will go away. It is not an unstable increase.

We know about unstable increase when we look all around us. Our economy rises very fast, and then what happens? It comes down very fast. There are governments that take over very fast, and then disappear just as fast. Look at the fashion industry. There are trends that catch on very fast, and then vanish just as fast, and something else takes their place. But Allah says that barakah is something that increases and yet remains stable. It stays. It does not go away.

And Allah says that His name is full of barakah. What does that mean? It means that the name of Allah, and the name of al-Rahman, is being mentioned—from the day creation came into existence, and it only increases and grows with every single passing moment, and it will continue to grow until the very end of creation. Allah and His name will remain forever, because they are full of barakah. Worshippers come and go, but the One who is worshipped remains. Those who glorify the names of Allah come and go. Many came before us, and many will come after us. We will all pass away, but the glory of Allah will always remain. This is the barakah of the name of Allah.

Barr is optimistic in nature.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
And what does this mean to us? How do we take advantage of this in our daily lives? It means that we mention the name of Allah. When we recite the basmalah, it contains the two names of Allah that are full of barakah. When we call upon the barakah of these names, then whatever we do will produce good, and it will produce good that is more than expected. Its growth will continue, and it will not disappear. Not only that, it will also be stable. It will keep going and going and going. Because of this basmalah, every single Muslim is meant to be an optimist, even if the task at hand apparently fails.

From that failure there will be growth. The temporary failure will produce spiritual growth and lead to bigger and better tasks. And because the name of Allah was mentioned before we began the task, with the intention of calling upon His blessing, that task will be recorded in our book of deeds, and its reward will keep accumulating for the hereafter. This is because the very mention of the name of Allah has now made it an act of worship. So if it takes me ten hours to complete that task, I have just performed ten hours of worship, simply by reciting the basmalah at the beginning of the task. The time it takes me to complete it is earning me rewards. And after I have completed the task, the effect of what I have produced is going to keep earning rewards for me for as long as it is fulfilling its purpose. Just consider that. Reciting one basmalah, with the right intention, and see the amount of reward it accumulates. So the basmalah before a task is the seed of blessing that we plant, which then blossoms into thousands upon thousands of trees bearing uncountable fruits of reward for us. SubhanAllah!

Every single good deed is an act of blessing. You help one single person. You teach one single person. And you do not know: what if that person ends up becoming a great scholar? He ends up teaching thousands of students, and you keep receiving a share of the reward in all his accomplishments, for as long as he is teaching and students are benefiting from him. And then some of those students become teachers, and they spread that knowledge, and the reward for all of this is accumulating in your book of deeds, because all of it started with the seed you planted, because you started that person on his journey. This is blessing! All by reciting the basmalah before beginning a good task. We cannot calculate the results that stem from the basmalah, because they are from Allah, and they will grow and grow beyond human expectation. Common sense, logic, and mathematics cannot capture it within themselves; they cannot encompass it.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
Now let us look at the word اللہ. Why did Allah choose this name to be His primary name? Not only in the basmalah, but also in numerous other places in the Qur'an. Over three thousand five hundred times the word اللہ is used in the Qur'an. There is no other name of Allah that even comes close to the number of times that this name is mentioned. What is the meaning of this beautiful divine name, Allah? It is the first name mentioned in the Qur'an, in the first surah, Al-Fatiha: بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم، الحمد للہ رب العالمین. And it is also the name mentioned in the last surah of the Qur'an, Surah An-Nas: الہ الناس. And even in our daily lives, Allah is the primary name we use. We say, "Oh Allah, give me this. Oh Allah, help me with this. Oh Allah, protect me from that." We use His actual name, His most glorified name, when we are addressing Him or referring to Him in our daily lives.

Now let us look at what this name means, and why our Creator, why our Master, chose this name for Himself. And this is not a name that is unique to our religion of Islam. Quite the contrary: this is the name that Allah chose for Himself and mentioned in every past scripture. Even in the Old and New Testaments we find the name Allah, in its Hebrew form. In the Old Testament, we find that God refers to Himself as eloh, أِلَوہ, and ألوھیم — Allah and Allahumma — and in the New Testament as well.

When they crucified Eisa (AS), the Bible records his words as: الائی الائی لما سبختنی، الائی الائی لما ترکتنی — "My Allah, my Allah, why did you abandon me?" Even the Nabateans, a very ancient people who lived six thousand years ago, called the ultimate god Allah in their own script; the name is Allah. These Nabateans had many idols, a great many idols of all their various gods, yet they had no idol and no physical form for this god Allah. In other words, even they understood that this Allah was too holy for them to depict, for He is the God of all gods.

So the name Allah is in truth the primary name, one that is not particular to Islam but belongs to every past religion, revelation, and scripture, through all the ages, to every civilization and to every prophet.

ILAH ALLAH — NISBATAIN

So Allah is Ahad and He is Wahid. These two are called nisbatain, the two attributions: نسبت اعلیٰ اور نسبت ادنیٰ, the greater attribution and the lesser attribution. Both are correct, but one is greater than the other. Let me give you an example. A bulb turns on and lights the room. You can look at the effect and you can look at the cause. What is the effect? The room lights up; there is brightness, there is warmth, there is a glow — all of this is the effect of the bulb turning on. And you say, "Wow, that is so amazing!" What are you praising? You are praising the effect produced by the bulb turning on.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
But there is another way to look at it: focus on the cause. What caused the bulb to light up? It was not the bulb itself, but the electricity that heated the filament inside the bulb and made it glow so brightly that it lit up the entire room. And when you realize this, again you say, "Wow, that is so amazing!" The same words again, but this time not because of the effect, but because of the cause that produced the effect. So you said, "Wow, that is so amazing," while observing the effect, and you said, "Wow, that is so amazing," while observing the cause. Both are accurate, but the amazement over the cause is of a higher rank than the amazement over the effect. Do you understand? You can appreciate the cause and you can appreciate the effect, but the appreciation of the cause is of a higher rank than the appreciation of the effect. Why? Because if there were no cause, there would be no effect. If there were no cause, there would be no effect! So in essence the praise, the amazement, is really only for the cause and not for the effect, is it not? Your appreciation of the effect becomes embedded in your appreciation of the cause. You need only appreciate the power of the electricity and the internal design of the bulb, and that appreciation will already contain within it the appreciation of the bulb turning on and lighting up a room. Does that make sense?

So Ahad and Wahid are both attributions, but Ahad is greater in rank than Wahid. Why? Because Ahad is the cause and Wahid is the effect. Wahid, or one, exists in the physical dimension. If I ask you how many Allahs you believe in, you will have to tell me that you believe in one Allah. But why is He one? He is one because He is unique, for when something is unique, what can it only be? It can only be one! If there were more than one of that thing, it would no longer be unique. So Allah is one, He is Wahid, because He is Ahad first. He is Ahad first, unique first, and that is what makes Him Wahid.

That is what makes Him one. So Ahad is the cause, and Wahid is the effect. And for this reason, from the standpoint of tawheed, we believe Allah to be Ahad. We choose the cause, because we know that the cause will inevitably resolve into its effect, which is oneness.

In the Arabic language there is a thing called Ishtiqaaq. Ishtiqaaq means that a word is built upon another word; it came from somewhere else. For example, you may have heard the word Aalim. It is mushtaq — it is derived from another word, Ilm, which means knowledge. So here you have one word derived from another word; it has its origin or its roots somewhere else. A word of this kind is called Mushtaq, meaning that it is a word, but its origin is some other word. It rests upon another word.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
Then there are words that are original. You cannot trace them back to any other word. They are as they are, and there is no going further back. These are the originals, the untraceable words, and they are called اسماء الجامدۃ. Jamid means solid. It has no building blocks. So it is like comparing a wall to a boulder. A wall is made up of bricks; it is a whole made up of parts. But a boulder is simply a boulder; it is not made up of anything else. It is one solid lump of mass. So the Ism Jamid is not made up of parts, whereas the Ism Mushtaq is made up of parts. Now which is the cause and which is the effect? Jamid is the cause, and mushtaq is the effect, because Alim exists only because Ilm exists.

So why am I telling you all of this? I am telling you all of this in order to explain the word Allah to you. Allah is a very unique word. There is no other word in the entire Arabic language that matches this pattern. It is the only word that is both Jamid and Mushtaq. It is both cause and effect, both at the same time. So the word Allah has two attributions, just as the tawheed of Allah has two attributions: a higher attribution, which is jamid, and a lower attribution, which is mushtaq.

Let us begin with the mushtaq, from our example: the wall that is made up of bricks. From this perspective, the word Allah is derived from the word Ilah. What does this divine name Allah mean? I am going to go over some of its meanings.

Mushtaq

The name Allah comes from the root word وَلِھَا. Waleha means to become astounded, to become astonished, to become amazed. It is as though the person who tries to think of Allah will become amazed and astonished, for you cannot understand who Allah, SWT, is. Allah is the One who, if you try to comprehend Him, you will fail; if you try to walk toward Him, you will exhaust yourself and never reach Him; if you let your thoughts and imaginations take flight toward Him, you will lose your wings and still not reach Him. Allah is an Entity beyond our comprehension.

The Sayings of Mawlana Ali

Another interpretation of Waliha is to lose one's mind because of the loss of a beloved. That is why in Arabic the mother who loses her son is called مُوَلَّا. This is the mother who suffers the extreme pain and grief of losing her child; she is called مُوَلَّا. Now, how does this relate to the name Allah? The one who does not have Allah in his life suffers from this same kind of ultimate grief and madness. The one who does not believe in Allah, the one who has no connection with Allah, is as though he is going to lose his mind, because there is nothing in his life to give him value, to give him meaning, if you do not believe in Allah.

If you have no concept of a god in your life, then your life has no purpose. This is one interpretation that is offered.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
Another interpretation is that the name Allah comes from اَلَہَ یَعلُہُ. Aliha literally means to worship. So Ilah is the entity that is the focus of worship and obedience. That is one meaning of the word aliha. Another meaning is the one to whom you turn for protection, the one to whom you turn for refuge. Therefore Allah is the one to whom each and every created being must turn for protection, the one to whom they must turn for refuge, for no one can exist without turning to Allah for their every single need. This is also the meaning of the name الصمد. Samad is the one to whom every being turns for every need, while he himself has no needs.

Another interpretation is that the name Allah comes from اَلِہَ, which is used of a child who is thirsty for the milk of its mother and is crying desperately for it. That is aliha. The verbal meaning derived from it is: the one to whom people turn in desperation in need of help. Ilah, or ilha—in fact, the masdar form—is the one to whom people turn for help in desperation.

On the basis of this, the scholars discuss that Ilah is the one who is to be worshiped, the one who is to be obeyed, and the one to whom people turn in desperation. There is nowhere else to turn but Allah. It comes from the words لاَہَ یَلِیہُ, and this means to be raised up. Therefore the one who believes in Allah has raised himself up, in this world and in the next. The one who believes in Allah will be honored, in this life and in the life to come.

Allah comes from the root word Ilah. Ilah is a generic term, close to the word God. It is a very rich word, a composite word, and it carries a whole range of meanings. The word Ilah means an entity that is worthy of worship, a deity. Ilah is also the object of devotion and love. Ilah is someone you turn to in desperate times. Ilah is also someone with whom you are passionately in love, someone you cannot stop thinking about. The word love is already embedded in the word ilah. And literally speaking, the word Ilah means something you lean on. When you are exhausted and you lean on something, that thing is literally called الہ.

Now the word Ilah is generic. There are several people I could love. There are several people I could turn to for help in desperate times. I could be in love with more than one person in a lifetime. I love someone intensely; things go bad; I can then fall in love with someone else. So the word Ilah is a generic term that could apply to multiple entities.

But when I apply the definite article to the word Ilah, when I add the alamat al-ma'rifa, al, to Ilah, then that particular Ilah becomes Allah. So Allah is in fact the Ilah. Allah is al plus Ilah; the two fuse together to form the word Allah. The al adds the clause of exclusivity to this Ilah. Now Ilah is no longer generic; it is an exclusive Allah. What does that mean? It means that Allah is the only one I will love. Allah is the only one I will turn to for help in desperate times. Allah is the only one with whom I am going to be madly and passionately in love. Allah is the only one on whom I will fully and completely lean.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
Jamid. Allah is the universal word for Allah, and it is not a derivative of another word. Allah is the word Allah chose for himself in every other language, and it is the name he revealed as his proper name to all the messengers, in all languages.

On the surface this sounds more like a matter of spiritual belief, while the other point sounds like a linguistic reality. But there is linguistic evidence for this as well, and I want to discuss at least a couple of examples.

We said that the derived form of Allah is in fact a compound of two words, al and ilah. Now, in the Arabic language, when you call out to someone, you use the word ya. For example, ya walad, ya rajul. But in the Arabic language I cannot add the definite article al to a word when I use ya. So I cannot say ya al-walad, or ya al-rajul. That would make no sense; that would be grammatically wrong. I cannot even use it for his ninety-nine attributes. Even though in their original form the attributes carry an al with them—we have الرحمن, الرحيم, الملك, القدوس, do we not?—when I call upon these attributes using ya, I have to drop the al. I cannot say ya al-raheem; I have to say ya raheem. I cannot say ya al-rahman; I have to say ya rahman. Ya malik, ya quddoos, ya mu'min, ya muhaimin. So even when referring to Allah's attributes, I cannot use the al with any of them. But when we call upon Allah, what do we say? We say ya Allah, which we know is in fact ya al-ilah. And we do that all the time. So in this linguistic sense, Allah no longer remains a derived word; it no longer remains a compound word. It becomes jamid, a solid word. Because when we say ya Allah, the al is clearly still there, and if it is there, then it is there because it is not really an al. It is part of the actual word itself. If that were not so, we would call him ya ilah; the al would have to be dropped. But we do not do that. We call him ya Allah. So that means the al is part of his name.

Second, the word Allah is never used generically anywhere in the Qur'an as an attribute. For ilah, or ilahiyat, is an attribute. But in the Qur'an he is not referred to as the ilah. He is referred to directly as Allah. And the greatest proof is in the basmalah itself. The verse says بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم—I begin with the name of Allah, who is Rahman and Raheem. Rahman and Raheem are descriptions, but Allah is the one being described. Allah is the noun, and Rahman and Raheem are the adjectives. Allah is the noun; rabb al-alameen, al-rahman al-raheem, malik yawm al-deen—these are all adjectives. Therefore Allah is the original name itself. It is jamid.

Then, in the context of Surah al-Ikhlas, we see that the disbelievers asked the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: Tell us, who is your Lord? Who is your master? Whenever such a question is asked—who is he? whom do you worship? what do you worship?—you do not answer with the descriptions; you always begin with the name. So this surah begins, ھو اللہ احد اللہ الصمد. Ahad can be a description, samad can be a description, but Allah itself is the proper name.
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
So this word defies every grammatical principle. We break the norm of the Arabic language for this word, and for this word alone. It defies every grammatical principle of the Arabic language. For that reason alone it is considered universal, a jamid.

One more point, more of an aside. As I mentioned, Allah was used in all the earlier languages; it was used in Hebrew, in Aramaic, and in all the earlier languages. So was this word Allah, then, a foreign word imported into the Arabic language? Well, the grammatical proof concerning that is this: when a foreign word is brought into the Arabic language, you cannot place a kasra, a zer, on it—that is a grammatical rule. So if Allah is a foreign word,

then we can have Allahu. we can have Allaha. But we cannot have Allahee. That is according to the principles of Arabic grammar. ممنوع من الصرف. ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ۚ لَيَجْمَعَنَّكُمْ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَمَةِ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ ۗ وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ حَدِيثًۭا. There is a kasra on the word Allah, which means it is not a foreign word. And if it is a word belonging to every language, and if it was a word taught to all the messengers, Arab and non-Arab alike, then how is it that it carries the kasra throughout the Qur'an? Therefore there is only one possible explanation: that the word Allah must be universal to all languages. Foreign things are those that are alien to me and native to you. But what word is native to every language? And who is native to every language? Allah, may His glory be exalted. So the notion of being foreign does not apply when we are dealing with the word of majesty.

Seeking Help

The "B" [بِ] in Bismillah is a "B" [ب] of Isti'anah (استعانة), which means "seeking help." So, we empower ourselves by seeking Allah's help before beginning an action.

Incomplete Sentence

Allah left the phrase "Bismillah" as an incomplete sentence. When we say "With the name of Allah," the verb or action is missing from the sentence. It is not included because the context of where it is used completes the meaning. For instance, when we say Bismillah before reading, the context and intention deliver the meaning as "With the name of Allah, I begin reading." Therefore, the phrase can be used in different situations.

Before the Action

Scholars also say that the phrase Bismillah should come before the action. Although it is acceptable as a sentence construction to say, for example, "I read with the name of Allah," there are two reasons why Bismillah should come first (that is, "With the name of Allah, I read"):

To seek blessings by beginning with the name of Allah first and not with your action.

To express the fact that the action is only for Allah. In the Arabic language, when you delay the verb, it signifies exclusivity. So, when we place our action or verb after "With the name of Allah," it means beginning exclusively with Allah's Name, seeking His help alone and solely for His sake.

The Basmalah is used for three primary reasons:

Ikhlaas (Sincerity) — the action is for His sake alone;

Barakah — seeking His help and blessing for the action;

Qabool (Acceptance) — that Allah accepts and is pleased with our action.

Meaning of the Name "Allah"

Linguistic or Literal Meaning

The term "Allah" is derived from a contraction of the Arabic definite article al- "the" and ilāh "deity, god" to al-lāh, meaning "the [sole] deity, God." [Encyclopedia of Islam]
body.topic_title_en: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

body.text_en:
All praise belongs to God; we are beginning our study of this remarkable surah, Surah al-Fatiha. Before we begin, there are a few things I want to mention, so that you have a sense of our overall aim here. Because some members have joined us only recently, I want to make sure we are all of one mind before we go any further.

One of the reasons I wanted to study this surah together with all of you is to offer a taste, a kind of example, of how the Qur'an is meant to be studied. We are forever hearing people say that you really ought to study the Qur'an, that it is so remarkable, so astonishing; yet we are never actually given the chance to see a practical example of what that means. What does it mean to undertake an in-depth study of the Qur'an? What is so remarkable about the words of the Qur'an that people keep speaking of? In these sessions, I hope to give you a practical demonstration of that idea. God willing, by the end of this surah, by the end of this study, you will be able to appreciate a few things.

First, the power of the Arabic language. And I do not mean colloquial Arabic, or formal Arabic, or even ancient Arabic; when I say to learn Arabic, I mean specifically the Arabic of the Qur'an. God willing, we will also try to address certain misconceptions.

One common misconception about the Qur'an is that we can understand this book on our own. Trust me when I tell you that we cannot. As you will soon see, God willing, this text is too profound for us to grasp by our own efforts alone. We need a guide, a teacher, an Imam or a Da'i who can solve the various puzzles that lie within this book, because the Qur'an can at times appear deeply contradictory. You can come upon one passage of the Qur'an that seems to contradict another passage completely.

For example, the Qur'an says: فَإِذَا ٱلَّذِى بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُ عَدَوَةٌۭ ؛ كَأَنَّهُ وَلِىٌّ حَمِيمٌۭ — this is said in the course of speaking about the call to faith and the ethics of that call. When you deal with those who deny the faith, God says: even if there is enmity between you and the other, treat him as though he were your most intimate friend. But then, in a different passage, speaking of those who deny the faith, God says: وَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ حَيْثُ ثَقِفْتُمُوهُمْ وَأَخْرِجُوهُم مِّنْ حَيْثُ أَخْرَجُوكُمْ ۚ وَٱلْفِتْنَةُ أَشَدُّ مِنَ ٱلْقَتْلِ — kill them wherever you find them, and drive them out from wherever they drove you out; the trial, the persecution, and the corruption they are causing is worse than their fighting.

So on the one hand we are told to treat them as our closest friends, and on the other hand we are told to kill them and drive them out. It looks like a grave contradiction. And it remains a contradiction until you understand the context of both verses, and only someone learned in the study of the Qur'an can explain that context to us. Once we understand that context, we discover that there is no contradiction between the two, because content set apart from its context is disastrous. Content set apart from its context is disastrous.

And the Qur'an, for reasons of great depth, does not explain the context; it delivers only the content. God does not say, "Look, one who denied the faith has just come to the Messenger of God in Mecca and asked him this particular question, and here is the answer to his question." The Qur'an does not do that. It simply answers the question. Now, why does it do this? It does it

to emphasize the need for one who can place this content in its proper context for us. This is why we have the institution of the Imamat and the duaat علیھم السلام, who supply us with the proper context for this content. It is why the Qur'an says, وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ — for every nation there has been a guide. This is a most interesting verse. When it speaks of the people, it uses the plural, قوم; but when it speaks of the guide, it uses the singular, ھاد. This is to stress that for every nation there will always be a single guide. Allah also says, فسْـَٔلُوٓا۟ أَهْلَ ٱلذِّكْرِ إِن كُنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ — ask the people of the book if you do not have the knowledge. This Qur'an is ذکر; it is remembrance. And the Imams are the اھل الذکر, the people of remembrance.

This is the beauty of the Qur'an, that it has separated the content from the context. The book holds the content, but only the people of the book, the اہل الذکر, possess the context for that content. So Allah divided the two, that each would be useless without the other. Consider how, in films about treasure hunts, the map that leads to the treasure is split into two parts and the parts are kept apart, so that only when one worthy of the treasure finds both pieces can he reach it. It is exactly the same here.

There is a very famous hadith of the Messenger of Allah (may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him): إِنِّی تَارِکٌ فِیکُمُ الثَّقَلَیْنِ مَا إِنْ تَمَسَّکْتُمْ بِهِمَا لَنْ تَضِلُّوا — I am leaving among you two precious things; as long as you remain connected with both, you will never be misguided. کِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَ عِتْرَتِی أَهْلَ بَیْتِی — the book of Allah and my progeny, the Ahl al-Bayt, the Imams who will come in my lineage. وَ إِنَّهُمَا لَنْ یَفْتَرِقَا — because, without a doubt, these two will not separate from each other. Which two? The Qur'an, the ذکر, and the Imams, the اہل الذکر, who hold the knowledge of the Qur'an; the two will never, ever separate from each other. حَتَّى یَرِدَا عَلَیَّ الْحَوْضَ — until they both reunite with me at the fountain. An extremely profound hadith. SubhanAllah.

So we need a guide who can place this miraculous content of the Qur'an in its proper context, that we may understand it. And because people disconnected from and abandoned the Ahl al-Bayt, because they abandoned the Imams and tried to understand the content of the Qur'an without the context of the Imamat, they went astray; and this Qur'an, this religion, turned from a message of peace into a message for terrorism.

On a tangent: if you can picture how every surah is connected to the surah before it and the surah after it, you can see that it forms the shape of a tasbeeh, a set of prayer beads, in which every bead is joined to the bead before it and the bead after it. And so if we compare these surahs to the beads of a tasbeeh, Surah Al-Fateha would without doubt be the Imam of that entire tasbeeh.

So that is what the word Surah means. Now let us look at the word Fateha.

The word Surah comes from the root word soor, which means the outer walls of a city. The word Fatiha comes from the root word فتح, which means "a way out." It is also the root word for فتح, which means victory. So Surah Al-Fateha gives us a way out of the situation we are stuck in, and it gives us victory over the challenges we face in life.

Then we spoke about why it is not just Fateha but Al-Fateha, meaning not just a way out but the best possible way out, and not just any victory but the ultimate victory. This best way out, however, and this ultimate victory rest not on our standards and goals but on Allah's standards and goals. If I have success at step one, which then results in failure at step two, then that success is not really a success. What matters is the final success. What matters is winning the war and not just the battles. So the Al in Fateha is the Al of faith. It is the Al of submission. It is the Al of trust in Allah, that O Allah, whatever outcome You decide for me is the best possible outcome for me.

10 names of Fateha

Fateha is in fact referred to by ten different names. I am not going to go through each and every one of them, but I will go over the important and more common ones with you, InshaAllahu Ta'ala!

Al-Faateha

The first name of this Surah is Al-Fateha itself, which means "The Opening Surah." The word fateha means opening. It is also called Fatehatul Kitaab, meaning The Opening of the Book. And this word Fatehatul Kitaab is mentioned by our beloved prophet Muhammad Mustafa (SAS) in various famous Ahadees. In one hadees he said:

مَن لَم یَقرأُ فَاتِحَۃُ الکتابْ ؛ فَلَیسَ مِنَّا

He who does not recite the Opening of the Book, he is not from among us. Meaning he has nothing to do with us!

What this means is that every single Muslim, man, woman, and child, must memorize Surah Fateha. If you do not know Surah Fateha, you are not a Muslim, because Rasul Allah said whoever does not recite; and when the ancient Arabs say یقرا, the interpretation is not just recitation. It is not just یقرأ, it also means یحفظ, to memorize. Therefore Rasul Allah says he who does not memorize Surah Al-Fateha has nothing to do with us. And we know that every single Muslim in the world has a relationship with Surah Al-Fateha. Even those who do not pray regularly, they know Surah Al-Fateha.

In another narration it is said that Rasul Allah (SAS) said to Ubay Ibn Ka'ab, a great sahaabi:

أَلَا أُعَلِّمُكَ سُورَةً مَا أُنْزِلَتْ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ ؛ وَلَا فِي الْإِنْجِيلِ ؛ وَلَا فِي الزَّبُورِ ؛ وَلَا فِي الْقُرْآنِ مِثْلُهَ؟

Would you like me to teach you a Surah, the likes of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms (Zabur), nor the Qur'an? He said: Of course, Yaa Rasulallah!

He said: Listen! It is Surah Al-Fateha!

He also said: Should I not inform you about the BEST Surah in the entire Qur'an?

أَلَا أُخْبِرُكَ بِأَخْيَرِ سُورَةٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ؟

Listen! It is Surah Al-Fateha! he said.

In another narration by Ibn Abbas, he says that Rasul Allah (SAS) said that one day he was sitting next to Jibreel (AS) when he suddenly heard a very loud cracking sound coming from above. Jibreel (AS) lifted his head and said: "Ya Rasul Allah! This is an angel descending from the skies to the earth, who has never descended before, and will never descend again after this day." When that angel arrived, he greeted Rasul Allah and said:

أَبْشِرْ بِنُورَيْنِ أُوتِيتَهُمَا ؛ لَمْ يُؤْتَهُمَا نَبِيٌّ كَانَ قَبْلَكَ

He said: Be pleased with two sources of light, two noor, which no other prophet has been given before you.

فَاتِحَةُ الْكِتَابِ وَخَوَاتِيمُ سُورَةِ الْبَقَرَةِ،

It is the Fatihatul Kitab and the Khawateem Al-Baqara. The opening of the Qur'an and the closing verses of Surah Baqarah.

لَمْ تَقْرَأْ مِنْهُمَا حَرْفًا إِلا أُعْطِيتَهُ

You will never recite even a single letter of these verses without receiving a reward for it. Meaning, anything you ask for after reciting these verses will be granted to you.

Again, in this hadees, the word used is فاتحۃ الکتاب, the opening of the book, which is Surah Al-Fateha, and the last three verses of Surah Al-Baqara, which are:

لِّلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَإِن تُبْدُوا۟ مَا فِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَوْ تُخْفُوهُ يُحَاسِبْكُم بِهِ ٱللَّهُ ۖ فَيَغْفِرُ لِمَن يَشَآءُ وَيُعَذِّبُ مَن يَشَآءُ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدِيرٌ

To Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and on the earth. Whether you reveal what is in your heart, or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He will forgive whom He pleases and punish whom He pleases; and Allah has power over all things!

آمَنَ ٱلرَّسُولُ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْهِ مِن رَّبِّهِ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ ۚ كُلٌّ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَمَلَٓئِكَتِهِ وَكُتُبِهِ وَرُسُلِهِ ؛ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍۢ مِّن رُّسُلِهِ ۚ وَقَالُوا۟ سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا ۖ غُفْرَانَكَ رَبَّنَا وَإِلَيْكَ ٱلْمَصِيرُ

The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Master, and so do the believers. They all believe in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers. They say, "We make no distinction between any of His messengers." And they say, "We hear and we obey! Grant us Your forgiveness our Master, and You are the final destination of all journeys."

لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا ۚ لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ ۗ رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَآ إِن نَّسِينَآ أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا ۚ رَبَّنَا وَلَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَآ إِصْرًۭا كَمَا حَمَلْتَهُۥ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِنَا ۚ رَبَّنَا وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِۦ ۖ وَٱعْفُ عَنَّا وَٱغْفِرْ لَنَا وَٱرْحَمْنَآ ۚ أَنتَ مَوْلَىٰنَا فَٱنصُرْنَا عَلَى ٱلْقَوْمِ ٱلْكَفِرِينَ

Allah does not place a burden on any soul that is greater than what it can bear. It will enjoy the consequence of every good it earns, and will suffer the consequence of every evil it earns. "Our Master! do not condemn us if we forget or fall into error. Our Master! do not lay upon us a burden, like the one You laid upon those before us. Our Master! do not lay on us a burden that is greater than what we can bear. And pardon us; and grant us protection; and have mercy upon us!"

You are our protector! Grant us victory over those who stand against our faith."

These are the ten verses: the seven verses of Surah al-Fatiha and the last three verses of Surah al-Baqara, which were given to the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) as a special gift to him. We will, God willing, see that both contain the exact same message. May Allah grant us the good fortune and the wisdom to memorize these remarkable verses and to truly understand their meanings.

There is another hadith, one actually related to the one I just mentioned, in which the Messenger of Allah said, "I have been given the Opening of the Book from the treasures beneath the Throne." لقد أَعطَیتُ فاتحۃُ الکتابِ مِن کُنُوزِ تحت العرش

We know that Allah has a throne that extends over and encompasses the heavens and the earth: وسع کرسیہ السموات و الارض We covered the Verse of the Throne in our sessions on the miracles of the Qur'an. If you remember, this is the imagery the Qur'an uses to depict Allah's glory and His majesty. These are all metaphorical terms. The throne is an abstract symbol that stands for, or points to, a specific reality. It is not that Allah is seated like a king upon a huge chair. But the Qur'an is speaking to the Bedouin Arabs, and so Allah uses this imagery to help them grasp the abstract in terms they can relate to.

So in this hadith the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) says that this surah is from beneath the treasures of Allah's Throne. Now what does that mean? By the way, the word کُنُوزِ comes from the root word کنز, and کنز does not merely mean ordinary treasure. Treasure is a generic term. You have a great deal of gold and silver and rubies and diamonds; all of that is treasure, and the Arabic word for it is ثروۃ. کنز, on the other hand, is used for treasure that is priceless: the very best of the best.

So in this hadith, the image is of a mighty king seated upon a throne that has priceless treasures beneath it. Now, ordinarily a king's treasure would be kept in the treasury and not beneath his throne. But the imagery shows the closeness, or the priceless worth, of this treasure that the king keeps near his throne. The throne represents the majesty and glory of Allah, and this Surah al-Fatiha is among those verses that describe Allah's majesty and describe Allah's glory, as we will soon see, God willing. And that is why they have been symbolized as treasures beneath Allah's Throne. As the Messenger of Allah says, لقد أَعطَیتُ فاتحۃُ الکتابِ مِن کُنُوزِ تحت العرش I have been given Surah al-Fatiha, which is among the verses that best describe the majesty and glory of Allah. Glory be to Allah!

Besides Surah al-Fatiha, the other verses that are from the priceless treasure are the last two verses of Surah al-Baqara and the Verse of the Throne.

So these are some of the narrations that explain the power and magnificence of Surah al-Fatiha, or the Opening of the Book.

The Meaning of the Word Fatiha

Now let us understand the word Fatiha. What does the word Fatiha mean? This word is literally translated as the Opening, because it is the opening verses of the Qur'an. It opens up the Qur'an for the reader. When someone begins reciting the Qur'an, the first surah they will recite will be Surah al-Fatiha; that is why it is called the opening of the Qur'an. So that is the literal meaning.

From a linguistic standpoint, the root word of al-Fatiha is فتح, which means "the way out." You are stuck.

and al-Fatiha gives you the way out of the place in which you are stuck. From فتح also comes the word أفتاح, which is commonly translated as "open." An Arab, for example, would say افتاح الباب — open the door! But what it truly means is: find a way out of the situation in which you are stuck. When you want to enter a room and the door is closed, you are stuck outside. That door blocks your path; it keeps you from moving forward. When you open the door, فتحُ الباب gives you a way out, and you get past that obstacle. That is why the Arabs would say افتاح الباب, which from a linguistic standpoint means: find your way out, or through, that door. Do you understand?

So al-Fatiha truly implies "the way out" of a difficult situation. That is why, in Arabic, a victory comes from this same root, فتح. أذا جاء نصر اللہ و الفتح — here فتح means victory. You were stuck. You were surrounded by an enemy. Then فتح comes, victory comes your way, and you find your way out.

So al-Fatiha creates an opening for us through every difficult situation we face in life. If you are struggling in school and find yourself stuck, al-Fatiha will give you an opening through your difficulties. If you are worried about your child, who is stuck in a certain situation, al-Fatiha will create that opening for your child and carry him through the challenges he is facing. If you are surrounded by worries, difficulties, anxieties, and depressions, al-Fatiha will give you victory over your problems. Al-Fatiha provides a way out of every problem of our lives, be it small or large. When we are surrounded, when we are outnumbered, when we are helpless, when we can find no solution, al-Fatiha will create that solution for us. So this surah is a "way out" of all our problems in life. It is also a "victory" over each and every struggle that we face in life. That is the true meaning of Surah al-Fatiha. SubhanAllah!

Now let us speak about the ال in Surah al-Fatiha. It is not merely Surah Fatiha; it is Surah al-Fatiha. We have seen this ال before, in the context of علامۃ المعرفۃ, to make something prominent. Here it carries the meaning of "the best." It is the ال of faith. Al-Fatiha does not mean merely a "way out" or merely "victory." Al-Fatiha means the perfect way out and the ultimate victory. It does not merely provide another way out; it provides the way out, the best possible way out. But by whose standards? By your standards and mine? In accordance with your desires and mine? No. It is by Allah's standards and in accordance with Allah's desires.

So you may want a way out of your financial crisis. You recite al-Fatiha for that way out, yet you end up falling deeper into your crisis, because that is what Allah judges to be the best way out for you. You want to save your house. You keep reciting al-Fatiha for a way out of the bank's foreclosure, yet you still end up losing the house, because that is what Allah judges to be the best way out for you. This is why I said it is the ال of faith: the faith that if anything happens after I recite Surah al-Fatiha, then whatever happened was for my best, because many times we lose battles only to win the war in the end. Allah made you struggle through your financial crisis.

only so that it would force you to acquire better financial knowledge, better management skills that would help you in a future situation, and in the end you make a great deal of money because of the financial knowledge you gained, knowledge you would never have thought to acquire had you not failed in that financial crisis. Allah made you lose your house only to give you a bigger and better house in the future. He made you lose the job you so desperately wanted to hold on to only so that He could open many more doors with a far better job that He wanted you to have. So the ال in al-Fatiha is the ال of faith in Allah, the ال of trust in Allah, the ال of submission to Allah: that O Master, You know what is best for me, You know the best way out for me, You know how I am going to win the ultimate war even if I lose the battle at hand. All of that faith is held within the ال of al-Fatiha.

Now, how does reciting Surah al-Fatiha give me the best possible way out? How does reciting Surah al-Fatiha give me the ultimate victory? If I have an examination and I do not prepare for it, will simply reciting Surah al-Fatiha carry me through the examination? If I have a difficult marriage, if I have difficult children, if I have difficult parents, will simply reciting Surah al-Fatiha give me the best possible solution? Of course not.

It is not the mere recitation of Surah al-Fatiha but the practical application of the teachings and the concepts described in Surah al-Fatiha that gives us the best possible way out. It is applying the teachings of Surah al-Fatiha that gives us the ultimate victory over our challenges in life. It is not simply the verbal recitation but the practical application of what Surah al-Fatiha teaches that mends marriages, that mends problems in families, that mends problems in societies, that mends problems in nations. If I have an examination in school and I have not studied for it, I can recite Surah al-Fatiha until I am blue in the face, and I will still end up with an egg on my examination, I will still end up failing my examination.

So then what is the purpose of this recitation of Surah al-Fatiha? The purpose of the constant recitation of Surah al-Fatiha is the constant reminder of its teachings. By constantly reciting the seven ayats of Surah al-Fatiha, I am constantly reminding myself that I need to apply its teachings in every aspect of my life, because what is the Qur'an if not a reminder? Allah says to Rasul Allah SWS:

وَذَكِّرْ فَإِنَّ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ تَنفَعُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ

Remind them! For the reminder benefits the believers.

So the recitation of Surah al-Fatiha is a reminder of its teachings. When I say Bismillah al-Rehman al-Raheem, I am in reality reminding myself that I am beginning my task in the name of Allah, for the sake of Allah's pleasure, because I am going to be held accountable for this task before Him, so what I am about to do had better be something that meets with His approval. When I say Bismillah al-Rehman al-Raheem, I am also reminding myself that He is gracious, that He is merciful, that He will help me accomplish the task I am about to begin by eliminating, or at least reducing, the possible challenges that could stand in my way in accomplishing it. So the mere recitation of Bismillah al-Rehman al-Raheem is meant to remind me of Allah, of His mercy, of His glory, of His approval.

So if I am in the habit of reciting Bismillah al-Rehman al-Raheem before I begin anything, that alone will restrain me from sin. Once I have remembered Allah, once I have reminded myself of His mercy, it becomes impossible for me to sin. When I remind myself of His glory, it becomes impossible for me to stand against Him in battle. When I remind myself of His companionship and His help in the task I am about to perform, it becomes impossible for me to fear anyone, or to dread any disappointment. All of this comes from the recitation of Bismillah al-Rehman al-Raheem alone.

So to remind myself of Allah constantly, through the constant recitation of His verses, gives me the strength to discipline my life, to work hard, to study hard, to play fair, and to enjoy the blessings of life every single day. It makes Allah my North Star. It makes Allah my Qibla, my compass. It gives me the spiritual strength I need to study hard and with sincerity, to succeed in my exams and in any other challenge I may face in life. It reminds me that even if I lose every single time, and lose to every single person, and lose every single thing in this world, yet Allah is pleased with me, then I am truly successful. It reminds me that if I win every single time, and win over every single person, and acquire every single possession I have ever dreamed of, yet Allah is displeased with me, then I am truly unsuccessful.

When I am faced with challenges and situations I cannot control, the recitation of Surah al-Fateha is a reminder that I must submit myself to Allah completely, remembering that He is al-Rehman al-Raheem. He will take care of me. He is always there for me. It is a reminder that He will carry me through the situation in which I am trapped, and a reminder that He will carry me through it in the best possible way.

So it is not the mere recitation of this Surah, but the practical application of its teachings, that leads to the ultimate success — that leads to الفَتْحُ, which means the ultimate victory; that leads to الفَتَحَ, which means the best possible opening, the best possible way out from the place in which I am trapped. The recitation of Surah al-Fateha is meant to be a reminder of the teachings we will soon learn, insha'Allah. Every time you and I recite these verses, we must remind ourselves of their teachings, so that we can apply them in our daily lives. Without that application, the recitation of the Surah means absolutely nothing.

This Surah is called Fatehatul Kitaab because it opens the Book of the Qur'an for the reciter. This is a sign from Allah that we must make it the opening of the book of our own lives. Just as the Qur'an is a book, our lives are also a book, one that we are writing day by day. Every single day we fill a page of this book with our good and bad deeds. And when we die, this book that we wrote with our deeds will be handed to us, as Allah says:

وَكُلَّ إِنسَنٍ أَلْزَمْنَهُ طَٓئِرَهُ فِى عُنُقِهِۦ ۖ وَنُخْرِجُ لَهُۥ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَمَةِ كِتَبًۭا يَلْقَىٰهُ مَنشُورًا

And We have fastened every man's deeds to his neck, and on the Day of Resurrection We shall bring out for him a book which he will find wide open.

ٱقْرَأْ كِتَبَكَ! كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًۭا

Read your book today.

It is sufficient as an accountant against you. So Allah made this Surah the Fatehatul Kitaab—the opening of His book—as a sign and a reminder for us, that we too must make the teachings of this Surah, the Fatehatul Kitaab, the opening for the book of our lives, so that what we write in it meets with Allah's approval on the Day of Judgment. This Surah Al-Fateha not only guarantees a successful life for us in this world, but also in the hereafter. And that is why you and I need to try this out. We need to give this Surah a fair chance. We need to begin applying its teachings in our lives as we continue to learn it, each week, little by little, and see for ourselves whether it makes a difference in our lives or not.

How do we determine whether something works for us or not? By trying it out. So let us try out the teachings of this Surah together. May Allah give us the strength, the knowledge, and the wisdom to bring these teachings into our lives.

So that is the literal and linguistic meaning of the words Al-Fateha and Fatehatul Kitaab.

سورۃ الصلواۃ

Another name for Surah Al-Fateha is Surah Al-Salaah—the Surah of Prayer. There is a hadith that begins with Allah Himself saying: I have divided the salaah half and half between Myself and My slave. The hadith then goes on to explain Surah Al-Fateha itself. Allah says: when My slave says Alhamdulillahi Rabbil Alameen, I say this back to him; when he says Ar-Rahman Ar-Raheem, I say this back to him; and so on. But how does the hadith begin? It begins by saying: I have divided prayer into two halves, and it then goes on to explain Surah Al-Fateha. For this reason, one of the names of Surah Al-Fateha is also Surah As-Salaah, as if this Surah is the essence of the entire salaah.

Also, what is interesting is the first sentence of this hadith. Allah says to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him): قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين. I have divided the salaah between Myself and My slave into two halves—the first half is for Me, and the second half is for My slave. ولعبدي ما سأل And the half that belongs to My slave, he shall receive it. SubhanAllah! Allah says that the half which belongs to His slaves, they will receive it. He made it a condition upon Himself to grant us our portion whenever we turn to Him in salaah. He did not say that His slaves will receive their half only if they pay Him His half first. He did not say that. He said that even if they stand before Me once a day, once a week, once a month, once a year, I will give them their spiritual sustenance for that particular prayer. SubhanAllah! Just as we have our three or five physical meals a day to keep our bodies alive and healthy, Allah has destined five spiritual meals for us to keep our souls alive and healthy. In every salaah we stand before Allah to receive that spiritual portion from Him, and He says that My slave will receive their half when he stands before Me.

Now, what are these two halves? The first half is the right of the Creator over His creation, as their master. The second is the right of the creation over their Creator, as His slaves. I will say that again. Allah is our master. He created us from a drop of liquid, shaped us, and gave us life. He provides us daily with our spiritual and physical sustenance; He takes care of us. For all His numerous blessings, His uncountable blessings,

He holds the right over our souls. He holds the right over our souls that we acknowledge Him as our master, that we turn to Him in obedience, that we acknowledge our need of Him and His place in our lives. That is Allah's right over us, as our Creator.

Then, as His creation, we hold certain rights over Him. When we are in trouble, we have the right to call upon Him for help, as a child turns to its parents, as a slave turns to his master, as an animal turns to its owner for its bodily needs. Allah did not create us self-sufficient. Instead, He created us with needs. We have bodily needs. He created us weak, and so we turn to Him to make us strong. He created us with hunger, and so we turn to Him to provide us with food. He created us naked, and so we turn to Him to clothe us. So for all our bodily needs, we turn to our one and only Master, who is free of all needs.

Then, alongside our bodily needs, we have spiritual needs, and in the Salaah we turn to Him five times a day to receive our spiritual sustenance from Him. We are spiritually weak, and so we turn to Him to gain spiritual strength. We are spiritually starving, and so we turn to Him for His knowledge. We are spiritually naked, and so we turn to Him for His beautiful garments of piety.

يَبَنِىٓ آدَمَ قَدْ أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكُمْ لِبَاسًۭا يُوَرِى سَوْءَتِكُمْ وَرِيشًۭا

O Children of Adam, I have sent down clothing for you so that you might hide your ugliness and appear beautiful. Here Allah is speaking of physical clothing.

وَلِبَاسُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌۭ

And certainly the clothing of piety is the best in the eyes of Allah. Here Allah is speaking of spiritual clothing.

So the lesson to draw from these verses is that we human beings have not only bodily needs but also spiritual needs. And according to this hadith:

قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين ۔ ولعبدي ما سأل

I have divided the Salaah into two equal halves between Myself and My slave, and My slave will have what he asks for, from both his bodily and his spiritual needs, when he stands before Me in the Salaah. SubhanAllah. This is why Surah al-Fateha is also called Surah as-Salaah.

أم القرآن  و  أم الکتاب

Another name for Surah al-Fateha is Umm al-Quran, and another name is Umm al-Kitaab. Two different names, and we will look at both of them together, because they are really the same thing.

In a hadith the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used this word for Surah al-Fateha and said: Every prayer in which the Umm al-Quran is not recited is mutilated.

کُلُّ صَلواۃٍ لَم یَقرأُ فِیھَا بِأُمُّ الکتابِ أبتَر

In any prayer, if the essence of the book is not recited, that prayer is considered mutilated. It is not a completed prayer. It is not an accepted prayer.

Most of you know what the word Umm means. It means mother. Even in Urdu we have Ammi, meaning mother. So, literally translated, Umm al-Quran means the mother of the Quran. But in reality the word Umm is deeper than merely mother. In fact the word Umm does not mean mother at all. Originally, in ancient Arabic, the word Umm means "the origin of" or "the basis of." So the Arabs called their mother Umm because she was the basis of their origin. Umm means the "Asal," or the "basis." So Umm al-Quran means the extract, the essence, or that which serves as the basis or the origin of the Quran.

Surah al-Fatiha is the basis... or the origin of the Quran... Meaning that if there were no Surah al-Fatiha... there would be no Quran... Therefore Surah al-Fatiha is the mother... and the entire Quran is its child.... The entire Quran is the child born from the womb of Surah al-Fatiha... So Surah al-Fatiha is the essence... and the rest of the Quran is nothing more.... than a commentary on Surah al-Fatiha... Surah al-Fatiha acts as an introduction to the book of Allah! You know, every author has an introduction... Whenever someone writes a book, he mentions the methodology, he mentions the overall goals... so al-Fatiha... if you will... is the introduction to the rest of the book of Allah... And therefore the meaning of the entire Quran has been summarized in Surah al-Fatiha... Or we could say... Surah al-Fatiha is the definition of the Quran... and the remainder of the Quran is the explanation and the examples in support of that definition.... For example... you have a definition for Newton's third law of motion... For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.... That is the essence, or the principle... And then there are explanations and examples that spell out that definition in detail... That is exactly what Surah al-Fatiha is... It defines the principles of Islamic theology... the essence... the motto... the mission statement of Islam.... and the remainder of the Quran is a detailed explanation of that mission statement... So how is Surah al-Fatiha the essence of the entire Quran?

Surah al-Fatiha begins with the primary names of Allah... بِسْمِ اللہِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِیْمِ ... The entire Quran speaks about His Mercy and His Grace.

Surah al-Fatiha praises Allah... الْحَمْدُ لِلہِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِیْنَ ... The entire Quran explains why Allah is to be praised and glorified....

Surah al-Fatiha reminds us of the mercy and kindness of Allah.... الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِیْمِ... The entire Quran is filled with examples, explanations, and details of that mercy.

Surah al-Fatiha mentions the day of judgment and accountability before Allah.... مَالِکِ یَوْمِ الدِّیْنِ... The entire Quran explains the details of the good and bad events that will occur on the day of judgment.

Surah al-Fatiha mentions our submission to the will of Allah — اِیَّاکَ نَعْبُدُ وَ اِیَّاکَ نَسْتَعِیْنُ ... The remaining Quran is filled with the examples and details of how to accomplish that submission, and the success stories of prophets and of people who lived before us... and how their submission to Allah protected them..

Surah al-Fatiha contains a prayer, a supplication... اِھْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِیْمَ ... The remainder of the Quran contains the prayers and supplications that various prophets made to Allah in their various times of trial and tribulation.

But this does not mean that we cannot or should not read the translation of the Qur'an until then. We must, however, also understand the difference between surfing the sea and diving deep into it. Reading the translation of the Qur'an is like surfing the sea. That in itself is remarkable, but it cannot compare to deep-sea diving, where a trained diver descends to the floor of the ocean and brings up the pearls of wisdom from its depths. So when I keep asking you children to understand the Qur'an, what I mean is this: at the very least, understand the translations of the surahs you recite in your salaah; you should at least understand what you are reciting. But for a deep understanding of the Qur'an, we will most certainly need a teacher, just as we would for any other subject in the world.

That is the first thing.

Secondly, we constantly hear that the Qur'an was revealed specifically to the Arabs, and one common question follows from this: if this Qur'an is such a universal message, why was it revealed only to the Arabs and not to everyone else? **An Illiterate Prophet**

On a different note: since we are speaking of **أم**, you may know that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is referred to as **أُمی**, which is taken to mean unlettered and illiterate by Muslims in general. And they quote verses of the Qur'an in which Allah too has called the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ummi: **ٱلَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ ٱلرَّسُولَ ٱلنَّبِىَّ ٱلْأُمِّىَّ**. They follow the messenger, who is an ummi prophet. This they translated as: They follow a messenger who is an unlettered and illiterate prophet.

This is the worst of allegations and the worst of accusations that could be made against the greatest teacher, the greatest **معلم**, the greatest Dai the world has ever seen (**نعوذ باللہ من ذالک**). And to soften their blow, they say: well, unlettered does not mean illiterate; unlettered does not mean ignorant. He simply did not know how to read and write, but that does not mean he was ignorant; that does not mean he was illiterate.

Ah, but that is the very definition of illiterate, my friend! Someone who cannot read and write! And ignorant is defined as someone lacking knowledge or awareness. They say Allah gave His prophet all his knowledge through inspiration, through wahi, which is true! So then my question is: why did He not give him the knowledge of the letters? Why did He not give him the knowledge of how to read and write? It simply does not make sense.

But I want to prove this from the Qur'an, so that there is not even a speck of doubt in our minds about his being the most literate, the most knowledgeable man who ever walked this earth.

Let us begin with the meaning of this word **أُمی**. In Arabic, **أُمی** means several things, all at the same time. It means unlettered AND illiterate AND ignorant. It is not either-or; it is AND. It means unlettered AND illiterate AND ignorant. This is one of the powers of the Arabic language; it is part of its **بلاغۃ**, its eloquence, that there are certain words that are composites, that combine several meanings together all at the same time.

If you remember the definitions of the word aqal from the previous sessions, that too is a composite word. We discussed that it is primarily a container, but it is also a scale, to choose between two goods and two evils; it is also a restraint. So is Aqal one of those three things at a time? No! Aqal is a composite word that means ALL of those things at the same time. The primary meaning, the literal meaning of the word aqal, is container. Now notice that the word container covers the other two definitions as well. Aqal is a container, and a container is also a measure of the quantity it holds; that is why we have measuring cups. And it is also a restraint for its contents; it holds them, binds them, and does not let them flow out. So Aqal is a cup AND a measure.

a scale AND a restraint all at the same time... We will see this same pattern when we analyze words like Rabb, Allah, Hamd, and so on. Each of these is a composite word, and each carries several meanings, and all those meanings apply ALL at the same time. So when an Arab used the word أُمی, he did not mean only unlettered; he also meant illiterate AND he also meant ignorant. Do you understand?

Now, why does the word أُمی mean all of these things? Linguistically, as we have just discussed, the word Umm means mother. One of the meanings of أُمی is "my mother," which was also used for a baby. Why? Because who is the baby's entire universe? His mother! That is why a newborn baby was called أُمی, because it has just come into the world from its mother. And when a baby is born, it is completely unlettered, it is completely illiterate, and it is completely ignorant. All three things at the same time. The baby is unlettered AND illiterate AND ignorant, all at the same time!

Therefore the Arabs would call unlettered, illiterate, and ignorant people Ummi, because they were like newborn babies, who are born with those three qualities: they are unlettered, they are illiterate, and they are ignorant. Hence the term أُمی! Do you understand?

Now tell me: not being able to read or write, being unlettered, being illiterate, being ignorant — are all these signs of honor, or are they signs of shame? We would have to agree that these are all signs of shame. Now, does it make sense that Allah AWJ would find this shame acceptable for his most chosen, most beloved prophet (SAS)? Of course not! نعوذ باللہ. Therefore, calling Rasul Allah (SAS) أُمی is the greatest and the most sinful accusation against him! How can the greatest teacher, the greatest داعی humanity has ever seen, be unlettered, illiterate, and ignorant? How could he be an أُمی!

And even for the sake of argument, if he were unlettered, how difficult was it to learn the twenty-eight simple letters of the Arabic language? Twenty-three years of tableegh, and he could not even learn twenty-eight letters? That makes absolutely no sense. And would his being an أُمی not have gone against him during his tableegh to the people of Mecca?

Being unlettered himself, when he said to others طلب العلم فریضۃ علی کل مسلم و مسلمۃ — Gaining knowledge is compulsory upon every male and female Muslim — would someone not object: O Rasul Allah, if gaining knowledge is so important that you are calling it a Farz, a compulsory duty, then how is it that you do not even have the basic knowledge of the Arabic letters? How is it that you are illiterate? How is it that you are ignorant? You cannot even read a sentence, and you are telling us to gain knowledge? Would it not have been hypocritical of him to do that? نعوذ باللہ من ذالک.

So then, what does the word Ummi mean, and in what context did Allah use it when he referred to his beloved prophet Rasul Allah (SAS) in the Qur'an? One of the names of Mecca at the time was "أُمَّ ٱلْقُرَىٰ," the mother of all villages. Qura is the plural of villages; a single village is called Qaryah. Mecca, as we know, was the center of trade in ancient Arabia, and because of that, it gave birth to many villages all around it. People settled in small villages all around Mecca, so that Mecca could be easily accessible to them.

They follow a messenger who is a Meccan prophet, so that they could conduct their business. And because Mecca was the primary village, the one that gave birth to all the small villages around it, it was called "أُمَّ ٱلْقُرَىٰ," the mother of all villages. And the people of Mecca, the local residents of Mecca, were called أُمی. Consider an example. Today the people who were born in Texas are called Texans, people born in Florida are called Floridians, and people born in New York are called New Yorkers. In the same way, the people of Mecca, the people of Ummul Qura, were called أُمی. The Messenger of Allah was from Mecca, and so he was an أُمی.

Now let us look at this verse again: ٱلَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ ٱلرَّسُولَ ٱلنَّبِىَّ ٱلْأُمِّىَّ. They follow a messenger who is a Meccan prophet. ٱلنَّبِىَّ ٱلْأُمِّىَّ, a Meccan prophet. وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ — and teach them the Book and wisdom.

If he himself were illiterate and ignorant, how could he teach the Book and wisdom to anyone else?

So it is the worst of accusations that we, as Muslims, could lay upon our beloved Prophet, the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), that he was unlettered. نعوذ باللہ نعوذ باللہ.

Now, why did the Messenger of Allah not display before the people of Mecca and Medina that he could read and write? That is a separate subject, and, God willing, we will speak of it on its own should we have the chance. But since we were on the subject of Umm al-Kitab, I wished to make that clarification.

We have discussed the meaning of the word Fatiha and al-Fatiha. We discussed the names Umm al-Kitab and Umm al-Qur'an. We discussed why it is called Surah as-Salah, the surah of prayer.

Saba' Masani. Another name for Surah al-Fatiha is سبع المثانی, the seven that are often recited, the constantly repeating seven.
