Either there is a giant meteor headed toward the earth and there is nothing humanity can do about it, or there is a giant tsunami so large that it is going to drown the entire Asian continent and then come after the Americas, and there is absolutely nothing humanity can do. There was a movie, 2012, in which the world essentially comes to an end and is destroyed.

Is there a description in Islam of such a day? Even in Christianity, that the world is going to end? What do we call it? Judgment Day. Doomsday, right? Buildings are going to collapse. Fire from the sky. The oceans going wild. Volcanoes are going to erupt. And, of course, my car will not start. All of this is going to happen, right?

Now, if you have seen any of these movies, what happens at the end? Some human beings still survive, do they not? They say.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
So reflecting on these four verses, we reach the conclusion that UBOODIYAH, servitude, is what is expected of us. The question then becomes, WHY should we choose to become Allah's slaves? Because slavery by definition means giving up our free will. It means to submit our will to the will of Allah. Not to DO what WE want, but to DO what Allah wants us to do. That is the concept of slavery. The only question is, WHY? And so we started looking at the slavery of Allah, and we began comparing it to the slavery of the world.

The first thing we saw was that slavery by definition is a humiliation.

whereas freedom is honor. And so, right from the start, Allah honored us by giving us free will. Free will can only be an act of the Rehman and the Raheem. Then we see that Allah is رب العالمین. He is رب السموات و الارض. He is not merely my master; He is the master of the alameen. He is the master of the heavens and the earth. And they are in constant uboodiyah, in constant slavery to Him. They are in a state of constant hamd. Consider the sun, the moon, and the stars. They know their task, and they carry it out constantly. They never take a break. They do not say, "I am tired today; I cannot do my work." The sun does not say, "I have been rising and setting for millions of years; I am burnt out; I need a vacation."

Then, in comparison to every other creation, we see that Allah gave us the most. And when you give someone a great deal, you expect a great deal in return. That is only fair. So if Allah gave us the most, He would be absolutely just in expecting and demanding the most from us in return. And yet He expects the bare minimum, the very least. SubhanAllah! Of all the creations, this master gave us the most. The rest of creation is constantly in ubudiyyah to Him. They are all working around the clock, in constant obedience to Allah, Azza wa Jal, to serve us. But then, despite giving us the most, al-Kausar, He expects the least from us in return. One hour of salaat in a day. One month of fasting out of twelve, and only from sunrise to sunset. Two and a half percent of our wealth in zakaat, the wealth He gave us in the first place. It is incredible. What kind of a master is this? What master in the world gives so much and expects so little in return? We have never heard of such a master.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
this evil that has come and attacked us. Human nature and the human will are strong enough to outlast and survive whatever attack comes our way. Have any of you seen Armageddon? It is an old movie with Bruce Willis. He had hair back then. That is how old it is. A meteor is heading toward the world, and they cannot do anything about it. They try to shoot it down with missiles and the like, and nothing works. So Bruce Willis and a group of his friends actually fly onto the meteor and blow it to pieces in midair before it reaches the earth. And then everyone on earth survives.

In other words, if a higher source, even if it sends punishment from the sky, if human beings come together, and they band together, and they work hard enough, they can overcome and survive anything. Throw whatever you want at us; we can survive it. Which is a kind of undertone for this: you can talk about judgment day all you want, but human beings will figure out a way to escape it. We will figure out a way to survive.

So there is a whole slew of movies built around surviving something like a judgment day. That is the subconscious message that is pumped into our brains constantly through movies. I am not one for conspiracies, so I am not saying that this is what the entertainment industry is trying to do. But regardless, that is the psychological impact of such movies upon us, subconsciously, whether we realize it or not.

If there is a catastrophic event, we will get over it. And if the world does come to an end, we will move to a different planet. Battlestar Galactica. If the world does go mad, we will simply move. We will move into the middle of the ocean. But human beings will survive! We will be fine! Go ahead, bring on judgment day. We will find another planet with giant cockroaches, or whatever, you know!

I bring all of this up because these movies, and beyond that a great deal of literature, and a great deal of discussion, all of it points to this argument: that God is an angry entity that wants to punish people, that wants to control people, that wants to impose upon them some kind of rules they do not want. They just want to be free and live their own lives. And I do not know why this so-called god keeps telling them to do things. And if you truly want to be free and happy in life, you have to be rid of this concept of God. You have to be rid of God.

With what words does the Fateha begin? Alhamdulillah. Allah says in the Quran that all human beings naturally praise, and naturally thank, Allah. He did not say, "Thank Allah!" He did not say, "Praise Allah!" He said that praise and gratitude belong to Allah. But now, if you look at this ayah, which we are about to begin studying, what does it say?

ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
O Allah, it is ONLY You we worship, and it is ONLY You we seek help from. I prefer this rendering of Iyaka nabudu: it is ONLY You we give ourselves to in slavery, and it is ONLY You we turn to for help. Is that what this ayah literally translates to? Now, when we say, "It is ONLY You we give ourselves to in slavery, and it is ONLY You we turn to for help," who is actually speaking? It is you and I who are saying that. We are saying to Allah that we give ourselves to YOU in slavery, and it is ONLY You we turn to for help. We are asking Him, we are begging Him, to allow us to be His slaves. Pay close attention to the tone of this ayah. The ayah does not say, استعباد أنفسكم لي.

Enslave yourself to Me. Is the Qur'an commanding us to enslave ourselves to Allah? Or are we saying to Allah, let us be Your slaves? What the Qur'an is doing is suggesting that we are saying it ourselves. The Qur'an is asking us to arrive at that conclusion on our own. The first four ayahs of this surah are meant to bring us to that conclusion ourselves. For when you believe in بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم, when you believe in الحمد, when you believe in ar-Rahman ar-Rahim, when you believe in Malik Yawm ad-Din, the natural conclusion you should reach is that you yourself should want to become His slaves. If you have not reached that conclusion, then do not say it. The Qur'an is not forcing us to say it.

Then we say: O Allah, guide us to the straight path. For once we have enslaved ourselves, having accepted Allah as our Master, the slave needs the Master to tell him what to do. So we, as slaves, as willing slaves, say اھدنا الصراط المستقیم. Surah al-Fatiha is the inner voice of every true human being. The purpose of the Fatiha is not, strictly speaking, to tell you what Allah wants from you. The purpose of the Fatiha is for you to say out loud what you are supposed to have within you already. It is not a conclusion reached from the outside; it is a conclusion reached from the inside, after you have understood the previous four ayahs.

I am now ready to become Your slave. And I have just realized that You have done a tremendous amount for me, and that I owe You a great deal. Now, once I realize that I owe Allah so much, once I realize that I have a great many assignments still to make up, is that easy or difficult? Is it overwhelming? Of course it is. Which means I cannot do this by myself. I need help. O Allah, I owe You a great deal, and in order to give You what I owe, will You help me? There is something almost amusing in it: we want to express our gratitude and our praise to Allah for all that He has done for us, but He is so lofty, and my capacity to praise Him and to thank Him is so weak. So we ask Him:

ایاک نستعین
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
O Allah, I need Your help. I do not know how to do this by myself. You see, Allah does far too much for us, and if we are going to speak of fairness, then He ought to expect a great deal from us in return, because He does a great deal for us. If I am paid a great deal, a great deal of work will be expected of me. We ask Allah for help, because in effect we say: Allah, I know You do so much for me, but I truly do not think I am capable of doing much in return. I need Your help. I need You to give me a few tasks that I can do, tasks that are worth a great deal of extra credit, so that instead of doing a great deal, I can do a little, yet it will count for much. We cannot do for Allah what equals what He does for us; that is simply impossible, and this is one of the reasons we ask for help. O Allah, I want to do a great deal, but I cannot. So You tell me a few things that I can do, that I can work on, that I can try to keep perfecting, and though they are only a few, they count for a great deal in Your sight.

Now remember, we asked Him for prayer. We said ایاک نستعین, and in response He gave us prayer. He did not force prayer upon us; He did not enslave us with prayer. All the practices we have — we asked Him for them. We came into His slavery, ایاک نعبد, and we asked Him for His help, ایاک نستعین. And prayer was His way of answering our request. You need help? Very well: perform prayer five times a day, and fasting and zakat once a year.

Hajj once in a lifetime. That is all you need. That is My help to you, the help you asked for. And, by the way, did He take the majority of things and make them forbidden? No. He took the majority of things and made them permitted. Only a few things are forbidden. Did He ask us to go on Hajj every year? Every month? Once in a lifetime. Did He ask us to fast every month? No. Once a year. Did He ask us not to marry? He could have said, do not marry, or you will be distracted by the wife and the children; stay celibate, so that you can worship Me. Did He do that? Does He allow us to travel? To do all sorts of work? Did He give us all sorts of freedom? He did. But I thought a slave is not supposed to have what? Freedom. I turned to Allah and said, I am ready to be Your slave. Allah said, very well. My slavery is truly easy.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
Understand that any other kind of slavery, to anyone else, when you are a slave to anyone else, is going to be oppressive. When you are a slave to Allah, it is very easy. And this slavery comes with some bargains. Allahu Akbar. This religion is so beautiful. Does Allah not give to every human being anyway? He does. But He says to the slave, if you will only become grateful, I will keep on giving to you, and I will keep on giving to you, and I will keep on giving to you, more and more and more without limit. I will give you more than anyone else. He told the Jews, وَلَوْ أَنَّهُمْ أَقَامُوا۟ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةَ وَٱلْإِنجِيلَ وَمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْهِم مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ لَأَكَلُوا۟ مِن فَوْقِهِمْ وَمِن تَحْتِ أَرْجُلِهِم. If they had only lived by the Book. Did the Book have endless rules, or only a few rules? Only a few rules. If they had only lived by the Book, then they would have eaten and enjoyed treasures that would have come from the sky, and treasures coming out of the earth, and they could have had an amazing life in this world. And to us, He is saying to His slaves, if you do these few things for Me, I will turn this world into Paradise for you. And then, on top of that, I will give you Paradise, which is beyond your wildest imaginations.

He is not asking us to do a great deal. ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین. O Allah, we want to become Your slaves; help us. What do You want us to do? When we become someone's slave, which is a great deal more than becoming someone's employee, is it not? It is a great deal more than becoming an employee. But even when you become an employee, do you not need instructions? You cannot simply have a job and have no instructions. You need to know what to do. If I am Allah's slave, I can only be His slave if I know what the Master wants. So we are asking Him, will You please give us some instructions? What do You want us to do? How do we ask that in the Fatiha? اھدنا الصراط المستقیم.

The summary of the entire Quran in two sentences. One: accept Allah as Master, and accept yourself as slave. Many people accept Allah as Master, but they do not accept themselves as slave. Internalize that: He is Master, you are slave. Two: accept that this guidance is only beneficial to those who accept themselves as slaves. ایاک نعبد, you have accepted yourself as slave. Once you have done that, then what do you do? ایاک نستعین, guide us. Slavery and guidance are the summary of the entire Quran.

Again, the Quran begins with Allah calling Himself Master, ایاک نعبد, and the Quran ends with Allah calling Himself Master of people, قل اعوذ برب الناس. So this is the heart of the matter. People refuse to accept themselves as slaves of Allah.

People do not really have a problem accepting Allah as the Creator. That is not the hard part, nor is accepting Him in any of His attributes. All of that is easy. Allah is one — wonderful; I am still going to do what I want to do. Allah is merciful — excellent; I still have my life. But when you say that Allah is Master, then what does that make me? That makes me a slave.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
To put it in very simple terms, what is the difference between a free person and a slave? It is very simple; it is not complicated. The difference is that a free person does whatever he or she wants. And what does a slave do? A slave cannot do what he or she wants. If a slave did what he or she wanted, he would no longer be a slave. The only thing that makes them a slave is that they do what the master wants. If you accept that, if you accept that your will comes under the will of Allah, that your will must be submitted like a slave before the will of the master, then you have understood what this book and this message are.

It sounds very simple. It takes a few minutes to explain, but internalizing it is a lifelong struggle, a lifelong struggle. Glory be to Allah.

The first example is obedience through fear. This is the case in which you force someone into submission through physical, emotional, and psychological pain. The person will comply only so that he or she does not have to suffer. Slavery is the perfect example. Slaves were beaten and tortured into unwilling obedience by their masters. Animals are beaten into submission to make them perform some sort of work.

The second example is obedience through hope. This is the case in which some sort of trade or bargain is established to achieve obedience. If you accomplish this, I will do this for you in return. You do what I need you to do, and in return I will do something for you. It is, in essence, a transaction.

So let us take a particular example in both scenarios. I want my children to learn their prayer supplications so that they can pray. Now, is this for my benefit, or is it for their benefit? Their learning the prayer supplications is not going to benefit me in any way, is it? It will only benefit my children. So my goal is not to have them do this for my benefit, but for their own benefit. My goal is for them to succeed in the afterlife. I am looking toward their eternal happiness, and I know that prayer is the way to that happiness, and for that they need to learn the supplications. So my intention is as good as it can be. Do you agree? Now my children, on the other hand, have no interest or desire in learning the supplications. So how do I achieve their obedience?

The first way is through fear. I can frighten them. I can threaten them — physically, emotionally, psychologically. I can guilt them. I can tell them that if they do not learn, I am going to take their toys away, make them eat broccoli every single day, whatever it may be. But I can make them comply. I can make them obedient through fear. They will do exactly what I want, even though what I want is for their own benefit, not mine. But they will end up doing it. But is this going to be willing obedience or unwilling obedience on their part?

The second way is through some sort of gift and reward system. I put together a reward system in which, for every supplication they memorize, I will give them a certain reward. So in the hope of achieving that reward, they end up learning the supplications.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
So this scene is built on hope. The one before it was built on fear, and this one is built on hope. They will become obedient. They will comply and learn the supplications in the hope of receiving the reward.

And there is a third kind of obedience, which is the truest form of obedience. In it, a person willingly submits to an authority out of love — not out of fear of punishment, and not out of greed for some reward, but purely out of love. It is love that drives it, because the person wishes to please the one they love. It is like the submission of a lover to every wish and desire of his beloved. Now this love, too, contains hope and fear, but they are not the same as in the earlier examples.

In the earlier example of hope, obedience took place in the hope of a reward that would benefit the self. So my children were learning the supplications for their own benefit, for the reward they would receive once they had memorized them. In this case, it is in the hope of pleasing the beloved. So here, actions are done only out of love for the beloved and out of the fear of upsetting the beloved. There is no desire for any kind of return or reward in this kind of obedience. It rests purely on love, on pleasing the beloved. The pleasure of the beloved is the sole aim and reward of this submission. And the only fear is not the fear of punishment, but the fear of upsetting the beloved. This third kind of willing submission includes both hope and fear — but the hope of pleasing the beloved, and the fear of upsetting the beloved. This is the obedience of love that Allah demands of the intellect.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
On top of that, as if that were not easy enough, He also sent us revelation to explain His reasons to us. Does a master ever explain his reasons to his slaves? Can any slave tell his master, "Explain the purpose of this command to me"? Can a slave negotiate with his master? Can a slave say, "I will obey your command only when you explain it to me, when you tell me why I need to do this"? Can a slave do that? No! But did this master explain things to us in the Quran? He did. Why? So that we could find ease in our submission to Him, to make uboodiyah easy for us. Because when we understand the benefits of something, it becomes easier to take advantage of it. يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلْعُسْرَ Allah desires ease for you. He does not desire hardship for you. This is a very unique master. No master in the world does this.

Now here is another question. Are these acts of worship meant to benefit Him, or are they meant to benefit us? Whom is slavery always designed to benefit? The master, or the slave? Always the master. But this master, He designed the alameen for us. He gave us the most. He asked the least in return from us. He explained the reasons of His commands to us. But whatever He asked us to do, whom does it benefit? It benefits us and only us. SubhanAllah! Every slave in the world is bought to benefit the master. Every command issued to a slave is for the master's benefit. What kind of a master is this, whose every single command is meant for the slave's benefit, and not one single command is for His own benefit? If that is not love, if that is not care, if that is not mercy, if that is not ease, if that is not Rehma, then you tell me what is. AllahuAkbar!

So the more we reflect on the rububiyyah of this master,

the more we realize that he is absolutely incredible. He is exceedingly loving. He is exceedingly merciful. He is like no other master we will ever find in this world. No master does for his slave what Allah does for us. No master loves his slaves. He may take care of them, be kind to them, but no master ever loves his slaves. No master grants his slaves al-Kausar. No master showers his slaves with countless and priceless gifts. No master grants his slaves free will. Masters enforce their own will upon their slaves. They make their slaves do what they themselves want done. No master judges the work of a slave by the slave's own capacity. A slave's work is always judged against the level of the master's standards and expectations. But Allah judges our deeds by our own limited capacity.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
No master buys a slave in order to benefit the slave. Masters buy slaves for their own benefit. No master rushes to fulfill the needs of his slaves. Slaves are always the ones made to rush to fulfill their master's needs and desires. But this master rushes to fulfill our needs. This master is unlike any other master we have ever seen in the world. There is no master so loving, so caring, so merciful, so lenient, that we forget our place before him. We forget that we are his property. Because he is Malik. He is the owner. And if he is the owner, then by definition that makes me his property. Which means he can do whatever he wishes with me. He can break me. He can rip me apart. He can burn me, drown me. He can do whatever he wishes with me. And if he chooses to do so, there is absolutely nothing that I can do, or you can do, or all of us together can do, or everything in this universe combined can do, to protect me against his wrath.

إِن يُرِدْنِ ٱلرَّحْمَنُ بِضُرٍّۢ . لَّا تُغْنِ عَنِّى شَفَعَتُهُمْ شَيْـًۭٔا وَلَا يُنقِذُونِ

If the Rahman decides to harm me, then absolutely nothing in existence will be able to help me. Look at that.

إِن يُرِدْنِ ٱلرَّحْمَنُ بِضُرٍّۢ

If the Rahman decides to harm you. SubhanAllah!

إِن يُرِدْنِ الجبار. إِن يُرِدْنِ القھار. إِن يُرِدْنِ ذوالنتقام.

If the Conqueror, the Subduer, the Avenger decides to harm you. No, no, no.

إِن يُرِدْنِ ٱلرَّحْمَنُ

If the Rahman decides to harm you. Even in his ضُر, in his harm, he is merciful. SubhanAllah!

And yet I constantly disobey Allah. I constantly fail in my uboodiyah, in my slavery to Allah. But he still allows me to exist. You know my phone, it was freezing up a bit. Every now and then it would freeze up and I would have to restart it again. You know what I did? I went to the store and I got a new phone. I got rid of the old one. Why? Because occasionally, not all the time, a few times, it acted up on me. So I got rid of it. Because that is what you do with property that is no longer doing its job. You discard it. We are all Allah's property, and we are not doing our jobs. Not occasionally, not sometimes, but constantly, all the time. So what should a master do? What should a master do with such useless property? Discard it, right? But does he do that? AllahuAkbar!

So we realize that this master is unlike any other master in the world. This is a master who loves us, intensely and constantly, and for that we want to love him back. There is not a single master in this world whom a slave would love. Slaves always hate their master. The first chance they get, they want to run away from that master. Is that not true? But we love this master, and so the only way

the only direction we want to run is *toward* this master. So what do we say? ایاک نعبد. It is you alone whom we willingly enslave ourselves to. In other words: O Allah, we want to become your slaves. O Allah, sign us up. It is you alone to whom we give ourselves in slavery. That is what this ayah literally means.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
I want you to notice the change in tone here. All of the earlier ayats are in the third person. They are informational. بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم — with the name of Allah, extremely merciful, intensely merciful. الحمد للہ رب العالمین — all praise and glory belong to Allah, who is the master of all that is known. الرحمن الرحیم — the intensely merciful, the consistently merciful. مالک یوم الدین — owner and king of the time when the debt of submission falls due. These are all in the third person; in these ayats Allah is speaking to us.

But when we say ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین, the tone changes. It is you alone to whom we give ourselves in slavery, and it is you alone to whom we turn for help. Who is the one speaking now? It is you and I who are saying this. We are the ones saying to Allah that we, willingly, are giving up our freedom in order to become your slaves. We are asking him. We are begging him to accept us as his slaves.

I want you to pay close attention to the tone of this ayah. The ayah does not say استعبادُ أنفسكم لي — enslave yourselves to me. The ayah says: it is you alone to whom we give ourselves in slavery. The Qur'an is not commanding us to enslave ourselves to Allah. We are the ones begging Allah to let us become his slaves. That is a huge difference in tone.

The Qur'an is asking us to arrive at this conclusion on our own through the first four ayats. Because when we truly understand بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم, when we truly understand الحمد للہ رب العالمین, when you truly understand الرحمن الرحیم, when you truly understand مالک یوم الدین, the natural conclusion we reach is ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین — that we want to become his slaves. That is the tone of this ayah. If you have not reached that conclusion, then do not say it. The Qur'an is not forcing us to say it.

And linguistically, ایاک means: you alone. We want to become the slaves of you alone. Because we now realize that there can be no master like Allah — intensely merciful, consistently merciful. And we realize that becoming the slave of Allah is freedom from all the slaveries of this world. O Allah, we realize that if we do not become your slave, we will end up becoming a slave to everything else in existence. We will become a slave of the عالمین. And this عالم is an extremely oppressive master, one who humiliates, who degrades, who decays. It is a master that takes the most beautiful thing and, in the end, turns it into something ugly.

So if you do not accept me into your slavery, I will become a slave to everything else. I will become a slave of money, of my house, my car, my children, my food, my provision. I will become a slave of my company, my branded clothes, my vacation homes. I will become a slave to constantly pleasing my friends and my relatives. Therefore, O Allah, it is you alone to whom we give ourselves in slavery, so that we may become free from all the slaveries of this world.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
The meaning of عون. Now, once we decide and commit to becoming Allah's slave, is it going to be easy, or is it going to be difficult? Are we slaves who are worthy of this honor? I want you to imagine a master going to the local "Slaves R Us" to purchase a slave.

What qualities would he look for in the goods he is about to buy? He would want someone who could be of use to him. No master purchases a weak or sickly slave; what good would that do him? When a master buys a slave, he looks for one who is strong and healthy. If servitude and slavehood — uboodiyah — are what Allah is looking for, what kind of slaves are we? Is our eman strong and healthy, or is it weak and sick? We are slaves of absolutely no use to this master. This is why there is a cry of desperation in ایاک نعبد. O Allah, we know we are useless, worthless slaves. Our eman and our uboodiyah will never be worthy of the Rabb al-Alameen. And yet we are willing to try. But we will need Your help. And so, ایاک نستعین: it is You alone whom we turn to for help.

Consider this again. Does a slave ask its master for help? When a master says, move this cupboard to the other room, can the slave answer, very well, I have this end, you take the other and let us do it together? Never. So ایاک نعبد is our way of saying: O Allah, we wish to become Your slaves, but we know we are weak. We are ruled by the desires of this world; we have countless distractions in every waking moment of our lives. We walk along a slippery slope, and it will not be easy to remember You without pause. We are surrounded on every side by four enemies working against us. There is our nafs, the soul that is weak from the outset. There is this duniya, the temptations of the world. There is ھوی, our overwhelming desires and passions. And there is the Shaytan himself. We are encircled on all sides by these powerful enemies. And so we will need Your help to pass through this, for You alone can help us: ایاک نستعین.

The word نستعین comes from استعانۃ, which in turn comes from عون, meaning help. There are many other words for help in Arabic. There is نصر, there is مُساعَدۃ, there is نجدۃ. Each of these is a different kind of help. So let us understand precisely what kind of help we mean when we use the word عون.

عون is this: when I try my level best but still cannot reach my goal, the help I then ask for — that extra push — is called عون. If you are in the gym doing your bench presses with a workout partner, and you want to do ten repetitions but can manage only eight, and your partner helps you push out those last two, that is عون. Do you understand?
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
If I am trying to fix a flat tire, struggling at my best with it, and someone stops by and helps me finish the job, that is استعانۃ. It is not عون if I have a flat tire and say to you, hey, please help me change this tire — while I sit here inside the car listening to my music as you change it, and, by the way, before you begin, could you please press play on this DVD player? That is not عون.

So we say ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین: it is You alone whom we enslave ourselves to, and we will try our level best to do what we are obliged to do, but we will need Your help to carry us all the way to the end. In those moments of weakness, we will need You to take our hands and bring us across the finish line. That is ایاک نستعین.

So ایاک نعبد is the making of a willing commitment to Allah, and ایاک نستعین is the asking of Him for His help to see the work through.

But consider the relationship between a master and a slave. What is the slave forever in need of from his master? Commands. Instructions. Where there are no instructions from a master, that, in effect, is what it means to be free. And so, as an عبد, we require instructions. When those instructions come from Allah, they are called ھُدی. O Allah, now that I have made myself Your slave, what would You have me do? How am I to repay this debt of submission, this debt of praise, this debt of gratitude? How do I begin to pay it down? Give me some instructions. And whatever You command me to do, I will strive with all my strength to fulfill it. Yet I know how weak and incapable I am, and so I will need Your help. I will need Your عون in carrying out those instructions. I will need Your ھِدایۃ. And therefore: اھدنا الصراط المستقیم.

Now there is something I wish to point out here about the sequence of these declarations. ایاک نعبد is a commitment. It is a declaration. It is a promise. O Allah, it is to You alone that we enslave ourselves. That is our عہد شریف, is it not? And then ایاک نستعین: whatever You tell us to do, we will do it with Your help alone. And only then comes the asking for instructions, for commands, for ھُدی. It is not, first give me the instructions, and then, if I think I will be able to do them, if I think they make sense, if I feel I will be able to make the time for them, then I will do them. No, no, no. All of that has already been settled in the first four verses. Now it is a commitment; it is a promise of عبودیت, made of one's own free will, to do whatever You tell us to do. Because that is entirely a part of being a slave. You do not become a slave and then say, I will do it if it makes sense to me. The making sense of it all was accomplished in the first four verses. At this point we are wholly convinced that anything and everything this master tells us is going to be for our own benefit. The homework, the research, all of it has already been done. Do you understand? From here on it is simply willing submission.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
For some ask this question: why must we make this عہد? Why is that so important? Why must I promise Allah anything? Because the Fatiha makes us promise first. And if you notice, ایاک نستعین is part of the same verse. Promise and help go together: ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین. Help is bound to the promise. The more sincere we are in our promise, the more Allah will help us in our efforts. And only then come the instructions.

Now this is commonly translated as: Guide us to the straight path. This is a most interesting verse. It is the most beautiful verse, and it is also the most misunderstood verse. I want you to pay close attention to this one; it is extremely powerful. First, let us look at it linguistically. When I say to you, Guide me to your school, what I am asking for is instructions, is it not? So how would you give me instructions? You might say: Take Route 786. Go three miles this way and turn right, then go two miles that way, then jump into the water, swim two miles in that direction, then walk three miles that way. That is how you give guidance to a particular destination.

Another thing you can do is this. You can say: Just stand right here. My school bus will arrive in ten minutes. You can take that bus, and it will bring you to my school. That is guidance through the bus, or with the help of the bus. Do you understand?

That's guidance through a medium, through an intermediary.

The third is this. You say: I am headed to school right now. Why don't you get in the car with me and let me take you all the way. And now, as you are driving there with me, you say: Look! You see this sign — this is where we turn right. You see that bird sitting on the tree — this is where we turn left. Now THIS is guidance ALONG the path.

In the first one, you simply gave me instructions. That is guidance TO the destination. In the second one, you told me to take the bus. That is guidance THROUGH an intermediary. And in the last one, you YOURSELF drove me to school. That is guidance ALONG THE WAY to the destination. Do you understand the differences?

Now listen to this carefully. Guidance TO the path, in Arabic, is اھدنا الی صراط المستقیم. Guidance THROUGH the bus would be اھدنا بالصراط المستقیم. Guidance ALONG the path is اھدنا علی صراط المستقیم.

Allah did not say الی صراط المستقیم. He did not say بالصراط المستقیم. He did not say علی صراط المستقیم. He did not use any of those words. He said directly: اھدنا الصراط المستقیم. Linguistically in Arabic, when you do not use ANY of these words, you mean ALL of them at the same time. The principle of Arabic is that if you are using none of them, you are actually using ALL of them. Otherwise you would have to use three separate sentences. So if you want to use ALL of them together, you use NONE of them — that is the principle.

So now, what اھدنا الصراط المستقیم means is: guide me TO the path. Guide me THROUGH the intermediaries that can get me to my destination. AND hold my hand all along the way, until I reach my destination. SubhanAllah! Isn't that amazing?
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
Now, what are directions? What are instructions? They are knowledge. So with اھدنا الصراط المستقیم, we are asking Allah for knowledge. But then we are asking him for more. We are ALSO asking him for the guidance of those PEOPLE who can practically demonstrate for us how to apply that knowledge, how to put that knowledge to use. And then, as we begin applying that knowledge ourselves, we are ALSO asking ALLAH for his constant companionship. Because we do not want to go on this path by ourselves. We want to walk this path WITH Allah by our side, EVERY step of the way, so that he never hangs up the phone. Do you understand?

We are asking for guidance TO the path. We are asking for role models who can serve as examples for us. But then we also have our own walking to do. Just getting to the path and observing how OTHER people are walking on it — THAT is not going to get us to our destination. In order to get to our destination, we ALL have to do our OWN walking. And for that, Ya Allah, we need your company. We need you to support us all the way through.

So we are asking Allah for his ھُدی. And ھُدی, or guidance, comes from HADIYA, which means a gift. Now for an Arab in the desert, if he is lost, what is the GREATEST gift you can give him? More than water! Water is not good enough, because water will last him one more day. Food will last him a couple more days. So what is the GREATEST of all GIFTS for an Arab who is lost in the desert? Guidance. Directions back to his home. That is the ULTIMATE gift. So we are asking Allah not for just ANY gift. We are asking Allah for the ULTIMATE gift.

Your school counselor's guidance is information. The traffic officer's guidance is information. The GPS's guidance is information. All of that is information. But Allah's guidance is more than information. Allah's guidance has to do with personal choices at every given moment. And we are not just asking for information. We are also asking for the strength to make those right decisions. These are two different things, because sometimes we have all the correct information and we still make the wrong decisions. We made them because we did not have the strength, or the will, or the commitment, or the right mindset to make the correct decision. That is why we ask Allah for guidance.
body.topic_title_en: You Alone We Worship, You Alone We Ask for Help

body.text_en:
Today we cannot even trust what our eyes see. The best thing to do is to pray for the right path.

There has always been conflict between men and women, between employer and employee, between government and people, between body and soul. The body is physical; the soul is spiritual. The soul says that we should do spiritual things: I need spiritual food, I need knowledge and prayer and worship and remembrance. The body says that we should do physical things: I want food, I want enjoyment, I want fun, I want parties, I want to have a good time, I need entertainment. So there is something inside us asking for spiritual sustenance, and something asking for physical sustenance. There is spiritual pleasure and there is physical pleasure. There is spiritual beautification and there is physical beautification. And where is this war taking place? Inside us, all the time.

Now, if you let the soul decide, if you listen only to the soul, who will suffer? The body. If you let the physical side decide, who will suffer? The soul. The Christians decided that they would take care of the soul only. They would dress in uncomfortable clothing. They would not marry, because marriage belongs to the body, it is physical. They would not live in beautiful homes; they would live in dark churches, because we only want to care for the soul and forget about the body.

There are people today who say that we should take care of the body only. Who cares about the soul? Do both of these groups end up harming themselves? Yes, and sometimes they even destroy themselves.

Now, when we asked Allah for guidance, the image given for that guidance is a straight path, which means a path that runs straight down the middle. So who is the only one who will not favor men over women? Who is the only one who will not favor the employer over the employee, or the employee over the employer, or the government over the people, or the people over the government? The only one who can be fair is Allah. The only one who can create a balance between the spiritual and the physical is Allah. When we call this the straight path, we call it the straight path because it is the path of balance. It is the perfect negotiation. Here is what women receive. Here is what men receive. Here is what the employer receives. Here is what the employees receive. Here is what the soul receives. Here is what the body receives. I will distribute it fairly, so that neither side is ruined. Everyone receives what he needs. This is the balanced path. This is اھدنا الصراط المستقیم. It could only have come from Allah.

Anyone else would be biased in one direction or the other. This is why we are asking Allah. Remember that we are the ones asking; He is telling because we are asking. This is absolutely critical in Islam. This is what justice is all about in Islam. It is a very beautiful and powerful concept in Islam.

Man versus woman — social conflict, and therefore social justice.

Employer versus employee — economic conflict, and therefore economic justice.

Government versus people — political conflict, and therefore political justice.

Body versus soul — personal conflict, and therefore personal justice.

Allah sent us the Qur'an to balance all of this. Why? Because we asked Him for it.

http://www.bayyinah.tv/posts/quran-for-young-adults-day-6 [Session 3]
body.topic_title_en: Guide Us Along the Straight Path

body.text_en: Siraat al-Mustaqeem is a balanced path between the conflicts that have been mentioned. And the verse speaks in the plural: guide US, اھدنا. It does not say اھدنی, guide me. It is a prayer for the group: guide us to the straight path. So this path is not for the one who is selfish. This path is not for the one who has no sense of justice. If you are not seeking justice, then you are not seeking guidance. The two are intertwined.
body.topic_title_en: Guide Us Along the Straight Path

body.text_en:
**Siraat**

The word *siraat* is translated as "path." It is in fact one of several words that Arabic offers for a path. But *siraat* is used for a path that is the only road leading somewhere. Imagine there are two islands, and a bridge connects them. The water between the two islands is so turbulent that you cannot take a boat from one to the other. The only way to go from one island to the other is the bridge, and there is no other path you can take except the bridge. No alternative route is available. That bridge, that one single path, is called *siraat*.

*Siraat* has a few characteristics. It is a wide path. It is a straight path. It is the only path possible. There are other words in Arabic that also mean path: سبیل، طریق فج. These are words for roads or paths for which an alternative path may exist. You can take another option. For example, if you are stuck in traffic, you can use your GPS to take you along an alternate path. Or you simply take a different path and your GPS keeps pestering you: turn around; turn around, I said; I said turn around. No! You do not own me. I own you.

So when there are alternate paths to reach a destination, the word *siraat* cannot be used, because *siraat* has no plural. These other words do have plurals. For instance, *sabeel* has the plural سُبُل. *Tareeq* has the plural *turuq* or *taraaiq*. *Fajj* has the plural *fijaaj*. So, basically, path and paths: you add an "s" at the end. Road or roads. But *siraat* is a word in Arabic that does not even have a plural. No plural exists for this word, because it would make no sense. By definition the word *siraat* means a single path. It is the only road to the destination, so you cannot have more than one of it. Do you understand?

**Laws versus Morals**

From this we learn that a law has in fact revealed one truth. There is only one true path. There is no such thing as multiple truths. There is no such thing. So among multiple choices, whenever you have multiple paths, the true path will always be one. If you consider all religions, then the singularity of the word *siraat* indicates that there has to be one true religion, and that religion is Islam. Now, within Islam, when you consider the many sects, then among all those sects there has to be one true sect, which we believe is Sulemaniyat.

For all the prophets from Adam, peace be upon him, to Muhammad Mustafa, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, the beliefs and the morals have been exactly the same. In other words, who Allah is and what His qualities are have always been the same. No matter which prophet you ask about Allah and His attributes, they would tell you exactly the same thing. If you ask any of the prophets what the rights of parents are, what our attitude toward parents should be, toward our neighbors, toward truth, honesty, and compassion, they would all tell you exactly the same thing. These are all morals, and they have always been the same.
body.topic_title_en: The Path of Those You Have Blessed

body.text_en:
But as time passes, societies grow more and more complex. If you examine history, we see that our lives are far more complicated than they used to be in the old days. In earlier times the laws laid down by the sharia were simple. But as time passed and societies developed and matters began to grow complicated, the laws also began to grow complicated in order to meet the needs of society. And as nations became more and more complex, Allah determined to reveal not only morals but laws as well.

One of the most advanced forms of these laws was given to Moses. Now the question is: why do we need laws at all? One of the most important reasons is this. Morals help a person become a better person. Belief, or faith, is meant to work in the same way. As time passes, faith and belief are meant to grow stronger and stronger. So morals and faith both have the potential to grow and to keep on growing. But do laws keep growing over time? No. The purpose of laws is entirely different. The purpose of laws is to ensure that you do not become a criminal. In other words, laws are there to define the bare minimum. That is, if you do anything less than this, or if you violate these things, then you are a criminal. That is the purpose of laws. If somebody is abiding by the law, that does not necessarily mean that person is a good person. That person is simply a law-abiding citizen. It only means that he is not going to jail. The whole purpose of laws is for people to work and function together peacefully and in harmony. Now law can be divided into two parts: things you must do, and things you cannot do. So what are some examples we can think of, in terms of governmental law, of things we must do — something the law dictates that we must do? We have tax laws. There are zoning laws. There are traffic laws. There are business laws about what kinds of businesses you may open. You cannot simply start any kind of business in any location. There are laws about trespassing. There are criminal laws: stealing, robbing, killing, hurting people. Break any of those laws and you get into trouble. So laws can be divided into two groups: things that you must do, and things that you absolutely must not do. But abiding by a law does not make you an admirable person. It only means that it does not make you a criminal.

Even in the Islamic sharia we have various different kinds of laws. For example, there is a law stated in the Qur'an that as a Muslim I cannot kill my children. وَلَا تَقْتُلُوٓا۟ أَوْلَدَكُم مِّنْ إِمْلَقٍۢ Do not kill your children because of poverty. So I cannot say that I am an admirable person because I am obeying the laws of Allah. I have not killed any of my children — yet. That is not really an accomplishment. I simply did not break a law.
body.topic_title_en: The Path of Those You Have Blessed

body.text_en:
Laws are based on morals. Now the idea is that most people in a society will try to do the right thing. For if everybody in the society were a criminal, then you would no longer have a society at all. But there are certain people in a society who will tend to break the law. And that is why laws are created: so that such people are prevented from causing damage to the other members of the society who actually want to obey the law. And that is why, every time we find a law, what we inevitably find alongside it is punishment. Wherever there is a law, there is going to be a punishment for breaking that law. There is no punishment for breaking a moral. If I speak to you very rudely, if I yell at you, I cannot be arrested for it, because that is a moral issue. If I lie to you, I can get into trouble with you, but I will not be arrested for it, because I have only broken a moral. But if I lie in a courtroom under oath, now I can get into serious trouble, because now I am not breaking a moral but a law. I can actually go to jail for perjury. So punishment is associated with laws, not with morals. Morals are personal, but laws are not personal. They have to be enforced by some form of government. So if there is a law,

any law at all, it will always carry a punishment for breaking it. And there has to be an authority that enforces that law. You and I cannot take that law into our own hands. If we see somebody breaking the law, we cannot carry out the punishment against that person ourselves. We have to report it to the proper authorities, and then they enforce the punishment for whatever was done. This applies to Islamic law as well.

So we have beliefs, morals, and laws. Morals and beliefs have to do with becoming a better person. Laws, which are a set of dos and don'ts, have to do with living together in harmony as a group. Now, there are two kinds of laws: there are spiritual laws and there are social laws. One of the laws in Islam is that you must fast for thirty days in the month of Ramadan. Is that a spiritual law or a social law? It is a spiritual law. In the same way, there is a law that we must pray five times a day. Is that a spiritual law or a social law? Again, it is a spiritual law. There is another law in Islam that you must pass on your inheritance to the right people in the right amounts. So if I die, a certain percentage of my wealth goes to my parents, a portion goes to my wife, a portion goes to my children, and so on. All of that is clearly laid down in sharia law. Now, is that a spiritual law or a social law? That is a social law.
body.topic_title_en: The Path of Those You Have Blessed

body.text_en:
So you understand. A spiritual law is something between me and Allah. A social law is something between me and other people. Do you understand that? The worldly punishments in Islam are overwhelmingly attached to social laws. I will say that again. The worldly punishments in Islam are overwhelmingly attached to social laws. We said that wherever there is a law, there is a punishment attached to breaking that law, or to not abiding by it. But the distinction to make is that, while we are in this world, punishment will only be enforced for breaking social laws. If I break spiritual laws — for example, if I do not pray five times a day, or I do not fast once a year, or I do not go on the pilgrimage once in a lifetime — then even though I am breaking spiritual laws, no punishment can be enforced upon me while I am in this world. But if I kill someone, if I steal, if I commit a fraud, then I am breaking social laws, and the sharia lays down a punishment against me in this world for breaking those laws.

So the true path is made up, for us, of three things: morals, beliefs, and laws. Now, which of those three things have always been there and have always remained the same? Morals and beliefs! So when it comes to morals and beliefs, we go back into the Qur'an and learn lessons from the people whom Allah favored in the past. Now, "favored" — in English, is that a past tense or a present tense? It is past tense. In other words, our role models for what it means to believe and what it means to live by good morals all exist in the past. The role models for beliefs and morals will always be in the past. And the Qur'an speaks of all these role models through the examples of the prophets who lived before us, and the morals and beliefs by which they lived their lives. The reason Allah described their lives in the Qur'an is that they lived lives founded upon timeless morals. So the morals they lived by and the belief system they held apply even today, for us.

And the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family, and Maulana Ali, peace be upon him,
body.topic_title_en: The Path of Those You Have Blessed

body.text_en:
and our Lady Fatima are the ultimate role models for us, in both senses: how to believe and how to live by morals. So we follow all of these people when it comes to morals and beliefs. But when it comes to the laws, the only one we follow is the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family. His law is the one that binds us. That is why in the Qur'an we do not find any of the laws that were enforced upon the nation of Moses, peace be upon him, unless they happen to be the same laws that are enforced upon us. We had no need to learn the laws that were laid down for Moses, peace be upon him, because we already have someone who gives us our laws, and that is Muhammad, peace be upon him and his family. What Allah does tell us about Moses, peace be upon him, is his patience with the Children of Israel, his courage before Pharaoh, his standing up for his faith, the miracles that were granted to him, and how Allah helped him when he needed that help and asked for it. All of these are things that either support our faith or strengthen our morals. Do you understand?

Now, the most important point about أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ: our true role models lie in the past. Our true heroes are all in the past. The best way to understand this is to think about whom you ask for career advice. You do not ask for career advice from someone who attends school with you, who sits in the same classes as you, who knows and studies the same material that you do, and who is the same age as you. If you need career advice, you would most likely go to someone who has already graduated, who already has a job, and who has already completed the very program you are studying now. So, for example, if you are in medical school, you would want advice from a doctor who graduated from that same school and who is very successful in life. And you would want to know exactly what steps he took to reach where he is. How did he apply for a job? Which professors did he take courses with? How did his career work out? What are the things he would advise you to do? What are the things he would advise you not to do? What should you focus on? What should you not focus on? The best advice comes from the person who has already walked down this entire path and already knows what the road is like. Do you understand?

But if someone is traveling along at your side, someone walking beside you who has never yet gone down the whole road, he may be very good company, yet he cannot guide you in the absolute sense about what to do and how to do it. He is just as unaware of what lies ahead as you are. Our true role models will always be in the past. And there is a list of them in the Qur'an. Who are our true role models?

وَمَن يُطِعِ ٱللَّهَ وَٱلرَّسُولَ فَأُو۟لَٓئِكَ مَعَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنْعَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْهِم مِّنَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ وَٱلصِّدِّيقِينَ وَٱلشُّهَدَآءِ وَٱلصَّلِحِينَ ۚ وَحَسُنَ أُو۟لَٓئِكَ رَفِيقًۭا
body.topic_title_en: The Path of Those You Have Blessed

body.text_en:
Allah says: among those whom Allah favored — again, the past tense — the first are the prophets. The prophets are our first role model. They are the first kind of people from whom we must learn. We must examine their lives and then try to follow their example. Next come the Siddiqeen. These are the people who believed in the prophet and stood by him no matter how difficult it became. They confirmed and acknowledged that what the prophets were saying was in fact true. So the first group is the prophets, and the second group is the Siddiqeen, the people who believed in the prophets. Then, وَٱلشُّهَدَآءِ.

And those who gave their lives. People who sacrifice their lives for their beliefs and their faith. People who were willing to die, simply so that they might go on believing. These are the martyrs, the shuhada. And the final group is the Saliheen, the righteous. They may not have been killed, yet they were great people all the same — great enough for Allah to mention them in His book. They were great fathers and great mothers, great brothers and sisters. They were great sons and daughters. And then Allah says about them: وَحَسُنَ أُو۟لَٓئِكَ رَفِيقًۭا

This is a most striking statement from Allah: how excellent these people are as company. In other words, if you follow their path, if you follow their way of living, if you live the life that they lived, then Allah will give you their company in paradise. You will be together with them in heaven.
body.topic_title_en: The Path of Those You Have Blessed

body.text_en:
The difference between those who earned anger and those who went astray is a very interesting one. Those who earned anger are the people with whom Allah is angry, and they are also the people whom you and I have a right to be angry with, because they are the ones who know that a thing is wrong and do it anyway. Someone who knows that a thing is wrong, does it, and goes on doing it — you are supposed to be angry with such a person. Someone who had no idea that a thing was wrong and did it was simply lost. Do you understand the difference?

غیر المغضوب علیھم means those who received anger, those who were the recipients of Allah's anger. And who are these people? Those who know the wrong thing and do it anyway. ولا الضالین: and we do not want to be among those who lost their way.

Those who earned anger are those who, once they have seen knowledge, once they have come to know, still do not care. At that point it is right that Allah should be angry with you. At that point it is just that the other creations of Allah should be angry with you. At that point it is right that on the Day of Judgment your own loved ones should be angry with you. Because once you know, you are responsible.

Some people develop this twisted attitude: do not tell me anything! Because once I know, I will become responsible, so I would rather not know. I do not want to know, because once I know I will be questioned about it. Ah — if you are clever enough to know that you are not supposed to know, that actually means you know, and you are going to be questioned. It was a nice try, though. It is cute. But Allah will question you anyway, because you were clever enough to know that you should know. You cannot pull a fast one on Allah. It does not work.

Now, interestingly, in the Qur'an, Allah mentions people whom Allah allowed to be misguided even though they had knowledge:

أَفَرَءَيْتَ مَنِ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَهَهُۥ هَوَىٰهُ وَأَضَلَّهُ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍۢ وَخَتَمَ عَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِۦ وَقَلْبِهِۦ وَجَعَلَ عَلَىٰ بَصَرِهِۦ غِشَوَةًۭ فَمَن يَهْدِيهِ مِنۢ بَعْدِ ٱللَّهِ ۚ أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُون

You would think that if someone has knowledge, how could they be misguided? People imagine that if you learn a great deal of Arabic, then you can understand the Qur'an, and then you will be a good person. Ah — Abu Lahab understood Arabic, and understood it very well too. We are never going to be as good in Arabic as Abu Lahab. Abu Jahl understood Arabic and the Qur'an. The Qur'an was given to them; it was being revealed for them. They heard it all the time. In fact, I told you about those incidents during the miracles of the Qur'an. They were addicted to it. They could not stop listening to it. And Allah says:

فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَهُ بِلِسَانِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُون

We have made it easy on your tongue so that they may remember it. Allah made this language easy so that the Quraysh could understand it.
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
So understanding something does not make us a good person. That is only knowledge. Knowledge simply is not enough. Some people think that everything stops at knowledge, so they gather all the knowledge they can lay their hands on. They become obsessed with knowledge. They know everything in the world, and yet their actions are completely ruined. Do we not see people like that in our lives? We did not come into this world merely to learn the Qur'an. Learning is a means to an end. We learn so that we can live according to what we have learned. If the second does not happen, that knowledge means absolutely nothing. Learning is all about thinking.

Very interestingly, Allah speaks very little about knowledge in the Qur'an.

and a great deal about thinking. He speaks a little about knowledge and much about reflection. There is a difference between the two. The problem with the Maghdoob Alayhim is that they possess the right kind of knowledge, but they do not possess the right kind of thinking. Knowledge does not necessarily turn into action. It is the right kind of thinking, arising out of the right kind of knowledge, that turns into the right kind of action. When you think about the knowledge you already hold, that is what converts it into action. That is the missing ingredient in between. You can have knowledge of things. Did you have knowledge of the Day of Judgment before you came to my sessions? Did you know that there is one Allah? Did you know that He is a loving Allah? You did. So then what did you gain from the session? I told you nothing new. I may have given you new examples and new explanations, but the underlying concepts were already there. You had the knowledge. So what is different about these sessions? What is different is that in these sessions we think, we reflect. The more you think, the more you reflect, whether with me or on your own, the more it passes into your daily actions. But if you do not think about it, nothing in you will change. Everyone here knew that they were slaves of Allah. Yet when we stop and consider what it means to be a slave of Allah, that is when transformation takes place. Giving all of this some thought changes something inside us. Thinking is the most important vehicle of all.

Do we not know that the Bani Israeel were people of knowledge? Of course they were; they were extremely knowledgeable. Yet Allah asks them in the Qur'an, افلا تعقلون؟ Why do you not think? Why do you not use your intellect? So the Maghdoob Alayhim are people who have knowledge but do not act upon it. Knowledge by itself is not enough.

The Dalleen are people who simply do not know, and so they act wrongly. But even though they do not know, what power do they still have? They still have the power to think, they still have the power to reflect. They can ask themselves: the way I am behaving, my conduct in life, what is it based on? I do not even know why I am doing it. At the very least I ought to want to find out. That much thought they are capable of.
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
Rasul Allah SAS was asked about the Maghdoob Alayhim and the Dalleen. He said that the Maghdoob Alayhim are the Jews and the Dalleen are the Christians: the people who receive anger are the Jews, and the people who are lost are the Christians. But Allah did not say غیر الیھود و لا النصری, not the path of the Jews nor of the Christians. Allah did not say that. Allah says: do not let me walk the path of those who earned Your anger, nor the path of those who went astray. That is what the Qur'an says. Yet Rasul Allah described them as the Jews and the Christians. How are we to understand that? What does it mean?

When we study the Qur'an, we see certain kinds of behavior in connection with which Allah speaks of the Jews. And when you study the Qur'an, you see certain kinds of behavior in connection with which He speaks of the Christians. It is that behavior which made them either Maghdoob Alayhim or Dalleen. So the label does not really rest on the people; the label rests on the behavior of those two kinds of people. And where are these behaviors described? In the Qur'an. Allah highlights these behaviors in the Qur'an. So this becomes a matter of studying and reflecting upon those behaviors. This is not about judging people.

So now the Muslims relax and say:

Oh, in these verses Allah is speaking only about the Jews and the Christians. He is not speaking about us. Listen! He is not speaking *about* the Jews and the Christians. He is giving you the Jews and the Christians as examples. What He is actually speaking about is you and me. He is speaking about us. If He were not speaking about us, we would not have to ask Allah to protect us from becoming like that. If it does not concern you, then why would you say, "O Allah, do not make me one of the maghdoob alayhim and the dalleen"? Do you understand? We would not be saying that unless we ourselves stood in danger of becoming such people.

So what is that danger for us? The danger is that we learn things, but we do not think about them. We do not reflect upon them. And, most important of all, we do not act upon them. That is what maghdoob alayhim and dalleen means.

The dalleen are people who do not know. They simply do things, but they cannot explain why they are doing them. And if you ask them about it, they will all give one and the same answer: because this is the way it has always been done. Now, is that a logical answer? I am doing it because that is simply the way it is done? It is not.

Let me give you a perfectly realistic example: marriages. It is a very controversial subject, but I will speak about it anyway. Today, in our marriages, we have at least six ceremonies — that is the bare minimum. Do these come from the Shariah? No. But if you ask someone, "Why do you hold all these ceremonies? What is their origin? What is their significance? Why do you do this?" — what is the answer you always receive? Because everyone does it this way. This is how it has always been done. That is dalleen. It is nothing but blind imitation.
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
And by the way, are these ceremonies cheap or expensive? They are extremely expensive. And what do families do in order to pay for them? Do you imagine that everyone pays in cash? No. They take credit. They pile on debt. Yet nobody stops and asks the logical question: why are we doing this? Why do you need so much extra food that will only be wasted? Why do you need such an enormous hall? No, no, no, no — we do not do that. When our family does things, we do them big. When we go into debt, we go big into debt. When we sink, we like to drown all the way to the bottom of the ocean. That is simply not how we do things. What are we, beggars? Are we poor?

And if you truly probe and probe and probe — why are we doing this? — and once you have gotten past the surface answers, "Oh, it is innocent fun, it is only so that we can have a good time," once all these surface answers are stripped away, the answer underneath is always the same: we simply do it, because that is the way things have always been done. That is the answer of a daal. I do not know why I am doing it. I am just doing it. And I do not like thinking about it either. Do not make me think about it. It makes me uncomfortable. It brings out the fact that I really do not know. That is the behavior of someone who is daal.

And the reason this is a Christian way of thinking is that they said Allah has a son, and his name is Eisa. Why is he Allah's son? Because he was born without a father. But Adam AS was born without a father and without a mother. So? He just is, all right! You simply do not have faith. Accept Jesus into your heart. He has paid for your sins. Accept Jesus into your heart. Very well! If he has paid for my sins, may I go and rob a bank? Why would you do that? Because he paid for my sins! I am not sinful now. So now I can go and rob a bank. I have been wanting to all this time anyway. I could probably get away from the police; getting away from God was my biggest problem.

And by your account, he has already paid for my sins, so I am fine! No! But if you were a true believer, you would be a good person, and you would not sin. Then what is he paying for? I am not sinning! I thought you said he paid for my sins!

Do you see what this is? This is simply wanting to go on doing as one pleases, without understanding any logic behind things. This is the Christian way of thinking. This is Christian behavior. This is the way of the Dalleen. And you and I do so many things in our lives in exactly that way. It is the attitude of: do not ask about it, just do what feels good, just do what is innocent fun. That is Dalleen.
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
I want to tell you something about the Christians. You may or may not know this. You will never feel as good in a masjid as you will feel in a church during their services. You may feel wonderful in your worship of Allah, but when you meet people in the masjid or jamaat khana, you will not feel wonderful, most of the time. But if you go to any church, let me tell you: the love with which you will be treated, the kindness, the courtesy, where everyone feels that things are so open, that they can share the problems of their lives with others who care about them. One man will come and complain on the microphone about his life, and about how he was angry with God, and everyone will weep for him, cheer for him. It feels so good. The whole experience makes you feel amazing, and you will walk out saying: why can we not do that at the masjid? How is it that we do not care about people? They care so much. They have so much genuine love for people.

Feeling that people care, feeling that you belong, feeling that people love you and understand you — all of this is an amazing feeling. It is a very powerful feeling. It is in fact so powerful that people become ready to accept Jesus as their lord and savior because it feels so good! You feel so excited. You never felt that way in the masjid. I have met people like that.

But that does not change the fact that what you believe is only out of emotion, and not out of reason.

The Jews became people who were all about knowledge and had absolutely no heart. The Christians became all about the heart and had no intellect. Knowledge is powerful, but the heart is also powerful. The Qur'an comes and says: I will give you a path right down the middle. I will give you a path where you can have both. You can have the feeling; you can feel the immense love of Allah. And you can also have the reasoning behind things. I will give you the middle path between the heart and the intellect. Your intellect will be able to make sense of things, and your heart will be able to feel the closeness, the connection, and the attachment with Allah. The Qur'an gives us both.

This is very serious matter. Look at what we are doing right now. We are learning the Fatiha. Everything I have taught you has been about learning and understanding the Fatiha. It has all been about knowledge. But in the next prayer, when you stand on your prayer mat and recite the Fatiha, you will be praying the Fatiha. Everything we are studying now about the Fatiha is about the intellect. After this session, when you stand before Allah and recite the Fatiha, it will not be about the intellect; it will be your heart attaching itself to Allah, praying to Allah, asking Allah for everything we have discussed. All this knowledge will become a personal cry, a very personal conversation with Allah. You are experiencing the Fatiha spiritually.
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
You are not studying it. This is the middle path. Outside of prayer, we learn it for the intellect. But inside prayer, during prayer, we experience it in our hearts. We feel the love of the Rahman, the Raheem. We feel the longing to ask Allah to make us His slaves, to guide us. The eyes begin to shed tears. It becomes a spiritual experience. So the Qur'an addresses the mind, and the Qur'an addresses the heart. That is balance. That is justice. That is what it is meant to do: not to let itself become one or the other. That is the balance in the Fatiha, between intellect and heart, between عقل and قلب.

انعمت علیھم are the people who walk this middle path. They have the knowledge, and they experience it and live by it in their lives. Their knowledge does not simply turn into academic knowledge, the kind where a person knows a great deal but cannot weep in prayer. One of the greatest tragedies of Islam is this: when people did not know much about Islam, they would weep far more in prayer. Now people know far more, but they weep very little in prayer. So knowledge increased, but the heart grew harder. When that happens, you have to work on the heart. Yet making the heart soft does not mean that you no longer need knowledge. People go either to one extreme or to the other. The Qur'an wants balance.

The first four verses of the Fatiha are about Allah. The last two are actually about us. We are asking for guidance. We are asking to walk the path of the good and not to walk the path of the bad. And the one in the middle of these two is ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین. The first half of this verse, ایاک نعبد, connects to what comes above it, and ایاک نستعین connects to what comes below it. It is what we want to give Allah, and what we want from Allah. What we want to give Him is ourselves in slavery, and what we want from Him is help in guidance. So the first part of the Fatiha is about Allah, the last part is about us, and the middle part is about both Allah and us. Everything is completely balanced out: Allah, both of us, ourselves. So this is our relationship with Allah, perfectly balanced.

Now, the first three verses: the conclusion of those verses is that I want to become Allah's slave. I am ready. Sign me up. That conclusion in Arabic is ایاک نعبد. That is the conclusion of the first part.

The next part is us, as slaves, asking the Master for help: ایاک نستعین. Notice that the rest of the Fatiha is us asking for help, for guidance, for walking the good path and not the bad path. Is all of that not asking for help? In other words, ایاک نعبد is the conclusion of part one, and ایاک نستعین is the introduction to part two. SubhanAllah!
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
The first three verses were about Allah. What did we learn about Allah in that part? That part was knowledge. Then, when we say that we want to be slaves, guide us, what is that? Action or knowledge? It is action. We want to take action on the basis of the knowledge of Allah, that we want to become His slaves. So the first part of the surah was knowledge, and the second part of the surah is action. Now, if you have knowledge and you have action, then you are on the straight path. Is that not true? This is why Allah mentions the straight path. The people on the straight path have knowledge, and they act on the basis of that knowledge.

What is مغضوب علیھم? What do they have? They have knowledge, but they do not have action. What is ضالین? People who do not have knowledge, but who still have action. The Fatiha began with knowledge, then spoke of action, and then spoke of the people who have both.

Then it spoke about those who have knowledge but no action, and then about those who have action but no knowledge. It is a complete picture of knowledge and action.

Now the grammatical point. In Arabic there are two kinds of sentences: sentences built around a noun and sentences built around a verb — noun based and verb based. A noun is a person, a place, an idea, an animal, or a thing. A verb is an action word, and it is fixed in the past, the present, or the future. Nouns are permanent; verbs are temporary. Nouns are timeless; verbs are locked into time. What I am telling you now is a matter of language itself.

The first part of the Fatiha is about Allah. The middle is about Allah and about us, half and half. The last part is about us. Part one of the Fatiha, according to Arabic grammar, is noun based. Part three, the part in which we are asking, is verb based. The middle part, even though it is verb based, begins with a noun, so it is a mixture of the two.

What did we say about nouns? They are timeless. What is the first part about? Allah. Is He permanent or temporary? Permanent. So the first part is timeless, because Allah is timeless.

The last part is about whom? About us. And what kind of language is used? Verb based. And what is that? Temporary — because we ourselves are temporary.

The middle part, according to Arabic grammar, is a mixture of both. It is a جملۃ فعلیہ with a مفعول بہ مقدم. There is a noun at the beginning, a noun standing first even though the sentence is a verbal sentence. It is a mixture of both. And was the middle verse not itself a mixture of both, something for us and something for Allah? Subhan Allah!

For someone to speak, without any editing, and to say: because I am speaking about One who is permanent, therefore I should use a noun based sentence; and because in the last part I am speaking about those who are temporary, therefore I should use a verb based sentence, a temporary style of language; and because the middle verse is a mixture, therefore I should make the sentence itself a mixture — and to do all of this in speech delivered aloud, with no process of editing. Subhan Allah! This is impossible for a human being. This is not humanly possible.
body.topic_title_en: Not of Those Who Earned Wrath, Nor of Those Who Went Astray

body.text_en:
Hamd, from the commentary of the Doctor. We have reached the verse الحمد للہ رب العٰلمین. This is one of the most profound and most compact verses in the entire Qur'an. The more you reflect upon it, the more you will see that there could not have been a better way to begin the word of Allah. In order to appreciate the meaning of this verse fully, we must first understand what the word AlHamd means. All Hamd belongs to Allah, the Rab Alalameen. What exactly does Hamd mean? And in order to understand the word Hamd fully, we need to compare it with other words that resemble it.
