A set of conscious and unconscious ideas that make up one's goals, expectations, and motivations. Now listen to this very carefully. When I accept God, that is my religion. It is my ideology, my way of life. When I reject God, that is my religion. When I accept half a god, that is a religion. When I consider science to be my path, that is my religion. So religion, by definition, is simply a way of life with a certain set of ideologies and rules.

Even an atheist has a religion, because even an atheist has a way of life. He has certain parameters, certain rules and beliefs that govern his day-to-day life. So make no mistake: atheism is a "faith"-based religion, with a blind "faith" in nature as a deity, because atheists attribute to nature the cause of everything. But in the end, anyone who is intelligent and capable of articulating an idea must have a religion, because to follow an ideology is religion. In other words, there is no human being, apart from one who is insane and incapable of reason, who does not have a religion — purely on the basis of the definition of the word religion.

Now, in Arabic, the word for religion is Deen. And Allah says in the Qur'an:

ان الدین عند اللہ الاسلام

No doubt, the religion of Allah is Islam. So if we replace the word deen, or religion, with our definition, the verse would read: No doubt, the way of life that Allah has outlined is Islam. And if we replace Islam with its meaning, which we know comes from the root word سلَّم, meaning to submit, then the verse reads: No doubt, the way of life that Allah has outlined is submission. So submission is the way of life. Submission is Allah's religion.

Every intelligent human being submits to one thing or another. Every human being holds some set of moral and ethical principles, some set of scruples. Name it whatever you like — call it Hinduism, Christianity, Judaism, Islam, atheism — it does not matter. The point is that everyone submits to some rules or some way of life. Even an atheist submits to certain specific principles that govern his day-to-day life. Do you understand?

So Allah created submission as the way of life for human beings. A Muslim submits to a way of life. A Christian submits to a way of life. A Jew submits to a way of life. An atheist submits to a way of life. An agnostic submits to a way of life.

So if submission is the way of Allah, does that mean that any kind of submission will be acceptable? No, because Allah also says: And whoever follows a religion, a way of life, other than submission to Allah, it will not be accepted from him, and on the day of judgment he will be among the losers. And that makes complete sense. I am a software developer. My employer asks me to develop an eCommerce website so that the company can sell its products online. Instead, I build a website that shows YouTube videos. Is that going to be acceptable to my employer? Of course not. That is not going to be acceptable, for obvious reasons. Allah says that the religion of Allah has always been submission to Allah, submitting to the way of life that Allah has prescribed. In the time of Nuh (AS), that way of submission was Hinduism. In the time of Musa (AS), that way of submission was Judaism.

During the time of Eisa (AS) that way of submission was Christianity. And now, during and after the time of Muhammad (SAS), that way of submission is Al-Islam. We discussed this earlier. In Arabic, (ال) is called علامت المعرفۃ. It is used to make something definite. In Arabic, "Kitab" means any book; "Al-Kitaab" means one particular book. So in these verses Allah did not say ان الدین عند اللہ اسلام. Instead He said ان الدین عند اللہ ال اسلام. He did not say ومن یبتغ غیر اسلام دینا; He said ومن یبتغ غیر ال اسلام دینا. My way of life is not any form of submission; my way of life is THE way of submission I have prescribed. It is not any form of submission that I will accept; it is only one particular way of submission that I will accept.

When we accepted Islam as our religion, as our way of life, we became employees of Allah. So, obviously, the employer will expect from the employee what he asked him to do, not what the employee feels like doing. Do you understand?

In any case, those are the definitions. Science is a methodology for understanding cause and effect, and religion is a way of life that is tracked by some ideology.

Now let us define body and soul. We human beings have a body, and we have a soul. The body we know; it is the tangible, physical structure of a person, including his inner organs. The difference between a living human being and a dead corpse is the absence of a soul, or essence. Otherwise, a dead body has all the same external form and internal organs as a living being, with one primary difference: the soul, or the essence, has been disconnected from the body.

The Arabic words used for soul are "nafs" or "rooh." But if you look up the general definition of soul, you will find, for example, that Wikipedia defines soul as "the spiritual or immeasurable part of a human being or animal, regarded as immortal." It is called the "identity" or the "essence" of the individual. This idea of the soul is wired up with the idea of a future life and a belief in a continued existence after death. It is the ultimate animating principle by which we think and feel, one that is not dependent on the body, even though it acts upon the body. And the proofs of its existence are attributed to consciousness during dreams and to common mental operations, such as imagination and memory, all of which suggest the existence of a vital life force that, even though it uses the body, still exists independently of the body. That is the definition.

Now, the soul is not something that can be seen under a microscope, because it is not in a physical or tangible form. But it cannot be denied, because of the existence of human emotions and other cognitive abilities attributed to it. A good falsification test for the existence of the soul is what we find in the study of robotics, or of artificial intelligence. What are robots? From a technical standpoint, robots are defined as a machine capable of carrying out a complex series of actions automatically, especially through a program or a defined set of instructions. Robots are basically programmed bodies. They do not have a soul; instead, they have a program. They can act and react according to a defined program. They cannot change their own programs themselves, and even if they can, they can only do so based on another defined algorithm written by someone else.

...that then enables these supercomputers to write new code for themselves. That is the entire premise of artificial intelligence. Yet even with all of these enhancements, Paul Cohen, the lead program manager at DARPA, says, "AI still cannot solve the problem of common sense. We still cannot endow a computer with the knowledge that every five-year-old has." Now this is quite an astonishing statement, made by the lead program manager at DARPA, who oversees all of the AI research.

But let us grant that perhaps it is not possible today. Perhaps a hundred years from now scientists will be able to build a supercomputer that rivals the human intellect. It is possible. Why not? After all, look at what is happening around us. But what they will never be able to do — according to the Turing Test, named after Alan Turing, a British mathematician — is make robots feel emotions. Robots may be able to detect the emotions of human beings and to "act" emotionally in response to them, but they cannot be made to feel an emotion. They could simulate an emotion on the basis of a program. They can speak and behave in patterns that give the appearance of being in love, but they can never feel love. They can be made to act angry, disgusted, or afraid on the basis of programmed code, but they can never be made to feel these emotions.

Why is that? It is because in the end they are man-made machines. They can compute, they can process, they can even be programmed to simulate and perform a certain emotion, but they cannot be programmed to actually feel the emotion. This is because emotions are attributed to that timeless, boundless thing called the soul, or "rooh," which we human beings possess. Even the most sophisticated computer a hundred years from now will still be, at bottom, a tin can with a highly sophisticated program. It will be only as good as the program written for it by human beings. There will never be morality or ethics associated with a robot, no matter how intelligent it is, because, once again, morality and ethics belong to the spiritual dimension, and robots exist in the physical dimension. Morality and ethics can apply to the developers, the programmers, and the people who construct these robots, but not to the robots themselves.

And that is why you should consider: when is the word "robot" used for a human being? It is used to refer to a person who behaves in a mechanical or unemotional manner. The key emphasis is on the word "unemotional."

So we as human beings have a body and we have a soul. We are not our bodies; we are souls that make use of our bodies in order to function within this world. Our bodies are bound by the laws of this universe. Our souls, on the other hand, are free and transcend the laws of this universe. And it is because of this limitless nature of the soul that the emotions it displays are also limitless, boundless, and timeless.

Let us do a simple exercise in order to understand. Do you love your parents? How much do you love your parents? How many pounds of love do you have? Quantify it for me. How many siblings do you have? You answered that one quite quickly. How is that? When I asked you to quantify your love for your parents, you struggled so much, but when I asked you to quantify your siblings for me, it was instantaneous. Why is that? It is because things can be quantified only when they occur within time and space. Your siblings have a body that is tangible.

and that exists within time and space, so you are able to quantify them. Your love is an emotion that transcends time and space, and it is intangible; that is why there is no way for you to quantify or measure it. Do you understand?

Now, do your parents love you? How do you know that? Only when their intangible love was expressed as actions within physicality, within the confine of time and space, were you able to detect it, identify it, observe it. Only then were you able to put some sort of conceptual measure around it. Correct? So the only way you can identify that intangible emotion of your parents' love is when it is expressed physically; only then does it become observable and noticeable. Do you agree? Therefore I can say that only by observing the tangible were you able to recognize the existence of the intangible love of your parents.

Now, when they acted upon their love and expressed it physically, how did you know it was meant for you? How did you know its relevance? Because it was directed toward you, and it was designed to meet your needs. For example, you are dying of hunger, and you say, "Ammi, I am really hungry. Can you make me something to eat?" and your mother comes and gives you a hug and a kiss on the cheek. Now, that is love, is it not? But it is not the kind of love you need right now. It will not register as love for you, because it is not designed to meet your current need. Do you understand? You will say, "Ammi, I do not need the hug-and-kiss kind of love right now; I need the edible kind of love right now." Do you understand?

So there are a few principles at work here that I want you to recognize. Emotions are qualities of the soul; they are not bound within time and space, and therefore they cannot be quantified. Bodies, on the other hand, are bound within time and space, and therefore they can be counted. The only way an emotion can be identified or recognized is when it is converted into a physical action. Once it expresses itself as a physical action or a physical gesture, it can be recognized. Therefore the physical expression of that emotion is proof of the existence of that spiritual emotion. If I need to recognize the intangible emotion, my only option is to see it through the expression of the tangible action. And finally, there is a specific design and a target for the expression of that emotion. Unless it is designed and structured to meet your specific needs, the expression of that emotion does not translate accurately. Does that make sense? Both of these elements have to come together:

1. The physical expression of the emotion
2. It should be designed and structured in a way that meets your specific needs

Only when both of these exist can you conclude that your mother loves you. Do you agree?

Now let us address some preconceived notions. What is science, again? Science is a methodology for understanding a reality based on a system of cause and effect. What is religion? Religion is an ideology that translates into a way of life; it is a way of life that is ideologically tracked. Let us understand their scope.

Science is an observation of cause and effect. It is a tool, and it has limitations. All scientists agree that science is still in its infancy in practically every single field. It is nowhere close to maturity. There is research being done, as we speak.

In every scientific area, new things are being discovered and existing scientific methods are being improved. The way science works is that a theory is put forward — an observation of something that fits our idea of how we see the physical world. Then data is gathered for or against the theory. The exceptions or deviations are called anomalies. A statistical analysis is then performed on the data that has been collected, and a conclusion is drawn. If the statistical probability is very low, the theory is disproved. I am simplifying this a great deal, but if you are interested, we can ask Anees to explain it in more detail.

You must understand, however, that science is not a perfect tool. Science is only as good as its measurements. In the end, it is only a statistical probability. It rests on trial and error. So, first of all, it is merely a tool, and secondly, it is an incomplete and imperfect tool. Please understand this. If you think that science is the hundred-percent absolute answer to everything, that is a complete misconception.

Let me give you an example. When Galileo, who was the first to use the telescope, observed the heavenly bodies, he was able to see facts that had never been known to mankind before. For instance, he found that the surface of the moon is not smooth; he found that Jupiter had four moons. Now, did these realities exist before 1600? Of course they did — but science was only able to prove them in 1600. Today we know about the universe only what science has told us so far, yet realities already exist that still need to be discovered. So if science cannot prove the existence of God, that means nothing. Perhaps it will be able to prove God's existence a hundred years from now, but you and I will not be here a hundred years from now. So we cannot really wait for science to give us the answers, can we?

Religion, on the other hand, speaks from a position of perfection, from a position of authority. You never hear that research is being done in religion to increase the rakats of Maghrib from three to four. Nor is research being done in the ethical or moral teachings of Islam to suggest that perhaps truth is not the best moral action, that perhaps lies could be made a moral standard. We never see that happening. The only research being done in religion is in understanding the existing and established principles of morality and ethics. But no new morality or code of ethics is being added to the set that already exists.

So, on the one hand, we have an imperfect tool called science. And I am not saying that it is not an amazing or an extremely relevant tool. It absolutely is. But it is, nonetheless, an imperfect tool. And on the other hand, we have a perfect religion in which no changes are being made, nor have ever been made, nor will ever be made. Societies have been functioning on these codes of morality and ethics for ages. The laws of government are all based on religious teachings. And I am stating these as plain and simple facts.

Now, religion — Islam, for example — and science take different positions when it comes to the creation of this universe and of man. From the Islamic perspective, it is absolutely clear that Allah is the fashioner, the creator, and the designer of everything, because we understand rationally that from nothing comes nothing. Something cannot come from nothing. Today we know that we are something.

and we know that before that we were nothing. And so we must somehow establish where we come from, where all of this began. This is a very important question to answer. Now, there are different arguments about it. Some say we came about through probability, that there is a chance we were created at random. There is another group that says no, it is impossible for something to come from nothing, and therefore there must be an intelligent designer who assembled us. The system we see around us is simply too complex, too intricate, and too structured. It is too well formulated and too universal to have appeared out of nowhere at random. It could not have simply emerged from this primordial soup. And even this primordial soup that we speak of had to come from somewhere. Where did this soup come from? There had to be something to bring the primordial soup about, because, once again, from nothing you cannot have something in the physical sense of the matter.

Now, if we could prove that what exists today has always, always existed, then that would be a different matter. But there is no evidence whatsoever to prove it, none whatsoever. In fact, there is clear and undeniable evidence that the universe had a beginning, that it exploded from a singularity, which is the big bang theory. It is very clear. Even Stephen Hawking speaks about this issue: that prior to the Planck moment, 1×10 to the power of 43 seconds after the big bang occurred, we cannot speak scientifically, because all the laws of science fall apart. And we understand that, so we must stop at that moment and not discuss anything earlier.

Now, if you wish to talk about things before that point, you can be philosophical about it, but you cannot speak scientifically about it, because, scientifically speaking, all the instruments of science cease to exist before that point in time. Thus there is nothing one can use to hold this conversation, unless one wishes to be speculative and philosophical about it. So you cannot go prior to the big bang on the grounds of science; you can only go there through philosophy, and religion is the only philosophy that allows us to do so.

The reason people have a problem with the existence of God is that it requires them to take a certain leap of faith, because we are speaking of a being that cannot be measured within the realm of science. Therefore one has to take a leap of faith, and this is where science has a problem, and I do not blame it. I do not expect science to take a leap of faith and say there is a God. Science is only a tool; it is a mechanism of observation. It is simply a methodology. Leave it there. No one has asked it to become a believer. It is a man-made tool, to be used by man to reach our own objectives within this spectacular system.

But we have also intelligently understood that this scientific system has a set of fixed laws that we call the laws of constants, for example the universal constants. These constants, which, by the way, were set in motion instantaneously at the Planck moment, did not go through an evolutionary process; they established themselves instantaneously at the Planck moment. These constants set the pace for the expansion of this universe. How can this whole sub-system of creation take place if this super-structure did not exist?

We are not speaking of some small piece of structure that sits within a larger structure; we are speaking of the entire system. Where did it come from? If it is something, how did it come from nothing? It had to come from something, because out of nothing you can obtain only nothing.

Now Bertrand Russell, a famous atheist, posed this question. Since you say that everything needs a maker, that everything must have a predecessor, very well: I will grant that God created this universe. But then my question is, who created God? For according to what you say, everything that exists must have a predecessor. So who was God's predecessor? This was the classic question Bertrand Russell asked. If you say that you cannot get something from nothing, then who created God? Now that is a very valid question.

But we have to understand this within the scheme of the realities of the lives we live. We must understand, first and foremost, that we are looking at a relative world. You and I exist in this relative realm, where time, matter, and space, the time-space continuum, are all part of the fabric of our super-structure. They give us what we have and make us who we are. Now, scientifically speaking, at the Planck moment, at the moment of the big bang, we know that all of these things did not exist. Time, space, and matter came into existence at that point; they did not exist before it. The question, then, is what it was that caused this.

We understand this from a philosophical argument, because we cannot carry on a scientific conversation beyond that point. Therefore, from a philosophical point of view, and using reverse logic, we must say that whatever began it cannot have been relative to this time-space continuum. It cannot have been bound in time, nor in matter, nor in space, nor in the time-space continuum. The argument of a predecessor applies within the realm of time, space, and matter; it is within this realm that cause and effect take place, not outside of it. Therefore the same rules of precedence do not apply. This, again, is a philosophical argument. Why? Because we are looking at a point where scientific conversation is not possible, and we can speak only philosophically.

Now, if we look at this argument mathematically, we begin with the assumption that God created this universe, and that in this process of cause and effect He created me. If I now establish the argument of a predecessor for God, then I will have to believe that His predecessor had a predecessor, who had a predecessor, who had a predecessor, and by the laws of mathematics I must carry this to infinity. This means that there is now an infinite wait for my God to exist. And if my God does not exist, the universe cannot exist, and therefore I cannot exist. Therefore the God who created this universe and me cannot have a predecessor.

These are the three signs of piety, the first of which is belief in the unseen. What is the unseen? God, the soul, and the afterlife. So the first component is belief in God, the soul, and an afterlife. And after that belief, notice:

After the unseen comes the prayer. Why? Because if you do not believe in the unseen, if you have no faith in it, if you do not believe in God, the soul, and the afterlife, then there is no point to prayer. The verse itself teaches us that prayer has something to do with the unseen; it has to do with faith. If this element of faith is absent, then prayer is nothing more than a physical, cardiovascular exercise. The word used in the verse is Salaah, which comes from the root صلو, from which we also get the word اتصال, meaning to connect. So the word Salaah literally means "to connect." Connect to what? To the unseen world. So the first thing is belief and faith in the unseen world, and after that comes connecting to it. And then comes spending from what Allah has given you. This carries a far, far deeper meaning than merely spending money; in fact, everything else within Islam falls within this third category. God willing, we will discuss "rizq" and "spending," and what they mean, at a later time.

But notice what is interesting. Right at the beginning of His revelation, in the first few verses of Surah al-Baqarah, Allah says that this book is a book of guidance only for the pious, not for everyone. He then states the three components of piety, the first of which is faith. He says that if you wish to approach Him, it will have to be on the basis of faith. This clearly explains the importance of faith. And in the previous session I showed you that we do a great many things purely on the basis of faith. There is nothing wrong with that; it is in fact a higher form of intelligence.

The way I now see it, after years and years of study, is that the only purpose of the intellect is to bring us to the point where we can operate on the basis of faith alone. It is like the training wheels on a bicycle. When a child learns to ride a bicycle, we put training wheels on it. Why? What is the purpose of those training wheels? So that the child learns how to balance the bicycle, in other words, so that he develops the faith and confidence that he can ride it safely. Once the child learns that, he no longer needs those training wheels. So I see the confidence to ride the bicycle as faith, and the training wheels as the intellect. The purpose of the intellect is to make us confident about riding the bicycle. Once we are confident, we no longer need the training wheels in order to ride. Similarly, the intellect is there to support faith. Once faith develops and grows strong through the training wheels of the intellect, we are no longer dependent on that intellectual backing, because we already possess the faith. We can simply operate on faith from that point forward.

Think about your closest friends in life. When you first met them, you were probably very careful in your interactions with them. You examined and weighed their every act, their every intention, until you developed faith in their friendship. And once you developed that faith in their love, loyalty, and sincerity, you now interact with them simply on the basis of faith. This does not mean that you have tossed your intellect aside.

It simply means that you have developed faith, and now you no longer need to question their intentions and motives at every turn. Faith, then, plays an enormous role in our daily lives, whether or not we realize it. So much of what we accomplish rests on faith alone. Does that make sense, at least as a matter of theory?

Today I would like to begin taking up some of those basic questions we arrived at in our last session, the questions about the existence of God. Does God exist? Do I even need a God? And above all, why should I care? How does it affect my life if I discover that there is no God? How does it affect my life if I discover that there is, in fact, a God? These are questions of the greatest importance.

Over the years, I have had a great many discussions and debates with atheists and agnostics on this very subject of the existence of God. A couple of years ago I had a friend at work named Igor. He is from Ukraine, and he used to be an atheist. His parents are atheists as well, and not merely atheists but very staunch ones. His mother actually teaches atheism at a college. At the time I did not even know that atheism was a subject taught in school. So we used to have these heated discussions on the question of God's existence, and through them I learned a great deal about atheism. It helped me enormously, because it compelled me to research, to study, and to learn more and more, and to work out counterarguments to his arguments, for the sake of my own faith more than anything else.

But in my discussions with him and with others over the years, I have come to realize that in the end atheism comes down to essentially two issues, two places where people of faith and people without faith see things very differently.

The first is in how we, the believers, and the atheists see created things. We look at the same sun, the same moon, the same stars, the same mountains, the same existence of all creation, of our very selves, down to the same protein, and yet the conclusions the two of us reach are very, very different. For the atheist, it is essentially chalked up to chance and chaos, and for him the universe has no purpose or conscience in and of itself. To him, the entire universe is without conscience, and from that it is easy to extrapolate that human beings themselves possess no conscience. And so the whole idea of right and wrong, the whole idea of morality, can be washed away, because it is left entirely to us to decide what is right and what is wrong. A consequence of believing in this chaos is that it actually brings this chaos into human existence. In other words, because we are not answerable to anyone, we therefore need have no order in our lives. So there are consequences to this belief in chaos, consequences that reach beyond a mere academic exercise about the origins of the universe. There is a direct impact on how we regard our own lives. This, then, is the first difference: how they and we see our own lives and existence as created things.

The second major difference lies in the attributes of God, in the objection that, if there is a God, how can He be so unfair. And this, in turn, comes down to either a personal matter or an observational one. In the personal sense: if God is so great, how is it that I was diagnosed with cancer? How is it that I lost my job? How is it that I lost my home? What did my child ever do to deserve to die? How is it that the tornado struck my house and not some other house?

Basically, it comes down to matters of justice and love. How did this injustice happen to me? So it rests upon some kind of personal trauma, and that points to the psychological origins of atheism. There is some personal, painful experience, and they lay the blame for it upon God. Why did He not protect me from it? Why did He not come to my aid? I prayed to Him so much, and still I failed and did not get into medical school, and so on. And therefore I do not believe in His existence. That is the personal side of it.

On the observational side: Why is there war? Why is there disease? Why are there diseases that still have no cure? Or whatever the case may be. Why are there catastrophes in which innocent people die? Look all around you: where do you see justice? How can you believe in a God who allows all of these things to happen? So on the one hand it is about how we view creation, how we observe the universe around us and within ourselves, and on the other hand it is bound up with matters of justice. That, in essence, is the substance of every conversation I have had with people who are undergoing a crisis of faith. And then they regard those who do believe as a kind of primitive, pre-modern creature that does not belong in this century.

I had these discussions with Igor for a couple of months, and at the end of them he arrived at the conclusion that he was not sure about the existence of God. Perhaps He exists, perhaps He does not. I was very pleased with that outcome, because he had moved from there is absolutely no God to I am not sure whether there is a God. He had gone from being an atheist to an agnostic, and so we left the matter there. Then, a couple of months later, he came to me and told me that he was now convinced there had to be a God. I remember being quite surprised by this, because I had not expected it. So I asked what had led him to this conclusion. He said that it had simply come together. It had simply clicked. Once he was able to gain a different perspective, the very same things in which he had seen chaos, in which he could see no order, he now saw as intelligent design. SubhanAllah! He still does not believe in organized religion, but he now does believe in a deity. So he went from being an atheist to an agnostic, and finally to a deist. Hamdulillah!

But I remember that, when we began, he would say so adamantly that there is absolutely no evidence to prove the existence of God. And that is the most common statement made in denying God's existence: that there is no physical evidence that God exists. And I stress the word "physical." They say there is no physical, scientific, empirical evidence to this day that can prove conclusively that a deity or a God exists, and therefore He does not exist. And I used to say to him that this statement was completely absurd to me. For a lack of evidence can never be evidence for an argument in a court of law. To say that God does not exist because I have no evidence is tantamount to absurdity in a court of law.

It is like standing in a courtroom before a jury and saying: because I lack the evidence to prove that this man is guilty, therefore he is guilty. Or: I lack the evidence to prove that this man is innocent, therefore he is innocent. That would be completely absurd. Evidence proves the existence or non-existence of something.

not the absence of it. It is therefore unacceptable, and entirely absurd, to say that I do not believe in God because there is no evidence for the existence of God. I may be agnostic and say that I am not sure whether God exists or not; that is acceptable, an acceptable starting point. But I certainly cannot say, on the mere grounds of a lack of evidence, that God does not exist. To any intelligent person, that is truly putting the cart before the horse.

I used to tell Igor: if you wish to speak with me about the non-existence of God, give me hard, irrefutable evidence that He does not exist; but do not tell me He does not exist on the basis of a lack of evidence. He could not, and to this day no one can.

Originally I had planned only to touch upon this subject of the existence of God. But after my conversation with you, Imran, I realize that there is a need for an in-depth study of it, because I too struggled a great deal with what you seem to be struggling with today. And I will assume that you are not the only one; there may be others in the group as well. So I went back to my notes to see how I had addressed these questions for myself.

But before we enter this topic, you need to understand my purpose in exploring and researching it. For I do not think that, unless and until you share the same purpose, we will be able to reach the same goal.

As I said earlier, my quest for knowledge and for answers began when 9/11 happened. It truly forced me to question the purpose of my existence. As some of you know, I worked in a building very close to the twin towers. And when this terrible atrocity occurred, I realized that it could have been me. Those people who died had families, just as I do; they had twenty-year plans for the future, just as I do. Some of them may not have believed in God. They came to work that morning thinking it would be just another day at the office, and now they are gone. I could have been one of them.

And my concern became this: if I die today, and if there is a God, am I ready to face Him? Am I prepared? What would happen if He does exist and I am standing before Him, completely helpless and completely empty-handed? These questions began to keep me up at night. So this quest to find the truth for myself was not some clever hobby I had taken up. It was not something I wished to gain knowledge or information about so that I could have interesting conversations and win arguments and debates with my friends. It was, for me, a matter of the very purpose of my existence. It was a deadly serious matter for me to discover these answers.

And the reason I raise this is that these are the questions you must ask yourself. How serious are you about finding these answers? And why? What will you do once you have found them? Are you willing to meet the demands of that answer once you find it? Because if not, who cares? Why should you trouble yourself with this question at all? Simply go on living your life as it is. These questions matter only when they are tied to an end goal.

When I began to deconstruct my religion, I needed certain validations. I realized that it was my duty and my responsibility, for the sake of my life, to find the right answers for myself and to validate what was being said to me. I did not want to be preached to.

I did not want to be told what to believe or not. I did not want to follow a religion out of fear of the punishments of a hell, or because I was enticed by a heaven. I did not want to be fooled by anyone, and I did not want anyone feeding me fairy tales. I wanted certainty, no matter what it was. If you tell me this is the truth, then no matter what it is, no matter its name, no matter its brand, I will accept it and I will follow it. And then, if that faith demands hard work from me, I will work hard at it. If it asks me to stay hungry, I will fast. If it asks me to spend my money, I will. If it means I have to face the ridicule of my friends, then so be it. If it means going against my parents and my family, then so be it. I decided I would fulfill any and every demand of that religion, but only if I were convinced it was the truth. It is as simple as that.

And it was "I" who needed to be convinced of it. It had to make sense to "ME." Not because my parents believe it is right, and not because my highly intelligent atheist friend, whom I look up to, believes it is right. So many times I found my judgments clouded by the people in my life who held an emotional influence over me, people I respected and admired. You know: if he does not believe in God, there must be some reason; after all, he is so intelligent, how could he be wrong? I had these kinds of biases. But I realized that this is my life, and it is my afterlife that I am talking about here. So the only person it needs to make sense to is ME, because in the end I stand alone before Allah in the afterlife anyway.

وَلَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونَا فُرَدَىٰ كَمَا خَلَقْنَكُمْ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍۢ
And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time,

وَتَرَكْتُم مَّا خَوَّلْنَكُمْ وَرَآءَ ظُهُورِكُمْ
and you have left behind whatever We bestowed upon you,

وَمَا نَرَىٰ مَعَكُمْ شُفَعَآءَكُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ زَعَمْتُمْ أَنَّهُمْ فِيكُمْ شُرَكَٓؤُا۟
and today We do not see with you your friends, your "intercessors," who supported you against your belief in Me;

لَقَد تَّقَطَّعَ بَيْنَكُمْ وَضَلَّ عَنكُم مَّا كُنتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ
today all those associates have been severed from you, and all your claims are now lost.

If this is the reality of the Day of Judgment, then who cares what anybody else thinks? If I am going to stand alone before Allah, then all that matters is what I believe. So that is the intention with which I started my journey.

So this is how I started my journey. But when I began researching the subject of the existence of a god, I kept getting stuck in this endless cycle of how I could be sure. What if there was another explanation? What if I made the wrong decision by believing in the existence of a god? So even though the answers were making sense to me, and they were passing all the falsification tests, I still just was not sure. And I could not understand what was wrong with me. Why does everyone else get it and I do not? But then, praise be to God, I was blessed with some amazing friends—may Allah bless them endlessly—who showed me that it was not the answers that were the problem; the problem was with my expectations about the answers. You see, when there is too much information, it can create chaos, it can overwhelm, and sometimes you cannot see the answers right in front of you. So this friend...

My name is Naoman—he asked me: do you even know what answer you are looking for? Do you even know what answer would satisfy you? Are you expecting someone to show you a photograph of God? Are you expecting to see God with your own eyes, to speak with Him? If He were to appear before you, introduce Himself to you, and shake your hand—would that convince you? These questions truly shook me. I had to ask myself what, exactly, I was expecting the answer to be. Seeing God physically is not possible, for very obvious reasons. So then I had to ask myself: if I cannot see a photograph of God, and I cannot see Him physically, then the only option left to me for recognizing His existence is through reasoning. Only intellectually, through logical thinking, can I arrive at His existence.

And this is where science came to my rescue. This is what I love about science: it has such a methodical approach to things. At its most fundamental level, science is deeply non-emotive; there is no emotion involved in it. It is pure methodology. So I wrote down everything I had learned about God, and then I organized those thoughts into a sequence, using a scientific and methodical approach. Today I think of them as, essentially, my test cases—my litmus test, if you will. I settled on certain definitions, certain principles, against which I would then put the existence of God to the test. And I decided that if the existence of God met these tests, I would accept it; if not, I would reject it. This is what we are going to try to do over these next few sessions, God willing.

So Naoman helped me break my inquiry down into three steps, and God willing, I hope to do the same for all of you. First: a clear definition of things. One of the challenges with conversations on the existence of God and religion is that they can be derailed very easily. A great deal of the time, either we do not understand the concepts clearly, or we have not defined our questions properly, or we do not fully grasp the meaning of the terms we are debating. As a result, we tend to segregate ideas, and then we fight over one side against the other—when in reality there is always an overlap between everything we discuss. That is simply the nature of this vast system of the universe: no matter what we address, or how we address it, there is always some sort of overlap—what we call a sharing of realities as well as of physical states. So it feels to us that if the question concerns an unseen entity like God, then the answer must be purely metaphysical, with no overlap with the physical. And that is not true, because we learned from the Qur'an that the only way to understand the unseen is through the recognition and understanding of the seen.

So when comparing and contrasting science and religion, the first thing for us to ask is this: are these two separate entities? Are science and religion two separate things that cannot be reconciled? Or are they really part of one single entity that somehow, over the span of time, became separated—through certain misunderstandings, or through particular positions that one side took against the other? What is the relationship between the two? Is one subordinate to the other? And how do we define science, and how do we define religion?

What does it mean to be scientific? What does it mean to follow *a* religion? To believe in *a* religion? When people ask, "Are you religious?" or when someone says, "I do not believe in a religion"—what is it that they mean by that? We need first to understand these definitions, and then to examine their strengths and their limitations. What is their scope? Do they have an upper bound, a limit, or are they limitless? Do they address the physical? Do they address the spiritual? Do they address both? Where does religion come into play? Is it for the heart or for the intellect? Is it abstract or concrete? Does it deal with the emotions or with the physical body? How far can science go? And what do we need if we wish to go beyond that limit?

Without a clear definition of these terms in my head, I kept ending up in circular or argumentative discussions. Because, as we now know, that is what intellect means: to restrain, to create a boundary within which we can operate safely. And definitions provide us with that boundary. They are like a logical pathway that allows us to correlate our conversations rather than end up in endless cycles.

In the previous session we talked about all these definitions of science and religion and body and soul. Later I realized this was getting too technical. The last session felt too bookish, too mechanical. I realized I had lost the simplicity of things. Islam is about simplicity. My goal for these sessions is to make things simple, not to overcomplicate them with loads and loads of data. And I was also reading a great deal from a paper, which I normally never do. I usually just have a conversation.

So I decided I am not going to go through all those mathematical and highly technical proofs, debates, and arguments that I have about the existence of God, because we really do not need any of that. I am going to make this very, very simple for you. If you are willing to see the truth, then what I am going to show you today will be more than enough, InshaAllah. If not, then nothing I say is going to matter anyway.

I personally think the problem lies with this leap of faith that religion requires. You can have all the scientific proof in the world, but that first step you take can only be a leap of faith. And what is interesting to me is that we do this all the time in our daily lives.

When you invest in the stock of a company, it is a leap of faith. You can have all the data and research on the company, but that is no guarantee that the stock will not tank. Yet we still make these investments.

Starting a new medical treatment
Starting a new job
Marriage
Friendship

We take these leaps of faith all the time. But I do not know what it is with religion: when it comes to religion, we find it so hard to make that leap.

You know, if your hands are cold, you have to rub them together to get them warm. Just knowing that you should rub them, or talking about it, does not warm your hands. You have to start rubbing your hands and see whether you feel the warmth or not. You cannot feel the love of Allah by merely talking about it. The only way you can feel it is if you actually begin to practice it.

I do not know; that is at least how I see things. In any case, what I have to say today will, I think, InshaAllah be enough information for you children to be able to take this leap of faith. If not, then InshaAllah whenever you are ready, and whenever Allah opens your heart to Him.

وما توفیقی الا باللہ ولا حول ولا قوۃ الا باللہ العلی العظیم

So let us begin. Yasu and Imran, I am going to pretend to conduct a scientific experiment with you. And I want you to play along and work with me. All right?

Let us say I walk up to you and show you a clock. Nothing fancy, just a simple, ordinary, battery operated, analog clock. And I hand you a screwdriver and ask you both: let us examine this clock, let us study it scientifically. What are some of the things we would see? We would see the face of the clock with numbers on it that run from 1 to 12. We would see 3 hands, one for seconds, one for minutes, one for the hour. We would see the seconds hand moving faster than the minute hand, and the minute hand moving faster than the hour hand. Then we unscrew the back of the clock and begin to look at the insides. I am sending you an illustration of what you would see.

Now let us examine what we see here. There is a battery compartment.

that holds a battery. We see a chrome solenoid, an oscillator, a few gears, and so on. The first thing we notice is that these components are not all alike. They are made from different materials, and they differ in shape and size. Some are made of metal, some of plastic. Some are round, some are rectangular. Some are delicate, others sturdier. Looking at the gears, we see that some are smooth while others have cuts and grooves in them, and they are not all the same size. Is that not so?

As for how these different components are put together, what do we see? We see that there is a power source, a battery, which charges the chrome solenoid, which in turn triggers the oscillator. This oscillator spins the first gear, and that gear governs the movement of the seconds hand, one turn per second. Then we see that the seconds gear is connected to the minutes gear in such a way that when it turns sixty times, it turns the minutes gear once; and when the minutes gear turns sixty times, it turns the hour gear to which it is connected once. I have not shown this in the diagram, but when we examine the matter further, we see that on the other side the first gear is attached to the seconds hand, the second gear to the minutes hand, and the third to the hour hand. Is that not so?

So there are many components, of different materials, shapes, and sizes, all connected to one another. When we watch this clock at work, do we find a single, unified purpose that all these components are laboring to accomplish? What is it? To tell the time. Now that is an interesting observation, is it not? All of these plainly unlike objects, of different materials and shapes, are coming together to accomplish one goal, which is to tell the time.

That is why, when the Greek philosophers came into contact with Islam for the first time, their greatest complaint about Islam was that these people do not talk about things that do not exist. They do not talk about abstract ideas. They talk about direct, concrete examples. Their way of thinking is too direct. There is no confusion in it. It is too straightforward. How terrible! The Islamic thought process has always, always been very straightforward.

A philosophical question was once put to an Arab bedouin, and the story is so beautiful. A Roman atheist was traveling through the Arabian desert — this is a very old story — and he met an Arab bedouin, and he asked: how do you know there is a God? The Roman asked the Arab bedouin, how do you know there is a God?

The Arab looked around, and he saw camel droppings. He pointed to them and said: a camel was here. And then he walked away. That was his answer! How do I know a camel was here? I see camel droppings. How do I know there is a God in the universe? Look around! He has left His signs everywhere! What do you mean, there is no God? To the Arab it was that simple. ترک البیع البیرۃ — the camel left its droppings. It was so simple. Look: this is here, therefore something had to be here before. Something left this. That is enough for me. Straightforward reasoning. They did not complicate matters at all.

Invitation to reflection

And this is why the Qur'an is so beautiful! It gives us roads to conviction through this same single argument. How are you absolutely convinced that this is the truth? How do you know for certain that this revelation is from Allah? How do you know that this is not merely a theory, not merely one more theology, but the absolute truth? Simply reflect upon the creations around you. Allah says that if you reflect genuinely and honestly upon the creations around you, there is no way you will arrive at any other conclusion. This is the Qur'an's argument:

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

Certainly, without doubt, in the heavens and the earth, and in the changing of night and day, there are miraculous signs for those of intellect.

Allah never proves His existence in the Qur'an

Do you know something interesting? Allah never used revelation to prove His existence. Why is that? This is His message! His Book! He should have filled it with proofs of His existence. Yet, interestingly enough, Allah did not use the Qur'an to prove His existence. Allah never speaks about the proof of His existence in the Qur'an. It is not even a subject in the Qur'an. If an atheist asks, show me a surah in which Allah proves that He exists, we cannot do that.

The Qur'an does discuss doubt. It absolutely discusses doubt, but it discusses doubt in revelation, whether this is revelation or not: ذلک الکتاب لا ریب فیہ. Nowhere in the Qur'an does Allah say ذلک الألہ لا ریب فیہ. It discusses doubt in revelation. It discusses doubt in messengers. It discusses doubt in the afterlife. It discusses every aspect of our faith that flows from belief in Allah, matters such as these: this God could not have left me without guidance; this God cannot be unjust to me; there must be some mechanism of justice. All of those conclusions are discussed. But when it comes to doubt in the existence of Allah, Allah simply asks a rhetorical question, as though it is not even a valid concern for Him:

أفی اللہ شک؟

Is there even the possibility of doubt in Allah? He does not even say أفی وجدود اللہ شک؟ He does not even say, is there doubt in the existence of Allah, but rather أفی اللہ شک؟ That can be understood as: Are you serious? Do you truly mean this? What do you mean, is there an Allah or not? Are you doubting My justice? My mercy? My love? My care? My guidance? Because if you do not believe in My existence, you do not believe in any of My attributes either. Can you really do that? With everything I have done for you, with everything you see around you, is that even a question for you?

Do you know why Allah never discusses doubt in His existence?

Because Allah's declaration in the Qur'an is that you already have another set of ayats — another set of signs that will bring you to that conclusion. Do you remember what the word ayah means? A miraculous sign. Now what is the purpose of a sign? It points to something. If you see a sign for your school, does that mean you have reached the school? No. It is a sign pointing to your school, which means that if you follow this sign, you will reach your school. You see a sign for the airport, and you know it is a pointer to the location of the airport. All you have to do is follow the sign and you will get there. Correct? Allah called the verses in the Qur'an ayats, and He referred to His creation as ayats:

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

He said: to see My existence, you do not need these ayats in My book. Look around you. Look at all the signs I have placed all around you and inside of you. Those will automatically bring you to that conclusion. What are those signs? The skies, the earth, the mountains, the clouds, the breeze, the rain, the plants, the animals — all of this will bring you to that conclusion if you reflect seriously and honestly. It will become impossible for you to say that this is the product of an accident. Nobody in their right mind will be able to say that all of this is the result of an accident.

How could this be an accident? We know the big bang was an explosion; scientific proof exists for that. What do we know about an explosion? Is it constructive in nature, or is it destructive in nature? Do explosions bring about chaos and disorder, or do they bring about structure and order? They are destructive. Explosions bring about chaos. What sort of an explosion was this, that created such magnificent design and order? Have you ever heard that there is a doctor, a lawyer, an engineer, and a Mulla in a room, and there is this explosion, and the doctor flies out and lands in his chair in his clinic, the lawyer gets thrown out into his courtroom, and the Mulla flies off and fits into his masjid? Does that ever happen? If there is a huge pile of rubble lying around and I throw in a stick of dynamite, does that explode into a twelve-story building, with lighting, wiring, and plumbing? Does that ever happen? So what kind of explosion was this, that was so intelligent that it created such amazing structure? Why did this explosion have the opposite effect of any other explosion in this world? Who reversed the effect of that cause? Is that not a sign? Who is the sign pointing to?

If this was an accident, explain to me why things like beauty exist in this world. Why would beauty exist as the result of an accident? You have seen accidents, have you not? When two people get into an accident, do they come out looking more beautiful or more ugly? Then why does this beauty exist as the result of this so-called accident? Why would delicious taste exist as part of an accident? How would that make any sense? How would symmetry exist in the universe as part of an accident? A little snowflake — why does it have such incredibly artistic symmetry? Today we have super expensive chandeliers designed in imitation of that snowflake. How could all of this be merely because of an accident? We should have chaos and ugliness everywhere. It should all be mangled and twisted.

Why is it so beautiful? SubhanAllah! Look at the symmetry in a leaf. Look at the beauty in a flower. How could this be an accident?

You know how it is when you walk into a store and pick up the new iPhone or the Samsung Galaxy and admire it. What is the first thing you notice? So sleek, so beautiful, such amazing symmetry. Who designed this? Who is the manufacturer? That leaf is Allah's design. He is the manufacturer of that leaf. Look at it. Appreciate it. It will give you a completely different experience.

Consider the phones again. Did the iPhone come together as the result of an accident? Did the flip phone, over time, all by itself, through some cosmic accident, evolve into the iPhone 6? No. Somebody designed the flip phone, and somebody designed the iPhone. Now, if you cannot believe that a simple device like a phone, a simple device like a clock, could come together by some accident, then how can you believe that this huge universe, this entire universe, these multiverses, came into existence by an accident?

You do not really have to be sitting in these Sunday sessions, or in any Islamic lecture, to experience faith. You only have to pay attention to the world around you. You only have to pay attention to the ayaats Allah created all around you.

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

Certainly, without any doubt, in the heavens and the earth, and in the changing of night and day, there are miraculous signs for those of intellect.

This is so beautiful. I love this ayah. Such amazing symmetry. SubhanAllah!

The verses of the Quran are called ayaats, and Allah also calls His creations ayaats. These ayaats, these signs of the Quran, push us outside into the world, so that we may examine the ayaats and signs that lie outside the Quran. And the ayaats that are outside push us back to the Quran, so that we may understand the One the signs are pointing to. SubhanAllah! The book forces us to look at the world, and the world forces us back to look into the book. SubhanAllah! How amazing is that? We are constantly moving back and forth between the book and the universe. Our entire life is spent going from one set of ayaats to another set of ayaats, back and forth.

It is truly incredible. Allah has placed so many ayaats, so many signs, in the Quran, and He wants us to use them to reach Him. If only we would follow the signs, instead of endlessly debating how we can know that He put them there. What if, what if, what if.

Allah says that you do not need the what ifs. Just look at the what is.

هُوَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ لَكُم مَّا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًۭا

I am the One who created everything in this world for you.

ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰٓ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَسَوَّىٰهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَوَتٍۢ ۚ وَهُوَ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمٌۭ

Then I turned to the skies and fashioned them into seven skies for you.

إِنَّنِىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ فَٱعْبُدْنِى وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكْرِىٓ

O My beloved creation! I am your Allah. There is no one but I. Worship Me, pray to Me, and mention My name.

You want to know about Me? I will tell you. Just take a step toward Me, and I Myself will tell you who I am.

ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ

Do you think I ever forget about you?

لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌۭ وَلَا نَوْمٌۭ

I do not sleep and I do not grow tired. I never rest.

How could I forget about you? What is it that I own? لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Me. How far does My knowledge reach? يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ ۖ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍۢ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ I know everything that has happened in the past and everything that is going to happen in the future. Nothing can take place without My knowledge. Nothing lies outside My authority. وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ ۖ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ My power encompasses the heavens and the earth, and guarding them, sustaining them, caring for them does not tire Me. Do you think I will not protect you? Do you think I will grow tired of caring for you?

Do you not see what I have done for you? هُوَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُم مِّن تُرَابٍۢ ثُمَّ مِن نُّطْفَةٍۢ ثُمَّ مِنْ عَلَقَةٍۢ I am the One who created you from this earth, and then turned a drop of fluid into a growing child in the womb. ثُمَّ يُخْرِجُكُمْ طِفْلًۭا Then you came into this world as an infant. ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوٓا۟ أَشُدَّكُمْ Then I gave you life so that you could grow into an adult. ثُمَّ لِتَكُونُوا۟ شُيُوخًۭا Until you grew old. وَمِنكُم مَّن يُتَوَفَّىٰ مِن قَبْلُ And some of you I take back before they reach old age. ‏هُوَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُم مِّن طِينٍۢ ثُمَّ قَضَىٰٓ أَجَلًۭا I am the One who gave you life and sent you into this world, and I am the One who appointed death for you so that you could return to Me.

Do you think you are the one in control? Do you think it is your education, your wealth, your standing in society that gave you your honor? قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ مَلِكَ ٱلْمُلْكِ۔ O My beloved Messenger, tell them: I am your Master. I am the King. تُؤْتِى ٱلْمُلْكَ مَن تَشَآءُ وَتَنزِعُ ٱلْمُلْكَ مِمَّن تَشَآءُ ۔ I grant kingdom to the ones I choose, and I take it back from the ones I choose. وَتُعِزُّ مَن تَشَآءُ وَتُذِلُّ مَن تَشَآءُ ۖ I honor whom I will, and I humble whom I will. بِيَدِكَ ٱلْخَيْرُ ۖ إِنَّكَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدِيرٌۭ Every good that you see comes from My hands. I am the One who has power over all things.

How can you deny Me? Do you not see My signs all around you? Do you not see My glory and My majesty spread out before your very eyes? وَٱلسَّمَآءَ بَنَيْنَهَا بِأَيْي۟دٍۢ وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ I am the One who built the sky with My own hands. رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّىٰهَا I raised it like a roof above your heads. ‏وَأَغْطَشَ لَيْلَهَا وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَىٰهَا And then I set in place this whole order of night and day for you. ‏وَٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ دَحَىٰهَآ And then I spread the earth out beneath your feet. ‏أَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا مَآءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا I brought out water and pasture from it for you. ‏وَٱلْجِبَالَ أَرْسَىٰهَا And then I set the weight of these mountains upon the earth. And for whom do you think I did all of this? ‏مَتَعًۭا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَمِكُمْ So that all of it might be provision for you and for your animals.

If I hold back the rain from falling, what do you think will happen? ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَأَنزَلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءًۭ فَأَخْرَجَ بِهِۦ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَتِ رِزْقًۭا لَّكُمْ Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth and then sent down rain from the sky.

and then brought forth from it fruits and sustenance for you. وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ ٱلْفُلْكَ لِتَجْرِىَ فِى ٱلْبَحْرِ بِأَمْرِهِۦ I made the ships your servants, and they float across the oceans by my will. وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ ٱلْأَنْهَٰرَ And I made the springs and the rivers subject to you, so that you could benefit from them. وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ ٱلشَّمْسَ وَٱلْقَمَرَ دَآئِبَيْنِ And I made the sun and the moon your servants; they labor day and night to serve you. وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ ٱلَّيْلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَ And I made the night and the day your servants, so that you could work and rest. وَبِٱلنَّجْمِ هُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ And I created the beauty of the stars for your delight. وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِى سَخَّرَ ٱلْبَحْرَ لِتَأْكُلُوا۟ مِنْهُ لَحْمًۭا طَرِيًّۭا And I made the oceans subject to you, so that you could enjoy the fresh meat I placed in them for you. I did this for your sustenance. وَتَسْتَخْرِجُوا۟ مِنْهُ حِلْيَةًۭ تَلْبَسُونَهَا And so that you could draw precious jewels from their depths and adorn yourselves with them. وَتَرَى ٱلْفُلْكَ مَوَاخِرَ فِيهِ Do you not see the ships slicing through the chest of the ocean as they sail across it? Who do you suppose carries them to the other side? وَلِتَبْتَغُوا۟ مِن فَضْلِهِ And I did all of this so that you could recognize my blessings upon you. وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِى مَرَجَ ٱلْبَحْرَيْنِ I am the One who brought together the waters of the two seas. هَٰذَا عَذْبٌۭ فُرَاتٌۭ This one is sweet. وَهَٰذَا مِلْحٌ أُجَاجٌۭ The other is bitter. وَجَعَلَ بَيْنَهُمَا بَرْزَخًۭا وَحِجْرًۭا مَّحْجُورًۭا And then I placed a barrier between them, so that they do not mingle with each other. أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُزْجِى سَحَابًۭا Do you not see that it is Allah who drives forth the clouds? ثُمَّ يُؤَلِّفُ بَيْنَهُ Then he rubs them one against another. ثُمَّ يَجْعَلُهُۥ رُكَامًۭا Then he arranges them layer upon layer. فَتَرَى ٱلْوَدْقَ يَخْرُجُ مِنْ خِلَٰلِهِ And then he draws the rain out of their wombs. فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِ O my creation, only look at the food you eat. أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَآءَ صَبًّۭا It is I who poured down this sweet water for you. ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّۭا Then I split open the chest of the earth, so that the water could enter it. وَفَٰكِهَةًۭ وَأَبًّۭا I created fruits bearing seeds. وَحَدَآئِقَ غُلْبًۭا And beautiful lush gardens. وَزَيْتُونًۭا وَنَخْلًۭا And olives and dates. وَعِنَبًۭا وَقَضْبًۭا And thick clusters of grapes. فَأَنۢبَتْنَا فِيهَا حَبًّۭا And for whom did I do all this? مَّتَٰعًۭا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَٰمِكُمْ I did this for your sustenance and for the sustenance of your animals. وَجَعَلْنَا نَوْمَكُمْ سُبَاتًۭا Who lays you down to sleep peacefully in the night? وَجَعَلْنَا ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًۭا Where does the darkness of the night come from? وَجَعَلْنَا ٱلنَّهَارَ مَعَاشًۭا Who brightened the day for you, so that you could earn your living? وَبَنَيْنَا فَوْقَكُمْ سَبْعًۭا شِدَادًۭا Who built these seven heavens above your head? وَجَعَلْنَا سِرَاجًۭا وَهَّاجًۭا Who hung that vast lamp called the sun in the sky for you? وَأَنزَلْنَا مِنَ ٱلْمُعْصِرَٰتِ مَآءًۭ ثَجَّاجًۭا Who brings down these heavy rains from the clouds? لِّنُخْرِجَ بِهِۦ حَبًّۭا وَنَبَاتًۭا And all of this so that you could raise your livelihood from this earth. وَجَنَّٰتٍ أَلْفَافًا And I created beautiful gardens for your comfort. إِنَّا خَلَقْنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍۢ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَٰكُمْ شُعُوبًۭا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓا۟ I created you as man and woman...

and then divided you into tribes and nations so that you might come to know one another...

هُوَ ٱلَّذِى يُصَوِّرُكُمْ فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ كَيْفَ يَشَآءُ ۚ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ

I am the One who shaped you within your mother's womb just as I pleased. There is no deity except Me. I am the Most Powerful and the Most Wise.

How can you fail to recognize Me? How can you refuse to believe in Me?

وَمِنْ آيَتِهِۦ خَلْقُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْض

And among My signs are the heavens and the earth upon which you live.

ِ وَٱخْتِلَفُ أَلْسِنَتِكُمْ وَأَلْوَنِكُمْ

I distinguished you from one another in your languages and in the colors of your skin.

ھو الذی یحی و یمیت۔

I am the One who gives life and brings death.

امات و احیا

I give you death, and then I raise you to life again.

اغنا و اقنا

From where do poverty and wealth come?

ادحک و ابکا

From where do you suppose joy and sorrow come?

فأقبرا

Who lays you in the dust and turns you into dust?

من ای شئی خلق

O My servants, you have crossed every height and every limit of ingratitude. Have you forgotten what you were created from? Let Me remind you.

من نطفۃ

From a filthy drop of water.

خلقہ ، فقدرہ

I created you. I gave you form.

ثمَّ سَّبیل یَسَّر

Then I brought you into this world.

ثم اماتہ ، فاقبر

Then I gave you death and placed you in the ground.

ثم اذا شاء انشرا

And then, whenever I wish, I will raise you up once more.

ذالکم اللہ ربکم الحق! ذالکم اللہ ربکم الحق! ذالکم اللہ ربکم الحق

That is your Lord, the ultimate Truth. King of the universe. King of the lands and the oceans. King of all that lies in the east and in the west. King of honor and of disgrace. I have no partner. I have no counselor. I cannot be likened to anything. I have no equal. I cast no reflection. You possess nothing with which you may compare Me.

احق من ذکر

There is no one worthy of remembrance except Me.

احق من عُبِد

There is no one worthy of worship except Me.

انصر من التُّغِی

There is no one else worth calling upon for help except Me.

لا تدعو مع اللہ احدا

Have I fallen asleep? Have I grown weak, that you should abandon Me and call upon My creation for aid? What injustice could be greater than this? How can you do such a thing when I am so near to you?

اقرب الیہ من حبل الورید

I am closer to you than your jugular vein.

و ھو معکم اینما کنتم

I am always with you, no matter where you are.

واسِرُّ قولکم وجھرُکم بہ

Whether you call upon Me softly or call upon Me aloud, I hear everything you say. I hear everything you think. I hear everything you feel.

Why then do you call upon created things rather than upon Me? My treasures have no limits. My kingdom has no boundary. My greatness has no measure. My glory has no height. My power has no limit. My magnificence has no end. I am present in the sight of your eyes and in the beating of your heart. My signs are in the horizons around you. My signs are within your own souls.

سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ

If only you would use your eyes. An eye that is clean of impurity. An eye that takes no pleasure in gazing at filth. An eye that does not search out the weaknesses and faults of others. Find that eye, and then look all around you with it, and you will see My signs in everything that exists outside of you and in everything that exists within you.

لا الہ الا ھو

There is no deity except Me.

فَلَا تَدْعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱللَّهِ أَحَدًۭا

So do not call upon others for your help.

You need no one besides Me. Say but once: Ya Allah.

And I will respond seventy times: لبیک یا عبد — Here I am for you, My servant! Allahu Akbar! What kind of Master is this? How can a Master love His servants in this way? He says: call upon Me but once, Ya Allah, and I will answer seventy times, saying that I am here for you — لبیک یا عبد. But call upon Me first! How can you expect a response when you do not call upon Me even once? Call Me once, and then, if I do not answer, bring your complaint to Me. Where shall we find a Master like this? Where shall we ever find love like this, loyalty like this?

Now let us think about this for a moment. All these individual components: in their separate existence, are they connected to this single purpose of keeping time? That is to say, if you consider a battery on its own, does it by itself have anything to do with keeping time? No. Does the solenoid have anything to do with time? Do these round plastic gears have anything to do with time? No. These sticks attached to the gears, do they have anything to do with time? Not at all. So what we conclude from our scientific observation is this: although these individual components have nothing to do with time by themselves, when they are brought together in this fashion, when they begin to function together, each performing its own particular task, then together they accomplish a specific goal, which is to keep time.

Now here is another observation. Do you see how delicately these components are joined to one another? Do you see that if any one of them were displaced, even in the slightest, this whole system would fall apart, and would no longer be able to accomplish its single purpose of keeping time? Do you agree?

So now we have established two things. The first is the science of the matter: how each component works independently and how they work collectively. That is the science of the clock. And then there is our interpretation of that science, which is that all these unlike components are coming together to accomplish one unified goal, which is to keep time.

So now, on this basis, after examining the clock scientifically, what would your final conclusion be?

Based on these observations, what would you conclude? Do you find design and order in this clock? Or would you say that you see chaos and randomness? As a person of intellect, you would have to conclude that you see design and order. You would have to say: I see various different components, of disparate shapes and sizes, made from different materials. I see them coming together in a particular array, a particular structure, to accomplish a unified goal of keeping time — a goal that has nothing to do with the individual components themselves. And observing the way these components are connected to one another, I see that if they are displaced even the slightest, their unified purpose cannot be achieved. Correct? Would either of you want to argue with anything I have said so far?

Now I ask you: how did all of these various items, these disparate objects of different shapes and sizes, come together in such a harmonious fashion to accomplish a unified goal? What would you say to that? [Somebody put this together.]

Now, that is not a very scientific answer, is it? I would have to disagree with you on that. You say there had to be a maker. How do you know that? Did you actually meet this maker? Do you know who he is? Have you seen a photograph? Did you actually see him making the clock? Did you see him putting all these various pieces together? So then how did you conclude that there had to be a maker?

All I see is cause and effect. Look. The battery is providing the power through these wires to the motor, and that motor is CAUSING this first gear to rotate. Because the first gear — the one connected to the seconds hand — because it is connected to the motor, the motor CAUSES it to turn. And do you see how this gear is shaped? And how it is connected to this second gear? It is because of this shape that when the first gear turns sixty times, it CAUSES this second gear to turn once. And you see how this second gear is designed in the same way, so that when it turns sixty times, it CAUSES this third gear to turn once. And because each of these gears is connected to its respective hand, the clock is keeping time.

That is my scientific observation about this clock. Where did you get a creator and a maker from? It is simple cause and effect! So explain to me: where do you see a creator in all of this?

You want to know how this clock came together? I will tell you. It is a very interesting and scientific story. You will actually like it! So do you know what happened? I have this table in my kitchen. I had all the parts of this clock spread all over the table for a different project I was working on. I had blocks of wood, I had these metal gears, a battery, some wires. Erum made me these cute stickers with numbers from one to twelve. I had these chopstick type of things. All of this was just lying on my table, and I was planning to do something else with it.

One day I was working in the front yard. I suppose I must have left the stove on or something. There was this huge explosion in the kitchen. When the dust settled and I was finally able to enter the house, guess what I saw? All these components I had on my table — I suppose because of the explosion they somehow must have mixed and mashed together — and I found this clock lying on the floor, in the perfect working condition that you see today. That explosion actually built this clock in the very form you see right now! True story!

Is that not utterly wonderful? It makes perfect sense, does it not? The idea is not so mad after all — is it? It could happen. Why not? This story of the explosion is in fact quite probable. I can demonstrate it to you in another way as well. Do you know what I might have done instead? I might have taken all those separate pieces off my table, placed them in a box, and then begun to shake the box. Now, granted, this may not be as powerful as an explosion, yet there is plainly some probability that on one of those shakes all the separate parts would assemble themselves into this completely structured and working clock. Is that not so? Why not? The probability may be low, but it is possible. I am certain that if I were to work out the numbers — mathematically, statistically — you would arrive at a probability close to zero. Would you not? So explain it to me scientifically: where did you get this creator from?

Even though you cannot prove it, you know that this clock could not have existed unless someone put it together. Merely because I observe cause and effect, and do not observe a maker, that does not cancel out the existence of the maker, the creator of this clock. Every single argument I have made — is that not the very same argument made about this universe and the existence of its creator?

I exist. I look upon this magnificent, marvelous universe around me. I study science, and I see this incredible order, this astonishing structure in the universe on every side of me. Should I not ask the question of a maker? Should I not use my intellect? If I, as an intelligent being, dare to step onto the altar of intelligence to question the integrity of my own existence, how can I not question the integrity of my maker? A small, simple clock cannot exist without a maker. Am I then to believe that this complex universe, with such magnificent design and order, came about by itself, merely through cause and effect, without a creator?

Wherever we turn in the universe, as students of science, we find the most perfectly planned arrangements. It is all simply stunning. The more knowledge we gain, the more we see how intricate the arrangement is, and how delicate the planning and the order within its design. How did that come about?

The larger and more complex a system is, the more robust and resilient it ought to be. Consider a tractor. Consider a tank. These are enormous machines, and they are extremely robust. Yet how is it that this universe is so grand, so splendid, and at the same time so delicate? How did these two entirely opposite qualities come together? Is this not a sign for the intellect to ponder? Is it not saying: look, my friends! I am showing you something unnatural, something incredible, so that you may think, so that you may reflect. There must be someone behind all of this.

When the big bang occurred, we know that two things came into being as a result: speed and gravity. Today we know that gravity is the weakest force in the universe, and yet it stands in perfect balance. If gravity were any stronger, the smaller stars could not form; and if it were any weaker, the larger stars could not form and no heavy elements could exist. We see all these different planets, each with its own gravitational field — huge, massive planets held within so delicate a system of gravity that if any part of it were to change even in the slightest, it would destroy the earth upon which we live.

And consider the scientific discoveries concerning the speed of these planets.

A second can be physically divided into a thousand parts — physically. Each part is called a millisecond. Beyond that, you cannot divide it physically. If a second must be divided any further than that, the division has to be logical; it cannot be physical.
