A scientist by the name of Paul Davies concluded the following: suppose you could logically divide a second into a trillion parts. If the speed of this earth were to change by one trillionth of a second — if it increased or decreased by that much — this entire planet would be destroyed.

What do all these different planets have to do with the earth? What has the sun got to do with the earth? They are entirely separate bodies of mass. Yet what happens if the sun loses heat or gains heat? What happens if it moves closer to the earth or farther away, even by the slightest amount? Would that destroy this earth? Absolutely. Is our climate dependent upon the interaction of these different planets in our solar system? Absolutely.

And what is the single, unified purpose of all these separate planets, of different shapes and sizes and temperatures? To support life on this earth. And out of all the species, which one is it that takes advantage of everything this earth has to offer? Human beings. Is that not true? Why do we care if the climate of the earth changes, if it boils up or freezes over? Because of human life. Who is affected by the resources of this planet? What is the only species that makes use of the resources of this planet? Human beings. Whose needs is this entire solar system meeting? The needs of human beings. Is all of this a coincidence? Is all of this merely cause and effect? A small clock cannot assemble itself and serve a unified purpose without its maker. Are we to believe that this entire solar system came together to support our existence all by itself? Tell me, what intellect can accept that?

See, Islam is simple. One of the greatest misconceptions we hold is that God, religion, all these things must be complicated. Who said so? Did you ever stop for a moment to consider whether that notion makes any sense? If there is a God, and He created all these human beings for the purpose of worshiping Him — as He says in the Qur'an:

وما خلقت الجن والانس الا لیعبدون

And I did not create jinn and man except to worship Me.

Then Allah obviously had to know that, in order for us to worship Him, we would first have to recognize His existence. Now, if a Creator wants His creation to worship Him, what would make sense logically? Would He make His recognition easy, or would He make it very hard? Are all human beings rocket scientists? Or are some of them simple peasants and uneducated people? Was His recognition meant only for the highly intellectual? Or was it meant even for a person of ordinary intellect? Which audience do you think He is addressing? In that verse He simply said Jinn wal Ins, meaning everyone. He did not say:

For when you live in the world of "what if," by definition you are denying the world of "what is." You are denying the world of "what is." The two are in complete contradiction. This is what is called the deductive reasoning of philosophy, as against the inductive reasoning of Islam.

There are three components to critical thinking: (1) deductive reasoning, (2) inductive reasoning, and (3) abductive reasoning.

Deductive reasoning is the process of reasoning from the general to the specific. It is also called top-down logic. You begin from a general premise and move to a specific logical conclusion. For example, the premise may be: all men are mortal, and Socrates is a man; therefore the conclusion is that Socrates is mortal. You see that we moved from the general to the specific. The Greek philosophers would use this logic to deduce things. If you have ever read The Republic, that is deductive logic as used by Aristotle and Plato.

Then there is inductive reasoning. Inductive reasoning is the process of reasoning from the specific to the general. You study the specific and then branch out to the generic. If what I observe specifically is true, then that would apply in the larger picture. My rifle recoils when I fire it, which is specific; therefore, for every action there must be an equal and opposite reaction, which is general. All the basketball players in your school are tall, so all basketball players must be tall. Every time you eat peanuts your throat swells up and you cannot breathe; therefore you are allergic to peanuts. Obviously!

So that is inductive logic. A simple clock has a design. A simple clock cannot exist without a maker. Therefore the perfect design I see in this universe cannot exist without a creator.

The philosophy of Islam is rooted not in the deductive "what if," but in the inductive "what is." That is the Qur'anic argument. Look around you! Have you not seen this? Have you not seen that? Have you not paid attention to your own self? Do you not see the birds? Do you not see the sky? Have you not paid attention to the earth? To the camel? To the mountain? To your parents? Simply pay attention to what is around you. Live in reality; do not live in the abstract. Now, the Qur'an does deal with the abstract in certain places. It does sometimes deal with "what if" questions. But overwhelmingly the Qur'an is all about the "what is."

But if you were to sit such a person down and ask: Who told you this? Who told you that it is enough merely to be a good person? Do you have an agreement with Allah on the matter? Did Allah say this to you? Did the Messenger of Allah say it to you? Are you aware of a verse that I have not read?

The best explanation is held to have two qualities. First, the more an explanation fits with everything we already know, the sounder the conclusion tends to be. Second, a simpler explanation is held to be better than a complicated one.

An example of abductive reasoning is this. Consider a detective who solves a crime. Suppose she knows that the murder weapon was found in the trunk of Smith's car; that Smith has no alibi; that Smith had a motive; and that Smith failed the lie-detector test. The best explanation for all of this evidence is that Smith committed the murder. She lays this evidence before a jury, and they convict Smith of the crime.

One way to challenge an abductive argument is to offer a better explanation of the data than the argument provides. Another is to look for further evidence to add to the premises. So, in the case of Smith's murder, suppose the detective discovers that Smith has a very clever enemy, one who had a motive to commit the murder and who had been plotting against Smith for a long time. In that case, Smith's guilt is no longer plainly the best explanation for all of the detective's evidence. There is now an equally strong rival explanation: that Smith was framed by his enemy. All of the evidence must be weighed before a conclusion is drawn.

Well, I am going to tie this observation in with this and this and that. All right!

At the end of the day, I can make all the observations I want. I can observe the atom, I can descend to the subatomic level, I can observe vast structures. And then what? Do I stop, simply because I am a scientist and I have completed my observation? What do I do with all of these observations? Do I tie them together with something? Do I make sense of them? Ah, make sense of them! And what does it mean to make sense of them? It means that I will now describe what is happening. But the moment I describe it, am I still being scientific? For my description is now deeply experiential, and it may be heavily biased, and I may be putting a certain spin on it in order to see it the way I wish to see it, according to how I see the world. What happens then? Suddenly you begin to tread into the philosophical realm. You begin to spin ideas out of what you have just seen. This is the classic difficulty when it comes to morality, for example. Ethics and morality cannot be observed by the empiricist. The empiricist cannot observe the concept of good and evil within physical observations. There is no concept of good and evil in the universe, cosmologically speaking. Even when you look empirically, if you study chemistry, for example, there is no such thing as good chemistry and evil chemistry. Chemistry is chemistry, and biology is biology. When I dissect a creature, I see what is happening. I study its mechanisms on the basis of my understanding, I write it down, and I manipulate it through cause and effect. Good, very good! And then what? Then why is there a board of ethicists governing the manipulation of DNA, deciding what kind of research is permitted when it comes to genetic engineering, for example? Why do I need a board of ethicists at all? If science is the foundation of everything, then science ought to stand above the board of ethics, and science ought to dictate what is ethical and what is not.

So we understand that there are questions of ethics, questions of morality, questions of emotion, of ideologies, of visions and imaginings. All of these are part and parcel of our existence. Consider the concept of intelligence. How do you measure intelligence apart from something that is directly measured? You cannot. How can you measure love? It is a concept that lies dormant within a being, and yet no one has ever observed love. It is impossible. Love can be observed only secondarily, through a reaction. When you react in a certain way toward another person or thing, I can say that you love that person or thing, and from that reaction we can conclude that this person loves this thing. These concepts lie outside of purely empirical observation.

Put all of these considerations together, and it brings forth the idea that, from an Islamic perspective, whatever systems exist in the physical world are part and parcel of this created system. So, to answer the question of who is the maker of God, we understand clearly from this argument, from a rational argument, that God has no maker. Someone may say: but is that not precisely what you just stated, that everything must have a predecessor in order to have a beginning? Yet if you step outside the relative world and break that space-time continuum, then yes, it makes sense that Allah has no beginning, because now time itself becomes a frame of reference. To give you a simple, logical example: my existence depends upon a predecessor, whose existence depends upon another predecessor.

Whose existence depends upon his predecessor, and so I would have to carry this logic mathematically to infinity. I would have to take it all the way to infinity — that is the concept. Now consider this notion of infinity that lives within the domain of science. If you examine it closely, what is its definition? Where does it sit within the whole scope of science? For in science everything runs from zero to infinity. Calculus is built entirely upon this idea of infinity, and yet infinity cannot be described. It lies outside the reach of description. Even mathematical computation breaks down when you try to operate upon infinity. But if everything runs toward infinity, and my predecessors stretch all the way to infinity, then logically I cannot exist, because for me to exist there is an infinity to wait through first. Yet I say, by reason, that I do exist. Therefore whatever created me cannot have depended upon a predecessor — and this is what we call the first cause, the unmoved mover. These are the cosmological and ontological arguments advanced for the existence of God.

From an Islamic standpoint — and this is very important for us to understand — we must not despise that science. Muslims often feel that science is a bad thing. I say no. Science is one of the greatest gifts Allah has given us. It is one of the greatest tools we have been given, and in my opinion, thank God for science. It has brought so much reconciliation of abstract concepts with concrete physical realities, in terms of observation, within our faith. It is a great gift that we exist in this age. Science is not something contrary to religion or contrary to belief in God. It grants us the knowledge to take a thing and turn it into something else, to understand the causes and effects of things and then to work them to our advantage. This is a phenomenal gift given to mankind.

The Qur'an is not a book of science. It is a book of everything, including science. It is a book of morality and ethics. The Qur'an gives us a holistic view.

Richard Dawkins, in *The God Delusion*, says that evolution is a process; it is a system.

What makes religion so powerful in contrast to science is that it holds the element of emotion. It has the component of faith. It has the component of tawakkal, which science does not have. And as human beings, we can never be purists when it comes to a methodical system. It is utterly impossible, unless we lower ourselves to a robotic level where we are no longer human beings at all. There is always some minor form of bias. Emotions can be very powerful; they can bond with science and make things clearer. Pure emotion can cloud judgment, but when emotion bonds with science, it can actually make things clearer, because the heart is receptive to the acceptance of new and unfamiliar ideas.

It is a wonderful thing that when you love someone, and a tear falls from your eye as that person is leaving, that single gesture cries out louder than a thousand words you could ever say to them. That emotion of love can manifest and shine brighter than the sun itself. That is an emotional state, and science cannot grasp it.

In any case, I demanded this methodology of myself because I did not want to be fooled, and I wanted to be certain that I was as unbiased as I could be in my approach. I found out that this is simply not possible. No human being can be free of bias.

It is impossible; the only thing we can do is limit our biases and control them so that our judgment is not skewed by them. Fundamentally, I believe that all ideas come from a single root. It is like studying a cell: you have to work at the level of the nucleus. Science shows us today that DNA is the root of life — the only molecule known to man that can replicate itself, a template that can decide how I am going to be as a living being. I love that. I wanted to know more about it. I am never going to be a molecular scientist, but I want to know more about it, because this double-helix system was astonishing to me: how Allah has condensed and contracted this formula into a very, very tight coil that is so functional, so elegant, so secure, and so rapid. What is the probability that something as structured as DNA came about by chance? I asked mathematicians; I asked statisticians: what is the probability of this happening by chance? Because I am seeing too much order — I am seeing far too much structure.

The point is that we have to go down to the level of the nucleus. No matter what you study, you will always find that there is a center that spreads out and expresses itself. Even when you study the universe, you will find that the galaxies are moving around in circles, in the shape of a disc, and there is always a center. Allah says: ان فی ذالک لآیات یتفکرون — these are signs for a community that thinks. So the more I studied things, the more I found that there is a core in everything. Then, logically, my belief system should also have a core; it too should have a center around which it revolves. What is my core? My core is a deity, because my origin needs to have a precursor, and that precursor must be at the center of the cause of who I am. Who is this one? Do you exist? How is it that I cannot see you? How is it that you do not show yourself? And why are you so great that I cannot see you? Could you not be great and still let me see you? These are the questions that I asked.

The more I dealt with these questions in a methodical way, the more I realized what a foolish question it is to ask to see God. I see nothing but God around me; I see nothing but God's creation all around me, inside me and around me. People may say that this is a leap of faith. Well, it really is not, because in science people come up with all sorts of conjectural arguments. Take, for example, Stephen Hawking. He wrote the book A Brief History of Time. He was one of the people who proposed the idea of black holes. When they studied the density of the universe, they noticed that the universe is far denser than what is visible, and they could not reconcile mathematically that huge discrepancy in the numbers regarding the density of the universe compared with what was visible and measurable. But they knew that there was some sort of dark matter out there that could not be seen, because light could not penetrate it, and they called it the black hole. It is infinitely dense; they call it infinitely hot; and they called it a singularity, since a singularity is that single point of origination where mass is ultimately and infinitely dense. So, interestingly, if you study this concept, Hawking reached this conclusion without actually seeing this dark matter. Now, is that acceptable in science?

Because if science is so tangible, and everything within it is measurable, can I measure a thing by negating another thing? Can I conclude that something exists by rejecting something? Or can I arrive at a scientific understanding without having to see a thing tangibly, yet observe the effect of that hidden thing through what is visible? Can I do that? We do it all the time in science. So many scientific concepts rest upon derivations. If this is acceptable in science, then why can I not believe in a deity who cannot be measured, cannot be seen, and is not tangible, when I can derive that deity in the same way?

Look at the systems of the universe around us. I exist. I look about at this universe that exists. I examine this grand and spectacular system that surrounds me on every side. Can all of this have come out of pure chance? Can pure chance govern order? Can a complete totality of disorder bring about order? These are absurd statements in science, for when you examine chance within probability, it is entirely controlled; it operates within a controlled system. There is no such thing as a totality of chance outside a controlled system. It is inconceivable. It is like saying that there was so much randomness that it suddenly formed a computer, which formed an operating system, which became Microsoft Windows. That is absurd.

There is a root here. There is a center here. No matter how much probability and chance may exist among the things that can happen, I see this vast consistency all around me in the design of Allah. And Allah has given me the ability, within this spectacular universe, to answer every coin with a counter coin, which is what makes life so beautiful. For if a thing had no consistency, then science itself should not exist, because science too must stand upon a consistent foundation in order to project its solutions and its answers.

Religion. Even evolution is a system. Even when gases collide to bring about life, that is a system; it is a mechanical system. Where did these gases come from? And gases cannot function without an environment. We know that, according to the laws of probability, when a thing has a probability of chance, it is always a product. So if it is one in a million, and there is another product that can happen one in a million, then these two must be multiplied: one in a million times one in a million. That is always the case; it is a mathematical rule. Now, when you multiply these probabilities through logical analysis, the numbers grow smaller. So regression is part of pure chance within probability. The probability has now become one in a million times one in a million; it is now one in ten to the twelfth, because the six zeros and the six zeros are doubled. The numbers grow smaller. That means pure chance is regressive, not progressive.

But we have a progressive system. We have faith. We have ideologies. We have morality. These are not products of pure mechanical sciences. So no one in their right mind can say that evolution, as a methodology of replication and of bringing about a complex, multicellular organism such as you and I, is the only reason for our existence. This notion is so childish, so myopic, that I cannot believe it is even entertained.

Religion once used to punish scientists, for they tortured and murdered scientists, and so science came back with a vengeance, saying: keep religion out of science. Any range in natural mathematics works between two extreme boundaries.

You have zero, and you have infinity. Everything in mathematics moves from zero toward infinity. Isaac Newton devised the system of calculus, which is natural mathematics, the very language of the universe. Einstein ran into a difficulty, because a number cannot be divided by zero; that is an illegal operation. So he would resort to a trick and arrive at an answer, and people would object that his science was flawed because he had cheated. Then a French mathematician found the true answer through limits. He said: do not divide the number by zero; rather, approach zero infinitely. As x approaches its value, it draws nearer and nearer to zero without ever reaching it, and that is a legitimate operation. It is called a limit.

Why do we need limits? Because the true language of science is infinity. SubhanAllah. In truth, the entire world of science is driven by infinity; without infinity nothing makes sense. Yet, as vital as this entity is, it is not tangible. I cannot touch it. I cannot measure it. I can speak of it, and I can apply things toward it, but I can never feel it. Something is always approaching infinity, and yet it can never become infinite, because the moment it became infinite you could no longer speak of it at all.

This infinity, in reality, is Allah. All ranks are moving toward infinity, because everything is approaching infinity, and all His attributes are approaching infinity. Nothing in the universe, once it emerges from zero, ever stops; it goes on approaching infinity. So people say: give me this tangible god; if you have no tangible god in your religion, you are speaking nonsense. My answer is: give me this tangible infinity; and if you cannot, then you are speaking nonsense in your science.

The proof of intelligence lies in the DNA, for one of the proofs of intelligence is language. The evolutionists carried out studies on monkeys and apes to find out how intelligent they were, how we might have evolved from them, and what the missing link between us and them could be. And they found that language was the critical thing. They tried to teach the monkeys to understand language, because language is the decisive mark of intelligence; one of the signs of intelligence is language. And language is composed of encoding and decoding. Right now I am encoding. As I speak to you, I am encoding words, I am encoding emotions, I am encoding gestures, I am encoding ideas, and you are listening and decoding them instantaneously. It is because of this encoding and decoding that we are conversing intelligently. This encoding and decoding is what all of life is about. DNA is precisely that: an encoding that is then decoded. Intelligence! SubhanAllah. Can we deny it? No.

An origin can never arise on its own; the Creator of the first cause is Allah. Allah tala shows us that, when it comes to the methodical system of discovery in science, the human race already possesses that ability. In fact, an atheist at the University of Colorado, a mathematician and a logician, posed this question: your Quran says that it contains everything, dry and wet; then why does it not contain all these scientific principles that are being discovered today? That is an excellent question. The answer is that God is very pragmatic with us, and He has already endowed us with the ability to uncover the natural laws for ourselves.

and we can ascertain them on our own. It would therefore be redundant for God to tell me what I am able to confirm for myself; that is why He gave me an intellect. But where we fall short is in the ability to understand morals and ethical principles, because there is nowhere in the universe where I can go looking for the moral arguments about what one may and may not do, about the lawful and the forbidden. So God gives me that in His book. Does that not make sense? Because in the end, no science in the world can compete on the moral level. God tells me in the Quran all the shoulds and should-nots of the lawful and the forbidden, which no science can tell me. God tells me how I ought to deal with the rest of creation in my daily life, which no science can tell me, because there is no morality in pure science. There is no evil or good in science. Yet in the end, life is about morality, not about whether I can decipher the laws and principles of the universe. It is not about what I can or cannot do scientifically. It is about what kind of life I lead in this world. It is morality that makes me a good person or a bad one, not as a Muslim but simply as a human being.

If I know science, I can answer many questions. I can manipulate cause and effect to build things, but that does not make me a good person. If I know how to push buttons and flip switches, that does not make me a good person, because if I am morally bankrupt, it still does not make me a good person. So the bottom line is ethics: ethics, ethics. And only God can teach us that. Hence the necessity of religion; hence the necessity of God.

Roger Penrose, the world-renowned mathematician, says that the probability of the universe coming into existence by pure chance is zero. That is from an expert in mathematics, and there are many mathematicians like him. Some have proposed that there is a possibility, but it is so negligible that it too leans toward the impossible. Yet even if, for the sake of argument, we take this blind leap of faith, it is absurd. No human being ever takes a step knowing that the probability is one trillionth of a percent. For example, if I say that there is a one trillionth of a percent chance that if you leave your house to go to school or work today you will have an accident, you will not take that into account; and if you did, it would call your intelligence into doubt, because even from a mathematical standpoint, even from a statistical standpoint, it is simply absurd.

Now let us look more deeply into the استعاذہ — the call for Allah's protection FROM the accursed Shaytan: أعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم, which is also a prayer. This ayah is commonly translated as "I seek refuge of Allah from the cursed Shaitaan." But linguists say that this is not the best translation, and, InshaAllah, we will look at why they say so and why they consider this a poor or weak translation.

To begin with, the first thing you must understand about this ayah is that it has two parts, or that it deals with two entities. There is the one whose protection we are seeking, and there is the one from whom we are seeking protection. This is the very first distinction we need to make. We are running FROM someone, and we are running TO someone. We need the protection OF someone, and we need protection FROM someone. So the first thing to notice is that there is a pair here. There are two questions that need to be answered: Whom are you seeking protection from? And whose protection or refuge are you seeking?

Now, the one whose protection you are seeking — the term for that is المستعاذُ بہ. It means the one whose protection you are seeking, and that, as we know, is Allah. We are seeking the protection of Allah. And the one from whom you are trying to seek protection, the one you are trying to escape from, is المستعاذُ منہ, who, as we know, is Shaytaan. So Allah is المستعاذُ بہ and Shaytan is المستعاذُ منہ. So "bihi" and "minhu." If we observe the استعاذہ carefully, it contains both: أعوذ ب اللہ من الشیطان الرجیم.

So if you look at the diagram I sent, you can see that it contains the بہ as well as the منہ. The ب is associated with Allah, and the من is associated with Shaytaan. Do you understand?

Now, why is this interesting to know? It is interesting because, in explanation of these two terms, المستعاذُ بہ and المستعاذُ منہ, we find two separate surahs in the Quran. One is devoted essentially to المستعاذُ بہ, and the other is devoted essentially to المستعاذُ منہ. These two surahs are called the المُعَوِّذَتَینِ, which literally means the two refuges, and these are Surah AlFalaq and Surah AlNaas.

The Istiaaza (أعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم) is basically the essence, or the summary, of these two surahs. So if we fully understand the meanings of these two surahs, we can fully understand the meaning of the استعاذہ.

So the first thing I want to do is a linguistic analysis of this surah with you. I want to show you the beautiful symmetry and perfection that exists in these two surahs, and to highlight the beauty and the miracle of this amazing book. We went over a basic definition of the word عاذ in the previous sessions, but, inshaAllah, we will study this word in far greater detail. We will compare the two surahs to see what connection they have with each other, and then what connection they have with the Fateha. We will also look at their historical context; we will look at the reasons and the circumstances under which these two surahs were revealed. And then, finally, we will look at how the teachings and lessons of this surah can help us in our day to day lives.

First, let us simply understand the meaning of these surahs from a generic translation.

Comparison of Surah Falaq and Surah Naas

So we can see that both Surahs have the same theme.

It is the seeking of the protection of Allah from Shaytan. So both surahs are المستعاذُ بہ as well as المستعاذُ منہ. Yet if one looks closely, Surah al-Naas is essentially about المستعاذُ بہ, the seeking of the protection of Allah, while Surah al-Falaq is more about المستعاذُ منہ, the seeking of protection from Shaytan. For if you study Surah al-Naas, you will see that the protection of Allah is mentioned far more often, whereas in Surah al-Falaq it is protection from Shaytan that is mentioned far more often.

Let us look at this. In Surah al-Naas, Allah is called upon three times:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

The protection of Allah is sought three times: رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ. But protection from Shaytan is mentioned once:

مِن شَرِّ ٱلْوَسْوَاسِ ٱلْخَنَّاسِ

From the evil of the whispering of Shaytan. The remaining verses that follow are simply the description and the details of وسواس الخناس. They are no more than an explanation of how Shaytan whispers into the hearts of men:

ٱلَّذِى يُوَسْوِسُ فِى صُدُورِ ٱلنَّاسِ مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ

The one who whispers into the chest of mankind, whether he be from the jinn or from men. But the subject is still one single thing: the evil whispering of Shaytan. So you see that in Surah al-Naas, Allah is called upon for protection three times, and protection from Shaytan is mentioned once. This surah is therefore directed primarily toward المستعاذُ بہ.

Surah al-Falaq, by contrast, is focused more on المستعاذُ منہ, because in this surah we find that Allah is called upon only once:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ

That is all. In every remaining verse, the surah speaks of seeking protection from the various evils:

مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ ... وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ ... وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ ... وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ

So we see that in this surah, Allah is called upon only once, while refuge and protection from the evils are sought three times. The first of these, مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ, is only a mention of the existence of evil in general: protect me from all evil that was created. It is all inclusive. But the specific evils from which protection is being sought are three:

وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ ... وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ ... وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ

These are the three specific things from which the surah seeks protection. And therefore we see that Surah al-Falaq is primarily المستعاذُ منہ.

So in Surah al-Naas (المستعاذُ منہ), Allah is mentioned three times and the specific evil of Shaytan's whispering is mentioned once. In Surah al-Falaq, which is (المستعاذُ منہ), Allah is mentioned once and the protection of Allah from three specific evils is mentioned. There is thus a beautiful symmetry between these two surahs.

There are also some further interesting connections between the two surahs. Surah al-Falaq deals with the kinds of trouble that afflict a human being which are not the product of his own doing; in other words, he has no control over them.

وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ

The evil of the dark night, which is not under our control.

وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ

The evil of those who engage in sorcery and black magic.

Again, this is something not under our control. وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ The evil of the one who acts against us out of jealousy — that too is not under our control. None of the evils mentioned here are actually under our control. We are the helpless victims of all of them. The evil of the dark night, the evil of sorcerers, and the evil of the one who acts out of jealousy: over none of these do we have any control. These evils are being done *to* us. And because we are the victims of these evils, which are inflicted upon us by someone or something else, we are not held accountable for them. There is no sin recorded against us. Do you understand?

Now, in contrast to this, Surah al-Nas deals with the actions of human beings for which we truly are held accountable. What is it that we seek refuge from in Surah al-Nas? مِن شَرِّ ٱلْوَسْوَاسِ ٱلْخَنَّاسِ We seek refuge from the evil of the whisperings of Satan, from his وسوسۃ. And when Satan works his وسوسۃ within us, what do we do? We commit an evil act. But that evil act which we commit — are we accountable for it before Allah? Or may we simply say, "Oh no, it was not my fault, it was a وسوسۃ from Satan"? No! We are indeed accountable for it. We are responsible for it.

In other words, what we seek protection from in Surah al-Nas is something we will have to answer for if we fail. But in Surah al-Falaq, the afflictions that come upon us are beyond our control; we are victimized by them. Yet in both cases, the only one who can help us is Allah (AWJ).

That is why we see greater desperation in Surah al-Nas. For if we end up committing an evil act on the basis of the وسوسۃ of Satan, if we fall victim to his whisperings, what will we end up doing? We will end up damaging our faith. That is why in Surah al-Nas Allah is called upon multiple times:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

So it is said:

فا الأولیٰ فی شَرِّ المصائب ؛ وَ الثَّانِیَ فی شَرِّ المعَائِب

The first deals with the evils of the afflictions that come upon us and are outside our control, but the second has to do with the evils that we ourselves may commit — sins for which we are answerable. Therefore the second calls for a more intense seeking of refuge. So when we say:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

this, from a grammatical standpoint, is what is called a بَدَلْ in Arabic. It means that these three verses of Surah al-Nas would be equivalent to saying:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ
قُلْ أَعُوذُ بمَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ
قُلْ أَعُوذُ بأِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

So it is as though (قل اعوذُ ب) stands in parentheses and is applied to all three verses. This is because we are far more desperate about losing our faith through the وسوسۃ of Satan. That is a far greater danger. Even though the dangers mentioned in Surah al-Falaq are quite enormous dangers — the dangers of the night, the danger of sorcerers, and of the one who is jealous — those are serious dangers as well. But when they befall us, we are not accountable; the people committing those evils are accountable. Yet when we *act* upon the وسوسۃ of Satan, we are responsible for that action, and therefore accountable before Allah for it. And that makes it a greater and a far more personal danger to us.

Do you understand? Then we find a remarkably eloquent ordering within this surah al-Falaq. Allah moves in this surah from the general to the specific, from the widely scoped to the narrowly scoped, growing more and more particular. Let us see how.

مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ — from the evil of all that was created. In this verse He speaks generally of all evil. Nothing is specified here, so the scope is wide. In the next verse He says: وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ — from the evil that takes place in the darkness of the night. The scope narrows. From all evil in general, He has now brought it down to the evils that take place in the darkness of the night. He then says: وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَ
تِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ — from the evil of those who practice sorcery and blow upon knots. This is more specific still, for He is naming a particular group of people. Notice that He uses the word النفثت, which is a plural form. He did not say نفث, which would have been singular. He used the plural form النفثت, which means that Allah is still speaking of a group. And then, finally, He says: وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ — from the evil of the one who is jealous, especially when he or she acts upon that jealousy. Here He uses the singular form حاسد.

So we find this beautiful movement from the general to the specific in this remarkable surah. He begins with all the evil that exists, then moves to the evils of the night, then to a particular group of people, and finally narrows in upon one specific evil act, the act that is the cause of all the other evils: jealousy. SubhanAllah!

Allah reveals that jealousy is the starting point of all evil, and that it leads to every other general form of evil. The verse before the one about the jealous person speaks of black magic: وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ. What is the underlying motive for working black magic upon someone? Jealousy. And when are the rituals of black magic performed? In the darkest hours of the night: غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ. Jealousy too is directly related to darkness, because whoever is jealous of you will always attack you from behind, when you are unaware. Such a person gossips about you behind your back, and you remain completely in the dark about it.

So in truth, the underlying, core emotion of evil is highlighted in this surah, and that emotion is jealousy. SubhanAllah!

And then this surah passes into Surah al-Nas, which speaks of the evil whisperings of Satan: من شر الوسواس الخناس — from the evil of the whisperings of Satan. And where does he place those evil whisperings? الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس — in the hearts of people. Where does jealousy live? In the heart! SubhanAllah. It is simply astonishing how these transitions unfold, and how both the physical and the spiritual causes of evil are brought to light in these surahs.

May Allah protect us from the whisperings of Satan, who creates jealousy in our hearts, jealousy that leads to every kind of evil in the world.

Now, before we begin to take these two surahs apart from a linguistic point of view, let us speak a little about the historical setting of this surah: when and why these surahs were revealed. Both of these surahs were revealed together. That is the first thing to remember. They were both revealed together.

But why were they revealed?

The historical setting of the revelation of both surahs

As soon as the Messenger of Allah, may peace be upon him, began to preach the message of Islam, it stirred up every class of people around him. As his message of Islam, his message of peace, spread further, the opposition of the disbelieving Quraysh grew fiercer and fiercer. At first their hostility was not so active, because they still hoped that they could stop him from spreading his message: by enticement, by bribes, by the lure of women, by wealth and riches. But he disappointed them completely, on every count. He said in particular:

والله لو وَضعُوا الشمسُ في يميني والقمرُ في يساري۔۔۔ ما تركت هذا الأمر

Even if you place the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, I will not give up this message. I will never stop, until either Allah gives His religion victory, or I die defending it.

When all of this failed, they tried to reach a compromise with him. They said: let us accept all the gods, all the deities, and let us make Allah the greatest of all the gods. So when enticement and bribery did not work, they turned to compromise. That is when Surah al-Kafirun was revealed, in which Allah declared that there would be absolutely no compromise with the disbelievers in the matter of faith. The Messenger of Allah, may peace be upon him, was commanded to state this plainly:

لَآ أَعْبُدُ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ ۔۔۔ وَلَآ أَنتُمْ عَبِدُونَ مَآ أَعْبُدُ ۔۔۔۔ وَلَآ أَنَا۠ عَابِدٌۭ مَّا عَبَدتُّمْ ۔۔۔ وَلَآ أَنتُمْ عَبِدُونَ مَآ أَعْبُدُ ۔۔۔ لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِىَ دِينِ

"I do not worship those whom you worship, nor are you worshipers of the One I worship. For you is your religion, and for me is mine."

So when every avenue was exhausted, their hostility reached its extreme, and now they turned to intimidation. Hazrat Zia Ali Sahab Muqaddas used to say that there are always three ways, three stages, by which someone attempts to stop us. They are ترغیب ۔۔۔ ترکیب ۔۔۔ ترھیب. The first is ترغیب, which comes from رغبۃ: incentives, tempting a person toward something with bribes and deals. If that does not work, then comes ترکیب: tricks, in an attempt to reach a compromise. And when neither of those works, then at last comes ترھیب, whose verbal noun form is رَهَّبَ: intimidation, the use of force and violence.

So when incentives did not work, they tried compromise; but then Surah al-Kafirun stated clearly that there would be no compromise of any kind with the disbelievers. So at last they resorted to tarhib, intimidation. They began to use violent force.

Another major reason for this growing hostility was that in many families some members, men or women, boys or girls, had accepted Islam. A son was turning against his father, a father against his son. So the disbelievers burned with rage within against the Messenger of Allah. They cursed him. They held secret consultations to kill him quietly in the dark of night, so that the Banu Hashim could not discover the murderer and take revenge. Magic and charms were worked against him, to try to kill him, or make him sick, or drive him mad.

Devils from among men and jinn spread out on every side, whispering evil into the hearts of the people, turning them against him.

Then there were people who burned with jealousy against him.

They simply could not bear it: how could a man from another clan, an ordinary man, not even a man who held some high rank in their society, be chosen for this work? Abu Jahl said this openly in a gathering. He said, "We and the Bani Abd Manaf, the clan to which the Messenger of Allah belonged, have always been rivals. They fed others, and we fed others too. They provided mounts for the people, and we did the same. They gave in charity, and we matched them. Matters went so far that the two of us have always stood equal in honor and nobility. But now they proclaim that they have a Prophet who receives inspiration from heaven. How can we compete with that? By God, we will never acknowledge him, and we will never affirm faith in him." So they rejected the Messenger of Allah, not because they disbelieved his message, and not because they doubted that he was a true prophet. They rejected him on the ground of jealousy alone: that he was doing something they would never be able to do.

All of this was going on in the background. Every attempt was being made against the Messenger of Allah to prevent him, to discourage him, or to frighten him away from spreading the message of Allah. Yet nothing seemed to work. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, had migrated to Medina, and Islam was spreading swiftly in Medina and in the surrounding villages. The treaty of Hudaybiyyah had been signed. Meanwhile the Jews, exiled for treachery and revolt, had settled themselves in a place called Khaybar. This is where the famous battle of Khaybar was later fought. These Jews caught wind of Hudaybiyyah, and they understood that, now that the Messenger of Allah had signed that treaty, his greatest concern would no longer be the disbelievers of Mecca. His entire attention would now turn toward the Jewish community, which had shown great hostility toward the Muslims over the past few years. So they began to put together a strategy for how to counter the moves that the Messenger of Allah was going to make.

There was a man called Lubaid bin Asim (لعنت اللہ علیہ). He belonged to a tribe called بَنُو زُرَیق. This man was the greatest sorcerer and worker of black magic of that time. He had several daughters who were his apprentices and who would assist him in performing these spells of black magic. So these Jews of Khaybar came to Lubaid ibn Asim and said, "Look! We have tried everything against Muhammad. We have tried to bribe him. We have tried compromise. We have tried intimidation. We have tried everything in our power to stop him. We have even tried magic, but our magic is not strong enough. You are the best and most powerful magician we know. Do something to him that will tear him apart. Do something that will break him down." So these Jews came to Lubaid bin Asim, seeking his help.

What Lubaid bin Asim did was this. He paid a Jewish boy who used to serve the Messenger of Allah, and he obtained the comb of the Messenger of Allah, with some of his hair still caught in the teeth of the comb. He took those strands of hair, tied them to a cord, and began to recite his spells. As he recited, he began tying knots in this cord. He tied eleven knots in all. He put together this contraption, this device.

He gave it to the Jews and told them to hide it in a place where no one could find it. So the Jews took this device and hid it in a well in Medina called ذُو اَروَان. They did not simply throw the contraption into the well. They dove down to the bottom of the well and set it there beneath a rock.

Now, what effect did that magic have upon our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family? That is the question that must be asked. Some narrations say that he began to feel troubled within himself. He began to feel anxious and distressed for no reason at all. He began to feel a great strain. He began to lose his sleep. Some narrations say that he would do something and forget that he had done it, or that he would not do something and yet think that he had done it. So his memory began to be affected. He was passing through all this turmoil. He was experiencing this discomfort inwardly. Yet he never showed any of it to his companions, so the companions around him noticed nothing wrong with him. Do you understand? All this disturbance was taking place within him, but no one on the outside saw any of these effects.

This is what black magic does. It sickens the soul, and the soul's sickness then shows itself in bodily and mental ailments. People who have been victims of magic say that they feel they are being squeezed from within, or that they feel a heavy burden upon them at all times. This is what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, was feeling and experiencing on account of this magic.

Throughout this time, the Messenger of Allah was turning to Allah for help and guidance. One night, while he was sleeping, he saw a dream in which Allah sent two angels in the form of human beings. The Messenger of Allah was asleep, and in his dream he saw two angels who came to him in human form. One stood beside his head and the other stood beside his feet, and they began to converse with each other. The one standing beside his feet asked the one standing beside his head, pointing to the Messenger of Allah, "What has happened to him?" The other replied, "Several powerful spells of magic have been cast upon him." The first asked, "Who did it?" The other replied, "Lubaid ibn Asim did it." The first asked, "How did he do it?" The other explained the whole process to him. The first asked, "Where did the Jews hide this device?" The other said, "It is at the bottom of ZooArwaan, beneath a rock."

So in the dream, through their conversation, the angels described every detail of the events that had taken place. They gave the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, a complete diagnosis, a complete and detailed account of exactly what had happened, who had done it, and how they had done it.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, awoke and told Maulana Ali about this dream. The two of them went to this well. The Messenger of Allah commanded Maulana Ali to bring out the contraption. He leapt into the well, brought out this device, and handed it to the Messenger of Allah. And it was then that the two chapters, Surah al-Falaq and Surah al-Nas, were revealed to him. Now, how many knots did the device have upon it? Eleven knots. And there are eleven verses in all between Surah al-Falaq and Surah al-Nas: five in al-Falaq and six in al-Nas. So the Messenger of Allah recited the first verse and untied the first knot. He then recited the second verse and untied the second knot.

And he continued in this way until all the verses of both surahs had been recited and all eleven knots were untied. At the end of the last verse, when he opened the final knot, he described himself as relieved. He said it felt as though an illness had been lifted from him, and that he felt cured. Another narration states that he felt as though he had just come out of darkness into light. Glory be to Allah!

Scholars argue that through this surah the proof of his being a true messenger was also revealed. In Surah al-Falaq there is the verse وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ. Until this verse was revealed, no one knew that someone was working magic upon the Messenger of Allah, for, as we recall, he never told his Companions about it. He bore these hardships patiently, but he never showed it or mentioned it to anyone. Now this is remarkable, because in these surahs Allah becomes very specific. He does not say وَمِن شَرِّ الساحرین, "from the evil of sorcerers" or magicians. That would have been general. Instead, Allah spells it out, down to the details of the act itself, which is also the purpose of QUL: declare it, out loud. قل اعوذ برب الفلق ؛ قل اعوذ برب الناس

And when he declared it, together with the Companions, those Jews who had hired Lubaid ibn Asim heard it too. And they wondered: we worked this powerful magic to try to harm him; how did he obtain this information that we did this, and then, ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ؟ How did he know that several spells had been cast upon knots? There was no way he could have known this except through revelation.

And Allah exposes not only the mechanics of the act, that is, black magic, but also the emotion underlying it, which was jealousy. For jealous people grow more active in trying to strike the final blow and to destroy the work that they cannot otherwise stop by insinuation, by evil suggestion, or by force.

So these verses inform the people, even his worst enemies, that he has a protector and a source of knowledge greater than theirs. They call upon their source of knowledge, which is magic, but the Messenger, peace be upon him, has been given the highest form of protection and the highest form of knowledge, which is revelation, and Allah's protection will ALWAYS overcome their evil. Glory be to Allah!

So that was the historical background of how and why these two surahs were revealed. They were both revealed together in a dream to the Messenger of Allah as an antidote to the magic of Labid ibn Asim.

Comparison of Falaq and Naas

Before we begin Surah al-Naas, let us go over a few comparisons between the two surahs. We have already discussed these earlier, so I will pass over them quickly.

We saw in Surah al-Falaq that its primary focus was on protection FROM evil. The protection of Allah is mentioned only once, قل اعوذ برب الفلق, while protection FROM specific evils is mentioned three times:

وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ
وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ
وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ

So it was primarily a surah dedicated to seeking protection FROM evil, مستعاذ منہ.

In Surah al-Naas, on the other hand, we see that its primary focus is on the protection OF Allah, because in this surah the protection of Allah is mentioned three times:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ
مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ
إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

And protection FROM a specific evil is mentioned just once:

مِن شَرِّ ٱلْوَسْوَاسِ ٱلْخَنَّاسِ

From the evil of the whisperings of Shaytan. The remaining verses are simply the explanation of that central evil, the evil of waswasa:

ٱلَّذِى يُوَسْوِسُ فِى صُدُورِ ٱلنَّاسِ مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ

The one who whispers in the hearts of people, whether they are from the jinn or from human beings. That is only the explanation of the actual evil, which is the whispering of Shaytan. Is this symmetry and difference between the two surahs clear?

Now, another interesting thing about these surahs is that in Surah al-Falaq the protection we are seeking is physical in nature:

وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ
وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّثَتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ
وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ

The effects of these evils affect us physically. In Surah al-Naas, however, the protection we are seeking is spiritual. We are asking for protection for our soul, from the waswasa of Shaytan.

Also, the evils mentioned in Surah al-Falaq are outside our control. We are helpless victims of those crimes. But the evil mentioned in Surah al-Naas is something we ourselves will be guilty of, because when Shaytan does waswasa to us, we will end up acting upon it and committing an evil. Therefore we will be liable and accountable for that action. The liability in the previous surahs was on the criminals, but the liability in Surah al-Naas is entirely on us. We will be accountable for the action that we commit on the basis of Shaytan's waswasa. For, as the Quran says, on the Day of Judgment Shaytan is not going to take responsibility. He will say to us:

وَمَا كَانَ لِىَ عَلَيْكُم مِّن سُلْطَنٍ

Do not blame me. I had no power or control over you. I did not hold a gun to your head.

إِلَّآ أَن دَعَوْتُكُمْ فَٱسْتَجَبْتُمْ لِى

I only invited you, I called you to that evil, and it was YOU who responded to it.

فَلَا تَلُومُونِى وَلُومُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُم

Therefore do not curse at me today. Curse at your own soul, because it was all your own doing. I did nothing. I only suggested; you responded. I only sent you the email; it was you who clicked on it. I only sent you the link to that filthy site; you were the one who went to it. I only made the call; you are the one who picked it up. I only sent you the address; you are the one who drove there. All I did was give you an invitation, that is all. The one acting on it was entirely you. You are the one who is alone responsible for your acts.

So the evils addressed in this surah, in Surah al-Naas, we are liable for. We will be held accountable for them on the Day of Judgment. The previous surah, al-Falaq,

deals with the harms of this duniya. But the waswasa of shaytan harms our deen, our akhira. Which is more precious? Which must be guarded more carefully? Our deen, of course, is the one that must be guarded more. So between these two surahs, from which one do we more desperately need to seek protection? Surah al-Naas. And that is why, in this surah, we ask for Allah's protection far more than we do in Surah al-Falaq. In Surah al-Falaq we called upon Him only once:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ

But in al-Naas we call upon Allah to protect our deen again and again, three times over:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

For when shaytan casts his waswasa into our eman, when he plants doubt in it, when he plants jealousy in it, when he plants greed in it, what is he attacking? He is attacking our faith, our taqwa. His waswasa can corrupt every one of those things. This is why we ask for Allah's protection so much more in this surah.

We have already spoken about Qul. It is uttered in obedience to Allah's command, and the lesson here is that you cannot enter Allah's protection unless you are obedient to Him. One who is disobedient to Allah has no right to ask for His protection; he must first come into Allah's obedience.

Qul is a declaration. You have to declare that you are seeking refuge. You have to set your ego aside and admit that you need help, that you need Allah's protection. Allah did not say:

استعیذ برب الناس

Seek protection from the master of people. He did not say that, because that could be done in secret. You could seek Allah's refuge quietly. But Allah says:

قل اعوذ برب الناس

meaning: declare your need of Allah openly. Say it aloud. When you say it aloud, you have crushed your ego and humbled yourself before Allah, saying, "I cannot protect myself. You can protect me." And this is part of the lesson here. Part of the lesson is humility before Allah, glorified and exalted, and the breaking of one's own nafs.

Why Rabb al-Naas?

Now, why does Allah call Himself Rabb al-Naas in this surah? And what is the relation of Rabb al-Naas to the remaining ayats? We now understand why He called Himself Rabb al-Falaq in the previous surah: because it had to do with tearing through and ripping apart all the evils mentioned in it. That is why Allah called Himself Rabb al-Falaq.

So why does Allah call Himself Rabb al-Naas? The word Naas means people, all of mankind. Notice that He did not say Rabb al-Momineen, Rabb al-Sulemani, Rabb al-Sunni, Rabb al-Shia. He did not identify Himself as the master of one particular group. He identified Himself as Rabb al-Naas, the master of all mankind. That is the first thing to appreciate.

But then He could have referred to His mastery over many other things. Indeed, in so many places in the Quran He associates His mastery and lordship with other creations:

رب السماوات والارض

Master of the skies and the earth.

رب العالمین

Master of the worlds.

Now let us look at the word "Naas." As we have seen, the wordings of the Qur'an are very precise. Every word is like a brick in a beautiful piece of architecture. You cannot move a single word from its place. So now, why does Allah use the word Naas, when many other words could have been used here? Nations, أقوام for example. قل اعوذ برب أقوام. Dawl. Umam. Many words could have been used, all of which mean a group of people. Now why Naas? And especially because this surah is named after this word.

The word Naas, in its origin, comes from the word Nisyaan, which means forgetfulness. One of the reasons human beings are called Naas is because they are forgetful. Because they forgot the promise they had made to Allah in the spiritual world before being born into His physical world. And do you know what that promise was?

When Allah created human beings in the spiritual world:

وَإِذْ أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِنۢ بَنِىٓ آدَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ

When their Rabb, their master, their owner, when He gave existence to souls from nothing:

وَأَشْهَدَهُمْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ

And He made them witness Him. That is, all these created souls were made to witness Allah AWJ. They all stood before Allah, and then He asked them:

أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ ۖ

Allah said: Am I not your master? Am I not your Rabb? Even then He introduced Himself as Rabb. We all said:

قَالُوا۟ بَلَىٰ ۛ شَهِدْنَآ ۛ

Of course You are, we all testify!

When He created us, and we were all standing before Him, Allah asked: أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ Am I not your master? Do you know what He did not ask? Do I exist? Do I exist? He did not ask that. Why? Because He is right there. We as souls are seeing Him. That would have been a foolish question for us to ask our master, when we are seeing Him.

Ya Allah, do You really exist? So He asked, أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ — Am I not your Rabb? And all of us, every single one of us, testified: بَلَىٰ ۛ شَهِدْنَآ. Of course, O Allah, we bear witness that You are our Rabb. You are our owner. But then, when we came to this world, we forgot.

Now let us think about that for a moment. We witnessed Allah in the spiritual world. We could not possibly have had any doubt about His existence, or His majesty, or His glory, at that point. He made us bear witness that He is our Rabb — not Malik, not Ilah, but Rabb. Yet then we are born into this world, and our memory is wiped clean, is it not? None of us remember that day when we saw Him standing before us in the spiritual world, do we? So why is that? Would it not be so much easier to believe in Allah if we could simply remember that one day? Then what is the point of this forgetfulness? Well, stay tuned for Season 2 of Sunday Sessions. I will explain that when we study AlHamdu Lillahi Rabb AlAalameen. Because we need to study a few more things in order to truly understand this concept.

But for now, understand this much: the word Naas comes from Nisyaan, which means forgetfulness. And we as human beings tend to forget. Our parents tell us not to do something; we go and do it anyway, and when they ask us why, what is our answer? I forgot! We forget things all the time. We forget birthdays, we forget appointments, we forget our prayers, we even forget our master and our lord. And all of this is thanks to the waswasa of Shaytan.

One of the only powers Allah has given Shaytan is the ability to make us forget. And what is the biggest thing that he makes us forget? That Allah is there — that is what he makes us forget. And then, once we do remember that Allah is there, he makes us forget that He is our master. I do not mean that you forget it for life, as though you had amnesia or something. That is not what I mean. What I mean is that he makes us forget Allah in the very moment when we needed to remember Him, when we needed to remember His ownership of us. That is when he makes us forget Allah.

In those five minutes when we were acting out our desires, when we were acting out our aggression, we forgot. For that evening, for that weekend, we forgot. When we took that turn toward the place we should not have gone, we forgot. When we raised our eyes and looked at what we were not supposed to look at, we forgot. In all of these moments, we forgot that we have a master. Shaytan can make us forget at the very moment when we needed to remember Allah. Listen to this ayah:

ٱسْتَحْوَذَ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلشَّيْطَنُ فَأَنسَىٰهُمْ ذِكْرَ ٱللَّهِ

Shaytan got a hold of them, and he made them forget the remembrance of Allah. That is all Shaytan wants to do: make us forget the remembrance of Allah.

This is why the word Naas is used in this surah: قل اعوذ برب الناس. Because Naas means people who have the tendency to forget. And when they forget, whose waswasa is it that makes them forget? Shaytan's! So part of the lesson of this surah is that we seek Allah's protection from becoming forgetful. We are asking Allah to help us become people of remembrance, and not people who forget — make us not among those who are heedless. And that is why Allah reminds us:

فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ ٱلْقُرْآنَ فَٱسْتَعِذْ بِٱللَّهِ مِنَ ٱلشَّيْطَنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ

When you recite the Qur'an, seek Allah's protection from Shaytan.

Because he will make you forget. Does this happen to you? You are reciting the Qur'an, or you are standing in salah, but your mind is already on a completely different planet? You are shopping at the mall, replaying that last episode of your favorite show in your head. You are in the middle of salah, but you have already changed the channel. You are on a completely different frequency now. You have no idea what is going on. You do not remember where you are, what you are doing, before whom you are standing. You even forget which rakah you are in. That is why, whenever you recite the Qur'an, seek Allah's refuge.

Even in Surah al-Kahf this lesson was mentioned in passing. You know how the young companion of Musa, peace be upon him, forgot? فَإِنِّى نَسِيتُ ٱلْحُوتَ وَمَآ أَنْسَىٰنِيهُ إِلَّا ٱلشَّيْطَنُ أَنْ أَذْكُرَهُ No one but Shaytan made me forget. The lesson from this is that one of Shaytan's greatest tactics is to make us forget the remembrance of Allah.

So now these two things — forgetfulness and being caught by Shaytan — are one and the same. And remembering Allah and being protected from Shaytan are likewise one and the same. If the heart is filled with the remembrance of Allah, then Shaytan has no room to enter. But when the heart is empty of the remembrance of Allah, a large sign is hung out: Vacancy available. And Shaytan enters. The only way he can enter is when you and I are not remembering Allah.

So because of this human tendency to forget, the word Naas is used so perfectly in this surah. رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ The Owner and Master of Naas — because people will forget that Allah is their owner. They will forget that Allah has ownership over them. مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ Because people will forget that Allah is their true king, who has complete authority over them. إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ Because people will forget that Allah is their God. They will forget that Allah is the only one to be worshiped. They will forget that and begin worshiping other things.

Firaun Taking the Place of Allah

Now the other side of this coin. When we studied Surah al-Falaq, we saw that the word Falaq was used in two ways, according to the audience it was addressing. When speaking to the victims of evil, it was a glad tiding to them, saying: Do not worry. I am the Rabb of al-Falaq. I will tear open the darkness of your afflictions and bring you out of them, just as I tear open the darkness and bring out the day. But at the same time it also speaks to the criminals, and warns them, and threatens them, saying: Falaq is also the name of a door in the Fire. So you had better not be doing these kinds of evils to others. So Surah al-Falaq is a double-edged sword.

Now let us see whether the same pattern exists in Surah al-Naas. In the Qur'an a great many evil people are mentioned. Many devils are mentioned. But who is the greatest of the enemies mentioned in the Qur'an? After Iblis himself, whom would you place at number two? Firaun! You would have to place Firaun at number two. And I want you to notice something about Firaun. But before that, very quickly, what are the three names of Allah that are mentioned? رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

Now look at what the Qur'an says. Let us take the first word, "Rabb." What did Firaun say about himself in the Qur'an? فَقَالَ أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ I am Rabb.

and not just any rabb. I am the greatest of all rabbs: أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ. This is the greatest waswasa of shaytan. What you are supposed to attribute to Allah, he attributed to himself. Rabb.

What was the second name that Allah mentioned for himself after Rabb? Malik. King! And we find another statement of Firaun in the Qur'an. وَنَادَىٰ فِرْعَوْنُ فِى قَوْمِهِ Firaun called out to his nation. قَالَ يَٰقَوْمِ أَلَيْسَ لِى مُلْكُ مِصْرَ Is the kingdom of Egypt not mine? وَهَٰذِهِ ٱلْأَنْهَٰرُ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِىٓ ۖ أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ Do these rivers not flow beneath my feet? Do you not see all of this? What did he call himself this time? King! He named himself as Rabb first, and then he named himself as king.

What is left? Ilah! Now let us see whether he committed this crime too. He turns to his chiefs and he says: وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمَلَأُ مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرِى My generals, listen: I know of no other Ilah for you than myself.

In the story of Firaun, we find him declaring three things for himself: Rububiyah, Mulk, and Uluhiyah. All three for himself. He calls himself Rabb, Malik, and Ilah. Now this sample that Allah has given us in the Qur'an is very important. It should not be overlooked, and it is not merely for you and me to say, "What a man Firaun was! He is such a horrible person. What a loser!" No! There is something here. There is a lesson to be learned here: that this is where the whisperings of shaytan can lead.

What was the greatest problem of Iblees himself? What made him Iblees? Arrogance! أنا خیر منہ. خلقتنی من نار و خلقتہ من طین I am better than him, because you created me from fire and you created Adam from clay. So the problem of Iblees was arrogance, which got him into trouble with Allah. So, to get us human beings into trouble, what is the greatest thing he can instill within us? Arrogance! And who is the worst manifestation of arrogance in the Qur'an? Firaun!

But you do not have to reach that level to worry that you are headed down the same road that leads to Firaun. Today we are not living in a time where people declare themselves god over others. But we are living in times where people declare themselves god over themselves. They declare that they are their own master. I am my own man! I am my own king! I am my own master! I am king of the house! I am king of my domain. We declare ourselves as our own Ilah. And the Qur'an says: أَرَءَيْتَ مَنِ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَٰهَهُۥ هَوَىٰهُ Did you see the one who takes his desires and turns them into his Ilah? We let our desires become our gods over us, and we begin to worship them. Desire says, "Smoke! It will make you look cool." And we say, "Yes, Master." Desire says, "Forget salah, watch a movie." We say, "Yes, Master!" Desire commands, and we obey.

We are living in times where we have all turned into miniature Firauns without even realizing it. You do not have to own great castles, fight with messengers, and be arrogant and outspoken against Allah AWJ. We do not need to do that to become Firaun today. Our egos have made us all Firauns today.

And that very ego is crushed at the beginning of these surahs when we openly declare: I need protection. I need Allah's protection. I am coming into his obedience. This is a very powerful lesson in submission. In fact, Iblees himself recognizes the lordship of Allah, but he wants human beings to forget it.

He himself said to Allah: You are the one who created me. خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ. When asked what had stopped him from prostrating, he answered that he was better than the human being: you created me from fire, and you created him from clay. He admits that Allah created him. He accepts that he is Allah's creation. He accepts that Allah is his Lord, his Master, and his God, even as he disobeys him. Even in his disobedience he gives Allah his due: You created me — خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ. Even then he himself acknowledged the oneness of Allah. Yet he wants the human being to forget that oneness. He wants the human being to become ungrateful. May Allah protect us all from the whispering of Satan.

So we see that this surah, like the one before it, is at once a reminder and a warning. It is a reminder to the one who seeks Allah's protection: do not be afraid, I am your Lord, your owner; I am your Master, your king; and I am your God. But at the same time it is a warning and a threat: do not dare to try to become a lord yourself. If I have given you ownership, it is only a trust. Do not let it deceive you into arrogance. If I have given you authority over a country, do not forget that I am the ultimate authority. Do not oppress the people I have placed under your control. And do not let your desires become your god, for I am the ultimate Lord, the ultimate Master, and the ultimate God.

Recap. من شر الوسواس الخناس.

Now that we have spoken about the "protection of" portion — قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ — which, to summarize, is this: قُلْ, I openly declare; I set aside my ego, and I willingly and openly submit in obedience; أَعُوذُ, I seek the spiritual protection of my God; بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ, of the owner of people; مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ, the king of people; إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ, the God of people. And now that I have submitted to the protection of Allah, what am I seeking protection from? من شر الوسواس الخناس. From the evil of the retreating whisperer.

There are two words here that we need to understand: الوسواس, the one who whispers, and الخناس, the one who retreats. Let us begin with الوسواس, the whisperer. And what does a whisperer do? He performs وسوسۃ. He whispers.

Now, there is another word in Arabic that is used for whispering, and that is ھمسۃ, which is also used in the Qur'an: وَخَشَعَتِ ٱلْأَصْوَاتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ فَلَا تَسْمَعُ إِلَّا هَمْسًۭا. On that Day of Judgment, everyone will stand silent before al-Rahman, and you will hear nothing except faint whispers.

Now the first question is: what is the difference between ھمسۃ and وسوسۃ? The first difference is that the word ھمسۃ means to whisper anything at all; it does not matter whether it is good or bad. I could whisper something good, or I could whisper something bad. For such a whisper, where the intention is beside the point, the word ھمسۃ is used. But وسوسۃ is used only and always for evil whispering. Do you understand? ھمسۃ can be used for both good and evil whispering, but وسوسۃ is used only for evil whispering. That is the first difference.

The second difference is what is called تکرار الَّفظ. This may become a little technical, but it is a truly fascinating science of the Arabic language. When there is a repetition of a syllable within a word, it alludes rhetorically to the repetition of the act itself. If a sound is repeated more than once within the word itself,

Then that alludes to the repetition of the act itself. Now, in the word وسوسۃ, which syllable do you hear repeated? The sound وس is repeated twice in the word: وس, وسۃ. So when a word in Arabic contains such repeating syllables, that automatically implies the repetition of the act itself. It is very interesting.

So ھمسۃ is someone who whispers. Listen carefully: ھمسۃ. No syllables are repeated. That means the ھامس whispers only once. But was-wasa, because the syllable وس is repeated, implies that a وَسواس, the whisperer, is someone who whispers, and then whispers again, and then whispers again, and then whispers again.

So الوسواس is someone who whispers all the time, continuously, until its purpose is achieved. Wass-wassaa, wass-wasaa, wass-wassaa. That is how that act of whispering is: it is constantly repeated until the goal is acquired.

A similar example is the word zal-zala, which means the shaking of the earth, an earthquake. But do you notice the syllable "zal" repeated? So zalzala means the shaking of the earth, but it is not just the earth shaking once. It is when the earth shakes, then shakes again, and then shakes again; that is zal-zala.

A series of mountains, one after the other: sil-silaa. Not just a mountain, but a series of mountains one after the other.

So when a syllable is repeated within a word, it describes the continuity of the act itself; it implies repetition. Do you understand? So just studying the root of the word وسواس tells us that this whispering that is mentioned is, first of all, taking place with evil intent, and secondly, it is not just happening once, but repeatedly. And by repeatedly, I do not mean a few times.

Now here is another subtle difference we need to understand. When I say several times, that could be a few random times, and that is it, right? And this is why you see that Arabic is such an eloquent and sophisticated language. If the act of whispering were repeated only a few times, then the word would have been المُوَسوِس, which is the active participle. But Allah did not use the word الموسوِس, or وِسواس, the whisperer. Notice that both words, الموسوِس and وِسواس, contain a kasra. A kasra would mean just a few sets of whispers. He would repeat his deed a few times and then walk away. But in the ayah, وَسوسۃ is used, with a fatha, or a zabar. This is called صیغۃ المبالغہ, meaning the one who whispers non-stop, the extreme whisperer, one who is obsessed with whispering. Do you understand?

If he were just a whisperer, he would have been وِسواس. But a وَسواس is an obsessive-compulsive whisperer; he is a whisperer with OCD. He does not stop. He keeps going and going and going, until he accomplishes his goal.

So now you see what just happened here? Just the word whisper, وسوسۃ, itself implied continuous repetition by the repetition of the syllable in it. But now tack on top of it the hyperbolized form of the whisperer, with the fatha (وَسواس and not وِسواس). That adds further strength to the act of continuous whispering. And this makes it a very, very, extremely powerful word to use, to describe the constant, never-ending, relentless whispering of shaytan. This is not an easy enemy we are dealing with. We are dealing with a very powerful enemy, and this is very important to appreciate. Because only after we truly appreciate the power of this enemy

we can understand our need to submit to the protection of Allah. When you are afraid of an enemy you believe you might be able to face on your own, your urgency in seeking protection from that enemy is of one kind. But when you know there is no way you can defeat an enemy, the urgency with which you seek protection changes entirely, does it not?

That, then, is the first thing to understand from this word, الوسواس: that Shaytan is one who whispers, and who will go on whispering without pause until the end of time.

The second thing I want you to notice is that this ayah seeks protection from the evil of the constant whisperer, not from the whispering itself. The ayah does not say من شر الوسوسۃُ الخناس, protection from the evil whispering of Khannas. After all, is it not the whispering that is bad? Are we not seeking protection from the evil whispering? So why did Allah mention the whisperer in particular, and not the whispering itself?

This is because the one who whispers can do more evil than the whisper alone. Do you understand? Whispering is only one of the tactics of Shaytan. So when we ask Allah for protection from the whisperer, we recognize that his constant whispering is only one of the ways he can harm us. He could harm us in countless other ways, the greatest of which is his whispering. And so we submit to the protection of Allah against all of it. We ask for protection from his whispers, and also from anything else he may do to harm us. If the ayah had said only, protect me from the whispering, then that is all we would be protected from. But we are asking for protection from his whispering and from any other act he may attempt against us. In truth, we are seeking protection from him, from everything he does, including his whisper. So it is far more comprehensive and all-inclusive to say من شر الوسواس الخناس than to say من شر الوسوسۃ الخناس.

Khannas

Then there is the adjective added to the whisperer, which is الخناس. The word literally means "the retreater," the one who draws back. This word is used elsewhere in the Qur'an as well:

فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِٱلْخُنَّسِ ٱلْجَوَارِ ٱلْكُنَّسِ

It is used to describe the stars, which appear to the eye to shine, and then step back and vanish. That is what the word خَنَسَ means: to step back, to retreat.

But the ayah is not من شر الوسواس الخَانِس. Khaanis is the one who steps back. خَنَّاسَ is the one who keeps stepping back. And if he keeps stepping back, then that in itself implies that he keeps stepping forward as well, and then again steps back. Do you know what this means? It means that he is not only whispering constantly, and where did we learn that? From الوسواس, the one who whispers without ceasing. But then, the moment he whispers, what does he do? He steps back.
