So it is as if someone were doing this to you: someone calls your name from behind, and when you turn around, he is not there, he has stepped back. That is خَنَّاسَ. And then, the moment you turn your back to him again, what does he do? He steps forward and whispers once more. You would think that after doing this several times he would stop, would you not? But not according to the word الخناس. For it is once again صیغۃ المبالغہ. It is used in its hyperbolic form.

just like الوَسواس. You know the word khabbaaz. It means the one who makes khubz. He makes bread over and over and over again. He does it for a living. He does not simply make one pita bread and then give up. He keeps making bread day in and day out. That is why he is called al-khabbaaz. He is going to do it for a living, all the time. In the same way, someone who KEEPS on giving gifts, who never stops, who keeps giving gifts over and over and over again, is وھَّاب. Hiba means a gift. وھَّاب is one who gifts over and over and over again. And this is in fact one of the names of Allah AWJ. Another name is غَفَّار. غَافِر is someone who forgives. غَفَّار is someone who keeps forgiving over and over and over and over again. It is not that Allah forgives only once, or that He is merely forgiving. He is غَفَّار, because He CONSTANTLY forgives, over and over and over again. Even for the same crimes that we keep repeating, as long as our intention is pure when we seek His forgiveness. So there is this hyperbole used in these words.

So الوسواس الخناس is someone who keeps coming at you from behind. He whispers a thought in your head, and then he retreats. He comes to you again, whispers a thought in your head, and then retreats. He comes again, whispers a thought in your head, and then retreats. Now, what do you think? From a psychological point of view, what do you think happens when someone keeps doing that to you? Someone keeps whispering to you over and over again, and keeps retreating over and over again. What do you start thinking? You start thinking that these thoughts are YOUR OWN thoughts. He instigates you, and you think that it is YOU who actually wants to do it. It is YOU who wants to see it. It is YOU who wants to feel it. You end up taking responsibility for committing the evil act, which began with someone else's whisper. How many times in your life have you caught yourself saying, I cannot believe I did that. I cannot believe I said that. I cannot believe I thought that? We do it all the time.

Shaytan, with his CONSTANT, never-ending whispering, with his constant retreat, makes us do things which at one time we had said, I will NEVER EVER do that. And then we end up doing those EXACT same acts that we detested in others. And it is all because of الوسواس الخناس.

So that is الوسواس الخناس. He keeps whispering, retreating, and then coming back, over and over and over again. He NEVER EVER quits. So his offense is الوسواس, and his defense is الخناس. And that is why Allah calls out to us, to give ourselves willingly, in submission to our Rabb, our Malik, and our Ilah. Because when someone tries to hurt a child, who comes between the child and his enemy? The parents stand in between. The Rabb AlNaas comes forth for protection. When civilians are being attacked by invaders, who comes forth to protect the civilians? The king does. That is Malik AnNaas. And when an enemy SO powerful, physical or spiritual, when such a powerful enemy that neither the Rabb nor the Malik (in the worldly sense) can protect against, when الوسواس الخناس attacks, who comes to our protection? Ilah AnNaas. SubhanAllah! So we have both of his attacks, of وسوسۃ as well as خنس, covered inside these two words.

So from this ayah, we are learning that Shaytan plants himself right in the heart of human beings, of the sons of Adam AS. And then, as soon as the human being grows lackadaisical.

As soon as he grows heedless, as soon as he forgets, Shaytan strikes him with waswasa. But the moment he remembers Allah, the moment he remembers his Rabb, his Malik, his Ilah, Shaytan withdraws. He steps back. So when we remember Allah, Shaytan takes a step back, and when we cease to remember Allah, Shaytan moves forward. And he never, ever stops. It is not that he sees an opening and says, "Ah, I am tired today. I do not feel like it. I am not in the mood. I have no wish to do waswasa today. I have had a long and busy few thousand years." No. He does nothing of the sort, because he is الوسواس الخناس. He never takes a rest. You and I will take a rest from remembering Allah; Shaytan never takes a rest. He labors at his work. He is working harder than any one of us.

And to defend ourselves against such an enemy, what must we do? We have to fight back, and fight back hard. This is not something that comes without effort. This استعاذہ from Shaytan does not come easily. He is truly excellent at what he does. To be protected, we must genuinely appreciate the hard work he pours into his task of casting people into the hellfire. This is a serious matter. These ayat give us a true measure of what the level of our defense against him ought to be.

Now, what is the end goal of his ceaseless whispering? What is the aim he is trying to achieve? What did we see his own affliction to be? It was Kibr. It was arrogance and pride, was it not? And that is precisely what he wishes to plant in the hearts of people, because he knows this is what ruined him. Therefore it will surely ruin others as well. And the easiest way to do this is through anger. Anger is a manifestation of what? Of arrogance. Of the ego. And Shaytan is very skilled at making us angry. He will work so cunningly to make you angry. He will work on you. And at the very same time he will work on the one he wishes you to be angry with. Then he brings the two of you together, and — boom. It is astonishing how this one operates. He will tell the thief to commit the robbery, and at the same moment tell the guard to be watchful tonight. He is the greatest double agent you will ever encounter in your life.

Even when you try to help someone — you see a person growing angry, and you go to remind him: "Asif Mamu, please do not be angry. Calm yourself. Say اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان ارجیم" — he will turn that very anger back upon you. "What do you mean? Are you calling me Shaytan? Are you saying I am possessed by Shaytan?" He will make that person angrier still. And then you grow angry. "I am trying to help you, and you are shouting at me? What is this?" And now you and I are at each other's throats, and Shaytan sits there laughing, saying, "I got them well. I even got him to stop saying اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان ارجیم." SubhanAllah.

So make no mistake. Shaytan is truly excellent at what he does, and it takes humility and a great deal of courage to take a step back and say, "This is not me. This is Shaytan whispering to me. I need to step back and humble myself before Allah." And to realize that anger is something befitting Allah alone, and not something befitting me. It is not something I should take upon myself. So if I feel anger rising, I should take a step back and say اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان ارجیم.

And the Qur'an warns us to be constantly aware of Shaytan's presence. مَا مِنکُم مِن احدٍ اِلَّا قَد وُکِّلَ بِہِ قَرِینُہُ — There is not one of you but a constant companion is assigned to him. Notice the word that is used: qareen, which means an associate. This hadith does not use the word Shaytan. So you must be careful about your associates, about the friends you keep. If he cannot reach you directly, he will reach you through your friends; through your associate he will whisper to you.

And understand that this whispering, this waswasa, is not directed against Allah alone. Shaytan also whispers about the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and about his Friends. He whispers about Maulana Ali, about the Imams, the duaat, the manaseeb. He whispers about your parents. He whispers about everyone. The easier attack is not upon our faith about Allah. Do you know what the easier attack is? It is upon our faith in the Messenger of Allah, and in the Friends of Allah. That kind of faith he can assail very easily, because there Shaytan brings our ego into the way.

So why, in this surah, did He extend His mastery, His lordship, specifically toward people, toward naas? It is because it is only people, only mankind, who need Allah's protection in this surah. The skies and the earth do not need protection from shaytan. The worlds and the universes do not need protection from shaytan. Who needs protection from shaytan and his whispering? It is people.

So Allah extended His mastery, His lordship, toward people. It is as if it is being said: I seek Allah's protection from the evil of the one who is the worst enemy of all mankind, and I seek protection with the master of mankind, the one who has authority over them and over all of their affairs.

Why is *naas* repeated every time?

Now let us look a little at the linguistic and grammatical dimension of these verses.

In this surah, Allah has asked us to seek His protection using three of His names:

رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

And notice that the word *naas* is mentioned three times. He did not have to do this, did He? From a grammatical point of view, the word *naas* is redundant.

If I say, "Nadia is a girl. Nadia is my friend. Nadia attends my sessions regularly," is that the best way to speak? No. What can I say instead? "Nadia is a girl. She is my friend. She attends my sessions regularly." Once I have said "Nadia," I do not need to repeat it again and again. I could simply use a pronoun, right?

So Allah could have done the same thing. Linguistically, He could have said:

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ; مَلِکِھِم، اِلٰہِھِم

He could have used a pronoun. But Allah used *naas* specifically with each verse. It seems redundant. So why is that?

Let us first speak about a psychological progression. Take a child, for example. One of the first realizations a child has is that his needs are cared for by his parents, by someone who has control over him, someone who takes care of his tarbiyah (his training). As a child, when you have a need, you go to your parents. That is why parents are also called *rabb* in Arabic, because they carry out the tarbiyah, or training, of the child. In that sense they have mastery over the child. Just as a slave, when he has a need, goes to his master, so this is captured in the word *rabb*.

But then sometimes there is a problem that your parent cannot take care of. The one who has mastery over you cannot resolve that problem. It is a problem bigger than that. Then do you know whom you turn to? You go to the government. You go to the sovereign. You go to the king. You go to the *malik*. You make that next step.

But then you have a problem so great that your *rabb* cannot solve it. Your *malik* cannot solve it. Even your king, your government, cannot solve it. No one on earth can solve it. Where do people turn when they have that kind of need? Where do people turn then? *Ilah an-Naas!* Now you can only ask God for help. So these are the three psychological steps within these verses.

بشرٌ یَھدُو لَنا؟ — This man is going to guide us? He is just like us. This is what they said about Eisa, upon him be peace: یمشی فی الأسواق — he walks about in the market just as we do. He goes shopping as well. How can he be a messenger? I saw him at the grocery store the other day, and he is a messenger? یأکل الطعام — he eats food just as I eat food. What makes him so special? Do you truly expect me to accept authority from him?

And this is the root of the ego. Human beings refuse to accept the authority of another human being. It is ingrained within our heads. When you are in class, you refuse to accept the authority of your teacher, and even when you accept it, you do so grudgingly. You are told to sit down, and only after much resistance do you comply. You cannot bear the authority of your parents over you. It is my life, you protest; simply leave me alone. Your life? Who gave you this life? Who carried you for nine months to give you the very life you are so arrogant about? And yet we cannot bear their authority over us.

Employees cannot bear to listen to their bosses. The only time you call someone a good boss is when he gives you no work to do, when he does not tell you what to do; that is when you love him. As soon as another human being holds authority over us, we grow irritated. What does he know, we say. You are pulled over by a police officer, and he exercises his authority over you, and you are irritated. You must stand before a judge, and you are irritated. Human beings simply do not like another human being holding authority over them.

And yet here is another human being, the Messenger of Allah, who has been given absolute authority over you. Absolute authority — and we do not like it.

For us, the Messenger is little more than another book, a story we read in books. But to Maulana Ali he was not merely a story. He was his master. He was the authority over him. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was Rabb and was Malik for Maulana Ali. To Salman Farsi, to Miqdad bin Aswad, to Ammar Yasir, the Messenger of Allah was not simply another person with authority; for them he was the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. How difficult do you imagine it must have been for them to accept his authority over them? These were people the Messenger of Allah had grown up among. He was their uncle, their relative, their friend. Can you appreciate how difficult it is to accept everything your closest friend says, no matter what it is? Do you know how hard that is? And you can no longer even address him as your companion. What must you call him now? Ya Rasul Allah.

How hard it is for a wife to accept EVERYTHING her husband says! Everything he says. And not even to say, "My husband said." No. She must say, "Rasul Allah said." They have to say قال رسول اللہ صلی اللہ علیہ و آلہ وسلم. Maulatina Fatima does not say قال ابی, "My father said." Maulatina Khadija does not say قال زوجی, "My husband said." They say قال رسول اللہ. Because they have completely and willingly accepted his authority over them. They have humbled their ego.

Accepting Allah is one thing. But accepting Rasul Allah requires much more humility, because now you must accept the authority of another human being over yourself, for this person is going to tell you what Allah wants from you. This is why people have so much trouble with the office of the Manseeb in our Jamaat. They say those who hold it do not know what they are doing, that they do not know how to run the Jamaat. But walk two steps in their shoes before you speak against them. Walk two steps in their shoes. It is so easy to sit on the sidelines and criticize. I have twenty people in these sessions, and I have realized what a challenge it is to deal with even a group. They must deal with the entire Jamaat, spread across continents. Yet we make this trouble because we as human beings do not like the authority of another human being over us. And this is what Shaytan takes advantage of.

Today we live in a time of inflated egos, and it is so easy to let that get in the way. That is really the psychological origin of our refusal to accept a master over us. I do not want to accept Allah as my master, because then I would have to do what He commands me to do, and that is not acceptable to me, for I want to do what I want to do. So what is the easiest way to manage that? You see it play out at every election. One party criticizes and assassinates the character of the other, because that is the easiest way to win. We do the same thing with Allah. Character assassination. What sort of an Allah is this? How is He merciful? Look what is happening to me. Look what is happening all around me. There could not possibly be an Allah. I am not going to believe in the existence of Allah. And once Shaytan gets you to do that, once he convinces you to reject the mastery of Allah over your soul, you have then, in effect, handed your soul over to the devil.

## Human beings cannot escape slavery

But sadly, do you know the most ironic thing about it? That in rejecting the mastery and ownership of Allah over you, you have inevitably accepted the ownership and mastery of Shaytan over you. You have now made Shaytan your Rabb. He now owns you. You are still a slave. You are still a slave, no matter what. The sad part is that now, instead of being the slave of the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate Master there is, you are the slave of a horrible, horrible master. He will make you do things that, pleasurable as you find them today, will destroy you in the hereafter. And on that Day, when you are being punished, he will back off completely and disown you.

وَمَا كَانَ لِىَ عَلَيْكُم مِّن سُلْطَنٍ

He will say: Do not blame me. I have nothing to do with your destruction today. I did not hold a gun to your head.

إِلَّآ أَن دَعَوْتُكُمْ فَٱسْتَجَبْتُمْ لِى

I merely invited you. I simply called you to that evil, and it was you who answered.

فَلَا تَلُومُونِى وَلُومُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُم

Do not blame me today. Curse your own soul.

Because everything you did, all of it was your own doing. This is the kind of friend Shaytan is. Tell me, children: is such a friendship worth it? Is this the kind of friend for whom we should abandon Allah? For here is what Allah says about these friends. You have just heard what Shaytan will say to his friends on the Day of Judgment. Now let me tell you what Allah says about His friends on that Day.

أَلآ إِنَّ أَوْلِيَآءَ اللَّهِ لاَ خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلاَ هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ There is no doubt about it: for the friends of Allah there will be no fear and no grief on the Day of Judgment. الَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا وَكَانُوا يَتَّقُونَ Those who believed in Him and adopted piety for His sake. لَهُمُ الْبُشْرَى فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَفِي الاَخِرَةِ For them is glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. And now listen to this. لا تَبْدِيلَ لِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ ذَلِكَ هُوَ الْفَوْزُ الْعَظِيمُ There is never any change in the words of Allah. Allah never goes back on His word. And for them is the greatest of all successes.

Notice that the words Fauz al-Azeem are used here. We spoke of this remarkable word before, of what this success actually means in its very language. I have just told you what Shaytan does with us. In this world he convinces us that we are his very best friend, and in the Hereafter he abandons us completely. He goes back on his word. But Allah, the true Master, the Rabb, the Malik, the Ilah, He says: لا تَبْدِيلَ لِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ Allah never goes back on His word. SubhanAllah!

So how incredibly foolish, how incredibly senseless would that person be who abandons Allah's mastery over his soul and accepts the mastery of Shaytan. For make no mistake: you always, always have someone who is a Rabb over you. If it is not Allah, it will most certainly be Shaytan. And if not Shaytan, then your own desires, inspired by Shaytan. But you always, always have a master over you. Why? Because Allah says: وما خلقت الجن و الانس الا لیعبدون I created the jinn and mankind to be My slaves. Slavery is what we are made of. We cannot escape it. Slavery of our soul, slavery of our desires, slavery of our friends, slavery of the fleeting attractions of this world, slavery of power, slavery of wealth, slavery of women. There is nothing but slavery. We cannot escape slavery, just as a flower cannot escape its fragrance, and filth cannot escape its stench.

These surahs are teaching us that if this is the reality, if we cannot escape slavery no matter what, then let us accept Allah as our Master. For He is the best Master you will or could ever have. And InshaAllah we will speak of the nature of His mastery in detail in future sessions. InshaAllah I will show you the mercy and the love of this Master. Compare it to anything else, and then choose for yourself.

So the immediate question, rather the immediate concern, becomes this: what are we to do? If Shaytan is so strong, and his whispers are so powerful, so constant, so unrelenting, what are we to do? We are all but doomed, for he can reach us at any moment, can he not? Now listen to this ayah, in which Allah declares whom Shaytan will never be able to touch. When Iblees was asking Allah for all these allowances, that You grant me time until the Day of Judgment, that I will attack Your creation from the left, from the right, and so on, when he was asking for all these allowances, there was a declaration that Allah AWJ made to him about us. He said: إِنَّ عِبَادِى لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطَنٌ There is no doubt about it: over My slaves,

the ones who accept themselves as My slaves. The one who accepts Me, who willingly submits to Me in obedience, who gives himself up to Me, who accepts Me as his Rabb, his Malik, his Ilah — over them you will have absolutely no authority. The moment they accept My mastery, your authority over them ends. You will no longer be able to harm them. As soon as they come under My protection, as soon as they submit themselves to My protection, your game is over. All they need to do is accept Me as their master, their owner, and submit themselves to Me.

All of this is captured in the word Rabb. Why do you think these surahs begin with the word Rabb? قل أعوذ برب الفلق؛ قل أعوذ برب الناس Why do they begin with Rabb? Because if Allah is Rabb — if we have sincerely, honestly, truthfully, willingly accepted Him as our Rabb — that acceptance makes us what? His slaves! That, by definition, makes us ‘abd. And Allah says: إِنَّ عِبَادِى لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطَنٌ No doubt, over My slaves, over My slaves, you will have no authority.

Look, He says My slaves. Why did He need to use the word My here? He could have simply said: إِنَّ العِبَادَ لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطَنٌ Why did He say My slaves? Because we are slaves no matter what. He created us as slaves. The My includes willful submission. Allah does not want to make us His slaves. We want Allah to become our master. I will say that again. Allah does not want to make us His slaves. We want Allah to become our master. He does not need our slavery. It is we who need His mastery over us! I cannot wait to reach the verses of al-Fatiha when we discuss this relationship of slavery and mastery with Allah. It is the most beautiful thing I have ever learned in all the years I have studied.

So the call is for us to submit ourselves into Allah's slavery. That is why He says My slave. Because accepting Allah's slavery, in and of itself, is true protection from Shaytan. To act as Allah's slave, to live a life as Allah's slave, is a protection from Shaytan.

So Allah said: إِنَّ عِبَادِى لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطَنٌ No doubt, over My slaves, you will have no authority. إِلَّا مَنِ ٱتَّبَعَكَ مِنَ ٱلْغَاوِينَ You will have authority only over those who choose you as their master. Only those will be from among the misguided.

Look at all the problems we face today. Problems with possessions. Psychological issues. Depression. These do not happen to people who are truly slaves of Allah. One of the clear, manifest proofs that we are not slaves of Allah is that we face these problems. God willing, I hope to do a few sessions on trials and tribulations — what they are, and why we are put through these tests in life. So, this was مِنْ شَرِّ الْوَسْوَاسِ الْخَنَّاسِ.

But Allah is teaching us something very unique here. He is teaching us that if you have a problem, no matter what age you are, you always turn to Allah alone. Because your *rabb* is Allah. Your king is Allah. And your *ilah* is Allah. Turn to Allah from the very beginning. This realization is the height of intellectual progression. The height of intellectual progression is that you understand that from your most basic needs to your greatest needs, you turn to Allah for everything. He is مسبب الاسباب. He will create the causes and the means for me through parents, teachers, jobs, employers, kings. But in the end He is the one doing everything for me. Nothing can happen, and nothing will happen, without His command. Therefore, for every single one of my needs, I must turn to Him alone.

فھو ربی و ملکی و الہی

Because He is my master. He is my king.

and He is my God. This is why the word *al-Naas* is mentioned specifically with every single verse.

Your parents may be your Lord. Your teachers may be your Lord. But I am your true Lord. So before you commit yourself to the protection of your parents, before you commit yourself to the protection of your teachers, commit yourself to My protection, because I am رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ. I am the King of all mankind. If I do not choose to protect you, your parents cannot protect you, and your teachers cannot protect you.

If you have a need that those who hold mastery over you cannot resolve, and you must go to the next level — whether it is the head of your company, the principal of your school, a minister of state, or the president of a country — seek My protection first. For though I have placed them in positions of authority, I am مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ. I am the King of all mankind.

And finally, if you have a need that neither those who hold mastery over you nor those who hold power and authority can resolve, then surrender to My protection, because I am الہ الناس, the God of all mankind. This is why we find the word *al-Naas* mentioned with every single verse.

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَٰهِ ٱلنَّاسِ

**How the names of Allah progress**

We see that the names of Allah in this Surah progress from *Rabb* to *Malik* to *Ilah*. So what is the connection between these three words? To understand it, let us look at the meanings of these words.

Let us begin with the word *Rabb*: رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ. *Rabb* is a very comprehensive word, and God willing, we shall study the word *Rabb* in great detail when we study the verse الحمد للہ رب العلمین. But for now, simply understand that the word *Rabb* means owner. Ownership implies value, and value implies love. So *Rabb* means the one who owns something that he loves, and because he loves it, he finds it valuable. Value does not necessarily mean monetary value. For example, if my daughter owns a doll that she loves, then because she loves it, she values it. In that case she is the *Rabb* of that doll. Do you understand? The doll itself may be very cheap in the monetary sense. But because she loves it, she values it, and that makes her its *Rabb*. So *Rabb* means the one who owns something that he or she loves and considers valuable.

Now this kind of ownership automatically carries certain implications. When someone owns something they love and consider valuable, they will take care of it, they will be concerned about it, and they will always try to set it right. For example, if you own a fine phone, and you truly value it, you will always take care of it and be concerned about it. You will not simply leave it anywhere; you will try to keep it close to you. And when you cannot, you will make sure to keep it safe. So if there are young children in the house, you will make sure to keep it in a place where they cannot damage it. You will always protect it. You will get a fine protective cover for it, to guard it from damage. You will make sure to get a case that looks beautiful and elegant, in order to enhance the beauty of the phone. You will make it stand out. You will also set it right when there is a problem. So if it becomes dirty, you will wipe it clean. If something is damaged, you will try to have it fixed. All of this is included in the meaning of the word *Rabb*.

So you can see.

That the word *Rabb* can be used in a worldly sense, even though Allah is the ultimate *Rabb*. Still, the word *Rabb* can be used in a worldly sense as well, simply because the definition of the word *Rabb* can apply to worldly relationships. Let us look again at the definition of the word *Rabb* in a worldly sense. A *Rabb* is one who owns something that he loves and considers valuable. His ownership includes care and concern for the property, and it also includes setting it straight when necessary. Now if you think about it, these attributes of love, care, concern, and setting straight are all attributes of training. *Tarbiyyah*, which means training and nurturing. A *Rabb* is someone who trains and nurtures. You understand?

That is why parents are called *Rabb*. Why? Because they have ownership over you. They have *Rububiyyah* over you. Suppose you are in a group and you get lost. When they try to find your parents, what will they announce? Whom does this child belong to? In other words, who has ownership over this child? You understand? And because your parents have ownership, which means they love you and consider you valuable, at least until you become a teenager, they take care of you, they are concerned for you, and they set you straight, meaning they correct you when you go wrong. These are all elements of *Tarbiyah*, and therefore that qualifies them for the word *Rabb*.

So Allah is *Rabb al-Naas*. He is the owner of mankind. Why? Because He loves them and He considers them valuable. And because of that, He takes care of them. He is always concerned about them. And He tries to set them straight when they stray.

Now what is مَلِک? The word مَلِک means king. A king is someone who has authority over you. Is it possible for someone to be an owner but not have complete authority? Certainly. I own a car, but I do not have complete authority over it. I cannot drive it on the sidewalk, or drive through when the light is red. Even though I own it, I do not have complete authority over it. But Allah is not just *Rabb*. He is not just the owner. He is also *Malik*. He has complete authority over His property. He can do whatever He wants, whenever He wants to.

So while *Rabb* is the ownership of Allah, مَلِک goes a step further to describe the authority of Allah. So what was missing in *Rabb* is captured in مَلِک. And in the final one, the combination of both is used. The only one who can have both, ownership and authority, both at the same time, is *Ilah*. So the third one is almost a result of the previous two. This is called عطف بیان in Arabic, which means explaining the first two with the third. Because Allah is رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ and because He is مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ, both at the same time. The natural conclusion of those two realities is what? That He is إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ. Because *Ilah* is the only one who can be رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ and مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ at the same time. And that is Allah AWJ.

So there is a psychological progression when it comes to *Naas*, or people. We humans, for our needs, first turn to our *Rabb*. They can be teachers, parents, uncles, aunts, grandparents, bosses. But then, when we have a need that the *Rabb* cannot fulfill, we turn to the *Malik*, someone in authority, like a city or state official, or the king or president of a country. And when they too cannot fulfill our needs, we finally turn to the *Ilaah*, who can take care of all our needs. So there is this psychological progression.

but there is also a literary progression that unfolds in the names used for Allah. It begins with the one who has ownership, رب الناس. It advances to the one with ultimate authority, مَلِکِ الناس. And then it concludes in the sum of those two attributes, which is الہ الناس, the god or deity of people. What does this mean? Why is He *Ilaah al-Naas*? Because He is *Rabb al-Naas* and *Malik al-Naas*. We will look at the word *Ilaah* in much detail later on, God willing.

## From General to Specific

Now I want to show you something truly remarkable. Consider this from a literary point of view. If we analyze these first three verses, or rather the names of Allah mentioned in them, رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ, we will see that they move from more to less, from the general to the specific. What does that mean? Let us take a look.

Let us begin with the word *Rabb*, رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ. Who is the *Rabb* again? The one who has ownership, who loves and values that which he owns. He cares for it. He is concerned about it. And he sets it straight. Now, based on that definition, how many people in your life could be called *Rabb*? Is it not so? Your parents, your grandparents, your uncles, your aunts, your siblings, your friends, your teachers, your bosses, your doctor. They all could be labeled *Rabb*, could they not? Because they have some ownership over you, they care for you, they are concerned for you, and they set you straight. So you can have many أرباب, which is the plural of *Rabb*, correct?

But for any society or any country, how many kings can there be? How many ultimate sovereigns can you have for one country? Only one. In any society you can have multiple ارباب in the worldly sense, but you will only have one king, one president. Right? But then, if you take the entire world into consideration, if you take all the countries in the world, do they each have a king or a president or a sovereign body? They do. So even though you will only have one king, one sovereign body, for one country or one society, overall, as a whole, there can be multiple kings. Yes?

But as you go further and you reach the name *Ilaah*, how many *Ilaah* can you have across the board? You can have only one *Ilaah*. The word *Ilaah* can never be taken in a worldly sense. *Rabb* you can take in a worldly sense. You can say رب البیت, the owner of the house, or رب الولد, the owner of a child. You can also take مَلِک in a worldly sense. For example, the king of Saudi Arabia, Malik Salman ibn Saud. So *Rabb* and *Malik* can both have worldly implications, but the word *Ilaah* can only have one implication, and that is Allah, Almighty and Majestic. أَنَّمَآ إِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌۭ وَحِدٌۭ. There is no doubt, your deity, your god, can only be one.

So when we look at the three words used for Allah, *Rabb*, *Malik*, and *Ilaah*, we see there is a progression from more to less, from the general to the specific, until it comes down to the one and only Allah.

But now, when you observe the word *Naas*, which means people in general, or mankind, it is in fact a progression from less to more. Think about this. When someone takes care of others in the worldly sense, they can only take care of a few. Your parents, how many children can they take care of all at once? A few. Once the number goes beyond three, the older siblings have to pitch in to take care of the younger ones. But the parents themselves can only take care of a few.

How many students can a teacher do justice to at one time? Only a few. How many patients can a physician keep under care? A few. If there are too many, a Rabb cannot manage. Is that correct?

But what about a king? What about a مَلِک? Does he take care of more than a few? He does. He has an entire kingdom to look after. He has many more people beneath him. So the number of people a king must protect and provide for is far greater than what a parent, a teacher, a Rabb must care for. Yes?

Now what about an Ilah? How many people does Allah take care of? The whole of creation! SubhanAllah!

So you see the words used for Allah — Rabb, Malik, and Ilah — they carry an implication that moves from more to less. But at the same time, the implications of the word Naas, as in رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ, move from less to more. SubhanAllah! That is why the word ٱلنَّاسِ each time carries a slightly different meaning. The repetition there is not merely for beauty or rhyme. It actually has a different implication each time, both from the standpoint of the one giving protection and the one seeking it. رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ can be many people — parents, teachers, company owners — each of them caring for and protecting a small group. مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ, on the other hand, is a much smaller group protecting a much larger group. And then the most comprehensive one is إِلَهِ ٱلنَّاسِ, a single deity caring for the entire universe. So there is this astonishing progression in eloquence within these verses.

Now, what was the surah we studied before this one? Surah al-Falaq. Do you remember seeing a similar pattern in the previous surah? What did we see in Surah al-Falaq? In that surah, the evils mentioned progressed from the generic to the specific. مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ — from all the evil that was created. Very general. وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ — from the evil of the dark night. It is no longer everything; only the evil of the night. وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ — from those who blow on knots. A specific group performing magic within the darkness of night. وَمِن شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ إِذَا حَسَدَ — from the envious who acts upon his envy. Down to a single entity: the envious one.

SubhanAllah. In Surah al-Falaq, which is primarily a Musta'az minhu — focused on protection FROM evils — the mention of evil moves from generic to specific. And Surah al-Naas, being primarily Musta'az bihi — focused on the protection OF Allah, the call to Allah — moves from generic to specific. SubhanAllah! And this is spoken text. How do you do this with spoken text?

Do you see how perfect and precise the text of these surahs is? Can we as human beings speak like this? Can we, at a moment's notice, say: All right, magic has been performed on Rasul Allah, so let me put together two surahs containing eleven verses, because there are eleven knots on the device used to work magic against him. In the first, I will seek protection FROM evil, keeping the ratio of three to one in protection from evil versus the call to Allah. In the next, since it is protection OF Allah, I will maintain the ratio of three to one between calling upon Allah three times and mentioning evil once. In al-Falaq, being a surah of protection FROM evil, I will move the mention of protection from evil from general evil to the specific evil of envy. In Surah al-Naas, being a surah of protection OF Allah,

I will transition the names of Allah from the generic Rabb specifically to Ilah. I will keep al-Falaq entirely about the protection of the body, and I will make Surah al-Naas entirely about the protection of the soul. I will begin Surah al-Falaq with the mention of the name Falaq, which means to rip and tear through the darkness of night to bring forth the day. So why should I not make sure that I mention darkness in all the remaining verses, so that they tie in perfectly with the word Falaq? Let Me use the word as glad tidings of relief for the victim, and at the same time use that very same word as a warning to the criminals. And since I am naming the next surah al-Naas, which means people, let Me bind everything I say after it to mankind. And I will do all of this on the spot, without any hesitation, without any editorial process or revision. Praise be to Allah! If this is not a miracle, then I do not know what is. If this does not bring me to my knees, if it does not leave me incapable of a response, then I do not know what else can.

And we have not even looked at Surah al-Naas yet. There is still a treasure of miracles yet to be seen in this surah, and then there is the relationship of these surahs with al-Fateha. It is simply incredible.

Consider the psychological progression from Rabb to Malik to Ilah, from owner to king to God. An owner is someone who loves his property and considers it valuable, and as a result he cares about it, is always concerned about it, and always sets it right. The king has authority, so what the word Rabb left out is captured in Malik. Allah is not only the owner; He also has complete authority. And then both of these words together lead to the natural conclusion that He is Ilah. He is the creator, the controller, and the sustainer of everything.

And because the words Rabb and Malik can be used in a worldly sense, Allah presides over all these terms and establishes His dominance over them. He declares that even though there are people to whom I have granted ownership over you, I am the ultimate Rabb. Even though there are people to whom I have given temporary authority over you, I am the ultimate Malik. And then I am Ilah, and no one has any partnership with Me in that respect.

Then the scholars point out something very interesting. As we saw, the word Rabb is associated purely with love, and the word Malik is associated purely with authority. And this surah begins with the word Rabb: قل أعوذ برب الناس. It begins with love, and then it proceeds to authority. So the first relationship Allah has with His creation is based on love. When does the need for authority come into play? When love is not being appreciated. When love is not being recognized. When we, as ungrateful human beings, begin to take love for granted, that is when authority is brought into action. This is exactly like parents with their children. No parent wants to start with authority. Every parent wants to start with love. All parents want love to be the emotion that they wish the child to accept. But then, when that does not happen, they are forced to switch to authority. We see this same principle in this surah, where Allah begins with Rabb. He begins with love, but then, when that is not enough, He has to resort to authority. And then He finally uses His ultimate identity, which is Ilah, which is also a very beautiful word. God willing, we will study this word soon, when we study the word Allah.

With the combination of the words Rabb and Malik, He wants us to appreciate this word Ilah. I will come back to this, God willing, when we study the word Allah. In any case, Allah wants us to accept Him as Rabb first. He wants us to recognize His love first. When we fail to do that, He moves on to His authority. And together these establish His ultimate identity of Ilah.

Then the word Naas is used with all three roles. As we studied, the word Naas comes from Nisyaan, meaning forgetfulness. And this is why, out of all the words, the word Naas is used, because we as human beings tend to forget that Allah is Rabb, that He loves us. We tend to forget that He has authority over us, that He is Malik. And we tend to forget that He is our creator, that He is our Ilah. And that is why Naas is used with all these roles so perfectly.

Then, from another point of view, studying the example of Firon, we saw that his arrogance, which in turn is nothing other than the whisperings of Shaytaan, misled him into believing that he is Rabb, that he is Malik, and that he is Ilah. And the purpose of that story is a warning to us, because in our lives we tend to do the same thing. We forget that we are Naas, and we begin to think of ourselves as Rabb. We forget that we are Naas, and we begin to think of ourselves as Malik. And forgetting that we are Naas, we make our desires and our passions our god, and we begin to worship them. So at the same time, these three verses are a warning and a threat to us, that we should always remember our place, and where we stand in relation to these three words: Rabb, Malik, and Ilah.

Meaning of Naas

We have looked in great detail at the various parts and components of the Istiaaza. We studied Surah al-Falaq and Surah al-Naas. We learned about the Protector, the kind of protection He offers, and the nature of the enemy from whom we seek protection. We also learned what is required of us when we seek that protection. Now, to conclude, I want to tie all of these pieces together. We have seen the parts; now let us look at how they come together to form a complete whole.

So what I want to speak about today, and over the next few sessions, is a passage from Surah Aale Imran that describes the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and the disobedience and rebellion of Iblees. This passage tells of when it all began. If we truly understand the purpose and the teaching of this passage, it will answer most of our questions, if not all of them, about what Shaytan is trying to do, what his ultimate aim is, and what we need to be aware of.

I believe I have said this before, but I will say it again: the purpose of the Qur'anic stories is never the story itself. We listen to bedtime stories like Aladdin and Cinderella, and all these "once upon a time" tales. And then we listen to the Qur'anic stories, and sometimes we begin to think of them in the same way. Just as Cinderella is a pleasant bedtime story for children, the story of Adam and Hawwa also becomes, in our minds, merely a pleasant story. So the first thing is that we need to change how we perceive these stories. And the first step toward that goal is to understand that the purpose of these Qur'anic stories is never the story itself. Through these stories, Allah is always trying to explain a principle from His book of law. He is explaining a divine law. He is giving us a clear warning, and news of how things work within His divine order. There is a framework within which we human beings operate, and there is a framework within which Allah operates, and the Qur'an is our window into that divine order.

So the idea behind these Qur'anic stories is that Allah is saying: Look! This is what happened to the people who came before you. This is how they were confronted with evil. This is how they fought against it, or this is how they gave in to it. This is what they used to say. This is how they used to think. So look where they ended up! Learn from it. Do not repeat the same mistakes they made, or what happened to them will happen to you too. And also study the lives of those who succeeded before you, for if you make the same wise choices that led them to success, you too will become successful.

That is the purpose of these Qur'anic stories: to give us working examples and to set precedents for us, because, as they say, history repeats itself.

And the Messenger of Allah stated this in a hadith:

لَتَتَّبِعُنَّ سَنَنَ مَنْ قَبْلَكُمْ شِبْرًا بِشِبْرٍ، وَذِرَاعًا بِذِرَاعٍ، حَتَّى لَوْ سَلَكُوا جُحْرَ ضَبٍّ لَسَلَكْتُمُوهُ

You shall follow the ways of those before you, inch by inch and mile by mile, to the degree that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would follow them into it too.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Today we all face the very same challenges that were faced by the prophets and the people of their times before us. Its form may be different, its outward appearance may be different, even its intensity may be different, but the principles are still the same. It is still rooted in the same fundamental evils: greed, arrogance, jealousy, passions, and desires.

Nothing has changed. And the Qur'an presents the solution to all of those problems. So if we truly wish to understand the workings and the true machinations of Shaytan, the only way to do so is an in-depth study of the story of Adam AS and Iblees. For this story of Adam AS is in fact our story. The challenges of Adam AS are in fact our challenges. He is the original template. What happened to him is what is happening to us.

Story of Adam and Iblees

So the story of Adam AS and Iblees is the story of humility and arrogance. And this story has three parts. The first part is the creation of Adam and the rebellion of Iblees. We will look at that first. The second part is the humiliation of Iblees and his revenge against Adam AS, in getting him and his wife Hawwa cast out of Jannah. And the third part is the response of Adam and Hawwa AS, set against the reaction of Iblees, once they are cast out of Jannah.

So let us begin with the first part, which speaks of the creation of Adam AS. Allah says in the Qur'an: وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَكُمْ ثُمَّ صَوَّرْنَكُمْ — We created you, We fashioned you. In other words, Allah says: I know who you are, and what you love, because I made you. I know how I formed you. I know the things I placed within you. I know every one of your body parts, and I know every single temptation and craving that you have. And then He says: ثُمَّ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ ٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِآدَمَ — and then I commanded all the angels to make sajda to you. I honored you above the angels. I created within you a potential that could raise you above the angels.

Linguistic meaning of SAJDA

Let us understand this word, sajda. It is a beautiful word. The ancient Arabs used the word sajada for a camel when it would lower itself before its rider, so that he could mount it. It was used in that sense. سجد الأبل, they would say, when the camel would lower itself and submit its will to the will of its rider — meaning that the camel would allow its rider to steer it in whatever direction he wished.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Clay, because of its humility, can be molded; it can be shaped into whatever form the maker desires, because it is humble. It submits itself to the hands of the potter, who shapes it in whatever way he thinks best. Clay is obedient; it performs sajda, because it submits itself to the will of its master, allowing Him to shape it however He desires. Fire cannot be molded. It cannot be shaped, because it is disobedient; it is arrogant. That is why clay is better than fire. We human beings were created from clay, which is meant to be humble. Evil, or sharr, which I told you comes from the word sharara, a burning flame, has arrogance for its nature.

Now, is fire bright and luminous and attractive? Of course; that is why there is so much allure in evil. That is why we are drawn toward evil, because of its bright, dancing, naked flames. It seduces us; it entices; it mesmerizes us; it draws us toward it. But once we come close, what does fire do? It engulfs us, burns us, destroys us. What happens to the most beautiful thing when it is burned? It becomes all black and charred and disfigured and distorted. That is what evil ends up doing to us. But in the beginning, is it attractive? Is it enticing? Absolutely. Partying all the time, drinking, smoking, watching filthy movies on the internet. Is there attraction in all of these things? Certainly. Are their rewards immediate? Do you get to have a good time right now? Certainly. But where does it lead? Where does that path end? Look at what alcohol eventually leads to. The person ends up an alcoholic. He began drinking because it looked cool. But that same person, when engulfed and eaten and burned by it, ends up an alcoholic. What does the so-called cool habit of smoking eventually lead to? Cancer. Heart attack. Stroke. Where does this shamelessness and internet filth lead? Broken marriages, where the only kind of relationship a man is capable of having with his wife is what a monkey has with a female monkey. Honestly, examine any thing that is forbidden in Islam. You will find two qualities in it. It will appear very attractive, and it will always end in destruction.

They all lead to a single final destination: destruction. For that is what it is. Fire. And however attractive, however brilliant, however beautiful fire may appear, it burns. It incinerates. It always ends in pain and horror.

Now, set against that, consider what soil does. Consider the work of a farmer. How appealing does farming or gardening seem? Not very. It seems rather dull, rather tedious, does it not? The farmer keeps investing his time and his effort, day after day, month after month, and sees nothing. After months, he sees something tiny sprout out of the dirt. The progress is exceedingly slow. Yet when the time comes to harvest, what sort of yield does that soil produce? Tons of it. The fruits that come of that slow, dull, hard labor must be weighed in tons. And what is the weight of those fruits compared with the weight of the seeds that were first sown in the soil? There is no comparison. The reward the farmer reaps at the end bears no comparison to the trivial value of the seeds he sowed at the start. Is that not true?
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Now, do the rules of Islam seem dull, exactly as soil seems dull? Certainly, because Islam is precisely that: soil. And we are farmers planting the seeds of our belief in that soil. It is not the most attractive profession in the world. But when we sow the seeds of our belief and our faith into it, and water it with the knowledge given to us by our elders, our daat, and farm them and cultivate them by striving day in and day out with our taharah, namaaz, fasts, zakaat, and hajj, what does that dull soil give us back? Beautiful, lush, fruit-bearing trees. Rewards that cannot even be compared to the initial investment. Is it a long, tedious, repetitive process? Certainly. But look at the quantity and the quality of the reward at the end.

The exterior of fire is beautiful, but its interior is destruction and death. The exterior of evil is beautiful; it is attractive; it is enticing; it is mesmerizing. But it will always result in pain, in suffering, and in destruction, in this life and in the life to come. The exterior of clay is dull, but its interior is growth and life. The exterior of Islam, the exterior of Shariah, may seem dull; it may seem inconvenient, demanding. But once we submit to it willingly, in obedience, its end result is immense growth. Its end result is life, the ultimate success in this life and in the life to come.

Fire brings death and destruction. Clay produces eternal life.

And that is what Iblees chose. He chose the outward attraction. He preferred the outward and immediate brilliance of fire to the inner essence of clay.

And this is the lesson we must learn from this story. We must learn from this terrible mistake of Iblees. He chose the outward form over the inner essence. This duniya is fire. Listen to this very carefully. This duniya, this world in which we live, is fire for the one who wants immediate rewards. If you wish to do what people call enjoying your life, go right ahead. You will have your immediate rewards; of that there is no doubt. And it will feel wonderfully good as well. So if you are craving to commit those forbidden things, then go ahead. But know this: that it will end in death and destruction, in this life and in the life to come. For this duniya is fire for the one who wants immediate rewards.

And this same duniya is clay for the one who is willing to defer his enjoyment.

his enjoyment for a reward incomparably greater. This duniya is both fire and clay, and now the choice belongs to you and to me: what we will choose for ourselves. Iblis preferred the fire, and we know where that led him. Adam chose the clay, and we know where that led him as well. Both paths lie open before us.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en: This is why, in using the Istiaaza, we declare our humility before Allah by seeking His protection and entering into it. Protection from what? From the fire of Sharr, from the allurements of evil. For we come to understand that although the path of Shaytan is attractive, brilliant, bright, and mesmerizing, it ends only in destruction and terrible pain, the pain of heat, the pain of burning. But once we submit to the protection of Islam and restrain ourselves within the bounds of Shariah, we sow ourselves, willingly and in obedience, into the soil of Rabb al-Falaq, Rabb al-Naas, Malik al-Naas, Ilah al-Naas. Then the end is magnificent: it is growth, it is beauty. The end is the delicious, life-giving fruits of the hereafter.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
So that is what sajda means in the truest sense of the word: to pay respect, or honor, by lowering oneself before a greater being. Just as the camel honors and glorifies its rider by submitting before him. And that takes extreme humility. For if you compare a camel to a human being from a physical standpoint, there truly is no comparison. A camel is massive compared to a human being. The strength of a camel is enormous compared to that of a human being. A camel can go for days in the extreme heat of the desert without water, while a human would die of thirst. A camel can lift loads that would be far beyond the capacity of even the strongest human being. And yet this extremely powerful, extremely capable, this mighty creature lowers itself before a human being. It submits its will to a human being, because it understands that it cannot find its path without its master.

When we fall in sajda before Allah, it is a gesture of surrendering ourselves, surrendering our will, of becoming humble before the will of our master. Because, like the camel, we too sometimes think we are superior. Our ego is our camel. Why do I need Allah in my life? I have money. I have power. I have status. Why do I need to submit to anyone? I am in control of my life. A camel could hold the same attitude toward man, but then it would die of thirst, would it not? Because no matter how powerful and capable the camel thinks it is.

It still needs a human being to guide it to water in the desert. That is why the camel submits itself to its owner. That is the camel's sajda.

In the same way, my true sajda to Allah would be to surrender the reins of my life, my will, my decisions, into the hands of my master. To let not my own will but the will of my master steer me through life. To let Him walk me through beautiful pastures of ease, if He so desires, and to walk me through the dry, barren, scorching lands of trials and hardships, if He so desires. That is the true meaning of the word sajda. To give up oneself, to surrender one's will to the will of our master, the way the camel gives itself up in the hands of its rider, the way the ship gives itself up in the hands of the wind. السَّفِینَۃُ تَسجُدُ لِلرِّیحِ, the Arabs would say.

Another beautiful meaning of the word sajda is to bend and lower oneself under the weight of the bounties that are placed upon it. For example, the Arabs would say سَجَدَتْ النَّخْلَۃ, the palm tree bent down under the abundance of its fruit. The weight of Allah's blessings in our lives should force us to fall in sajda before Him.

So this is what sajda is, and especially during salaah. Look, putting our forehead on the ground is only a symbol. The true sajda is that of the heart. It is not a sajda if, after my salaah ends, I am still going to do what I want.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
And consider even the physical act of sajda. What are we doing? We place our forehead on the ground, the head being the most superior part of the body, because it contains the intellect, through which we plan and design and scheme. We place that intellect on the earth, on the dirt that lies beneath our feet. It is a symbol of surrendering our thoughts, our knowledge of what we think is best, our plans, our schemes, before our master. It is a symbol of testifying that, O Allah, even though You have blessed me with this amazing intellect, the greatest gift of all, my plans, my desires, my thoughts are nothing more than dirt before Your will. That is the true level of obedience that is captured in this symbolic act of sajda. And therefore the perfect symbol of obedience, the perfect representation of obedience to Allah, is sajda.

So Allah commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, to honor him, to respect him, first and foremost in compliance with Allah's command, because Allah commanded them to honor him. But then also as an acknowledgment that Adam had knowledge of that which they did not. وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ ٱلْأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ فَقَالَ أَنۢبِـُٔونِى بِأَسْمَآءِ هَٓؤُلَآءِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَدِقِينَ. Allah taught Adam all the names, then presented him before the angels, and asked the angels, Tell me all these names if you are truthful in your claims. First Allah established the superiority of Adam, peace be upon him, over the angels, by knowledge that they did not have. Then He asked the angels to prostrate to him. So the sajda of the angels was for two reasons: first, in obedience to Allah's command, and second, in recognition of Adam's superiority in knowledge over them. فَسَجَدُوٓا۟, they all fell in sajda, إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ, with the exception of Iblees, لَمْ يَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّجِدِينَ, he was not going to be from among those who would prostrate. Instead of saying مَا سَجَدَہُ, he did not comply, Allah says لَمْ يَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّجِدِينَ.

He was never, ever going to be among those who would prostrate. Subhan Allah. Allah knew all along that he would not do it. Allah knew his intentions from the very beginning. And it is worth pausing on why Allah still commanded Iblees to prostrate, knowing full well that he would disobey. But I will turn to that a little later.

So Allah questions Iblees. قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ إِذْ أَمَرْتُكَ. Allah said: what could possibly have prevented you from prostrating when I told you to? When I commanded you! Why did you not obey?

Notice this carefully. Allah did not say: why did you not prostrate when you plainly saw that Adam is more knowledgeable than you? Why did you not comply with My command once it made sense to you? Look at what Allah says. This is the part that you and I must attend to very closely. قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ إِذْ أَمَرْتُكَ. Why did you not prostrate when I commanded you to?
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Prostration must be done in obedience to the command. We sometimes think: I will pray once I understand that it is important, once I understand its purpose. In other words, once I have more knowledge about it. Is that not so? That is not what Allah questions Iblees about. Allah gives preference to His command over everything else. There is nothing wrong with learning why we should pray. In fact, we must learn it. But the reason for prostration, the only reason for prostration, must be that Allah commanded us to do so. Obedience is the first and foremost reason for prostration. Why? Because the very word prostration means that we have already accepted Allah as our master. We have lowered ourselves before Allah so that His commands may ride us, so that His command may steer us in whatever direction He pleases.

That is why, when someone asked Imam Jaffar as-Saadiq, peace be upon him, یا امام ! ھل الدین ؟؟, O Imam, what is religion? He replied, الا الطاعۃ, nothing except obedience. A camel's guidance begins when it prostrates before its rider. Our guidance begins when we prostrate before Allah.

Fire versus Clay

So Allah asks Iblees: what could possibly have prevented you from obeying when I commanded you? Now listen to what he says. And this is the true subject of today's conversation. Everything else hinges upon it. Iblees says: أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهُ ۖ خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ. Iblees at last gives voice to his arrogance and says: I am better than him. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.

Within this single statement lies the root cause of disobedience. As a matter of language, what Iblees said is what is called a statement of arrogance. بیان الاستکبار. The tone of this statement makes it plain that Iblees had already made up his mind. Had he not used this tone, the statement could have been open to debate. It could have been argued that perhaps Iblees did not understand, perhaps he had doubts and was trying to resolve them with Allah. But that is not what his tone suggests. Look at his words within their context. To whom is he speaking? He is speaking to Allah. He is speaking to the King of kings. He is speaking to his Creator. And he says: I am better than him. It is a wholly definitive statement. It is a wholly obstinate statement. There is no room for argument or discussion in it. In other words, there is absolutely no humility in his tone. It carries the sense of: this is how it is, and this is how it is going to be.

There is nothing wrong with asking questions when we do not understand. There is nothing wrong at all with questioning things, with seeking answers. The one thing to keep in mind is never to let go of humility in that line of questioning. For the manner in which a question is put reveals everything about the feeling beneath it. One can tell at once whether the person is filled with arrogance or whether there is humility in him.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Humility in a question means weighing other possibilities: that perhaps it is I who does not understand; that perhaps I am missing something; that perhaps this person knows something I do not; that perhaps I might learn something from his experience; that perhaps my parents do in fact know what they are speaking about. Arrogance, on the other hand, says: this is how I see things, this is what I believe, here are the facts, and I do not care what you think. I will not even try to understand what you have to say, because you plainly do not know what you are talking about. It is my way or nothing at all.

That is the tone Iblees uses. I am better than him — and that is the end of it. You created me from fire, and you created him from clay; fire is better than clay. These are simply facts. It is mere observation. It is basic science. And so, O Allah, I do not know what You had in mind when You commanded me to bow down to him. I do not think You know what You are doing. You clearly do not understand the difference between fire and clay. You are asking me to bow down to him? Are You serious?

All of this arrogance is voiced in this one statement: أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهُ.

Now, does it not all seem absurd when we look at it from the outside? What a dreadful thing to do. Wicked Iblees, wicked Iblees, is that not so? But now place the commands and wishes of your parents in the position of Allah, for Allah is Rabb, and so too are your parents. Allah is Rabb, and so too are our religious elders. We studied precisely this in Surah Naas. This passage is about the relationship of a creation with his Rabb. For what did Shaytan say? خَلَقْتَنِى — You created me. And to create is to own, and the Arabic word for that is Rabb. Allah has granted a share of His Rububiyah to parents over their children. Allah has granted a share of His Rububiyah to teachers over their students. When you, a child, answer back to your parents with arrogance, you place yourself in the very same position as Iblees.

Understand this: there is nothing wrong with holding a dialogue with your parents when you disagree; that is perfectly acceptable. It is arrogance that is not acceptable. It is all right if you cannot see eye to eye with your parents, but it is not all right to think that you are better than they are, that you understand more than they do. You do not, and you cannot. You are children. Most of you have not yet stepped into the real world. They have. So they may well know what they are speaking about. Place some trust in them. For this verse is teaching us the importance of humility in dealing with our Rabb. Parents are the nearest Rabb. If you cannot be humble before them, how do you expect to be humble before Allah?

Another very important lesson it teaches us is that disobedience is not the real problem. What leads to disobedience is the problem. Notice that the corruption in Iblees took place first within his soul. His statement has two parts. Consider the first part: أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهُ.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
I am better than him. That is the corruption of his soul. That is the arrogance in his soul. And then, inevitably, what follows is a justification for his disobedience. خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ. You created me from fire and you created him from clay. So what he did was justify his arrogance with what he thought were logical facts, leaving no room for any kind of dialogue. And it is not as though Allah was closed to dialogue, because we have just seen that Allah asked him: قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ إِذْ أَمَرْتُكَ. What stopped you from prostrating when it was I who commanded you? Did Allah need to ask Iblees for his reasons? Does an owner, especially an owner like Allah, need his property to explain why it is not behaving as it is supposed to? My pen stops writing. Am I going to ask it to present valid reasons for no longer writing? No. I would simply throw it away and move on. So why does Allah ask Iblees for a reason? Because it is a gesture of disappointment. It is the gesture of an intensely loving Lord who is disappointed with his creation. You know that I love you. You know who I am. You know my status. You know that my knowledge encompasses all things. You know that I would never, ever give an unjust command to obey. You know these things about me. I honored you by making you the leader and teacher of all the angels. What possible reason could you have for disobeying me?

Scholars and linguists say that this question, which Allah asked Iblees, carries a tone of humility in and of itself. But what makes it extremely humble is when you consider the context of who is asking whom. The Creator, the Lord, is asking his creation. The King of kings is asking his slave. That makes this statement extremely humble. And it also highlights the relationship of our Creator with his creation. Allah, being the only one worthy of pride, deals with his creation with extreme humility. SubhanAllah!

Now let us play devil's advocate for a moment. Is it possible that Iblees was actually confused? Is it possible that Iblees, in his ignorance, made a mistake because of his observation of the physical properties of fire and clay? Is that possible? It is not. He knew exactly why Allah had commanded him to bow down to Adam. He knew perfectly well that Adam, peace be upon him, was superior to him in knowledge, and there was absolutely no reason for him to disobey. How do we know this? Because of this verse, where Allah speaks about Iblees and says: وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ ٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوٓا۟ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ أَبَىٰ وَٱسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلْكَفِرِينَ. And when I commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, they all did so except Iblees. He refused, became arrogant, and was thus among the disbelievers. So the word disbeliever, Kafir, is used for Iblees in this verse. In another verse Allah says: وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ ٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوٓا۟ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَفَسَقَ عَنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّهِ. And when I commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, they all did so except Iblees. He was one of the jinn, and he transgressed against, or broke, the command of his Lord. So in this verse the word Fasaqa is used.

The Difference Between Kufr and Fisq
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
So let us look at these two words. Kafir comes from the word Kufr, which means to hide something intentionally, to conceal a truth deliberately, to deny a reality while being fully aware of it. That is all Kufr is. If you accidentally hide something, or you deny it because you do not understand,

that is not disbelief. That is forgetfulness. Disbelief is when a person knows something and deliberately covers it up. Do you understand?

But the word for the disbeliever is the intensive form of that word, and it means someone who deliberately and continually hides the truth. It is not a single act. The disbeliever is one who always, without pause, without fail, covers things over. This is why, in Arabic, a farmer is called by this same word. He has the seeds, and he hides them in the ground. He buries them in the earth and covers them over with soil, and he does this for his livelihood. So he does it again and again. The one who covers the truth continually, consistently, and deliberately is called a disbeliever.

The transgressor takes his name from the word فِسْق, which means to break an agreement, to step outside the bounds. On the same pattern as the word for the disbeliever, the transgressor means someone who is always stepping outside the bounds, who deliberately and continually oversteps.

So Iblis is both a disbeliever and a transgressor. He knew that Allah was his creator. He knew that Allah was his Lord. He understood that he was owned property and that Allah was his owner. He knew the reality that Adam, upon him be peace, was superior to him. Still he deliberately refused to accept that superiority. He knew his limits when it came to obeying Allah's commands. He knew his own place before the glorious station of Allah. Yet he deliberately overstepped.

He did both of these things. He rejected the truth, and he broke through his bounds — both in one single act. His disobedience.

So the problem was not that Iblis did not believe in Allah as his creator. An atheist does not believe that Allah exists, but Iblis did. His belief is plain in his own words. He said:

خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ

You created me! He does not merely believe in Allah; he acknowledges Allah as his creator. He is speaking to Allah, and he is accepting Allah as his creator. His disbelief — listen to this very carefully — his disbelief is not in saying, "I do not believe Allah exists." His disbelief lies in his disobedience. I will say it three times.

His disbelief is his disobedience. His disbelief is his disobedience. His disbelief is his disobedience.

Why am I saying it three times? Because you and I also believe in Allah as our creator, yet we still disobey Him all the time. And we say, it is not so bad. At least I still believe in Allah. It is not as though I am a disbeliever. I know I do some very wrong things. I know. But it is not as though I deny the faith.

The disbelief of Iblis was his disobedience.
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Iblis does not need to make you and me deny Allah. All he needs to do is get us to disobey. That is all he needs. That is all he is trying to do. You and I truly need to understand this. Because at the end of the day, after disobeying Allah, all we say is, well, at least I believe in Allah, and that ought to be enough for me. But guess what? Iblis believed in Allah too. He did exactly that. This is why I repeated it three times. The disbelief of Iblis, the disbelief of Iblis, was his disobedience. Because through his disobedience he deliberately rejected and covered up the truth.

And through his disobedience he became a transgressor. He overstepped his bounds, and he broke his agreement with Allah. Have we made an agreement with Allah? Something called the noble covenant. A promise we made with Allah: to pray five times a day, to fast, to give the alms, to do good, to keep away from evil. Did we make that agreement with Allah?

Iblees broke his agreement with Allah through his disobedience. What are we doing? And the root cause of it all was arrogance. Once our ego gives birth to arrogance, disobedience will follow, naturally and inevitably. That is why both prayers of refuge, Falaq and Naas, begin with the same word. Qul! Declare! Declare your submission. And, as we learned, our declaration of our own need removes arrogance from our hearts. It humbles the heart, because that is precisely what we learned Shaytan attacks. الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس. He attacks the chest of mankind, and what does the chest contain? The heart. Through his whispers he instills arrogance and pride within our hearts.

So what got Shaytan into trouble was not his disbelief in Allah, but his arrogance. His pride. What got him into trouble was his thinking that he is better than Adam, peace be upon him. What got him into trouble was his thinking that he knows more than Allah, for Allah, obviously, does not know that fire is better than clay, is that not so? Astaghfirullah! His arrogance is what got him thrown out of jannah. But the greatest, and, sadly, the most common sickness of our time, is arrogance. That is why you will notice that all religious activities are designed around humility. They are all exercises in humility. That is why, when we pray, what do we constantly say? Allahu Akbar. Allahu Akbar. Allahu Akbar. Allah is greater. Allah is greater. Allah is greater. Which means: I am not. I am not. I am not. And Allah says that when you disobey Me, you are saying that you are greater. You think that you are greater. That is disobedience.

Attributes of clay and fire
body.topic_title_en: He created me from fire and him from clay
body.topic_title_ur: Allah created me from fire and him from clay

body.text_en:
Now the scholars have presented another beautiful dimension of how flawed Iblees was in his logic that fire is superior to clay. So let us now look at the statement in a different light. Iblees said, خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ. Let us first understand the meaning of the word Teen. Teen means damp mud, or damp dirt. It is commonly translated as clay, which is basically damp dirt, or damp soil, if you will. In Urdu it would be translated as گیلی مٹی, or گارا. Now there is another word in Arabic, Turaab, which means dry dirt, or dry mud. You add a little water to Turaab and it becomes Teen. And, incidentally, this word Turaab is also used in the Qur'an. On the Day of Judgment, وَيَقُولُ ٱلْكَافِرُ يَلَيْتَنِى كُنتُ تُرَبًۢا, the kafir will say on the Day of Judgment: I wish I were dry mud today. We will look at this ayah in one of the future sessions, InshaAllah.

So the first thing I want us to understand is that Teen and Turaab are both the same thing. They are both dirt, or soil. Turaab is dry soil and Teen is damp soil. All right? But we will simply call it clay. All right?

The argument Iblees made was based on a comparison of the external attributes of the substance each was made from: fire and clay. We spoke about this earlier in some detail. He said that fire is brighter, it is hotter, its flame rises. Clay, on the other hand, is dull, it is cold, and it falls to the ground. Therefore I am better than him. But what he intentionally chose to reject, what he intentionally chose to ignore and cover up, was that Allah did not ask the angels to prostrate before Adam until He had blown His spirit into him. And the soul is always greater than the body. Spirituality is always superior to physicality. This is what we spoke about the last time. But now, if we look at it even from a physical standpoint,

Allah was completely just in commanding fire to bow down before clay. For even if the outward attributes of fire may seem superior to those of clay, the inner attributes and the inner qualities of clay are far superior to those of fire. The greatest reason is that clay is humble. It submits itself to the farmer who sows seeds within it. And because of its humility toward the farmer, the soil permits growth within itself.
