So the question is: what is a tribulation? What is its purpose? And what should our response be in the face of a trial or tribulation? One of the reasons we are disquieted by these tribulations is that we do not understand the wisdom behind them. That is one of the real problems.

So when Allah gives us trials and places us in trying circumstances or situations, the difference between the one who believes in Allah and the one who does not is that the believer will draw benefit from it. Consider this: if you do not believe in a god, then you will live a life that is godless. If you do believe in a god, you will live in a world filled with god. For a believer, Allah is everywhere. Everything is a sign pointing to Allah. So whether you believe in god or not, you will be constantly confirmed in what you already believe. A believer will be constantly confirmed in his belief, and a disbeliever will be constantly confirmed in his disbelief. That is why we see that the atheist cannot understand people who believe in god, and people who believe in god cannot understand the atheist. Both of them are seeing proof of what they hold. They truly are.

أَنَا عِنْدَ ظَنِّ عَبْدِي بِي فالیَظُنَّ بِمَا شَآء

I am in the opinion of my slave. So if my slave thinks I am nothing, that is what he finds. Allah is in the understanding of the believer. If you believe Allah is with you, then Allah is with you. If you do not believe in Him, then He is not with you. That is why despair is forbidden in every Abrahamic tradition. And in Catholicism, despair, to despair of the mercy of god, is an unpardonable sin. It is the one sin that they believe will never be forgiven. And we have Iblees, Ablasa: that was his disease. He despaired. And now he wants everyone else to despair.

أَنَا عِنْدَ ظَنِّ عَبْدِي بِي وَأَنَا مَعَهُ إِذَا ذَكَرَنِي فَإِنْ ذَكَرَنِي فِي نَفْسِهِ ذَكَرْتُهُ فِي نَفْسِي وَإِنْ ذَكَرَنِي فِي مَلَإٍ ذَكَرْتُهُ فِي مَلَإٍ خَيْرٍ مِنْهُمْ وَإِنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَيَّ بِشِبْرٍ تَقَرَّبْتُ إِلَيْهِ ذِرَاعًا وَإِنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَيَّ ذِرَاعًا تَقَرَّبْتُ إِلَيْهِ بَاعًا وَإِنْ أَتَانِي يَمْشِي أَتَيْتُهُ هَرْوَلَةً

I am in the opinion of my slave. I am with him when he remembers me. If he remembers me in privacy, I remember him in privacy. And if he remembers me in a crowd, I remember him among a crowd that is better than his crowd. If he moves toward me an inch, I move toward him an arm's length. If he moves toward me an arm's length, I move toward him a yard. If he comes to me walking, I come to him running.

The atheist says: look around you, this is a horrible world; how can you believe in a god? I say to that same atheist: look around you! How can I not believe in a god? So where is the problem? The problem lies in what they call evil. And this is ultimately the basis of every argument against the existence of god. It rests upon what they call the problem of evil.

Christians cannot explain evil, because they say god is all good and god is all powerful. Well then, how do you explain evil in the world? For if he is all good, he would not create evil, and if he is all powerful, he would remove it from the world. This is what they call, in philosophy, the problem of evil.

They see good and evil as separate entities. We do not. We say that Allah created good, and every good carries the possibility of a deviation from that good, which is bad. Freedom of choice creates that departure from good, and thus evil comes into being.

Allah did not create evil; creation created evil. Islamic scholars argue that one should not look at a thing and call it evil, because you do not know.

An Imam is a paragon — a person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality, someone who embodies something. أَمَّا ؛ یَأُمُّ means to move toward a particular goal, and أُمَّۃ is a group of people moving toward the same object. That is what an Umma is: a group of people bound together by the same goal. That is why we are called the Umma of Rasul Allah, because we have the same goal as his, which is to reach Jannah. The word for mother is also related to this same root.

He is معتمد الأنام, the one upon whom all creatures depend. Anaam means all creatures that sleep, but it also means the ins and the jinn.

Hujja is a level, a rank that certain scholars reach, where they become a proof for the existence of the truth of the Imam. The fact that such a person exists is a proof that the Imam exists.

Rutba is a rank. In modern Arabic the word is used in the military: rutab are the ranks that people hold. Here they are ranks in relation to Allah, just as you have them in any military. وما یعلمو جنود ربک الا ھو — And nobody knows the army of Allah except Him. So Allah has junood, an army. We have generals and colonels, and within those there are further ranks: majors, captains, lieutenants, generals, and corporals. Now, people with ranks in the Zahir wear uniforms so that everyone knows what their rank is. In Islam those ranks are hidden. We do not know the stations that people hold with Allah. It is something Allah has concealed.

One of the scholars said that Allah hid three things in three things: أَخفَا اَلثَّلاثَۃ فِی الثَّلاث; أَخَفا اَلرِّضائِہِ فِی طَاعَتِہِ؛ وَأَخفَا سَخَتِہِ فی مَعصِیَتِہِ؛ وَأَخفَا أَولِیَائُہُ فِی عِبَادِہِ — He hid three things in three things.

He hid His contentment in His obedience. In other words, we do not know what Allah will accept from us. Allah might not accept a great thing you did that was an act of obedience, yet He might accept a small act.

He hid His wrath in disobedience. In other words, we do not know which act of disobedience will incur His wrath. We may think of some huge sin we committed that might get us into trouble on the Day of Judgment, but it could be a sin we considered very small that actually incurs His wrath — as with people who are abusive to animals. We may think that is nothing, but for Allah it may be an enormous thing. That is one reason why all the prophets were shepherds: they learned to be gentle with animals, because that is a transitional phase into being gentle with human beings, who stand at the top of that chain. If you are kind to animals, it would certainly seem that you would be kind to humans, because we are the highest on that chain. We are at the top of the hierarchy of beings.

And the final one is that He hid His Awliya among His servants.

So he says that the benefits are based on the differences in the ranks of people. For some people, a tribulation removes wrongs. Scholars say that there are wrongs committed in this world that are removed only by depression. If you are wondering why people become depressed —

People become depressed because of *zunoob* — their sins — because sin sickens the soul. People suffer trouble within the soul. You may numb it. You may keep yourself occupied. You may entertain yourself. You may do all of these things in order to avoid facing the anguish the soul is undergoing, but you cannot remove that anguish. It is not possible. This is why Karl Marx is reported to have said that religion is the opiate of the masses. An Islamic scholar then replied that opium is the religion of the masses. That is precisely what it is: an escape from reality. That is the idol. That is what they are worshipping, and they will do anything for that idol. All they are trying to do is numb the pain of existence. What they do not understand is that existence is painful because you are not fulfilling your function. And when you do not fulfill your function, there is always trouble.

Whenever anything in the body is not fulfilling its function, what is the first sign that tells you to go to a doctor? Pain. There is some sort of disquiet in the body to let you know that the body is not fulfilling its function. So if you suddenly have this pain in your liver, and you go and are told you have hepatitis, that pain was there to let you know that the function has been disrupted. The same is true of the soul. If you are not fulfilling your function, which is to worship Allah, may He be exalted, to testify to His unity, and to behave accordingly, then you will be in pain and suffering until you come into accord with it. And that is a gift from Allah, in the same way that pain, signs, and symptoms are a gift to people so that they may go to a physician and be made well. If there are no signs and symptoms — for example, they say that the worst kind of cancer is the kind in which there are no symptoms. Why? Because by the time the cancer is detected, it is too late.

You see, what *kufr* is, essentially, is a covering up. If you have a headache and you go and take Tylenol, you are not really getting rid of the headache. You are suppressing the symptoms. So if you are sick in your soul because of *kufr*, and you go and do things in order to remove the pain of that *kufr*, you are only covering it up further. And because of this there is الظلمات فوق ظلمات — it is darknesses over, covering, darknesses. You keep covering up more and more and more, until the soul becomes so completely diseased that it becomes a hopeless case, unless Allah intervenes. And that is what happens to people.

Now, when it comes to the Prophets, when they pass through trials and tribulations, the purpose is not to free them of their sins but to raise them in rank. It is not to remove their wrongs. It is رفع الدرجات, the elevation of ranks, to move them upward in degrees. اشدنا ابتلاءُ — they are the ones who are tried the most. Then those closest to them, then those closest to them, then those closest to them. It is like that.

There are non-Muslims in the world, or even Muslims, and you see them in tribulation. You see them in pain and you wonder about them. It is genuinely difficult to assess what is happening to them. This is one of the problems in religion: the rules are different for a Muslim than they are for a non-Muslim.

Entering the domain of Islam gives a Muslim certain advantages and privileges from which non-Muslims are excluded. This resembles any institution in this world. So matters do not become any easier for people of faith. But what happens to those who have reached the rank of the Saliheen? They arrive at a point where they are completely content with the trials and tribulations that Allah has chosen for them. It is no longer painful, because they can now see something that others cannot.

There was a woman, one of the Salihaat, who was walking along when she stumbled on a rock and hurt her foot. She began to laugh. One of the bystanders saw this and thought she had lost her mind. He asked her, "Are you insane? ھل انت مجنونۃ" She replied, "No! I fell and was hurt. But when the pain came, I remembered the saying of my Prophet: a believer does not even get a thorn in his foot except to remove his wrongs. And the sweetness of my wrongs being removed overwhelmed my pain." Now that is faith. That is emaan. Those were her spiritual endorphins kicking in.

Trust me, there are spiritual endorphins. Everything we see in the physical realm is only a symbol. It is a symbol for the spiritual realities. So imagine that you are wearing gloves on your hands. Imagine that your hand is in fact the soul and the glove is the body, because in reality that is what it is. The soul has put on the body like a glove. Now, when you see the glove moving, you know that it is really the fingers inside the glove that are moving. The glove is only a symbol, and so is the movement of the glove. It symbolizes that there are in fact fingers behind it doing the moving. So what we see in the seen, physical world is only a metaphor for the unseen, spiritual world. In this world we have opium that can put out our physical pain. There is also such a thing as spiritual opium. Belief in Allah can provide us with that spiritual opium.

When Maulana Ali was struck by an arrow that pierced his shin, they tried to remove it, and he found it extremely painful. So he asked that the arrow be removed while he was in the state of prayer, while he was in the state of Sajda. That is what they did, and he did not even flinch. After he had finished the prayer, he asked for the arrow to be removed and discovered that it had already been taken out.

Do you think these are merely stories? Things that people simply made up, like fairy tales and the like? Seriously! These are not invented tales. These are things that people witnessed with their own eyes. And if you think about it, it is not such an impossible thing either. Today we have drugs like fentanyl. Once you take that drug, they can break your leg in seventy places and you will not feel a thing. You will not care. You will be in complete bliss, and all of it from a drug. That is nothing more than a chemical reaction happening in the brain. That is all it is. So do not think that such things are only stories. People do enter those states of devotion with Allah.

Where the entire physical world around them ceases to exist. So he says: أَحَدُھَا مُعرِفَتُ عِزِّ الرُّبُوبِیَّۃِ وَ قَھرِھا. The first benefit is that you come to recognize the power of His lordship over you. You realize that Allah is Rabb, that He is the owner, and that you are marboob, that you are His property. The nature of lordship is that lordship lords over you. This is why, when tribulations come to you, the Qur'an says: ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَصَبَتْهُم مُّصِيبَةٌۭ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَجِعُونَ

These trials and tribulations are meant to remind us that there are things beyond our control. There are certain things you can control within your environment. When I am thirsty I can drink water. When I am hungry I can eat food. When I need to pick something up I can use my hands. When I need to go somewhere I can use my legs. Allah has given me all of that. He has blessed me with all of these capabilities and gifts. But He can take them away from me any time He wishes. He is علی کل شئی قدیر. He has given me the ability to breathe normally, but He has the power to put me on a ventilator whenever He wills. It is when things like these happen that the believer actually sees reality. For this life we are living is an illusion. The illusion is that I am free, that I am independent, that I can do whatever I want, that I am the king of my domain, that I am at liberty to do anything I please. All of this is a delusion. We have six billion people walking on the face of this earth inside that delusion. But then a calamity comes, and suddenly the delusion is stripped away.

In my first job here in the United States there was an older gentleman. I still remember his name. His name was Jim Cramaldi. He was a staunch atheist, and he used to make fun of me and my beliefs constantly. He would joke about God and about the existence of God. He used to say that human beings are the architects of their own destiny, that we humans are in control, and that the existence of God is nothing more than a delusion. Then one day he found out that he had cancer. Throat cancer. He began going for chemotherapy and radiation and whatever else. Finally the doctors told him that they could not treat his cancer any longer and that he had only a few months left to live. I remember I was sitting in my cubicle when he came to me one day and said, "Will you please pray for me?" I was shocked. I honestly did not know how to respond. So I asked him about the fact that he did not believe in God, since he was an atheist. He said that he had realized he was not in control. He had gone to every doctor and tried every medicine, but there was nothing anyone could do to help him. Now he was willing to take the chance that he might have been wrong, and that if there really is a God, he was in deep trouble. I could see the desperation and the pain in his eyes. And he asked me, "Do you think your Allah will forgive me?" I told him that my Allah says He will forgive every believer. "So are you a believer?" He said yes. So I said, then He will forgive you. But it was so striking that this man, a staunch disbeliever,

A man who mocked God and made light of Him. When this calamity fell upon him, and there was no one else who could help him, he too had to turn to God in the end. The illusion that he was the one in control had been shattered. For some people, that is what it takes. That is what it takes for them to learn that lesson.

So the first benefit is to learn that Allah is Lord, and that He is قاھر فوق عبادہِ — that He overpowers His servants.

The second benefit is this: مَعرِفَتُ ذِلَّتِ العُبُودِیَّۃِ وَ کَسْرِھَا. It is to recognize your utter servitude, your complete resignation and brokenness before the will and the power of Allah. The words of Allah point toward this when He says: ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَصَبَتْهُم مُّصِيبَةٌۭ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَجِعُونَ — those who, when an affliction strikes them, say: without doubt, surely to God we belong, and to Him we will return. At last they admit that they stand within His Dominion. When a calamity strikes them, they finally admit that they are inside the Dominion of God. Inna Lillahi — we belong to Allah.

Put it another way. If I take something I own and throw it away, and you say I cannot do that, then why can I not do it? This is my property. I may do whatever I wish with it. I own it. That is the very nature of property. The one who owns a thing has the right to do with it whatever he wills. If you can stop him, then it is not truly his property.

Now, because this world, this Duniya, is not our property, we cannot do with it whatever we wish. Can we? Yet we do understand the idea of ownership. This world is the property of God. We are the property of God. And only Allah may do with it whatever He wills. The difficulty lies in perspective.

Take an example. Suppose I am a well-known scholar and I own a book, and I tear the pages out of it, or I burn it. You may say: that is wrong, you cannot do that. What kind of scholar are you? You are supposed to love books. You are supposed to respect them. You cannot simply burn them like that. And I can answer you: it is my book, I may do with it whatever I want. If I wish to burn it, I will burn it, and no law can stop me. So now you see me doing something you completely disagree with, because you are looking at it from your own perspective.

But then I tell you that this book is full of mistakes, that everything mentioned in it is wrong, that people who read it are actually being harmed by it, that it is spreading confusion, and that this is why I am burning it — to protect people. At that point you will say: now I understand. And now you may well agree with me. So the trouble was only your perspective, the way we were looking at my act of burning the book. Once I explained myself, that same act of mine you found acceptable.

This is the story we are taught in the Qur'an about Moosa and Khizr, peace be upon them — the story of the problem of evil. That story resolves the problem of evil. For Moses is looking with the eye of the outward, and everything he sees Khizr do appears wrong to him. But when it is explained to him by a servant who has been given knowledge, suddenly Moses is saying: I did not realize. Now I have an explanation.

So now I understand. Now the reality of the situation is this, whether we like it or not: we are the ones on trial. Allah is not on trial. Our master is not on trial. It is we, as his servants, as his property, who are on trial. So Allah has no need to explain anything to us. He need only command, and expect our obedience. But that is not what he did, is it? He sent the message for our guidance, and then he sent messengers to show us living examples of that guidance. Our master actually explained himself to us — something he had absolutely no need to do. But he did it anyway, out of his mercy toward us. He explained all his actions to us in the Qur'an. The difference between a believer and a disbeliever is that we are saying, in this world, that we have proof enough to believe in our master. For on the Day of Judgment both the believer and the disbeliever will see the realities that we do not understand while we are in this world. Everything will become clear to us. But at that point it will be too late.

We are saying that we trust Allah. But they are saying, "No! This is all wrong!" Well, how do you know? You do not have all the information. You cannot pass judgment on a thing unless you understand that thing completely, until you have complete information about it. To judge a thing is only one aspect of conceiving that thing in its entirety. This is the first principle in logic. And that is why a judge must have all the facts before he can judge. If you judge beforehand, it is called prejudice, and to be prejudiced is considered a moral vice. So we cannot prejudge Allah. We do not have the right to do that, because Allah is the one who knows all things.

وَمَآ أُوتِيتُم مِّنَ ٱلْعِلْمِ إِلَّا قَلِيلًۭا

And you have been given only a small amount of knowledge. So how can you judge the master on the basis of the little information the master has given you?

We do not even know how our brain works — our brain, the vessel of our intellect. Neurologists admit that we have not even scratched the surface of the potential of the human mind. So how is it possible that, with this limited capacity, we aspire to understand our master? It simply makes no logical sense. A great deal of the how can be explained, and is explained, by science. But of the why we know very little. We know how the heart beats. We do not know why it beats. There are many other ways in which blood could be supplied to the body. Why by this expansion and contraction in particular?

We do not even know our coordinates in the universe. The only reason we know our coordinates on this planet is a system of reference. It is based on cardinal points that do not even exist in reality; they are experiential. It is all flat earth. It all rests on pre-Copernican theories about the universe. But that is all we have. So if you ask about my coordinates in New Jersey, they are based on points of reference, such as Greenwich. Who chose Greenwich? The English happened to be the most powerful people at that time, so it was Greenwich. It could have been Timbuktu. It is all arbitrary. You do not even know your own coordinates in this universe.

How do you expect to know God's coordinates? How do you expect to know where God is? But this is the ignorance of man. Man lives in a deluded state. And the trouble with delusions — which I think is the most troubling thing of all — the trouble with delusion is that no one who is deluded sees his own delusion. That is the very problem of delusion: we do not understand that we are deluded. Arrogant people are, most of the time, entirely unaware of their arrogance. They do not realize that they are being arrogant. Yet they see themselves as better than you. And to see oneself as better than another is a deluded state of mind, because in reality they do not know whether they are better than you or not. They may be or they may not be, but they do not know it for certain. Still, they believe that they are.

Someone chose Greenwich to be that point of reference for our coordinate system. But what are our coordinates in this entire universe? We cannot even identify that. And yet we dare to ask questions about the coordinates of where Allah is. That is a very unfair question.

There are, quite literally, dozens of verses that touch on the concept of *Museebah*. This word, *Museebah*, comes from the Arabic verb اصابۃ, and *Asaaba* means to hit a target. When you strike the target perfectly, when you land a bull's-eye, that act of hitting the mark exactly where it was meant to land is called صواب. This is why another word for "correct" in Arabic is صواب: to hit the right target is the act of اِصَابَۃ. The word *Museebah*, then, is something that strikes you, and strikes you at precisely the point where it was meant to strike. So the first thing we learn from Allah is contained in the very term chosen to describe what befell us.

Many other words could have been used. *Kaarisah*, *Haadisah*, *Waaqiah* — any of these could name something bad that happens. But Allah does not use these words. He uses the word *Museebah* specifically. Why? Because Allah is telling us that, as far as His *Qadar*, His decree, is concerned, as far as His planning is concerned, this calamity was like an arrow that was loosed and struck its target with perfect accuracy — exactly when and where it was meant to reach you. How deep it went and how grievously it wounded were all decided beforehand. The calamity that struck you was a perfect hit.

Then there is even the *taa marboota* at the end. We do not say *museeb*; we say *museebah*. Adding the *taa marboota* introduces the concept of *Hadaf* (target). This means that every single thing is aimed. Consider how we reason: first my transmission broke down; as a result I was late to the meeting; because I was late I lost my job; as a result of that I was divorced; then I lost my health; then, as a result, and then, as a result, and then, as a result. We string all these events together — cause and effect, cause and effect, cause and effect. But Allah is calling each and every event, each and every difficulty, an individual thing. Even though they appear to follow from one another, they are the result of Allah's allowance. Allah permits every single one of those events to occur.

There are people who walk into the very same situations you do, and yet the same things do not happen to them. That chain of events that unfolds for you does not unfold for them. Allah decrees something else for them entirely. That is the first thing we need to notice about the word *Museebah*: it is highly specific, and it is aimed specifically at you.

There are two verses about the word *Museebah* that we should never forget. He says:

وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم بِشَىْءٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْخَوْفِ وَٱلْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْأَمْوَلِ وَٱلْأَنفُسِ وَٱلثَّمَرَتِ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ ٱلصَّبِرِينَ

Allah says: congratulate the people who have *Sabr*, who have patience. What strange language Allah uses. When you and I meet with a difficulty or face a calamity, we are expected to have *Sabr*. We do not ordinarily need *Sabr* when we are happy. You are meant to have *Sabr* when you are distressed, when something is wrong, when something has gone badly — when you were supposed to graduate, and it was delayed on account of some problem.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
You are expected to have a little *Sabr*. You fell ill, and you are expected to have *Sabr*. Now consider this. When you and I are speaking together, and one of us is in a difficult situation — meaning that something bad has happened to one of us, so that we are expected to have *Sabr* — you do not go to that person and offer congratulations. You do not do such a thing. It makes no sense. You do not smile at them and say, "Brother, congratulations, you broke your leg." One does not ordinarily do that. When do you congratulate someone? You congratulate someone when there is a happy occasion, when things have actually gone according to plan. You applied for a job, the offer came through, and you got the job. You applied for admission to a college, and you were accepted. You asked for a raise, and you received an increment. You were hoping to marry, and everything came together. When things truly work out, that is when you congratulate one another.

Now look at the language that Allah uses in this verse. He says, وَبَشِّرِ ٱلصَّبِرِينَ — congratulate the people who have *Sabr*. SubhanAllah! Why? Because for the believer the attitude is entirely different. Perhaps this whole ordeal, this whole calamity that confronts you and that you are passing through, is there for that one reason: so that you learn to have *Sabr*. For if you can have *Sabr*, you are worthy of congratulations. Perhaps I thought the goal was to get the job. Perhaps I thought the goal was to make the sale. But perhaps, to Allah, the real goal was that I learn *Sabr*. That is a greater goal than anything else. It is an opportunity for the believer to be congratulated by Allah. We hold goals in our minds that we wish to accomplish. We hold goals in our hearts that we wish to accomplish. And Allah says that there is something far more valuable in your heart, and if you accomplish it, if you realize what it is worth — and I will tell you what it is worth — it is worth congratulation.

And this congratulation is in the singular. He did not say و بَشِّرُو الصبرین. He said وَبَشِّرِ ٱلصَّبِرِينَ. It is singular. Congratulate the ones who have *Sabr* — and that congratulation is singular. When Allah gives a command in the singular, it is in truth a direct command to Rasul Allah SAS. It means that Rasul Allah SAS, from his own mouth, is to congratulate those who have *Sabr*. So this ayah is about the Rasul himself congratulating the one who is patient on the Day of Judgment. May Allah make us among them. You know that when a family member says congratulations to you, it means one thing. When the principal of your school says congratulations to you, it means another thing. When the dean of your college congratulates you, that is something else again. When the president of a country congratulates you, that is something altogether different. Now imagine when Rasul Allah SAS congratulates you. What an honor that would be. And Allah has actually commanded him to do so. That is the gift in this verse.

And then, right after this congratulation, Allah says, ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَصَبَتْهُم مُّصِيبَةٌۭ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَجِعُونَ. Whom should you congratulate? These patient people.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Let us say that I am a millionaire, and I buy Erum a Lamborghini, or a Porsche. What good is that going to do for her? She does not know how to drive. What possible benefit could she take from that gift? Would it not be better for me to give that car to you, because you could actually make use of it? Stop smiling. Do not get any ideas. I am not buying you a Porsche, ha ha.

Now, when we actually begin to examine the tests, which in Allah's terms are our trials and tribulations, the question becomes this: how are we going to perform in this test? Our worry becomes not so much about the test itself, but about our performance in it.

Then we see that these trials and tribulations are not the same for everyone. Some are put through more difficult trials than others. In the example of the school system, when would a teacher give a student more difficult questions than the rest? When he expects more from that student. Is that not the case?

Now we come to these tests that Allah puts us through, and we sometimes feel that the tests are not fair. O Allah, very well, I am a bad person, so it is acceptable if You do this to me. But my child is only four years old. Why would You put him through this affliction? Why did that happen to him? He did nothing. Why is this world full of suffering? Why do bad things happen to good people?

Let us look at this question and try to answer it on different planes: the intellectual plane as well as the spiritual plane.

I want to begin with the story of Malik ibn Deenar. This man later became the most righteous person of his time. But Malik ibn Deenar says that he began his life very far away from Allah. He said, I did everything wrong. There was not a single sin that I did not commit. In fact, I used to get drunk. I was a habitual drinker. And he said that he continued his life in that fashion, in amusement, in entertainment, in drinking and partying. He would say La Ilaha Illa Allah, yet that was the kind of life he was living. Until one day he saw a little girl, who was three or four years old.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
And he says that on that day something changed within his heart. He longed for a little girl of his own. So he resolved to marry, and Allah in His bounty granted him a beautiful daughter. He says that although Allah knew full well what I was doing, He still gave me a beautiful daughter. Malik Ibn Deenar named her Fatima. Then he says that as his daughter grew, he began to change from within. He says I loved her so dearly that her love began to transform me, and I started to become a better man. He says he understood that he was now a father and could no longer go on living as he had. He says that one night he was sitting in a room drinking wine, as was his custom. His daughter came and sat in his lap. As he raised the cup to drink from it, she pushed it away. When she did this, he resolved to stop. He said that from that day onward he would never touch a drink again. And he kept his word. He gave up drinking entirely. He says my life began to change little by little. He began to pray, step by step. And he says that faith entered his heart, and he could feel himself becoming a better man day by day.

But then one day his daughter fell ill. And he says I grew deeply anxious. He said that his daughter was the light of his life. He began to pray with all his strength. Please, O Allah, do not take her from me. Yet the daughter grew sicker and sicker, and in the end she died. Now those who have passed through this know that it is indeed the greatest calamity of all. There is no greater anguish for a parent than to watch their child suffer and die before their very eyes. And he said I could not bear that pain. He said there was no way I could be patient over her loss. He said, O Allah, how could You do this to me? She was the light of my life. Because of her I was becoming better. I had begun to change. How could You take her from me? From that point on, he says, he relapsed. He says he became far worse than he had been before. He began to drink even more than he once had. One night he said, tonight I am going to drink as I have never drunk before. And he drank and drank and drank until he lost all his senses. He says I drank myself into a stupor and passed out.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
That night, he says, he had a dream. He said it was the Day of Judgment, and he was truly afraid. And then, all at once, everyone was raised up, and he stood alone amid an immense crowd. And then he heard the angels calling people by their names. And then one of the angels called my name. مالک اب دینار!! حَلُمَّ علی الارضِ عَلی الجَبَّار Malik Ibn Deenar! Rise! You are to be brought before the Almighty. He said that when he learned this, he was terrified. And suddenly all the people around me vanished. And I stood alone in that vast plain with an enormous serpent before me. And that serpent, its mouth gaping open, came straight toward me. He says he was so terrified that he began to run. But the serpent kept chasing him. And as I ran, I came upon an old man. I ran to him and begged for protection. I said, help me, the serpent is about to attack me. The old man said, I am so weak, there is nothing I can do to help you. So, he says, he kept running.

As he ran, he came upon the same old man again and again. Each time he begged him for help, and each time the old man gave the same answer: that he was too weak and too old to help him. But at last the old man said, "There is a hill over there. Run to the top of it; perhaps you will find protection there."

Malik ibn Dinar says that he ran toward the hill. When he climbed to its top, he saw on the far side a great open ground where many young children were playing. One of the children looked up at him and knew him, and called out, "Fatima! Look, your father is here. Go and help him." And his four-year-old daughter came running to him. She stood between him and the serpent, and as the serpent came to strike him, she raised her hand and commanded it to stop. The serpent stopped. Then she commanded it to turn back, and it obeyed.

Malik ibn Dinar says: I was so exhausted and so terrified that I collapsed and fell to the ground. And Fatima came and sat in my lap, just as she used to sit when she was in this world. I asked her, "Fatima, what is happening? I do not understand what is happening here." And she answered, "Father, did you not know? Did you not know that the deeds we do in the world come before us in the hereafter in a physical form?" For Allah says in the Qur'an:

وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَبُ فَتَرَى ٱلْمُجْرِمِينَ مُشْفِقِينَ مِمَّا فِيهِ وَيَقُولُونَ يَوَيْلَتَنَا مَالِ هَذَا ٱلْكِتَبِ لَا يُغَادِرُ صَغِيرَةًۭ وَلَا كَبِيرَةً إِلَّآ أَحْصَىٰهَا ۚ وَوَجَدُوا۟ مَا عَمِلُوا۟ حَاضِرًۭا ۗ وَلَا يَظْلِمُ رَبُّكَ أَحَدًۭا

And the Book will be placed, and you will see the guilty, fearful of that which is within it. They will say, "Woe to us! What sort of Book is this that leaves neither a small thing nor a great thing but has recorded it in full!" And they will find all that they did present before them, and your Lord treats no one with injustice.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
On the Day of Judgment, you and I will find what we did in this world set before us. And then she said, "That serpent that was chasing you and trying to strike you—those were your evil deeds, the deeds you did in the world. You made it so strong, you made it so powerful, because you did so many of them, and today they were going to destroy you. And that old man—those were your good deeds. You made him so weak by doing so few of them, and he could not help you on this day. He could not protect you.

"When Allah saw this—when He saw that your evil deeds were going to destroy you in the hereafter—He took me away from you, so that you might be patient over the loss of me. And through your patience over the loss of me, Allah would forgive your evil deeds and admit you into paradise." And then she said, "My dear father, is it not time?"

أَلَمْ يَأْنِ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوٓا۟ أَن تَخْشَعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ لِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا نَزَلَ مِنَ ٱلْحَقِّ

Is it not time for those who believe that their hearts should grow humble at the remembrance of Allah and at the truth that has been revealed? Is it not time?

And Malik ibn Dinar says, "It is time, it is time, it is time." He says he woke from the dream, weeping and crying out, "It is time, it is time, it is time."

And it was the time of Fajr. He says that he immediately performed his ablution and ran to the mosque to join the prayer. As he joined it, the imam was reciting: أَلَمْ يَأْنِ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوٓا۟ أَن تَخْشَعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ لِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا نَزَلَ مِنَ ٱلْحَقِّ. He says that on that day he changed completely. He made a full about-turn and became one of the most righteous people of his time. He is the one who, later in his life, used to say: poor are the people of this world who departed from it without ever tasting the sweetest thing it has to offer. And what is that sweetest thing? It is the sweetness of the remembrance of Allah, and the sweetness of His obedience.

Now, what is the moral of that story for us? What do we learn from it? He lost his daughter. Was that good for him, or was it bad for him? In the long run, in the afterlife, was it good for his daughter or bad for her? When he met her in the dream, was she happy or unhappy? Where is Malik ibn Dinar now? Where is his daughter now?

The scholar says: رُبَّمَـا أَعطـَـاكَ فَمَنَعَـك ورُبَّمَــا مَنَعَـكَ فـاعْطَاك. It might seem that He has given you, when in reality He may be depriving you; and it might seem that He is depriving you, when in reality He is giving you. Allah gives at times by depriving, and He deprives at times by giving. Sometimes matters may not be going well and everything seems bad, yet that may in truth be a blessing from Allah. And sometimes life is wonderful and I am enjoying the best days of my life, yet it may in truth be a punishment from Allah. Now, how do we tell the difference? How can we know whether what is happening is good or bad? That is what we will speak about today.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
But if we look at the story of Malik ibn Dinar, he himself admits at one point that he could no longer be patient after the death of his daughter. Yet one dream, one single dream, changed his entire life. He became one of the most patient of people. What brought about that transformation in him? First of all, what was his dream about? It was about the hereafter, the reality of the afterlife. It is the afterlife set against the present life. The reason we find it difficult to be patient, the reason we suffer pain, the reason we find existence unbearable, is that we live our lives upon a wrong premise. We live with incorrect expectations. And when things happen that were in fact meant to happen, but that go against our expectations because of our mistaken premise, the mistaken perspective through which we view life, we are shocked.

We live as though life is everlasting. We live as though nothing will ever change. I have my parents, I have my children, I have my house, my car, my job, my health, and the silent expectation is that nothing will ever change. But the truth is that all of it will change. The only constant thing in life is what? Change. The very first thing we must learn about this life is that it is temporary. Life is transient. This is not my home; it is merely an examination room in which I have been placed for a short period of time. When you go into an examination room, you do not take your sofa set with you.

You do not take your closet and all the clothes in it with you. You do not take a bed with you. Because it is a temporary place. Your home here is your temporary place. It is what you came from, and it is what you will eventually return to.

According to a hadith, Nuh, peace be upon him, was once asked a question. Among all the prophets, Nuh, peace be upon him, had the longest life. When he was asked about the span of his life in this world, he said, کیف وجدت الدنیا؟ How did you find the life of this world? He answered that it was like a house with two doors: I entered through one, and I left through the other.

This long life we are living today is going to seem like a dream. When you are having a bad dream, it feels very real. It seems as though you are truly suffering. But what happens when you wake up? All praise is due to God, it was only a dream. In the hereafter, this life is going to seem the very same way. We have lost sight of this reality. We are living in a dream and mistaking it for reality. We expect everything in this life to be permanent; we expect nothing to change. And yet God, glorified and exalted, tells us in the Qur'an, ۘ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ۚ كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Everything. Every single thing. I am a thing. My feelings are a thing. The property that I own is a thing. Emotions are things. Sorrow is a thing. Happiness is a thing. Colors are things. Beauty is a thing. Everything is going to perish, except the face of God. Do not attach your heart to that which is going to perish. Do not expect it to last forever. Because when we do, we suffer. We suffer when we expect from life what it is not. Enjoy it while it lasts. Be grateful for it while you have it.

Now the question is this: why did God create the world in this manner? Why are things arbitrary? Why is everything temporary? God created this world, and he made it imperfect on purpose. He made it a place where things change constantly. Good turns into bad. Beautiful turns into ugly. Strong turns into weak. Young turns into old. Nothing stays the same. And he made the world this way deliberately. Why? So that it would be easy for you and me to detach ourselves from it. He wanted to turn us away from this world. He wanted this world to unsettle us, so that nothing would hold us back from moving toward him.

Mawlana Ali says that this world is like a beautiful woman who seduces and entices the one who looks upon her. But the more the man comes to know her, the more he is repelled by her, for this world is a disloyal woman. She is unfaithful. In another of his sayings, he says that this world is like a snake: smooth and soft to the touch, but filled with deadly poison.

But look at what we are doing. Knowing full well that this world gives a little only so that it can take away a great deal, it binds us to itself, and then it changes. Yet we are killing ourselves over this world. God created the hereafter for us. And so that we would never forget it, he designed this world in a way that pushes us away from it. You run toward something, a person, a place, or a thing. You try to find peace in it. You try to find tranquility within it. And that very thing ends up becoming the source of your misery and unhappiness.

And there you stand, asking yourself this very question. Why did I invest so much in it? In this project? In this person? In this relationship? And yet, once again, we repeat the same mistake, over and over and over. This world is pushing us away. It treats us badly. It tells us to go away, go away, go away. And still we keep running after it, the way a dog keeps running after a bone. So Allah created this world in a way that constantly reminds us that we were not created for this world. But that does not mean he asked us to give the world up. He never asked us not to enjoy life. The Qur'an says in fact that Allah wants us to have a good life, and we saw those verses in the earlier sessions, where he calls the life of this world معیشۃ, which means a life of pleasure and ease. So it is our perspective, the way we look at this world, that is the real problem.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
The second reason for our misery, the second reason for our grief, is that we live this life thinking that we own something, that we are entitled to something. Life is not an entitlement. Life is a trust. It is not mine. I have no ownership over it. My body, my car, my house, my parents, my children, my business, my intelligence, my money, my power. My, my, my. My what? Do I truly own anything? This is a reality we never pause to consider. Nothing here is mine. I am nothing but a guest. Consider how it is when you go to visit someone's house and you are a guest there. The host tells you to sit here, and what do you say? Certainly. Of course. He says, do not go into that room, and you say, certainly, of course, I will not go into that room. Why? Because it is not my house. If I enter someone's house as a guest and I say, I do not like the color of your walls, let us paint them black, how do you imagine that conversation goes? He will say, this is not your home, you are not free here, my house, my rules, you are only a guest in my house. But because our host, because Allah is so exceedingly generous with us, because he gave us so much and so many gifts, we forgot that we are guests in his house. He made us so comfortable in this world that we began to think it was our home. We began to think we owned it. And when he takes things back, we do not like it. When he says, now it is time to leave, we are troubled by it.

It is just like my children. I love them so much that sometimes I buy them gifts for no reason at all, simply as an expression of my love. I buy a lovely, beautiful toy for my child. I wrap it up. I make it look truly nice. I walk over to my child with that gift. And what am I thinking? Why am I giving her this gift? Because I love her. And to show her my love, I get her this gift that I know she will truly enjoy. The gift I got her is beautiful, but there is something far greater than the gift itself, and that is my love for her. Look, I am giving you a gift to show you what? That I love you. I give her the gift. And what does she do? She says thank you once. She perhaps gives me a hug once. And then what? Hand it over, Bubu. I give her the gift, and she takes it and begins to unwrap it.

And she looks at it and loves it so much. She becomes completely absorbed in the toy. She begins to play with it. And she forgets about me. I no longer exist for her. She is now wholly consumed by it. She is having a wonderful time with it. And now it is time to sleep. I go to her and say, "All right, that is enough, it is time to sleep now." And she says, "No, no, no, no. I want to play with my toy."
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Your toy? Did you just see my toy? Did you buy it? Did you earn it? No, I gave it to you. But I say nothing. The next morning she is playing with it again when it is time to leave for school. I tell her to put it down and get ready for school. And she tells me, "No! I want to play with my toy." Your toy? I brought you the toy. My toy? And I am not going to go to school?

When I see this, and because I love her, I know that school is important for her. It is more important for her than playing with that toy. So what do I do? I say, "Give the toy back to me." And I take the toy away. When I do that, what happens? She becomes upset. She begins to scream. She cries. "Why did you take my toy away from me? My toy?" Your toy? And then she says, "You took my toy away from me. You are making me suffer. How could you make me suffer? You do not love me. You are not my father."

I do not love you? Because I took the toy away? The toy that I gave you in the first place because I love you? You enjoyed my gift and ignored the love that bought you that toy in the first place. I do not love you? I am not your father? I do not exist for you?

Are these not the very complaints of the atheist? Why did you take my daughter away from me? Why did you bring this calamity upon me? How could you make people suffer? You do not love me, and therefore you do not exist. Astaghfirullah. Astaghfirullah.

Nothing is mine. The way I behave in times of calamity is a direct reflection of my attitude during my times of peace. If I am not patient during my trials and calamities, that is a clear reflection that I was not grateful during my times of ease and comfort. We are veiled by the gifts of Allah. The gift has kept us from the giver. Like my daughter: I gave her the toy, but that very toy masked from her something far greater than the toy — my love for her. The toy was only an expression of my love. I gave her that toy solely to show her that I love her. But she saw the toy and not the love behind it. She could not see my love. She could not see me. I was veiled from her eyes by that very toy.

We are just like her. We look at all the toys that life gives us, placed all around us, and we begin to think that this is all mine. I own it. I am entitled to it. I deserve it. I am never going to give it back. I never wanted to change. We take Allah's gifts. We take all of his gifts. And then we use them against him. He gave us the greatest gift of all, the intellect, and we use that very intellect to put Allah on trial. How am I able to take interest? Because Allah gave me money in the first place. How am I able to wound other people's feelings with my speech? Because Allah gave me the ability to speak in the first place.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
How am I able to go over to filthy websites? Because Allah gave me eyes and sight in the first place. How am I able to disrespect my parents? Because he gave me the gift of parents in the first place. We take the very gifts that Allah bestows upon us, and we use them against him. Allah gives someone a great deal of beauty — mashaAllah — and now she begins to think: my beautiful hair, my beautiful eyes, my beautiful body. Allah says, cover your hair. No! It is my hair. Allah says, conceal your beautiful body. She says, no! It is my body. Your body? Your hair? For how much did you purchase it? How much did you pay for it? Every good thing given to you and to me is a gift from Allah. And when Allah sees that you are disobeying him with the very gifts that he gave you in the first place, he takes it away. Why? Because it is distracting me from what I am meant to be doing. Because I am too caught up in the gift, and I am forgetting the one who gave me the gift, and I am forgetting the love that was at work behind that gift.

Another reason is this: I want to take this puzzle away from my daughter so that I can give her something better. She has already learned how to solve it. I want to give her a more challenging puzzle, because I want her to grow intellectually. So I take away the first gift, only so that I can give her the next one. But in that stretch of time between taking away the first gift and giving her the new one, what does she do? The same thing. How could you do this to me? How could you take away my toy? You do not love me? You do not care about me! I do not love you? I do not care about you? I am the one who gave you the first toy. I am the one who wants to give you a better toy.

This is how we deal with Allah. He takes away my present job, only so that he can give me a better job. But what do I do in the meantime, in that gap between losing my job and finding the next one? I weep. I complain about how bad life is, and about how a great many terrible things happen to good people like myself. But then, after all my complaining, to whom do I turn? I turn to al-Razzaq, the Sustainer. I begin to pray five times a day. I begin to remember Allah, calling out to him for his help. Perhaps that is what he wanted for me. Perhaps he wanted me, once again, to become regular in my prayers.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
The reason we suffer is that we do not understand why we are being tested. Depression and calamities cause pain. Why? Because I do not understand what Allah wants from me in it. What helps a person bear afflictions is when Allah opens the gates of understanding to him. What does that mean? These are scholarly words that carry a very deep meaning. Let me give you a practical example. Have you ever had a toothache? May Allah protect us all from it. It is one of the most dreadful things. Trust me, I know. I have had seven root canals. It is not a pleasant experience. Now, when I have this pain in my tooth — but let us say I have a toothache for the very first time in my life. I have never seen the inside of a dentist's office before. I go to him and tell him that I have this terrible toothache, which has kept me up all night. He examines my tooth.

Realizes that it has decayed. And it needs to be pulled out. Now what is the very first thing he is going to do? He is going to take out that syringe and fill it with novocaine. Then he walks toward me to give me that shot. And when he does that, my response is: Are you crazy? I am already in so much pain. I just told you I have been up all night with it. And now you want to give me a shot on top of that? You want to hurt me even more? What is wrong with you? I get up and leave. All dentists are horrible. I never want to see a dentist again in my life. I am going to do my very best to keep other people from going to the dentist too. Why? Because when I was in pain, he tried to hurt me. He tried to stick a needle into my gum, right where it already ached so much.

But now understand this. Simply because I did not trust the dentist, simply because I did not put my faith in him, I am going to spend the rest of my life in pain. I am going to live in pain and keep complaining about the dentist. But why was the dentist trying to give me the shot? Was he doing it to hurt me? Or was he doing it to numb the pain, so that he could pull out the decayed tooth, so that I could be free of pain? The dentist was actually trying to help me. But the only way he could help me was by giving me that shot.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
That whenever a specific, targeted calamity strikes them, the first thing that comes out of their mouths is *Qaloo* — not even *fa-qaaloo*, not even *summa qaaloo*. Not "THEN they say." There is a *when* and there is an *it then*: when this happens, then they say. But in this verse there is not even time for a "then." There is not even a *fa-qaaloo*. Why not? Because it is meant to be an immediate response. It is like an immediate reaction, an instant reflex. This verse is teaching us that when the difficulty comes upon you, there is meant to be an instant reflex. And a reflex is not a controlled movement; it simply happens. So for the believer, this statement simply comes out, like a reflex. And what comes out? إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَجِعُونَ. There is no doubt about it: we belong to Allah. There is no doubt about it: we belong to Allah. And there is no doubt about it: we are going to be returned to him. We are his property. He is our owner. And the property will, without doubt, return to its owner.

Now, why is this statement important when something difficult happens? We really have to stop and think about the wisdom here. When the difficulty comes, why does a believer say *Inna Lillahi Wa Inna Ilayhe Rajeoon*? Let us look at a few examples. Let us say I am driving my car. I have just bought a brand-new car, and I am driving it, and I have engine trouble. That makes me angry, because I just paid good money for this car. How can this happen? This was supposed to be such an outstanding car. I am getting late to work. I have an important meeting. I am stuck here in the middle of the heat. The air-conditioner is not even working. Now all these things are going through my head. But the first thing that I think as a believer is *Inna Lillah*.

Why? Because I am angry at this car since I own it, and I am actually reminding myself that I own nothing. I myself am owned. Allah owns me. Without doubt, I belong to Allah. How can I complain about anything, when I myself am not the owner of anything? You see, people become angry when they think they are entitled. It was my turn. I deserved it. I was supposed to get that promotion. I was supposed to win that debate. I was supposed to make it into college this year. I was supposed to be the president of my school. My phone is not working. My car is not working. The lights are not turning on. When you think you deserve something and you do not get it, that is when you become angry. But in the verse — *Inna Lillah* — right at the outset, you admit that I deserve nothing, because I own nothing. I belong to Allah. Allah deserves; I do not deserve. It completely puts things into perspective. It makes things easy. Everything that you receive in life is then considered a gift. It is not something that you earned; it is a gift. So when you do not have it, you realize it was not mine anyway.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Now, on the other hand, suppose I did place my trust in this dentist. He walks toward me with that syringe. I know it is going to hurt when he puts it in my mouth. But if I simply bear that pain, if I simply stay patient through the prick of that needle, what will it lead to? It will make me free of pain. The reason I will be free of pain is that I trust him. I may not understand what he is doing. I do not know what he put in that needle. But I trust that he knows his work. I trust that he knows what he is doing. And I trust that his goal in the end is to help me, to take away my pain. Because he has cured a hundred people before me. He has a fine reputation. That knowledge helps me trust him. So what is it that lets me stay patient in that dentist's chair? It is my trust in him. It is my patience that makes all the difference. A momentary, temporary patience that, I trust, will grant me eternal freedom from that pain.

We, as creation, do not know our Creator. We do not know Allah. When an affliction comes our way, we see the affliction. We do not see the doctor who is afflicting us in order to remove a greater affliction from us. We all claim that we know Allah, that we trust him. But when the affliction strikes, we show that we do not trust him at all. We do not understand what he is doing. And this veil makes it very hard for us to be patient through his decrees. And that is one reason why we are not patient.

So what are the things we have said so far? Life is transient. Life is a trust, and we own nothing. And the third: life is a test. Life is a test. And we, as human beings, do not like that. We do not like to be tested, in any situation. Nobody likes to sit in that examination hall at the end of the year. But we have to, because it is the measure of our success or failure in our present grade.

Depends on the outcome of our test.

Seventeen benefits of trials and tribulations

وَلِيَبْتَلِىَ ٱللَّهُ مَا فِى صُدُورِكُمْ وَلِيُمَحِّصَ مَا فِى قُلُوبِكُمْ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُو

Allah explains the purpose of a test. All tests are directed at my heart. He says: so that I can bring out and place before you what lies hidden in your heart. What does that mean?

أَمْ حَسِبَ ٱلَّذِينَ فِى قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضٌ أَن لَّن يُخْرِجَ ٱللَّهُ أَضْغَنَهُمْ
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Did these people really think that Allah is not going to bring out the sickness in their heart? What does that mean? Let us try to understand it in practical terms. When I am sick physically, is that a good thing or a bad thing? It is a bad thing. And what is the sign that tells me that something is wrong with me physically? It is pain. Do I like pain? Do I enjoy pain? No, I do not. But what is that pain telling me? It is telling me that something is wrong. Fix it. Pain is a messenger. Pain is informing me: look, there is something inside you that you are not aware of. Pain is the messenger telling you to stop. Stop what you are doing. Something is wrong. Look at it. Fix it. The worst type of disease in the world is the one in which you feel no pain, the one that has no symptoms. Why? Because by the time you find out, it is too late. When I do not know that there is something wrong in me spiritually, then I continue my life, living in the same way, doing the same bad things over and over again, thinking that I am good, thinking that all is well. And that ignorance eventually kills me.

Just like my body, my heart can be sick too. And I do not mean the physical heart; I mean the spiritual one. Spiritually my heart can be sick. It can be diseased. And I could be completely unaware of it. I imagine that I am a very modest person. I have no such thing as arrogance. Allah knows that I do not have modesty in my heart. He knows that I am a very arrogant person. It is only that I do not have the circumstances to exercise that arrogance. So what does He do? He tests me. How does He test me? He gives me ideas: go ahead, make patents upon patents, earn wealth upon wealth, become a millionaire, start your own company, become a CEO, gain power! He puts me in a position of power. And as soon as that happens, what happens to the arrogance in my heart? It surfaces. It comes out. That money and that power were a test for me, only so that Allah can bring out that arrogance from within my heart and show it to me and to the world. Why? So that I can do something about it. So that I can fix it. So that I can cure it. If I pass that test, that same money and wealth now become a blessing for me. It becomes a tool by which I can earn heaven. But if I do not fix it, if I continue to remain arrogant, then that same money and wealth become an enormous affliction for me. Because now, with that very wealth and power, I will earn hellfire.

Similarly, Allah gives us another chance if we fail the first time. Why is that bad? What does Allah want us to do? He wants us to pass the test. So He keeps giving us another chance, over and over again. Some have learned their lesson, and the test is over.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
And others do not, and they must keep repeating the test. The affliction stops only when we understand what is happening, and when we have fixed the source of the pain, so that we may live a happy life in the hereafter. Affliction and calamity are from Allah's mercy. They are from Allah's love. It is our perspective, how we choose to see it, that turns it into such torture to bear.

I may think that I love Allah. But Allah knows, in the depths of my heart, that I do not. So He places me in a test. He places me in a situation that draws out the true reality and shows it to me. I do not learn from it. I do not take a step back and try to correct it. So He places me in that situation again. And again. And again. Until I either learn my lesson, or I gather so much proof against myself that, on the Day of Judgment, I will not need Allah to pass judgment against me. I will pass judgment against myself on that day.

So the very first thing I should do, when I find myself afflicted with a calamity, is to observe myself and see how I react to it. Was I arrogant? Was I humble? Was I ungrateful? Was I patient? How did I perform in the test? And even if I failed that test, failure in a test is not a bad thing, so long as I learn something from it. When you go for your driver's license, and you take the test and fail, what happens? They give you another chance. Is that bad? No, it is not. Then you take the test again and fail. What do they do? They give you another chance. And they keep giving you chances, over and over again. Until what happens? Until you finally pass the test.

So the first thing to do is to observe our reactions to that calamity. Observe how we reacted to that affliction, because Allah brings out what is hidden in our hearts through tribulations. If you struggle to be patient, if you are trying very hard to be patient and you are struggling because of it, then know that your patience in that struggle is the expiation and elimination of your sins. And if what comes out is contentment, if in the face of affliction you find contentment in your heart, then Allah is elevating your ranks.

Once again, there are two reactions in the face of trials: sabr and rida. Sabr is the elimination of sins, and rida, or contentment, is the elevation of ranks. Consider the example of Imam Hussain, peace be upon him. He was not patient in his trial. He was content. He was grateful for the trial. And that state is a far superior state. But it can only come about when one's heart is filled with the love of Allah.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Let me give you a practical example to explain the difference between patience and contentment in the face of trials. Let us say there is a believer who was completely paralyzed from the neck down. And the paralysis is so severe that even his or her speech is impaired. This person cannot even speak properly to express his needs. And then somebody comes to you and says, "Can you please take care of this person? Can you take this person into your house and care for them around the clock?" Would that be a good deed? Of course. But would that be easy? Absolutely not. If somebody asked me to do that, would I be able to do it? I do not think so. If I were placed in this trial, if I were placed in this test,

I do not believe I have the patience within me to see that person through. And if I truly had no choice but to do it, I know I would struggle. I would struggle a great deal, because care of this kind demands enormous patience, and I do not feel that my heart holds strength enough to be so patient. To care for this person means that I must feed him, bathe him, change his clothes, and tend to him in every way imaginable. If he falls ill, I must carry him to the doctor. I must see that he takes his medicine at the proper time. I must attend to his every need, even in the middle of the night. Can I do that? I do not think so. It would be extremely difficult for me to show patience of that measure. I understand that it is a great deed. I understand that its rewards are immense. But I do not think I hold within my heart the strength and the patience to actually do it. That would be my answer if someone asked me to care for such a person.

But now I am asked something else. "No, I am not asking you to be patient in caring for this person. I am asking you to be content. Can you do that? Can you care for this person and be genuinely happy while you do it?" My answer to that would be: now you are asking too much of me. To be patient is one thing, but now you want me to be content and happy while caring for this person? That is simply too much to ask. I may have had my doubts about being patient, but I can tell you with certainty that I will not be content while caring for this person. Do you understand?
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Yet here is the striking thing: most of us in this gathering are either doing this very thing already, or have done it in the past. Truly? What do I mean? I mean those of us who have children. When Allah gave us a baby, how was it? That baby was wholly dependent upon us. It could do nothing for itself. We had to feed it, clean it, bathe it, take it to the doctor, give it medicine, change diapers, change diapers, change diapers, change diapers. We had to do every single thing for that baby. And all the while we had to forget the very idea of sleep. Is that not so? Yet while I am doing all of this, am I suffering? If you have one of these night-screamers—and I have one, so I am allowed to say it—suppose I came to you and said, "Oh my, what a calamity life has burdened you with! My brother, my sister, please be patient. May Allah be with you. I feel such sorrow for you." Your answer would be: "What on earth are you talking about? This baby is no affliction. He is no burden to me. He is the coolness of my eyes. He is the best thing I have ever had in my life. I thank Allah every single day for this gift." What? A gift? This baby works you like a slave all day and does not let you sleep at night, and it is a gift from Allah? What made us able to be so patient with this baby, and why was it so hard to be patient with that person? After all, I am doing the very same things. What made me able to bear this great trial? It is love. It is love that makes the difference. The love I hold for my child, I do not hold for that person.

And so caring for that person is a burden to me. But doing the very same things for my own child is a blessing. Caring for that person, I must force myself to be patient. Caring for my child, I am content. The only reason we understand this difference is that we were given the gift of love. So Allah gave us the gift of a child. And the only reason we are happy, the only reason we are content with it, is that He filled our hearts with love for the child. He did not only give us the gift; He also gave us the provision for it. And that provision is love.

When we are afflicted with hunger, is hunger bad? It is very bad if you have no food, is it not? But if I am hungry and my refrigerator is loaded with food, is hunger bad now? No. AlHamdulillah, when I am hungry I have the provision for it. The problem is when I give you money, and instead of buying food and filling your refrigerator with it, you go and spend it elsewhere. And then, when you feel hunger, and you open the refrigerator, it is completely empty. The problem is not hunger. The problem is, why is the refrigerator empty? The problem is, why do you not have the provision?

Allah, glory be to Him, sends an affliction, and for every affliction that He sends He first provides a provision. If we accept the provision, then the affliction is no problem. You will be able to bear the affliction very easily.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
فَإِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا. إِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًۭا. There is no doubt about it: WITH difficulty there is ease. And then Allah says it again. There is no doubt about it: WITH difficulty there is ease. SubhanAllah. I want you to examine this verse carefully. He says ان مع العسر یسرا. He did not say ان بعد العسر یسرا. He did not say AFTER difficulty there is ease. He says مع العسر یسرا, WITH difficulty there is ease. Side by side. You do not have to worry about the difficulty, because I am giving you the ease along with it.

Yes, I am afflicting you with a sickness, but I have created the doctor who will examine you. Before the affliction I am giving you, I have already created the medicine that will cure your sickness. I have already given you the money you will need to pay the doctor's bill and to buy the medicines that will cure you. I have given you all of this, and now I am giving you the affliction. I have given you people who will take care of you during your time of difficulty. I have put love in their hearts for you, so that they take care of you during this trial. I have taken care of everything, before and after. All you have to do now is be patient with what I am trying to do. With this I am trying to clear away your sins, to make you realize something, to teach you something, so that you can grow, so that you can be purified, so that you can learn. So that when you come to Me, you are eligible for the gifts that I have in store for you. I am giving you this shot of novocaine so that I can pull out your decayed tooth, so that you can enjoy a long-lasting comfort.

This awareness is what changes the attitude of a disbeliever in the face of trials.

أِنَّمَا یُعِینُوھُم عَلی حَمْلِ البَلایَا؛ وَارِدَاتَ العَطَایَا. What aids a person to bear afflictions is not from the person himself.

It is from Allah. And that is precisely our problem: why are we unable to be patient? Because we are relying upon ourselves. Patience is a gift from Allah. When I am afflicted, the question is not why I am hungry; the question is why my fridge is empty. Why am I far from the love of Allah? Why is my heart empty of the love of Allah? That is the real question. If I attempt to bear the affliction entirely on my own, without the love of Allah, I will surely suffer.

Consider how Allah cares for us at every step of the way. There is a hadith that when you go to visit a sick man, you should ask him to pray for you. Now, that hadith sounds backward, does it not? Let us understand how Allah cares for the one who is afflicted by troubles. The way to make this most relatable to us is to look at examples from our own lives. If any one of you has been through such a situation, you will probably be able to relate to this far more than those who have not; but, God willing, I am certain that conceptually we will all be able to take something from it.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
In fact, I will use myself as an example. Imagine that my son falls very ill. May Allah protect all our children from trials. But, simply as an example, let us say that my son Amir falls gravely sick, and he is admitted to the emergency room. The doctors come and tell me that he is in a great deal of pain and that he is unable to breathe properly. I cannot even imagine what state I would be in if that ever happened. I cannot imagine what state Nazneen would be in if that ever happened. There is nothing more painful than to see your own children suffer, whether physically or spiritually. So the doctor comes to me and tells me that my son cannot breathe and that he needs to be placed on a ventilator. What would my reaction be to that? What would be the state of my heart at that moment? Is there any other place in this world where I would want to be at that moment? Of course not. I would not leave my son's side even for a second. I am a father. I imagine Nazneen would be in far more pain than I. If I told Nazneen to go home and rest while I stayed at the hospital, would she listen to me? She would not leave his side for a second. She would sit day and night beside his bed, holding his hand, praying for him.

Now, my daughter Erum is waiting for her brother to wake up. So she goes and buys a helium balloon for Amir, and she ties it to the bed of Amir, who is now completely sedated. Nazneen and I are sitting beside him. He is our son, and we love him so much. We are sitting there next to him, weeping by his side, praying for him constantly. I know that I would want to remove all those tubes from his mouth as soon as I possibly could. I would want to ease his suffering as quickly as I possibly could.

And then Allah listens to our prayers, and at last he wakes. And when he does, being a child, he sees the balloon and smiles and points to it. Now, when I saw him do that, what do you think I did? You want this balloon? Take it. Take it. Of course. Here you are. What else do you want? What else can I bring for you? Anything you want, anything you ask for right now, I will bring for you. In that moment,
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
No matter what my son asked for, I would give it to him if it were in my power. Can you imagine how close I would feel to him at that moment? How dear he would be to my heart? How dear Woody would be to his mother's heart? SubhanAllah. If this is how much we love our children, can you even imagine how much Allah loves His creation? Because according to the Hadith, Allah holds the love of seventy mothers for every single one of His creatures. If, in an affliction of this kind, I draw so close to my son, then when a human being is passing through his own afflictions, can you imagine how close Allah would be to him at that moment? Look how ready I was to answer anything Amir might ask of me. And I am limited by my capabilities. But when a human being, a creation of Allah, is in pain, and he asks for something, whether for himself or for someone else, do you think Allah would refuse the one He loves so much at that moment?

When we are in the state of affliction, at that moment Allah is closer to us than any other human being. In that moment, when the person asks Allah. Now imagine that when my son wakes and, instead of pointing to the balloon, says to me, Babu, there is something I want from you. I would say, anything you want, whatever you want I will get for you.
