And he says to me, please forgive me, because I was not a good child, because I was not an obedient son, please forgive me. In that moment, what do you think would rise from my heart? In that condition, seeing my son in that condition when he asks me for forgiveness, what do you think would be my natural response? Of course I forgive you, my son. SubhanAllah.

When I am in such an affliction, and during that affliction I turn to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and I ask Him for forgiveness, do you think Allah would not forgive, no matter what sin I may have committed, no matter how terrible I may have been? Do you think Allah would not forgive me at that moment? If I, as a human being, if I, being only a father, not even carrying the heart of a mother, would be willing to forgive every disobedience, every rudeness, every harshness of my son at that moment, can you even imagine Allah, the One who identifies Himself with love, who holds the love of seventy mothers in His heart for His creation, do you think He would refuse to forgive?

If, in that moment, my son wakes and, instead of asking something for himself, instead of seeking forgiveness for himself, he says, Baba, please buy for her the gift she always wanted, please forgive Erum, do you think I would refuse? Oh my God, Amir. You are in such a difficult state, you are in so much pain, you are suffering so much right now, and yet you are concerned about your sister. You want me to forgive her? Your request will surely be granted. Of course I will give her anything. All you have to do is ask. SubhanAllah.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
If only, during my affliction, as I am passing through this calamity, I raise my hands and ask Allah to fulfill the needs of a brother, or to forgive the sins of a brother, will Allah turn down my request? Do you really think that Allah is not going to respond?

Not only will he respond, but how close I will be to him in that moment. So the trial becomes the perfect opportunity for us to ask Allah for our needs. Trials can become one of the best experiences a person can have — an experience of awareness of the closeness of Allah in that moment. Why does Allah need to do this for me? Why does Allah need to fulfill every request that I make, disobedient creation that I am? And that led me to ask a question: why do good things happen to bad people like myself? When I see this kind of love from Allah, it truly makes me wonder. My life is nothing more than a collection of acts of disobedience to Allah in every single moment. You ask why bad things happen to good people; I ask you, why do good things happen to bad people like myself? Why me, ya Allah? Because he is generous. Because he is loving. And I am certainly not the best person in this group. If so much good can be given to a person like me, how much would Allah give to someone like you? Do not despair of the mercy of Allah.

What makes us bear the pain of the affliction is the closeness of Allah in the moment of that affliction. When his light enters my heart, there is no affliction anymore. The reason we suffer is that we are veiled from seeing Allah. When I try to bear the affliction by myself, I fail. When I walk the journey of this life alone, I fail. And all along Allah is offering himself to me, telling me that I do not have to take this journey alone: I want to be your wali. I want to be your wakeel. I want to be with you. And when we make Allah our companion, then there can be no affliction in the journey, no matter how difficult it may seem.

The poet says: ما تجِدَهُ الْقُلوبِ مِنَ الهُمُومِ والأحزَان فَلِأَجْل مَا فَقَدَت من وجود العيان. The pain, the sadness, the anxiety that the heart experiences is because it is veiled from seeing the divine. This veil is what causes pain. The essence of all blessing, enlightenment, happiness, and joy is being close to the divine. The core essence of pain, anxiety, and sadness is the existence of a veil between my heart and Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala. Because it means that I am by myself. I am alone. I am far from him. I do not see him.

فَسَبَبِ العَذاب بِوُجُود الحِجَاب..... و تَمامِ النَّعِیم بِالنَّظَرْ اِلی وَجہِ الکَرِیم. The cause of all torment is the existence of this veil, and the utmost pleasure is when we are granted the sight of the most Generous in the hereafter. The reason affliction is so painful is that we are veiled from our companion. We are veiled from his immense love and mercy even during the time that we are suffering. We consider ourselves alone. We think we are by ourselves, and that there is no one there to help us. That is the essence of all pain.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
For the one whose refrigerator is filled with good things, hunger does not trouble him, because he knows that he has provision waiting in it. The one who is certain of getting water does not feel thirsty. We are people whose refrigerator is empty; that is why, when we grow hungry, we have nothing to turn to. This is why it becomes so difficult to remain patient during afflictions — because patience is not from me. Allah says: وَٱصْبِرْ وَمَا صَبْرُكَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِ. Be patient, and you do not attain patience except through Allah.

except from Allah. Your patience is with Allah. It is by Allah. This is something we witness when we study the events of Karbala. The kind of affliction those people faced, and the patience they demonstrated within it, no one in this world has ever seen before, nor will anyone face such a calamity in the future. The reason they were able to bear all of it is that they knew they were not alone. They knew that Allah was with them.

On the other hand, when Allah is not one's companion, then losing a phone can feel catastrophic, and not being able to buy the toy you wanted can feel disastrous. When Allah carries us on the wings of His mercy, the greatest tribulation feels easy. And when we are alone, all by ourselves, in those moments even the smallest discomfort feels like an enormous burden.

The lesson we learn from this is that we should not have to wait until an affliction falls upon us in order to feel close to Allah. Our concern should be the question: Am I close to Allah right now, during my time of ease and comfort? Because if I am close to Allah, if Allah is my companion in my day-to-day life, then when the affliction actually strikes me, I will be with Allah. I will be with His light. And if that becomes the case, then there is no harm in being in any sort of affliction. This is why the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: عَجَبًا لأمرِ المؤمنِ إِنَّ أمْرَه كُلَّهُ لهُ خَيرٌ وليسَ ذلكَ لأحَدٍ إلا للمُؤْمنِ، إِنْ أصَابتهُ سَرَّاءُ شَكَرَ فكانتْ خَيرًا لهُ وإنْ أصَابتهُ ضَرَّاءُ صَبرَ فكانتْ خَيرًا لهُ. How amazing is the affair of the believer. Everything is good for him — and that is for no one but the believer: if good times come his way he is thankful, and that is good for him; and if hardship comes his way, he has the provision for it from Allah that helps him become patient, and that is good for him. Everything becomes good for a believer.

The moral of all this is that we have to live life according to what it is, not according to how we would prefer it to be. That means that in every single moment I should be grateful to Allah — grateful for my children, grateful for my house, grateful for my safety. We have to remain always in a state of constant gratitude, because all of these things are temporary. And this awareness of the presence of Allah in my life will help me when the afflictions strike me, for in that moment I should expect that everything will change. That is the way to live.

Secondly, I do not own anything, including my body and my soul. I do not own any of them. They are blessings given to me, and I should be thankful for them, because Allah can take them away at any time.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
We take our hands for granted. We take our feet for granted. Our eyes, our sight, our hearing. We take our ability to speak for granted. The very fact that right now I am speaking to you — I take this capability of speech for granted. I think that I am the one giving you this knowledge. I take this ability of transferring this knowledge for granted.

But this tongue that I am speaking with does not belong to me. This knowledge that I am giving to you does not belong to me. I did not pay for it. It belongs to Allah. So when it begins to stutter — Inna Lillah.

And now for the second part of the remedy. It is remarkable how Allah gives us solutions within our faith, what wisdom there is in the words He gave us. The second statement is Wa Inna Ilayhi Raji'un: there is no doubt that we are returning to Him. Why does this matter? Because every problem that you and I are facing right now is not permanent — because you and I are not permanent. Whatever the problem may be, it will not last. Whether it is financial trouble, ill health, difficulties within the family or the marriage, emotional pain or physical pain, it makes no difference: none of it is permanent. And do you know why? Because you and I are not permanent. If even you and I are not to remain, how can our problems remain? We ourselves must be returned to Allah. Forget the problem for a moment: one day I myself will depart. Not only will this problem no longer be here — one day I too will no longer be here. I will be returned to Allah. This puts things in their proper place. Setting things in their proper place makes you concern yourself with what truly matters; when you do not, you can fix your attention on the wrong things.

If you are standing inside a building and the building is on fire, you do not debate what color you should paint a wall — "I think white would sit better against the blue." The building is on fire; you leave it at once. There are priorities. When you grasp the larger picture, you see that there is a greater problem, and that greater problem is that we have not acknowledged that we belong to Allah. Perhaps at times you and I are made to pass through hardship only so that Allah may set it back in our hearts that we belong to Him and that we will return to Him. Perhaps you and I are passing through certain trials today only so that Allah may give us the gift of being able to say it — not merely with our tongues, but with our hearts: Inna Lillahi wa... That is a gift in itself. If we can truly take that in, then patience can become easy. And if we are able to be patient, then the congratulation of Allah — given through a direct command to His beloved Prophet — is for us.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Third is the focus on the afterlife, considering the afterlife permanent in comparison to this temporary existence. If I am constantly thinking about heaven, and I aspire to reach that ultimate goal, then I live in this world focusing on the things I need to do that will enable me to live in heaven. Because if we do not imagine heaven as our ultimate home, if we do not think of heaven as our ultimate home, then this world becomes our home, and when it is taken away from me I collapse. But if in reality my home is heaven,

And someone wants to take away my home in this worldly life. It will not matter to me, because I never considered this to be my home in the first place. As long as I have heaven, I am all right. As long as I am saying *La ilaha illa Allah*, I am all right. As long as I am following in the footsteps of my Prophet, I am all right. As long as I have the love of my Prophet in my heart, I am all right. I am all right. We are patient over the hardships of going to school, of working hard to earn a degree, of going to work day in and day out. Why? Because we can see what the immediate outcome is.

There was once a man who was afflicted with something, and he kept calling upon Allah, praying to Him, asking His help constantly, for twenty years, but nothing happened. One day another man saw him doing this and asked him, "What are you doing? Why are you making this supplication?" He said, "Because I want Allah to remove my affliction." The other man said, "But you have been praying for twenty years, and Allah has not yet removed your affliction." The man thought, "He has a point. Why do I keep calling upon Allah when nothing happens?" So he stopped praying, and he stopped calling upon Allah. One night, as he was sleeping, he was called upon in his dream: "Why did you stop making your supplication? We no longer hear your voice in the heavens!" He said, "I have been asking, I have been making supplication for twenty years, but there has been no response." And he was told, "Your making supplication for twenty years is your response. Your calling upon Allah constantly for twenty years is far better than what you were asking for. That was Allah's response to you, but you did not realize it."

So we must call upon Allah constantly, because calling upon Him is itself from His enabling grace. It is from His divine blessings. He does not give everyone the desire to call upon Him, and every call is recorded in the books for the hereafter.

اِن أَقاَمَکَ تَبَت وَ اِن قُمتَ بِنَفس‏ِکَ سَقَط

If Allah makes you stand, you will never fall; and if He lets you fall, if He leaves you to yourself, you will always fall. I want to stand with Allah, never by myself.

The Messenger of Allah, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, used to say:

یا ارحم الراحمین ... بِرَحمتِکَ أَستَغِیث ... لا تَکِلنِی اِلی نَفسِی طُرفَۃَ عَینِ وَلا أَحدٍ مِن خَلقِکَ

O most merciful of all who are merciful, by Your mercy I plead to You: do not leave me to myself for even the blink of an eye, nor to any of Your creation.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
In the Qur'an there are two kinds of verses. In one set of verses, Allah says that whatever befalls you: مَآ أَصَابَ مِن مُّصِيبَةٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ إِلَّا فِى كِتَبٍۢ مِّن قَبْلِ أَن نَّبْرَأَهَآ. There is not a single calamity that ever occurs — whether in the heaven or on the earth, anywhere and to anyone, it does not matter where — but that it is already recorded in the Book that We have decreed. That is to say, it was a decree of Allah, and it was bound to happen.

This means that you do not get to say of someone who died young that he had his whole life ahead of him. He did not. There is no such thing. It was already decreed. This was the length of his journey upon the earth. My journey upon the earth is decreed, and so is yours.

When you go to the graveyard, you see all these different tombstones. On some you read that a person was born in 1901 and died in 2013. But then you also come upon a tombstone that says born in 2013 and died in 2013. You find those kinds of graves too. This has already been decreed by Allah. It has already been decided how long each and every one of us will remain upon this earth. It is already settled. You and I do not get to say, oh, if only he had been given more life today. No, no, no. It is all decreed.

The other thing Allah says is this: مَآ أَصَابَ مِن مُّصِيبَةٍ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ. No difficulty, no calamity, no affliction will strike you except by Allah's permission. And look at the people of faith, at the beautiful thing they say: قُل لَّن يُصِيبَنَآ إِلَّا مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَنَا هُوَ مَوْلَىٰنَا ۚ وَعَلَى ٱللَّهِ فَلْيَتَوَكَّلِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ. They did not say kataba alayna. This is truly remarkable. The believer is told that no difficulty will strike us except what Allah has written for us. They could have said, what Allah has written against us, because when you speak of difficulty, you think in terms of against. This difficulty is striking against me. But the verse says مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَنَا, for us. Huwa maulana, He is our master. Allah teaches the believers that even when difficulties come, they are written not against us but for us. And that is the attitude of the believer toward difficulties and calamities.

But then there are several verses in the Qur'an that say whatever happens to you is because of your own sins: وَمَآ أَصَبَكُم مِّن مُّصِيبَةٍۢ فَبِمَا كَسَبَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ وَيَعْفُوا۟ عَن كَثِيرٍۢ. Whatever difficulty strikes you, it was because of what you did. Allah says it is your fault. Certain difficulties, Allah says, are entirely your own doing, what your hands have earned for yourselves. Now how do we reconcile these two things? Is it because of Allah, or is it because of our own wrongdoings?
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
The first thing to note here is that Allah never says qul. He never says, say, it is your fault, except in one place, in Surah Aal Imran: أَوَلَمَّآ أَصَبَتْكُم مُّصِيبَةٌۭ قَدْ أَصَبْتُم مِّثْلَيْهَا قُلْتُمْ أَنَّىٰ هَذَا ۖ قُلْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ أَنفُسِكُمْ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدِيرٌۭ. In other words, we are not supposed to say to someone that this is happening to you because it is your fault. Do you know why you were diagnosed with cancer? Because you do not pray five times a day. That is why you have cancer. You and I do not get to say that. We do not get to say that. This one verse, in which Allah actually uses the word qul, is a reference to the battle of Uhud, in which Allah commands Rasool Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to say to them that this defeat was their own fault. When these people ask you, why did this happen, how could this have happened, tell them it was your own doing. Because in the specific case of the battle of Uhud, what happened? The believers were winning. They were winning. They were in an advantageous position, and the enemy was fleeing. But then some of the archers left their position, even though the Prophet had commanded them not to. And when they left their position, the tide of the battle turned.

And so it all unfolded, and the believers were defeated. But now the believers do not get to blame Allah, because you abandoned your strategic positions. You must take responsibility for your own actions.

So what we come to learn in this verse is that we do not get to blame Allah. You were driving over the speed limit, and you got into an accident. It is your fault, and you do not get to blame Allah. You cannot say that Allah decreed this accident for you. This was entirely your own doing. You were speeding. You were driving like a maniac. You did not put your seatbelt on. And that is why you were injured. This is من عند انفسکم. This is because of what you did.

You do not study for your exam. You spend the entire year playing video games. And then, when you fail the exam, you do not get to blame Allah. You do not say Inna Lillahi. It was not Allah's will that I should have passed. No, no, no, no, no. This is من عند انفسکم. You have to take responsibility. You cannot simply place everything upon Allah. You are not applying for a job. You are sitting at home all day. No job is coming to you. Allah is not sending angels to your house with an offer letter. And you say, when Allah decides, I will get a job. Inna Lillahi wa inna. No.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
There is this balance in the Qur'an. When things happen to you that are outside your control, they are from Allah. But when you place yourself in a disastrous situation, that is not from Allah. That is from your own wrongdoing. A flood is outside your control. Someone else's car striking yours is outside your control. You were diagnosed with some sort of disease; that is outside your control. But if that same disease came to you because you are smoking five packs a day, and your doctor keeps telling you that you are heading toward diabetes, and you are still in the habit of mixing a little tea into your sugar — you know, you are that kind of person — then you do not get to blame Allah. This is ن عند انفسکم.

The Qur'an is such a balanced approach to this problem. The believer has to understand how to take responsibility. But in either of these cases, whatever came to you — unless it is death, unless it is death — it is a gift from Allah, so that you may learn your lesson and move on in life, so that you may do better. You are not truly doing justice at work. You are coming in late every day, not completing the tasks that were assigned to you. And then you are fired. You cannot blame Allah for that. And that, in fact, is a gift from Allah to teach you a lesson, so that in the next job you get, you do not repeat the same mistakes. These difficulties actually make us better human beings. They make us better believers. They make us stronger as people. They make us more responsible.

So, just to recap all of this: the lesson we learn from these verses is that the first thing we must do when we are afflicted or placed in a difficult situation is to train our tongues. Train our tongues and our hearts to say, Inna Lillahi wa inna ilaihi rajioon. That is number one. Number two: do not suggest to other people that the bad which is happening to them is because of Allah. Do not say this to people.

If you wish to say something to people—before you say it to anyone else, first think about yourself. You do not get to decide whether something has come from the unseen. Something comes from Allah, and you do not get to decide why Allah did this to them, because Allah did not offer you His explanation. So you do not have that license.

And when it comes to ourselves, we need to make the distinction between the things that are out of our hands and the things we can control. For the things beyond our control, we say, Inna Lillahi wa inna ilaihi rajioon. And for the things that are within our control, we need to take responsibility for them. We must acknowledge that we were the ones who fell short. We are the ones who should have done better. What is happening to me is the result of my own misconduct.

From the sermon of Hassan Elwan.

Allah tells us about this reality of our lives in the Qur'an. He tells us what to expect.

أَحَسِبَ ٱلنَّاسُ أَن يُتْرَكُوٓا۟ أَن يَقُولُوٓا۟ آمَنَّا وَهُمْ لَا يُفْتَنُونَ ‏وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ ۖ فَلَيَعْلَمَنَّ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا۟ وَلَيَعْلَمَنَّ ٱلْكَذِبِينَ
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Do people really think that they can say they believe and be left untested? Without any doubt, We have tested the people who came before them, so that it becomes known—so that it becomes completely plain—who among them were true in their claims and who were not, who were the liars.

What does this verse mean? What is the whole idea of a test? Why are we tested in school? The entire purpose of a test in school is separation. There are two kinds of students who go to school: those who actually study and actually learn, and those who are there to have fun, who are simply there for a good time. Now, both types of students can claim that they go to school and that they truly want to study, and they can back up their claim by pointing out that they are indeed there in school, and therefore true to the cause. But when a teacher needs to separate out the ones who actually studied from the ones who did not, what must he do? He has to conduct a test.

Now, does this teacher not already know which students study and which do not? Does a teacher not already know the studious ones from the clowns? He does. Then why does he actually need to give a test? There are two reasons for this. The first is so that the good can be separated from the bad, with actual proof provided by the hands of the students themselves. So when a student does poorly on the test, his grade is a witness against him. The teacher is exempt from the charge of injustice. The student cannot claim that the teacher is prejudiced, or biased, or unfair, because the proof is in the pudding. The incorrect answers to the questions are proof against the student himself, and the correct answers of the student who actually did study are proof in his favor. So in both cases the teacher is free of any blame.

The second reason is that the test allows the students to know where they truly stand. There could be a student who really believes he is studying and holds some delusions about his work ethic. But when he receives a bad grade, when he simply cannot perform well in an exam, it is an eye-opener for him.

He comes to realize that whatever method he has been using is not working. He must change something if he is to do better. The purpose of the test, then, is to distinguish the good from the bad, so that when the good is rewarded and the bad is punished, the student cannot blame the teacher. And secondly, if there are any delusions of grandeur in the student's mind, they can be shattered, and the student can be brought back to reality.

Now, does a teacher make his students aware that there will be a test at the end of the school year? And does he tell them of it two days before the final examination, or at the beginning of the year? He tells them at the beginning of the year. So every student knows that an examination is coming, and that his future will depend upon its results. Once again, this frees the teacher of any charge of injustice. He informs the students about the examination the moment the school year begins. He teaches all of them the same subjects, and at the end of the year he tests them with the same questions.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Now, do all the students in the school possess the same intellectual capacity, or do they differ in their levels of intelligence? They differ in their levels of intelligence. They come from different backgrounds. Their circumstances and situations are all their own. But does the final examination take any of this into account? Does it ever happen that the teacher says, "Listen, you come from a poor household, and I know you must help your parents with other matters on top of your homework, so I will grade you differently"—while to another student, who comes from a well-off family and carries no outside responsibilities or pressures, the teacher says, "I will grade you differently, more strictly, because your circumstances were easier"? He does not do this. It does not happen in life. Every student, whatever his situation, whatever his intellectual capacity, faces the same test at the end of the year, and all are graded and judged equally. This is what happens in the academic world. This is what happens in the professional world. This is what happens all around us in the physical world. This is the standard.

Now, what is a test? A test is a difficult situation into which you are placed. You have been taught a certain subject, and now you are asked questions about that subject, to see whether you give the correct answer or not. In the movies we see soldiers put through rigorous training; but to graduate, they must pass through a live simulation that is made very difficult for them. Is that not so? They have already endured harsh physical training. Why, then, is there a need to make the final test even more demanding and more difficult? Why are they pushed to their very limits? And what would happen if this were not done, and the final test were made very simple? Let us think about it. When an army pushes its cadets to their limit in order to select only a handful, what is it trying to choose? It is trying to choose the best. That is, if the country takes pride in its soldiers, it would not want just anyone to become a soldier.

They would want the very best, because the honor they are about to bestow is itself the very best. And so the best of the best receive one rank in the army, those below them receive another, and those below them a different rank again. Placement is decided by final performance. You would agree that this is the fairest way to decide who receives which position. The purpose of a test, then, is to establish ranking.

Now Allah says:

وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم بِشَىْءٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْخَوْفِ وَٱلْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْأَمْوَلِ وَٱلْأَنفُسِ وَٱلثَّمَرَتِ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ ٱلصَّبِرِينَ

And certainly, We shall test you with something of fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives and fruits, but give glad tidings to As-Sabirin.

This life, for a believer, is a test. We are all in Allah's examination room. And what is the training we gain through this test? What is the correct answer to these tests? It is sabr. Patience. Patience is the correct answer to the tests we are placed in. I will say it again: patience is the correct answer to the tests we are placed in. For Allah says, Wa Bashir al-Sabireen — to the patient, glad tidings. It is the patient one who will be congratulated in the end.
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
Now, when do you congratulate someone? When you are giving them a reward. The soldiers are put through their training. They are put through that grueling test. And then those who make it through — you have seen it in the films, where they are all lined up, and the general goes to each of them one by one, shaking their hands, giving them a medal. What is he saying? What word does he certainly use? Congratulations. Congratulations is a word used when giving a reward. So with Allah, what makes us worthy of congratulations? It is sabr. It is patience.

And for that patience, what is the reward we are going to receive? The reward is Jannah. Heaven. And we know that there are ranks within heaven. Heaven is not a single, level plane. There are ranks within it, and the highest ranks are given to the highest performers. And if the performance expected of us is patience, then who receives the highest rank? The one who is the most patient.

And in order to test whether someone is the most patient, what must the examiner do? He must put that person through a difficult test. For the more difficult the test, the greater the need for patience. And the greater the difficulty, the harder the test, the greater the reward, and the higher the rank in heaven. So the reason Allah places us in trials and tribulations is to see how patient we can be. Patience is the price of Jannah. There are all these different ranks in heaven, and each rank has a price, which is determined by the measure of our patience.

Allah says:

أَمْ حَسِبْتُمْ أَن تَدْخُلُوا۟ ٱلْجَنَّةَ وَلَمَّا يَأْتِكُم مَّثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ خَلَوْا۟ مِن قَبْلِكُم ۖ مَّسَّتْهُمُ ٱلْبَأْسَآءُ وَٱلضَّرَّآءُ وَزُلْزِلُوا۟ حَتَّىٰ يَقُولَ ٱلرَّسُولُ وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ مَعَهُۥ مَتَىٰ نَصْرُ ٱللَّهِ ۗ أَلَآ إِنَّ نَصْرَ ٱللَّهِ قَرِيبٌۭ

Did you think you will enter Paradise without such as came to those who passed away before you?

They were afflicted with severe poverty and illness and were so shaken that even the Messenger and those who believed along with him said, "When will the help of Allah come?" Yes! Surely the help of Allah is near.

Now the question people ask is this: why does Allah need to put us through these trials in order to grant us our ranks in Heaven? Well, the answer to that is this. Why does a teacher not simply pass every student and move them on to the next grade? Why must he put them through a test? That is very cruel of the teacher, is it not? But is it? Is the teacher truly being cruel by refusing to pass every student to the next grade without a test? He is not. It is in fact the mercy of the teacher not to pass everyone to the next grade. Why is that? Because the student who has not grasped the level of knowledge required at that particular grade will not be able to survive the next grade. He will not be able to benefit from the knowledge offered at the next level. The person who has not earned the measure of patience required for a particular rank in Heaven will not be able to take advantage of the gifts and pleasures offered by that rank in Heaven. Do you understand?
body.topic_title_en: Why Bad Things Happen to Good People
body.topic_title_ur: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People

body.text_en:
In the previous session we studied the meaning of the ayah من شر الوسواس الخناس. We know that in this surah we seek Allah's protection from one specific evil in particular: from the evil of الوسواس and الخناس, the one who whispers without ceasing and withdraws without ceasing. We came to understand how relentless, how incessant, and how oppressive Shaytan is in his whispering. For this reason we must continually seek the protection of Rabb al-Naas, Malik al-Naas, and Ilah al-Naas from the evil of this الوسواس الخناس. Now, having described this evil being — Shaytan himself — Allah proceeds to describe his evil deeds. So the surah continues: الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس, the one who whispers constantly into the chests of people; من الجنۃ و الناس, whether he be from among the jinn or from among mankind.

Let us look at the first ayah: الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس, the one who whispers constantly into the chests of people. The first thing to notice here is that Allah mentions whispering once again. He had already mentioned it in the previous ayah, من شر الوسواس الخناس. Yet now He says it again: الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس. So let us begin by understanding the reason for this repetition.

In the previous ayah we see that Allah mentioned the identity of this evil being, and here He mentions the action of that evil being. And He used the present-tense form یُوَسوِسُ for it as well. So we saw that Shaytan is الوسواس, that Shaytan is one who whispers, and one who will continue to whisper without cease until the end of time. The next thing I want you to understand is that الوسواس is an ism; it is a noun. الاسم یدُلُّو علی الدوام: a noun signifies permanence.

In the Arabic language, as in every other language, you can use nouns and you can use verbs. What is the difference between a verb and a noun? Between nouns and verbs, which of them has tenses — present tense, future tense, past tense? Verbs have a tense. Nouns do not have a tense. There is no past-tense noun, no present-tense noun, and no future-tense noun. Is that clear? When I say, "I am eating," it means I am eating now, but at some point I will stop. A verb is bound to time. It has happened, it is happening, or it will happen; but it is temporary, and at some point it ceases. A noun, however, is permanent. It does not change its state. A book is a book, was a book, is a book, and will always remain a book. It is not going to change its state. Do you understand?

So, if Shaytan is al-Waswas, let us first understand what identity is. When I say to you, "I am a teacher," do you know what that means? It means that this is who I am; this is what I do. Shaytan has been identified as الوسواس الخناس: one who constantly, incessantly, relentlessly whispers and withdraws. That is his identity. That is why in the previous ayah the noun الوسواس is used. But in this ayah Allah uses a verb, یُوسوِسُ. Why? Because Shaytan actually lives up to that title as well. It is one thing to be given a title, but it is another thing altogether to earn that title by actually doing the deed.

That is what the present tense یُوسوِسُ tells us. For in ancient Arabic, when the present tense was used, the future tense was implied within it. So this word یُوسوِسُ tells us that not only is Shaytan known for being a whisperer, known for his constant and unrelenting whispering, but that he is actually doing it now, and that he will continue to do it in the future. So you had better be ready. You had better always be prepared.

He is never going to stop. There is never going to be a time or a moment when you can imagine that you are free from his whispers. And this in turn means that there is never going to be a time when you and I will not need Allah's protection. We are constantly under attack; therefore we constantly need Allah's protection. Even when we are engaged in acts of religion, such as prayer, fasting, alms, and pilgrimage, he will whisper to us in every single moment.

But then Allah added something quite remarkable. He said فی صدور الناس — in the chest of people. The word صدر, chest, according to the Arabic lexicon, is ظرف مکان. It is in fact a place. In the Quran, sadr is always used in the sense of a place or a space. رب الشرح لی صدری — Master, expand my chest. Once again in the sense of space.

In contrast to this, there is the word قلب, which is a thing. Allah did not say الذی یوسوس فی قلوب الناس — he constantly whispers, and will continue to whisper, in the hearts of people. Allah did not say that. He did not use the word heart. He used the word chest. Now what is the difference?

There is in fact a great difference between saying that he whispers in the heart and saying that he whispers in the chest. In the earlier sessions, we spoke about how the heart is the center of all human activity. Everything a person does, the desire for it first arises in the heart, and is then turned into action with the help of the intellect. But the origin of desire is always the heart.

Now consider the image this verse creates. Think of it in this way. The heart is like a castle, and around the castle there is some open ground — a front yard, a side yard, a backyard. So there is all this ground around the castle. The castle is your heart, and the surrounding ground is your chest. The heart lies inside your chest. Allah says that he gave Shaytan access to what? To the chest. But Allah did not give Shaytan access to the heart.

So Shaytan is lounging in the front yard, or he is sunning himself in the backyard. In short, he is all around, but he is not yet where? He is not in the heart. The heart is locked. And the only one who holds the key to the door of your heart is you. He is constantly knocking on the door with his whispers. He is waiting outside, patiently. He is always there. الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس. He is constantly knocking on the door of your heart, hoping that one day you will open that door for him and let him enter your heart.

A true believer has the same relationship with the Qur'an. He enters the fortress of the Qur'an to replenish his energies, to revitalize himself with the teachings of the Qur'an. But where is he going to actually carry out those teachings? In the outside world. In the dunya. So the idea is that we, as momins, as believers, we keep coming back to the Qur'an constantly, to remind ourselves of its teachings, and then go back into the world to act upon what we have learned.

But as soon as we step outside, whom do we encounter? Our greatest enemy, who has openly declared his hostility against us. We encounter Iblees, or one of his shaytans, who openly declared to Allah:

قَالَ فَبِمَآ أَغْوَيْتَنِى لَأَقْعُدَنَّ لَهُمْ صِرَطَكَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ

Because you were the one who expelled me from jannah, I will sit waiting for them, to ambush them on your straight path. صِرَطَكَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ. Which surah mentions the straight path? اھدنا الصراط المستقیم. Surah Fateha mentions the straight path.

We are asking Allah to protect us from Iblees, because he is on a mission to get us off the straight path. We learn the details of how to walk on the straight path in the Qur'an. But when we step outside and try to walk on that straight path, whom do we find sitting there, waiting to ambush us? Iblees. And that is why these two surahs of protection, Falaq and Naas, are so intimately connected with Surah AlFateha. Because we need Allah's protection when we are walking that straight path, because we know that Iblees is going to be there, trying to get us off.

Then, from a thematic standpoint, the themes of these two surahs, Falaq and Naas, have powerful connections with AlFateha. Surah Fatiha is about the استعانۃ. We will study this term later. But استعانۃ means seeking help, which is what Surah AlFateha is all about. ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین. It is you we worship, and it is you we turn to for help. So in Fateha we have two statements for the Istiaana: ایاک نعبد and ایاک نستعین. And here we have two surahs for the Istiaaza, for protection: Surah Falaq and Surah Naas. There we ask Allah for help; here we ask Allah for protection. You have heard of positive and negative reinforcements, right? In Fateha we ask Allah for help in accomplishing a task; in معوذِتین we ask Allah for His protection against elements that are trying to keep us from completing that task.

Then the words of these surahs, especially Surah Naas, complement the words of AlFateha. In Surah Naas we seek the protection of the owner and master of all people, رب الناس. In AlFateha, what do we call him? رب العلمین, owner and master of all worlds. In Fateha we say مالک یوم الدین. In Surah AlNaas we say ملک الناس. Both Maalik and Malik, they both have the same root word. In Fateha we say ایاک نعبد, it is you we worship. And whom is worship done for? A deity? An Ilah? Right? So in Surah AlNaas we say الہ الناس.

Then we see that the معوذِتین are the two surahs of protection, and in Surah AlFateha we ask Allah to keep us away from two kinds of people, or two bad influences: مغضوب علیھم ولا الضالین. And then in Surah Fateha, just as we have these two negative influences, the مغضوب علیھم ولا الضالین. In Surah Naas.

we have two categories of evil from which we seek protection: من الجنۃ و الناس, from the jinn and from people. SubhanAllah! There are these remarkable connections between these two surahs and Surah al-Fateha. The way in which the Qur'an begins perfectly complements the way in which it ends.

Then there is another striking thing: the parallel between the singular and plural forms used across the two surahs. The very word used in the معوذتین for seeking protection is in the singular form, اعوذ. But the words used in the Fateha for seeking guidance are all in the plural. We say ایاک نعبد, not ایاک أعبدُ. So there is this balance between singular and plural, because the things we ask for in the Fateha are things we need as a group: as a group of Muslims, or a group of momins, or a group of Sulemanis. Look at it however you wish, but the Fateha has a group theme running through it, because our communication with Allah in the Fateha is as a group, not as individuals. We speak to Him, seeking His guidance, collectively.

But when it comes to the waswas of the shaytan, is it a collective thing or an individual thing? It is an individual thing. Therefore, in the معوذِتین, the theme is individual, not collective, because these two surahs ask for Allah's protection on a very personal and individual level, and so the verb usage is singular as well.

I misjudged the level of my audience. These sessions are not for children.

Now think of استعاذہ as a security guard that you have posted outside the door of your heart. The moment you say اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم, the guard appears and does not let Shaytan come near the heart. He throws him back into the front yard. But if you do not keep calling upon that guard for protection, Shaytan will keep knocking, and knocking, and knocking. And what will happen? Eventually you will open the door, and Shaytan will step inside.

Do you know what happens next? What do you think will happen when Shaytan walks from the chest into the heart?

You know people who have iman, people who have faith. Do you know what is the most beautiful thing to them? Their faith itself. وَلَكِنَّ ٱللَّهَ حَبَّبَ إِلَيْكُمُ ٱلْإِيمَنَ وَزَيَّنَهُۥ فِى قُلُوبِكُمْ — Allah has made the love of faith.

She has made faith beautiful to the hearts.

وَكَرَّهَ إِلَيْكُمُ ٱلْكُفْرَ وَٱلْفُسُوقَ وَٱلْعِصْيَانَ

And He has made ugly disbelief, lewdness, shamelessness, and disobedience. This is the original state of the hearts. It is natural for a human being to find beauty in what is good. It is natural for a human being to find beauty in modesty, in courage, in truth, in respect, in obedience. Because this is the fitrah, this is the nature upon which Allah created us. By nature we are drawn to fragrance and repelled by stench.

When there is faith in our hearts, the heart stays soft. And a thing that is soft can be molded. It can be changed, it can be transformed. A soft thing is always open to change. But once Shaytan enters the heart,

وَلَكِن قَسَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ ٱلشَّيْطَنُ مَا كَانُوا۟ يَعْمَلُونَ

then the heart becomes hard, and evil deeds begin to look beautiful. They begin to look tempting, they begin to look good. If the remembrance of Allah is in our hearts, evil deeds will naturally look ugly. وَكَرَّهَ إِلَيْكُمُ ٱلْكُفْرَ وَٱلْفُسُوقَ وَٱلْعِصْيَانَ, because Allah made disbelief, corruption, and disobedience disgusting to the hearts. So if you have faith in your hearts, those things will look disgusting to you, naturally. You will not even be tempted toward them. You could drive past a club and feel the urge to say استغفر اللہ، لا حول ولا قوة الا بالله. What a waste of humanity. What a disgrace to the son of Adam. Allah honored Adam with such intellect, and to what level have his children stooped. Leaping like monkeys in the name of enjoyment. What a life of animals they are ready to live. By your fitrah, by your nature, you would spit at it. You would be repelled by it. That would be your natural response, if faith is in your heart.

But if Shaytan has made his way into your hearts: Let me just pull over and check it out a little. Oh, that skimpy dress on her looks really good. She looks really hot. They look so cool smoking and drinking. He sounds so cool using profanity, throwing the F bomb into every sentence. I should try that. Let me dress in a way that shows my body to the world. Sexuality, shamelessness, lewdness, all these things become very attractive when Shaytan is in our heart.

This is the difference between the heart that has kept Shaytan out and the heart that has invited him in. Now the question this ayah asks us is: where do we stand? When we see such things, are we disgusted by them, are we repelled by them, or are we fascinated by them, are we attracted to them? The honest answer to that question will tell us the true state of faith in our hearts. If faith is beautiful, then disbelief, corruption, and disobedience will look evil, they will look disgusting. And if Shaytan has entered the heart, it will be the other way around. It is as simple as that.

So it is in fact from the mercy of Allah that He gave Shaytan access to the chest but not to the heart. Had He allowed Shaytan to whisper into the hearts, we would have no defense against him, we would not be able to use our will against him. That is why Allah did not give Shaytan direct access to the heart. It is you and I who open the doors of our heart to him. That is on us. We are the ones who do that.

Now if Shaytan is already in our hearts, what do we have to do to get him out?

We have to call the guard. We have to dial the spiritual emergency line, which is the Istiaaza: اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم. We have to recite these two surahs. We have to submit to Allah willingly, in obedience, seeking His constant protection from the constant waswasa of Shaytan. We have to call upon رب الفلق; we have to call upon رب الناس، ملک الناس، الہ الناس, in order to evict Shaytan from our hearts. And once he is out, we have to place these security guards outside our heart again, to prevent him from entering once more. That is through the constant remembrance of Allah.

The surah then moves to its final ayah: من الجنۃ و الناس. Allah classifies the evil whisperers by declaring that they belong to two categories. What is also so remarkable about this surah is that, if you recall, we saw a progression in the names of Allah. We saw how Rabb progressed to Malik, the King, and then Malik progressed to Ilah. Now we see a similar progression here in the details of the evil entity. Allah begins by describing the entity itself: من شر الوسواس الخناس. He then progresses to describe the act and the place he attacks: الذی یوسوس فی قلوب الناس. And now He progresses to describing the two categories to which these evil entities belong: من الجنۃ و الناس. They are from the Jinn and from mankind. Allah uses three ayats to describe the protector. He then uses three ayats to describe the evil from which we are seeking protection. You can see how beautifully this surah is balanced: three ayats speak of Allah, and three ayats speak of evil.

And do you know why that is? Because there are, fundamentally, only three evils in the world. If you take the common denominator of all evils, it comes down to three things: کبر، حرص، حسد. Pride, Greed, and Jealousy. These three are called امہات المعاصی, the mothers of all evils. Every evil that you know of in this world stems from these three root evils: Pride, Greed, and Jealousy. And that is why these three particular names of Allah are called upon: Rabb, Malik, and Ilah.

Jealousy is always bound up with love. You love someone or something, but the one you love favors somebody or something else, and you become jealous. Which of the three names of Allah is associated with pure love? Rabb. That is why, to guard against jealousy, we say what? قل اعوذ برب الناس. We seek the protection of the One who has the ultimate love, against the evil of jealousy that stems from a deviation in love.

Similarly, Greed is always bound up with possessions. You have something, and you want more and more of it; that is greed. Who has the most possessions of all? A king does. That is why we call upon ملک الناس. We seek the protection of the One who holds the ultimate kingship over all.

And finally, Pride. Who alone is worthy of ultimate pride? It is the Ilah, the Deity. Pride befits only the Ilah. Therefore we seek protection from pride and arrogance by turning to the Ilah: الہ الناس. The ultimate, and the only One, truly worthy of pride.

So there is this beautiful symmetry between the three primary roots of evil — Jealousy, Greed, and Pride — and the protection sought through these three specific names of Allah against those three evils. SubhanAllah.

So now Allah classifies the whisperers into two categories: Jinn and human beings. Now the first thing is the order in which these two categories are mentioned.

Allah mentioned the jinn first and mankind second. Now why is that? Because there are other places in the Qur'an where, when the subject is Satan, Allah mentions human beings first and the jinn later. وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلْنَا لِكُلِّ نَبِىٍّ عَدُوًّۭا شَيَٰطِينَ ٱلْإِنسِ وَٱلْجِنِّ — And in this way, for every prophet We appointed an enemy from among the devils of mankind and the jinn. In this verse we see that the human devils are mentioned first, and the spiritual devils, the jinn, are mentioned second. But in Surah an-Nas we see that the order is reversed: the jinn are mentioned first and الناس are mentioned second. Why is that?

There are several reasons. The obvious reason is that in the verse I just mentioned, وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلْنَا لِكُلِّ نَبِىٍّ عَدُوًّۭا, the verse is speaking about the prophets. And when it comes to the prophets, the animosity against them always originates from human beings first. Human beings go outright against the messenger of Allah. Since they take precedence in their animosity against the prophets, human beings are mentioned first in this verse.

But because the context of our surah, Surah an-Nas, is not animosity against the prophets — it is وسوسۃ against human beings — who takes the primary role? The jinn. That is why in this surah the jinn are mentioned first and human beings later.

Another reason the jinn are mentioned first and human beings later is that one is spiritual and the other is physical. The jinn is a soul without a body; it is in spiritual form. Naas, human beings, are in physical form. And we see that this surah is all about the attack upon our soul. Surah al-Falaq was about seeking protection from physical attacks, but Surah an-Nas is about seeking protection from spiritual attacks. And because of that, the jinn, the ones in spiritual form, are mentioned first, and Naas, the ones in physical form, are mentioned second.

Another reason is that it is the corruption of the soul that leads to the corruption of the body. It is the evil desire, that feeling of arrogance, of contempt, of jealousy, that comes first. And where do these evil desires and feelings originate? In the heart, which is placed where? In the chest — which is exactly where Satan attacks. So the intention behind these whisperings is to corrupt the soul first, because that will inevitably lead to the corruption of physical actions through sins. That is why the spiritual form, the jinn, is mentioned first, and the physical form, Naas, is mentioned second — because the corruption will happen first in the soul and will then proceed into actions.

Another reason the jinn are mentioned first is that the scholars comment, وسوسۃ الجن، ھو الاصل — the whispering of the jinn is primary. This means that if a human being is whispering evil to you, it may not even be his own whisper. He may be taking it from the whispering of his own Satan. Because Satan could not reach you directly, he is now using someone you are associated with in order to reach you. Do you understand? It is possible that the human being whispering to you is being moved by the whisperings of a jinn. So when a human being carries out waswasa, it could be because a jinn is controlling him. But when a jinn carries out waswasa, it is always his own doing. That is why من الجنۃ comes first, and then, secondarily, و الناس.

So what we are learning here is the concept of vehicles. Satan uses vehicles.

This means the whisperings of Satan can reach you through your best friend. They can come through your favorite cousin, a relative. You hear their voice. You do not hear Satan's voice. But do you know what? At that moment, that person is a puppet for Iblees.

And do you know why you young people find it so hard to fight these emotions and desires? Because Satan's attacks are fiercest against the young. Why? Because you are the future. If he manages to corrupt your minds, he not only has you in his pocket, he also has the next generation. You are the greatest return on his investment, as the saying goes. And also because young people today have no locks on the doors of their hearts. Forget locks; some of you have removed the entire door. There is a huge opening, with a sign hanging out: Let us party. All devils welcome aboard!

Because this is how Satan works. Even if the man is religious, Satan will still whisper to him. The man walks into a bookstore and sees a beautiful young woman buying a book. Even if it is the Qur'an, he will walk up to her. Hey, what are you buying? Oh, the Qur'an? Nice. What is your favorite surah? Oh really? Surah Fateha. Mine too. I am actually attending these Sunday sessions about it. Would you like to join? Can I get your number? Ha, ha. Do not get any ideas. I am joking, but this is truly how he operates.

And now he does not even need to use people. He has websites and television channels and Hollywood and Bollywood; he has his work on DVD. We have made his job easy for him, through modern mass media. Now of course, mass media could be used for great things. But for the most part, what is it used for? To promote shamelessness and evil things.

Now, the complication in this word naas. In the Arabic language there is a word نفر, nafar, which is commonly used for a group of people, and there is also the word رجال, which is typically used for a group of people. The Qur'an says:

قُلْ أُوحِىَ إِلَىَّ أَنَّهُ ٱسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَقَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا سَمِعْنَا قُرْآنًا عَجَبًۭا

a group of people from among the jinn. The word nafar is typically not used for jinn; it is used for human beings. But in this verse it is used for jinn. Similarly we have:

وَأَنَّهُۥ كَانَ رِجَالٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْإِنسِ يَعُوذُونَ بِرِجَالٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَزَادُوهُمْ رَهَقًۭا

There used to be men from among the human beings who sought refuge with men among the jinn. So here rijaal is being used for men as well as for jinn.

Now, in one of the narrations it is said that some men met a group of people who looked very strange. So they asked them, من القوم, who are you? What nation do you come from? They replied, أناسٌ من الجن. Very interesting language. They said, we are people from the jinn. But what word did they use for themselves? The plural of naas, unaas.

So another interpretation of this verse is that Allah says الذی یوسوس فی صدور الناس, the one who whispers into the chest of the naas. من الجنۃ و الناس, those naas, those people, can be from among the jinn as well as the human beings. So this surah is not only a protection for believers among human beings; it is also a protection for believers among the jinn. So the word naas in this interpretation encompasses both.

The human beings as well as the jinn. So the same verse can be taken in two entirely opposite ways.

These, then, are the two kinds of whisperers named in this surah. We now understand the whispering of the jinn: that it appears in the form of thoughts and desires in our heads. He keeps prodding and probing at us, and because he keeps drawing back, we begin to imagine that these are our own thoughts. So we can see how an unseen jinn whispers to us. But what of the whisperings of the human devil, or of someone who is being used as a vehicle by a jinn? How do those whisperings appear? For this verse names both.

A whisper. The first thing to grasp is that it is a whisper. Now we usually think of a whisper as someone sitting beside us and saying something to us under their breath. wswswswsws. That, we think, is whispering. But there is another form of whispering that is far more common. And it happens all the time on the phone, in the form of texts. We do it all the time, and it is done to us all the time as well. It sounds something like this. Hey! I will tell you something about this person, but just do not tell anyone I told you, all right? Blah blah blah blah blah. Does that sound familiar? Be very careful of that.

Now if this person is telling you something in confidence, with the intention of protecting you or helping you — for example, if someone is trying to warn you about the evil intentions of someone who is trying to harm you — that is a different matter. That is not waswasa; that is hamasa. It is not being done with evil intent. That kind of whispering is being done with good intentions, in order to protect you. There is a difference. That is not waswasa; that is hamasa. I explained the difference between the two words last time.

But more often than not, what is being done is waswasa, especially when it is about a third person. Someone fills you up with anger and hostility against your friend or your cousin, and then this whisperer draws back by saying, "Do not tell anyone I told you." And now, the next time you meet this person, everything about him seems wrong. The way he walks, the way he is dressed, the way he talks, the way he laughs. And you sit there wondering, why did I ever like this person in the first place? Has that ever happened? What suddenly changed? You liked this person before; now, all at once, you do not like anything about him. It is because of that silent whispering, done to you under the cover of, "Do not tell anyone I told you," "I tell you everything because you are my best friend," "I trust you so much that I feel I can tell you anything." wswswswswswsws. Be very careful of that!

A man once came to one of the sahabas and tried to slander another Muslim brother. He said, you know this man; he pretends to be a Muslim. He is such a hypocrite. He drinks alcohol and he gambles, and he does all sorts of evil deeds, and still comes and prays in the masjid. And the sahaba replied to him, could Shaytan not find a better postman than you? Could he not find a better messenger than you to deliver this gossip to me?

Be very careful of that. Many people in our lives act as messengers of Shaytan, and they do not even know it. Many times we act as the messengers of Shaytan without realizing it. Be careful!

And the recitation of this surah gives us insight, and a reminder to recognize this in ourselves as well as in others. So, to summarize: the protection we are seeking is the protection of the master of people who forget, رب الناس; the king of people who forget, ملک الناس; the god of people who forget, الہ الناس. And this protection is from the evil entity, الوسواس الخناس, who attacks through his whispers, الذی یوسوس. And where does he attack? فی صدور الناس, in the chests of people, which contain what? The heart. And these attackers, to which two categories do they belong? من الجنۃ و الناس; they are from the jinn and from human beings.

In the first meaning, the Shaytan who does the whispering may take a spiritual form as well as a physical form. In the second meaning, the Shaytan who does the whispering may whisper to human beings as well as to the jinn. For we know that Allah created not only human beings but also jinn for the purpose of worshipping him. وَمَا خَلَقْتُ ٱلْجِنَّ وَٱلْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ — I did not create the jinn and human beings except to worship me.

Now, are the angels not a creation of Allah too? Then why did he not mention them in this verse? Are they not created for his worship as well? Why did he not say, وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الملائکۃ و ٱلْجِنَّ وَٱلْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ — I did not create the angels, the jinn, and human beings except to worship me? Because the angels are already doing what they are meant to do. They are always occupied in worshipping him, and they are not affected by the whisperings of Shaytan. Shaytan cannot reach them in any way, shape, or form. They are always under the protection of Allah. It is human beings and jinn who fall prey to the whisperings of Shaytan. And once Shaytan enters their hearts and takes over their hearts, he uses both of them to advance his cause. This is the same idea as a virus: it infects other cells and makes them like itself in order to advance its cause.

Appreciation of protection through danger

That concludes our study of these two surahs. Now the question is this: how are the Istiaaza and these two surahs even related to Surah al-Fateha? Why are we studying the Istiaaza instead of studying the Fateha?

Imagine there is a great storm coming. Where would you rather be when the storm strikes your town? Most likely in your house. Your house is a symbol of safety against the storm. But the reason you value that safety is that you understand the dangers of the storm, yes? You cannot appreciate safety until you understand the danger you are being protected from. You appreciate the air conditioning in your house because you have felt the heat outside. You appreciate the heating in your house because you have felt the freezing cold outside. We human beings understand things through contrast. The one who truly appreciates and values food is the one who has a real understanding of hunger, someone who has genuinely experienced hunger. You know, you can tell, simply by looking at someone who wastes food, that this person has never experienced hunger. I am not speaking of the hunger you feel after a tennis match, when you come home and the refrigerator is full. I am not speaking of that hunger. I am speaking of the hunger in which you have not eaten for days, and there is nothing in the refrigerator at home. That man, when he gets food.

you can see him appreciating the value of that food. So Surah al-Fateha is a fortress. It is a safe haven. But in order to truly appreciate its value, to truly appreciate what it has to offer us in terms of security, what must we first understand? The dangers. We needed first to understand the dangers, the evils that surround this fortress. The Istiaaza is the door of that fortress, the door that keeps the evils out and keeps us safe within. So we began with the Istiaaza. We began with the dangers of evil, so that we could truly appreciate the comforts within the Fateha. That is why we began with the Istiaaza, and this is what Allah commanded us to do.

فأذا قرأت القرآن فستعذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم

Before you enter the fortress of the Quran, seek protection. Close the door on Shaytan al-Rajeem. But first, understand what the Quran is protecting you from, so that you can truly appreciate its protection.

But then I began with these two surahs, Surah al-Naas and Surah al-Falaq, because they are deeply connected with Surah al-Fateha. I want to go over some of these connections quickly, InshaAllah.

The first connection is the cyclic pattern in the recitation of the Quran. When we recite the Quran, which surah do we begin with? We begin with the Fateha. And before we begin the Fateha, what do we recite? The Istiaaza. We say اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم. So we begin with the Istiaaza, then we begin Surah al-Fateha, which is the essence of the entire Quran, and then we continue reciting the surahs until we complete the recitation of the Quran. But at the end of our recitation, what are the last two surahs we encounter? Surah al-Falaq and Surah al-Naas, both surahs of the Istiaaza. We begin with the Istiaaza and we end with the Istiaaza.

So think of the Quran as a beautiful and comfortable house, a safe haven, your fortress of solitude. Before you enter it, you seek protection from evil, and then you enter the house. Why? So that you can enjoy all the comforts the house has to offer. That is the recitation of the Quran. And then, when you are ready to step outside, you again pass through the Istiaaza in the form of Surah al-Falaq and Surah al-Naas, so that you remain protected while you are outside the house. So it protects us on both ends, when we enter the fortress of the Quran and when we leave it.

But then, once you complete the recitation of the Quran, what do you do immediately after that? You read a dua, the dua recited at the completion of the Quran, and then you recite which surah again? Surah al-Fateha. You began the Quran with the Istiaaza, you ended it with the Istiaaza, and at the end of it you recite the Fateha again. And then you begin the entire process again.

When you step out of your house, you go to school or work. Where do you end up returning in the evening? Back to your home again. So there is this cyclic pattern in the recitation of the Quran, with protection on both ends.

There is something truly important to understand about this analogy between a house and the Quran. As I said, we always begin our day by leaving our homes, and at the end of our day we return to our homes. But where do we spend our entire day? Outside the house. At school or at work, at tennis or basketball, at tutions, at whatever. We spend most of our time outside the house. Yes? So the home is not a place where we spend most of our time. We spend it outside. But the home is a place where we gather our energies, where we eat and drink and relax and sleep.

those are all actions that replenish our energy. They recharge our battery. Correct? These things refresh us. They revitalize us. But where do we actually spend this energy? Outside our homes. Is that clear?

We are studying the story of Adam, upon him be peace, and Iblees through this passage from Surah al-A'raf, the seventh surah, whose name means the Heights, or a place of elevated station. One thing to grasp is that although we regard this as a primordial story, the truth is that it is unfolding still. This story of Adam, upon him be peace, and Iblees is being played out in our own lives, again and again. And it is, above all, a story of two characters, or two creatures: Adam, upon him be peace, and Iblees. Hawwa is mentioned as well, but she is joined together with Adam. In every place where Adam is named, the word ھما is used, which is the dual form, signifying the two of them together. So Allah says in Surah al-A'raf: وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَكُمْ ثُمَّ صَوَّرْنَكُمْ — And we created you both and fashioned you both. ثُمَّ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ ٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوٓا۟ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ — and then we commanded the angels to bow down to you. They all did so except Iblees. لَمْ يَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّجِدِينَ — He was never going to be among those who submit. We spoke at length about what the word sajda means. It is when the camel kneels, or submits itself before its rider, and surrenders its control to him. The idea of sajda is to give up our own will for the will of Allah.

So Iblees refuses to prostrate, and Allah asks him: قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ إِذْ أَمَرْتُكَ — What could possibly have stopped you from prostrating to Adam when I commanded you to do so? قَالَ أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهُ خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ — He said: I am better than him. You created me from fire, and you created him from clay. And we spoke in considerable depth in the previous session about the differences between fire and clay.

The two most important things to take away from this ayah are these. First, the realization that it was the arrogance of Iblees that led to his disobedience: أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهُ. And then what followed was خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ — You created me from fire, and you created him from clay — which was his very logical justification for his disobedience. The disbelief of Iblees was not that he failed to believe in Allah as his creator. The disbelief of Iblees showed itself through his disobedience.

So in almost every single case, when we wish to disobey Allah, when we wish to disobey a command of Allah that in our heart of hearts we know to be true, we will always devise a very good, very logical justification for it. And that justification will almost always be rooted in this physical world, because what Iblees used as his justification were material things. He said: I am fire and air, and Adam is earth and water. So the elements he used to justify his superiority were all material things; they were all physical things. He used مادۃ (material) to justify his disobedience — which, if you consider it, is exactly what we do as well. All the desires and pleasures that lead to the disobedience of Allah are grounded in this physical and material world. And that is a very powerful realization to hold, because many times we can recognize our own disobedience simply by examining our justifications.
body.topic_title_en: The Devil's Plan to Lead Astray

body.text_en:
So Allah says to Iblees: how dare you be arrogant before me. قَالَ فَٱهْبِطْ مِنْهَا — Fall out of here. Leave! I am casting you out. فَمَا يَكُونُ لَكَ أَن تَتَكَبَّرَ فِيهَا — You no longer deserve to remain in this place because of your arrogance. You cannot show pride here.

In other words, you are in the divine presence. This is not a place for pride. If you are truly aware of the glory of Allah, and if you know your own place in relation to Him, you cannot possibly stand before Him in a state of pride. فَٱخْرُجْ إِنَّكَ مِنَ ٱلصَّغِرِينَ. Get out of here, for you are among the Saghireen. Saghireen comes from صغر, or صغیر, which means small. Allah says that it is because of your pride: by being prideful and arrogant, you have placed yourself beneath the very one you imagined yourself to be above. So your own thinking, that you were superior to this other creature, is precisely what made you inferior to him.

And then Iblees says, قَالَ أَنظِرْنِىٓ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ. He says, give me some reprieve. Give me time, until the day these people will be raised again. Give me until the Day of Judgment. Once again, notice that Iblees not only believes in Allah as his creator; he also believes in the Day of Judgment. So this is not an atheist who disobeyed Allah. This is, in fact, a firm believer. This is a Momin, one who believes, who is disobeying Allah. And this is a very frightening reality when you think about it, because we too claim to be Momins. We too claim to be believers, do we not? Well, Iblees was a believer. And what made him Iblees was his disobedience. We are Allah's creation, just as he was. We disobey Allah too, just as he did. If his arrogance and disobedience turned him into Iblees and had him cast out of Jannah, why would that same justice not apply to us? So this is a very frightening reality if you think about it seriously. How are we any different, when we too disobey Allah and devise the most logical justifications for doing so?

Allah says to him, قَالَ إِنَّكَ مِنَ ٱلْمُنظَرِينَ. Very well. I give you time until the Day of Judgment.

Wait. What is happening here? Why is Iblees asking for time, and why is Allah granting him time? Before we answer these questions, let us understand something else first. It is a very common misconception that Iblees, or Shaytan, stands against Allah, that Iblees is somehow Allah's adversary (نعوذ باللہ من ذالک). That is absolutely incorrect. No one can stand against Allah. No one has the capability to stand against Allah. Iblees is a creation of Allah, and by his own words he accepts this. And a creation cannot stand against its creator. So this is the first thing we need to understand. Iblees is not standing against Allah. Iblees is standing against Adam and the children of Adam AS. He is standing against us. He is our enemy, our adversary. He is not Allah's adversary. The only reason he is even able to do what he does is that Allah has permitted him to. He does what he does with Allah's permission.

Let us begin with the second part. Why did Allah grant Iblees this time, in which he could misguide us? Would it not have been wonderful if Allah had simply imprisoned Iblees right there and then? So what made Allah accept the challenge of Iblees? Let us understand this part first.
body.topic_title_en: The Devil's Plan to Lead Astray

body.text_en:
Wait. What is this? Fill hellfire with all of you? Where did that come from? Allah is speaking about Iblees and his army; He should have said, "I will fill hellfire with them." But He did not say منھم اجمعین. He said منکم اجمعین. He does not say "all of them"; He says "all of you"! This is in fact لی الطوعیۃ, to frighten you; لی التحدید, to challenge you.... The one reading the Quran thinks: wait!

"Where did you come from? I thought Allah was going to say, 'I will fill hellfire with them.' Instead He says, 'I will fill hell with you!'" You are reading the Book, and all at once it is pointing at you. It is pointing at you and at me. "Wait — me?" And you resolve that you had better not follow Iblees, for the only way it can be pointing at you is if you follow Iblees. So this switch in subject is in fact a means of warning and of striking fear into us, and it is used throughout the Quran.

Allah giving Adam everything

Now, after expelling Iblees, Allah addresses Adam and Hawwa and says:

وَيَٓـَٔادَمُ ٱسْكُنْ أَنتَ وَزَوْجُكَ ٱلْجَنَّةَ

Adam, you and your wife, settle in Paradise. Notice this word Zawj. The word Zawj in fact means "companion," or partner. Allah referred to Adam and Hawwa as partners. I point this out because some men hold a certain way of thinking, and some mothers-in-law hold it about their sons — that when it comes to their perfect sons, the relationship of husband and wife is a relationship of master and slave. It is not. Had it been so, Allah would have said, وَيَٓـَٔادَمُ ٱسْكُنْ أَنتَ وَعَبدُک — Adam, you and your slave, settle in Paradise. He did not say that. He used the word Zawj: partner, companion.

In any case, Allah says: ٱسْكُنْ أَنتَ وَزَوْجُكَ ٱلْجَنَّةَ. And Allah did not even say Fil Jannah, that is, He did not point to a particular place or location within Paradise. He said AlJannah — all of heaven. Allah says that your new home is Paradise itself. You are not moving into a single house, inside a city, within a province of Paradise. The whole of it is your house. Every building there, every house there, every location there — all of it is your house. Adam and Hawwa, take it. Take all of it. And then He says:

فَكُلَا مِنْ حَيْثُ شِئْتُمَا

Eat and drink from whatever you desire. You need not check the label on anything; everything is halal. Eat and enjoy. Nor is it the case that one thing will turn out disappointing, so that you say, "That was not so good; we should go to the other one." That is us and our restaurants: sometimes the biryani comes out well and sometimes it does not. But in Paradise, eat whatever you wish. Everything will be excellent, all the time. Then, however, He says:

وَلَا تَقْرَبَا هَذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونَا مِنَ ٱلظَّلِمِينَ
body.topic_title_en: The Devil's Plan to Lead Astray

body.text_en:
But do not go near this one tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers. Allah forbids them to go near a single tree. Little attention is paid to the word هَذِهِ — this tree. Allah did not say تلک شرجۃ — that tree. He did not say that tree; He said this tree. What is the difference between this and that? This is near. So the forbidden is always near; the haram, the forbidden thing, is always near. Allah said to them: you have a great many options among what is permitted, but do not imagine that the forbidden is far away. It will always be near, and because it is near, you must guard against it. You can never say, "I am far from the haram." As vast as this universe of Paradise is — and how large is Paradise? Allah says:

وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا ٱلسَّمَوَتُ وَٱلْأَرْضُ

Its expanse is something like all seven heavens and the earth combined. The size of Paradise is the size of all seven heavens and the earth combined — and even that is only something set beside Paradise, not exactly equal to it.

Today we possess telescopes that reveal to us a magnification of the universe that humanity has never seen before. And Allah says that this vast expanse still does not compare to the size of Paradise. Yet even though Paradise is so immense, Allah uses the word "this" to point to the forbidden tree. He made this nearness, this accessibility of the forbidden, a part of the trial set before humanity: that the forbidden will always be near you, that it will always be within your reach, and that it will stir your curiosity.

I know it is forbidden, one says, but I am only curious. I am not doing anything. I am only wondering. I wonder what beer tastes like. I will never drink it; I only want to know its taste. I want to know what smoking feels like. I will give it up after one. I am only curious. I am only wondering. I only want to try it once. This is the meaning of وَلَا تَقْرَبَا هَذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةَ.

And here is something worth noticing. Allah did not say لا تأكل من هذه الشجرة. He did not say, do not eat from this tree. He said, do not go near this tree. The command was not about the eating. For it is not the tree we are drawn to; we are drawn to eating its fruit. Yet Allah says, do not even go near the tree. My command is not about the fruit; my command is about the tree. Do not even go near it. Do you understand what that means? It is not, do not drink alcohol. It means, do not even go near alcohol. It is not, do not take drugs. It means, do not even go near drugs.
