You can touch the bark of a tree. But to reach the fruit, you must climb the tree, and only then reach the fruit. Did Allah tell Adam, do not eat the fruit? Did He say, do not approach the fruit? No. Did He say, do not climb the tree? No. He said, do not go near the tree — فلا تقرب ھذہ الشجرۃ.

In Surah Isra we learn that فلا تقرب ھذہ الشجرۃ becomes, for humanity, ولا تقرب الزنا. لا تقرب ھذہ الشجرۃ turns into لا تقرب الزنا.

We will speak about that, God willing, later.

So when Allah says, فَلَمَّا ذَاقَا ٱلشَّجَرَةَ — so they tasted the tree. This means they did not even reach the fruit. The point is that merely by reaching out toward the tree, they disobeyed Allah, because Allah's command was not to approach the tree, and Iblees made them approach it. This is very important to understand. Do you know why? Because as the revelation unfolds, فلا تقرب ھذہ الشجرۃ turns into وَلَا تَقْرَبُوا۟ ٱلزِّنَىٰٓ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ فَٰحِشَةًۭ وَسَآءَ سَبِيلًۭا — do not go near adultery; indeed, it is the most extreme form of shamelessness, and the ugliest path to walk on. Do you see the use of the word saa'a here? Ugly. Remember what Iblees wants — to remove our clothing and expose our what? Our ugliness. Allah does not say, do not commit adultery. He says, do not go near adultery. What does that mean? Do not take even the first step that will eventually lead you to adultery.

So they both tasted the tree, and then what happened? بَدَتْ لَهُمَا سَوْءَٰتُهُمَا — their ugliness was exposed. Iblees completed his mission. What did Allah say Iblees wanted? Why did he whisper? What was his ultimate goal? فَوَسْوَسَ لَهُمَا ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ لِيُبْدِىَ لَهُمَا مَا وُۥرِىَ عَنْهُمَا مِن سَوْءَٰتِهِمَا — he whispered to them in order to expose their ugliness to them. And now Allah says he succeeded in doing what he set out to do. He got their clothing removed. He had them dishonored before Allah. Iblees got their ugliness exposed. The clothing of the Garden is what made them look beautiful, and the removal of that clothing exposed their underlying skin, which is referred to as ugliness, سوءا, because it is unnatural for human beings to be naked, especially after Allah honored them with the gift of clothing. وَطَفِقَا يَخْصِفَانِ عَلَيْهِمَا مِن وَرَقِ ٱلْجَنَّةِ — so now they are trying to wrap themselves using the leaves of the Garden. A state of desperate humiliation.

And Allah calls out to them. وَنَادَىٰهُمَا رَبُّهُمَآ أَلَمْ أَنْهَكُمَا عَن تِلْكُمَا ٱلشَّجَرَةِ وَأَقُل لَّكُمَآ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنَ لَكُمَا عَدُوٌّۭ مُّبِينٌۭ — did I not forbid the two of you from that tree? Did I not tell you both that Shaytan, without doubt, is your clear enemy? Did I not tell you that? Why did you go back there? Notice how Allah says here, that tree. What did He say before? فلا تقرب ھذہ الشجرۃ — He used the word this, ھذہ. He said, this tree. But now Allah says, that tree, تلک الشجرۃ. Did I not forbid you from that tree? In other words, you were both doing so well; you were getting further and further away from what was forbidden. Why did you let Iblees rope you back to it? Why did you have to come close to that tree again? You had gotten away from it. You were not even tempted by it. Why did you go back? And had I not told you that Shaytan is your clear enemy? Why did you believe him? Even if he swore to you, even if he gave you all the rational, logical explanations in the world, why did you choose to believe him over My command? Why did you choose to trust him over Me?

What we are learning here is that Allah's command supersedes all of Iblees's logic. Now, does this mean we do not use logic? Of course not. Use all the logic you need to come to the conclusion that Allah is your master. Take all the time you need. Make use of all the signs Allah has created.

both inside and outside of this book. Use your intellect. Use your heart. Allah says: take as much time as you need to reach the conclusion that I am your master. But once you have reached that conclusion, then submit to Me. And what does submission mean? It means giving up my own logic to the will and command of my Master. That is true submission. "O Allah, I accept. I admit that no one else is my master. You are my one and only master. لا الہ الا اللہ. I have no master except You. And now I submit my intellect, my logic, my will, to Your logic, to Your intellect, to Your command." That is true submission. That is true prostration. Just as the camel submits to its master: "I will no longer go wherever I wish to go. Once you are on my back, I will go wherever You want me to go." That is prostration. But that requires an immense amount of trust. So study the message. Study the miracles. Understand how and why all of this is beneficial only for you. That is why I sent this message in the first place. That is why I sent My messengers, to explain everything to you. But once you submit, then give up the logic that would set you against My commands.

Consider this. When you enroll in college and you have multiple offers, you have options. You can choose which school you want to join. When you apply for jobs and you receive multiple offers, you have options. You can choose which job you want. You can take the tour. You can visit your college. Look at the classrooms. Meet the teachers. Look at the academic structure. You can speak with other graduates. With a job, you can visit the building, meet the other employees, find out what is what. You have that option. But once you accept an offer, once you join the school or accept the job, once you sign on the dotted line, do you still continue investigating? No. Because you made a very deliberate choice before you joined that institution. Now you gladly do whatever is required of you. Is that not true? It is the same with religion. It is really not such a difficult thing to understand.

The matter with Iblees is this. He will not prevent you from joining Islam. Once you have joined, he will force you to use your own logic against the commands of Allah. He will make you devise the most perfect arguments, arguments based on your incomplete knowledge of the facts, mixed together with your experiential biases, and he will make you submit to your desires, your passions, and your caprice, which will run against the commands of Allah.

This is what he did with Adam and Hawwa علیھم السلام. He got them to disobey Allah after they had signed on the dotted line. He got them to lose their clothing. He got them to be dishonored before Allah. He brought them down from the ultimate honor, where the angels are prostrating before them, to this level of humiliation where they are patching themselves with leaves. There is remarkable imagery here. Look at their state of desperation, trying to patch themselves with leaves. Can you imagine that helplessness? Allah did not put them in that state, did He? No. He was the One who robed them with the beautiful garments of paradise. He put clothes upon them. And then He also warned them: "Look, do not follow Shaytan. He is your enemy. He is going to try to drive you out of paradise. Do not let him deceive you." But they did not listen. They disobeyed Allah. The natural consequence of which was that their honor was removed from them, and now they are helpless.

trying to cover themselves again with leaves. How can these lowly leaves compare with the robes and beautiful garments of paradise? A picture of intense desperation is drawn here. How desperate we, as creatures, are for our Creator. If He takes His blessings away, look at the pitiful state into which we would fall. SubhanAllah! And look at the state into which Iblees wishes to bring us down. (نعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم)

And so Allah rebukes them. Did I not tell you to stay away from that tree? Did I not warn you that Shaytan is your clear enemy?

The difference between the reactions of Adam and Iblees.

قَالَا رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا

They said, our Master, we have wronged ourselves. Now they are both weeping. They are repenting, and they are saying:

رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا

Our Master, we have wronged ourselves.

وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَسِرِينَ

And if You do not forgive us for our mistake, and You do not have mercy on us, we will surely become among the losers.

Now, in this verse, we also learn about this stark difference between Adam and Iblees. They both disobeyed Allah. They both disobeyed Allah. They both disappointed Allah. Iblees was asked to do something, and he did not do it. Adam and Hawwa were asked not to do something, and they did it. Both forms of disobedience occurred in this story. What we learn from this story is that disobedience to Allah happens in both forms. There is disobedience of commission, and there is disobedience of omission. There is disobedience when we do not do what Allah has commanded us to do. And there is disobedience when we do what we are commanded not to do. That is the first thing.

But the greatest lesson in this story is their response to their disobedience. It is an extraordinary lesson. Iblees disobeys Allah. Allah asks him why he refused to believe.

قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ إِذْ أَمَرْتُكَ

Why did you not prostrate when I commanded you to do so? What was his reply?

ۖ قَالَ أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهُ خَلَقْتَنِى مِن نَّارٍۢ وَخَلَقْتَهُۥ مِن طِينٍۢ

I am better than him. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay. Correct? Arrogance was his reply. Justifications for his disobedience were his reply. Rationalization was his reply. A lack of accountability, a lack of taking responsibility, was his reply. Ego. Pride. Jealousy. Greed. That was his reply. Correct?

Now, do Adam and Hawwa also disobey Allah? Yes! Does Allah question them both as well about their disobedience? He does!

أَلَمْ أَنْهَكُمَا عَن تِلْكُمَا ٱلشَّجَرَةِ وَأَقُل لَّكُمَآ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَنَ لَكُمَا عَدُوٌّۭ مُّبِينٌۭ

Did I not tell you not to go near that tree, and did I not tell you that Shaytan is your clear enemy? Correct? But look how they both respond to Allah's question.

قَالَا رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا

Our Master, we, we have wronged ourselves. We admit it. We take complete responsibility for our actions. You are right. We are wrong. SubhanAllah! What a beautiful response. What a beautiful response. Complete accountability. Complete responsibility. We are the ones who wronged our own souls. Not: it was Iblees who wronged us. Not: O Allah, he swore by You, and we did not believe him. He kept trying for months and months, and we did not believe him. It was only when he lied to us and swore by Your name that we believed him. You should punish him, not us! O Allah, come on. You can understand.

We do not know what a lie is. We have never experienced deception before. So You can understand why we were fooled, despite the fact that You told us, despite the fact that You warned us. Could they have said that? They absolutely could have. But instead, what do they say?

قَالَا رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا

Master, it is we who wronged ourselves. That is all. We are at fault. We take full responsibility. We failed. They do not even mention Iblees. Think about that. They do not even mention Iblees. SubhanAllah. Because no—O Allah, You commanded us, and we disobeyed You. Khalas. We are the wrongdoers. It does not matter why we did it, or who made us do it. In the end, we disobeyed Your command, and we are responsible for our own actions. What a beautiful response from a true servant, and what a fitting response to such a glorious Master. SubhanAllah. And then:

وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا

And now, if You do not forgive us, and if You do not have mercy upon us,

لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَسِرِينَ

we will be doomed. We will be destroyed. Complete humility. Not a shred of arrogance. O Allah, we are completely dependent upon Your mercy, and we are completely dependent upon Your forgiveness. Without those two things from You, we are finished.

This is the greatest lesson for us. What we are learning here is that disobedience can come from anyone. It can come from a jinn; it can come from a human being. Disobedience will happen. It will happen because of our desires, because of our caprice, because of the heat of the moment, because of anger, because of haste, because of not thinking things through, because of deception by others—as in the case of Adam, peace be upon him—because of making the wrong kinds of friends, because of listening to the wrong kinds of people, or simply because of our lack of knowledge. Disobedience will happen. But it is not the disobedience; it is our response to the disobedience. It is our response, after realizing a mistake—how we respond—that will differentiate us between becoming an Iblees or an Adam.

We have completed the Istiaaza, which concerned seeking Allah's protection from every kind of evil. Now that this is done, the next logical step, after asking Allah to guard us against external threats, is to ask Allah to bless us with the right thoughts within. This is what Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim and the Fateha are all about. In other words, the Aozubillah and the Bismillah work together in cooperation with one another, and that is the whole point. We begin by seeking refuge from evil because we wish to be rid of the bad first. Once that is done, once we have entered Allah's protection, the next thing is to ask Allah for the good.

This is in fact the entire premise of our religion. Islam rests on these two primary pillars of the negative and the positive, of rejection and acceptance. Allah says:

فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بِٱلطَّغُوتِ وَيُؤْمِنۢ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدِ ٱسْتَمْسَكَ بِٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ

Whoever rejects the false gods, the false deities, and accepts Allah, that is the one who has taken hold of the strong handhold. So we must first reject evil, and only after we have done that can we affirm the good.

You can see that this concept is perfectly aligned with our kalima. What is our kalima? لا الہ الا اللہ. You can see that it has two parts, لا الہ and الا اللہ. The first part, لا الہ, deals with the eradication of the negative. We first negate everything that is bad; we negate all false gods by saying لا الہ. And only then does the second part come into play, which is the affirmation of the one true God, الا اللہ. That is what the sequence of this kalima teaches us. We must negate or reject evil first, and only then can the affirmation take place. Why? Because unless and until we negate the bad, it is not possible to affirm the good.

When we fall sick, the doctor must first work to eliminate the disease. Once the disease has been eradicated, only then does he work on improving the patient's health. A teacher must first remove a student's misconceptions before he can establish new concepts. You have to take down an old, broken, dysfunctional structure before building a new, working structure in its place. So this principle of لا الہ الا اللہ is a universal principle. You will find it at work everywhere. In the same way, the Istiaaza and the Basmallah work together to accomplish the same goal. The Istiaaza is the removal of all evil, and therefore it must precede the Basmallah, which is the establishment of all good, through the names of Allah who is Rahman and Rahim.

Importance and virtue of the Basmallah

Now, there is so much to be said about the importance and virtue of the Basmallah. It is the essence of Surah al-Fateha. I told you earlier, quoting the hadith of Rasul Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), that Surah al-Fateha is the essence of the Quran. And there is another very famous saying of Maulana Ali, in which he says:

إن كل ما في الکتب السماویۃ، في القرآن

Indeed, whatever exists in all the previous divine books, their essence, exists in the Quran.

و كل ما في القرآن في فاتحة الكتاب

And everything that is in the Quran is in the opener of the book, meaning Surah al-Fateha.

و كل ما في الفاتحة في البسملة

And everything that is in the Fateha is in the Basmallah, the very first ayah of the Fateha.

و كل ما في البسملة في الباء
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
And everything that is in the Basmallah is in its letter Ba.

which is the first letter of the Basmallah. و انا النقطة تحت الباء. And I am the dot beneath the Ba. This is a most profound saying from the master of all knowers, سید العارفین. In other words, Maulana Ali says that the entire Quran is condensed within the Ba of Bismillah. And concerning the Basmallah, Maulana Ali, peace be upon him, said to one of his companions, Ibn Abbas, لو شئت لأَوْقَرتُ سبعين بعيراً من باء بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم — If I wished, I could tell you so much about the Ba of Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim that seventy camels would have to be loaded with the books that held that knowledge.

This saying points to the sheer amount of knowledge that has been gathered and condensed into the single Ba of the Basmallah. And this is not an exaggerated or overstated remark. Our duat have in fact written whole volumes on the Ba of the Basmallah.

For this session, I will describe only a portion of this saying of Maulana Ali, where he calls the Basmallah the essence of Surah al-Fateha. First, let us understand what he means by the essence. I will give you a very simple example of how to understand this saying. If you ask me, Asif Mamu, tell me everything that Allah wants from me. How do I understand who Allah is and what He expects of me? I will say, read all the revealed books. Read the Taura, the Injeel, the Zaboor, the Psalms of Solomon, and you will know what He wants from you. You tell me, no, no, that is too much. Give me a summarized version of all of those books. So then I will say, fine, read the Quran. Everything described in all of these divine books has been summarized in the 114 surahs of the Quran. You say, no, Mamu, that is still too much. I have homework to do. I have television shows to watch. I have to play tennis. I have so many more important things to do. I cannot sit and read 114 enormous chapters. Give me something simpler. I will say, all right, fine, just understand Surah al-Fateha. Just understand the seven verses of Surah al-Fateha, and you will understand the essence of the Quran. Because the rest of the Quran is simply an explanation of these seven verses. Everything the Quran speaks about is summarized in the seven verses of the Fateha.

Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim speaks of identifying the creator and His primary attributes. The name of Allah, who is intensely merciful and consistently merciful.

Hamdu mentions the praise of Allah and how we must be grateful to Him for all His blessings.

Rahman al-Rahim describes His mercy.

Malik Yaum al-Deen speaks of the day of judgment and everything that will happen on that day.

Iyyaka Nabud wa Iyyaka Nastaeen is an explanation of how to enter the servitude of Allah, and how to attain the rank of becoming His slave and seeking His help through prayers and supplications.

Ihdina is about seeking His guidance for the straight path that leads to success.

Siraat speaks of the stories of three kinds of people: those who were successful, those who incurred Allah's wrath, and finally those who went astray.
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
but when you add "the." THE CAR. It is now one specific car. The same thing happens here. When you add the Al — which is the same as the definite article "the" in English — when you add this Al to Ilah, it is no longer any generic Ilah. It is now one particular Ilah. It is now exclusive. It has now become Allah. That is what Allah is: where the Al and the Ilah both fuse together to form the exclusive word Allah. The Al adds a clause of exclusivity to this generic Ilah. You understand?

So when I say Allah, the generic Ilah now becomes exclusive. What does that mean? It means Allah is not someone I worship. It now means Allah is the only entity that I worship. He is the only entity that I make Sajdah for. Allah is not just someone I am devoted to. He is not just someone I am loyal to. Allah means the only one I am devoted to, the only one I am completely loyal to. He is not someone I turn to in times of desperation; Allah becomes the only one I turn to in times of desperation. He is not just someone I am passionately in love with; He is the only one I am obsessively and passionately in love with. He is not just one of the things I lean on, or depend on, or put my weight on; Allah is the only one I completely lean on and put my weight on.

You see how this Al, this exclusivity, affects and changes the word Ilah? And this is fundamental to our understanding of religion, because this exclusivity is the very concept our Kalima is built upon. La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no Ilah except the Ilah, except Allah. We reject and deny all the generic Ilah and affirm the one and only exclusive Ilah. Our concept of Tawheed dictates that we do not believe in Allah as a deity in a hierarchy of deities. That is not what we believe. We do not say Allah is the ultimate deity in a hierarchy of deities. No! Our concept of Tawheed is that there is no other deity. لا الہ — the complete annihilation and extermination of all other deities. الا اللہ — except the one and only deity, which is Allah. This transference of Ilahiyat from the generic to the specific is the challenge of لا الہ الا اللہ.

False Deities

Because we are the ones who create false gods in our lives. Think about it. We have all created false gods, generic Ilahs, in our lives, in every meaning of the word. I have chosen my desires, my caprice, my ھوی, as my deity, as my Ilah. My desires are a deity that I worship, one that I constantly make Sajdah for. I hand over my intellect into the hands of my desires and feelings and let them take control of me. I let that false deity rule me. I worship it. I submit to its every whim and desire. And that is why we have been given this sword of لا الہ الا اللہ. With this sword of "La Ilaha," there is no deity, I cut down the idol of my desires, my caprice, my hawa, and replace it with the worship and submission of my one true and only Allah.
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
There are many people I am devoted to in life; there are many people, many causes, I am loyal to. But when I am placed in a situation where my devotion and my loyalty are challenged and come into conflict with my devotion and loyalty to Allah, لا الہ الا اللہ dictates that I negate and deny all my other devotion. I reject all my loyalties and replace them with devotion and loyalty to the one and only Allah. This is key to understand. My devotion and loyalty to Allah is not a devotion in a hierarchy of devotions.

It is the only devotion and loyalty that I have. All my other loyalties exist because of my loyalty and devotion to Allah. Do you understand?

In the same way, suppose I am madly and passionately in love with this world. I am obsessed with it. I cannot stop thinking about it. I have made it and its pleasures a false god. I have made this world my ilah. And now, once again, لا الہ الا اللہ demands that with the sword of la ilaha I cut down, reject, and deny my love and obsession for this world, and aim that passionate love toward the one to whom it belongs, and become wholly obsessed with the one and only Allah. That is illa Allah.

I am astounded and amazed by the marvels of creation, by wealth, by glory, by power. Here is yet another ilah I have created. I must now replace it with لا الہ الا اللہ. I must now be amazed and astounded by my creator alone, by my one and only Allah.

There are many false gods I have created, many an ilah I have made, that I turn to for help, that I lean on, that I place my weight upon. Now لا الہ الا اللہ is the journey from that state of depending on false gods to the state of turning to Allah alone for help in times of desperation, leaning on Allah alone, placing my weight on Allah alone.

Now understand this. لا الہ الا اللہ does not mean that I cannot turn to my parents or my loved ones for help, or that I should not love anyone in this world other than Allah, because all of that is part and parcel of this life. It is part of Allah's design. The idea is that when they are set beside Allah, when they are measured against Allah, all these other relationships become false gods.

So even when I turn to someone for help, لا الہ الا اللہ teaches me that it is Allah alone who can help me, and that the one I am turning to is only a means through which I am seeking Allah's help. For what we end up doing is thinking that it is this person who is helping me, and so making him a false deity, making him an ilah. And that is where لا الہ الا اللہ comes into play, that la ilaha, it is not this person who is helping me, but illa Allah, it is in fact Allah helping me through this person. Do you understand?
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
It is Allah alone who can cure me of what afflicts me. The doctor is merely a means by which Allah is curing me. But the moment I see the doctor as the one who cures, I have now turned him into a false god, into an ilah. So now I must use لا الہ الا اللہ to break that idol, and place my gratitude, my hope, and my fear where they belong.

Even though there are many I love in this world, that love stems from my passionate love of Allah. I love them because it makes Allah happy. For in essence, Allah is the only one I am passionately and obsessively in love with.

Even though I am devoted to various people and various causes in life, the origin of that devotion and loyalty comes from my devotion and loyalty to Allah. And if that devotion ever comes into conflict with my devotion to Allah, I will reject it and replace it with my devotion and loyalty to my one and only Allah.

This is the constant journey and the constant battle of لا الہ الا اللہ: replacing every false deity, replacing every false god that we have created, with the one true deity, which is Allah.
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
That is it! That is the entire Quran in seven verses for you. You say, Mamu, I know seven seems a small number to you, but I have the memory of a goldfish. So I cannot remember so much. Can you simplify it further for me? So then I will say, fine, Goldie! If you cannot remember all of that, just remember Allah, and His two primary attributes of mercy with which He has identified Himself, al-Rahman and al-Rahim. He is intensely merciful and He is consistently merciful. Because the entire Fateha

the entire Quran. Every revealed divine scripture is nothing more than an identification of Allah and a description of His intense and constant mercy — His Rahmaniyya and His Rahimiyya. For it is the Merciful who showers you with His blessings, the One you must be grateful to and praise. It is the Merciful who will establish the Day of Reckoning. It is the Merciful who helps, who provides guidance, who leads people to success, who distinguishes the true path from the false, who shows us which road to walk upon and which to avoid. The whole of the Fateha is a manifestation of Allah's Rahmaniyya, His intense mercy, and His Rahimiyya, His constant mercy.

So forget everything else. Simply remember the name of your Creator, which is Allah. And understand that He is intensely merciful and that He is consistently merciful. That is all. This name, Allah, and His two primary attributes of mercy — that is what faith and Islam are all about.

This is the meaning of that extremely eloquent statement of Maulana Ali. إن كل ما في الکتب السماویۃ في القرآن — indeed, the essence of all the previous divine books exists in the Quran. و كل ما في القرآن في فاتحة الكتاب — and everything that is in the Quran is in the Fateha. و كل ما في الفاتحة في البسملة — and everything that is in the Fateha is in the Basmalah.

So the entire essence, the meaning of all the previous divine scriptures, has been summarized and condensed into the one hundred and fourteen surahs of the Quran. The essential meaning of one hundred and thirteen of those surahs has been condensed into the seven verses of Surah al-Fateha. And then the six verses of al-Fateha have been condensed into the Basmalah.

He then goes further and says that the Basmalah is condensed still further into the letter Ba of the Basmalah, and that he is the dot beneath the Ba. I will explain this part later. For now, I hope you understand what he means when he says that the essence of all the previous divine scriptures has been condensed and reduced to this one statement, بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم.

Now, as things are condensed, the surface area shrinks, but what happens to the density? It increases, does it not? And if this density is of something extremely precious, what happens to its value? Its value rises. It becomes even more precious.
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
So if the Basmalah contains the essence of all the previously revealed divine scriptures, including the Quran itself, you can imagine how dense, how lofty, and how valuable this statement must be. And then you can imagine how dense the Ba of the Basmalah must be, if it is the essence of the entire divine mass. So, just like the big bang theory, you can see that this Ba is, in reality, the singularity that exploded into this enormous universe of revealed scriptures. Subhan Allah. Just as the whole universe came into existence from an extremely dense mass, this entire universe of religion also originated from this incredibly divine mass of the letter Ba. And Maulana Ali says, I am the dot beneath that Ba. Subhan Allah. God willing, I will explain what this means in a future session.

But I think that if you truly comprehend and reflect upon what I have just told you, then this in itself is enough to appreciate the power and the strength of the Basmalah. It is no wonder that this statement precedes every single act we perform in our daily lives. There is no divine action that is done without reciting the Basmalah.

In fact, the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said: كُلَّ شَئیٍ أَبتَر بِدُونِ بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم — every act is severed and disfigured if it is not preceded by "In the name of Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful."

Now, the Basmalah is made up of four words: Ism, Allah, al-Rahman, and al-Rahim. Well, technically five words, if we count the letter Ba at the start. Of these words, the most important, the most virtuous, and the most magnificent word is obviously "Allah." Everything else, all the other words, revolves around this central word, Allah. So I thought it best to begin our discussion with this word. What does the word Allah mean? And what are these ninety-nine names of Allah? Because Allah is itself a name, is it not? Allah is the name of the deity that we worship. So then, if Allah is a name, why does He need these other ninety-nine names? And why do we say, "In the name of Allah, the intensely merciful, the constantly merciful"? Why not simply "with Allah the merciful," or "with the help of Allah the most merciful"? Why the name of Allah?

If I am working on a project with Hussain, I would not say, "I completed this project with the name of Hussain." I would not do that. I would simply say, "I completed this project with Hussain." So then, why does this verse insist on the name of Allah? What does the name symbolize?

And also, who is Allah to us? How do we see Him in our lives? Do we see Him the way He ought to be seen? Do we give Him the place He deserves? Do we truly love Him? Do we truly love Allah? In fact, what does it even mean to love Allah? What are the primary components of love?
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
So let us think about love in the worldly sense. Think about two people who are madly in love. What is the most important thing for a lover? The contentment and happiness of the beloved. That is all that matters to a lover. If I truly love someone, the only thing that will matter to me, the only thing I will be obsessed with, will be what? To make my beloved happy. Even if that means going against my own will and desires. That is what true love is: an obsession with the happiness and contentment of the beloved, at any cost. Why? Because I recognize the importance of that person in my life. I recognize my need for my beloved's love, and I will do everything in my power to keep that person in my life and to make sure that person is always happy with me. Is that not true? In one sentence, that is the philosophy of love: an obsession for the happiness of the beloved.

And the outcome, the manifestation, of true love takes the form of hope and fear. Hope that my beloved will be pleased with my efforts. Hope that my efforts will be good enough for my beloved. Why do you see young men buying flowers, writing poems in their own blood, trying desperately to impress the girl they love? Why? Hope! Hope that she will accept the gesture. Hope that she will find the effort satisfactory and grow in her affection for him. Hope that she will reward him with more care, more love, more affection. So that is how love manifests, in the form of hope.

And then also fear. Fear that I might accidentally do something to offend the one I love, to displease her in any way. So that she does not become upset with me, or reject my efforts, or punish me. And what is the greatest of all punishments for a true lover? Do you know what it is? It is abandonment. There is nothing more painful for a lover.

than when his beloved abandons and rejects him, when the beloved does not return his love. The fear of abandonment is the greatest of all pains for a lover. To be whipped, stoned, beaten, and burned is nothing. The real torment, the greatest of all fears for a lover, is rejection by his beloved. A poet says:

و مِنَ الشَّقاَوةُ أن تحبَ، وَ مَن تُحِبُّ يُحِبُّ غَيرَك

The greatest of miseries is to love someone while that person does not return your love, or loves someone else.

So these are the three primary emotions of love: love, hope, and fear. حب، و الرَّجاء والخوف. Now the question is this: do we have this relationship of love with Allah? When we deal with Allah in our daily lives, do our actions take the form of hope and fear? Are we consumed by the hope of pleasing Him? Do we fear, or are we even concerned about, displeasing Him, or offending or angering Him? If not, why not? What is missing? How do we develop that awareness of Allah that will lead us toward that kind of love?

And then, what are the conditions and obligations of love? What are the rights of the beloved? As Maulana Ali said:

عَرَفتُمُ اللہ فَلَم تُأَدُّو حَقَّہُ

You claim to know Allah, but you do not fulfill His rights. That is the first problem. For Allah says:

فَعلَم! أنَّہُ لا الہ الا اللہ
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
Know that there is no god but Allah. And to know that there is no god but Allah, and to say that there is no god but Allah, are two different things. You see, even the hypocrite says La ilaha illa Allah. But knowing and saying are two entirely different things. So Maulana Ali says that you claim to know Allah, but you do not fulfill His rights upon you.

So we need to learn about this. We need to gain that knowledge. Because knowledge of Allah gives rise to love. That is the very nature of the knowledge of Allah. The more we know about Allah, the more we will love Him. The more we know about His messenger, the more we will love him. The more we know about Maulana Ali, the more we will love him. Knowledge gives rise to love.

Now the lover is always obedient to the beloved. That is the very nature of love. If you have someone who claims to love you, and then they never do what you ask, then you should know that this is a false claim. They do not love you. They are only giving you lip service. Because the very nature of love is that you do what the beloved asks.

اِنَّ المُحِبُّ لِمَن یُحِبُّ، مُطِیعُ

For the one who loves someone is always obedient to that person.

A poet came to a woman and told her about his friend who was madly in love with her. She said to the man, "Tell me about this friend of yours who claims to love me. Do not detract and do not embellish. Just give me the plain truth." And so the poet said:

اِن کَانَ یَظُنُّ الموتُ بِالظَّمَا وَ قَال لَك لا تَشرِبُ المآءَ وَلَم یَرِدِ

If he thought he would die of thirst, and you said, "Do not drink," he would not drink.

That is the state of a true lover. The one who claims to love, and the one who actually loves, are two different things. Many people claim to love. Shakespeare said, "Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds, / Or bends with the remover to remove. / O no! it is an ever-fixed mark / That looks on tempests and is never shaken." That is love. Love is not something that changes when the situation changes. People claim to lose their faith.

Some misfortune occurs in their life, and they lose their faith. You know how it goes: I lost my faith. But they never had faith in the first place, because faith cannot be lost. You either have it or you do not. Faith is tested in trials. That is when the true metal of a person is revealed — not when all is going well. Anyone and everyone is a believer when things are going well. It is when things are going terribly wrong that the real test of faith comes.

So knowledge engenders love and gives it birth. That is what we are going to try to do. That is what Surah al-Fateha is all about; that is the goal of this surah — to develop an awareness of Allah. Who is Allah? What does the love of Allah mean? How does that love take shape in the form of hope and fear? What are the obligations and conditions of love?
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
So let us begin with the word Allah and first understand what this word Allah means, for this is a name that Allah, exalted and glorified, took for Himself. Usually names are given by someone else. No one names himself; people are named by others. But Allah is a name that Allah took for Himself.

إِنَّنِىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ فَٱعْبُدْنِى وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكْرِىٓ

Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer to remember Me.

So if He chose this name, Allah, for Himself, it must hold incredible significance and depth within it. I want to begin by exploring this name Allah first, and then we will move on to His ninety-nine names, or attributes, and finally look in detail at how the Basmallah is used. Why do we say it before we begin any action? It is meant to create Barakah in our actions — so what does Barakah mean?

Then there are the words al-Rehman and al-Raheem. I am actually going to set these two words aside for later, because we will encounter them again in the Fateha: al-Rehman and al-Raheem.

Now let us take a look at the word Allah. Why did Allah choose this name to be His primary name? The Quran opens with the Fateha, and the Fateha opens with the Basmallah: بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم. In this very first verse of His very first surah, He introduces Himself with the name "Allah." And this name, "Allah," is not used only in the Basmallah; it is used in numerous other places throughout the Quran. The word Allah appears over three thousand five hundred times in the Quran. There is no other name of Allah that even comes close to the number of times this particular name, "Allah," is mentioned.

Interestingly, when we refer to Him in our daily lives, we always use His actual name. Have you noticed that? We always call upon Him by saying "Allah." We say, O Allah, give me this. O Allah, help me with this. O Allah, protect me from that. So we always use His actual name, as opposed to other names such as Rehman, Raheem, Quddus, Salaam, Momin. We do not generally call upon Him using these other names, even though they too are His names. We almost always call upon Him by His most glorified name when we address Him or refer to Him in our daily lives.

Now what does this word Allah mean? And, by the way, this is not a name unique to our religion of Islam alone. Quite the contrary: this is the name that Allah chose for Himself and mentioned in every past scripture. Even in the Old and New Testaments, we find the name Allah in its Hebrew form. In the Old Testament,

we find that He refers to Himself as eloh, أِلَوہ, and ألوھیم, which are equivalent to the Arabic Allah and Allahumma. And in the New Testament as well: when they crucified Eisa (AS), the Bible records his words as الائی الائی لما سبختنی; الائی الائی لما ترکتنی — My Allah, My Allah, why did You abandon me?

So the name Allah is in fact the primary name, one that is not specific to Islam alone but has been used in every past religion, revelation, and scripture throughout the ages, given to all civilizations and to all prophets.

Linguistic meaning of ILAH and ALLAH
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
Now, to understand the word Allah, you must know something about Arabic. In the Arabic language, words are always built on tri-literal roots. For example, you may have heard the word عالم or علیم — these are its derivatives. They come from the tri-literal root علم, meaning knowledge. So in Arabic you will always find words derived from two- or three-letter roots. The word Allah too actually comes from the three-letter root "Ilah" — Alif, Laam, Haa — Ilah, which means deity. Allah is in fact AL + ILAH, THE DEITY. The definite article Al and Ilah combine to form ALLAH. So in order to understand the meaning of the word Allah, we must first understand the meaning of the word "ILAH."

Now, the word Ilah is a very rich word. It is a composite word, and it carries a whole range of meanings in ancient Arabic.

Primarily, the word Ilah comes from Alaha, اَلَہَ یَعلُہُ, and the verb Alaha literally means to worship. So Ilah is the entity that is the focus of worship and obedience. That is one meaning of the word ALAHA.

Another meaning: Ilah is the one to whom you are completely devoted, someone to whom you are completely loyal, someone you turn to in every single moment of happiness and grief. That too is an Ilah. Another meaning of the word Ilah is from اَلِہَ, which is used for a child that is thirsty for its mother's milk and is crying desperately for it. That is Aliha. And the verbal meaning derived from it is the one to whom people desperately and inevitably turn when they are in need of help. The one you turn to in times of desperation, seeking their protection, is also an Ilah. That is why one of the names of Allah is الصمد. Samad is the one to whom every being turns for every need, and who Himself has no needs.

Then there is another very beautiful meaning of the word Ilah: someone you are passionately in love with, someone you cannot stop thinking about, someone you are obsessed with. That person too is called Ilah. One of its derivatives is (وَلَھَا) Walaha, which means to lose one's mind because of the loss of a beloved. In Urdu they say والھانہ محبت — mad love. That too is from Waliha. That is why in Arabic the mother who loses her child is called مُوَلَّا. This is a mother who is suffering that extremely excruciating pain and grief over the loss of her child; she is called مُوَلَّا. It is that kind of passionate and obsessive love. Because the one who loses Allah, who no longer has Allah in his life, would suffer from this type of ultimate grief and madness. The one who has felt the love of Allah and then fallen from the grace of Allah, who no longer has that connection with Allah, feels that he is going to lose his mind, because now there is nothing left in his life to give him value.

to give him meaning. For if you do not believe in Allah, if you have no concept of an Ilah in your life, then your life has no purpose. So this too is one of the meanings of the word Ilah: to be passionately and obsessively in love with someone, the way a mother loves her child and is forever consumed with worry for its safety. You see, then, that this extreme form of love is already embedded within the word Ilah.
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
You know the story of Hazrat Ayyub. He was placed in great trials to test his faith. According to a hadees of Rasul Allah (sallalahu alayhi wa aalihi wa sallam), Allah once spoke to his angels of the patience and gratitude of Hazrat Ayyub, peace be upon him. So Iblis spoke to Allah and said that the only reason Ayyub is grateful to you is that you have blessed him with so much. You have given him so many possessions, so many children; that is the only reason he is grateful to you. Take it away, and you will see that he is grateful no longer.

So Allah began to take things from him. He took his possessions away. His house collapsed before his very eyes, killing his children. Can you imagine that? And when he saw it happen right in front of him, do you know what came instinctively from his mouth? AlHamdulillah. That is what he said. And not only that: he was struck with a terrible disease, his body infected with worms that would eat away his flesh. God willing, we will speak of these trials when we study AlRahman AlRahim: why the prophets are placed in trials, and why we are placed in trials. It is a most interesting and eye-opening subject.

But the point is this. Allah put Hazrat Ayyub through this extreme form of trial to test his faith and his love of Allah, and he passed with flying colors. When his test was complete, Allah told him to bathe in a spring of water he had set out for him. He bathed in it, and his disease was completely cured.

The reason I bring this up is that, years later, someone asked him, "How is your health now, Ayyub?" He sighed and replied, "The days of my illness were more beloved to me than these days of health." The man was astonished to hear this and asked, "How can that be?" Ayyub replied that when he was ill, every single day Allah would ask him, "How are you today, Ayyub?" But since he had been cured, Allah no longer asked him that, and he missed that love and care from Allah. This is Waliha. This is Muwalla. Extreme, passionate love, so that a person is driven to madness without the beloved. So that is another meaning of Ilah.

And also, speaking literally, not linguistically but literally, the word Ilah means something you lean on, something upon which you place your entire weight. When you are exhausted and you lean on something and put all your weight upon it, that thing is literally called الہ. So you see, the word Ilah means many things.

Another derivative of the word Ilah is وَلِھَا یعلُہُ. وَلِھَا means to become astounded, to become astonished, to become amazed. And that is because when we try to conceive of Allah, we become amazed and astonished, and we come to realize that we cannot comprehend who Allah, azza wa jall, is. Allah is the one whom, if you try to comprehend Him, you will fail; if you try to walk toward Him, you will wear yourself out yet never reach Him; if you let your thoughts and imaginings fly toward Him, you will break your wings in the attempt and still be unable to reach Him.

Allah is an entity beyond comprehension. This is why, in the very first sermon of the Nahj al-Balagha, Maulana Ali, in praising Allah, says — and this is one of the words of praise I recite at the beginning of our sessions:
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
الحَمْدُ للهِ الَّذَي لاَ يَبْلُغُ مِدْحَتَهُ القَائِلُونَ

Praise and gratitude belong to Allah, whose worth those who speak cannot describe,

وَلاِ يُحْصِي نَعْمَاءَهُ العَادُّونَ

whose bounties those who count cannot number,

ولاَ يُؤَدِّي حَقَّهُ الُمجْتَهِدُونَ

and whose rights of obedience those who strive cannot fulfill;

الَّذِي لاَ يُدْركُهُ بُعْدُ الهِمَمِ

the one whom the far reach of aspirations cannot attain,

وَلاَ يَنَالُهُ غَوْصُ الفِطَنِ

and whom the deep plunge of understanding cannot reach;

الَّذِي لَيْسَ لِصِفَتِهِ حَدٌّ مَحْدُودٌ

the one whose description has no fixed limit,

وَلاَ نَعْتٌ مَوْجُودٌ

for whom no eulogy exists,

وَلا وَقْتٌ مَعْدُودٌ

for whom no counted time is set,

وَلا أَجَلٌ مَمْدُودٌ

and for whom no extended term is fixed.

فَطَرَ الخَلائِقَ بِقُدْرَتِهَ

He brought forth creation through His power,

وَنَشَرَ الرِّيَاحَ بِرَحْمَتِهِ

He spread the winds through His compassion,

وَوَتَّدَ بِالصُّخُورِ مَيَدَانَ أَرْضِهِ

and He anchored the trembling expanse of His earth with rocks.

So that is the meaning of the word Ilah: to become astonished and dumbstruck. Another meaning that comes from the same root is وَلاَہَ یَلِیہُ, and it means to be raised up. For the one who believes in Allah has raised himself up, in this world and in the next. He is the one who will be honored, in this life and in the hereafter.

So those are some of the meanings of the word Ilah. As you see, it is a very comprehensive term. Let us go over these meanings again. What is an Ilah? An Ilah is a deity that is worshiped. He is the one to whom we submit our will. An Ilah is the one who becomes the focus of our complete devotion and loyalty. An Ilah is the one to whom we turn for protection and refuge in times of desperation. An Ilah is the one with whom we are passionately in love, the one with whom we are obsessed. An Ilah is the one whose glory and magnificence astound and astonish us — one whom we recognize to be so lofty, so far beyond our capacity for comprehension and understanding, that we would be dumbstruck each time we tried to approach him. An Ilah is the one on whom we lean, on whom we place our weight.

The Linguistic Meaning of Al-Ilah

Now that we understand what the word Ilah means, let us understand the difference between Ilah and Allah. As I have said, Allah is in fact The Ilah. The word Ilah is generic. All its meanings can be taken in the generic sense. If you take the meaning of worship, I could worship many gods, as the Hindus do. If you take the meaning of devotion and loyalty, I can be devoted and loyal to many people, to many causes; I can be devoted to many projects at the same time. In the meaning of love, there can be several people whom I love. There can be several people to whom I could turn for help in times of desperation. I can lean on many things over the course of a lifetime. So the word Ilah is a generic term that can apply to multiple entities. Do you understand?

But when I apply this definite article, "the," to the word Ilah — when I add this "Al," called علامت المعرفۃ in Arabic, to the word Ilah — it no longer remains generic; it becomes specific. Just as in the English language, "book" can mean any book, but "the book" means one specific book. "Car" can mean any car.
body.topic_title_en: The Meaning of the Word Allah

body.text_en:
In the previous session we spoke about the meaning of Ilah and of Allah. We learned that Allah is in fact the definite article "THE" applied to Ilah, which makes it exclusive. But the root word underlying Allah is Ilah, and that is a VERY comprehensive term with a whole range of meanings. My Ilah, for me, is the one I worship, the one to whom I surrender my will. Ilah is the one who is the focus of my complete devotion and loyalty. He is the one to whom I turn for protection and for refuge in desperate times. My Ilah is the one with whom I am passionately in love, the one with whom I am obsessed. He is a being whose glory and magnificence astound and astonish me. When I set out to understand Him and to recognize Him, I realize that He is so LOFTY, so far beyond my powers of comprehension and understanding, that I am left dumbfounded every time I try to approach Him. And then, finally, in the literal sense, my Ilah is the one on whom I lean, the one on whom I place my entire weight.

Now the use of the word Ilah is very general. It can be applied to many beings at the same time. But when we say Allah, we add the definite article THE to the word Ilah, and now it is no longer a general being. It is VERY specific, VERY individual. It becomes ONE and ONLY ONE particular being.

And so our kalima, La Ilaha Illa Allah, there is no ilah except Allah, becomes a journey. It is a journey of breaking the idols we fashion with our own hands, and of applying each meaning to its true and sole owner. So:

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no Ilah except Allah. That is, there is no other being I worship, or to whom I surrender myself, except Allah.

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no other being who is the focus of my complete devotion and loyalty, except Allah.

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no other being to whom I turn for protection and for refuge in desperate times, except Allah.

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no other being with whom I am passionately in love, and with whom I am obsessed, except Allah.

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no other being with whom I am passionately in love, and with whom I am obsessed, except Allah.

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no other being whose loftiness and glory astonish me, astound me, startle and daze me, whose loftiness overwhelms me, except Allah.

La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no other being on whom I will place my weight, on whom I will lean completely, except Allah.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
This is the journey of La Ilaha Illa Allah. It is a very difficult journey. And every journey requires provisions that help you get through it. The provision for this journey is knowledge of Allah. The more knowledge we have of Allah, the more we will be amazed by His glory. The more amazed and astonished we become, the more passionate our love for Him will grow. The more passionately we love Him, the more obsessed with Him we will become. The more obsessed with Him we are, the more we will worship Him and submit to His commands. The more we worship Him, the more we will turn to Him seeking His refuge. The more we find ourselves under His powerful shelter, the more we will lean on Him, and the more we will place our weight on Him.

And so Allah means ALL these things together, all at the same time. This is the perfection of the Arabic language. There is SO much depth in the Arabic language, which SO many people, Arabs among them, do not appreciate, because many Arabs carry a compounded ignorance when it comes to the Arabic language.

Just because they can speak dialectal Arabic, they make assumptions about the language that are not true at all. There are many Arabs who do not understand its subtleties, and they truly miss some of the extraordinary nuances of the Qur'an and of rhetoric: بلاغۃ معانی بدیعۃ والبیان. These sciences genuinely open up the power of the Qur'an to the person who studies them.

Now consider the Arabic language. There is a word that the ancient Arabs used for non-Arabs. They called them عجمی. Now, there is another word, also عجمی, which is used in the Qur'an: بھیمۃٌ عجما, meaning a dumb animal. So the word عجمی has come to carry that sense in general usage: someone who is mute, or dumb. But if you actually study the words Arab and Ajam linguistically, the word عجمی comes from عجمۃ, which does not mean to be dumb. It means to try by biting. To try by biting. Now look at the word Arab. It comes from the verb عربَۃ, which means to cut. It means to cut, or to eat fully; that is one of its meanings as well. So عجمۃ means to bite, whereas عربَۃ means to cut. The difference between biting and cutting is that biting is not precise, whereas cutting is very precise. Such is the nature of the Arabic language: it is a very precise language.

Arabic is part of revelation

In fact, those who have studied Mabda Maad and Haqaiq know that Arabic is a language that was put into place precisely so that it could absorb and take in the message of the Qur'an. The Qur'an was not revealed in one of the best languages that happened to exist at the time. Do you see what I mean? It is not as though there were fifty languages out there, and from among them Allah chose Arabic because it was the best of those in existence. It is not like that. The Arabic language was specifically designed for the Qur'an. It was put in place before the time of the Messenger, so that the Qur'an could be revealed in this precise language. This is because the entire grammar of the Arabic language is based on events that occurred in the spiritual world. So this is not a language that came out of the ding-dong theory.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
Most of the languages we have today are based on what is called the ding-dong theory. It is in fact a linguistic theory; you can look it up. But the Arabic language is based on what is called توقیفیۃ. This is not a conventional language. One of the Orientalists has said that Arabic is the most artificial language in existence. All other languages are what are called pidgin languages, where different peoples with different original languages came together and tried to communicate with one another, and then a new language evolved. This new language was basically a mixture of all these different words drawn from different languages. Urdu, for example, is a pidgin language. It is not an original language. All its words come from other languages such as Arabic, Persian, and Sindhi.

Arabic, on the other hand, is not a pidgin language. It is not an arbitrary, glued-together language. It is, in a sense, a divine language, put in place for a divine message.

And so today I want to point out some of these incredible nuances and subtleties in the Arabic language, so that we can truly appreciate its depth and have some idea of how intricate and sophisticated this language is. Now, those of you children who have studied the science of Tajweed and Makharij from a proper madrasa or from a Maulvi Sahab.

Those of you who know the proper pronunciation of the letters will appreciate what I am about to show you. The younger children in the group may find it difficult. So I ask the parents to help the children wherever something is not clear. I have prepared some diagrams for each topic, which I will send along as I share this with you. Hopefully that will make it easier for you to understand and follow along, InshaAllah.

One of the most fascinating things about the Qur'an is that meaning reaches down to the letter itself. There is no other language that can do this. You can look up a word in Arabic and understand something of its meaning simply by looking at how its letters are pronounced. Some of the great linguists of Arabic, such as Ibnul Faris, have documented this entire science on the basis of phonetics, on the basis of how letters sound.

Take a word such as نَفَسَ, nafasa. It is built on a root of nun and fa. The third letter then changes, and as the root changes the meaning changes with it. The change rests on the qualities of the letter itself. So نَفَسَ means to blow or to breathe. Then you have نفث, which means to blow lightly. Observe the difference in sound between the way س and ث are pronounced. س is pronounced in a very ordinary tone, just like breathing. ث, on the other hand, is pronounced very softly. And so, when it is added to the same root of nun and fa, the meaning becomes to blow softly, because the pronunciation of the letter ث is soft.

Then you have نفح, which means breeze, the breeze of the winds. Here you get the ح sound, which is in ریح, meaning winds. The sound that the winds make is in the pronunciation of the letter ح itself. ریح. You can hear the wind in the letter ح. This is incredible. This is not some dingdong theory. This is truly a divine language. It is amazing.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
Then you have the word نفخ, which is استعلاء. It is a very strong letter because of the way the letter خ is pronounced. And because of the force in the letter kha, نفخ means to blow forcefully. Notice the sound the letter خ makes. It is explosive, like a blast. خ. There is friction in it. It has a bang to it. And that is why you have the word خلق, which also begins with the letter خ, and which means to create. Khalaq means to create. As Allah said:

ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ

Why is that? Because creation took place with a Big Bang. Is that not so? The singularity exploded into this universe with the Big Bang. That is the خ in the word خلق.

So you have four words: نَفَسَ, nafasa, nafaHA, and nafaKHA, each taking its meaning from the sound of the final letter. And you will find this throughout the Arabic language. It is deeply sophisticated in the way Allah has designed it. You simply cannot make this up. It is too incredible. And these are signs of Allah. These are signs of Allah, placed into the very fabric of the one thing that was given to human beings and was not given to any other creation: language.

سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ

We will show them, and keep showing them, our signs in the horizons and in their souls, until it becomes clearly manifest to them.

that this message is the truth. These linguistic dimensions of the Qur'an are signs that prove it to be a divine message in fact.

The Kalima Is Made from Ilah

Now consider the word Allah. It is made of two syllables formed by a combination of three letters. Two syllables: All-Laah. And three letters: Alif, Laam, and Haa. Allah. Now look at how these letters are pronounced. You have three letters: Alif, Laam, and Haa. The Alif, or the Hamza, is articulated at the deepest point of the throat. The name of Allah issues from the very point at which human vocalization becomes possible. It comes from the depths of the vocal tract. And when you say Allah, it returns to the Haa, which also lies at the depth of the vocal tract. Both the Hamza and the Haa are what are called huroof al-halq, the letters of the throat, because they are articulated from the base of the vocal tract. So the word Allah begins from the depths of the throat and returns to the depths of the throat. But in the middle of it stands the letter Laam, which is articulated from the ceiling of the mouth, the lisaan. Notice where your tongue must touch in order to pronounce the Laam correctly: the ceiling of your mouth. Now this is incredible. The name of Allah begins from the depth of the throat, travels all the way up to the ceiling of the mouth, and then returns to that same depth. It covers the entire range of vocalization, from the bottom to the top, and then back to the bottom again. The whole range is covered by the name Allah, because He is the one who encompasses all. This is incredible. Even the manner in which His name is pronounced points to His glory and magnificence.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
Then some scholars have pointed out something found in the Greek language. Lu-Laan is a Greek word meaning to soothe or to comfort. And it has been recognized throughout history that the sound Laa is a soothing and comforting sound, especially for children. That is where the word lullaby comes from, and that is where La La comes from. This is what mothers sing to their children: La la la la la la la. Because babies find it comforting. Why? Because it is a soothing sound. It brings a kind of tranquility, sakeena, to the heart. So the name of Allah is in truth something that brings tranquility and peace to the heart of a human being when he says Allah. You will also find that most forms of meditation are built on the sound La, because it is believed that when this is done as a regular practice, it connects all the meridian channels in the body.

Now look at our Kalima, upon which our entire religion rests: La ilaha illa Allah. There is a constant repetition of the sound La, because this is a sound of tranquility, because it is a sound of comfort. Just as our religion, Islam, is a religion of peace, a religion of tranquility and comfort. And it is truly amazing that Allah has built His entire Kalima upon this comforting sound. Anyone in the world is able to recite this Kalima.

And then this Kalima, this statement, has four words made up of twelve letters: La, ilaha, illa, and Allah. But what is amazing is that this entire Kalima is composed of only three letters: Alif, Laam, and Haa. And what word do these three letters combine to form? Ilahun. And when you recite the Kalima, what are you saying? La ilaha illa Allah. There is no ilah except Allah. And you are saying it with the very letters that make up the name Allah. Allah is using the three letters of His name.

Alif, Laam, and Haa, forming this supremely eloquent statement, which is the basis of His entire divine revelation. This is far too perfect to be a coincidence. There is simply too much perfection here for it to be a random accident. Who can do this? Do you think any human being, alone or all of them together, is capable of this kind of perfection? It is impossible. This is clear proof that this is indeed a divine message, and that it is from Allah AWJ.

All combinations of Allah are found in the Quran

Another fascinating fact about this name "ALLAH" is that it is the only and most perfect four-letter name that exists in the world, in the sense that no matter which letter you remove, its meaning does not change. Normally, in any language, when you begin removing letters from a name, its meaning changes. Take "Jameel," for example, which means beautiful. Remove the Ya from it and it becomes Jamal, which means camel. Remove the Jeem and what remains is میل, which means dirt. Remove the Meem and it becomes Jail. So whichever name you choose, as soon as you begin removing letters from it, its meaning begins to change. But Allah is such a unique and amazing name that no matter which letter you remove, its meaning does not change. And every variation points to Allah Himself through a verse of the Quran.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
If I call His name Allah with all four letters, ا ل ل ہ, the Quran says: إِنَّنِىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ فَٱعْبُدْنِى وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكْرِىٓ‎. No doubt I am Allah. There is no Ilah except Myself. Worship Me and establish prayer to remember Me.

If I remove the first Alif, what remains is للہ, and the Quran says: لِلَّهِ مُلْكُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.

If I remove the first Laam, what remains is Ilah, and the Quran says: وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِى فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِلَهٌۭ وَفِى ٱلْأَرْضِ إِلَهٌۭ. And He is the Ilah in the heavens and the Ilah in the earth.

If I remove the first Alif and the first Laam, what remains is لہ, and the Quran says: لَهُۥ مُلْكُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.

And if I drop everything — the first Alif, the first Laam, and the second Laam — and leave behind only the last Haa with the sound of Pesh upon it, Hu, the Quran says: لَّآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ. There is no deity except Him.

So Hu points to Allah. Lahu points to Allah. Ilah points to Allah. Lillah points to Allah. And Allah is Allah Himself. Every single variation of His name is referenced by the Quran itself, and all of them point to Allah Himself. SubhanAllah! What a magnificent word Allah chose as a name for Himself.

You know that in Arabic there is a number attached to each individual letter. Alif is 1. Ba is 2. Jeem is 3, and so on. It is called Ilm AlAdad, the knowledge of numbers. That is how you arrive at the number 786 for Bismillah. If you add up the weight, that is, the number assigned to every single letter in the Basmala, it comes out to 786. La Ilaha Illa Allah comes out to 165. Ali comes out to 110. Muhammad comes out to 92. And that is why these numbers are sometimes used in place of the name itself.

Now, the name Allah has two syllables and three letters, does it not? The two syllables are All—Laah, and the three letters are Alif, Laam, and Haa. Two and three make five.

Consider how many times the two letters Alif and Laam are repeated in the Kalima. Each of them is repeated exactly five times. The letter Ha is repeated twice. And for those who know the science of numbers: what is the weight of the letter Ha? What is the number assigned to it? It is 5. And it appears twice in the Kalima: once to balance the Ilah, and again to balance the Laam, both of which are repeated five times.
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
Now look at the number for Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. For those who understand the science of numbers: what is the total for Bismillah? It comes out to 786. And what is the sum of those three digits? What is 7 + 8 + 6? It is 21. That is, 2 and 1. And if you look at Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim, it contains the one primary name of Allah, followed by two of His attributes. Two and one. And then, what is 2 + 1? It is 3 — the three letters Alif, Laam, and Ha, which make up the name Allah. This is beyond incredible. Everything is connected to everything else in such mathematical perfection. And what I am telling you is only the tip of the iceberg. There is so much more that exists in these verses, mathematically. There is so much mathematical proof within these verses that it lifts this message far beyond the shadow of any doubt that it could have been produced by any human mind. It is impossible.

Now add up the numbers of La ilaha illa Allah — there is no god except Allah. We know that Allah has ninety-nine attributes, which are called اسماء اللہ الحسنی. Now look at this diagram of the Kalima. Look at the weight of the numbers that make up La ilaha and illa: 31 + 36 + 32. They come out to 99. And what remains? Allah! You have Allah and His ninety-nine attributes.

Now, what is the weight of the word Allah? It is 66. What is 6 + 6? Twelve. And how many letters is the Kalima made up of? Twelve letters. SubhanAllah! What is the weight of the entire Kalima? It is 165, is it not? What is 1 + 6 + 5? That is also twelve.

Now look at the numbers that make up the weight of the word Allah. You have 1 for Alif; 30 + 30, which is 60, for the two Laams; and then 5 for the Ha. Now, in the science of numbers, when you have a figure greater than ten, you take the primary number and separate it from the number of times it is repeated. So, for example, you have 60 for the two Laams, which is in fact 6 repeated ten times. The primary number, then, is 6. So if you reduce it, what numbers do you get? You get 1 for the Alif, 6 for the two Laams, and 5 for the Ha — the very same numbers as the weight of La ilaha illa Allah: 1, 6, 5, in the same order.

This is simply incredible, miraculous. Who could devise perfection of this kind? This is truly Allah's word in action.

سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ

We will keep showing them Our signs in the horizons and in their own souls, until it becomes clearly manifest to them that this message is the truth. SubhanAllah!
body.topic_title_en: The Miracles of the Name Allah

body.text_en:
We are studying the first verse of Surah al-Fatiha, which is the Basmala: بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم — With the name of Allah, the intensely merciful, the consistently merciful. Within this statement we are studying the meaning of the word Allah, which comes from the word Ilah. When the definite article "the" is applied to the word Ilah, it becomes exclusive, and one arrives at the word Allah. My Allah, then, is the one to whom I should submit completely, the one to whom I should be completely loyal.

كَذَٰلِكَ يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُسْلِمُونَ

I will complete my blessings on you if you submit to me.

My Allah is the one I turn to for protection and refuge in desperate times.

وَإِمَّا يَنْزَغَنَّكَ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ نَزْغٌ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ

And if an evil whisper comes to you from Shaytan, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing.

My Allah is the one I am passionately in love with, the one I am obsessed about.

قُلْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ فَاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ

O Muhammad, say to them: If you should love Allah, then follow me, so Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

My Allah is the one whose glory and magnificence astounds and astonishes me. When I set out to understand Him and to recognize Him, I realize that He is so lofty, so far beyond my capacity to comprehend and understand, that I would be dumbfounded every time I tried to approach Him.

قُل لَّوْ كَانَ ٱلْبَحْرُ مِدَادًۭا لِّكَلِمَتِ رَبِّى لَنَفِدَ ٱلْبَحْرُ قَبْلَ أَن تَنفَدَ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّى وَلَوْ جِئْنَا بِمِثْلِهِۦ مَدَدًۭا

Say, "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement."

Finally, my Allah is the one I lean on, the one on whom I place my entire weight.

إِن يَنصُرْكُمُ ٱللَّهُ فَلَا غَالِبَ لَكُمْ ۖ وَإِن يَخْذُلْكُمْ فَمَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَنصُرُكُم مِّنۢ بَعْدِهِۦ ۗ وَعَلَى ٱللَّهِ فَلْيَتَوَكَّلِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ

If Allah helps you, none can overcome you. If He forsakes you, who is there, after that, who can help you? In Allah alone, then, let believers put their trust.

These, then, are all the different meanings of the word Ilah that apply exclusively to Allah once the definite article "the" is applied to Ilah. But of all these meanings, the most prominent and the loftiest is this: my Allah is the one I worship and obey.

إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ

It is You we worship and You we ask for help.

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُمْ وَٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ

O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous.

The word used here is عبادۃ, which is commonly translated as worship. But the word actually means two things. The word عبادۃ means to worship and also to obey, both at the same time. And the Ilah who is worshipped and obeyed, the one for whom عبادۃ is done, is called معبود: the one who is worshipped and obeyed. These words are not interchangeable, as they are in the English language. Instead, both of them are embedded inside a single Arabic word, inside the word عبادۃ.

If you open any English Qur'an, a great many oversimplified translations say there is no one worthy of worship except Allah. That is the common translation.

There is no one worthy of worship except Allah. And when we think of the word worship, what comes to mind? The five daily prayers, fasting, zakat, and so on. Are these not the first things? All of these are different forms of worship. And we assume that is the whole of it. We stop at those activities. That is precisely the point I wish to highlight today: the difficulty with translating the word عبادۃ as worship is that worship does not necessarily include the idea of obedience, and especially obedience that grows out of love and trust.

The word obedience can carry a very negative overtone. People can be forced into obedience. Children are often bullied into obedience through threats or worse. So obedience sometimes has a very negative feeling attached to it. That is not the kind of obedience we are speaking of here. We are speaking of the obedience that arises naturally as the product of all these definitions of الہ. When you love someone passionately, when you are absorbed in that person, when you are wholly devoted and loyal to that person, when you can lean on that person completely and put your entire weight upon him knowing that he will not let you fall, when you are so impressed and astonished by the loftiness of that person's greatness and his magnificence, when you know that he is the only one you can turn to for protection and refuge — then what comes out naturally, as the product of all these feelings, is obedience. An obedience that grows out of love. A lover's obedience, offered to make his beloved happy. One that rests on passionate love and on complete, unshakable trust. Do you understand?

So عبادۃ, and specifically عبادۃ offered to an الہ, has these two ideas embedded within it: worship and obedience, both of which grow out of passionate love and not out of force or compulsion.

Now let us understand this idea of obedience from the point of view of the Qur'an. I want you to observe how the word الہ is used in these verses. In the story of Moses, peace be upon him, one of the things Pharaoh said to his commanders was:

وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمَلَأُ مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَهٍ غَيْرِى

When they saw Moses, peace be upon him, coming forward, and Pharaoh noticed his own authority over his commanders weakening, he said: I do not see anyone other than myself as an الہ for you. Now, when a king is speaking to his commanders and calling himself an الہ, is he thinking of worship or of obedience? He does not need them to make supplication to him at that moment. What does he need? He needs their obedience. So in this verse the word الہ is used in the sense of obedience.

Then there is the verse:

أَرَءَيْتَ مَنِ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَهَهُۥ هَوَىٰهُ

Have you seen the one who has taken his desires as his الہ?

Let us draw up a list of some desires. One person has certain temptations. Another has greed. Another is offered a highly profitable but forbidden business opportunity. He has that desire: to become rich, to become powerful.

Now, do people carve a statue out of money or out of power and then go and worship it? What do people do with their desires? They obey them. They have an itch and they scratch it — as the advertisement for Sprite says, obey your thirst. The point is that when you have a temptation you do not worship it; you obey it. Now, sometimes one of these shades of meaning takes control over the other, but in some measure both are present.

So now, when we use the word Allah, which means THE الہ, we arrive at a different meaning.

He is the being who is to be worshiped, and also obeyed. To put this in practical terms, why do these two things matter? Suppose we are about to pray in fifteen minutes. Fajr is fifteen minutes away and we must perform عبادۃ. Now what sort of عبادۃ is that? Worship, or obedience? Worship, is it not? But from Fajr until Zuhr we may not be worshiping Him. Yet what had we better be doing? Obeying Him. Between two prayers you and I are not necessarily worshiping Him, but we had better still be obeying Allah AWJ. This is why the concept of ibadah in Islam is so comprehensive. You go out and earn a lawful income at your job: that is an act of obedience. You go to school and sincerely fulfill the purpose for which you went there. That is عبادۃ. That is obedience to Allah. You obey your parents, love them, and respect them: that is عبادۃ. You are kind to your brothers and sisters, generous to those in need, respectful to your elders. All of these are acts of servitude and slavery to Allah SWT. All of these are acts of ibadah. And when the time for salah arrives and we stand before Him in prayer, that is an act of worship, and that too is ibadah. So you see that ibadah is a very comprehensive term. And the meaning of the word Allah is this: the One for whom we perform ibadah is the One we constantly worship, and He is the One we are constantly obeying.
