Now that we have some understanding of the name Allah, it is time to speak about His ninety-nine attributes. In the previous session I sent you an image in which I showed you how La Ilaha Illa Allah contains Allah and His ninety-nine attributes.

There is one thing I forgot to mention, which I would like to mention now, since we are on the topic. Last time I showed you that the weight of the kalima, La Ilaha Illa Allah, is 165, based on the Ilm al-Adad presented by Imam Jaffar as-Sadiq AS. Now look at the numbers that make up the weight of the word Allah. You have 1 for the Alif, then 30 plus 30, which is 60, for the two Laams, and then 5 for the Ha. In Ilm al-Adad, when you have a number greater than 10, you take the primary number and separate it from the number of times it is repeated. For example, you have 60 for the two Laams, which is really 6 repeated 10 times. So the primary number is 6. Now, if you reduce it in this way, what numbers do you get? You get 1 for the Alif, 6 for the two Laams, and 5 for the Ha, which are exactly the same numbers as the weight of La Ilaha Illa Allah: 1, 6, 5, in the very same order.

In any case, Allah has ninety-nine attributes. The questions commonly asked are these: what are these attributes? Does He need these attributes, or do we need these attributes in order to understand Him? Let us begin, then, with a very basic understanding of name and attributes. This is in fact a very complicated subject, so today I only want to give a basic understanding of the difference between the name Allah and His ninety-nine attributes. The concept of name and attributes is the same as the concept of noun and adjectives. And the combination of the two helps us understand the entity itself, does it not?

If we wish to gain a complete understanding or comprehension of an entity, the scholars state that we need to understand its attributes. If we understand all the attributes of an entity, we understand the entity itself. In other words, to understand the noun, I need to understand all its adjectives, and my knowledge of the attributes is directly proportional to my knowledge or awareness of the entity itself.

If I gain only a partial understanding of the attributes, I will have only a partial understanding of the entity. I will still understand something, but my understanding will be incomplete. In Arabic this is spoken of as ذات and صفات. The Zaat is the being, the entity itself, and the Sifaat are the attributes of that being or entity. We as human beings are a composite of a spirit and a body. So I have a soul and I have a body, and these two things together are called the Zaat. Each of these components then has its own attributes. My soul has certain spiritual attributes, and my body has certain physical attributes. Once I have recognized the attributes and capabilities of my soul, I have in effect gained an awareness of the capabilities of the soul itself. In the same way, once I recognize and understand the attributes of my body, I understand my body. By understanding the Sifaat, I can understand the Zaat itself.

What you and I refer to in the first person is the Zaat. When I say, "I am Asif," the "I" that I am referring to is my Zaat, my being. Do you understand? It is always the Zaat, the being, that is given a name. Asif is the name of my being, my essence. My being is the actual entity that is being identified by the name Asif.

Suppose I am meeting you for the first time, and we have never met before, and I introduce myself by saying, "AsSalaamAlaykum, I am a teacher." You will respond, "WalaykumAsSalaam, and you are also a weirdo." Is that not so? Because you do not introduce yourself by your attributes. You introduce yourself by your name, the name given to your existence.

Now, attributes, or Sifaat, are the things that further describe your Zaat. Does that make sense?

So, for example, if we know there is a man named Zaid, we understand that the name of his Zaat, his being, is Zaid. We can identify his being through his name, and then we can gather additional information about him through his spiritual and physical attributes, the attributes that describe who Zaid is. He is intelligent, he is smart, he is witty, he has a fair complexion, he is slim, he is a tennis player, he is a brother, a son, a husband, he is brave, he is handsome, and so on.

Now, between the being and its attributes, which is the essential entity? Between Zaat and Sifaat, which is the key thing? It is obviously the Zaat. All these additional pieces of information that we have about Zaid exist only because Zaid himself exists. If there is no Zaid, none of the attributes can exist. Adjectives exist only because the noun exists. If there is no noun, there can be no adjectives for that noun. Do you understand? So between the two things, the key element is the Zaat, the entity itself, which is given a name: Zaid.

Now let us say we are having a conversation, and I say, "Hey, did you hear about Zaid?" As soon as I say Zaid, assuming we are both speaking about the same Zaid, all his attributes flash through your mind at the mere mention of his name, do they not? Simply by hearing Zaid's name, you know that I am speaking about the Zaid who is intelligent, who is smart, who has a fair complexion, who is a tennis player, and so on. So merely by mentioning the name Zaid, I have in effect mentioned all fifty-two of his attributes.

It is the same with Allah. We know that a deity exists, and if He exists, He has a being, a Zaat, and that being needs to have a name.

so that He may be identified. And therefore, for the identification of His being, He chose the name Allah. Allah is the name of His Zaat, His being. And this is the name — this name, Allah — by which He introduced Himself to us in the Qur'an: إِنَّنِىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ Without doubt, I am Allah, or I am THE ILAH. There is no Ilah except Me.

And once there is a Zaat, there will obviously be what? Sifaat. Where there is a noun, there are always going to be adjectives. So the name Allah has ninety-nine adjectives, ninety-nine descriptions of who Allah is. Who is Allah? He is AlRehman, the intensely merciful. Who is Allah? He is AlRaheem, the constantly merciful. Who is Allah? He is AlMalik, the king. Who is Allah? He is AlAzeez, the powerful. So there are ninety-nine attributes, or ninety-nine adjectives, that describe who Allah is.

But the word Allah is the primary name, the name of the being, which encompasses within itself all ninety-nine attributes. The ninety-nine attributes exist ONLY because Allah exists. Just as when I said Zaid, all his attributes were included in his name, so too, when I say Allah, it is equivalent to my saying الرحمن، الرحيم، الملك، القدوس، السلام، المؤمن، المهيمن، العزيز، الجبار، المتكبر، الخالق، البارئ، المصور، الغفَّار، القهَّار، الوهَّاب ، الرزَّاق ، الفتَّاح ، العليم، القابض، الباسط، الخافض، الرافع، المعز، المذل، السميع، البصير، الحكم، الحکیم، العادل، اللطيف، الحلیم، الخبير، العظيم، الغفور، الشكور، العلي، الكبير، الحفيظ، الحسيب، الكريم، المقیم، الرقیب، الجلیل، المجيب، الواسع، الودود، المجيد، الباعث، الشهيد، الوكيل، القوى، المتين، الولي، الحميد، المحصى، المبدئ ، المعيد، المحيي، المميت، الحي، القيوم، الواجد، الماجد، الواحد، الصمد، القادر، المقتدر، المقدِّم، المؤخر، الأول، الآخر، الظاهر، الباطن، الوالي، المتعال، البِر، التواب، المنتقم، العفو، الرؤوف، المالك الملك، ذو الجلال و الإكرام، المقسط، الجامع، الغني، المغني، المانع، الضار، النافع، النور، الهادي، البديع، الباقي، الوارث، الرشيد، الصبور ، الحنان، المنان، الدیان، البرھان.

All these attributes, all these ninety-nine attributes, are combined within this one name, Allah. That is why, when we refer to Him by His name Allah, simply by mentioning His name we are mentioning all His attributes. Do you understand?

Now, so that you may understand, I am going to use a metaphor. But understand that this is only a metaphor. So do not confuse it with anything other than a metaphor.

Consider light. We know that light is white. They call it white light. White light has no color. Now, what happens is this: if you take a prism — a prism is a medium of glass — and this light, this white light, strikes the glass, it refracts. It bends. There is a bending of the light. And then what happens is that the color spectrum appears. You see a whole spectrum of colors, from violet to red and everything in between.

This is exactly what happens with creation. There is the light of Allah, may He be exalted, because He is اللہ نور السموت والارض. He is the light of the heavens and the earth. But what happens is that when this light of Allah strikes His creation, the divine attributes refract within creation. So you get all these different manifestations of the essence of Allah, may He be exalted, appearing in His creations. So in one instance you see that Allah is Kareem (the generous). In another instance He is Jabbar (the compeller). In another instance He is Qahhar (the subduer). And in another instance He is Azeez (the powerful).

In another instance He is Muzil (the humiliator). In another He is Moiz (the bestower of honor). And He is all of these attributes at one and the same time. In creation we are able to see these attributes only one at a time, because they are a refraction of the divine essence of Allah within His creation. So we see them individually. But Allah is all of these attributes at the same time, just as white light is all seven colors at the same time.

This world, then, becomes a theater for the divine manifestations of these attributes. And this is how we come to know Allah: not directly through Him, but through His creations.

لا تفکر فی اللہ . ولاکن تفکر فی خلق اللہ

Do not reflect upon Allah. Reflect instead upon the creations of Allah. And as Maulana Ali said:

العجز عن درك الإدراك إدراك . والبحث عن ذاتِهِ كُفرُ وإشراكُ

The inability to know Allah is the true understanding of Allah. And to attempt to discuss the essence of Allah is shirk. It is assigning partners to Him. It is shirk. Accepting our inability to know Allah is the true comprehension of Allah. This is why the essential act of worship in Islam is to place our intellects on the ground, surrendering the capacity of the intellect to know Allah.

So the divine essence of Allah refracts when it meets His creation and splits into these ninety-nine attributes, because that is the only way in which we can know Allah: through the attributes present in His creation. We know mercy because we have seen mercy in His creation. We know generosity because we have seen generosity in His creation. We know revenge because we have seen that attribute within His creation. Were that not so, we would have no way of understanding the idea of mercy, of generosity, of love, of abasement, of honor, of victory, of protection. For we, as human beings, need some practical example of an attribute in action in order to understand it.

But these attributes within creation can cause confusion for us, just as the components of white light can cause confusion. How can white light be violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, and red at the same time? For Allah is Kareem (the generous), yet He is also Qahhar (the subduer). He is Rehman and Raheem (intensely merciful and consistently merciful), yet He is also AlMuntaqim, the avenger. So how can these two attributes exist at the same time? How can one who is Kareem, who is benevolent, be Qahhar and Jabbar (the compeller) at the same time? How can the Qahhar be Rehman? How can the subduer be intensely merciful at the same time? To us this seems a paradox. But that is the very nature of the essence of Allah. He is all of those things at the same time.

So I will give you an example: rain. The Kareem, the benevolent, sends rain as His mercy. But He can use that same rain to deliver Azaab. He can use the same medium to deliver His wrath, causing floods and death and destruction. It is the same medium: rain. In one instance it can be a source of Rehmah, of mercy, bringing life. But in another instance He can take that same rain and make it a manifestation of His Azaab. He can use it to bring death and destruction. As a scholar said:

اِذَا الکریمُ . تَجَلّٰی بِسمِ المُنتَقِمِ

When the generous one manifests as the avenger. AlMuntaqim is one of the attributes of Allah. It is when Allah takes people to account. He takes people to account for their actions.

Yet even in doing this, He does not lose His attribute of being AlKareem, the generous. Even when He manifests as the avenger, He remains AlKareem, because this is what the Kareem does. The Kareem Alqaum, the most generous of a nation, can at times do things that people do not associate with generosity. This is what is called tough love. But when He manifests as the avenger, that does not mean He has lost His attribute of being generous. He manifests as the avenger BECAUSE He is generous. It is just as parents scold and discipline their children BECAUSE they love them. And we as human beings find this paradoxical. How can you punish me if you love me? Well, I am punishing you because I love you. And this is what Allah does.

We are studying Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Within that statement, we are looking at the word of highest rank, the Ismul Jalalah, the most majestic name of all: Allah. We said that Allah comes from the root word Ilah, with the definite article THE applied to it, which makes it exclusive and personal.

So then my Allah becomes the one to whom I should submit completely, the one to whom I should be truly loyal. He is the one I turn to for protection and refuge in my desperate times. He is the one I am passionately in love with, the one I am obsessed about. He is beyond my imagination and beyond my capacity to comprehend and understand. He is the one whose glory and majesty leave me dumbfounded every time I try to approach Him. He is the one I can trust completely, lean on, and put my entire weight upon, knowing that He will not let me fall. And finally, and most important of all the meanings, He is the one I worship. As I explained last time, worship, or عبادۃ in Arabic, means two things. It means worship and it means obedience, both arising out of all these different meanings of the word Allah.

After discussing the word Allah, we began to speak about His attributes. The Quran gives us 99 attributes of Allah. And so we said that there is a being and there are attributes. There is zaat and there are sifaat. Noun and adjectives. Allah is the name of the being; it is the name of the essence. And whenever there is an essence, it will manifest through its attributes. In order to understand the essence, or the being itself, we first need to understand its attributes, because without the attributes there is no way for us to understand the essence. Once we understand all the attributes, individually and independently, we can then put them all together to understand the capabilities of the essence itself.

And as Gestalt stated — he is the famous German psychologist — he said that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Because what happens is that when you combine the power of these individual parts, these individual attributes, and they all come together to form a complete whole, that whole takes on a reality of its own, which is now independent of the parts.

So, for example, I have a body that is made up of parts, both internal and external components. I can understand what these individual parts do. The eyes can see, the ears can hear, the tongue can taste and speak, the hands can do different things, the legs allow me to move, the heart does this, the liver does that. I can understand the capabilities of all these parts individually. And no doubt, they are all powerful in their own right. Even individually, they are all capable of amazing things.

But I cannot construct a building with these parts working independently. I cannot run a business. I cannot cure patients in a hospital, or build computers, or travel into outer space. I cannot do any of those things by means of these parts alone. But when I put all these parts together, and they begin to work together to accomplish a unified goal, when I begin to use their abilities collectively, now I have a body, an existence, that can do amazing and brilliant things. Hence the whole is always greater than the sum of its parts.
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
Now, in the previous session, to explain the divine essence and its attributes, I gave you the metaphor of white light. When white light hits a prism, it refracts into its respective colors.

If I can understand the attributes of these seven lights independently, I can gain a complete understanding of white light itself. Professional photographers understand the importance of this, especially today in digital photography, because they have to manipulate the settings of these seven colors, or hues, in order to achieve what is called white balance.

So, using that analogy in a very broad sense, and not in a literal one: when the divine essence of Allah (subhanahu wa ta'ala) strikes His creation, it refracts into these ninety-nine attributes. It is only through these attributes that we can understand anything about His essence, because without them there is no way for us human beings to form even a vague idea of the essence.

Suppose someone has never seen light. Let us say a child is born in a dark cave and has never once seen light. How will you explain the idea of light to him? You may talk about it, you may describe it as much as you please, but even your finest description of light will not come close to the real experience of light. Is that not so? You have to experience light in order to gain even some understanding of it.

And then that experience of seeing and feeling light is still not the experience of the sun itself, which is the source, the creator of that light. Light is only an attribute of what the sun has created. It is simply the experience of photons generated by the sun, is it not? So even when you and I experience light, we are not experiencing the power of the sun. We are experiencing an attribute of that which the sun has produced. Do you understand?

So Allah placed a tiny refraction of His divine attributes within His creation. Allah is so lofty that we human beings do not possess the capacity to understand His attributes directly, let alone His divine essence. So He refracted His divine essence into the attributes of His creation, so that we could experience them. These attributes that we find within His creations are His signs, and they point back to His own divine attributes. This is how we understand and experience — or rather, how we gain an inadequate, feeble understanding of — the divine attributes of Allah.

Now, how do we do this? How is it possible to understand a creator through the attributes of its creation? I will give you an example, and again, this is only a metaphor, an analogy that I am using to explain an idea. So I will need you to work with me here in order to understand what I am trying to explain.

The Martian and the iPad.

We human beings created computers and laptops. We created iPads. These are all our creation. Now let us say that one of these iPads finds its way over to the planet Mars. A Martian finds this iPad, and as he handles it, he begins to wonder who created it. Now, this Martian has never once seen a human being. He has no idea what a human being looks like. All he has is this iPad. So, simply by observing the attributes, or features, of this iPad, what could a Martian possibly come to know about human capabilities?
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
He could see that the iPad has a screen with a display. From that he could conclude that the human species has the ability to see things, that they possess the faculty of sight, because if they could not see, why would they need a display? Then he observes that the iPad has speakers, which produce sounds.

From this it concludes that the human species must also be able to hear. And since there is a volume control, perhaps human beings can hear a range of sounds. Then it looks at the keyboard, at the way the keys are designed, and perhaps arrives at the conclusion that human beings must have fingers, simply because of the way all the keys are set apart from one another. Then it opens the iPad and begins to study its architecture. It sees that the iPad, like any other computing device, works by binary signals: on and off, ones and zeros. On that basis it could conclude that the human mind must think logically, in terms of binary signals — positives and negatives, yes and no, benefits and disadvantages. Then it notices that the iPad is very light and easy to carry. So it could conclude that human beings are capable of movement, that they can go from one place to another, which means that perhaps they have feet. Do you understand? Simply by observing what the iPad can do, the Martian may be able to make some intelligent guesses about its maker. This iPad has these features, therefore its maker must have these capabilities. Do you understand?

But however much it studies and grasps the structure, the architecture, and all the features of this iPad, there is no way for it to arrive at a complete understanding of what a human being looks like or is capable of. How he thinks. His genetic makeup. How his body works. All of that is impossible for the Martian to determine from its observations of the iPad alone. Yet it could certainly gain a preliminary understanding of the human being. Is that not so?

The only way this Martian will be able to understand more about human beings is if a human being describes himself to it. Is that not so? Now suppose this same Martian finds a book on human physiology and human psychology. By studying it, the Martian can understand far more about the human species than it was able to work out by taking the iPad apart. The point I am trying to make is this: simply by observing the features and attributes of creation, it is not possible to understand the creator. We need a description provided by the creator himself, to supplement and support that preliminary understanding which we gained through our observation of his creation and our experience of dealing with it.

So in this example of the Martian and the iPad, we spoke of two things: its experience, or its logical deductions about human beings, drawn from its handling of the iPad, supplemented by its knowledge of human physiology and psychology. But even with all this, the reality is that the Martian still cannot gain a complete, one hundred percent understanding of human beings, because the Martian is not human. Books and descriptions and explanations can take you only so far.
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
Forget Martians; look at ourselves. You know that research is constantly being carried out in the fields of animal physiology and animal psychology and behavior. And these researchers say that they barely know anything. And this is a form of life lower than the human being. We cannot fully comprehend the lower forms. How then is it possible to fully understand our own creator?

So I hope that with this example I have laid the foundation for the conversation I wish to have with you today. As human beings, in order for us to understand the creator, we need two things.

An experiential interaction with the attributes of His creation, supplemented by the description of that creation given by the creator. And finally the realization that both of these together are still not enough to comprehend the creator fully, because the whole is always greater than the sum of its parts. For when it comes to understanding Allah, we are nothing more than Martians trying to understand Allah through His iPad, which is this universe. And even though we can understand something about the attributes of Allah THROUGH the attributes of His creation, we cannot, we can NEVER, understand Allah completely. That is why Maulana Ali said:

لا تفکر فی اللہ . ولاکن تفکر فی خلق اللہ

Do not reflect upon Allah. Instead, reflect upon the CREATIONS of Allah.

So Allah gave us His creation, this world that we live in and interact with. AND He gave us a description of Himself through the Quran, in which Allah described Himself to us through His attributes. So that by combining the two, we join our experience of our interaction with the attributes of His creation, which is the Zaahir (the external form), with the description of His divine attributes, the baatin (or the interior), in order to gain some preliminary understanding of Him — enough to be able to approach Him, to move toward Him, to begin our journey toward Him. But will we ever be able to reach Him? No. That is impossible.

So now let us look at how we combine the zaahir and the baatin. For example, the Quran tells us that Allah is merciful. He is Rehman and Raheem, the intensely and consistently merciful.

وَإِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌۭ وَحِدٌۭ ۖ لَّآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلرَّحْمَنُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

Your Ilah is one. There is no ilah except Him. He is AlRehman and AlRaheem — intensely merciful and consistently merciful.

Then the Quran tells us that Allah is Kareem. He is generous.

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ

Oh my beloved human being, what has deceived you against your generous master?

The Quran says that He is AlRazzaq.

إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلرَّزَّاقُ ذُو ٱلْقُوَّةِ ٱلْمَتِينُ

No doubt Allah is the one who is your provider. He is of immense power and very steadfast.

Studying the attributes of this world

So Allah uses these attributes to describe Himself in the Quran. Now, when we observe His creations — rain is one of His creations, pure water that falls from the sky, which is the source of all life on this planet — when we observe rain, we can find a reflection, or a refraction, of these same divine attributes in rain and in the sky that provides the rain.
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
Because Rehma means mercy, and mercy is shown by the powerful to the weak. Allah is العزیز الجبار, the one of great might and of great power. And we know that mercy is an act of compassion shown by the powerful toward the weak. Without that act, the weak would suffer. Rain certainly has that property, the property of mercy. If the sky were to hold back its rain, we would not be able to survive, and there is nothing that we could do about it. And even though all we do is keep corrupting and polluting the ozone layer, still the Raheem, the sky, continues to bless us with its rehma, its mercy, by sending us water. So Raheem, or Rehma, mercy, is the attribute of the sky, which sends us this mercy in abundance. The sky is not stingy about showing its mercy. When it rains, it pours. That is generosity. That is Karam.

That is an attribute of the Kareem. So we find these attributes, Raheem and Kareem, in one of Allah's creations: the sky. And we find them in what the sky produces: rain, or water, which is the source of all life.

This rainwater is then absorbed by the earth, and the earth produces vegetation, and vegetation is the secondary source of life for animals and human beings. So the earth reflects the divine attribute of Razzaq, the Provider, because it provides for human beings and animals. It is also a manifestation of the divine attribute of AlMuqeet, the Nourisher. And when there is balance in the water that comes from the sky, and balance in what the earth produces, there is Salaam. There is peace, there is tranquility, and this is another divine attribute of the Creator reflected through His creation. SubhanAllah.

Another thing we find in abundance in this universe is balance. Everything balances out everything else. That is AlHakam, a divine reflection of the Judge, the Arbitrator.

Look at the enormous size of this universe. Look at its expanse. That is a reflection of AlAzeem, the Magnificent. The عالی, the Exalted. AlKabeer, the Great. AlJaleel, the Majestic. Look at the divine beauty reflected in nature, in sunrise, in sunset, on the mountains. Look at the beautiful colors of the sky, at the raw beauty of nature. That is the Jameel, the Beautiful, manifesting Himself through His creation.

Look at gravity, and how it binds all creation to itself. No creature can escape the confines of gravity. Even those who can defy it for a time, such as the birds, what happens to them when they stop flapping their wings? And planes, what happens to them when they run out of fuel? All of them are eventually subdued and compelled by gravity. Why? Because He is AlJabbar, the Compeller, and He is AlQahhar, the Subduer.
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
And we know today that human beings are the cause of every natural disaster occurring across the world. We are constantly interfering with nature, and this leads to all sorts of environmental problems: global warming; overpopulation, which depletes natural resources; the destruction of forests; ocean acidification, the rising acidity of the oceans that is killing marine life. We human beings are the cause of most of the problems on this earth, if not all of them. Yet these problems take a very long time to surface. Human beings transgress against nature and act in such selfish ways for a long time before the harmful effects begin to appear. Why is that? We have to abuse our health for a long time before the effects begin to show. Why do these problems not follow immediately? Because He is Saboor, the Extremely Patient. He gives time. He grants relief for a long while, hoping that His creation may correct itself, hoping that His creation may restore the balance.

But when they do not, He grows angry, and He must intervene. When human beings become arrogant, and despite all the time granted to them by the Saboor they continue to inflict harm, then Allah uses that very creation which they have harmed. He uses that same creation to humble them and put them back in their place. The victim now becomes the avenger. Rain, which was meant to be a source of His mercy, can now become a source of death and destruction. The earth, which was created by the Razzaq and the Muqeet to sustain and nourish human beings, can now shake and quake.

and destroy everything upon it. That is the manifestation of the Generous One as the Avenger, Al-Muntaqim.

اِذَا الکریمُ . تَجَلّٰی بِسمِ المُنتَقِمِ

When the Generous One manifests as the Avenger.

He is warning us: do not take advantage of My mercy, because I can also grow angry. And nothing angers Me more than injustice. When I grow angry, I will put you back in your place, because I am Al-Hakam, the Judge. I am Al-Qadir, the All-Able. I can do whatever I wish, for I am Al-Muqtadir, the Dominant. Even though My inherent quality is النافع, the Benefactor, I can also be Al-Darr, the Distressor, the Harmer.

Then we see that everything, every creature on this planet, has a life span. It comes into being, and then it inevitably perishes. Who brought it into being? Who caused it to perish? That is المبدع and المعید, the Originator and the Returner. And through this temporal condition of His creation, He manifested Himself as Al-Hayy, the Ever-Living. By the constant state of change that He placed within His creation, He manifested as Al-Baqi, the Immutable, the One who never changes. SubhanAllah.

So Allah's divine attributes are reflected through His creation. Allah sent down His divine revelation, the Qur'an, and in it He described who He is through His divine attributes. The verses of the Qur'an are His inner, batini signs. And then He created this entire universe around us, manifesting those same divine attributes as His outward, zahiri, physical signs (آیات الکونی). This is so that we may experience the manifestation of His divine attributes through His creation. He joined the zahir and the batin together for us. Why? Because He is الظاہر and He is الباطن. SubhanAllah.
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
So I hope you now understand how the divine essence of Allah, His zaat, refracts when it strikes His creation and splits into these ninety-nine attributes. And how, through the attributes of His creation, we are able to experience a little, a very small fraction, of the reflection of His divine attributes.

But what is very, very, very important to understand is this: simply because we grasp a little from the reflection of His divine attributes through the attributes of His creation, we cannot confine Him within the attributes of His creation. We cannot say that Allah is Raheem, that He is Kareem, that He is Salaam, just like rain. We cannot do that. We cannot say He is Al-Jabbar, just like gravity. Because if we do that, we are now reducing Him, bringing Him down, to the level of His creation. In the example of the Martian that I gave earlier, this would be similar to the Martian thinking that human beings are like the iPad, or that the capabilities of the iPad truly reflect the capabilities of the human being itself. Nothing could be further from the truth. We human beings are far, far, far more powerful and capable than the iPads we have created. The iPad is merely a reflection of our capabilities, is it not?

So it is the same with Allah. We cannot equate the attributes of His creation with His divine attributes. The mercy we see in this universe through this creation is nothing like Allah's mercy. His mercy is far beyond comprehension. What we are seeing is nothing more than a tiny reflection of a fraction of His divine mercy. His mercy is incomprehensible. His powers are incomprehensible. His majesty, His magnificence, His compassion, His love, His generosity, His divinity are far, far, far beyond anything we can ever comprehend. This is truly important to understand.

This is because we are very limited in the mental images we are able to form. So when we looked at the attributes of the sky, for example, we gained a point of reference, a mental concept of this attribute called mercy, and of generosity, and of peace and tranquility. So rain is merciful. But how merciful? Human beings are merciful, but how merciful? Merciful like the rain? If not, then merciful like whom? Like me? Like you? Like him? Like her? Like them? What is the level of Allah's mercy? What is the most merciful creation you can possibly imagine? Is Allah merciful in the way that creation is merciful? If the answer is yes, then we have just brought Allah down to the level of that creation, because now that thing or that person is equal to Allah, a partner in this mercy of His. Rain and Allah become equally merciful. And that is the very definition of shirk: to associate partners with Allah. That is shirk. Do you understand?
body.topic_title_en: The Refraction of Divine Attributes in Creation
body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
This is the shirk we are constantly negating, purifying Allah of it through our kalima. This is what subhan Allah means. Subhan comes from the word sabh, which means a great distance, or being far from something. It also comes from the word sabaha, which means to swim. When someone is swimming, he is always on top, and there is always a distance between him and the floor of the ocean. From the same root we get the word tasbeeh: creating a distance between Allah and His ninety-nine attributes. Consider what we do in our daily tasbeeh. Thirty-three times we affirm AllahuAkbar, Allah is great. Why is He great? Because of His divine attributes. AlHamdulillah, all praise and gratitude belong to Allah. Why do we praise Him? For what are we grateful to Him? Because of His divine attributes. SubhanAllah: He is lofty, and there is a great distance between us and Him. Why is that? Because of His divine attributes. And then, after declaring and affirming His ninety-nine attributes, what do we say at the end? La Ilaha Illa Allah. There is no one, no Ilah, no creation that reflects His divine attributes. Illa Allah, except Allah. We are negating from Him all the attributes of His creation. We are purifying Him of any and every resemblance that we may, in concept or in thought, place between Him and His creation.

And He Himself says: هُوَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِى لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱلْقُدُّوسُ ٱلسَّلَمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُ ٱلْمُهَيْمِنُ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْجَبَّارُ ٱلْمُتَكَبِّرُ — He is Allah, there is no Ilah other than Him. He is the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfect, the Bestower of Faith, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. And then, after saying all of this, what does He say? سُبْحَنَ ٱللَّهِ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ — He is Exalted above whatever they associate with Him. And what is it that they associate with Him? They associate the attributes of His creation with Him. The entire concept of tawheed is the purifying of Allah from the attributes of His creation. That is why the kalima of tawheed is La Ilaha Illa Allah: there is no Ilah except Allah.

Scholars say that one way to understand the kalima in the light of these divine attributes is to replace the word Ilah in that kalima with each of the divine attributes. So instead of saying La Ilaha Illa Allah, you now say La Rehma Illa Allah: there is no creation that has mercy like the mercy of Allah. La Karam Illa Allah: there is no creation that has generosity like the generosity of Allah. La Salaam Illa Allah: there is no creation that can provide tranquility like the tranquility of Allah.

body.topic_title_ur: Refraction of divine attributes in creation

body.text_en:
La Jabar Illa Allah: there is no creation that can compel like the compulsion of Allah. La Intiqaam Illa Allah: there is no creation that can avenge like the vengeance of Allah. And when you carry out this exercise of the intellect for each and every attribute, when you strip away from the attributes of Allah AWJ all these attributes as they appear in His creation, that is when you truly understand the meaning of La Ilaha Illa Allah: there is no Ilah except Allah. And when nothing exists that is like Him, then I can never completely understand Him. For there may be many an Ilah sharing in, or reflecting, the divine attributes of Allah, yet neither singly nor all together can they compare with the very attribute of Allah that they reflect. That is why the weight of La Ilaha Illa is ninety-nine. It is the complete negation of ninety-nine attributes reflected in and through His creation, before the affirmation of that one word, Allah. Speaking of this inability, this incapacity of human beings to approach Allah AWJ, Maulana Ali AS said:

العجز عن درك الإدراكہُ إدراك . والبحث عن سِرِّ ذاتِهِ إشراك

The inability to know Allah is in fact the true understanding of Allah, and to attempt to discuss the essence of Allah is Shirk. For it is my inability, my incapacity to comprehend Him, and it is His superiority over me, that make Him worthy of my worship and worthy of my obedience.

لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَىْءٌۭ

We are forced to negate, and to purify Allah of, every attribute we find in ourselves and in His creation, because there is nothing comparable to Him. And He explains this to us beautifully through one single word in the ayah:

لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَىْءٌۭ

No matter how hard you try, no matter how high your imaginations fly, no matter how deep your thoughts dive, there is no way you can ever understand My attributes. لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَىْءٌۭ There is absolutely nothing you can compare Me to. SubhanAllah.

I want you to pause for a moment and think about this paradox. He created this magnificent universe around us, every single entity within it reflecting His divine attributes, for us human beings, who possess intellects. Why? So that we might gain some semblance of an understanding of His powers, His attributes. And then, once we have gained that understanding, even at a subatomic level, He says: لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَىْءٌۭ. Whatever little you now think you know about Me, know that I am not like it. I am far beyond it. And what is so amazing is that He does this linguistically, through the use of one word: كَمِثْلِهِ. This is not a word in common use, nor was it used in ancient Arabia. It is a word used only in balagha, in the eloquence of the Quran.

We have already established that in order to understand something, we must compare it either in being (zaat) or in attributes (sifaat). From a grammatical standpoint, the word کمثلہ is in fact two words: KA and Mislihi. Both are words of comparison. KA is used for comparison, and Mislihi too is used for comparison. But the two are never fused together in this manner, as Allah has fused them in this ayah. So let us try to understand the subtlety in the use of this word:

کمثلہ

body.text_en:
In Arabic, when you wish to compare someone in attributes, you add the letter KA. For example, suppose I want to compare the bravery of Zaid with a lion. If I want to say that Zaid is brave like a lion, I will have to use the letter KA to do so.

I would have to say: زیدٌ کل أسدِ — Zaid is like a lion. What am I comparing here? Clearly I do not mean that Zaid has fangs and claws and a tail, and that he roars. I am not comparing Zaid in his being to a lion. I am comparing his bravery to the bravery of a lion. That is why I use the letter KA: زیدٌ کل أسد. So KA is used to compare two things in their attributes.

But when I need to compare in Zaat, that is, in being, I cannot use the letter KA. Grammatically that would be wrong. I would have to use the word Misl. For example: الشبل مثل الاسد — a cub is similar to a lion. The son of a lion is like the lion. Here I am not comparing in attributes, not in Sifaat. I am comparing in Zaat. I am comparing the essence, the being itself.

This, then, is the rule of the Arabic language. KA and Misl are used with great precision, and we find this distinction throughout Arabic poetry. For example, this poet is praising the generosity of a king, and generosity is an attribute. He compares the king's generosity to the ocean, and so he uses the letter KA. He says Kal Bahri:

کل بحرِ یَقذِفُ لِلقریبِ لآلیۃ     جوداً و یبَعَثُ لِلبَعیدِ سحائِبا

He says that the king is generous like the ocean: when I come closer to him, he gives me pearls, and when I move away from him, he sends clouds heavy with rain. Why does he use KA? Because he is comparing the attribute of generosity.

But when the being itself, the entity, the Zaat, must be compared, the word Misl has to be used:

أنا السُّروجِیُّ وَ ھذا وَلدی   و الشِّبلُ فی الِمخبَرِ مِثلُ الاسد

I am a lion and this is my son; without doubt the son of a lion is like the lion. Here, because the comparison is in being, in Zaat, the poet uses the word Misl.

I hope all of you grasp this subtlety, because it is precisely this that makes the verse so beautiful. Allah says:

لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَىْءٌۭ

To speak of comparison with Himself, Allah fuses both the KA and the Misl together: Ka-Mislihi. KA is used for attributes; Misl is used for the being itself. So Allah says: whether you try to compare Me in attributes, KA, or you try to compare Me in being, Misl, it will not be possible. لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَىْءٌۭ — there is nothing in existence, neither in attribute nor in being, that you can use to compare Me to. Do you see the beauty of this word?

Ka — there is no one comparable to Me in attributes.

Mislihi — there is no one comparable to Me in being.

KaMislihi — there is no one you can compare Me to, in attributes or in being. SubhanAllah!

body.text_en:
We're studying the linguistic meaning of the word Allah. We have been slowly building upon that concept — what the word Allah means, what his attributes mean. Hopefully by now you have a clearer understanding of who Allah is, and what he is supposed to mean to us, what place he is supposed to have in our lives, in our day-to-day dealings. Let me give a very quick recap of what we have discussed so far.

We spoke about nouns and adjectives, essence and attributes. He named himself, his essence, Allah. إِنَّنِىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ — Indeed I am Allah; there is no deity except me. And then, when this divine essence meets his creation, it refracts into these ninety-nine attributes, so that we, his creation, could recognize certain things about him. I gave the example of a Martian and the iPad — how the Martian is able to understand or experience certain attributes of human beings simply by interacting with the iPad. And then, when he finds a book describing human physiology and human psychology, he can combine the two: his experience and his knowledge of human beings, to understand more about us. But we also saw that understanding the iPad alone does not provide a complete understanding of human capabilities.

In the same way, we interact with this world, which is Allah's creation, and we experience some of Allah's attributes by interacting with his creation and with nature. And then our experience is supplemented by the knowledge of the Qur'an, which is Allah's message, delivered to us by Him, through His messenger, in a language that we human beings can comprehend, explaining who Allah is: the what, the how, and the why of his creations. And he did this so that we could intellectually reconcile the two things together. Allah says in the Qur'an that He is merciful (raheem), and then we do experience his mercy in the form of rain falling from the sky, providing us the means of a good life, and we say, indeed, Allah is merciful. It is the same for all the other attributes of Allah. We find them manifest in various different ways in his creations. We see them within us, within our souls, as well as in the horizons, in the creations outside of us. And this is what Allah is referring to when he says:

سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ

I will keep showing them my signs, my proofs, through the attributes of my creation, in their own souls and in the horizons — meaning within themselves and all around them. I will keep showing them these undeniable proofs. حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ — until they are truly convinced, until it becomes perfectly clear to them that this message is the truth. And today, with the advances that science has made, we are finding these attributes manifest even at the cellular level.

And why is it important to realize this? The reason it is important to understand this is because Allah speaks about a great deal of the unseen in the Qur'an, does He not? Things that we are incapable of seeing or proving while we are in this limited physical realm. So what He has done is this: He has made what we can see, what we can understand, what we can experience, a proof for that which we cannot. So in essence He is saying, I am telling you who I am through my attributes, which I have placed abundantly in my creation. They are manifesting inside you and outside of you, so that you can experience it for yourself.

And if what I am saying about this physical, seen world is true, then what I am saying about the spiritual, unseen world must also be true. So He used what we can see and experience as proof for that which we cannot see and experience. And He did all of this through the manifestation of His attributes all around us. And then He said that even though you will be able to get a small taste of My attributes, you can never completely understand My divine attributes to their fullest extent, because لیس کمثلہ شئی — there is nothing exactly similar to Him. کمثلہ: not in attributes, and not in essence.

So that is the first thing I want you to understand: why He designed everything this way, so that He could use what can be seen as evidence, as daleel, for that which cannot be seen. Because the unseen world is a far greater manifestation of His divine attributes.

Then we began studying Surah al-Ikhlaas, which is the most perfect description of how Allah is different from His creation. Because when things become relatable, the human intellect tends to equate. The human intellect computes: if A equals B, and B equals C, then C must be equal to A, correct? If two sides of a triangle are equal, the third has to be equal as well. So if the sky is manifesting Allah's attributes, the sun, the moon, the stars, the earth — if all of these are manifesting Allah's attributes, then they must all be gods. If human beings can manifest attributes of Allah, then why can Jesus not be the son of God? Because a son resembles his father, correct?

So Surah al-Ikhlaas responds to that line of thinking, using the word "Ahad," which we studied in the last session. Allah says, قل ھو اللہ احد — Say, He is Allah, the unique. And I explained to you how Allah is unique in His attributes, how, even though creations can manifest some of Allah's attributes, they can never be equal to Him, by virtue of three things: Allah's attributes are timeless, they are limitless, and they are inherently owned by Him. This means they were not learned, because then they could have been forgotten. They were not given to Him, because then they could have been taken away. They are all part of His essence, like fragrance is part of a flower. You cannot separate a flower from its fragrance. Like the shape of a chair is part of its body — you cannot separate the shape of a chair from its body. Like cold is part of ice — you cannot separate cold from ice. If they are separated, it will no longer remain ice. So these attributes are inherently, fundamentally His own. That is all encapsulated in the meaning of the word "Ahad."

And the reason He did this is اختصاص, to single out. It is ONLY Allah who has no counterpart. This means that everyone other than Him will necessarily have what? A counterpart. If there is a general, there will be another general. If there is a king, there will be another king. If there is a president, there will be another president. If you have one false god, you can have another false god. If there is one rich person, there will be another rich person. You will have one planet, and there will be another planet. One star, another star. Everything that exists, everything that is created, will have a kufu. But it is ONLY Allah who has no kufu. And where did we get the ONLY HE part? We got it from this grammatically rearranged sentence, ولم یکن لہ کفوا احد, because the lahoo comes earlier.

Even though we do not understand classical Arabic, we are still compelled to appreciate the eloquence of this message. It took me what — five, six sessions to explain Allah to you. Allah does it in four short, simple sentences, without losing a fraction of the meaning. We human beings are simply not capable of such perfection. If Allah truly opens up our hearts, this is speech, this Quran, that is truly miraculous. It leaves us completely defeated, incapable of a response. We have no choice but to submit. Glory be to Allah.

And now the last thing, to wrap up this topic of Allah. In one of the previous sessions I mentioned that saying the name Allah is equivalent to saying all the ninety-nine names of Allah. Allah equals ninety-nine names. Some of you asked me, how is that? How is Allah the sum of all ninety-nine names put together? And I promised you that I would answer this question in the final session on the word Allah. And now that you understand Ahad and Samad, you will, God willing, be able to truly appreciate this.

Imagine ninety-nine different colors, each color being unique (Ahad), and each color being absolute (Samad). When you combine all these ninety-nine colors together, what do you get in the end? You get the PERFECT ILAH, AL-ILAH. You get ALLAH. The perfection of ALL His attributes.

And now you know what you must think when you hear the word "perfect" applied to Allah. You must think unique and absolute. So the perfection of ALL His attributes unites together to manifest the perfection of His one true essence, which is named ALLAH.

Aligning Ilah with Ikhlas

Let us look at some examples. I want you all to keep all the different definitions of the word Ilah in your mind. One of the meanings of the word Ilah is: someone I completely submit to. Right? Now, when we look at the perfect attributes of Allah, we see that He is Jabbar. He is Qahhar. The compeller, the subduer. He is Al-Khafid, the abaser. He is Ar-Rafi, the exalter. He is Al-Qawi, the extremely powerful. And what do you do to someone who is the compeller, the subduer, the abaser, the exalter, the extremely powerful — all of that in the most unique and absolute sense? What do you do to someone with those attributes? You submit to them. You understand? And the one you submit to is called an Ilah. So you see how this works?

When we study the linguistic meanings of any of these ninety-nine attributes, we find that they all trace back to one of the different meanings of the word Ilah. It is really incredible!

So, for example, Ilah is the one we turn to for protection and refuge in our desperate times. Why do we turn to Allah in times of desperate need? Because He is Al-Wakeel, the trustee. He is Al-Wali, the most protecting friend. He is المانع, the one who prevents harm. So because of these perfect attributes — He being trustworthy in the most unique and absolute sense, He being Wali, my protecting friend in the most unique and absolute sense, He being Al-Mani, the one who prevents harm from reaching me — what is my natural reaction to that? I turn to Him for all my needs. And the one I turn to for all my needs is what? An Ilah!

Ilah is the one we are passionately in love with and are obsessed about. The kind of love that, if I lose Him, I would become like the مُوَلّا, like the mother who goes insane at the loss of her child. Now, why do I have this crazy love for Him? Because He is Rahman, He is intensely merciful. Because He is Raheem, consistently merciful, in the most unique and absolute way. Because He is Ghaffar, the always forgiving, in the most unique and absolute way. Because He is Sattar, the one who constantly covers up my faults and sins. Imagine if the world knew every horrible thing you and I have done. Imagine if the world knew the filth going through my head all the time. I would not have a single friend in this world. But Allah has protected me from others knowing my sins and my faults, because He is Sattar, the one who covers faults — again in the most unique and the most absolute way. He is As-Saboor, the extremely patient one. He is Al-Wadood, the extremely loving one. He is Al-Mujib, the one who responds to my every prayer.

So because He is intensely merciful, always merciful, always forgiving, constantly forgiving, extremely loving, always listening to my needs — السمیع — always keeping an eye out for me, protecting me — البصیر — because He is all these things to me in the most unique and absolute sense of the word, my natural reaction to all of this is what? It is that I am passionately in love with Him. I am always thinking about Him. Again, a definition of the word Ilah.

Because He is Al-Malik, the king. Because He is Al-Mutakabbir, the greatest. Because He is Al-Jaleel.

the majestic, in the most unique and absolute way. I am in awe of Him. I am dumbfounded by His glory, which is another meaning of the word Ilah. So you see, the word Ilah encompasses the qualities of all ninety-nine attributes. And because, when it comes to Allah, these attributes are ahad and samad, unique and absolute, it makes Him THE ILAH, or ALLAH, for me. This is why calling Him Allah is equivalent to calling Him by all ninety-nine of His names, because all ninety-nine attributes trace their meanings back to one of the various meanings of the word Ilah. Allahu Akbar. This is incredible. You cannot make this up. It is simply too perfect.

I hope you now understand the relationship of the word ALLAH to His ninety-nine perfect attributes. All His attributes connect back to one of the various meanings of the word Ilah. And this is why calling out to Him by His most majestic name, ALLAH, is the same as calling Him by His ninety-nine attributes. And because He is Allah, because He is ahad and samad in all His attributes, what do we say? We say, La Ilaha Illa Allah. We say there is no deity, there is no one who is ahad and samad, who is unique and absolute, both at once, except ALLAH, THE ILAH.

Now consider this. This is one of the reasons this Surah is called Surat Al-Ikhlaas. Ikhlaas means sincerity, and sincerity is when we do something completely and only for the sake of Allah. Sincerity is when we make Allah unique in our lives. We place Him before everything else in our lives. Ikhlaas comes from the root word Khalasa, which means to make pure. And how do you make something pure? By removing its impurities. The more we understand the meanings of ahad and samad, and the more we bring the practical application of these two words into our daily lives, the higher we will rise in spiritual rank. All progress in spiritual rank, all the ranks of Jannah, rests upon our creation of Ikhlaas. The greater our ikhlaas, the higher our rank will be in the eyes of Allah.

That is the true purpose of creation. That is the true test set before us: to come into the midst of creation, to come into the midst of temptations, and then to give up those temptations and desires completely, willingly, and unapologetically, for the sake of Allah. That is true worship. And no one reached the heights of Ikhlaas, no one practiced the true principles of Allah's ahadiyat and samadiyat, other than Rasul Allah and Maulana Ali. May Allah grant us all the knowledge and the wisdom, and create within us the burning need, to place Allah before everything and everyone else.

Then, after declaring His احدیت, His uniqueness, He says, اللہ الصمد — Allah is as-Samad. So now let us understand this word, Samad. It has a wealth of meanings.

Linguistically, الصمد is the one who is enough. He is المقصود لقضاء الحاجات. He is the one to whom we constantly turn, to fulfill our needs and to answer all of our questions. That is the first meaning of the word صَمَد: Allah is someone who is enough for me, to fulfill all my needs and answer all my questions.

The second meaning of the word صَمَد is someone or something that you set as your goal, or your ultimate destination. When you aspire to reach someone, when you aspire to please someone, when you make someone your final destination, they become الصمد. So Allah is saying, He is the one.

we should set as our ultimate goal. Allah is calling Himself the ultimate goal of His creation. Every action we perform must be aimed at Allah's pleasure.

Another meaning of صَمَد is the one who has no need of others, the one whom no one can overpower in any way at all. In battle, for instance, or in rank, or in any other quality. You cannot surpass Him in dealing, in leadership, or in eloquence. That too is صَمَد, because no one can overcome Allah.

Then the scholars say: الصمد الذی لا عیب فیہ — the صَمَد is the one who has no blemish, no fault, no impurity within Him. And Allah is pure of every fault and impurity.

It also implies عظیم الجلالۃ, the one who is immense and great in His glory and His majesty. And it means الدائم الخالد, the one who is ever living and everlasting.

So you see that the word صَمَد carries a number of meanings. But if you cannot remember all of them, do not worry; that is all right. The one meaning I truly want you to remember for صَمَد is this, because it holds the rest of the meanings within it.

The scholars say a thing is صَمَد — شئٌ الصمد، ھو مُصمَد، لا جوف لہ. A thing is called صَمَد when it is completely solid, with no holes and no emptiness inside. Something that is through and through one pure substance, like a pure brick of gold; a brick of pure gold could be called صَمَد. Or a boulder into which there is no way for air or water to enter — that is صَمَد. Something with no gaps whatsoever in its make — that is called صَمَد. Something absolute and solid and without any flaw — that is صَمَد.

And this meaning is a very important one to appreciate. For what happens when there is a gap in something? What happens when something is hollow? It cracks. And where there is a gap, impurities can settle in, and corruption can set in. But when something has no gaps, when it is through and through one solid block, it cannot crack, and impurities can find no way in. This is important to understand, because this is the state of each and every one of Allah's attributes. His attributes are not merely Ahad — He is not merely unique — they are also As-Samad. They are complete and whole. They lack nothing within them. So when He is Rahman, and He is Rahim, He is uniquely merciful, and He is, through and through, absolutely merciful. There is no gap in His mercy for injustice or wrong to settle into, because He is Samad. Do you understand? His mercy is constant, and consistent, and intense, because He is Ahad and As-Samad.

An attribute is like a shell. It is possible to describe someone with an attribute such as "noble," because that is how he appears on the outside. But is it not also possible that he is only pretending to be noble? Or that he is not so noble all the time, that he has fits of rage now and again? That is possible. You may call someone powerful because of their rank and position, but could there be weakness inside them? That too is possible. So we may give attributes to creation, and they may fulfill those attributes at times, perhaps even most of the time, but never all of the time. Yet when we call Allah by any of His attributes, because He is As-Samad, because there are no gaps or holes in His attributes, He truly manifests

and fulfills each and every single one of His attributes, in the most perfect and absolute sense. And that is why الصمد has the AL before it. It is because of the absolute — اِستِغرَاق — meaning absolutely. In no way, shape, or form does He lack anything.

So each and every attribute of Allah is unique — Ahad — by virtue of being timeless, limitless, and inherently owned. And they are complete and absolute, through and through, without any holes or emptiness — Samad — which makes them perfect. And these two qualities, Ahad and Samad, both exist at the same time. Because is it possible for something to be unique and not absolute? Is it possible for something to be absolute and whole, but not unique? Sure, very easily possible. A brick of gold is Samad, but it is not unique; there are several other bricks of gold. But Allah is Ahad and Samad, both at the same time. And this fact exists grammatically in these two verses. Grammatically, these two verses are highlighting the words Ahad and Samad and putting an AND between them. You know the difference between OR and AND, right? If Allah were Ahad OR Samad, then He could be one or the other, not necessarily both, right? But what Allah is highlighting in these two verses, grammatically, is that He is both at the same time. And I want to show you how.

So Allah says, قل ھو اللہ احد — say, He is Allah, the unique. Then He says, اللہ الصمد — Allah is Samad. Now, if you look at this grammatically, He did not need to use the word Allah again in the second verse, because He mentioned Allah in the first verse. He could have just used a pronoun. In fact, even in the first verse, He did not need to use the word ھو. Why is He using a pronoun before using the noun? Normally you use the noun first and then a pronoun. Mariam is in my sessions. She is my niece. I do not say: She is Mariam, who is in my sessions. Mariam is my niece. Right?

So Allah could have said, قل اللہُ احد — say, Allah is unique — and then in the next one He says, اللہ الصمد, instead of ھو الصمد. You understand? There are incredible taweelaat and haqaiq behind this. Unfortunately, I am not at liberty to discuss them. But I do want to hint toward these things, so that hopefully you will want to advance and find out why Allah said things this way. But for our purpose, these serve to highlight the importance of these words, Ahad and Samad. And grammatically, what this does in classical Arabic, when you bring back a noun where you could have used a pronoun, is that it puts an AND between the two qualities and brings them onto equal levels. Meaning, Allah is Ahad AND HE IS Samad, both at the same time. He is unique AND He is absolute, both at the same time.

And when you have someone or something that is unique AND absolute, both at the same time, you have perfection. So from this point on, when I use the word perfect for Allah, what it should mean to you is: perfect equals Ahad plus Samad. You understand? Perfection for Allah's attributes should mean unique — by being timeless, limitless, and owned — and also complete and absolute, lacking nothing. Because nothing else in creation is Ahad and Samad both at the same time. Therefore, nothing else in creation is perfect before the perfection of Allah.

Questions?

Another meaning in the words Ahad and Samad that I want to point out is that, just because the Qur'an mentions these ninety-nine attributes, it does not mean that Allah only has ninety-nine attributes.

Someone in the group asked me this question. Why do we confine Allah to just these ninety-nine attributes? Is he not more exalted than that, too exalted to be confined within ninety-nine attributes? It was an excellent question. But I needed to explain Ahad and Samad before I could answer it.

Using the metaphor of light, I said: white light refracts into its seven component colors when it strikes a prism. In the same way, when the essence of Allah strikes this physical, material plane, it refracts into these ninety-nine attributes, so that we human beings can experience them, so that we can wrap our intellects around them. But that does not mean that Allah is limited by, or confined to, these ninety-nine attributes. We are! Our intellects are confined to them. Not Allah. He is far more exalted, far more majestic, far more divine than these ninety-nine attributes. These ninety-nine attributes are what we human beings, with our limited intellects, are capable of experiencing and understanding in this physical realm. And even that is only a fraction. Otherwise, Allah's attributes are far too exalted, and infinite in number, for us human beings to grasp. And Allah himself says in the Qur'an:

سُبْحَنَهُۥ وَتَعَلَىٰ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ

Allah is far exalted, far superior, above what is attributed to him. Because these attributes are confined within the physical realm, and our intellects are confined within the physical realm. Allah is not. Allah is not confined within the physical realm, because he is the creator of the physical realm. Just as the Martian cannot confine the human being to the features of an iPad, so too we human beings, with our limited imagination, cannot transcend this physical realm. So the best we can imagine, the best we can dream of, the best we can wrap our minds around, are these ninety-nine attributes. Do you understand? His uniqueness, his completeness, his absoluteness is not something our minds can comprehend.

Let me give you an example. This one actually comes from the teachings of Maulana Ali, peace be upon him, which were explained beautifully by Hazrat Zia Ali Sahab. You see, when we human beings think of these divine attributes—let us take an example, let us use the same example we used last time, which is being knowledgeable. When we human beings think about knowledge, we need that thing to exist before we can gain knowledge of it, is that not so? Because minerals and metals exist, that is why we have the knowledge of chemistry. The human body exists, diseases exist, medicine exists, and that is why we have the knowledge of physiology and medicine. Computers exist, and that is why I am a computer engineer. If computers did not exist, the knowledge of computers would not exist, and I would not be able to acquire that knowledge to become a computer programmer. Do you understand? So our knowledge depends on the existence of the thing about which we are acquiring knowledge. If the thing did not exist, there would be no way for us to be knowledgeable about it.

So then there are three components to our knowledge. The thing, called the معلوم; the knowledge of the thing, which is the علم; and the one acquiring the knowledge, who is the عالم. Right? So there is علم, knowledge; the عالم, the knower; and the معلوم, the thing being known. And all of this depends on the existence of the thing.

So now, when we think of Allah being knowledgeable, of Allah being علیم, the question is: what is he knowledgeable of? We can say he has knowledge of the universe.

So if he is knowledgeable because the universe exists, does that mean he was not علیم when the universe did not exist? For we know that this universe did not always exist. And what happens when, one day, this universe no longer exists? Would he still be علیم then? Would he still have complete knowledge of the universe, even when there is no universe?

Do you see the problem here? We human beings cannot process this, because we cannot think outside these physical confines. For us to be knowledgeable, the thing must first exist; then we can gain knowledge of it and so become knowledgeable. But this is not the case with Allah. He is forever knowledgeable, because his knowledge is timeless. He is forever, he is infinitely علیم, because his knowledge is limitless — even when there is no thing to be knowledgeable of. For this attribute of being knowledgeable, of being علیم, is part of his divine essence.

So Allah is علیم, not because of his creation. He is not dependent on the existence of his creation to be علیم. He was علیم before he created anything. He is علیم today. And he will remain علیم even after his creation no longer exists. For his علم, his knowledge, is not dependent on the existence of his creation. Do you understand?

Similarly, Allah is powerful; but what does power mean? We can only understand Allah's power in reference to how we see power. For we too, as human beings, share a time-bound, limited, and externally acquired version of Allah's divine attribute. We too are powerful. But we are powerful only because some thing exists that can be overpowered. When we come across a thing that is insurmountable and overwhelming, we no longer remain powerful. But Allah is powerful even when there is nothing to be overpowered.

That is why, in the sajda supplication of Shafa, what do we say?

وارحم ذلی بین یدیک — Have mercy on my weakness before you.

و تضرعی الیک — and on my cries before you.

و وحشتی من الناس — and my panic and horror and trepidation is because of people.

و انسی بک — and my peace and tranquility is with you.

And then we say:

یا کریم یا کائنا قبل کل شئی — O the one who is generous, and the one who existed before anything ever existed.

و یا کریم و یا کائنا بعد کل شئی — And O the one who is generous, and the one who will exist after everything is destroyed.

What a beautiful way to call Allah, AWJ. Two attributes are mentioned here: Karam, generosity, and کائنا, his existence. For this universe around us is a refraction of these two attributes. These attributes answer the two most fundamental questions about the existence of this universe. Why does this universe exist? To show that Allah exists. Why did he create this universe? Because he is generous. SubhanAllah.

This universe exists to show that Allah exists, and that he is generous. He is Kareem. Generosity is not something you have to do. When you do not have to do something, but you still do it — that is what makes you generous, is it not? Allah did not have to create this universe for us to live in and enjoy. But he did it anyway. Why? Because he is generous. And the magnificence, the glory, the majesty, the immense size of this universe is screaming and pointing toward its creator, saying: I exist because my creator exists. And my immensity, my glory, my beauty is a refraction of the majesty.

the glory and the beauty of my creator. SubhanAllah.

And look, even with us. Today we are called generous because we are able to give things, because we are able to donate, to give money. But we first need to have money before we can give it in charity, is it not? Would we be capable of generosity if we had no money? How would we show generosity without possessing things to be generous with? So we need created things in order for generosity to exist.

But Allah is generous even when there was nothing to give. He was generous even before he created this universe. And he will be generous even after this universe is long gone. He existed before this universe was created, and he will exist even after his creation is destroyed. His generosity and his existence are not because of his creation. His creation is because of his generosity and his existence.

I will say that again. His generosity and his existence are not because of his creation. His creation is because of his generosity and his existence, so that it could experience his attributes.

So when we think about the attributes of Allah, we are forced to think of them within the boundaries of this physical realm, within the boundaries of our limited experiences. And there is no doubt that Allah and his attributes are far beyond the confines of this physical realm, and far beyond the boundaries of our imaginations. So Allah is not confined to these ninety-nine attributes. His capabilities are infinite. These ninety-nine attributes are only those that manifest within this physical realm, so that we human beings can experience a tiny fraction of who Allah is. But Allah is far beyond the confines of time and space, and far beyond our limited understanding of what these attributes mean.

And that is why he says:

وَتَعَلَىٰ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ

He is far above what you attribute to him.

سُبْحَنَ رَبِّ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَرْشِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ

Glorified is the master of the heavens and the earth, the master of the throne, above what you attribute to him.

And that is why he says:

لیس کمثلہ شئی

There is nothing you can use as a point of reference to compare to me. Because nothing can be compared to me, neither in my attributes nor in my essence.

After stating his ahadiyat and samadiyat, his uniqueness and completeness, Allah says:

لم یلد ولم یولد

He did not father anyone, nor has he been fathered. In the old English wording, he did not beget, nor was he begotten.

I will skip over the grammatical nuances of this verse. But just know that there is a great deal of beautiful commentary by scholars about why he did not say لا یلدُ ولا یُولَدُ. Allah used the word Lam, and not La. And why he used the past tense and not the present tense. Lam forces the meaning of a verb into the past tense. So I am translating it as: he did not beget, nor was he fathered.

So the first thing we need to work out is the benefit of the past tense in this verse. Why use the past tense? Why not say, he does not father, and he is not fathered? Why not? Well, the second half makes logical sense. ولم یولد makes sense, because birth happens in the past, so that follows. But then why not guard against shirk in the future too, by saying ولا یلد, he does not give birth? The problem with "he does not give birth" is that it does not necessarily negate that he did give birth. It does not eliminate the possibility that he did father.

So it leaves room for shirk in the past. That is why Allah used لم یلد. He covered the past tense, and He covered the future tense. Subhan Allah.

In any case, what I want you to understand for our purpose is how this verse connects with the previous two. The first two verses already established that He is ahad and samad — unique and absolute — which means there will never be anyone comparable to Him.

Now, what does having a child do? A human being begets a human being; a cat gives birth to a cat, a dog to a dog. An animal gives birth to its equal, to one of the same species. And we have already established that He cannot have a second. That is not possible for Him. Because to have a child, or even to be born, means that you have a beginning and an end. When you are born, it naturally follows that you will also die. And the very fact that you were born implies that at some point you did not exist in this world. That takes away from godhood and from divinity itself. So we never attribute these things to Allah.

Allah says in another place: أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لَهُۥ وَلَدٌۭ ؟ وَلَمْ تَكُن لَّهُۥ صَحِبَةٌۭ — How can He have a son, when He does not even have an associate, a spouse? One word for a spouse is صاحب, and another word for it is کفو, and that is coming ahead in the next verse. Allah says: ولم یکن لہ کفواً احد. So now, if He does not give birth, and He is not begotten, and the matter of children is out of the way, what about the spouse?

On a side note, it is interesting that the word kufu, in Arabic literature, is also used for an enemy who is your equal in battle. If two men are equally skilled in a fight, they are kufu. And it is also used in marriage. The word enemy says it all — I am joking. So why is a spouse a kufu? Because they are the enemy — again, I am joking.

The word kufu is used when someone is comparable to you: someone who can go toe to toe with you, who is on par with you, who has the same skills, the same status, the same rank, the same social circles. Such a person is called a kufu. So you generally marry someone who is compatible with you, the same as you, of the same level of intellect, with the same interests, and so on. Such a couple are called kufu of one another.

Now this word is used for Allah: ولم یکن لہ کفوا احد — and He never had any counterpart, anyone who could be compared to Him, anyone who could go toe to toe with Him. All of this lies in the details of a single word. What word is that? Ahad. قل ھو اللہ احد. Ahad is the primary word, the entire purpose of the surah. Every other word we are learning is a consequence of it. Allah is Ahad; therefore He is samad. He is Ahad; therefore He does not beget a child, nor has He been begotten. He is Ahad; therefore there is no one comparable to Him.

Remember, I told you that Allah changed the normal pattern of how the word Ahad is used in the first verse. It is supposed to be used only in the negative sense, but Allah used it in a positive way. It is the same with this verse. Grammatically, what should have been said is: ولم یکن أحدٌ کفواً لہ — and there is no one comparable to Him. That should have been the grammatically expected order of the sentence; the lahoo should have come at the end. But Allah rearranged it.

and brought it to the beginning. Now here is something very striking from a grammatical standpoint, and this is one of the amazing benefits of grammar. It is a technical subject to study, but its rewards are remarkable, glory be to Allah. The verse reads: ولم یکن لہ کفوا احد. This is not, in fact, the expected grammatical sequence. It should have been: ولم یکن أحدٌ کفواً لہ. That would have been the grammatically expected order of the sentence. But Allah rearranged the order of the words.
