Ahad stands at the end, lahoo at the beginning, and kufu in the middle. In the natural order, Allah would have been mentioned at the end, and the one being set up as His counterpart would have been mentioned at the beginning.

So why did Allah change this order? In this sentence, which is the most important entity? Lahoo refers to Allah, kufu to the counterpart, and ahad to anyone else. Of these, which is the most valuable word? Lahoo. And part of Arabic rhetoric is الاھم الاول — the most important comes first. Therefore Allah mentions Himself before everything else. And one of the meanings of Ahad is الاول, not merely لیس لہ ثانی, the one who has no second, but also the one who comes first. Even in this sentence, the Messenger of Allah mentions Allah first, because had he not done so, it would have literally negated the first verse. Glory be to Allah.

We're studying the highest-ranking word: Allah, which is the Ismul Jalalah, the most majestic name of all names. It comes from the root word Ilah, and it means THE ILAH. So, with this exclusivity clause applied to it, Allah is the one I completely submit to, the one I am truly and completely loyal to. He is the one I turn to for protection and refuge in my desperate times. He is the one I am passionately in love with, the one I am obsessed about. He is beyond my imagination, and beyond my capabilities of comprehension and understanding. He is the one whose glory and majesty dumbfound me, every single time. He is the one I can completely trust, lean on, and put my entire weight on, with the certainty that He will never let me fall. And finally, the most important meaning of all: He is the one I worship. And my worship, my عبادۃ, comprises two things: worship and obedience, both stemming from the sum of all these different meanings of the word Ilah.

Then we learned that for a creation to understand its creator, it needs two things. First, an experiential interaction with the creation that reflects the attributes of the creator, supplemented by a description of the creator Himself. So we experience the attributes of Allah through our interaction with His creation, which is this universe. And our experience is supplemented by His description, which He provides for us in the Quran. These two things together help us understand our creator.

Then I explained how we must separate out, or distinguish, the attributes of the creation from the attributes of Allah. Because if we do not do that, we end up committing shirk, and we partner the creation with the creator in those attributes. And Allah has no partner. He can have no partner, because لیس کمثلہ شئی. There is nothing comparable to Him. We looked at the linguistic beauty of the word کمثلہ. Ka is used to compare in attributes, and Misl is used to compare in essence. And Allah says, لیس کمثلہ شئی. There is nothing comparable to me, neither in attributes nor in essence. Both are captured by this one word, کمثلہ.

AHAD vs WAHID

So if there is nothing comparable to Allah, neither in essence nor in attributes, what does that make Him? That makes Him unique! And the Arabic word for unique is Ahad. But we also hear the term Wahid for Allah, which means one. So the question becomes: is Allah Ahad, or is Allah Wahid? Is He unique, or is He one? To answer this question, let us turn to the Quran. What does the Quran say about this?

According to the Quran, Allah is both. He is Ahad, AND He is Wahid. Allah says, قل ھو اللہ احد. Say He is Allah, the unique. But the Quran also says, وَإِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌۭ وَحِدٌۭ ۖ لَّآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلرَّحْمَنُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ. Your ilah is one; there is no other deity except Him, and He is rehman and raheem.

Now the first thing we need to understand is the difference between Wahid and Ahad. Wahid means one. So how come Allah does not say قو ھو اللہ واحد, Say Allah is one? That would have been true as well, would it not? We know the language of the Quran is extremely precise. You cannot change any single word in any single ayah. So this forces us to recognize that this word, Ahad, must then have been used in a very particular context. To understand this better, we need to understand a little bit about the Arabic language.

In the Arabic language, certain words can only be used in a particular way, and in no other way. Suppose I say right now — and listen carefully to this — لیس واحدٍ مَوجودٌ فی المسجد. Which word did I use? I used Wahid. There is not ONE in the masjid. Do you know what that means in Arabic? It means there is not one, but two, three, four in the masjid. In other words, what I am saying is that there is not JUST one; there could be more than one in the masjid. As opposed to that, if I say لیس أَحدٍ موجودٌ فی المسجد, do you know what that means? It means there is not a single person in the masjid. When I say لیس واحد, it means there is not JUST one in the masjid — there COULD be one, but probably there are more. But when I say لیس احد, then what it means is that there is not even a single one in the masjid.

Ahad is ALWAYS used negatively. It is never used in a positive sense. It always means NOT anyone at all, NOT anything at all. For example, Allah says وَلَا يُشْرِكُ فِى حُكْمِهِۦٓ أَحَدًۭا — NO ONE at all can be His partner in His command. وَلَا يُشْرِكْ بِعِبَادَةِ رَبِّهِۦٓ أَحَدًۢا — let NO ONE at all commit shirk with Allah. So Ahad is used as absolute negation. Do you understand? When you want to negate absolutely, you use the word Ahad. But when you want to speak in the positive, you use the word Wahid.

Now here is the interesting thing. In Surah Ikhlaas, Allah says قل ھو اللہ احد — Say, He is Allah, the Unique. Here Ahad is NOT being used in the negative. It is being used in the positive. And this is very interesting, because the only place in the entire Arabic literature where this word is used in the positive sense, without any further attribution, is Surah al-Ikhlaas. The word Ahad is NEVER used anywhere else in the entire Arabic literature in the positive way, except for Allah. So, linguistically speaking, Allah broke the rules for this word Ahad when He used it for Himself.

First let us understand what Allah is saying in the context of this word Ahad. Ahad is a unique singular entity that cannot be compared to any other entity, that no other entity can compete with. Ahad is a singular entity for which no comparison is possible, no competition is possible. It does not have a synonym; it does not have an antonym. ANY sort of affiliation is ABSOLUTELY impossible for this singular entity that is Ahad. The One who has no second is Ahad! The One for whom a second is impossible — that is Ahad.

with Allah's knowledge. I would be committing shirk. But when I say, "InshaAllah, we will have a session again next week," meaning "if Allah so desires, we will have a session next week," now, by using the word InshaAllah, I have placed my knowledge of the unseen with Allah, where it belongs. If Allah chooses, if Allah so desires, we will have a session again next week. I have taken all the power away from myself and placed it with its rightful owner. Once again, the word InshaAllah shifted my focus from myself to my Creator. I am no longer a partner with Him in His knowledge of the unseen.

Now the last one. And I am using this example for the benefit of both parties, the giver and the receiver. When I say to one of you girls in the session, when I say, for example, "You are very beautiful. You are gorgeous," what is your natural reaction going to be? "Oh, thank you!" Right? Hee hee hee. But the question is, when I am saying that you are beautiful, to whom am I giving the credit for that beauty? I am giving you the credit. And when you say thank you, what are you doing? You are accepting credit for that beauty, are you not? Why am I saying that you are beautiful, and why are you saying thank you? You did not make yourself. You did not create your beautiful features. You did not choose your skin color, the color of your eyes, your hair. You have no part in it. So then why am I giving you credit for your beauty? And why are you accepting it by saying thank you?

One reason you are saying thank you is that you either believe you own your beauty. You believe in your heart that it is you who made yourself look beautiful. Or you could be saying thank you for the compliment I am giving you. But even in that case, your question should be, who am I to pay this compliment of beauty to you? Because that is what I said, did I not? I said you are very beautiful. We both know that you did not create yourself. So then who am I to assign that beauty to you? And why are you accepting it with a thank you? We are both assigning the credit of beauty to the wrong object. The credit for your beauty belongs to your Creator. When you praise a painting, you do not talk to the painting, do you? You do not say, "Mr. Painting, you are really awesome!" No, you do not do that. You praise the artist who made the painting. Similarly, you and I are all Allah's artwork. So who is the true owner of our compliments? It is Allah.

Now, if we switch these statements around, and I say, "MashaAllah, you are very beautiful!" and in response to that, instead of saying thank you, you say AlHamdulillah, now what did we just do? I just attributed your beauty to the one who gave you that beauty in the first place. MashaAllah, you are beautiful because Allah chose that beauty for you. My focus immediately shifted from you to the one who created you. And when you said AlHamdulillah, praise and gratitude be to Allah, you too shifted your focus from yourself, from your own beauty, to the one who made you beautiful. Both of us, just by using the words MashaAllah and AlHamdulillah, changed our conversation from shirk into worship. SubhanAllah.

What a beautiful religion we have! What immense beauty there is in our humility toward Allah. This is true عبدیت. This is true servitude, true worship. And this can only be done, in the most complete sense, by the one who sees Allah as THE ILAH.

This can only be done by the one who is passionately in love with Allah, who is obsessed with Allah, who is completely dependent on Allah, who is constantly turning to Allah.

Qul is a lesson for the messenger himself, and it is also a command that he must go out and teach. This is "teacher training." When Allah says Qul, the messenger cannot simply keep it to himself; he has to declare it. If Allah were to say اِعْلَمْ هُوَ اللّٰہُ اَحَدٌ, then that would be something for him alone to know. But when Allah says قُلْ هُوَ اللّٰہُ اَحَدٌ, now it is not just for him; he has to go out and spread the word.

Huwa is a pronoun here. Now, a pronoun is used in place of a noun. So there is both a pronoun and a noun in this verse: you have Allah. There was no need for Huwa. Even without Huwa, the sentence is complete. قُلِ اللّٰہُ اَحَدٌ is a perfectly valid sentence. So why, then, is the word Huwa, "HE," used here?

A pronoun is used when it is already known who is being talked about. For example, if I said to you right now, "You know, he graduated from college," your first question would be what? Who are you talking about? Who graduated from college? But when there is someone so well known that you do not even need to mention his name, then you can simply use the pronoun, because it is so obvious who the subject is. His greatness is so universally acknowledged that there is no need to mention his name first. I can say only "He," and you will know whom I am speaking about. In Arabic this is called شَأْن. Because of the universally known greatness of the subject at hand, you can just say Huwa. So the Huwa is a sign pointing to the greatness of Allah AWJ.

And of course it is also an answer to the questions مَنْ هُوَ؟, who is He? and مَا هُوَ؟, what is He? And the answer to that is هُوَ اللّٰہُ اَحَدٌ, the one you asked about is Allah.

If we break this down further grammatically, from the standpoint of خبر مبتدا, subject and predicate, then in an actual English translation this verse reads: Say! He is Allah. And then: Say! He is Ahad. Allah is خبر الاولی and Ahad is خبر الثانی. So from a grammatical point of view these are two sentences fused into one. So we would translate this as: Say, He is Allah — comma — the Unique!

Now, back to the question of why Allah changed the grammatical rule when using this word. In order to understand that, we have to go back in time and understand the ancient Arab mentality first, because this word, Ahad, used for Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, created earthquakes among the Arabs. They too had gods; they believed in gods. But for every one of their gods, they also had another god. I can have my god, you can have yours. They believed in Allah, but then they said He took angels as His daughters. The Christian community said He took a son. So they attributed sons and daughters to Allah. In some of the Hindu traditions, what do they do? They say god BECAME the universe. God is in the bug, and in the tree, and in the rock, and in the stone. God is running in my veins. Right?

This is similar to the American transcendentalism of more recent times. In American literature too, one hears that god is in the tree, or in nature, or in us, and so on. But what happens is this: if you begin to compare Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with other things, or you begin to pair Him with them, or to associate Him with anything else, what is lost? Ahad. Ahad is lost. And if you set Allah apart from every attribution belonging to human beings, if you set Allah apart from every attribution belonging to all of His creation, then what you gain as a result of that exclusion is Ahad.

This was a wholly revolutionary conception of the uniqueness of Allah. It is a conception that the Christians and the Jews and no other religion accepted. They all said, we are content with قل ھو اللہ واحد. Say Allah is one; that is acceptable to us. When you study their creed, you will find that they have no difficulty with wahid. But what do they have difficulty with? Ahad. They are not willing to accept قل ھو اللہ احد.

So Allah broke this rule of language in this verse when He used the word Ahad for Himself in the affirmative sense. For what happens is this: when you break the ordinary pattern of speech, it alerts the listener and forces him to pay attention.

There is another grammatical subtlety. If you notice, in the word Ahad there is no AL. But it is present in the word Samad: اللہ الصمد. We do not say اللہُ صمدٌ. We say اللہ الصمد. In the same way, Allah could have said اللہ الاحد, but the AL is omitted from Ahad, even though it is present in Samad. So why not place AL there as well? Well, this is a grammatical difference, and it carries a rhetorical benefit. The first benefit is that removing the AL and placing a tanween upon the word sets an exclamation mark upon the statement. He is Allah. AHAD. Only consider that, and how astonishing it is. And in the ancient Arabic that can be accomplished with a tanween. You and I cannot accomplish it in English; we have to raise our voices and bang our fists upon the desk to drive the point home. But that is what Allah is saying when He says Ahad. The power of that word is made manifest in that tanween.

The second thing is that the tanween is used, by convention, for a khabar, the predicate of a sentence, and the predicate is used when someone asks a question. And of course Ahad was a response to the question that the Arabs were asking at that time: Who is Allah? And to answer that question fittingly, the alif and the laam are not there. You must place the tanween there. Who is Allah? He is Allah, the unique.

And as I said, this was an enormous point of resistance for them. This is the one word that earned people beatings. This is the one word that would get Hazrat Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, tortured. It was this one word that got him pinned to the scorching sand of the desert, his bare skin exposed, with a heavy boulder placed upon his chest, all so that he would give up this one word. You may have read this story. His master tortured him in this way so that he would give up Islam. He would pin him down, his bare back against the scorching heat of the desert, a heavy boulder upon his chest. And then he would whip him. And with every lash Hazrat Bilal would say, Ahadun Ahad. Ahadun Ahad. Ahadun Ahad. Beat me as much as you wish. With every lash, the word Ahad will come out upon my tongue.

So this was an enormous point of contention for the ancient Arabs.

Saying Allah was never the problem. Accepting Allah as Ahad was the problem. And so, what an amazing word Allah gave us by which to understand Him.

Now, the idea behind this word Ahad is that Allah created the human being with knowledge of Himself. He inherently placed this goal within every single creation: to want to willingly accept Him as its master and to become His slave. The ultimate goal in the life of a human being is to become Allah's slave. His عبد. That is what Allah created him for.

وَمَا خَلَقْتُ ٱلْجِنَّ وَٱلْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ

And I did not create jinn and mankind except that they should become My slaves. لِيَعْبُدُونِ

To be an عبد is the more desirable state. Indeed, this is the greatest honor that Rasul Allah received. What do we say in the azaan and the Iqamah? اشھد ان محمد عبدہ و رسولہ. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the slave and messenger of Allah. Not messenger and slave. Not اشھد ان محمد رسولہ و عبدہ. No, but اشھد ان محمد عبدہ و رسولہ. Slave first, messenger later.

The pride and honor of Rasul Allah was not in being Allah's messenger. It was in being His slave. And even when Allah called His beloved to the seventh sky on the night of Mairaj, the greatest honor bestowed upon any living soul, He did not call His messenger. He called His slave.

سُبْحَنَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِۦ

Exalted is He who took His slave. His slave, not His messenger. Allah could have said سُبْحَنَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَسْرَىٰ بِرسولہ, Exalted is He who took His messenger. But no. Allah distinctly honored him with the title of His "slave." And that is why, when Rasul Allah formulated his kalima, he placed the word Abd before the word Rasool. اشھد ان محمد عبدہ و رسولہ. He gave precedence to his slavery of Allah over his prophethood.

So to become Allah's slave is the need that Allah created every human being with, just as He created us with thirst and hunger. It is inherent in us. We cannot escape it. But when our appetite is not filled with healthy food, what do we fill it with? If we do not get the right meal, are we going to say that we will not eat at all? No. When a person is starving and there is no healthy food available, he will turn to whatever he finds his hands on. Even if there is filth, even the bark of trees, will the human being still start chewing on that? He will. When we lose sight of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and He is no longer our goal, then necessarily we will find a replacement. It is inevitable. Necessarily we will have to aspire toward something else, because that hunger, that thirst, is inherently placed within all of us.

And for those who choose Allah, and who find the love and slavery of Allah, what happens to them? Oh my God.

ان صلواتی و نسکی و محیایا و مماتی لی اللہ رب العالمین

It becomes very simple for them. The one who has truly found Allah, his statement becomes: My salaah is for Allah. My sacrifice is for Allah. My life is now for Allah. And my death is now for all. All is for Allah. The way they live. The way they eat. The way they earn their living. The way they sleep. What they want to do with their lives. Their long-term goals. Their short-term goals. What they are going to do with their children. Why they are getting an education. Where they are going to work. Everything becomes for Allah. Allah becomes their ultimate goal.

But for the one who does not have that goal, they have to find another goal.

And in the old days it used to be idols. There were various other religions. People would find themselves some other god. But in our times it has become far more pathetic. Far more pathetic. Now we have the person obsessed with his body, working out eighteen hours a day, whose only goal in life is to grow bulkier and bulkier. To stay on top. To keep in shape. To impress the girls. That has become his god. His body has become his god. He has made an idol of his body. He has become a slave to his own body.

Now we have the person whose entire life has become about money. Have we met people like this? They cannot talk about anything other than their bank balance, their cars, their branded clothes, their houses. There is nothing else in life they can talk about. There is nothing else they can think about. And the moment they lose that money, they become suicidal, because that is all they ever thought about. Money has become their god, their idol, the thing they worship. They have become slaves to their own money.

For some people it is their children. They live for their children. They live through their children. My son came first. My daughter did this. My son did that. That is all they can do — boast about their children. Day and night they think about their children. There is no other thought running through their minds. There is no other goal in their lives beyond their children. They build their whole purpose around their children. They make their children their god.

There are children who play twenty hours of video games. They become slackers. Their goal becomes to entertain themselves. Their lower self becomes their god. They simply enjoy frying their brain cells sitting behind a screen.

When you do not find Allah, you will find something else. And you will chase after it. And you will give your life to it. You will inevitably create an idol, begin to worship it, and become its slave. And we know what happens to all idols: eventually they all break.

So these are the psychological implications of understanding tawhid. It is very easy to say that Allah is one, that He is unique. But is He one in my life? Is He the one for me? Is there really no one like Him, no other god, in my life? Or do I have some other god that I am chasing? Is there some other thing, or some other person, that I place before Allah?

And Allah asks us this question in the Qur'an, rhetorically:

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ؟

What deluded you concerning your gracious Lord? What was so important that you left Me for it? Subhan Allah.

So when He uses this word, أحد, it carries certain psychological implications with it. It carries implications for our attitudes toward Allah. And the way we think about our lives changes completely. After this realization, suddenly there is nothing more important to me than making Allah happy. Nothing more important to me than Allah being pleased with me. Nothing more important to me than Allah forgiving me. Nothing more important to me than Allah speaking to me on the Day of Judgment and telling me that I am successful. What becomes important is that He will look toward me.

and tell me that I will not be among those He will turn away from. إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَشْتَرُونَ بِعَهْدِ ٱللَّهِ وَأَيْمَنِهِمْ ثَمَنًۭا قَلِيلًا. أُو۟لَٓئِكَ لَا خَلَقَ لَهُمْ فِى ٱلْآخِرَةِ. وَلَا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ. وَلَا يَنظُرُ إِلَيْهِمْ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَمَةِ. وَلَا يُزَكِّيهِمْ. وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌۭ Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Judgment. May Allah not make us among them. That is what we learn from this one word, Ahad. قل ھو اللہ احد. Say: He is Allah, the Unique. Unique in my life. Unique in my heart. Allah has a place in my heart, in my life, in my work, in my thought process, in my decisions, in my prayers, in my sacrifice, in my life, in my death, in my existence. Allah has a place that no one else has. All of that is captured in this one word, Ahad.

What makes Allah worthy of worship

Now let us look at the attributes of Allah in the context of this word Ahad. One of the easiest places where we can become confused is when a word is used for Allah and is also used for us. For example, Allah calls Himself علیم, the Knowledgeable. Have you ever heard that word used for a person as well? That a person is knowledgeable? That a person is علیم? Certainly! Allah calls Himself حکیم, the Wise. Can a person also be called wise? Certainly! It is possible. Allah says, for example, that He is غفور, the Forgiving. Can you describe a person as forgiving? Yes, you can. It is the same with the other attributes of Allah. سمیع, the One who hears everything. بصیر, the One who sees everything. Can these words be used for a human being as well? Certainly they can.

But this is now a problem, because the same word that is used for Allah is now also used for a human being. Now, there are certain attributes of Allah that are unshared, that apply exclusively to Him alone. Ahad. Samad. Rehmaan. These are attributes that are used exclusively for Allah and not for any human being. But a majority of the attributes of Allah are shared by human beings as well. For example, one of Allah's names is رؤف, the Compassionate, and رحیم, the Merciful. But these same attributes are also used for Rasul Allah in the Qur'an. و بالمؤمنین رؤف الرحیم

Now this seems to violate the definition of Ahad, because now the attributes of Allah are no longer unique. They are now shared with His creation. So how do we reconcile these two things? Because sharing an attribute with Allah is what? It is Shirk, the greatest sin of all. So now, how do we understand this clearly? If a word is used for Allah, and the same word is used for entities other than Allah, then how do we not end up committing shirk?

So what I want you to remember is three differences. If you remember these three things, you will never fall into shirk. So what we will do, InshaAllah, is use one attribute or name as a sample, and then these three rules will apply to all the other attributes of Allah. Let us take the name Knowledgeable, علیم. So we say Allah is علیم, the Knowledgeable, and we compare that to another human being who is also علیم, knowledgeable.

Timeless

Here is the first thing. Allah's attributes have no beginning and no end. So if we take knowledge, Allah's knowledge does not have a beginning, meaning there was never a point when He was not knowledgeable, and it has no ending, meaning there is never going to be a time, ever, when He will not be knowledgeable.

Now compare that to your knowledge and mine, or to the knowledge of all creation gathered together. What does it have? It has a beginning, and it has an ending. That is the first difference. Allah's attributes are timeless. All of Allah's attributes are timeless: they have no beginning and they have no ending. Ours, by contrast, is temporary; ours is bounded in time; ours is caged. That is the first point.

No Limits

The second is that Allah's attributes have no limits and no confines. His knowledge encompasses everything; there is nothing that He does not know. Your knowledge and mine, by contrast, necessarily has limits. I do not know which game you are playing on your phone at this moment. I do not know whom you are texting at this moment. I do not know which level of Candy Crush you have reached. I do not know how many heartbeats I have left upon this earth. I do not know what will happen in the next thirty minutes. I have some knowledge, but I do not have all knowledge, whereas Allah has all knowledge, without any limit.

So the first difference is that Allah's attributes are timeless, and the second is that they are limitless.

Inherently owned

Now the third difference, and the most important. Everything I have — and here I am speaking of knowledge — the knowledge that I possess is not something I own. It is something that was given to me. I was not born with it; it was given to me by others. It does not inherently belong to me. Allah, by contrast, when you speak of His knowledge, it is His own. It belongs to Him inherently, innately, naturally, essentially. It was not given to Him by anyone else; it is His own. It is part and parcel of His essence. It is not acquired.

So these are the three things to keep in mind when thinking of Allah's attributes. They are timeless, limitless, and inherent.

Now let us consider any of the other attributes of Allah. Take power, القوی. You can have a person who is strong, but his power has a beginning and it has an end, whereas Allah's power has no beginning and no end. The power of Allah has no limits; it is infinite; it is limitless, whereas the power of a human being has limits. And then the power of Allah is essentially, fundamentally, His own. He did not receive it from anyone else; it is His own. But the power of a human being comes from whom? From Allah, Subhanahu Wa Ta'ala.

Now remember what I told you when we were looking at the definitions of the word Ilah. I said that the greatest of all its meanings is أَلِہَ یَعلُہُ بِمَعنیٰ عَبَدَ یَعبُدُ — Ilah in the sense of the one who is worshipped. Now I am tying that meaning to what we have just learned, so listen to this carefully.

How are Allah's attributes unique? How are they Ahad in comparison to the attributes of His creation? They are unique in three ways: His attributes are timeless, limitless, and inherently owned. And when these three features are applied to an attribute, what do you get as a result? You get perfection. These attributes are perfect, because they are timeless, because they are limitless, and because they are inherently His own — and so they will never disappear.

They will never change.

Because if these three things were not present. If He were not timeless. If He were not limitless. If He were not the inherent owner of these attributes. He would not be worthy of my worship. I will say that again. If He were not timeless. If He were not limitless. If He were not the inherent owner of these attributes. He would not be worthy of my worship. If He were not السمیع in this PERFECT sense. He would not be worthy of my worship. If He were not بصیر in this PERFECT sense. He would not be worthy of worship. If He were not علیم in this PERFECT sense. If He were not رحمن. If He were not رحیم. If He were not غفور. And we can go on and on, listing all ninety-nine attributes of Allah. In other words, if He were not PERFECT in each and every one of these ninety-nine attributes. He would not be worthy of my worship.

It is the PERFECTION of these ninety-nine attributes that makes Him AL-ILAH. That is the true meaning of أَلِہَ یَعلُہُ بِمَعنیٰ عَبَدَ یَعبُدُ. The one who is so magnificent that He is worthy of worship! So Allah, because of His perfection, is the ultimate being who is worthy of worship and obedience. And this is why, linguistically, the highest meaning of the word Ilah is the one that is worshipped. The deity that deserves to be worshipped. The one and only entity that deserves to be called ALLAH. Because, as I shared with you in one of the previous sessions, Allah combines all ninety-nine attributes within it. And that is why He says in the Quran:

وَلِلَّهِ ٱلْأَسْمَآءُ ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ

To this one name, Allah, belong all the other beautiful names. To this one name, Allah, belong all the other beautiful names. The name Allah combines in itself the power and the perfection of all ninety-nine attributes, that are timeless, limitless, and inherently belong to Allah. It is this PERFECTION that makes Him worthy of veneration, of prostration, of love, of hope, of fear, of dua, of being the one to lean on, being the one I can put my weight on. And finally, the one who is worthy of my worship and obedience. And that is our Kalima as well. لا الہ الا اللہ. There is no deity worthy of being an Ilah other than Allah, who is THE ultimate Ilah. That is what our Kalima implies.

So if you keep these three distinctions in mind, then you will maintain what Allah calls Ahad. If you do not, then you will commit shirk each and every time. Which, by the way, we do all the time. All the time! We literally do it a hundred times every single day. Whenever we praise someone, or something. When we make statements about the future. When we fear someone or something, we are constantly committing shirk. Even if that is not in our hearts. But we are committing shirk with our tongues.

And that is why, to counter that, we have been given three words: انشاء اللہ، ماشاء اللہ، سبحان اللہ، حمد للہ. InshaAllah; SubhanAllah; MashaAllah.

First of all, what do these words mean? انشاء اللہ. IF Allah desires. ما شاء اللہ. Whatever Allah desires or chooses. سبحان اللہ. Exalted is Allah. Glorified is Allah. حمد للہ. Praise and gratitude belong to Allah.

Again. انشاء اللہ. IF Allah wishes. If Allah chooses. ما شاء اللہ. Whatever, or for whomever, Allah desires. And, سبحان اللہ. Exalted and Glorified is Allah. حمد للہ. Praise and gratitude belong to Allah.

Now let us look at these words individually. When I see something and appreciate it. For example, I see a beautiful sunrise.

or a sunset, or a beautiful waterfall. And I say, "What a beautiful waterfall." What I am unknowingly doing is using the word *beautiful* for the waterfall. And beautiful is an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He is *Jameel*. When I said the waterfall is beautiful, I equated the beauty, the *jamal*, of the waterfall with the *Jameel*, the Most Beautiful. I partnered the beauty of the creation with the Creator. Even though that was not my intention, even though I did not say it deliberately, I still committed *shirk*.

*Shirk* means, in its literal sense, "to partner." The Urdu word *shareek* comes from the Arabic root *shirk*. It means to partner, to associate, to attribute. So when I called the waterfall beautiful, I partnered its beauty with the beauty of Allah. And that is *shirk*. It is called *shirk-e-khafee*, hidden *shirk*. There are two kinds of *shirk*. There is *shirk-e-jalee*, which is manifest *shirk* — such as saying that Christ is the son of Allah, or worshiping the tree and the cow as gods. That is clear and open *shirk*. But partnering the attributes of the creation with the attributes of Allah is also *shirk*. It is *shirk-e-khafee*, hidden *shirk*. So by calling the waterfall beautiful, I committed *shirk-e-khafee*.

But when I say, "What a beautiful waterfall — *SubhanAllah*!" I at once purify my statement. I at once purify the timeless beauty of Allah, the limitless beauty of Allah, the beauty innate to Allah, from the beauty of the waterfall — which is limited, which is bound in time, and which has an owner. I exalt and glorify the beauty of Allah above the beauty of the waterfall. In saying *SubhanAllah*, I become consciously aware of this fact. I remind myself that this beauty, this *jamaal*, is refracting the *Jameel*. It is refracting the beauty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. At once my focus shifts from the beauty of the waterfall to the beauty of the *Jameel*. Do you understand? And so now I am using the attributes of the creation to turn toward the remembrance of Allah. That is the idea behind saying *SubhanAllah*.

There are many who use *SubhanAllah* only as a parroted phrase. "Oh, *SubhanAllah*! *SubhanAllah*! *SubhanAllah*!" — they say it about everything. But does their heart actually turn toward their Master? Are they consciously thinking of Allah and remembering Him when they say it? If not, then it is still *shirk*. It means nothing. So be mindful of this the next time you say *SubhanAllah*. At the mention of this word, your heart should shift its focus. It should turn from the object you have just praised to the One who created that object, realizing that the object is simply refracting one of the beautiful attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So that is *SubhanAllah*.

Now the next one. When I say, "We will have a session again next week," in that statement lies an assumption — a knowledge, rather a certainty — of the fact that there is going to be a next week. But only Allah has knowledge of the unseen. Only Allah knows whether I will be here next week or not; whether my Skype will work next week or not; whether my computer will work next week or not; whether I will have electricity next week or not. Because next week's session lies in the unseen future, and only Allah has knowledge of the future.

So by saying, "We will have a session again next week," I am unknowingly, unintentionally, partnering myself in the knowledge of the unseen that belongs to Allah alone. I partnered myself in the knowledge of the unseen.

We studied the meaning of the word Allah. I hope that by now you all have a good understanding of what this remarkable word means, both in its linguistic sense and in what it is meant to signify in our lives. The word Allah stands for a concept, a concept of what Allah is meant to mean in our lives. We also looked at how the meanings of the ninety-nine attributes all trace back to one of the meanings of the word Allah. These ninety-nine attributes are a refraction of Allah's divine essence within this physical realm. All of Allah's creations — not only we human beings, but anything and everything that has been created — are manifesting the divine attributes of their creator.

Why have these attributes been placed within them? They are placed in them as a reminder, as a reminder, as a sign, so that the creation never forgets who its creator is.

Is that not what a sign or a logo is? It is a reminder. That is all it is. If you own any of the Apple products, you will surely find the logo of an apple upon it. Flying windows, if you own a Microsoft product. Every company stamps its logo on its product, so that the consumer never forgets who created that product.

So Allah refracted his divine attributes in his products, within his creation. And then he gave us human beings the intellect, the consciousness, to witness those attributes. Because no creature other than the human being is fully aware of its own existence. Human beings are the only creation that has been given this gift of awareness. And so he placed his signs, his attributes, all around us and within us. سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَٰتِنَا فِى ٱلْأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ, so that we might constantly recognize these signs and keep being reminded. Reminded of what? حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ, until it becomes absolutely clear to us that Allah is the only truth.

So if you ask me, if you say to me, Asif mamu, you keep telling me that Allah is magnificent. He is majestic. He is so glorious. How do I understand that? How do I wrap my mind around it? What does it mean that he is so exalted and so powerful? Give me some example of that glory and majesty you speak of. What does he mean when he says in the Qur'an, وهو الخلاق العظیم, He is the greatest of all creators.

I will tell you: look at the size of this universe! And look at your own size in comparison to the size of that universe. And you will get some sense of where you stand in relation to Allah. Because we human beings create, and Allah creates. Look at what we are capable of creating, and look at what he created. Just reflect on the size of this universe for a second! You know, NASA has reported this — true or false, I do not know — but they say that from what we have observed through the eye of the telescope so far, we have found so many stars in the known universe. Not the unknown universe. Just the known universe. They say we have found so many stars that if you were to start counting these stars at an interval of one star a second — so every second you count one star — it would take approximately three hundred trillion years to count all of them. Three hundred trillion years. And this is just from the part of the universe that has been explored so far. وهو الخلاق العظیم. Allahu Akbar.

Explanation of size of universe to Moosa

And we have known this all along, long before science found this out.

The old testament recounts this in one of its ancient stories. Moses, peace be upon him, asked Allah: "O Allah, when you commanded the heavens and the earth to submit to you — فَقَالَ لَهَا ٱئْتِيَا طَوْعًا أَوْ كَرْهًۭا قَالَتَآ أَتَيْنَا طَآئِعِينَ — submit to me whether you do so willingly or unwillingly, and they said, 'We submit to you willingly' — had they refused to submit, what would you have done?" Allah replied: "I would have unleashed a beast upon them that would have swallowed them both."

Moses began to think. A beast that could swallow — not chew — for when you chew you must break a thing down, and you can only swallow something very small in size. So Moses, utterly amazed, thought: if this beast could swallow both the seven heavens and the earth in a single gulp, how vast must its jaw be, its throat, its body — how enormous must this beast be to swallow the heavens and the earth! And so, wholly dazed, he asked Allah: یا اللہ! أین تلک الدابۃ؟ — O Allah, where is this beast? Allah replied: فی مَرجٍ مِن مروج — He is grazing in one of my pastures.

Moses, peace be upon him, was entirely undone. He was astounded. Here he had been thinking that the beast was immense — what is the size of a pasture compared to the beast? If this beast can swallow the heavens and the earth in a single gulp, then to graze, how vast must the pasture be? And then Allah said: فی مَرجٍ مِن مروج — in one of my pastures — meaning that there are many pastures. Yes? So Moses, peace be upon him, asked: أین ذالک المرج؟ — O Allah, where is this pasture? Allah replied: فی علمٍ من علومِ، موسی — It lies within the treasures of my unseen knowledge, Moses! What you see around you is not even a tiny fraction of what I have created. وھو الخلاق العظیم — He is the greatest of all creators.

The spiritual heart is constantly beating to the tune of La ilaha illa Allah. It is contracting and expanding, to testify to a message that is itself made up of contraction and expansion. La ilaha illa Allah is the beat of our spiritual hearts. It is what constantly removes shirk and kufr from our actions and replaces it with the life-giving oxygen of faith. And it is a continuous and constant process of purification, just as the heart is constantly and continuously engaged in the purification of the blood. Once the heart stops pumping, what happens to the body? It dies. What happens to the spiritual heart that stops purifying itself of shirk and kufr? It dies.

The Pronunciation of the Word Allah

And now look at how the word Allah is pronounced. When you hear the heart through a stethoscope, doctors say it is lubb-dubb, is it not? They say it makes that lubb-a-dubb sound. But when one of the Imams was asked, "I hear my heart beating and making a sound. What is my heart saying?" — the Imam replied, "It is saying: Allah, Allah." Now, if you actually listen to the sound, you do not hear the word Allah, do you? So then what did the Imam mean? This is not the word of an ordinary man; these are the words of an Imam. کلام الامیر. امیر الکلام. The speech of a king.

and the king of all speech. So what does it mean that the heart is saying Allah? Consider how this name, Allah, is pronounced. It too is a contraction and an expansion. That is what it is. That is what the tongue is doing. All-lah! All-laah. That is what it is doing. Say the word Allah right now, and see what happens when you pronounce the laam. You have to press your tongue against the top of your mouth. That is contraction. That is La Ilaha. And then you have to expand the tongue, bring it down, open your mouth, to complete it. That is expansion. That is Illa Allah. The name Allah is contraction and expansion. La Ilaha Illa Allah is contraction and expansion. In both, contraction comes first and expansion comes second.

The heart is constantly contracting and expanding, calling out to its master, Allah, because the heart remembers its master. But the nafs, the soul, has forgotten who its master is. And this is because we have become tainted with the duniya. We have become so absorbed in this physical and material world that we have forgotten who our Lord is. And that is why Allah, exalted is He, sent us messengers, to remind us who our master is, so that we can return, so that we can return to Him.

You see, we as Muslims today, as Sulemanis, our hearts are dead. We went onto auto-pilot a long time ago. And now we are in this state called "Ghafla," or heedlessness. And that is what a pilot does when he gets up in the air. If you ever opened that cockpit door, you would have a heart attack, because they are snoring, they are in deep sleep, and the plane is on auto-pilot. And that is what has happened to us. We have gone into this mechanical mode. We say Allahu Akbar, Allah is great, without meaning it in any way at all. We begin our namaz and a few minutes later forget which rakaat we are in. Did I do one sajda or two sajda?

That is why in Islam everything begins with an intention. A niyah. Why is that? Because the intention controls the action. And where does the intention lie? محلُ النِّیَّۃ القلب The place of intention is in the heart. But we say the niyah, and then we go onto auto-pilot. This is what we do. We go to sleep. And then there are different levels and degrees of sleep. That is why Maulana Ali said, الناس النیام. The people of this world are in a state of sleep.

Someone asked Maulana Ali: What is all of this? What is all this creation? He replied: ھباءٌ لا یُرَا اِلَّا حِ‏ینَ ما یَقَعُ عَلَیہِ النُّورَ اللہ This is like the dust in the air that only becomes visible when the light of Allah strikes it. You see, this was an Arif Billah. He was a man who knew Allah, exalted is He. What a profound description of the atomic realm. All of these atoms that are floating in this ethereal space that Allah has created. And the only reason it is visible is because Allah is Noor as-Samawat wal-Ard. Allah illuminated the heavens and the earth. And the heart is the organ of the human being that is capable of perceiving that light in the most profound and deepest ways. Our heart is a precious gift from Allah, and we have to protect this precious gift. Just look where He put it. He put it behind the sternum, the strongest thing in the body, and then He put a rib cage around it. He did not put it like the other organs that are out there, where a person has no protection. And that is why, if you want to bring down a man in martial arts, that is the first thing they teach you.

Go for the groin, because there is no protection there. Both physically and spiritually, it is the lowest-ranking organ of the body. But for the heart, Allah placed a protection, a powerful protection. And then He gave it this oscillating power, by which the blood flows into every single cell of the body with every pulse. That is the reason the blood reaches every single cell of the body.

This is entrainment. If you know anything about oscillatory physics — a large word, only just learned, and so used here — you know that oscillatory physics is the study of entrainment: how one thing entrains with another. The word "entrain" means this: when there is a rhythm that causes other things to fall gradually into synchronism with it. When the rhythm of one oscillating device brings the rhythm of another device into step with it, that is called entrainment.

We know that soldiers entrain naturally when they march. It becomes hard to walk with someone who is out of step; you naturally entrain and fall into step with the other person, do you not? That is why soldiers entrain naturally. And this entrainment results in amplification, which is more frightening still. You know what happens to a bridge when soldiers walk in entrainment. That is the first thing taught to every engineer. When soldiers cross a bridge in a single step, the force of their weight is amplified exponentially, because it was all together. That is the power of being unified. When you are unified, you have power; and when you are disunited, you are weak.

Now consider the heart, the beats of the spiritual heart, the understanding of the meaning of this beat of La Ilaha Illa Allah. It entrains the mind, the body, and the soul. And when this entrainment occurs, when everything is synchronized, there is an exponential amplification in the form of actions. The intensity of every action changes.

And that is why Rasul Allah said: Know that in the body of a human being there is a lump of flesh; if it is sound, the entire body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the entire body is corrupt. Why? Because the entire body is in entrainment with the heart. If the heart is diseased, the entrainment will be diseased. If the heart is sound, the entrainment will be sound.

La Ilaha Illa Allah is the constant entrainment for the soul. Look at salaah, which is the practical application of this testimony, La Ilaha Illa Allah. The heart is turned toward Allah, and the body is turned toward the Qibla. Everything is being entrained all at the same time. And then there is the sajdah, the ultimate contraction. I told you that sajdah, in ancient Arabic, means the moment when the camel relinquishes its control and submits to the will and command of its master. In sajdah we contract the entire body, bringing everything close together — is that not so? And we place our foreheads, that which contains our intellect; we place that intellect on the ground. And we do this to elevate the heart. That is an incredible gesture. In our day-to-day life, when we are standing up or sitting down, the intellect is always above the heart, is it not? The sajdah in salaah is a deliberate act of lowering the intellect in order to elevate the heart. It is a symbol that highlights the precedence of the heart over the intellect. SubhanAllah. There is not a single action in this beautiful religion that is without profound wisdom within it.

And so we truly need to protect our hearts. We must protect this amazing gift of Allah.

Because just as the physical heart dies, the spiritual heart too can die. And so, to keep the spiritual heart alive, we have the knowledge of this Qur'an. This is why we have تلاوۃ القرآن بالتدبر — the reading of the Qur'an with reflection. And this matters, because you need to know the reason. Why do things happen? Once you understand why Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, has asked us to do these things, it strengthens the heart, and a desire grows within you to fulfill that thing. For you are now using your intellect, and when the intellect stands behind something, it is not the same as following something blindly. To believe with conviction is a powerful belief. Where there is conviction, there is action. And where there is action, there is change. And so you will change, and the things around you will change. It is the recitation of the Qur'an with understanding and reflection, then, that keeps the heart alive.

And I find this story remarkable, considering that it was told several thousand years ago, when man had no knowledge whatsoever of the size of this universe. So Allah created this immense universe, because He is Kabeer, He is Jaleel, He is Musawwar, the fashioner. He is Azeem, the great. And if you wish to understand how powerful He is, then simply consider how long it would take you and me — all human beings combined — to create a fully functioning universe of this size. And then consider how Allah created this universe with a single command: Kun — Be. Fa Yakoon — and it was.

So Allah created this universe around us as a constant reminder for us, so that we never forget who He is.

Life is a journey. See, whether we like it or not, we are all on a journey. And every journey has a beginning, it has a middle, and it has an end. And we are in the middle right now. This worldly life is, in fact, the middle, and anything that is in the middle is in a temporary, transitional phase. It is not something permanent, because it is not the destination.

There are three worlds. There is the عالم الجبروت, the world of omnipotence — that is where Allah resides. Then there is the عالم الملکوت, which is the spiritual world, and then there is this عالم المُلک, the physical world. And Allah is the Malik, He is the king. He is مالک الجبروت و مالک الملکوت و مالک الملک. He is the owner of these three realms. He is the king of the Mulk, the Malakoot, and the Jabaroot. So this world in which we live is the lowest of all the worlds, and it comes forth out of the Malakoot, the spiritual realm in which Allah created us.

And the Malakoot comes from the Jabaroot. So when we were in the Malakoot, in the spiritual realm, we were in the state of witnessing, مشاہدۃ. This is why Allah made all the souls testify, اشھد الارواح. And what did he make them testify to? الست بربکم؟ — Am I not your lord? بلا شھدنا — No doubt, we testify! Every one of us testified, regardless of what our belief is today. Whether we believe in Allah now or not does not matter. We all testified. We were all made witnesses to Allah AWJ, and we all testified.

And then, when we crossed over into this physical realm, Allah placed our soul into this vessel, which is the body, much like a bird in a cage. So we are in this cage, and this cage is made of flesh and blood. This is the Mulk. This body of ours is from the Mulk. It is made from this earth. But the rooh, the soul that resides within this body, is from the Malakoot. And so the soul is a prisoner inside this body. Every prisoner will leave the prison at the end of its sentence. It is going to move on and return to the world it came from. It is just like opening the cage: the bird flies out and leaves the cage behind, and it does not look back. If you open the cage, the bird will fly out and it will not look back at the cage. It simply flies out and it is gone.

So we came into this world. And what happens is that, when you come into this world — see, the nature of this world is zulmaani, it is darkness. But the nature of the Malakoot is noor, it is light. And Allah created the heavens and the earth from light. ٱللَّهُ نُورُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ. ٱللَّهُ مُنَوِّرُ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ — Allah is the illuminator of the heavens and the earth. All of this physical realm came from light. There was a time when all of this was light, and then a degradation took place, and the light dimmed, and eventually it degraded into darkness, and this physical world came into existence.

And so Allah AWJ has made us human beings this interstitial space. سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ — I will show them my signs on the horizon. If you look at the horizon, the horizon is the meeting place of the heavens and the earth. The horizon is where the heavens and the earth meet, and you can only really see this in the ocean. The ocean is the place where you can truly see the heavens and the earth meet at the horizon. And Allah says that we will show them, within their own existence, that this is the meeting place of the heavens and the earth, of their soul and their body. The human being is where the soul and the body, the heaven and the earth, the Malakoot and the Mulk, both come together. Allah made the human being the microcosm, set against the macrocosm of our solar system. The horizon is the macrocosm, and we are its microcosm.

Because today modern science wants to tell us that we are insignificant, does it not? That we are nothing. Science today tries to reduce us to nothing. They say, look, you are from an insignificant planet, in an insignificant solar system, in an insignificant galaxy, in the midst of billions of galaxies. You are nothing. And all of that is true. They are not lying.

But if you go inside a human being, all of those vast spaces that are out there in the solar system, in the horizon — they are also within you. Maulana Ali said: وتـَحسب أنك جِرم صغير . وفيكَ انطوى العالمُ الأكبرُ — you think you are some insignificant speck, yet within you the whole cosmos is folded. All of the cosmos is within you. This is from one of the verses of Maulana Ali's poems: لدواؤك فيـكَ وما تـُبصـِـرُ . وداؤك منـــكَ وما تشــعرُ وتـَحسب أنك جِرم صغير . وفيكَ انطوى العالمُ الأكبرُ — your medicine, your cure, is within you, but you do not see it. Your ailment arises from you, but you are not aware of it. You think that you are an insignificant thing, yet this entire universe around you exists within you.

So you have planets within the solar system, each one functioning independently and also collectively. We have organs within our bodies, each one an independent planet, performing its own function and also working together to keep the human body alive and functional. If there are shining stars in the sky, we have eyes that shine with light. If there are oceans and rivers flowing within this world, we have blood flowing within our veins. If there are mountains with deep caves in them, reflect on the structure of the nose and the nostrils. If there are trees and forests in the world, we have hair and facial hair. If there are minerals and metals in this earth, we have bones and teeth and nails. If this earth contains the four primary elements of water, fire, earth, and air, we too have all four of those elements inside us, in the form of heat, water, gases, and carbon. If this world passes through four seasons — spring, summer, fall, and winter — our life passes through four seasons of birth, childhood, youth, and old age. If this world is able to produce beautiful, soothing sounds, like the sounds of a waterfall and of rain, and the music of the winds and the oceans, and at the same time is able to produce loud and harsh noises, like that of thunder, then human beings too are capable of both — beautiful speech as well as hideous speech. If this world is in a state of constant change, human beings are in a state of constant change.

I as an individual, you as an individual, we are each an entire solar system that exists within the galaxy of our families. Each member of our family is an entire solar system on its own, living together with other families, other galaxies, within communities, that exist within towns, that exist within states, that exist within countries. So now you tell me: are we human beings not the perfect symbol of these billions of galaxies that contain billions of solar systems? For we too are billions of people, living in billions of families, each one operating independently as a complete universe. وتـَحسب أنك جِرم صغير . وفيكَ انطوى العالمُ الأكبرُ — you think you are an insignificant thing, yet this entire universe exists within you.

So we are not insignificant. We are not nothing in the grand scheme of things. We are the universe itself. We are the purpose of this physical universe. This immense universe that we see outside of us, in the horizon, is only a reminder of the universe that exists within us, within our selves.

And so Allah created us within these powerful bodies. This body is very powerful because it is sensory. It is Hiss. And Allah gave us these five senses, and these are the inroads of our experience.

سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ

All of our knowledge comes from our sensory perceptions. That is the source of all knowledge. We arrive as a blank slate, and then we come into this world, and we begin to be filled with experiences. And experience comes only from and through this physical world. So Allah placed His signs, His divine attributes, within this physical world all around us, and within us as well. I will show them My signs, My attributes, these reminders, within the horizons and within themselves.

We human beings are not nothing. We are the astonishing representation of Allah's power. We are not a random event. Nothing in this external universe, in the horizon, is random, and nothing within our internal universe, within our existence, is random. Everything is for a specific purpose. We have a hadaf; we have a target.

ایحسبُ اَنَّ الانسَانُ یَترُکُ السُّدا؟

Does the human being think that he has been left in vain, that he is simply a sudaa, a random event? This is what Allah asks us in the Quran. Does he truly think that all of this was created for nothing? That this remarkable design I placed into the universe, and then condensed within him, is all for nothing? That the universe passed through all of these stages, one by one, all the way to its final creation, and that the human being passed through all of these stages as well? First of all, you had to be nutrition. Because there was a time when your material body was being formed inside someone else. For semen and ovum to exist, they must first be created, and they are created from nutrition. So there was a point when we were merely nutrition. And if you go back further, there was a point when even that did not exist, because it too came from something else.

هَلْ أَتَىٰ عَلَى ٱلْإِنسَنِ حِينٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلدَّهْرِ لَمْ يَكُن شَيْـًۭٔا مَّذْكُورًا

Does the human being not see that there was a time when he was nothing, and then he was made into something? And then all of these events that took place, stage by stage, nine months of systematic and purposeful development.

ثُمَّ خَلَقْنَا ٱلنُّطْفَةَ عَلَقَةًۭ — Then We made the sperm into a clinging clot,
فَخَلَقْنَا ٱلْعَلَقَةَ مُضْغَةًۭ — and We made the clot into a lump of flesh,
فَخَلَقْنَا ٱلْمُضْغَةَ عِظَمًۭا — and We made bones from the lump,
فَكَسَوْنَا ٱلْعِظَمَ لَحْمًۭا — and We covered the bones with flesh;
ثُمَّ أَنشَأْنَهُ خَلْقًا آخَرَ — then We developed him into a complete creation.

Do you think that you passed through all of these stages, one after another, until you developed into a complete human being, and that all of this happened for nothing? That all of these events simply took place at random, so that one day you would be sitting in these Sunday sessions playing candy crush on your phones?

ایحسبُ اَنَّ الانسَانُ یَترُکُ السُّدا؟

You think you were created to be enslaved to diversion and entertainment. This is what the world today wants us to believe: that the only reason we are here in this world is to be entertained, to be diverted, to watch movies, to play games, and to listen to music all the time. That is what they say we are here for.

We're here, in the end, only to entertain ourselves to death, and then another group takes our place and does the very same thing, and so it continues, on and on, until one day it ends. There is some cosmic collision, or a giant asteroid wipes us all out. This is the modern belief now: that there is no real purpose to the human being, no real meaning to existence.

How can this make sense? How can it possibly make sense when I look into the horizons and into my own self?

The human soul is trapped within this body, and the body by its very nature, when it perceives, becomes overwhelmed by the sensory experience. This is why God placed a reminder within his creation, so that the human being could use his powers of sense perception and witness the divine presence in all that is created, refracting the divine attributes. Through these divine attributes he could be reminded — reminded of the testimony he gave in the spiritual world.

This is why, when a baby is born, the first thing done in Islam is that the Azaan and the Iqamah are recited into its ears. It is to remind him, in this physical world, of the testimony he made in that spiritual world. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would never command us to do anything meaningless. Everything he guides us toward is haqq; it is the truth. So when the Azaan and the Iqamah are recited into the ears of the child, it is his soul that is being addressed, not the baby. The baby is flesh and blood, but the soul has access to the senses, you see, because the soul has been given a body. The hearing and the sight, they all affect the soul, and this is why what you look at will affect you, and what you listen to will affect your soul.

إِنَّ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْبَصَرَ وَٱلْفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُو۟لَٓئِكَ كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْـُٔولًۭا

Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — you will be questioned for all of them. God will ask us about our hearing, our sight, and our heart. Why the heart? Because the heart is the ultimate source of our consciousness. At the root of the human being is his consciousness, and this consciousness is something you always possess, even when you are a child. For a child knows to speak the truth, and this is why a child will never lie. It does not matter whether he is born in the house of a Muslim, a Christian, a Jew, or an atheist; it does not matter. The child will always speak the truth.

Why does a child not lie? Because it has witnessed the attribute of al-Haqq, the Truthful, in the spiritual realm. And that is why, instinctively, by default, a child will always speak the truth.

Learn Islam from a child. His parents and this world, this duniya, will later teach him to lie. But the instinctive response of a child will always be to speak the truth. Instinctively, a child will always be merciful, because it has witnessed the Rahman; it has witnessed the Raheem. It will be kind, because it has witnessed the Raouf. It will be loving, because it has witnessed the Jameel. A child constantly manifests the beautiful attributes of God, because it has witnessed those attributes in the Malakoot. And that is why it is so easy to love a child. It does not even have to be my own child.

The love that comes gushing out of us when we take a child into our hands does so because the child is subconsciously reminding us of the love of Allah that we once had. If you want to learn about Islam, learn it from a child. No one exhibits the traits of Islam the way a child does. And that is why the Messenger of Allah said:

مَا مِنْ مَوْلُودٍ إِلَّا يُولَدُ عَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ فَأَبَوَاهُ يُهَوِّدَانِهِ وَيُنَصِّرَانِهِ وَيُمَجِّسَانِهِ

Yuhawwidanihi, wa yunassiranihi, wa yumajjisanihi.

Every child is born upon the instinct — in a state of "Fitrah" — and then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Zoroastrian, just as an animal gives birth to a whole and unblemished offspring:

كَمَا تُنْتَجُ الْبَهِيمَةُ بَهِيمَةً جَمْعَاءَ . هَلْ تُحِسُّونَ فِيهَا مِنْ جَدْعَاءَ

Just as an animal gives birth to a whole offspring — have you ever noticed an animal that was born mutilated? Animals are not born mutilated; we mutilate them. In the same way, all human beings are born believers, and we turn them into disbelievers.

Study of the Heart

So when Allah created us in this physical realm, and placed His divine attributes in all of His creation — outside us and inside us, فی الافاق وفی الانفس — He gave us a gift. He gave us something very special, something that could help us recognize these attributes and connect back with Him. And that is the heart. He gave us a heart, a qalb, a medium through which to see and recognize His divine glory. He gave us this spiritual heart, and He made it the center of our consciousness, so that we can recognize His attributes, His signs, His mark in everything around us. And He made the physical heart a symbol for that spiritual heart.

Just look at the physical heart. It is the most astonishing organ of the body. We now know that the human heart beats approximately forty million times a year. Over an average human lifespan, your heart will beat about three billion times. It moves about forty gallons of blood within us. If you were to take forty buckets — not forty gallons, just forty buckets — and fill them with water, and begin carrying those buckets from one room to another, you would see how quickly you grow tired. And yet this extraordinary organ that Allah has placed within our bodies keeps pumping throughout our lives, effortlessly, without asking us for anything in return — not even asking us to tell it to pump this blood for us.

And what is even more unusual is that we now know the human heart is not only self-regulating; it begins to beat before there is a central nervous system. During embryonic development, the heart is one of the few organs that must function almost as soon as it is formed. And the fact that the heart is one of the earliest organs to develop speaks to its importance. The human heart begins to beat and to pump blood through the embryo around the twenty-second day of pregnancy. Who made the heart beat before there was even a central nervous system? Who made the heart beat? The One who created the heart made it beat, and He sustains its beating. Why? Because it is the heart that has been created to recognize Allah. That is why it is the first thing to develop — to symbolize the human need to understand its Maker. And it keeps doing its work until, one day, it stops beating. And then this form called the soul — the Rooh — leaves this physical realm and passes into a different realm.

And this heart, this Qalb — Qalb is spelled qaf, laam, and ba. Now, if you take those letters and switch them around,

you get the word *qabal*, which means to come before, to precede, to be first and foremost. And there is a science in the Arabic language, that when you switch the letters of a word around, they remain connected in meaning. Take a word like علم, which means knowledge. When you rearrange those same letters, you get عمل, which means action — because knowledge is bound up with action. So whenever the letters of a word are rearranged to form a different word, the two words are always related in meaning. This is another of the miraculous features of the Arabic language. And that is why *Qalb* and *Qabl* — the heart, and to precede, or to come before — are related. And the word *Qabl* is related to *Qibla* as well. *Qibla* means direction, and a direction is always pointed toward a destination. If there is no destination, there is no need for a direction.

So then, what is the direction of the heart? Who is the destination of the heart? It is the one it learned about before it learned anything else. Who is this heart yearning for? Who is it pointing toward? Whom does it take precedence for? It does all of this for Allah, because the heart knows something that it knew even before it came into this realm. You see, the heart knows: *Alastu bi rabbikum* — Am I not your Lord? The heart knows the answer to that question. Am I not your Master? *Bala shahidna* — Indeed, we testify that You are. So every human heart that came into this world knows this truth, this spiritual truth. I am certain you feel it even now, because everything I am saying, you already know to be true.

So we were made witnesses in the spiritual realm, and now, in this physical realm, the human being has been given the task of testifying again — by recognizing the divine attributes of his Master within the horizons and within his own soul. He is charged with repeating his testimony, the same testimony he gave in the primordial world, with Allah, the Almighty and Glorious. He must now testify to that same thing in this physical world, with *Sidq* — صدقاً من قلبہ — testify the truth, with sincerity of heart.

The heart is saying *La ilaha illa Allah*. And what is it that he must testify? What is it that the heart must see, understand, believe, and then testify to? It is لا الہ الا اللہ. It must testify that there is no god except Allah. He must purify the uniqueness and absoluteness — the *ahadiyat* and the *samadiyat* — of Allah from all His creation. He must purify his faith. Purify it with what? With his heart. And what is the human heart constantly doing, even in the physical realm? It is purifying blood. *SubhanAllah!* It is forever at work exchanging the deoxygenated blood for the oxygenated blood. Oxygen is life. *Iman*, faith, is spiritual life. The heart is constantly exchanging disbelief for faith, and then supplying that oxygenated blood to the various parts of the body.

And so the human heart has been made a symbol for the spiritual heart. Why has He made it a symbol? Because Allah, the Most Glorified and Most High, manifests Himself from an unseen realm. You see, in the spiritual realm Allah was manifest; He was *Zahir*, apparent. But in this physical realm He is *Batin*; He is hidden. Allah has hidden Himself from us by manifesting Himself — through His attributes, in creation, from an unseen realm. And it is only the human heart, the spiritual heart, that can recognize this. This is why the heart is the organ of cognition. It is not the brain.

Now, why does the heart beat? Why does the heart beat?

Why does it move from contraction to expansion? You see. Diastolic. Systolic. Why does it do this? There are many ways Allah could have carried the blood around to the different parts of the body without a beat. Why did Allah make it a beat? And then why did Allah make the breadth, the expansion and the contraction? You see, doctors can tell you the how. A doctor can tell you how the heart beats, how it gets the blood to the body, how the expansion and the contraction work. But what they cannot tell you is the why. And so they say — I do not know whether it is true or not, and there are quite a few doctors present in the group — but I have heard them say that the easiest way to stump a doctor is to switch from how to why. So why did Allah create this process of the heart, working through contraction and expansion? Doctors cannot answer that, because medical science can explain the how. How does the heart beat? Medical science can explain that. Why does it beat? Why is there not some different mechanism to pump the blood? That, science cannot explain. But the Quran can!

The heart beats. It expands and contracts, because one of the attributes of Allah is Al-Baasit. He is the Expander. He is Al-Baasit, and He is Al-Qabid. He is the Expander and the Contractor. And that is what the heart is constantly doing. It is constantly contracting and expanding. Why? Because it needs to testify. It needs to testify that there is no ilah except Allah. That is La ilaha illa Allah. La ilaha — that is the contraction. That is the negation of every ilah, the narrowing down of all forms of false deities, the contracting of the space, the removing and squeezing out of every drop of deoxygenated blood, until there is no ilah left in our lives. That is contraction. That is La ilaha. And then there is illa Allah, filling it back again with the life-giving oxygen of emaan, of faith. Recognizing and affirming Allah through His divine attributes, and testifying that there is only Allah. That is expansion. That is the oxygenated blood being pushed into every tissue, every muscle of our spiritual deeds. Our salaah, our fasts, our zakaat, our hajj.

We considered the meaning of the word Allah. Today, God willing, we will begin to consider two of His attributes: al-Rahman and al-Rahim.

Let us recall briefly what we have already said. Allah derives from the word Ilah with the definite article al- applied to it, so that Allah is al- plus Ilah. Because of the grammatical rules of Arabic there is اِضغَام, there is annexation: the alif of Ilah drops away, the two lams merge, and the result is Allah. Once this clause of exclusivity is applied to the word Ilah, Allah becomes the One to whom I should submit completely, the One to whom I should be truly loyal. He is the One to whom I turn for protection and refuge in my times of desperation. He is the One with whom I am passionately in love, the One with whom I am wholly consumed. He is beyond my imagining, beyond my capacity to comprehend and understand. He is the One whose glory and majesty confound me every time I attempt to approach Him. He is the One in whom I can place complete trust, upon whom I can lean, upon whom I can rest my entire weight, knowing that He will not let me fall. And, finally and most important of all, He is the One I worship. As I explained earlier, worship, or عبادۃ in Arabic, means two things: it means worship and it means obedience, both arising from the sum of all these different meanings of the word Ilah.

We then considered the perfection of His attributes, perfect because they are unique and because they are absolute, which in turn makes Him worthy of my worship. For the One who is worthy of worship must, by His very nature, be characterized by all the attributes of perfection, all the attributes of majesty, all the attributes of glory. So, because Allah is Allah, He must also be Ghafur. Because Allah is Allah, He must also be al-Rahim. Because Allah is Allah, He must also be al-Sami, al-Alim, and so on. Each and every attribute of Allah, by virtue of being unique and by virtue of being absolute, is an explanation of why Allah is Allah. And because He possesses these ninety-nine perfect attributes, Allah is worthy of my worship.

Now that we have studied the meaning of the word Allah and of His attributes, we find two attributes mentioned alongside His name: al-Rahman and al-Rahim. Out of all His ninety-nine attributes, why did Allah choose these two in particular? Notice, too, that this is not the only verse in which He employs these two attributes. Just one verse later, after He says الحمد للہ رب العلمین, He at once says again, al-Rahman al-Rahim. From this we can see, right at the outset, that this surah gives prominence to these two attributes, showing how important they are to Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala. Consider an example. Suppose I say, "Erum is my daughter, and I love her. I truly love her." What have I just done? I have stated two facts: first, that Erum is my daughter, and second, that I love her. But by saying that I love her a second time, what I am doing is emphasizing my love for her. I am giving greater weight to the fact that I love her than to the fact that she is my daughter. Do you understand?
body.topic_title_en: The Meanings of ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim

body.text_en:
So let us now come to the meaning of these two words, al-Rahman and al-Rahim. Their meanings are so extraordinarily beautiful. I remember that I had goosebumps when I first experienced the beauty of these words. First let us look at how these two words are commonly translated. If you open any English translation, you will find: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." Or: "the Merciful, the Merciful." "The Most Beneficent, the Most Merciful." "The Merciful, the Most Kind."

The merciful, the beneficent. The beneficent, the beneficent. The difficulty is that these words are so hard to process in English. When do you ever use the word "beneficent" in ordinary, day-to-day conversation? If someone helped you with something, would you say, "Oh, you are so beneficent"? You do not do that. I, at least, do not. My point is this: the purpose of a translation is that we come to understand the text. But if we begin to use words in our translation that we ourselves do not use and cannot relate to, then the whole purpose is defeated. We need translations that are close to the text, and that are also close to us. That is how a translation makes sense.

Both of these words, AlRehman and AlRaheem, have to do with the word رحمۃ. That is the word that underlies them both. And the word رحمۃ is generally understood as "mercy," but that is not the best translation for the word Rehmah. I am not saying it is the wrong translation; I am saying it is a weak one. The word "mercy" is generally used in English when you are being spared from a punishment. Consider: "The soldiers showed no mercy." What does that mean? It means they did not spare anyone. "The criminal asked the judge for mercy." In other words, he asked the judge to spare him. So the idea of mercy is generally that something bad was about to happen, and then someone intervened and showed you mercy. Do you understand?
