Because the soul can only be brought back to life by recognizing why it was created, what purpose it was created for, and then setting out and striving to achieve that goal, recognizing that we WILL have shortcomings, that we WILL make mistakes, that those mistakes are part of our humanity. This is why we were created. We were created to respond to our Uboodiyah, to Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala). And the only way a slave feels its Uboodiyah, its servitude to Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala), is in its abject nature. It is in its subjection to Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala), and that occurs by desiring the atonement when one has done wrong. It is in desiring to reconnect with one's true nature. And this is why we were given Wudu. What a gift this gift of wudu. What a gift. The gift of purifying ourselves. What a gift is the gift of salaah, to pray to Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala). What a gift to be able to recite munajaat.

and to call upon him. We are literally wasting away the preciousness of this life on our distractions. Allah gave us this beautiful life; He bestowed upon us His countless blessings, and we are throwing all of it away on entertainment and distraction. We have one short life in which to do something, to prove to Allah that He did not make a mistake by creating us. Yet here we are, crashing birds into buildings in the name of entertainment. The things we do, only to feel that rush of adrenaline, only to feel alive.

There is a man who jumps off a bridge tied to a rubber cord. He sees the cement sidewalk rushing up toward him, and suddenly he feels alive. He is literally trying to kill himself, and he feels alive. Then he wants to repeat that experience again and again, simply because he wants to feel alive. But that is not the life the human being was created for. It is not found through rushes of adrenaline. It is not found through the rush of drugs flooding the brain. It is not found through the rush of leaping out of a flying airplane, skydiving. It is not found through meaningless affairs and sleeping around for fleeting pleasures. It is not found through intoxication. Those are not the things that will make you feel alive. The only thing that will make you feel alive is to become the slave of the Hayye, the Ever-Living. To become a slave of the Ever-Living who never dies: that is the real secret of true life. This is the challenge set before the human being, and this is what we must wake up to.

The reason Huquq Allah comes first, and Huqooq afterward, is that once the heart becomes soft toward Allah, it will become soft toward people.

Huqooq Al-Ibaad. And then, finally, there is Huqooq Al-Ibaad, the rights of creation. Now that we have recognized Allah as our Master through His divine attributes, and we have trained our hearts in the divine light of those attributes, it is time that we reflect those divine attributes in our dealings with Allah's creation. We trained ourselves to be generous with ourselves; it is now time to reflect that generosity onto others in our dealings with them. We trained ourselves to be truthful, to be sincere with ourselves; it is now time to reflect that truthfulness, that sidq, that sincerity, in our dealings with others. We have recognized how Allah is forgiving with us, how He is patient with us; we must now reflect those attributes by being patient and forgiving toward others.

And this begins with blood ties. The first group of people upon whom we must reflect these attributes is our own family: parents, grandparents, uncles, aunts, even that annoying cousin of yours. That is where it begins. Silatur Reham, blood ties, kinship. Allah said, I work for you as a mother's womb works for the fetus. I have made Myself a mother's womb for you. Now you must reflect those same qualities toward the people of your family; you must become a mother's womb for them in your dealings with them. That is why it is called Silatur Reham, the ties of the Reham. To forgive your brother for Allah's sake, to forgive your sister for Allah's sake, not for them, but to do it for Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala). Truly, there are people who have not spoken to their brothers and sisters for years. There are some who have not spoken to their parents for years.

We are studying the Basmalah, and over the last several sessions we have examined the words Allah, al-Rahman, and al-Rahim in considerable detail. What remains is the word Bism. God willing, we will study this word today, and then complete our study of this verse by drawing everything together.

Bism is in fact two words. It is Ba joined to the word Ism. Ba is a preposition, and one of its meanings is with. Then there is Ism. So the Basmalah is actually made up of five words, in which the first word, "Bism," is a fusion of the Ba and the Ism. Now, what does Ism mean? In classical Arabic, Ism means noun. So there is اسم and there is فعل — noun and verb. The second meaning of Ism is name. So one meaning is noun, and the other is name. The reason for this is that every noun has a name. Anything and everything that is a noun always has a name. There is an animal, which is a noun, and it has a name: lion, tiger, dog, cat. An object is a noun, and so it has a name: table, chair, fan, computer. These are all names. So noun and name go hand in hand. That is why Ism, in classical Arabic, carries both meanings.

Now, what is so interesting about this statement, Bismillah, "With the name of Allah," is that one could argue the word Ism to be entirely unnecessary — redundant, even. For we have discussed at length that Allah is itself a name. It is the name of the divine essence. So I could instead say باللہ الرحمن الرحیم, and I would lose nothing in meaning. After all, we constantly say اعوذ باللہ, "I seek refuge in Allah." We do not say اعوذ بسم اللہ, "I seek refuge with the name of Allah," because it is Allah's refuge that I need, not the refuge of His name. So then, why must I say بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم, when I could just as easily say باللہ الرحمن الرحیم, and it would mean the same thing? If I am working on a project with Nadia, when it is finished I will not say, "I completed this project with the name of Nadia." I will say, "I completed this project with Nadia." There is no need to say with the name of Nadia.

In the same way, the word Allah can be used with the Ba, without the Ism. In fact, it is used in this manner throughout the Quran, constantly. وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ آمَنَّا بِٱللَّهِ — not آمنا بسم اللہ. يَحْلِفُونَ بِٱللَّهِ, "They swear by Allah" — not يَحْلِفُونَ بِسم للَّهِ, "They swear by the name of Allah."

So then, why is the word Ism used here? The only conclusion we can draw from its use in this place is that it does not, in fact, refer to Allah Himself. It must refer to something else. For if it were speaking of the name Allah, it would be entirely redundant, and this would introduce a linguistic imperfection — and then this Quran would no longer be the linguistic miracle it claims to be, which is impossible. So we must understand why Allah has used the word Ism in this verse. This is a subject of taweel, but I have expressly asked Javeed bhai for permission to share it with you.

ISM — NAMES

Now, since the beginning of time, since the creation of the first man, the concept of the name has been of the utmost importance. Indeed, the Quran draws attention to the importance of names in the account of the creation of Adam AS. For the name was the one thing that raised Adam AS in rank and gave him preference over the angels. If you recall the story: when Allah resolves to create Adam AS.

all the angels object to it, at once. They dispute with Allah; they contest His decision. وَإِذْ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ إِنِّى جَاعِلٌۭ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ خَلِيفَةًۭ — when your Master told the angels that He was going to place His representative upon the earth. قَالُوٓا۟ أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسْفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ — they said, Will You truly create one who will work corruption in the earth and shed blood? وَنَحْنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَ — if praise and thanks and glorification are all that You desire, we are more than enough for that. And then Allah says to them, قَالَ إِنِّىٓ أَعْلَمُ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ — I know that which you do not know. And then, in answer to that challenge, what is the very next thing that Allah does? وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ ٱلْأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا — Allah taught Adam AS the names, His ninety-nine divine names. Consider it well. ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ فَقَالَ — and then Allah presented Adam AS to all the angels and said, أَنۢبِـُٔونِى بِأَسْمَآءِ هَٓؤُلَآءِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَدِقِينَ — now tell Me these names, if you are truthful. And they could not answer. The angels could not answer, because they did not know the names, for they were not the ones who had been taught them. Adam alone was taught the names. And so what made him worthy of prostration was precisely this: the names. The name, then, is an exceedingly important thing that was given to Adam AS alone, and that raised his rank above the rank of the angels. And after Adam AS, this is something that has been given to us, for we are Banee Adam, the children of Adam.

Now what is a name? A name is the capacity for symbolic thought. That is the essence of naming. To name a thing is to take a symbol, which is linguistic in nature, and to apply it to something material or empirical that we can perceive. Or a name is something we may use as an abstraction, to draw distinctions between things. Animals cannot do this; animals cannot use symbolic language.

The second reason is that the "BA" indicates the desire for companionship. When I say "BA" before beginning my task, I am saying, O Allah, I need you at my side for this task. I need you to be with me. This is called الباء للمصاحبۃ. I want Allah, Azza wa Jal, to be with me. I want his Rahmaniyat, his Rahimiyat, to be with me. It is the confession of a weak and humble slave before his all-powerful master: that I cannot do this task without you, O Allah! If you do not help me in this task I am about to do, I will not be able to do it. I will not succeed in it. If you do not help me get to work in the morning, I cannot get to work in the morning. If you do not help me pass this exam, I cannot pass this exam. So Bismillah — O Allah, with your help I wish to begin what I am about to begin, so that I can reach the final goal, which is to meet with your approval. This is the "BA" of Musahaba, of companionship.

Now, generally in life, we do not see this. I mean, I see that I do not say "BA" and yet my tasks are completed without any trouble. You must have succeeded countless times without saying "BA." So then what is going on?

Well, this again goes back to the difference between al-Rahman and al-Rahim. As I said in the earlier sessions, Rahman is general love and mercy. The Rahman gives to all, whether they call upon Allah or not, believers or disbelievers — it makes no difference. But Rahim is a very special kind of mercy that is ONLY for the believers.

And then, the love and mercy of the Rahman is ONLY for this life, but the love and mercy of the Rahim is for the life to come. So if I succeed in my task without saying "BA," it is because of the Rahman. But I will have no reward for that worldly task in the life to come. So, for example, if I am beginning a task at work or at school, and this is not a religious task but a worldly one, yet because I called upon Allah for it, a reward from the Rahim has now been made obligatory for me. The Rahman may help me succeed in the task regardless, and I will receive praise and reward for that task from my teacher or my boss in THIS world, but this task will give me no benefit in the life to come. But if I called upon Allah with both his names of love, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, then the Rahman may or may not let me succeed in the task of this world, but the Rahim will DEFINITELY reward me for it in the afterlife. This is a VERY, VERY important thing to remember. Just imagine how many actions, how many worldly actions, we perform in a single day. Simply by remembering Allah, by saying "BA," that same action can turn into worship. So this is something we must all try very hard to discipline ourselves into. And another way in which remembering Allah before an action helps is that we would never commit a sin after reciting "BA."

By our very nature, we would not be able to do such a thing. And if we did — if even after reciting "BA" we still went on to commit a sin — then our whole stance would change completely. We would no longer be standing merely in disobedience to Allah. We would in effect be saying: O Allah, though I am aware of Your glory, though I am aware of Your power, I am committing this sin all the same. Do what You will. نعوذ باللہ من ذالک. But as a believer — indeed, as any decent human being — this verse cannot even rise to our lips when we are about to commit a sin. So if we make it our habit to recite "BA" before everything we do, it will serve as a powerful reminder and a strong guardian that protects us from sin.

And the final reason for reciting "BA" belongs exclusively to our religious acts: it is البائُنَا القبول, the "BA" of Allah's acceptance. Although we do want Allah to be pleased with our worldly deeds, we especially want Him to accept our religious ones, for the two do not weigh the same upon the scales on the Day of Judgment. So reciting the Basmalah is not only calling upon Allah with sincerity and true intention, seeking His help and His companionship; it is also asking for His final acceptance. For if Allah does not accept my act, it is as though I never performed it. Imagine that you labor over a project for months, working night and day, and its whole purpose was to count toward your final grades — and then, on the last day, you discover that your project will not be graded. How disappointed would you be? It is the same here. All the acts of worship we perform — we pray, we fast, we give zakat, we do all of this — and then, on the Day of Judgment, if these acts are not accepted, what would be the measure of our disappointment and grief? That is what the "BA" of the Basmalah does for us. It says: O Allah, I want Your acceptance of my deed. I want You to accept my effort in this worship, for I offer it with sincerity and with the intention of pleasing You, seeking Your companionship and Your help. I want my act to rise and ascend to You.

The Purpose of the Basmalah Is Barakah

And now, finally, what is the effect of the Basmalah? We have seen its reasons, we have seen its purpose. Now the last question: how does the Basmalah help the task at hand? What benefit does "BA" give me in the very action I am about to perform? That benefit is barakah, which is commonly translated as abundance. There is a hadith that the Prophet relates, in which Allah says: أنی اذا اُطِعتُ رَضِیتُ. وأذا رَضِیتُ بَارَکتُ. وَ لَیسَ لِبَرَکَتِی نِھَایَۃ — When you obey Me, it pleases Me; when I am pleased, I grant you barakah; and there is no limit to My barakah. In the Qur'an as well, in Surah al-Rahman, Allah says: تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ ذِى ٱلْجَلَلِ وَٱلْإِكْرَامِ — The name of your glorious and benevolent Master is full of barakah. The name of Allah is full of barakah — تَبَرَكَ ٱسْمُ رَبِّكَ. So all the divine names of Allah are full of barakah. And then, in another verse, He says — but here Allah does not mention which name is full of barakah, does He? It simply said that the name of your Master is full of barakah. Yet what did this surah begin with? Al-Rahman. And what is the first attribute of Allah named in the Basmalah? Bismillahi, al-Rahman, al-Rahim. So Allah is telling us something about the word "al-Rahman," in Surah al-Rahman.

Allah is saying that this name of His, the one with which I began — meaning al-Rahman — is full of barakah. Yet we also know that Allah Himself is full of barakah, because He says so in the Qur'an: تبٰرَکَ اللّٰہُ اَحۡسَنُ الۡخٰلِقِیۡنَ — Blessed is Allah, the best of creators! In this verse He joins barakah to Himself, not to His name. So we find both flavors in the Qur'an: the name of the essence, Allah, is full of barakah, and then all of His divine names are full of barakah as well. But in this final verse of Surah al-Rahman He does not say تبٰرَکَ اللّٰہُ; He is not speaking of Himself. He is speaking of His name. He says تَبٰرَکَ اسۡمُ رَبِّکَ — the name, al-Rahman, of your Master is full of barakah. So Allah is full of barakah, and His name al-Rahman is full of barakah. Do you understand?

Now when we recite the Basmalah, do we have these two names in that verse? Bismi Allahi al-Rahman al-Rahim. Both Allah and al-Rahman — both names of barakah — are used in the Basmalah. So the reason we recite the Basmalah, the reason we mention Allah's name before beginning a task, is barakah. Why? Because the Basmalah is overflowing with Allah's names. We have the bism, and we have just seen that the ism carries barakah: تَبٰرَکَ اسۡمُ رَبِّکَ — the name of your Master is full of barakah. The second word is Allah, and we saw تبٰرَکَ اللّٰہُ — the name of the essence, Allah, is also full of barakah. And then we have two explicit names, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, which are also of barakah, because both are among the divine names. So you can see that this verse is composed of words overflowing with barakah, and so when we recite this verse before any task we undertake, it spills that barakah into the task we are about to perform. And so, by reciting the Basmalah before every task, we are deliberately asking Allah to bless the task with the barakah of His names in the Basmalah.

Now, there is no word in the English language that can fully encompass the meaning of the word barakah. So we need to understand this word barakah through certain concepts. In Arabic, barakah is defined thus: البَرَکَۃُ النَّمَاءُ وَ الزِّیَادَۃُ. The first meaning of barakah is growth — something that rises, something that increases, that makes progress, that goes further and further and increases فوق التوقع, beyond expectation. If you plant a seed in the ground, how many trees do you expect? Just one! But if you put one seed in the ground and you get ten trees, with fruits producing hundreds of thousands of seeds — that is barakah. You planted one seed and eventually received thousands of seeds; that is growth beyond expectation. That is what you call barakah. Barakah means: logic says I should get one tree, but I got a whole forest. How did that happen? That is barakah. And also, what comparison is there between a tree and a seed? There is none. It is beyond comparison, because a seed is tiny and a tree is huge; a seed is delicate and a tree is strong; a seed has no value, while a tree bears hundreds upon hundreds of fruits, season after season after season, for years and years. If you truly think about it, what we receive from a tree, compared to a seed, is beyond all comparison. Yet that entire tree came from that one seed. SubhanAllah! That is barakah — unprecedented growth, unlimited increase. The Arabs say:

The Arabs also say **أَبْتَرَكَتِ السَّمَآء**, meaning that the rain keeps coming and coming. So continuity is another characteristic of the word barakah — something that stays continuous.

You cook food for two people. Suddenly ten guests arrive at your door. You all sit down together, and from that same food meant for two, twelve people eat and rise completely satisfied. That is barakah. It is not logical. You cooked for only two; it should never have been enough to satisfy twelve. Yet it satisfied them completely. How did that happen? That is barakah.

This actually happened in the time of Ali bin Syedna Suleman, may his soul be sanctified. There was a wedding in the house of a man who was not well off. He invited a few people from his village to attend, but word spread, and two whole villages gathered for the wedding. The man grew very worried, so he came to Syedna Ali bin Syedna Suleman and explained what had happened. He said, "I do not have enough food to feed them all." Syedna Ali said, "Go back and recite the name of Syedna Suleman three times over each cauldron." A few hours later, the man returned to Syedna Ali with a large tray of food in his hands. Syedna Ali asked him, "What happened?" He said, "My master, I did as you told me. Everyone ate from the food and left completely satisfied, and there is still food left over for my own family. So I have brought some of it to you." This is barakah. This is one of a thousand documented miracles of Syedna Suleman, may his soul be sanctified. Because the name Suleman carries barakah. Why? Because, as the Qur'an says, **إِنَّهُۥ مِن سُلَيْمَنَ وَإِنَّهُۥ بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ**.

I began this session with five people, and I held twelve sessions. Now, mashaAllah, there are more people in the group than Skype allows, and we are on our forty-fifth session. How did that happen? I did nothing. I did not go out inviting people. Yet I ended up with so many more people in the group. This is barakah. Why? Because of what we are doing in these sessions: we are mentioning Allah's name, for we are speaking about Allah, and al-Rahman, and al-Rahim.

So the meaning of barakah is growth, or increase beyond expectations. Barakah is also used in another way in the Arabic language. For example, the Arabs would say **أِذَا أَنَاخَ الْجَمَل**, when the camel settles onto the ground and does not move or budge. That too is barakah. And this is truly beautiful. Because when you grow something, and you grow it too much — I will give an example so you can understand. When children play with building blocks, they build up a huge tower, block upon block upon block. Now, as the tower grows taller, does it become more stable, or less stable? It becomes less stable. The taller the tower, the less stable it becomes. Eventually it will fall and break, and there will be no tower anymore. Is that not true?

So when something increases rapidly, and increases too much, it becomes less stable. But when something has barakah, it means that it will increase, and keep increasing beyond expectations, yet remain as stable as a camel sunk into the sand. SubhanAllah! In other words, do not think this increase will slip away. It is not an unstable increase.

We know unstable increase when we look all around us. Our economy rises very fast, and then what happens? It comes down very fast. There are governments that take power very fast, and then vanish just as fast.

Look at the fashion industry. Trends catch on very fast, and then disappear just as fast, and something else takes their place. But Allah says that barakah is when a thing increases and yet remains stable. It holds constant. It does not go away.

And when Allah says that His name is full of barakah, what does that mean? It means that the names of Allah, and the name ar-Rahman among them, have been spoken since the day creation came into being, and they only increase and grow with every passing moment, and they will go on growing until the very end of creation. Allah and His name will remain forever, because they are full of barakah. Worshippers come and go, but the One who is worshipped remains. Those who glorify the names of Allah come and go; many came before us, and many will come after us, and we will all depart, but the glory of Allah will always remain. This is the barakah of Allah's name.

And what does this mean for us? How do we draw upon it in our daily lives? It means that when we speak the name of Allah, when we recite the Basmallah, we are speaking names that are full of barakah. When we call upon the barakah of these names, then whatever we do will bring forth good, and it will bring forth good beyond what we expected. Its growth will continue, and it will not disappear. Not only that, it will also be stable. It will keep going and going and going.

Because of this Basmallah, the scholars say that every single Muslim is meant to be an optimist. Even if the task before us appears to fail, out of that failure there will be growth. The temporary failure will produce spiritual growth and lead on to larger and better tasks.

And because the name of Allah was spoken before we began the task, with the intention of calling upon His barakah, that task will be recorded in our book of deeds, and its reward will keep accumulating for the life to come. This is because the very mention of the name of Allah has now made it an act of worship. So if it takes me ten hours to complete that task, I have just performed ten hours of worship. Simply by reciting the Basmallah at the start of the task, the time it takes me to complete it is earning me reward. And after I have completed the task, the effect of what I have produced will keep earning reward for me for as long as it fulfills its purpose. Only consider that. Reciting a single Basmallah with the right intention, and see the amount of reward it accumulates. So the Basmallah before a task is the seed of barakah that we plant, which then blossoms into thousands upon thousands of trees bearing countless fruits of reward for us. SubhanAllah!

Every single good deed is an act of barakah. You may help one person. You may teach one person, and you do not know what may come of it. What if that person goes on to become a great scholar? And so we cannot calculate the results that flow from the Basmallah, because they are from Allah.

They will grow and grow beyond human expectation, beyond common sense, beyond logic. Mathematics cannot capture that number; it cannot encompass it.

The Arab scholars have agreed that human beings possess essentially three dominant modes of symbolic language. It is in its linguistics. The Quran is a linguistic miracle. And the recognition of this linguistic miracle comes from our ability to recognize things through names. Language unifies. This is the secret of the human being: that we have the ability to abstract, to differentiate, to identify — through names. We, as human beings, have the ability to see the *ONE* in the many. That is the only way we can communicate. Think about it. The only way we can communicate is by seeing the one in the many.

When we talk about a lecture, for example, when I tell you that there is going to be a session next Sunday at 9:30 a.m., how do you know what a session means in this context? Because the word SESSION has many meanings in different contexts. For example, I could say: this is a religious session. School is in session. The courtroom is in session. Yasmeen had a great tennis coaching session. The Federal Act was passed in the session of 1908. So the word session has so many different meanings in various different contexts. So when I say there is going to be a session on Sunday, how do you know which meaning of the word session I am talking about — that this is going to be a religious session? And how do you know exactly which Sunday I am talking about? Because a month has four weeks, and each week has a Sunday. Every Sunday has a 9:30 a.m. So out of all these multiple meanings for these words — Sunday and session — you are able to extract ONE particular meaning, understand it, and then show up on the correct day at the correct time for the correct reasons. This is the ability we human beings have. This is because we have the capability to abstract the one out of the many. And when we are not able to do this, when we are not able to zero in on THE one particular meaning, we are forced to say: Wait a minute. I just want to make sure. Did you mean this coming Sunday, or the one after that, or the one after that? Because every sentence needs to boil down to one particular thought from a sea of possibilities.

And so what this enables us to do is to speak intelligently about the oneness and the unified nature of words. Because that is who we are. We are all unifiers by nature. This is what we do as human beings. We are مُوَحِّدُون; we are constantly making one out of the many. And how do we do that? How do we make one? We do that through language. We can only communicate because of the oneness of language. And so through names, we were given this gift of unification, so that we could perform the ultimate unification: Tawheed. That is what the word Tawheed means. Unification. Tawheed comes from the root word "Hadd," which means a boundary, or a confine. And hadd is the root word for "Wahid," which means ONE, and also Ahad, which means unique. So Tawheed, Ahad, and Wahid all come from Hadd, which means a boundary. And what does a boundary give you? It gives you one distinct entity. It separates the one from the many.

So this ability to unify things through language is a sign that we have been created to perform the ultimate abstraction and the ultimate unification.

It is to recognize that this diverse creation must also have a single and unique source. Just as we can abstract the essence of the word "session" out of all its diverse meanings, we can also abstract the essence of existence out of all this diversity around us. And the essence of existence is Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala. He is the master of all creation, because he is the Creator of all creation, and it is only through his creation that we can identify him. This identification, this unification, is the purpose of creation. وما خلقت الجن و الانس الا لیعبدون And we did not create jinn and man except for Ibadah. And Ibadah, or worship, necessitates the extraction of the one Ilah out of multiple Ilah. That is what truly lies at the heart of Ibadah: the unification of the Ilah, choosing the one from the many. And this is how you reach Allah. La Ilaha Illa Allah. That is the ultimate abstraction, that is the ultimate unification. Out of multiple Ilah, you arrive at the one Ilah, and that is Allah. That is Tawheed. And this Tawheed, this unification, is the heart and soul of Ibadah, the worship we were created for.

So the Basmalah begins بسم اللہ, with the name of Allah, because we know Allah through the power of symbolic understanding. We cannot know Allah the way we know things. We cannot know Allah the way we know a tape recorder, or a laptop, or a computer. Because essences are hard to understand, even in the case of things, but when it comes to Allah it becomes absolutely impossible. The only way we can know Allah is through symbolic language, which is his ninety-nine divine names, or divine attributes. Because Allah has no likeness. He has no misaal.

A misaal is an analogical symbol for something we already know, used to let us know something we do not know. If you understand something that you already know, a person can use that as an example to explain to you something that you do not know. And you say, "Aaah, I got it! It is like this." But when it comes to Allah, لیس کمثلہ شئی, is that not so? Allah has no equivalent likeness.

And so we have these ninety-nine divine names as linguistic symbols, so that we can have some concept of who he is. So, for example, Allah is called مالک یوم الدین, Owner or King of the Day of Judgment. Now, because we understand Malik, because we understand the concept of a king, we can now relate to the position that Allah will take on the Day of Judgment: the position of a king, the position of the ultimate owner. We can understand that through that symbolic reference. But we now know that Allah is not limited to our concept of what a king means. He is far more exalted than that. Yet whatever concept we have is enough to get the point across.

So there is this distinction between Allah and the names of Allah. There is a distinction between Ism and Allah. The names of Allah, because of our ability to use names as symbolic thoughts, allow us to understand and identify Allah. Because that is the only purpose of a name: to identify the noun. My name is Asif. When you children hear my name, you are able to uniquely identify my essence. And you go, "Ahh, it is that guy who tortures me for an hour every Sunday."

So a name is a symbol for abstraction. A name is a symbol for identification. Names help identify nouns. That is why the word Ism means both things: name and noun.

because names help identify nouns. So keep this idea in mind. And now read the Basmallah again. At this point we are venturing into Taveel, so this is not common knowledge; it is something particular to the knowledge that we Sulemanis possess.

So: بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم. With the name of Allah, who is AlRehman and AlRaheem. That is the common translation. But in the language of Taveel, we can now translate it in this way: With the nouns who can identify Allah for us. Listen carefully. With the nouns who can help identify Allah for us. And what about Allah? His Rehmaniyat and His Raheemiyat toward us. So BARR, with the nouns. These nouns are certain very specific, chosen people, who can identify, clarify, and explain Allah's Rehmaniyat and Raheemiyat for us. That is why the word Ism is used specifically in this verse: to point to these people, who can explain to us and transmit to us the knowledge of how Allah is AlRehman and AlRaheem.

Now who are these people, and how many are they? Well, how many words are there in the Basmallah? There are 5 words in the Basmallah: Ba + Ism + Allah + AlRehman + AlRaheem. These represent the 5 people whom Allah has chosen to explain the Rehmaniyat and Raheemiyat of Allah, to clarify His intense mercy and His permanent mercy to us. These are the ones we know as the Panjatan-e-Paak: Muhammad + Ali + Fatima + Hassan and Hussain. These are the Ahlul Bait, the members of the house of Rasul Allah, who have been chosen to show us Allah's Rehmaniyat and His Raheemiyat, both conceptually and practically.

If you are not convinced, count the letters in the names of the Panjatan: Muhammad (4) + Ali (3) + Fatima (5) + Hassan (3) + Hussain (4). That is 19. Count the letters of the Basmallah. They are 19 as well.

If you are still not convinced, look at the letters of the Basmallah. They fall into 2 categories. There are the repeating letters and the non-repeating letters, and these too are 5 in number. There are 5 repeating letters and 5 non-repeating letters. I am not going to go into the Taveel of who the non-repeating ones are, but for now understand that the repeating 5 are the Panjatan Paak. Just as in the Kalima, la ilaha illa Allah, you have two categories, which also contain 5 repetitions. You have the Alif, which is repeated 5 times, and you have the Laam, which is repeated 5 times. And this is because there is a direct relationship between the Basmallah and the Kalima Ikhlaas.

So Ism in the Basmallah represents the 5 nouns, or the 5 people, the Panjatan, who are the true names of Allah, because they are the only ones who can identify Allah's attributes for us, especially the attributes of AlRehman and AlRaheem. So the presence of the word Ism there is to indicate that if you try to approach Allah without the guidance of these 5 chosen people, you will not be able to understand the love, the care, the concern, and the mercy of Allah. Not in this life. Not in the afterlife.

Now that we have covered the individual words, let us understand the entire ayah. We are told to recite this ayah before every single act that we do. Even the act of revelation. When the first ayah was revealed upon Rasul Allah (SAS), what phrase did it contain? اقرأ باسم ربک الذی خلق. Read, with the name of your master who created you. It really is the essence of the phrase. Now in this case the verb comes first. Why? Because it is the beginning of the Quranic revelation.

and notice that the name Allah is missing from this ayah. It says اقرأ باسم ربک; it does not say اقرأ باسم اللہ. That is why the verb came first in this ayah. But whenever the most glorious name "Allah" is mentioned, the verb always comes after the name Allah. It is always a subsequent verb. For example, when Allah commanded Nuh to board the ship, what did He say? وَقَالَ ٱرْكَبُوا۟ فِيهَا بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ مَجْر۪ىٰهَا وَمُرْسَىٰهَآ Allah said to Nuh (AS): go and ride upon the ship, and when you get onto it, say bismillah before you actually begin to ride it. So the verb, the riding of the ship, comes after bismillah, because the name Allah is mentioned in this ayah.

And when the prophet Sulaiman wrote to the queen of Sheba, and when that letter was read out to her, what did the letter say? إِنَّهُۥ مِن سُلَيْمَنَ وَإِنَّهُۥ بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ This letter is from Sulaiman, and before it is read out, it begins with the Basmala; then the letter is read out to her. The verb again comes after the bismillah, because the ayah contains the name Allah.

And we know that whenever Rasul Allah (Salawaat) would begin a task, he would begin by reciting Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. He would begin his lectures, his khutbas, his salaah. Anything he did, he would begin with the Basmala. And in one hadees he says: کلُّ أمرٍ ذِی بَال لَم یُبدَأ بِسم اللہِ تَعالیٰ . فَھُوَ أَقْطَعْ فَھُوَ أَجْزَمْ That every single deed of importance that does not begin by saying bismillah, it is as if the deed has been amputated. It is not whole. It is ugly, or it is mutilated. Every single deed of importance that does not begin with bismillah is then اقطع, it is cut off; it is اجزم, it is mutilated. That is why we say bismillah before everything of importance that we do.

Even when Rasul Allah (Salawaat) would write letters to the non-Muslim kings. For example, when Heracles, the emperor of Rome, received a letter from Rasul Allah (SAS), and when the translator opened up the letter and read it, the first thing it had was: بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم۔ من محمدٍ رسول اللہ الی حِرَقَل العظیم الرُّوم The Basmala. This is a letter from Muhammad the messenger of Allah to Hiraqal the emperor of Rome. So you see, even when he began a written document, he began it with the Basmala.

Why recite the Basmala before every action? Now let us see what that is. Why do we say the Basmala before beginning any action? If we think about this translation of the Basmala: With the name of Allah, who is al-Rahman and al-Rahim. If you just look at this sentence, even without knowing any Arabic grammar, you can immediately tell that this is an incomplete sentence. With the name of Allah. With the name of Allah what? What with the name of Allah? And even from a grammatical standpoint, the ba is a preposition; therefore, by rule, it has to be associated with something. It has to be associated with either a noun or a verb, because a preposition cannot just exist by itself. So with the name of Allah what? What am I doing with the name of Allah? So it is obvious that something is missing here.

And if you look at each of these words grammatically: Bism is a preposition combined with a noun. Allah is a proper noun. Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are adjectives. So you have a preposition, you have a noun, and you have adjectives. So then, grammatically, what is missing here? What is missing here is a verb. It is missing what they call a PERTINENT and SUBSEQUENT verb. The scary lingo for that is.

جار والمجرور متعلق بہ و متأخر بہ. So I'm sure that makes sense to everyone. Moving on. I'm kidding. I'll explain. All right. So what is missing from the Basmalah is a verb that is pertinent — متعلق بہ — and that is subsequent — و متأخر بہ.

Let us look at the pertinent verb first — متعلق بہ. You children know what pertinent means, right? Something related to the matter at hand, something relevant.

First of all, why is it missing a verb in the first place? Because verbs are actions, and actions are not normally nouns. Actions are verbs. So my action — the action I am about to perform after reciting this ayah — provides the missing verb and the context of my action, and thus completes the sentence. Do you understand? The reason the Basmalah is missing the verb is that I have to provide the verb by my action.

So when I say بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم and then I begin to read a book, the action of reading provides the missing verb, the missing context, and that then completes the sentence of the phrase. And so what the ayah transforms into is this: With the name of Allah, who is al-Rahman al-Rahim, I am reading this book. With the name of Allah, who is al-Rahman al-Rahim, I am entering my house. With the name of Allah, who is al-Rahman al-Rahim, I am drinking this glass of water. With the name of Allah, who is al-Rahman al-Rahim, I am beginning this exam. So my action provides the pertinent verb, the context, that was grammatically missing from the original sentence of the phrase. And so my action then completes the sentence grammatically.

This is the reason the verb is missing from the original sentence: so that we may put in the verb through our action. If Allah had added the verb Himself, if Allah had made the verb a part of the ayah, then we could not use this ayah for anything other than what Allah used it for. If Allah had said بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم أتلوٰ ھذا القرآن — With the name of Allah I recite this Quran — then the verb would have been tied to the sentence itself, and we would not be able to use this ayah for any other action except for reciting the Quran. So Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, removed the verb from this ayah so that we could use this sentence before every action we perform in our daily lives. So that is the meaning of the pertinent verb — متعلق بہ.

Now, what was the other thing I said? A pertinent verb and what? A subsequent verb. Now, what does subsequent mean? Something that comes later — متأخر بہ. So, for example, if I want to recite the Basmalah before reciting the Quran, I can say it in two ways. I can say I recite in the name of Allah, or I can say in the name of Allah I recite. I can put the verb recite before the name of Allah by saying I recite with the name of Allah — أقرأُ بسم اللہ. In this case I put the verb recite first. Or I can put the verb after the name of Allah by saying With the name of Allah I recite — بسم اللہ أقرأ. Now, what is the difference? Who cares whether it is before or after? Who cares whether it is I recite with the name of Allah, or With the name of Allah I recite? Tomatoes, tomatoes, right? Who cares? Well, actually we do care, and we care for two reasons.

1. We always want to mention the name of Allah first. Because, as I explained,

The ninety-nine names are symbolic representations of Allah's divine essence, so we call upon the name of Allah first, in order to bind our action, which is yet to come, within the confines of his attributes. It is a call for Allah's help. It is a supplication, asking Allah that the action I am about to perform be made a manifestation of his divine attributes, and that he include his Rehma, his love, his care, his genuine concern, and his infinite mercy within my action. So by making my action subsequent, by delaying my action until after I have called upon the names of Allah, I am doing two things.

First, I am calling upon Allah's help in making my action a divine manifestation of one of his divine attributes, by including his Rehma within my action. Second, I am glorifying and honoring Allah by calling upon him before my action, in order to remind myself that he is my master and I am his slave. So I remind myself that Allah is my true north, and therefore this action I am about to perform must be in accordance with his will and his command. That is the first reason we care to make the action subsequent.

The second reason we cannot express in English, so we need to understand this one in Arabic itself. In Arabic, the reason we delay the verb is to imply exclusivity. It is called الحصر. In Arabic, when I place the verb first, when I say, "I recite this Qur'an with the name of Allah," this does not eliminate the fact that I could be reciting for other reasons as well. It is possible I could be reciting to show off. I could be reciting to make sure my neighbors do not sleep. I could be reciting because I want to be paid for my recitation. I could be reciting because of this, or because of that. But in Arabic, when you place the verb after the noun, when I say, بسم اللہ أقرأ, then what that means is, I am reciting only for the sake of Allah. There is no other reason that I am reciting. Do you understand?

When we push the verb to the end, we add a clause of exclusivity to the action. The only reason I am reciting, the only reason I am entering the house, the only reason I am drinking this glass of water, the only reason I am sitting for this exam, is exclusively for Allah, who is AlRehman and AlRaheem. I have no other deity, no other god in mind. This is why the verb must be subsequent.

So that is the reason the Basmallah is recited before every action: because it is missing the contextual verb, which I supply by my action. And the verb must also be subsequent in order to call upon Allah's help, asking him to include his Rehma with the task I am about to perform, to glorify him, and then also to remind myself that I am doing this task exclusively for Allah. And this produces sincerity, IKHLAAS, in the action I am about to perform. I am not doing this to show off. I am not doing this for praise. I am not doing this for any reason other than to please my master, and to acknowledge that I am in complete need of his love, his care, his concern, and his mercy in order to complete this task to the standard with which he would be pleased with me.

BA of BISMILLAH

Now, what does the preposition "BA" mean? The BA has several grammatical implications. The first is intention. I am placing the intention of pleasing Allah before I even begin the task.

I am setting the pleasure of Allah as my goal. And when the goal is clear, when the priorities are clear, the proper actions that follow fall into place naturally and of their own accord. This is why the messenger said, انما الاعمال بالنیات — without doubt, actions will be judged ONLY on the basis of intention. So when I open the book of Allah and I say "BA," I am saying, O Allah, I begin with your name. I begin with you in mind. Your pleasure is the final goal of my recitation. By this I wish to come closer to you. And so the intention here is placed before the action as proof of sincerity.

These are ayahs from Surah Aal-e-Imran, the third chapter, verses 190 to 193. Allah says:

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

There is no doubt about it—especially when it comes to the creation of the heavens and the earth, and especially when it comes to the struggle between night and day. In the conflict that takes place between night and day, there are signs for the people of sound essence. The first thing I want you to notice is that it does not say لَآيَتٍۢ لمسلمین, there are signs for Muslims, nor لَآيَتٍۢ لمؤمنین, there are signs for believers. It says لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ. So let us first understand the meaning of these two words.

The word ayah means many things. It carries the meaning of something valuable: خرج القوم بآیاتھم, the people came out with their valuables. So an ayah is something valuable, something that has purpose and meaning. Ayah also means to separate one thing from another, or to make one thing distinct from another.

Now the Qur'an is made up of ayahs, or verses. And so each verse is valuable; it has a specific purpose, it has a specific meaning, and each ayah is distinct, or separate, from another ayah. Do you understand?

The word ayah also means a sign. We spoke about this earlier. A sign is something that points to something else. The wind is a sign that life is being delivered. Life being delivered is a sign that I am being cared for. Which is then a sign that I am not, in fact, my own caretaker. Which is then a sign that someone else is providing for me. One sign leads to another sign, which leads to another sign, which leads to another sign. Do you understand?

And we see this in the Qur'an. Reciting one ayah leads to another ayah, which leads to another ayah. And this is how the Qur'an is formed, is it not? A group of ayahs becomes a ruku. A ruku becomes a juz. A group of juz becomes a Surah. A group of Surahs becomes a para. Thirty paras become one single Qur'an. This is similar to the distinct creations on this earth. Each creation of Allah, azza wa jal, is an ayah. Each creation is something valuable; it has a purpose, it has a meaning, it is distinct from every other creation. And then these creations group together to form one single planet, within a cluster of planets, to form a solar system, within a galaxy, that exists within billions of galaxies, within one universe. Do you see the correspondence between the Qur'an and the universe? This universe is a physical Qur'an.

just like the Qur'an is a spiritual universe. I will say it again. This universe is a physical Qur'an, just like the Qur'an is a spiritual universe. And so Allah says:

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

There is no doubt. In the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of night and day, there is something of value. There is something meaningful. There are distinct things to observe, and various lessons to learn. There is a kind of reminder. There is a kind of indication. There is a kind of clue. This is not for everyone, but for a certain kind of person: for the اولی الاباب.

The Meaning of Ulil-Albaab

اولی الاباب is commonly translated as people of sound intellect. But what is truer in meaning is people of sound essence. Albaab is the plural form. Its singular form, Lubb, is in fact a very beautiful word. In Classical Arabic, when you crack open an almond, the kernel you find inside is called lubb. The kernel inside a nut, the seed inside a fruit, is called lubb. Why? For two reasons. First, it is the essence of the fruit. The seed contains the entire tree within itself in a dormant form. Second, it is protected on every side by the nut or the fruit. And because it is always protected from any and all external influences, its essence remains pure. So اولی الاباب means pure essence, or a clean mind, one that is not polluted by useless things. That is the definition of the word lubb: a person whose thoughts are not polluted by useless things, a person who truly thinks about things that matter.

This mind that Allah gave us is in fact a very powerful gift. It is extraordinarily capable. We can memorize entire books. We can store incredible amounts of information. There are people who, when they set their minds to something, become extremely knowledgeable in the very area on which they focus. For example, there are commentators who can tell you sports statistics from fifty years ago, all off the top of their heads. I am the one who consumes them, for food, for clothing, for ornament. And because this is by design, it is consistent. Every creation is doing exactly what it is supposed to be doing, consistently. I never see an apple tree producing mangoes.

I never plant a rose garden only to be surprised by tulips instead. Everything functions the way it was designed. Everything fulfills its purpose. And who is it who benefits from all of this that the world has to offer? Who stands at the center of it all, gathering in every benefit? It is I. It is us, human beings. And so now I think: how astonishing! Allah did all of this for me. He designed this entire machinery, He assembled this solar system, for me, so that I might benefit from it. Why would He do such a thing? He must truly love me. He must truly care for me. He must be genuinely concerned for my well-being. And I think: how perfect He is! He is so powerful, and yet so merciful toward me. And more than that: I see that He is exceedingly merciful, and unceasingly merciful. For I know that all of this will exist tomorrow as well. I know that the sun will rise again, that the moon will come out again, that the earth will still provide sustenance. How overwhelming this is. I can depend on Him completely. I can trust Him. I can rest my whole weight upon Him. And that is the definition of what word? Ilah. He is my Ilah.

Then I begin to reflect upon His mercy, and I ask myself: does He actually need to be merciful? Does a sovereign and powerful king, with absolutely no fear of retribution, no fear of accountability, no one to answer to — does He really need to be merciful? For Allah is accountable to no one. He needs nothing. Everything and everyone needs Him.

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ أَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱللَّهُ هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ

O people, you are all in complete need of Allah, and Allah is entirely self-sufficient, without need of you.

إِن يَشَأْ يُذْهِبْكُمْ وَيَأْتِ بِخَلْقٍۢ جَدِيدٍۢ

If He so wills, He can remove all of you and bring in your place a new creation.

So I ask myself: what if, instead of mercy, He had characterized Himself with power and justice? For that would mean that the moment I do something wrong, the All-Powerful would decree His justice against me. He would punish me at once. For that is the rule of this world, is it not? If I am caught stealing, the officer will not say, "Oh, it is all right, I know you really wanted that Xbox, it is fine, only do not do it again." No. My parents will not do that for me, will they? I would be punished immediately.

So when I miss a prayer, I would expect angels to descend from the sky and beat me to a pulp. For prayer is Allah's right over me, and He has every right to demand that right of me and to punish me if I do not fulfill it. Can He do that? Can He compel me to fulfill His rights, whether I want to or not? We all pay taxes every year, so we know what that feels like. We cannot escape a government; do you suppose we could escape Allah? What if Allah, being my creator, imposed a property tax upon me? He would be entirely justified in it. He would not be wrong to do so. After all, He is my creator, and that makes me His property. So He may do with me whatever He pleases. Does He do that? What if my sustenance and my daily ration of food, water, sleep, even oxygen — what if all of this were granted to me according to my level of obedience to Him? Does He have the power to do that? He surely does.

مَّا مِن دَآبَّةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ آخِذٌۢ بِنَاصِيَتِهَآ

There is not a single moving creature that Allah does not hold by its forelock.

When we begin to think in this way, we begin to develop a very special kind of appreciation for our maker. What an amazing creator!

What a loving creator. What a caring creator. What a merciful creator. His love, His care, His mercy are beyond this world. They are so intense, and so vast, that I have no way of measuring them. So now, when I realize all of this, what is my natural response? What is the most natural response, as a decent human being, as even a barely decent human being — what should my response be to the One who shows me this kind of extreme love? I want to love Him back, passionately. I begin to think about Him constantly. I become obsessed with love for Him. Do I not? Because if I want to be among the Ulul-Albab, that is the very quality He described: ٱلَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ ٱللَّهَ قِيَمًۭا وَقُعُودًۭا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ وَيَتَفَكَّرُونَ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ Those who think about Allah constantly and reflect constantly on His creation. They are obsessed with Allah. They are passionately in love with Allah. Are they not? Now wait — that is the definition of what word again? Ilah.

So now I feel a sense of obligation, driven by this extreme form of love that is being shown to me. Now I want to do something for the One who loves me so much. I want to make Him happy, because He is my ilah. Notice that I have not yet heard a single word of the revelation. I have not yet heard a single verse of the Qur'an. I am reaching these conclusions simply by observing the creation around me. Do you understand? The Martian is merely studying the iPad and thinking about its designer. He has not yet found that manual which speaks of human beings.

So now I am thinking: this creator loves me so much, and I want to do something in return for Him. But what can I do? What need does He have of me? What could I possibly do in return for the One who has absolutely no need of me? That is another thing. Why is He doing this for me, when He does not even need anything back in return? Because there is nothing I could possibly offer to Allah. He is As-Samad, absolutely self-sufficient. So then why is He being so merciful to me? It must be because: لا یکون من الکریم الا الکرم The generous cannot help but show generosity.

So then, now, what is it that I can do? What could I possibly do for the One who has absolutely no need of me? The only thing I can do is be grateful to Him. That is the only thing I can do in return for everything He has blessed me with — to be grateful to Him. Now I think: how do I show gratitude to Him? How can I express my gratitude to Him? The only way I can express my gratitude to Him is by fulfilling the purpose He created me for. So now, what is my purpose? I mean, I must have a purpose. If everything around me, everything for me, has been created with a particular purpose, to serve me, then I too must have a purpose. Right? Otherwise it simply does not make sense. How is it possible that all these magnificent creations around me have a purpose to serve me, to make life possible for me, to feed me, to clothe me, to give me my sustenance, to give me modes of transportation, to give me riches — how can it be that they all have a purpose, and I do not? So then, what is my purpose?

So now I begin to think about my own existence, and I begin to witness the universe within myself. I see that I have a body, with different parts, internal as well as external. And they too are bound, just like all the other creation outside of me. I can see, but my sight has limits; I cannot see beyond a certain point. I can hear, but my hearing has limits.

I can speak, but only across a certain distance. I can reach out with my hands, but only to a certain limit. I can take a step, but only so far. I am restricted. I am confined. I am bound by design, just like every other creation. I can walk, but I cannot fly. And then I see that some unseen force is controlling my body. I could not be my body, because if I were, I would not be able to control it. The car does not drive itself; it needs a driver. Planes do not fly themselves; they need a pilot. The car cannot decide where to turn, and when to accelerate, and when to brake. It needs the driver to make those decisions for it. So then, who is controlling my body? Who is making decisions for it? What to see, what to hear, what to say, where to go, what to pick up. My body must have an operator. I must have a soul.

Now, here is something remarkable to which I want to draw your attention. When this person was reflecting upon Allah and His creation and had arrived at his various conclusions, what word did he use to call upon his Creator? How did he address his Creator for the very first time? Let us look at the verses again. He begins the work of his reflection:

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ‏ ٱلَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ ٱللَّهَ قِيَمًۭا وَقُعُودًۭا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ وَيَتَفَكَّرُونَ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ

At this point he arrives at his conclusion and finds the purpose, and now he is about to speak with his Creator. Observe what he says:

رَبَّنَا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَذَا بَطِلًۭا

The word he used is Rabb. He did not say اِلٰہُنا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَذَا بَطِلًۭا — "O Ilah, You did not create this in vain." He did not say خالقُنا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَذَا بَطِلًۭا — "O Creator, You did not create this in vain." No. He says رَبَّنَا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَذَا بَطِلًۭا — "O my Rabb, You did not create this in vain." Why did he use the word Rabb? Of all the attributes he saw reflected in the creation, he could have used any attribute, could he not? جلیل, جمیل, کبیر, عظیم, علو. Why did he choose Rabb?

Now, then, let us look at the meaning of the word Rabb, so that we may truly appreciate the course of his thought. In fact, I wish to show you something of the beauty of the Qur'an, this symmetrical beauty of the Qur'an. I hesitated over whether I should share this or not, on account of the constraints of time, but I cannot resist it. I find it simply too wonderful. I want to show you this symmetry between the words Allah and Rabb.

When we look at the very first surah of the Qur'an, which is al-Fatiha, we see that Allah is mentioned twice, and then Rabb is mentioned once after that. We have بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم; Allah is mentioned here. Then after that we have الحمد للہ; Allah is mentioned again. And then we find رب العلمین. So Allah is mentioned twice before the word Rabb is mentioned once, correct? And after that, in the remaining verses, neither Allah nor Rabb is mentioned again. So this is the beginning of the Qur'an.

Now if we go to the end of the Qur'an, to Surah al-Nas, and if we work our way backward, what do we see? What is mentioned in al-Nas — Allah or Rabb? Rabb is mentioned: قل اعوذ برب الناس. You go to the surah before that; what is mentioned, Allah or Rabb? قل اعوذ برب الفلق. Rabb is mentioned again. But now, if you go to the surah before that, Surah al-Ikhlas, what is mentioned, Allah or Rabb? قل ھو اللہ احد. Allah is mentioned.

From the beginning, Allah is mentioned twice and Rabb is mentioned once. From the end, Rabb is mentioned twice and Allah is mentioned once. SubhanAllah! And, moreover, in the last two surahs you see the word Rabb used, but you see no mention of the name Allah. And in Surah al-Ikhlas, you see only the name Allah mentioned, and you do not see the word Rabb mentioned at all. SubhanAllah! Not bad for spoken words, is it?

Very well. Now let us understand this word Rabb. The word Rabb is commonly translated as "Lord." I do not know what that word means. I know of no lord, except the lord of the rings. To the linguists of Arabic, "Lord" is not a good translation of the word Rabb.

Let us first understand the meaning of the word Rabb in classical Arabic, before we try to find a single English word to stand for it. Rabb is an extremely powerful word, used in a great many contexts, and, like the other words we have studied, it is a composite word carrying several linguistic implications. You will remember that when we studied Surah al-Naas, I told you that even though this word is used for Allah, it is not reserved for Him. It can also be used for human beings — for parents, for teachers, for guardians. Do you remember? So the first thing to know is that, in classical Arabic, it is a word used for Allah as well as for human beings.

The linguists define Rabb as: الرَبُّ ھُوَ المَالِکُ وَ السَّیِّد وَ المُرَبِّی وَ المُرْشَدُ وَ المُنعِمُ وَ القَیِّمُ. Allah as Rabb is six things: Malik, Sayyed, Murabbee, Murshad, Munim, and Qayyim. Six things, and He is all of them at once, all at the same time. Now let us look at each of these meanings on its own.

The first meaning is al-Malik, which means owner. One who holds ownership is called Rabb, and the thing he owns is called Milk — not the English milk that cows produce. In Arabic, Milk means property. That is why property is called مِلکِیَّۃ, and the owner of that property is called Maalik.

Now, do we own things? Do we own a phone, an iPad, a computer? We do. So that makes us Rabb as well. Do teachers hold some ownership over their students? Certainly. Do your parents hold ownership over their children? Certainly — despite the way you sometimes feel about it. It is my life, mother. It is my life, father. You cannot tell me what to do. You do not own me. Despite these fine sentiments that we sometimes entertain, whether we like it or not, whether we agree with it or not, our parents hold ownership over us. Your parents hold ownership over you. They do, in fact, own your life. Why? Because this "my life" of which you speak — you would not have it at all, had they chosen not to have you. And however you may feel about it, you owe them a great deal of gratitude for allowing you to have an existence. In that sense, parents too are Rabb, because they hold ownership.

But do parents hold ultimate and absolute ownership? No. For although they gave birth to you, they did not create you. Allah created you. Allah created you and your parents both. So ultimate and absolute ownership belongs to Allah alone. Do you understand? Allah as Rabb is thus the absolute owner of His creation. He is Maalik. And if He is Maalik, what does that make us? It makes us His property. It makes us His مِلکِیَّۃ.

The second meaning is the word Sayyed, and this goes together with the previous meaning of Maalik. Maalik means owner; Sayyed means one who has authority. Sayyed is the one who is in charge. Do you see the difference? Malik is one who has ownership; Sayyed is one who has authority.

When I introduce myself as the Sunday session teacher, what am I telling you? What am I characterizing myself as? What am I saying is WAY more important to me than all my other attributes? My being a teacher, right? Even though Allah is glorious beyond comprehension, magnificent beyond comprehension, powerful beyond comprehension, what He is saying to Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam), and to us THROUGH him, is that when I interact with you, the MOST important thing to me, the way I want you to think of Me, is NOT Jaleel, NOT Azeem, NOT Qawee, NOT Kabeer, NOT Mutakabbir, but what? Rabb.

I just want all of you to take a moment and let this sink in. When a king introduces himself, does he do it in a humble way? Does he say, I'm your neighbor, I'm your father's friend, I'm your caretaker? NO!!!!! He says I AM YOUR KING. KNEEL. BOW DOWN BEFORE ME! Right? And if Allah did that, would it befit Him to do so? ABSOLUTELY! But what does He say instead? RABB. Can you imagine how important this word must be to Him.

That he introduced his most beloved messenger with this name? So today let us see if we can understand this word Rabb. I will show you one more remarkable thing before we study this word. Let us look at the very first ayah that was ever revealed to the messenger of Allah, and the very last ayah that was revealed. The first ayah, we know, is:

ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ

And the very last ayah that was revealed to the messenger of Allah:

ٱلْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِى وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلْإِسْلَمَ دِينًۭا ۚ

On this day I have perfected your religion for you, and I have completed my blessings upon you, and chosen Islam as the way of life for you.

فَمَنِ ٱضْطُرَّ فِى مَخْمَصَةٍ غَيْرَ مُتَجَانِفٍۢ لِّإِثْمٍۢ ۙ

Now here is the final part of the ayah:

فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ

There is no doubt about it: Allah is All-Forgiving and All-Merciful. He begins the revelation with the word Rabb, and ends it with Allah. And also, what are the two attributes with which he begins the Quran? بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم. And with what does he end it? غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ — the constantly forgiving and the constantly loving. He begins with his intense and constant Rehma, and ends with his constant forgiveness and constant Rehma. SubhanAllah!

Is it possible to own something and yet not have complete authority over it? Certainly, it is possible. For example, I own a car. But must I still have it registered? Must I still have it inspected every year? Must I drive within the speed limits? Must I drive it on the road? Can I simply drive it on the sidewalk if I please? No — unless I am in Pakistan. So even though I own my car, I do not have complete authority over it. Do you understand? And this holds true the other way as well. I may have complete authority over something.

I may be able to do whatever I want with it, but I may not have complete ownership of it. Take, for example, the computer in my office. I can do whatever I want with the software installed on it. I can install new things. I can uninstall things. I can change what is already there however I like. Nobody is going to stop me. But do I own that computer? No. My company does. So I can own things and not have complete authority over them, and I can have complete authority and not necessarily own the thing. Do you understand?

But Allah as Rabb has absolute ownership, and He has absolute authority — both at the same time. He can do whatever He wants, whenever He wants, with what belongs to Him. If He wants to burn it, He can burn it. If He wants to tear it apart, He can tear it apart. If He wants to drown it, throw it aside, discard it, He can do so as He pleases. You and I do not get to question Him about it. Why? Because He has complete ownership. He has complete authority. And even if we do complain, guess what? He does not care. It makes no difference to Him. When your parents ground you, when they take away your phone, when they take away your Xbox, you can cry and complain as much as you want; you are not getting it back. Because they are the owner, and you are the owned. And if our crying and grumbling gets us nowhere with our parents, who are limited lords, it certainly will not work with the One who is the absolute Rabb. We are the creation. He is our Creator. He is not the one on trial. We are. That He lets us understand the wisdom of His design, through the Qur'an, is a favor from Him to us. He is not obligated to do anything for us. But He does it anyway. Because that is what the Rabb does.

The third meaning of the word is Murabbee. Now this is a very powerful word. Murabbee means one who ensures growth, one who takes care of something, who nurtures something so that it can grow. A Murabbee is one who is responsible for the growth and development of the one placed in his care. Now, is it possible for me to own something, to have authority over it, and yet not take good care of it? Certainly. I will send you a picture of my backyard. I could own a car, but it is quite possible that I never get it serviced, is it not? We own our bodies, and we have authority over them, but we do not necessarily take good care of them, do we? So we can have ownership, and we can also have authority over a thing, but that does not necessarily mean that we also take good care of it. A Rabb is one who not only owns, who not only has authority; He also takes complete care of it. He ensures its proper growth. He nurtures it. And this process of His taking care of it is called Tarbiyyah.

A poet says: The depth of the ocean nurtures the clear white pearl. So even the ocean is called Rabb, because it helps develop the pearl within its shell. So there are all these different kinds of tarbiyah. Tarbiyyah is all about setting limits, setting boundaries. That is what Tarbiyyah is.

The tarbiyah of a plant would be your taking care of it, watering it at the right time, making sure it gets enough sunlight but not too much, protecting it from insects and bugs. So a whole set of do's and don'ts, until it matures into a tree and begins to bear fruit. Do you understand? If you simply leave the plant to grow by itself, that is not tarbiyyah, because you are not setting any boundaries.

The tarbiyah of a child is taking care of their physical needs.

their diets, their clothing, their mental needs. Educating them. Protecting them. Basically, monitoring their progress, from birth until they mature into a healthy, sound, decent human being. From a physical point of view, from a psychological point of view, and from a social point of view. This is تربیۃ الاولاد. Now, is tarbiyyah an easy process, or is it a VERY long, VERY time-consuming process? It is VERY hard work! In fact, it is THE MOST DIFFICULT process there is. It is a FULL-TIME job. And that is why its appreciation, and the gratitude for it, has been placed by Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) in التحیات, which we recited in EVERY SINGLE Salaah. What do we say in the last sentence? اللھم مغفرلی. Oh Allah, forgive me. و لوالدی. And my parents. والرحمھما کما ربیانی صغیرۃ. And have mercy on them, as they had mercy on me during the period of my tarbiyyah, when I was young. Why is EVERY child being forced to say this in EVERY single prayer? It is a reminder for every child to be grateful, and to honor the rububiyyah of his parents.

Some children today do ALL sorts of nasty things at school with their friends. Just to fit in. Just to appear COOL. Just for some attention. They do things that are completely against the TARBIYYAH of their parents. And then they so proudly plaster it all over the internet for the world to see. You have to understand that when you are out in the world, you are representing the tarbiyyah of your parents. When you and I do nasty things, in the name of whatever, the world does not see YOU behind those actions. They see the RUBUBIYYAH of your parents. You think you are just expressing your freedom. Being honest. Being who you are. But what you do not realize is that you are embarrassing your parents in the process, and tarnishing what their rububiyyah represents. Because that is not what they have TAUGHT you. That is not what they have SLAVED over you for. You are DEFINITELY better than that.

And this is the most natural principle that you will find, no matter where you go in life. You go to college and you do not represent the training, the tarbiyyah, of your high school. What is the first thing your professor will say? Did they not teach you anything in school? Why? Because you are a representative of their training. You start your first job and you cannot represent the skills your CV shows. What will your boss say? Is this what your teachers taught you in school? What school did you go to? The second anyone messes up, immediately their Rabb is questioned. You act crazy in life, and the world will point fingers at your PARENTS' rububiyyah, not at you! Is that justice? Is that fair? Is that not Zulm? What did we learn about unjust people? Where do they end up? And after EVERYTHING they have done for you ALL YOUR LIFE, the VERY LEAST you can do is not dishonor their Rububiyyah.

You know, a tree is called a Rabb for the fruits it bears. The fruit represents the tree. In ancient Arabia — in fact, even today in agricultural places like Pakistan — you go to one of these farms, and people will tell you: Do not pick from that tree. Stay away from that tree. It has the most horrible fruit. Pick fruit from THAT tree. THAT tree bears the sweetest fruit. The fruit represents the tree. It honors the tree by being sweet. YOU are the fruits of your parents. You REALLY need to think about that. We all do.

We need to conduct ourselves in ways that honor the tarbiyyah our parents gave us before the world, and never disgrace them, not after everything they did for us. This applies to you as children, it applies to us as adults, and it applies to us as Muslims, for Islam itself is tarbiyyah. Why do you think Islam holds such a wretched standing in the world today? Because we, as Muslims, have disgraced it. We have dishonored the tarbiyyah of the ultimate Rabb. For we represent Islam, whether we wish to or not. People look at us and judge Islam, just as people look at you and judge your parents. This, truly, is something all of us need to consider.

So Rububiyyah, or the Murabbee, is the one who is responsible for the maturing and the growth of someone or something. And how does the Rabb discharge his responsibilities? With Rehma. Rehma is the primary component of Rububiyyah. If there is no rehma, then there is no rububiyyah. And what does the word Rehma mean? Love, care, concern, and mercy — remember? That is what rububiyyah is made of.

Have you ever seen people who tend to plants very gently, with a great deal of tender, loving care? They will spray each single leaf with water and then clean it gently. That love, that care, that gentleness — that is the true image of Rububiyyah. It is not harshness. It is not beating. It is not psychological, emotional, and physical abuse. It is not guilt-tripping someone into submission. It is love, it is patience, it is kindness. That is the Islamic way of Rububiyyah. The Islamic way of Rububiyyah has always been Rehma.

Our Prophet (salawaat) took the most vicious of people, he took the most barbaric of people, and without a single slap, without a single taunt, without a single sarcastic remark, without a single insult, he turned them all into رضی اللہ عنہ, the greatest title possible for a human being: رضی اللہ عنہ. We do not mention the names of these sahaba without saying RA. Our Prophet accomplished that. How? With love, with gentleness, with kindness, forgiveness, open arms, patience, Akhlaaq. That is Rububiyyah.

So these are the two sides of the coin. Rububiyyah must come with Rehma. And then the Marboob, the child, must show gratitude for that Rububiyyah by honoring its Rabb, just as the fruit honors its tree by being sweet. So from now on, every time we recite the Tahayyat and we reach the sentence اللھم مغفرلی ولوالدی ورحمھما کما ربیانی صغیرا, let it be a reminder to us as parents that Rehma should be the primary component of our Rububiyyah, especially when we discipline our children. And for you children, let it remind you that you have to honor that rububiyyah, that you have to make your parents proud by displaying and reflecting their tarbiyyah to the world around you.

Both will make mistakes, and that is all right. You will fail at times, and your parents will fail at times. This religion does not demand perfection. All it demands is sincerity and effort. That is all. And this is why that sentence contains اللھم مغفرلی ولوالدی. Oh Allah, forgive me, and forgive my parents. Forgive what? Forgive me for the mistakes I make, for my shortcoming in reflecting the tarbiyyah of my parents; and forgive my parents for their weakness in not being able to live up to your name of Rabb. Forgive them for the mistakes they make in their tarbiyyah, because I know they are doing the very best they can. And forgive me for the mistakes I make in not being able to reflect their tarbiyyah.

I hope no one takes offense at what I am saying. I am only explaining what this word means, as the scholars have explained it. I will be the first to admit that, when it comes to the inability and the injustice of failing to reflect the tarbiyyah of my parents and my spiritual teachers, I find myself to be the worst — both as a child and as a parent. May Allah forgive me and grant me the ability to fulfill the requirements of this trust of Rububiyyah with which He has honored me.

So this is what we have learned so far: that Allah, as Rabb, has complete ownership. He has absolute authority. And He takes care of all of His creation with rehma — with love, care, concern, and mercy.

Now, at this point, you may wonder: if that is the case, then why is there so much misery in the world? If Allah is such a loving and caring Murabbee, why are people in such terrible conditions? We will speak about that, God willing, when we study Malik Yaum al-Deen. There are always rules, and then there are exceptions to the rules. What we are looking at today is the rule. We will speak about the exception later.

But let me give you something to think about, and I hope this example will help you understand. Suppose you hear about a truly amazing teacher. Everyone who graduated from his class tells you, "You have to get into his class. He is so wonderful." You keep hearing this from many people — how amazingly wonderful this teacher is — and you are intrigued. But then you also notice that a number of students fail his class every year.
