At that time the man becomes a rabb of his own body. The body complains on the Day of Judgment. When that is complete, he becomes the rabb of the next generation.

When mature, children become rabb of the body.

Barkah is because of Reham — sperm to baby.

All six meanings of rabb are manifested by Reham.

Now, how are we to understand this relationship? Our Rabb is in the unseen dimension, and we are in the seen dimension. There is no way for us to see him or to hear him directly. So how do we, as human beings, as creation, understand that he is in fact our Rabb? What is the proof, or the evidence, of his being Rabb within my own personal life? I can understand that he is the Rabb of the rest of the creation, in the skies and the earth. But how do I, on a very personal level, appreciate him as Rabb? How is he a Rabb to me? That is the question.

In order to enable us to answer this question, what he did, by design, was to surround us with Arbaab. Arbaab is the plural of Rabb. Rabb is singular; multiple Rabb are Arbaab. He created us from weakness, and we increase toward strength. He created us in ignorance, and we progress toward knowledge. There is a constant progression that we see in the design of this universe. Nothing simply comes into existence in its final stage. It grows, it evolves, until it reaches its final stage.

So what Allah as Rabb did was to design everything around us as rabb, as breadcrumbs, so that we could follow those breadcrumbs to reach the ultimate Rabb. Do you understand? Look at life. When we set a final goal — let us say you decide that you want to become a doctor — that is the goal you set for your academic endeavors. How do you reach that goal? You have to set up similar short-term academic goals, is it not so? You first have to pass middle school, then high school, then get into a medical school, and then complete all those years of training, and then the internship, and then at last you reach the end of the ultimate academic goal that you had set, and you become a doctor. Right? So you had to break down your final academic goal into smaller academic goals.

I will give you another example. You want to get stronger, so you take up body building. You start lifting weights. Your goal is to bench press 300 pounds. Right now you are barely able to push 20. So what do you do? You keep working at it, constantly increasing the resistance, using heavier weights. And you keep slowly building up your strength until one day you are able to bench press 300 pounds. Right?

Allah created this same design for us so that we would be able to reach him. He is the ultimate Rabb, and he wanted us to get to him. So what did he do? He surrounded us with intermediaries. He starts us with the first rabb, and then moves us to the next rabb, and then to the next, until we conclude what? That Allah is my ultimate Rabb. Do you understand?

body.text_en:
There is a progression in Rububiyyah that he created for us: Ibrahim and the star, the moon, the sun, and then Allah. It was Allah who brought us into this world, but in the seen world, in the visible sense, we were brought into this world by our parents. Allah provides all of our food, but in the physical sense, whom did Allah make the means of providing us with food? Our parents. Allah protects us, but in the physical sense, to whom has he given that responsibility? To our parents. God clothes us, but in the physical sense our parents clothe us. God teaches us: علم الانسان مالم يعلم — he taught the human being what he did not know; علمہ البیان — he taught the human being how to speak. Yet technically, who teaches us how to speak? Our parents.

In other words, much of what God did for us, he did for us through our parents. Parents are themselves gifts of God. They are doing the work of God, the work that he wants done for us. He did not directly teach me how to speak; he did that through my parents. He did not directly give me clothes; he gave me clothes through my parents. He did not directly feed me; he fed me through my parents. Do you understand this point? What this means is that my parents are in fact the ambassadors of God in raising me. They are God's ambassadors. They represent him. They represent his work. Everything that I have received from Allah, I have received through them.

The entire life that we live in this world is depicted in the womb of a mother: الدنیا رحم الاخرۃ

body.text_en:
Intro. What is love? A benefit, from *Hubb*, the seed. Let me explain gratitude to you. In classical Arabic, the word for gratitude is شکر. Even in Urdu you say شکریہ, and in Arabic you say شُکراً. So the tri-literal root of these words is شکر. You can see that the three letters are joined; there is no gap between any of them. The first letter, *sheen*, stands for the gratitude of the heart or the mind, which is the recognition of the benefit. The second letter stands for the tongue praising, or eulogizing, the benefactor. And the third letter is the fulfilling of the purpose of the benefit. So gratitude, or شکر, involves the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. The heart recognizes the benefit, the tongue praises the benefactor, and the limbs busy themselves with acquiring the benefit as the benefactor intended.

You insert yourself into the benefit. You begin to use it for your own advantage, in ways not intended for us, and you get شرک — the same letters, in a different sequence. SubhanAllah! You start using the benefit in ways that are not intended. For example, Allah gave me a tongue to articulate my emotions and, ultimately, to praise him. But instead I use it to hurt people. I use it to sing foolish songs. I use it to gossip, to backbite, to slander. In other words, I corrupt its purpose. And now what happens? It is no longer gratitude; it is ingratitude. That is why, when I change the sequence of the letters in شکر, what do I get? I get شرک.

And *shukar* rests on five foundations:
1. humility toward the benefactor
2. love for him
3. acknowledgment of the benefit
4. praising the benefactor
5. not using the gift in a manner the benefactor dislikes.

And what that produces is کَشْرٌ. The same three letters? It means the act of uncovering, or exposing to view, that which was hidden, which is the blessings of Allah that result from *Shukr*.

شَکَر is when a camel's udder fills with milk to the point that it looks as though it will burst. That is شَکَر. And when the baby camel sucks the milk out of such a full udder, that process is called شَکِرَۃ — to benefit completely from the abundant blessings of Allah. And what happens when the baby drinks the milk? It becomes strong.

The word begins with the letter *sheen*, which is for شئی. And I have just told you that شئی is the manifestation of the will. شئی comes from مشیئا. All right? So in this example, Khala's مشیئا, her will, was love, and what came out of it, the شئی, is the meal, which is a manifestation of her love. Does that make sense? That is *sheen*. How many letters come after it? *Kaaf* and *Ra*. I will not go into the linguistics of it, because it will grow too complicated and overwhelming, and I will lose the focus of today's session.

The idea of saying "Thank you," of verbalizing the words "Thank you," falls under the category of praise, not gratitude.

Grammatical Analysis. Today we are going to do a linguistic analysis of the words الحمد للہ. There is a twofold purpose to this. The first is that through this analysis we will come to understand the true meaning of *Hamd* from the Quranic perspective. Because gratitude is a very subjective word. We can each have our own definitions of the word *Hamd* in our heads. What does Alhamdulillah mean? Praise belongs to Allah. Gratitude belongs to Allah. Thank you, Allah. You are wonderful, Allah. So there are various mental images of الحمد للہ. And so it becomes important that we understand the one definition that actually counts.

The only definition that matters is the one the Qur'an holds to be *Hamd*. My second purpose is to show you the perfection in the very use of this word, الحمد للہ, and I want all of us to understand why no other words could have stood in its place. As I said earlier, in Arabic the word *Hamd* is a composite of two words. The first is المدح, which means praise. The second is الشکر, which means thanks, or gratitude. Why, then, did Allah not say المدح والشکر للہ رب العلمین, praise and gratitude belong to Allah?

Let us begin by understanding the difference between the two words. You are walking down the street and you see a beautiful car. What do you do? Do you thank it, or do you praise it? Let us hope you do not thank it. Let us hope you do not walk up to the car, pat it on the hood, and say, thank you so much, BMW. The natural thing to do would be to praise it. It is a beautiful car. You praise it. If you go to the house of someone who has just had a baby, do you thank the baby, or do you praise the baby? You praise it. Oh, what a cute baby! Such a beautiful baby. You do not thank a baby.

Thanks is something entirely different. Thanks is offered only when someone does something for you. If somebody lends you money, you say *shukran*. If somebody gives you something, if somebody donates to your cause, when somebody helps you in your effort, when somebody shows you a kindness—in other words, when somebody does something for you—you say thank you. And if you do not say it, you show the person your thanks, because *shukr* can also be shown. It does not always have to be spoken. That is why Allah says, ٱعْمَلُوٓا۟ آلَ دَاوُۥدَ شُكْرًۭا: show me through your actions that you are grateful. So *shukr*, or gratitude, must be in return for something, for a kindness or a benefit done for you. Whereas when you see something impressive, when you see something beautiful, when you see something that intrigues you and interests you, you will praise it.

Understand this distinction as well: someone you thank is not necessarily someone you praise. In conversation these two are generally used together. I can say, thank you so much for doing this for me, you are so amazing. In that case I have thanked and praised together. But it is also possible for me to thank someone without praising them. Let us consider that for a moment. How do you thank someone without actually praising them? Let us look at an example or two from the Qur'an.

In Arabic, when you alter the sequence, do you know what that means? So instead of saying "I ate lunch," if I said "Lunch I ate," what I am actually saying is that I did not eat anything else — I ate only lunch. But the ancient Arabs did not have to use the word "only." They would simply change the order of the words, and the clause of exclusivity would apply automatically; it would automatically convey the word "only." If I say, "They went to school," it is normal. But if I say, "To school they went,"

In the Arabic sense — that means they only went to school and nowhere else. They did not go to the movie theater. They did not go shopping. They did not go to work. They only went to school. Nowhere else. Do you understand? So it adds the word "only" to the meaning, when you change the sequence of the words.

Imagine you are teaching a class, and two students are talking in the back — Zainab and Fatima. And I can tell you one thing about girls, because I have one of them: boy, can they talk! So the teacher is teaching and these girls are chattering away in the back. And the teacher says, "Zainab!" And she says, "I wasn't the only one." Now, when she says, "I wasn't the only one," what is she actually saying? If I am going to the principal's office, Fatima had better come with me! But she did not have to use that second sentence. She just used one word strategically: "only." So if you use the word "only" strategically, you can actually be saying two things by saying just one thing. That is the wonderful thing about saying the word "only."

So if I say, "You are not the only people I am teaching," I did not say more, but you get the message: there must be others I am teaching as well.

Now Allah sometimes says فَلِلَّهِ ٱلْحَمْدُ — praise belongs only to Allah. Fill in the rest. What is implied? Praise belongs only to Allah, and to no one else! It does not belong to anyone else. Full stop. When you say "only," you are saying that praise belongs only to Allah and to nobody else.

In Surah al-Jathiyah, in the second-to-last verse, Allah says: فَلِلَّهِ ٱلْحَمْدُ رَبِّ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَرَبِّ ٱلْأَرْضِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ. And in this entire surah, Allah is addressing the mushrikeen — the people who commit shirk, who praise and are grateful to other than Allah. So Allah reverses the sequence of the words and says: Listen! Praise belongs only to Allah and to nobody else!

But when you and I speak, we do not say وللہ الحمد. We simply say الحمد للہ, because we do not have that confusion. We do not have that confusion. We do not speak to a Muslim and say, "Listen! Praise belongs only to Allah!" No. We simply say al-Hamdulillah, because the person already knows that praise belongs only to Allah. So there is no need for a debate, no need to use that tone.

وللہ الحمد is the tone of a debate. It is the tone of an argument. It is the tone of anger. When Allah introduced Himself to us with Surah al-Fatiha, He did not want to make it a debate. He did not want to make it an argument. He did not want to yell at us. He spoke to us in a tone that indicates that al-Hamdulillah — all praise belongs to Allah — is not a debate. It is not an argument. It is something you already know in your hearts. So there is no reason for me to say lillahil-Hamd.

So what did Allah say instead? Al-Hamdulillah. And do you know what that is teaching us? That al-Hamdulillah is already in my heart. The disbeliever lost it. The polytheist lost it. He had to be given it again. He had to be reasoned with. He had to be debated with. He had to be convinced of this. That is why he had to be told: فَلِلَّهِ ٱلْحَمْدُ.

So you see, every phrase in the Qur'an, starting with al-Hamdulillah, is so perfect in the way Allah says it that no matter what variation you try to come up with — you try to use a verb, you use inna, you try to change it into a command, you use alternate words like shukr and madh — you do not get what Allah actually communicated. You do not get what Allah Himself said. And the perfection of what He said is lost.

SubhanAllah! Allah has at least ninety-nine names. Allah did not say الحمد للمالک، الحمد للقھار، الحمد للوھاب، الحمد للغفور. All of those would have been correct. All of those are correct; none of them are wrong. The Fateha is Allah introducing Himself to us, and when you introduce someone, you use his name. الحمد لی رب العلمین — praise belongs to the Lord of the worlds. But could it be that others hold a different idea of the Lord of the worlds? "Praise the lord" could mean something else to a Christian. It could mean something else to a Jew. But "Praise Allah, the Lord of the worlds" leaves no room for confusion.

This actually happened. Which prophet was set to face off against magicians? Musa, peace be upon him. Musa, peace be upon him, faces off against the magicians. They throw their ropes and their rods; he throws his staff, and it swallows everything they came up with. What happens to the magicians? What do they do? They fell into prostration. Firawn is standing on the stage, and the magicians are in prostration, and he is confused. What is going on? Are you getting ready for round two? Or is this part of the act? What is going on? So the magicians stand up from prostration, and they say قَالُوٓا۟ آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ — we believe in the Master of the worlds. Firawn is still confused. Why? Why is he confused? Because what had Firawn declared? أنا ربکم الاعلی — I am your greatest master. He had declared himself to be the Lord, and the magicians are saying قَالُوٓا۟ آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ — we believe in the Master of the worlds. So Firawn is confused, because he believes he is the Lord they are prostrating to. He is thinking, "And? Go on?" And they say, "No, you fool! رَبِّ مُوسَىٰ وَهَرُونَ — the Lord of Musa and Harun, the Master of Musa and Harun." They had to make it clear, because if they had simply said "the Lord of the worlds," he would have had no problem with that. Do you understand? So the word Allah is critical.

But there is something else too, and it is so beautiful. When I look at a painting and I say that it is beautiful, what am I praising the painter for? His art. I am praising one particular skill of his. When I thank a teacher, what do I thank him for? For teaching me something. Thanks is specific; it is for a particular favor that was done for me. Praise is also specific. You praise the beauty of a flower because it is beautiful. You praise the freshness of the air because of how it makes you feel. So if we said الحمد للخالق — praise belongs to the Creator — then the only thing we are thanking Allah for is creating. If we say الحمد للحکیم — praise and thanks belong to the Wise — then the only thing we are appreciating about Allah is His wisdom. How do I appreciate every single thing about Allah without missing anything? The things I can think of, and the things I cannot even think of — how do I include everything in one concise statement, so that I truly get to thank Allah in the way He truly deserves to be thanked when praising Him?

What did we study about the name Allah? When we say Allah, what does it combine? It combines all of His attributes. So when I say الحمد للہ, I am praising Him and I am grateful to Him for every single attribute that He possesses. That is only possible through the use of the word Allah.

Now, this exercise I did with you, this exhaustive exercise of just exploring what Alhamdulillah is, and what the alternatives are, and how the alternatives are not good enough — can you imagine? This exercise exists for the entire Quran.

word by word by word. And it gives you an appreciation of the power of the Quran like nothing else. To understand the Fatiha is to open the doors to the rest of the Quran. Why? Because that is precisely what Fatiha means: an opening. When we underestimate the power of al-Fatiha, we will naturally underestimate the power of the rest of the Quran. When we begin to appreciate the beauty and the depth of the Fatiha, it will make us want to explore the rest of the Quran. That is why Fatiha means the "opening," or the "opener." The more you reflect upon it, the more it opens the rest of the doors; and if you do not reflect upon it, the door remains closed. That is what we are trying to do today. That is why the Fatiha.

You know that Moosa, peace be upon him, was raised in a rather interesting home. Where was he raised? What was his address? He had, in fact, a rather famous address. He was adopted and raised by Firon. Years later, when Moosa, peace be upon him, returned to him and delivered to him the message of Allah, Firon in effect said: how dare you? How dare you speak to me this way? قَالَ أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًۭا . وَلَبِثْتَ فِينَا مِنْ عُمُرِكَ سِنِينَ. Did we not raise you as a newborn in this house? Did you not spend many years of your life here? How dare you speak to me like that? In other words, what is Firon saying? Are you not grateful? And then Moosa responds: وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌۭ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَىَّ. That is the favor you did in fact do for me. Thanks. That is the way Moosa, peace be upon him, expresses his gratitude. So even though Firon is a man who will never be praised—the man will never be praised, and certainly not by a prophet—when he does a favor, he will still be what? Thanked.

Thanks can exist without praise. The Qur'an speaks of the rights of parents, and Allah says concerning parents:

أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَلِوَلِدَيْكَ إِلَىَّ ٱلْمَصِيرُ

Be grateful to Me and to both of your parents!

وَإِن جَهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُشْرِكَ بِى مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلْمٌۭ

If your parents strive against you, if they are the ones telling you to disbelieve, to commit shirk, do not obey them. But you still have to be what? The verse began by saying it: you still have to be grateful to them. In other words, if your parents are committing shirk, will you praise them? No, you will not praise them. But you still have to be what? You still have to be grateful to them.

Consider Abraham, peace be upon him. He does not praise what his father does, and yet he is still thankful to him, is he not?

So the first thing I want you to understand is that the words الشکر و المدح, gratitude and praise, are two different things, and they are mutually exclusive. Sometimes you can have praise without thanks. And there are other times when you can be grateful to someone but not praise them. But the word حمد necessarily means both things together. When Allah says الحمد للہ, He is saying that praise is for Allah, and He is also saying that gratitude is for Allah. He is not saying merely one or the other. He is saying that they both exist together.

مدح

Now, what if the verse read المدح للہ رب العالمین, all praise is for Allah? What would be the problem with that? The problem is that المدح is praise that is not always genuine. Praise can be insincere. Let us say you come home with a very bad report card. You walk in, and the moment you enter the house you say, "Mother, your cooking smells so delicious"—and she has not even begun cooking yet. So you are praising her, but it is not genuine. Do you see? Praise can be false. There is false praise offered to kings, to bosses, to judges. It is done all the time. People praise physical appearances: "You look so beautiful." That is a false praise, because you are not worthy of that praise—you did not make yourself look beautiful. Allah made you look beautiful by giving you these features. That is why, in Arabic, when you praise someone's appearance, you do not say Hamida. You would say Madaha, because it is a false praise. Consider, even so, the time and energy some women put into makeup. There is a woman in my office who wears a great deal of makeup, so much powder that I always imagine that if I went over and struck her, a cloud of powder would rise all around her.

So Madah can be false praise; it can be insincere praise. But Hamd cannot be a false praise; it cannot be insincere. Why? Because Hamd is generated in the heart by the awareness of the magnificence and the glory of the one being praised. I will say that again. Hamd—the praise element of hamd—occurs when the heart becomes aware of the magnificence and the glory of the one being praised. It is done because of the knowledge one acquires about the glory, the brilliance, the greatness of the one being praised. It can therefore never be false. Once I gain the knowledge of gravity and experience it, I can never afterward lie about gravity, because I have now witnessed it as a fact, and so I have no choice but to declare it. It is the realization that if I say gravity does not exist, this does not affect the law of gravity in any way, shape, or form.

Gravity will still exist. Only I will be hurt by ignoring and rejecting its principles. Therefore my statement about gravity can now never be false.

It is the same with praise, with hamd, offered to Allah. He is worthy of praise through the knowledge of who He is, made known in His ninety-nine attributes. He is worthy of praise not because you and I praise Him. He is worthy of praise even if there is absolutely no one praising Him. He does not depend on our praise. We depend on praising Him. He has no need of our praise. He has no need of our hamd. It is we who have the need to praise Him. The more knowledge we gain about Him, about His being, about His ninety-nine attributes, the more we are compelled to turn to Him in hamd. He has no need whatsoever of our hamd.

When you praise someone and do not truly mean it — when, for example, you praise in order to gain something in return — that is madah. Hamd means: O Allah, You are worthy of every last and ultimate praise because of who You are. Not because of what You have given me. Even if You had given me nothing. Even if I did not exist, You would still be worthy of praise. You would be worthy of my hamd. Not because of what You have done for me, but because of who You are.

Sometimes praise is offered merely to impress someone, though you do not necessarily mean it. Suppose I go to a job interview and it goes terribly. It is the worst interview I have ever had. I thoroughly dislike the men who interviewed me. Yet even so, as I am leaving, I say: it was nice meeting you. It was not nice meeting him, but I say it all the same. It is false praise, do you understand? So when the word مدح is used, it may be false; it carries the possibility of being insincere, and that very quality makes it unfit for Allah. But hamd cannot be insincere. Linguistically, the word hamd can be used only for genuine praise.

Now let us consider شکر. If Allah had said الشکر للہ رب العلمین, which means that thanks, or gratitude, is for Allah, what would be the problem with that? Thanks is offered only when you are acknowledging a favor. Something was done for you, and you recognize and appreciate that something was done for you, and then at last you thank the one who did the favor. You had a flat tire. Someone came and helped you. You say thank you. Thanks can arise only when you have a reason to give thanks. In other words, gratitude is a reaction. Is that clear to everyone? Thank you is always a reaction. Thank you is never something you begin with. Ever. You do not meet someone simply passing by and say, hey, you, thanks. You never do that.

When Allah uses the word hamd, linguistically this word joins together both praise and thanks, under certain rules. And the rules are these: that the praise must be genuine, that it can never be false, that it cannot be manufactured; and, second, that the gratitude is not reactionary. Therefore, linguistically, to say الحمد للہ is more powerful than to say المدح للہ, and it is more powerful than to say الشکر للہ. It is more comprehensive than either of them. Allah chose to say something that is better than both of them combined. Subhan Allah.

Now here is another thing. In English, so far, how many words have I had to use to render the single word hamd? I had to use two. I had to use gratitude, and I had to use praise. But how many words did Allah use? One. So here we are learning of a difficulty that arises the moment we begin to translate the Qur'an. Allah uses a single word, but to convey the idea we need several.

But what if Allah himself had used both words? What if Allah had said المدح و الشکر للہ رب العلمین — praise and gratitude belong to Allah? Had he done so, would it have been the same? In truth, no. It would not have been the same, and this is because of a beautiful principle of the Arabic language — indeed, a principle of all languages. In Arabic they say: خیر الکلام ما قل و دل, which means that the best kind of speech is the speech that uses very few words yet still conveys its meaning completely. To use fewer words and still make your point — that is eloquence. Now, some of us, mashaAllah, have friends who will speak to us for thirty minutes and still have not made a single point. They say a great deal, but they do not actually say anything, and you keep hoping they will reach the point at last, perhaps before Christmas. Some people use far too many words even to describe the simplest of things. The best kind of speech is the speech that is brief, that is easier on the tongue, and that conveys its meaning. So hamd, from the standpoint of eloquence, is better than saying المدح و الشکر للہ.

There is another reason for not saying المدح و الشکر للہ رب العلمین. In classical Arabic, when you place the word AND between two things — which is the letter و — it separates the two words even in their meaning. When I say المدح و الشکر للہ, what I am saying, linguistically, is that praise belongs to Allah for some things and gratitude belongs to Allah for other things. They are not always joined together, because the words themselves are not joined together. This is a remarkable feature of the Arabic language: you do not say what you do not mean. So if we take the two words gratitude and praise and join them with an AND, in classical Arabic that means that sometimes I am in the mood to praise him but not to thank him, and at other times I am in the mood to thank him but not to praise him. But when Allah says AlHamdulillah, it means that for every act he performs and every blessing he gives, genuine praise and unconditional gratitude belong to Allah, both at the very same time. You do not get to pick and choose between the two.

So now, if you own a fine car and you say AlHamdulillah, what have you just done? You have genuinely praised Allah for giving human beings the ability to create cars, to design them, and to manufacture them, and you have thanked Allah for allowing you to own one. So you are praising and thanking Allah both at the same time. All of this is captured in this beautiful word, hamd. And this is why AlHamdulillah is the attitude of a true Muslim, for AlHamdulillah is optimistic in its very nature. You know how it is: sometimes you are going through a difficult time, and someone comes and asks you how you are doing, and you simply say, "Oh, you know, life is miserable, but AlHamdulillah." You are not really praising him or thanking him when you say it that way. AlHamdulillah is not something we merely say or throw around. It is a reminder of an attitude. Allah is not interested in what comes out of our tongues; he is more interested in what comes out of our tongues that is also connected to our hearts. So we must mean what we say when we say AlHamdulillah. If I am going through a difficult time and someone asks me how it is going — AlHamdulillah! I am grateful to Allah, because whatever I am going through, it could always have been worse.

Someone in the world right now is going through a much harsher version of what I am going through. I am grateful to Allah that He is lenient with me. And so, AlHamdulillah. I praise Him, because it is only He who can and will bring me out of my situation. A sincere AlHamdulillah is therefore an attitude of hope toward Allah. This may seem somewhat contradictory at the moment, but, InshaAllah, it will become much clearer when we speak about trials and tribulations, and whether they are a curse or a blessing.

Now let us look at this phrase, الحمد للہ, grammatically. In the Arabic language you may use nouns and you may use verbs. Between nouns and verbs, which of them has tenses? You know the present tense, the future tense, the past tense. A verb has a tense. A noun does not have a tense. There is no past-tense noun, no present-tense noun, and no future-tense noun, is there? Now, when I say, "I praise Allah," did I use a noun or a verb? I used a verb. And what tense is it? It is the present tense. But when I say, "Praise belongs to Allah," is the word "praise" a noun or a verb? It is now a noun.

Allah could have used a verb. He could have said احمدُ اللہ, "I praise Allah." He could have said نحمد اللہ, "We praise Allah." But Allah did not use a verb. He used a noun. Why?

Here is what makes this so beautiful. When I use a verb, there is obviously going to be a tense attached to it, and when I use the present tense to say, "I praise Allah," then I am speaking only about the present. I have said nothing about the past, and I have said nothing about the future. If I use the past tense, then I am guaranteeing nothing about the future or the present, because a tense has to be one or the other. A verb is limited. It is temporary. But Allah used a noun. And nouns are what? They are permanent. Allah's genuine praise and unconditional gratitude are described with permanence. Do you know what that means? It means that I may be praising Allah now, but the praise of Allah has always been there. And I am not going to be in this world forever, yet the praise and gratitude of Allah will always remain, forever. His praise and gratitude do not depend on me. A tremendous reality within AlHamdulillah is that the praise and gratitude of Allah are permanent, and they do not depend on me. They are not because of me.

You see, when we use a verb, someone has to do the verb. That someone is called the subject, or the فاعل in Arabic. There has to be a doer. You cannot simply enter a conversation and say, "Failed the test!" Who failed the test? You cannot simply say, "Disappeared!" What disappeared? Oh, my book disappeared. You see? When you use a verb, you need someone to do it. You need a subject. You cannot have a verb standing all by itself. It does not make sense. It creates confusion.

But a noun does not need anyone to do it. A noun does not need a subject. A noun is independent on its own. An apple is an apple; it can exist all by itself, independent of any doer. So when Allah used the word AlHamd, He made it a noun. He made it independent. He does not need anyone to perform the actual praise, and He does not need anyone to be grateful. Had He used a verb, that would have meant that He needed someone to praise Him, and that He needed someone to be grateful to Him.

Even if Allah had said that everything and everyone praises and is grateful to Allah, that too would have been limited. Why? Because "everything and everyone" implies everyone and everything that exists now.

in the present. It leaves out everything and everyone in the past, and everything and everyone in the future. That is why Allah used a noun for His praise and gratitude. He used the word Hamd as a noun, so that it would not be confined to time and place. For Allah does not need His creation to praise Him and be grateful to Him. Even if there were not a single creature in this world, the Hamd of Allah would still be there. His praise and gratitude require no doer. SubhanAllah! All of this is captured in a single word.

Now, what if Allah had said أِحمد اللہ رب العلمین? What if He had used a command: praise Allah, the Master of the Alameen? Would that not have been better? After all, He is the Master, so a command would make sense. So why did He not make it a command? Let me give you an example to help you understand. I tell my daughter Erum to bring me a glass of water. I say, "Erum, bring me a glass of water!" I am giving her a command. Once she hears me, she has two possible choices. She can either bring me the glass of water, or she can bring me the glass of water. Those are the only two clear choices as far as she is concerned.

Now, if Allah had said to praise Him as a command, what are the two things that could happen? Some would praise Him. Some would obey His command. And then there would be others who would disobey Him. When you tell someone to do something, the matter is now in their hands. It depends on them. Perhaps they will choose to do it. Perhaps they will not. Allah did not speak of praise and gratitude in a way that depends on us. He did not place the matter in our hands. He said that whether you do it or not, whether you are grateful to Me or not, whether you praise Me or not, My praise and gratitude are always there. My Hamd is still there. It has been there forever, and it will be there forever. Human beings will come and go. Nations will come and go. Generations will come and go. This world will come and go. But the Hamd of Allah will always be there. It is a matter of fact. SubhanAllah!

Now, what if Allah had said انَّا الحمد للہ رب العلمین? Certainly. For sure. Without any doubt. Absolutely, Hamd belongs to Allah. Now, which sounds more powerful? Is "All praise and gratitude belong to Allah" more powerful, or is it more powerful to say, "Definitely, certainly, absolutely, Hamd is for Allah"? Clearly the latter. So how is it that Allah did not say انَّا الحمد للہ رب العلمین? A Khateeb uses it all the time. I myself say it at the beginning of sessions all the time to glorify Allah: انا الحمد للہ نحمدہ و نستعینہ و نستغفر بہ ن. So how is it that Allah did not say it?

If you remember our sessions on the miracle of the Qur'an, on the topic of conversation, I told you that there are two kinds of communication. A communication can either be informative, or it can be emotional. جملۃ انشائیۃ and جملۃ خبریۃ. Either you have speech that expresses your feelings and emotions, or you have speech that conveys information. These are the two kinds of speech that human beings are capable of. That is all. Let us look at an example. Right now, when I am teaching you about Hamd, am I delivering information, or am I expressing my emotions? I am giving you information. This is informative speech. But when I am talking to my friend, and I am telling my friend how I feel about someone or something, what kind of communication is that? That is an emotional conversation. So those are the only two types of speech that we, as human beings, are capable of.

The point is this: in Arabic linguistics, when you use *Inna*, the statement can only be informative. It can only be factual. It can never be emotional. But if you do not use *Inna*, the communication can now be both informative and emotional. By not using *Inna*, Allah made His praise a statement that we can use to speak to others about the praise and gratitude owed to Allah, to give them information about it. But He also made it a statement by which we express our own emotion. SubhanAllah! The beauty of it is that it can now be used to communicate the emotions of our heart, as well as a message we wish to convey to someone else. Right now, by saying الحمد للہ رب العلمین, I am giving you information about the praise of Allah. A few hours later, when I use the same words, الحمد للہ رب العلمین, I will be expressing my own gratitude and praise to Allah. We can now do both.

If *Innal Hamda* had been used, technically it could not have been used to express emotion. It would only have been meant for speaking to someone else. It would remain for the intellect alone, and not for the heart. So Allah said *Alhamdu lillahi rabbil-Alameen*, so that it could serve the heart as well as the intellect. SubhanAllah! And the very same phrase could be used for both emotional and informational conversation.

For example, right now I am telling you about *Alhamdulillah*, and this conversation is informational. Now, as I am speaking, I grow thirsty. I take a sip of water, and then I say *Alhamdulillah!* What was it this time? It was emotional. I actually expressed gratitude and praised Allah. It is the exact same phrase, *Alhamdulillah*. But when I am telling you about it, it is informational; when I am expressing it for myself, it is emotional. So the same phrase, *Alhamdulillah*, can be used as information, and it can also be used as emotion.

I will say two sentences, and you tell me which one sounds normal. "I ate lunch." "Lunch I ate." Which one sounds normal to you? "They went to school." "To school they went." Which one sounds normal? But if I say, "To school they went," do you still understand me? So one is normal and one is strange, yet both are understandable. I am not telling you this to explain how Yoda speaks in *Star Wars* — "Strong the force is!" — or whatever. In the Arabic language, sometimes the order of a sentence is changed, and it is made strange.

Now, in the Qur'an we find a different variation. Allah says: فَلِلَّهِ ٱلْحَمْدُ رَبِّ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَرَبِّ ٱلْأَرْضِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ. He begins the verse with وللہ الحمد, but *al-Fatiha* begins with الحمد للہ. They are the same words, but they have been placed in a different order. So what is the difference between the two? Allah could have said فَلِلَّهِ ٱلْحَمْدُ رَبِّ رب العلمین — "To Allah belongs all praise, who is the Master of the worlds." What is the difference?

The Meaning of Wisdom

We are studying the second verse of the opening, الحمد للہ رب العلمین. We have already examined its words: Allah, Rabb, and Alameen. Today I wish to begin discussing the word Hamd, and how it is bound to the words رب العلمین.

In classical Arabic, Hamd carries two meanings. It means gratitude, and it means praise. Let me say this again: Hamd means gratitude, and it also means praise. There is a difference between the two. Gratitude is the quality of being thankful when something good is done for you. Praise is admiration for something amazing or brilliant. Hamd holds both of these at once. We will undertake a linguistic analysis of the word Hamd in later sessions. Today I wish only to speak of gratitude, which is in itself an enormous subject. We will therefore be able to cover only a portion of it today. In the next session we will resume where we leave off today, God willing.

Allah says in the Qur'an: وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ . أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom. Be grateful to Allah!" Luqman is the wisest man of his time. وَمَن يَشْكُرْ فَإِنَّمَا يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ And whoever is grateful — his gratitude benefits none but himself. وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌۭ And whoever is ungrateful, and denies Allah's favor — then indeed, Allah is free of all need and praiseworthy.

Let us look at this first verse. Allah says: وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ . أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. We have certainly granted Luqman wisdom.

For those who do not know the story: Luqman was a black man from Sudan who lived before the time of Musa, peace be upon him — around 1100 BC, I believe. He was a deeply perceptive man. One day, while he slept beneath a tree, an angel came to him and said, "Allah wishes to bestow a gift upon you: either wisdom, or prophethood." And Luqman chose wisdom. When he awoke from his sleep, he found that his senses had been heightened and his understanding sharpened. He suddenly felt himself in complete harmony with nature, and he could perceive the inner meaning of things, beyond their outward reality. When he realized this, he at once fell into prostration, and thanked and praised Allah for this wonderful gift. He did two things. He thanked Allah for the gift he had been given. And he praised Allah for the things he was now coming to perceive through the use of that gift.

Later he was captured by slavers and sold into slavery. The scholars say this was his first trial: his training in bondage and servitude. He was made a slave so that he might learn how to become the true slave of the divine Master. And because of his servitude, his عبودیۃ, he attained such a rank in the sight of his Rabb that Allah mentioned him by name in His final message. So Allah says: وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ We have certainly granted Luqman حکمۃ, wisdom.

Now, what is wisdom? When we consider wisdom, what sorts of things come to mind? Someone very knowledgeable. Someone old and rich in experience, like Gandalf in The Lord of the Rings. Or someone who utters such epically profound things that, upon hearing them, we are left astonished — unable even to grasp what was said, yet certain that it was something deeply profound. That kind of thing. Most people, then, hold this hazy notion of what wisdom means.

One of the most remarkable things about ancient Arab culture is its love of simplifying things. They loved simplicity.

And they had a wonderfully simple definition of the word wisdom, which I want to share with you. Their definition of wisdom was this: you are wise when you possess correct knowledge, and you act upon it. That is all. Wisdom has two simple parts. The first is to gain beneficial, correct knowledge. The second is to act upon it. When these two things come together, that is what it means to have wisdom. It is nothing hazy or mystical. It is not a grand quotation. It is something practical. To the Arabs, wisdom is a practical thing.

Now let us put that to the test, so that we understand what they mean by it. Here is a piece of correct, beneficial knowledge: fire burns. That is correct knowledge. That is beneficial knowledge. Wisdom, then, would mean that you did not place your hand in the fire, because you knew that fire burns. If you did not place your hand in the fire, young man, you have acted wisely. You have chosen well, because you acted upon the knowledge that you have.

Let us take it a step further. Smoking can cause all sorts of health problems, and in the end even cancer of the lungs. This too is correct knowledge. In light of this knowledge, what do you decide to do? You choose not to smoke. If you make that decision, you are acting wisely. Reckless speeding on a highway can cause a crash. You can kill yourself, your friends, and other innocent people who have nothing to do with your recklessness. That is sound knowledge. So if you do not weave through traffic, if you do not try to force your way past a bus just as it is about to take an exit, that is a wise decision.

Now Allah says, وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ — We gave Luqman wisdom — which means that Luqman has two things. On the one hand, he possesses beneficial knowledge; and on the other, whatever knowledge he has, he puts to practical use. He acts upon it. His knowledge somehow changes the way he thinks. It changes the way he makes a decision. This is very important for all of us to understand as well, because in the end what the Qur'an most demands, especially from the young, is not knowledge. It is wisdom. At your age, studying is easier, memorizing is easier, retaining is easier, and taking a test is easier. In fact, if I had to return to school and study the things that you are studying today, and try to sit the same tests that you sit, I would do poorly in comparison to you. Why? Because I am no longer in the mode of a student. My mind is not as sharp as it was when I was a teenager. So gaining knowledge is very easy for you. But what is difficult? Acting upon it, is it not?

Your friend shows you an amazing project he has been working on, an utterly, incredibly astonishing gadget he has put together. Hey, look at this. What do you think? You look at it and say what? Whatever, man. It is nothing. Best Buy has a better version of that. Who cares? The right answer should have been praise, given all the effort and design he poured into it, but that would be so uncool to do, would it not? Your cool factor would take a plunge if, God forbid, you said: Wow, that is wonderful.

So we are surrounded by so many comforts, and in most cases we do not even need to lift a finger for them. It is done for us, constantly, until we begin to think we are entitled to it. I deserve it. And we begin to believe we own things. This belongs to me. We have developed this notion of my stuff. It is my stuff, and I am not going to share it with anyone, because it is my stuff. Why are you touching my stuff? Do not touch my stuff. It is mine. Mine, mine, mine. You children turn, quite literally, into that bird from Finding Nemo. Mine, mine, mine.

This is us today. But the thing about these people of sound essence is that they do not believe they own anything at all. They understand that they do not actually possess anything. Why? Because they are slaves, and slaves own nothing. And not only do they own nothing, they themselves are owned by their master. This realization is what truly makes them grateful. For they understand that everything they own is not, in fact, ownership; it is a temporary possession granted to them by their Rabb.

To be sure, they worked through the day to earn a living and make money, so they do deserve a paycheck, which they then use to buy things. But would they have been able to make that living if they had no eyes, or hands, or feet, or intellect? They may have worked for the paycheck that bought them the iPad, but did they work to gain their sight, their hearing,

their heartbeats? Their very existence? No. So that paycheck, the one buying them their toys and gadgets, rests upon certain undeserved, unearned gifts that their Rabb graciously and generously blessed them with. And if they do not own their existence, along with everything that comes with that existence, then technically they do not own their paycheck either, and therefore they do not own anything they bought with that paycheck. So then who owns all of it? The one who gave them existence, is it not?

These people of sound essence realize that in the true sense they own nothing and deserve nothing, because they are slaves. This is why, when they witness the favors and blessings of their master, they feel truly and completely grateful. And Allah confirms this in the Qur'an when He says:

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ كُلُوا۟ مِن طَيِّبَٰتِ مَا رَزَقْنَٰكُمْ

O you who have believed, eat from the good things which We have provided for you — and then do what?

وَٱشْكُرُوا۟ لِلَّهِ

and be grateful to Allah,

إِن كُنتُمْ إِيَّاهُ تَعْبُدُونَ

if you truly consider yourselves His slaves.

When we understand this, it completely changes how we see the world. Because now we realize that whatever you and I have — the clothes we are wearing, the devices we are using, the possessions we are so proud of, the cars we drive, the homes we live in, the schools we attend — none of it is actually something we deserve. These are all gifts that have been given to us. This morning all of you woke up and simply jumped out of bed. But there are children who wake up in the morning and whose parents must carry them to their wheelchairs, because they cannot walk. You woke up and the first thing you did was reach for your phone to check your messages. There are so many children who woke up in complete darkness this morning, who will not be able to see anything for the rest of their lives. This morning some of you ate your breakfast, and you did not like the taste of what was set before you, so you dumped it all in the garbage simply because it did not taste right. Yet there are children who picked through garbage pails this morning just so they could find something to eat.

These are realizations. These realizations are the soil in which true gratitude is cultivated. This mental exercise, of submitting ourselves as slaves to Allah, is the key to unlocking the treasures of His gratitude. In other words, gratitude is directly proportional to this realization of being a slave.

Complaint is the litmus test of ingratitude

Now, if you want to truly test this concept, the concept of whether you believe you are a slave or not, the litmus test for it is to catch yourself complaining. Scholars say that complaint is the proof of ingratitude. It is the physical evidence of ingratitude. I am not talking about complaining when someone is hurting you, or bullying you, or when you have a pain in your arm or something like that. I am not talking about that. I am talking about the complaints we have that are related to possessions or desires. You understand the difference? If someone is hurting you and you inform your parents about it, that is not a complaint. That is simply you being smart.

The complaints I am talking about are related to possessions and desires. They stem from ingratitude, and they are of two types. The first is the complaint when you do not get something you want. And the second is the complaint when the thing that you have

is not good enough for you.

When you complain about something you did not receive, you believe that somehow you deserved it. You believe you were entitled to it. Consider, for example, a student who studies hard and does very well on an examination, and yet the professor gives him a C. He complains, because he believes he deserved an A. And when your parents will not buy you a certain thing that you want, and you complain, you somehow imagine that you are entitled to it, or that your parents owe it to you. That is not true. They owe you nothing. Everything they do for you flows from their love, their care, their concern, and their mercy toward you. And if they truly owe anyone, they owe Allah, not you, because Allah has made them a Rabb over you. To you, directly, they owe nothing at all. That is the first kind of complaint.

The second kind of complaint is when you already possess something, and it is not good enough for you. Consider how ungracious that is. Someone gives you a gift, and you complain about it. Suppose I buy my daughter a violin for her birthday, because I know she has wanted one for a long while. So I save my money, and I buy the one I can afford for her. She takes it in her hand, looks at it, and says to me, "Babu, you know, there is a better one than this in the store." Is that ungracious? Yes, and it is unacceptable. And if she did that, what would I do with the gift? If I handed her the violin and she said there was a better one, what would I naturally do? I would take it back. And if you know me at all, I would take back not only the violin, but every other thing I had ever given her as well, for surely there is a better version of all of those gifts out there too. And when I did that, she would say, "No, no, I did not mean it."

But in truth, we human beings do not appreciate the gifts we have until they are taken from us. Children have so many complaints against their parents. Sisters complain against brothers, and brothers complain against sisters. A child goes to school, and someone asks him, "Tell me about your mother." And he says, "She is such a trial to me. She is always after me, always nagging me about my homework, about my chores. She is always shouting at me, always troubling me about my prayers. I cannot wait to turn eighteen and leave this house. I am so weary of her." But then, God forbid, something happens, and Allah takes his mother from him. At that point you ask him the same question, and he says, "I had the most perfect mother. She loved me so much. She always cared for me. She always made certain I was fed, and never let me go to bed hungry. She would wash my clothes, iron them, and fold them for me. She made my bed for me every day. When I fell ill, she checked on me constantly. She took such wonderful care of me. I miss her so much."

What happened? What changed? Only yesterday you could not stop complaining about her. What has come over you today?

So be grateful to Allah for the parents you have. You do not own them. Allah owns them, just as He owns you. And one day the Owner will take back what belongs to Him. On that day, you will be able to remember only how good she was to you. If you wish to be among the wise, be grateful now.

The same holds true for parents.

I have never once heard a parent complain about a child who has died. I have never heard a parent say, "My son was irresponsible. He never finished his homework, never did his chores, always argued with me." Never. They say only one thing: my son was perfect. My brother was perfect. My sister was perfect. Cherish the people you have in your life today, before you lose them. Nothing in this world lasts forever. That is the essence of wisdom.

Let us summarize what we spoke about today. Wisdom means to have knowledge and then to act upon it. And the summit of all wisdom is this: أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. Be grateful to Allah! The ultimate wisdom is to be grateful to Allah. That is the ultimate wisdom. For only the wise person realizes that to be created, to be granted existence, is Allah's ultimate gift.

وَٱللَّهُ أَخْرَجَكُم مِّنۢ بُطُونِ أُمَّهَتِكُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْـًۭٔا — And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing. That is our original state: complete ignorance. And then what?

وَجَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْأَبْصَرَ وَٱلْأَفْـِٔدَةَ — and He made for you hearing and sight and intellect. These are the three primary gifts by which we acquire knowledge: by seeing and hearing things, and by using our intellects. So that we may study the عالَم, and become an عالِم, and so understand the علیم. Without these gifts, could we have any decent life in this world? Absolutely not. So Allah created us in ignorance. He created us in a state of ingratitude, and then He gave us three gifts — hearing, sight, and intellect — to help lift us out of our ignorance, to help us move toward wisdom. And why did He do this? لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ — that perhaps you would be grateful. And He said لَعَلَّكُمْ — perhaps. Why perhaps? Because He knew that the human being is an ungrateful creation. And so we need to move toward gratitude. Gratitude is something that must be cultivated. It is a muscle that must be developed. And how do we do that? By realizing that we are slaves. We are slaves who deserve nothing. We do not, in truth, own anything. Everything and everyone we have in life is a temporary possession. They are all as temporary as our own lives. They are all gifts and blessings from our gracious and generous Rabb, who will one day take them back. انا للہ — there is no doubt about it, we belong to Allah. We are His possessions. و انا الیہ راجعون — and there is no doubt about it, one day we will return to Him. One day the Owner will take back His possessions.

You see, ingratitude happens when we believe that things are permanent. But if everything is temporary, the only logical conclusion is to enjoy these things while they last, and to be grateful to the One who gave them. An Urdu poet says:

سدا نہ باغی بلبل بولے، سدا نہ باغ بہاراں
سدا نہ قائم حسن و جوانی، سدا نہ صحبت یاراں

This nightingale will not sing in this garden forever, nor will the beauty of this garden last forever. Beauty and youth do not last forever, nor does the company of the beloved last forever. So be grateful to Allah while you still have these things.

This means that although knowledge can be acquired at an earlier stage, what takes time to develop is wisdom. You may learn a great deal about the Qur'an, yet not truly know how to use it. Wisdom has not fully settled in. So in order for us to develop wisdom, we must begin to apply the teachings of the Qur'an in our practical, day-to-day life. We must begin to put them into action. In these sessions we are gaining knowledge. Once the session is over, what must we do? We must find a way to act upon it. Otherwise, what is the point? If we merely acquire this knowledge and do nothing with it, then کمثل حمار یحمل اسفارا, as Allah says in Surah Jumuah.

These people are like a donkey that carries a huge load of books upon its back. But do those books actually benefit the donkey? No. So the aim of these sessions, or of any knowledge for that matter, is not to carry its burden upon our backs, but to actually benefit from it. And how does one benefit from it? By putting it into action, which is the true goal of the Quran. The goal of the Quran is wisdom.

Now Allah says that We gave Luqman wisdom. And what is the pinnacle, what is the climax, of all his wisdom? Consider this. أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. Be grateful to Allah. Be grateful to Allah. I want you to understand this part. Allah did not say, We gave wisdom to Luqman to be grateful to Allah, nor, We gave wisdom to Luqman so that he could be grateful to Allah. Rather, We gave Luqman wisdom; be grateful to Allah! Now what is the difference between the two? When your mother tells you, do your homework, is it a suggestion? Is it a request? Or is it a command? It is a command. Allah, after granting Luqman wisdom, is not suggesting to him that he be grateful. He is commanding him to be grateful. Which means that Luqman understood that being grateful is obligatory. It is not something that is merely nice to do; it is not something you do once in a while; it is not something you kind of, sort of should do. He realized that this is something he absolutely must do. That is captured grammatically within أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. In other words, at the end of his life, at the end of all of life's experiences that Luqman had, he realized just one thing: that being grateful is the ultimate wisdom. Gratitude is the ultimate wisdom. SubhanAllah!

You will find people in life who have a great deal of knowledge about the Quran. But even though they have knowledge, they do not act upon it, which means they do not have wisdom. You can be highly knowledgeable, yet still not be wise. And what lies at the heart of wisdom is gratitude. So the idea is that the more knowledgeable we become in this religion, the wiser we are supposed to become by acting upon that knowledge. And the wiser we become, the more grateful we should become to Allah (Azza Wa Jal). That is the purpose of the Quran.

Then the ayah continues, وَمَن يَشْكُرْ فَإِنَّمَا يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ. The one who is grateful is only, in fact, truly grateful for himself, for his own benefit. If you are being grateful, who is it that you are benefiting? You! You are becoming a happier person. You are becoming a more satisfied person. You are making the most of what you have in your life. You are not constantly looking at what you did not get, or what you do not have, or what you could have had. You are actually taking advantage of what you actually do have. The glass is never half empty for you; it is always half full for you. In other words, being grateful is, in a sense, now the same as being positive. And by being positive, you are only helping yourself; you are only improving the quality of your own life.

There are numerous TED talks about this today, about how becoming grateful and satisfied for what you do have tremendously increases the quality of your life. You will lead a happier, more fulfilling life. They are discovering all of this now, and everyone says that this is such an epic discovery, and the Quran stated this fourteen hundred years ago. Listen! If you are going to be grateful, it is only going to help you. This, by the way,

is one of the first and foremost things about believing in Allah. Belief in Allah is not merely a statement about our conviction that he exists, or a conviction in someone with divine powers who does everything, who created the universe, who created us, who controls all things. That is not enough. That is only the knowledge that surrounds belief. The fruit, the result, of belief is that we develop certain kinds of attitudes. And the first attitude that the Quran speaks of is gratitude. We become people who cultivate a positive outlook on life. We become appreciative. We always see the value in the things around us, even in bad situations.

Hazrat Luqman's master was a very rich man. And he respected Hazrat Luqman so much that he treated him as a great friend and companion, to the point that he made it his practice, whenever he had something special to eat, to feed Hazrat Luqman from it first and only then eat what remained. Is that not remarkable? But do you know what we learn from this? Wisdom is such a wondrous thing that it can turn a slave into a master and a master into a slave. Where on earth would you find a master who would eat from his slave's leftovers? Yet this was the kind of love and respect that Hazrat Luqman awakened in the heart of his master, simply through his wisdom.

In any case, one day during watermelon season, someone gave his master a watermelon. He calls Luqman, peace be upon him, and then he slices the melon and begins offering Hazrat Luqman one slice after another. Luqman begins eating the slices with great pleasure, and as he eats them he expresses his gratitude to his master and sings his praises. The more he praised his master, the more his master gave to Luqman. Why is that? In life, when you are grateful, when you are appreciative of someone, does that increase their affection toward you or lessen it? It obviously increases it, does it not? When we are grateful to Allah for his gifts, when we are appreciative of Allah's gifts, will that increase his affection for us or decrease it? Even though this is the story of a slave, Hazrat Luqman, and his master, it holds a wealth of wisdom for us about our own relationship, as slaves, with our master.

In any case, so the master is handing Hazrat Luqman the slices, and as he eats them he praises his master and expresses his gratitude to him. This in turn makes the master so happy that he keeps handing Luqman, peace be upon him, one slice after another. Finally, when there is one slice left, his master thinks, Let me too try a slice of this delicious melon. So he takes a bite from that last slice. That slice was so horribly bitter that his master almost choked. Some narrations say that he passed out. When he came back to his senses, he asked Luqman, How have you been eating these slices all this while with such a smile on your face, praising me and expressing gratitude? This thing is more bitter than poison!

Hazrat Luqman replies, O generous master, from your hands I have received hundreds of beautiful gifts. The burden of gratitude I owe you breaks my back. So I felt ashamed that the hand which granted me the sweetness of so many favors—if one day some bitterness should come from it, how could I turn away? O master, the pleasure of knowing that it comes from your hands turned the bitterness of the melon into sweetness! SubhanAllah! You see, this is true gratitude!

At every single moment of our lives, we are surrounded by Allah's blessings.

But when one thing does not go our way, we turn against our master. So Allah says that He gave Luqman wisdom. It was Allah who gave Luqman his wisdom; Luqman did not acquire it on his own. Allah gave it to him, and then He commanded him: أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. Be grateful to Allah!

وَمَن يَشْكُرْ فَإِنَّمَا يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ. The one who is grateful is only being grateful for his own sake. The true essence of belief is gratitude. And, by the way, consider what the opposite of gratitude is in Arabic. In English it is ingratitude. But do you know what the opposite of Shukr is? It is very interesting. It is Kufr. And what is another meaning of the word Kufr? Disbelief. So, to the Arabs, disbelief and ingratitude are one and the same thing. For them there is no difference between the two. Someone who is not grateful might as well not be a believer at all. Why? Because the first thing that results from your being a believer is that you become grateful; you become positive. And this is why the first words of the Qur'an in Surah al-Fatihah are what? Alhamdulillah. If we do not learn this one lesson, we have learned nothing from the Qur'an. We truly need to internalize this.

Allah then continues and says: وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌۭ. And whoever is ungrateful, then certainly Allah is free of all need, and He is praised in and of Himself. Now, this is a very powerful statement made by Allah, so let us try to understand what He is saying here. Allah is saying that He does not need you to be grateful to Him. In fact, He does not need you for anything at all. People ask this foolish question: Why does Allah need me to be grateful in the first place? Why does He constantly need my gratitude? In truth, He needs absolutely nothing from you, because He is غنی. غنی means one who is completely independent, who has no need of anyone or anything. In fact, the only one who truly has any need is us.

We do not thank Him for every breath, yet He still provides it. We do not thank Him for every single heartbeat, yet He still allows it. We do not thank Him for every blood vessel filling with blood, yet He is still doing it for us. The fact that we can see and blink, the fact that we are not overwhelmed with pain in every pore of our skin—all of that is from Allah. And despite the fact that we are not necessarily grateful to Him, nor do we constantly express our gratitude to Him, He still provides these things for us. So the truth of the matter is that, if there is anyone who deserves gratitude, it is He. And no matter how much we imagine we pray to Him, no matter how much we try to carry out our religious duties, in the grand scheme of things we can never truly thank Him. So we cannot think, even for a moment, that we have in fact accomplished the task of thanking Allah, because that will never be the case. We are never, ever going to be able to thank Allah for what He does for us.

Allah says: وَآتَىٰكُم مِّن كُلِّ مَا سَأَلْتُمُوهُ. وَإِن تَعُدُّوا۟ نِعْمَتَ ٱللَّهِ. لَا تُحْصُوهَآ. We give you everything that you ask of Us. And if you were to try to fully understand, to fully appreciate, even a single blessing of Allah, you would not be able to do so. You would not be able to fully grasp it or fully appreciate it; it is simply not humanly possible.

إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَنَ لَظَلُومٌۭ كَفَّارٌۭ. There is no doubt about it: human beings are truly unjust and extremely ungrateful. Allah is saying.

You cannot thank Me properly, nor thank Me completely, for a single favor I have done for you — the favors you actually see and experience. You cannot be truly grateful even for those. So what, then, of the rest? وَأَسْبَغَ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعَمَهُۥ ظَهِرَةًۭ وَبَاطِنَةًۭ Allah has poured out His favors upon you: the ones that are plain to you, and also the ones you never even see. There are so many unseen ways in which Allah is helping us that we do not even realize.

There are ways in which Allah protects us in our sleep. We are walking down the street, and around us are insects that carry deadly toxins. One bite from them could kill us. They carry deadly viruses and disease, and they pass right by us at Allah's command. They bite someone else, and that person dies, and we do not. This was never within our control. Had it been decreed for us, there is nothing we could have done about it. So we do not even know the ways in which Allah is protecting us. He says in the Qur'an: وَيُرْسِلُ عَلَيْكُمْ حَفَظَةً We send down guardian angels over you. He has literally assigned angels who are on full-time duty, only to watch over you, only to take care of you.

You are driving your car perfectly well, within the speed limit, within your lane, and there is a drunk driver right beside you who could crash into you at any moment, through no fault of your own — but Allah's angels are protecting you. We cannot even conceive of the ways in which Allah is protecting us, providing for us, doing us these constant favors we know nothing about. We invent illusions of home security, job security, social security — all of which can crumble in an instant. We have seen it happen. All of this is merely an illusion of security. Allah is the One who truly keeps us safe.

So Allah says: وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌۭ He does not need you, because He is ghanee. He is self-sufficient. In truth, it is you who need Him. Then He adds the word Hameed. Hameed is one who is praised and shown appreciation entirely on His own account. In other words, He does not need you to show Him praise and appreciation. If no one in the entire world were to praise Him and show Him appreciation, He would still be worthy of praise, and He would still be worthy of gratitude. If Allah had created absolutely nothing — if there were no human beings, no animals, no plants, if there were nothing at all in this world — Allah would still be worthy of praise. He would still be worthy of appreciation. He does not need creation to show Him gratitude.

The only thing our gratitude does is increase His favors upon us, which is simply a part of His justice, because that is what justice dictates: give more to the appreciative, give more to the grateful. In school, when you show appreciation to your teachers, they will naturally try to teach you more, because you are showing that you appreciate and value what they are doing for you. It makes them glad to do more for you — but not because they have to. They do not. It is only your gratitude and your appreciation that draws their favors more.

Anjum apa once told me that she was teaching her students how magnets attract metals, and she said it got her thinking that Allah's justice must be like that: that if you contain certain qualities, certain metals within you,

It will automatically be attracted to the magnet, which is his blessings. I thought that was a really beautiful example. Gratitude is that metal within us that attracts Allah's favors. The more gratitude we have, the more strongly we will attract his blessings. Which means that if I feel I am not seeing his favors in my life, then what is missing? My gratitude is missing.

Now what is gratitude? We need to understand what gratitude, or shukar, is. There are two meanings in the statement أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ. The first is: be grateful TO Allah. And the second is: be grateful THROUGH the intermediaries of Allah. I will say that again. Be grateful TO Allah. And the second is: be grateful BECAUSE of Allah, or be grateful FOR THE SAKE of Allah.

So let us begin by talking about gratitude TO Allah, in the context of the ulil-Albaab, the people of sound essence. Once again, Lubb, the singular form of Albaab, is the kernel inside a nut, or the seed inside a fruit. And because a seed is always PROTECTED and covered from all sides, its essence remains pure. It does not get influenced by external factors. In other words, it maintains its original pure state. That is why ulil-Albaab are called people of sound essence, because they have protected their hearts from satanic influences, and so they have been able to preserve their original purity. But that also implies that they started off with some basic purity, right?

You guys play video games, right? If you have played any RPG-type games, role-playing games, the character always begins with some basic capabilities. He can walk. He can jump. He can kick, punch. But these are not at their maximum level yet. They are at a very basic level. And then, as he progresses through the game, he possesses additional powers, new equipment, new weapons, attack combos, and so on. So now he can jump higher, run faster, have a three-punch combo, and so on. And then eventually you can buy in-app upgrades, and synch everything up to 100%, and now your character is fully awesome. Now it is exactly what you always wanted it to be, right? But when you started the game, your character is kind of weak, yet there are still some basic capabilities your character possesses, in order for you to be able to play the game. You understand? I am sorry, girls. I have not played any princess games, so I cannot make reference to those.

So according to Islam, EVERY ONE of us, ALL human beings, are created with some basic pre-programmed spiritual capabilities within the Ruh, the soul! It is called Fitrah. It is those basic capabilities we are all created with in this game of life. That is why Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) said مَا مِنْ مَوْلُودٍ إِلَّا يُولَدُ عَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ. There is not a single child that is not born upon this pure state, "Fitrah," فَأَبَوَاهُ يُهَوِّدَانِهِ وَيُنَصِّرَانِهِ وَيُمَجِّسَانِهِ. You-havvi-danihi, wa Yu-nassi-raanihi, wa Yu-majji-saanihi. It is then his parents (i.e. external influences) that make him a Jew, Christian, or a Zoroastrian. But the original state of a child is pure. You smile at a child, and it will smile back at you. You look at it in anger, and it will start crying. A child never lies. It will just look at you in the eyes, smile, and say, YOU FAT! You do something nice for the child, it does not even know how to say thank you yet, but it will hug you.

Or it will give you a toothless smile, or lick your face, or do something else that is kind. This is because we are all born with this innate capacity to be a decent person. Decency is not something you are upgraded into. Gratitude is not a power you download later. Kindness is not an in-app purchase you have to make at some later point. These are abilities that every human being is born with.

This is the stance that Islam takes toward the first creation. Christianity does not believe this. It holds that every human being is born in sin. But we Muslims believe that the starting point of every human being is good, no matter what family or religion he is born into.

And so one of the fundamental proofs of possessing a sound essence is that when something kind is done to you, you respond in kind. For example, if I do something kind for you, or if you do something kind for me, what should I do at the very least? I should be grateful to you. I should have that basic decency within me to say thank you. I should not require an upgrade for that, should I? When someone does something kind for us, is kind to us, feeds us, does us a favor, or gives us gifts, we simply and naturally become grateful to that person, and we thank him. Gratitude, then, is one of those fundamental emotions we are born with.

There is another. When we see something beautiful, when we see something amazing, such as a beautiful waterfall or a breathtaking view, when someone shows us something magnificent, we appreciate it and we praise it. So gratitude and praise are among that basic decency with which Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, created us all.

This is how we saw that when these people of sound hearts and sound minds, the ulil-albaab, reflect upon the creations of the heavens and the earth, they become aware of the existence of their Rabb. They become aware of His ownership and His authority over them. They witness how their Rabb is nurturing them, maintaining them, and putting them to their purpose, and how everything within themselves and outside of them is designed as enormous gifts and blessings from their Master. So they accept Him as Rabb, and in doing so they submit themselves to Him as His obedient slaves.

Taking Blessings for Granted

Now, in the previous session I told you that this act of submission as slaves is in fact an extremely difficult task. That is why I said that the greatest challenge you and I are constantly going to face in life, every waking moment, is accepting that Allah is Rabb and that we are His slaves. It is not easy, especially not in these times in which we live, and especially not for you children. Why is that? It is because of the amount of luxury and convenience that we all enjoy today. There is no blame here. It is not a bad thing that you have luxuries and comforts; al-hamdulillah for that. I am simply acknowledging the fact that yes, it truly is very difficult in this day and age for us to submit ourselves genuinely as slaves. And that is because we are all surrounded by comforts. When a master surrounds his slaves with comforts, it becomes very easy for us to forget what? That we are still slaves.

We have a great deal of what we want at the tip of our fingers, literally. We can order things online. We can download things. We have the devices to do so. We have the constant connections to do so. And we have all grown used to this kind of convenience. We have all become slaves of instant gratification for most things in our lives.

When we want something, we want it now. And the trouble is that most of the time we do get it right now. So being without it becomes simply unthinkable. Consider ourselves and our phones, and this need to be online without pause. We are literally enslaved to it. To spend a single hour without the internet feels devastating. In fact, if I asked all of you children to switch off your phones this very moment, some of you would go out of your minds. What? Turn off my phone? Are you out of your mind, Asif mamu? It is bad enough that my parents make me sit for an hour and listen to you, and now I cannot even use my phone? Oh, I hate you so much. Is that not so?

And do you know why this is a problem? We have grown so accustomed to getting whatever we want, whenever we want it, that we begin to believe we are actually entitled to it.
