We believe we truly deserve everything we have. So in the moments when these gifts are given to us, it feels like nothing at all. Whatever.

Today we live in a world where our hearts are afflicted with a disease called "Whatever." Your parents say to you: Look how much I love you and how much I do for you. I take care of you. I feed you. I buy you everything you need. And your answer is: Whatever. Your answer should have been gratitude, and instead it is: Whatever. Why? Because you feel, so what if you do all this for me? It is no great matter. You are supposed to do this for me, and so, whatever.

The most controversial verse comes from Surah Taubah. Surah Taubah is very uncompromising and very unforgiving. It is so vicious in its antagonism against the disbelievers that it does not even begin with BARR; it does not even mention God's mercy. Maulana Ali was asked why this surah does not begin with BARR. He said that it is like a sword that came down out of its cover. This surah came down like a sword out of its cover — that is how he responded. It is a very uncompromising, even politically incorrect surah. But do you know what is so amazing about this chapter? It did not begin with God's mercy, but it ended with His Messenger's mercy: لَقَدْ جَآءَكُمْ رَسُولٌۭ مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ عَزِيزٌ عَلَيْهِ مَا عَنِتُّمْ حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُم بِٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَءُوفٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ ‏It begins with the wrath of Allah.

But it ends with mercy. You see, God sent messengers throughout history. We know that, the Christians know that, and everyone else knows it too. All the People of the Book know that God sent messengers. Then these messengers came, and the majority of the people — did they follow them or did they not follow them? The majority did not follow them. And when that majority chose not to follow them and decided to remain disbelievers, God sent punishment down upon them. Not only in the Fire of Hell, but where else? In this world as well. God destroyed them by a flood, or an earthquake, or a fire from the sky, or the town was turned upside down. All kinds of terrible punishments are mentioned in the Qur'an. And what is the crime? The crime is not kufr. The crime is not disbelief. The crime is disbelief in a messenger to his very face. You are living in the time of a messenger. It is not that you merely heard about him. You met him. You spoke with him. He was your neighbor. And still you were disbelievers! And you stayed that way decade after decade after decade. How dare you? Not only will you be punished in the hereafter, you will also be destroyed right here and right now. Do you understand that? The crime is this disbelief in a messenger while he is present among you. That is the crime. And again and again and again, God destroys the nation that disbelieves its messenger while he stands before it. This has always been the way of Allah. This is how He has always acted through history. This is how He does things. And He says in the Qur'an: ولن تجد سنۃ اللہ تبدیلا — you will not find any change in the way God does things. Now, will the Christians believe that God destroyed earlier nations that did not believe their messengers? Absolutely. Because their Bibles are full of it too. Their book is filled with what our book contains. They have it as well.

Now let us take the next step. We believe that Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family and grant them peace) is His Messenger too. And not just any messenger, but His most beloved messenger. Correct? Now, the other messengers came to their nations and warned them that if they did not believe, a punishment was coming: انی اخافُ علیکم عذاب یوماً عظیم — I am afraid for you of the punishment of an enormous day. I am afraid for you, I am afraid for you. Did the people take those warnings seriously? No. Come on!
body.topic_title_en: Islam Is a Religion of Hate

body.text_en:
We have been hearing your warnings for a long time now. Bring it already. When is it coming? ویقولون متی ھذال الوعد — when is this promise that you keep talking about going to be fulfilled? We have been hearing you talk about this forever. We are tired of it. You know what, just bring it. If you can actually bring it, we can handle it. That is how they began to speak to their messengers. And then, finally, the punishment came. And when the punishment came, when that storm of fire came down from the sky and was about to strike the disbeliever on his head, it is not as though God pressed the pause button and then asked: do you see it now? Do you believe now? In other words, the floodwaters came and they were about to crush the disbeliever's house, and then God pressed the pause button, the way we see in movies when everything comes to a standstill, and then Nooh (peace be upon him) walked over to the disbeliever and asked: did I not tell you? Do you want to believe now? Were they given that opportunity? No. Once the floods begin, they are not going to stop until everything and everyone is destroyed. Do you understand? In other words, the opportunity to believe is not after God overpowers them. The opportunity to believe does not come after it, but before it. That is what I am saying. You can only believe before God brings the punishment, not after it. This is the way God has always worked.

Now let us come to the times of Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). Who are the criminals? The Quraish are. They disbelieved the messenger to his face. What do they deserve according to the sunnah of Allah? That they be annihilated. Perhaps a fire from the sky, or earthquakes, or that the earth should swallow them, or that they should be drowned in a flood. Something should happen to them, because this is what has happened in the case of every other messenger before him. Fine.

But God did not bring punishment down upon them from the sky. He did not bring the punishment upon them from beneath the earth. He did not afflict them with diseases. What was their punishment? The divine wrath against them was the sahaba, the Companions of the messenger. God sent the believers upon them, and the believers defeated them in battle despite their small numbers. They overpowered them and conquered Mecca. In other words, God overpowered them through the believers. And when God overpowers the disbelievers, what is supposed to happen? What happened in the case of any previous messenger? In the case of Nooh, or Salih, or Shoaib, when God overpowers the disbelievers, what is supposed to happen? They die. They are completely annihilated. Now Mecca has been conquered, and the swords of the Companions are at their necks. But at this point God says stop. Has he ever said stop before? No. He says stop.
body.topic_title_en: Islam Is a Religion of Hate

body.text_en:
He presses the pause button. Give them four months. Let them think it over. And in the meantime, during those four months, if anyone comes to you and says, "I never took you seriously. For all these twenty-three years I was simply amusing myself. I was busy with my PlayStation 3. I did not really hear the message. Could you please explain it to me once more?" — God says, do not even say to him, "Where were you all this time? You should have been paying attention. It is too late now." No, no, no. وَإِنْ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ ٱسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ حَتَّىٰ يَسْمَعَ كَلَمَ ٱللَّهِ Even now, if one of the disbelievers comes to you, give him time, until he has heard the word of God. And then do not stand over him and press him, "Tell me now, what is your decision?" No, no, no. ثُمَّ أَبْلِغْهُ مَأْمَنَهُ Let him return to a place of safety where he is no longer intimidated by you, and then let him make his decision on his own. SubhanAllah! Has this ever happened before? This is a special mercy given by God to His beloved Prophet Muhammad (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). Such special treatment was not given to any other messenger before him.

And on top of this, within these four months you have options. If you believe in God now, all your previous crimes are forgiven. I have been telling you that you would be overcome. I have been telling you, اذا جاء نصر اللہ والفتح. I have been telling you, لتُغلَبُنَّ — you will soon be overpowered. And you were not taking it seriously. Now that it has happened, now you should believe. So if you believe now, the whole previous record is wiped clean. You have a clean slate. Full immunity. You are an equal citizen. But if you do not wish to believe, then I am not placing you under house arrest either. Do you know what you may do? You may simply move. You may go to any other place outside Mecca, and you will not be hurt or harmed. You may simply leave.

The punishments for the crimes you committed — you killed innocent civilians, you drove people out of their homes, you engaged in acts of aggression — even though you did all of these terrible things, O people of Quraish, you have four months to believe, and I will forgive and forget. I am willing to let bygones be bygones. And if you still choose not to believe, then leave this place within four months, or be prepared to fight after four months. I do not know what else you would call this but mercy. I do not know what else you can call it. Unfortunately, we hold the seerah in such low regard. Tell me, which nation before this was given such mercy? Which was given such an opportunity?
body.topic_title_en: Islam Is a Religion of Hate

body.text_en:
In the previous session we considered the meaning of the word wisdom, and how the ancient Arabs defined it. They understood it as beneficial knowledge joined to action upon that knowledge. And the essence of the wisdom that was being taught to Hazrat Luqman was this: وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ — We granted Luqman wisdom. And what, then, was he to do with it? أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ — Be grateful to Allah. Allah is teaching us that gratitude is the essence of wisdom; it is its very pinnacle.

This gratitude, this capacity to praise what is good and to value good things, springs from a basic decency with which Allah created every one of us. Gratitude is not something we acquire in the course of life. It is already present within us. Yet there are people who lose this basic decency and are no longer grateful for anything at all. They become wholly selfish. They come to believe that every good thing that reaches them is purely the fruit of their own effort. They deserve what they have. They are entitled to all that they possess. They owe thanks to no one for anything. They owe no one anything. They are entirely self-sufficient. To such people, this message will make absolutely no sense. Islam will make no sense to such people. They will never be able to reach the stage of hamd. For according to the Qur'an, hamd requires two things. You must feel gratitude for the favors that are done to you, and you must also possess the ability to appreciate the design and the worth of things. Anyone who lacks these two things is in the wrong place.

For this is how the Qur'an begins its conversation. It opens with the introduction of Allah — بسم اللہ — and then the very first attribute it names is His love, His care, His concern, and His mercy: الرحمن الرحیم — that He is intensely merciful, consistently merciful. For only the One who loves, who cares, who holds genuine concern, and who has mercy — only One possessed of these attributes can be Rabb. For only a Rabb can nurture, nourish, sustain, and shower gifts, raising the one who is nurtured, the marboob, from their present condition to a higher one. Only a Rabb can do that. And this is why what immediately follows that introduction is the idea of gratitude: الحمد للہ رب العلمین — Praise and gratitude to the Rabb al-Alameen. It is that simple. It is that straightforward.

Then we learned that true gratitude is cultivated in the soil of servitude — in recognizing and seeing ourselves as who we really are: that Allah is our Rabb, and we are His slaves. Now slavery, as Razia apa said, carries a very negative connotation. But the slavery we are speaking of is very different. In fact, it is completely different. And the reason it is completely different is that this Master with whom we are dealing is very different. I will speak of these differences in detail when we come to ایاک نعبد و ایاک نستعین. But some of the ways in which this Rabb is different can be seen right at the outset. Historically, masters are not loving. At best they are kind, or just, or generous. But masters do not love their slaves. They do not shower their slaves with gifts so lavishly that the slaves in fact forget that they are slaves at all. So that is one of the first things that sets this Master apart. He did not merely provide His slaves with what was required.

He went above and beyond in His gifts. Islam is not for the ungrateful.

If we reflect upon nature, even in scientific terms, there is no reason why we should enjoy food. There is no scientific explanation for taste, no reason we would need it. Cows eat grass, and they do not put salt or ketchup on it. They do not mix it with tomatoes and apples and make a Russian salad out of it. They simply eat grass, and they are perfectly content doing so. Lions eat deer, and they just tear through them. They do not pause and say, "Hmm, this could use a little rabbit topping. Or perhaps a turtle on the side would be nice." They do not do that; they just eat the deer. You know how people feed their cats all the fine things you can buy at a grocery store. Yet a cat can eat a cockroach and be happy with it, just like that. It does not need to dip the cockroach in chocolate first. It will just eat it, no problem.

Human beings, however: Allah gave us these strange taste buds, did He not? And so there are certain fruits you like, and some you do not care for. Some of us have a sweet tooth. We love sweet things, certain kinds of chocolate you adore, and certain kinds you do not. There are certain restaurants you are obsessed with, and others you cannot stand. I do not like that place. Scientifically speaking, did we actually need taste, or the enjoyment of taste, when eating food in order to survive? No! It is a gift! You and I could be eating grass and meat and bugs with no taste at all; we could simply eat to live. We did not have to fill our stomachs and say, "Oooh, that was gooood!" We did not have to do that.

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ ٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَٱبْتَغُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِ ٱلْوَسِيلَةَ — O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the INTERMEDIARIES to approach Him. Do not just come directly to Allah; come to Allah THROUGH His means, through His intermediaries. What does this mean? If it is gratitude, BE grateful to them FIRST in order to be grateful to Allah. Obey them FIRST in order to obey Allah. LOVE them FIRST in order to love Allah. Acknowledge them, honor them, APPRECIATE them first, in order to acknowledge and glorify Allah. وَٱبْتَغُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِ ٱلْوَسِيلَةَ. These intermediaries are the milestones for us on the path to Allah. This is where the training of gratitude begins. And the VERY FIRST milestone for us is our parents.

This is why the Quran's argument is not that you simply have to find a creator. No, no, no. That comes much, much later. The Quran's argument is: Do you not want to be grateful? Are you not a decent person? Is gratitude not something I built inside of you? And if you ARE a decent person, and you DO want to be grateful,

Be grateful to the Rabb right in front of you, the one who exists in the seen realm. Because if you are not going to be grateful to your parents, your immediate Rabb, how are you going to be grateful to me? If you cannot see your parents as Rabb, how will you ever be able to see me as Rabb? Because Rububiyyah, just like anything and everything else in the world, is a progression. It is a training. Do you want to be truly grateful? Be grateful to your parents. Be grateful to your grandparents. Be grateful to your teachers. Be grateful to your teachers' teachers. Be grateful to the Imams. Be grateful to Maulana Ali. Be grateful to Rasul Allah. Because being grateful to all of them will be your gratitude to your ultimate Rabb.

The meaning of drinking water

Consider this; I will tell you something. What are the etiquettes of drinking water? We Muslims, following the teachings of Rasul Allah (salla Allahu alayhi wa aalihi wa sallam), when we drink water, we hold the glass in our right hand, and then we sit and drink the water. Is that not so? Now why is that? It is to honor, to show gratitude to, the greatest blessing there is for human life, which is water. It is the ultimate blessing for all living things. We would die without water. An arrogant person does not even think about this. But a true abd, an obedient abd, remembers and appreciates this fact every single time he takes a drink; the fact that, had his master not provided him with water and made it so accessible to him, he would not be able to survive. So how does he show gratitude to his master for that blessing? He humbles himself before Allah for that blessing. And he displays that humility in action, by lowering himself before it, by sitting down and drinking it.

But then this slave also realizes that he would not be able to drink the water unless it were held in a glass. Of course, he could dunk his face in the sink and drink like an animal. But to be able to drink in a civilized, honorable way, he needs to use a glass or a cup. Now, is water the real blessing of Allah, or is the glass the real blessing of Allah? Obviously it is the water! The glass is only a means, an intermediary, to a goal, which is to drink the water.

But look; our Prophet (salla Allahu alayhi wa aalihi wa sallam), in his vast wisdom, made it compulsory to pay respect to the glass as well. And this is why we hold it in our right hand and not our left hand, to honor it, to express our gratitude to it. Because we Muslims use our right hand only for honorable things, and we use our left hand for foul things. So Rasul Allah made it obligatory that when you drink water, you hold the glass in your right hand, to show gratitude to the glass, to honor it! Now notice which honor comes first. Do you hold the glass first, or do you drink the water first? You hold the glass first. So you have to honor and show gratitude to the means, to the intermediary, before you can show gratitude to the blessing. Is that not interesting? Even though the real blessing is the water, you have to honor the glass first. And then you have to lower yourself before the glass, and elevate it, in order to drink from it. I want you all to think about this act of drinking water. You have already lowered yourself, humbled yourself before Allah's blessing. You have honored the glass by holding it in your right hand. But that is not enough. As you are drinking the water,

you are continuously ELEVATING the glass. For you have to raise the glass in order to drink more water. Is that not so? It is not possible to drink more unless you keep lifting the glass higher. The more of the blessing you want, the more you must elevate and honor the glass, the intermediary. SubhanAllah! This entire structure of gratitude is set before us as a reminder, for every single time we drink a glass of water. AllahuAkbar. There is not a single thing in our religion, not a single hadith, not a single act commanded by our beloved Prophet (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam), that is not filled with immensely beautiful and profound meanings. SubhanAllah!

Parents are immediate intermediaries

So what I want you to understand is that your parents are the glass through which you are enjoying the blessings of Allah. You have to honor them first; you have to be grateful to them continuously, in order to be grateful to Allah. For parents are the first of all the intermediaries between us and Allah. He says in the same surah, Luqman:

وَوَصَّيْنَا ٱلْإِنسَنَ بِوَلِدَيْهِ

And We have made it obligatory upon man to care for his parents.

حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُۥ وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍۢ وَفِصَلُهُۥ فِى عَامَيْنِ

His mother carried him, which increased her in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years.

أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَلِوَلِدَيْكَ إِلَىَّ ٱلْمَصِيرُ

Be grateful to Me and to your parents. To Me is your final destination.

أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَلِوَلِدَيْكَ. Be grateful to Me and your parents. This is so beautiful. If you notice, Allah has joined the two extreme ends together. He says, be grateful to Me. Allah is the furthest link, all the way at the other end. And He joins it with وَلِوَلِدَيْكَ, and to your parents, who are the closest link to Me. Notice that when He speaks of gratitude, He mentions Himself, but He does not use the word shukr again for the parents. He does not say:

أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَ اشکر وَلِدَيْكَ

Be grateful to Me and be grateful to your parents. No, He uses the word shukr only once, with Himself. أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَلِوَلِدَيْكَ. Be grateful to Me and your parents. Why? Because being grateful to your parents is a part of your gratitude to Me. You cannot be grateful to Me if you are not grateful to your parents.

We were brought into this world by Allah. But in the seen world, in the seen sense, we were brought into this world by our parents. Allah provides all of our food and sustenance, but in the physical sense, whom did Allah make the means to provide us with food? Our parents. Allah protects us, but to whom has He given that responsibility in the physical sense? To our parents. You know, today, when you are older and you get scared, you say اعوذ بالله. But when you were a child and you got scared, when a two-year-old gets scared, what does he say? Mama, mama. Do they do that or not? Because everything that Allah is to us in the grand scheme of things, when we are a child, we do not see Allah, we do not even understand the concept of Allah. The only thing we understand is what? Mama. Parents. SubhanAllah. Allah clothes us, but in the physical sense our parents clothe us. Allah teaches us. علم الانسان مالم يعلم. He taught the human being what he did not know. علمہ البیان. He taught the human being how to speak. But technically, who teaches us how to speak? Our parents. In other words,

ALL of what Allah did for us, he did through our parents. The most important entity for a child is its parents. Their refuge is the parents. Their source of love is the parents. Their protection is the parents. Their provision is the parents. EVERYTHING that you can later think of with Allah, in the beginning of your life, as a child, is your parents. Parents are the GREATEST GIFTS and BLESSINGS of Allah, because they are doing the WORK of Allah, the work that he wants done for us. Parents are, in truth, the ambassadors of Allah in raising you. They are Allah's ambassadors. They represent him. They represent his work. And do you know what Allah's goal is for you and me? Do you know what he is using parents for? To make us a Rabb. That is what a parent is doing. They are nurturing you in order to elevate you from the status of a Murabbee and turn you into a Rabb. How? So that your SOUL now becomes the Rabb of your body. They elevate you from the pathetic, helpless state of a child to the elevated intellectual state of a Rabb. Look at a child: the parent needs to make every decision FOR it. From that state, your parents brought you to the state where you are now able to manage your own Rububiyyah. If you honestly reflect on it, that is no small task. That is not a small favor. That is an INCREDIBLE favor. And if you are a decent person, if you have not lost that decency that Allah created you with, you will feel immense gratitude for your parents. Because if you do not feel gratitude for them, you will never reach the next stage. You will not be able to be grateful to the spiritual parents who are now going to raise you from this pathetic and helpless state of mortal physicality to the glorious and immortal state of spirituality. If you cannot be grateful to your parents, you will never be grateful to your teachers, and you will never be grateful to Rasul Allah, and you will never be grateful to Allah. Because it is all a chain of command. This is why he says, وَٱعْتَصِمُوا۟ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ — hold strongly to the rope of Allah. وعتصمو comes from عصم, which means the following. You know that sport of bull riding? When you are on the bull and you are holding that rope, and the bull is trying to throw you off, how would you hold that rope? What kind of a grip would you have to maintain? A REALLY strong one, right? That kind of a hold is called عصم. Allah says, وَٱعْتَصِمُوا۟ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ — hold tightly to the rope of Allah. What is this rope of Allah? It is these intermediaries between us and Allah. Imagine this. Imagine a rope is hanging down from the heavens and coming all the way down to you. Now you have to climb this rope all the way up to heaven. How will you do it? You will grab what is closest to you with one hand, right? And then where will your other hand go? Directly to Allah? No. You will grab the rope right above your other hand. Is that not how you climb a rope? So what does this mean?

You will grab the first intermediary, which is your physical parents, and that intermediary will nurture you, give you life, and help elevate you from your current rank to the next higher rank of knowledge, which are your spiritual parents. And then your spiritual parent will lift you to the next parent, until you reach the final parents. There is a hadees of Rasul Allah: انا و انت یا علی ابوین المومنین — O Ali, you and I are the parents of all the believers.

But if you cannot love your physical parents, you will never be able to love your spiritual parents. It is simply a fact of nature. If your relationship with your parents is not good, then I guarantee you that your relationship with Allah is not good either. You can see this for yourself. And so the only way to set right your relationship with Allah is to set right your relationship with your parents.

## Definition of Hamd

So we are speaking of gratitude, hamd, which means two things. It means gratitude, and it means praise. Let us begin by defining these two things and understanding how they are related. Gratitude and praise are emotions that arise in the heart when one realizes that an undeserved gift, or an unearned benefit, has been provided by a benefactor. In other words, when someone does something kind for you, you feel this emotion of love in your heart for two things: love for the person who provides the benefit, and love for the gift itself. Do you understand? Love for the person who gave you the gift, and love for the gift itself. The love for the gift is experienced as praise, and the love for the giver is experienced as gratitude.

Let me give you an example. Your father buys you your brand-new dream car, and he is dangling the keys before you. What do you feel? Toward your father, you feel: Oh, thank you, thank you, thank you. You are the best father ever. I love you so much. I cannot believe you have done this for me. Thank you, Father. Thank you. So toward your father, you feel gratitude. And when you look at the car, examining the leather interior and the gleaming rims, you exclaim: How magnificent this is. How truly wonderful this is. So for the car, for the gift, you feel praise. Do you understand? Gratitude toward your father, and praise for the car.

Now, does your father simply hand you the keys to your new car? No. Obviously not. You know that a lecture comes along with it. You know it. Your father will say, Listen, you need to stop at the stop signs. You need to stay under the speed limit. You must not be out after nine o'clock. You need to, you need to, you need to. He is not going to give you a thousand rules. He will most likely give you ten. He will say, Here are the five things I do not want you to do, and here are the five things I do want you to do. Keep it clean. Be sure to change the oil, and so on. He will say, Listen, you did not buy this car. I did, and I am giving it to you. It is hard-earned money that I labored for, which I am using to buy this car for you. You have absolutely no share in this. You do not deserve this car. You did not earn this car. I am not asking you to pay me for it. The only reason I am giving it to you is because I love you. But in return, all I expect from you, all I ask of you, are these ten things. Please do not do them. And by the way, these ten things I am telling you are for your own safety. Obeying me does not benefit me; it benefits you. Please do not speed, for you will get a ticket. Please do not crash into a tree, for you will be hurt. I do not care about the car; I care about you. For the car, I have insurance. Please do not let your friend drive the car. Is that right? So he sets these few rules for you. Is that fair?

With undeserved gifts come responsibilities, because the gifts are being given to you for a reason. And you can fulfill that reason, or you can ignore it. Do you understand? Allah has given us numerous undeserved gifts.

Allah says: I will give you five fingers on each hand — use them wisely. I will give you two nostrils. I will give you working lungs. I will give you a beating heart. I will give you two legs, and every toe on each of them. I will give you a stomach that works. I will give you a chest. I will give you bones — bones that do not break the moment they touch something. There are people, after all, whose bones are very brittle; they break with the slightest force. An ordinary handshake can break the bones in their hand. Allah gave us eyes, ears, hands, and feet. But with these gifts came responsibilities.

So *hamd*, in its truest sense, is to appreciate the worth of the gift. When you appreciate the worth of a gift and the benefit it brings, what rises in the heart is praise for that gift. And that praise moves out of the heart, comes to the tongue, and is spoken aloud, in the words *AlHamdulillah* and *SubhanAllah*. That is the *hamd* of the heart and the tongue. And there is also the *hamd* of the *jawarih*, of the body parts. In other words, the gratitude and the praise do not remain confined to the heart and the tongue; they move on to the limbs, and the limbs busy themselves in carrying out the very purpose for which they were given. It is not merely lip service; it is not only on the tongue. It becomes visible in the actions of the human being. This is why: شکر نعمت العین…. خِفضُ البَصَر. The eye itself is a blessing, and the gratitude for the eye — the way we thank Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, for the blessing of the eye — is to lower it away from the forbidden. We do not look at the things Allah has forbidden us to see. The gratitude for the blessing of hearing is not to listen to the forbidden: the *gheebah*, the gossip, the backbiting. For on the Day of Judgment the hands and the eyes will bear witness against the human being. بَلِ ٱلْإِنسَنُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٌۭ . . وَلَوْ أَلْقَىٰ مَعَاذِيرَهُۥ. The human being knows what he is doing, even as he begins to offer his excuses. This is why the Arabs say: العُزرُ اَقبَح مِنَ الذَّنب — the excuse is uglier than the wrong deed itself. For all of us have excuses; life is simply filled with excuses.

And so *hamd* is the praise and the gratitude made manifest within action. This is why the Prophet said: لا الہ الا اللہ المفتاح الجنۃ……. وَلِکُلّ مِفتَاح اثنان. *La ilaha illa Allah* is the key to *jannah* — but then he said: every key has teeth. You must have the locksmith cut the teeth into it so that it will fit the lock. And the teeth of *La ilaha illa Allah* are acting according to it. They are entering into the circle of the people of *La ilaha illa Allah*. For it is a circle. And when you bind yourself within a circle, you are leaving behind everything that lies outside it. So to enter the circle of *La ilaha illa Allah* means to leave all that is bad outside. This is true gratitude.

This is why we find every creation that Allah made in a state of constant gratitude. What does that mean? Does it mean they are saying "thank you" all the time? No. It means they are doing what they were created to do. They are fulfilling their responsibilities. أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُۥ مَن فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ. Do you not see that Allah is praised by whoever is within the heavens and the earth.

This is true praise: doing what you were created to do. The sun is in a state of hamd. The moon. The solar systems. The galaxies. The animals, the birds, the plants, the minerals. EVERYTHING is in a state of hamd. Everything is doing what it is supposed to do. This is the ESSENCE of hamd. Is this not also the meaning of wisdom? To gain knowledge and then to act upon it? This is why Allah said that He gave Luqman wisdom, and then, Be grateful to Allah. Because the two are connected in meaning.

And our being grateful to our parents is, indirectly, a way of being grateful to Allah. Allah provides for us from the unseen. Allah protects us from the unseen. Physically, I received the check in the mail, or the deposit in the bank. But we know, as part of our faith, who is actually paying us. Allah is. Yet that is in the unseen; you cannot physically see it. You cannot trace the bank deposit or the transfer directly back to Allah. But what your parents did for you—was that in the unseen, or was it something you can see and experience? Your mother physically carried you in her stomach. She physically delivered you. She physically fed you. Your father physically raised you. They did. That is not some matter of faith, something you have to believe even though you have not seen it. You have experienced it for yourself. If you cannot even be grateful for what you experience in the seen world, how can you be expected to be grateful to Allah, who does everything for you from the unseen world? That does not make any sense. That is why Allah mentioned the parents first.

Now we learn that Luqman was given wisdom. And the first piece of wisdom that he shared with his son was this: do not commit shirk with Allah. In other words, the opposite of being grateful is being a person of shirk. And then we spoke about slavery and the elements of slavery, and we discussed how you can be committing shirk in any of those categories.

Now let us take one more step. If you agree with everything I have said, then let us take one more step forward. If not, this is where you get off.

Your father buys you a brand-new car. What do you owe him? Thanks! That is it? Thanks! Thanks, Dad. And the car races off. Fathers do not just hand you the keys to a new car. There is a lecture that comes with it. You know it. Your father is going to say, Listen, you need to stop at stop signs. You need to stay under the speed limit. You have to not be out after nine at night. You need to, you need to, you need to. He is not going to give you a thousand things. He will most likely give you ten. He will say, Here are the ten things I do not want you to do. Listen! You did not buy this car. I did. And I am giving it to you. It is hard-earned money that I worked for, that I am using to buy this car for you. You have absolutely no share in it. You do not deserve this car. You did not pay for it. You are not going to pay me for it. You did not work for it. The only reason I am giving it to you is because I love you. But in return, all I expect from you, all I ask of you, are these ten things. Please do not do them. And these ten things I am telling you are for your own safety. They do not benefit me.

Please do not speed, or you will get a ticket. Please do not crash into a tree, or you will be hurt. As for the car, I have insurance; that is not my concern. Please do not let your friend drive the car. He sets these few rules for you. Is that fair? At the moment he is about to hand you the keys, you say, "Of course, of course. Anything you say, Dad! Absolutely! Your wish is my command!" While your father is dangling those keys before your eyes, you agree with everything. Yes or no? And what happens next?

Your very intelligent friend gets into the car. "Whoa, can I drive it?" And you say, "Sure, brother, just do not tell my dad." He is driving, and your friends in the back seat are taking a picture. The genius is taking selfies as he drives the car. And then one day your father works it out. The world has moved on, and he actually does open a social media account, and he figures out how to add you as a friend, and your friends as friends, and he ends up seeing the picture. Is he disappointed? Yes, he is. "Look! I did not ask you for much. I only asked for these simple two hundred things. How could you not manage even that?" Does he have the right to take the car away at that point? You may cry and complain all you wish. It is not fair. It was not my fault. You are so cruel. Boo hoo. But the point is this: you are the one who broke the rule. You are the one who violated it, and so he has the right to do what? To take the car away.

Now, has Allah given us a car? Consider this. You realize that your father has done one thing for you. Your mother has done more things for you. How many things has Allah done for you? Allah says, I will give you five fingers on each hand; use them wisely. I will give you two nostrils. I will give you working lungs. I will give you a heart that beats. I will give you two legs, and every toe on each leg. I will give you a stomach that works. I will give you a chest. I will give you bones, bones that do not break upon contact. There are people, by the way, who have very brittle bones. They can break very easily. Even a handshake can break their hand; an ordinary handshake can break the bones in their hand. I know a family like that; their child has this condition. Even as a baby, if you tried to hug him, you would crush his ribs. He is very delicate.

The idea is this: you were given certain things. Did you pay for them? Now, when your father was handing you a car, what were you saying to him? He has not even handed you the keys yet. You are simply looking at the car, and he is dangling the key, and you are saying, "Thank you, Baba. Thank you, Baba. Thank you so much." Are you not thanking him? First, you are thanking him. And you are also looking at the car and saying, "Wow, that is so wonderful." You are praising it. You have not taken the keys yet, and already you have two feelings: praise for the car, and gratitude toward your father. Is that true?

Allah is doing a great many things for you. A few things, or many things? Many things that you notice, and, beyond that, many things you do not even notice. Far more than you could ever notice. And is He doing it once, or constantly? So He is doing a great deal for you and for me, constantly. Now, if He is doing so much, is it possible that He expects something from me? Is that possible? Because when someone gives you something, does it not sometimes come with expectations? Your mother gives you a great deal of love. She gives you breakfast. And you behave as though you were three years old at home.

"Mother, I am so hungry," and your mother answers with tender, cooing nonsense. But at the very least, what do you owe your mother? Even if she expects nothing, you, as a decent human being, born with basic decency, owe her something. Some gratitude? Some respect? Some consideration? When she calls you the first time, do you show up? You owe her something. And that is if she expects nothing at all. What if she does expect it? Would she be acting absurdly? Of course not. And is that asking for much, or for little? Now, if you are an indecent human being, that is a different matter; then the praise is not for you. But as a decent human being, that is the very least you could do for your mother: show gratitude. Do you agree?

Similarly, human beings did not need to have color. This earth did not need to be beautiful for us to live here. It could have been completely flat. We would have survived just fine if this world were not beautiful. But are there sceneries in this world that are absolutely stunning? Are there flowers that are incredibly beautiful? Are there waterfalls that are simply breathtaking? These beautiful creations of Allah inspire us to make beautiful designs and decorations. The entire fashion industry is inspired by flowers; they use floral patterns. The colors of the sunrise, of the sunset — they are inspired by the colors of the sky, by the patterns of clouds. Million-dollar chandeliers are designed after snowflakes. SubhanAllah! Why did there need to be beauty? We could absolutely have survived without beauty. But it is a gift, to His slaves from an amazing Master.

Fragrance. Why do we need fragrance? There are expensive perfumes, inspired by the fragrances that exist in the world. Amazing smells. It did not have to be this way. We did not need a good sense of smell to survive. There are people who have no sense of smell, and they survive fine. They live out their entire lives with no problems.

So this Master did not just give us life; He made life beautiful for us. This is something to be appreciated. This is something to be grateful for. Some people, though, are simply not interested in appreciating it. When something bad happens in life, most people say, "How come this happened to me? What did I ever do to deserve this?" Right? But when good things happen to them, they never ask the same questions. They never say, "How come this good happened to me? What did I ever do to deserve this blessing?" But then there are some who do.

And it takes gratitude and praise in the heart to be able to do that. This is the argument of Islam, the argument of the Qur'an: if you feel appreciation for what you see around you, then please read on. But if you feel no appreciation at all, if you are wholly wrapped up in yourself, if nothing is ever good enough for you and all you can do is complain, then that is fine — only do not trouble yourself to read any further, because you will simply be wasting your time. Good luck to you. I will see you in hell, and the pun is intended. Remember what I told you the last time: the word kafir carries two meanings. It is the one who disbelieves, and it is the one who is ungrateful. So if you wish to be a kafir, go ahead. If you wish to be a disbeliever, that is no problem. Live your life as you please. The Qur'an is not for you. Allah has no need of you.

This is the heart of opening this ayah with al-Hamdulillah. Praise and gratitude belong to Allah whether you choose to praise him or not, whether you choose to be grateful or not — it makes no difference. But a true servant, an obedient servant, a servant of pure essence, sees his master's favors and his gifts all around him and within himself, and he feels praise and gratitude even before he hears the revelation. He becomes a witness to the truth that his master loves him. And this alone sets this master apart from every other master in the world, because no other master will love his servant in this way.

A different kind of slavery

Enough about you and your mother, though. We are speaking about God. Is God constantly at work, day in and day out, day after day, week after week, month after month, year after year, in more ways than you could ever imagine? At the very least, what should you and I have? Some gratitude? Some appreciation for the gifts?

How offensive it is when someone gives you a gift and you complain about it. Suppose I buy my daughter a violin for her birthday, and I hand it to her gladly. Now Erum takes it in her hand, looks at it, and tells me, "Babu, you know there is a better version of this out there." Is that offensive? Yes. It is unacceptable. And if she did that, what would I do with the gift? If I handed her the violin and she said, "You know, there is a better version," what would I naturally do? I would take it away, and then take all the others away too. I am sure there is a better version of all of those as well, my girl! Come on. "No, no, I did not mean it!" If you receive a gift and you do not appreciate it, is it possible that the one who gave it grows angry with you? "You do not appreciate it? Fine. I will give it to someone who does." Is that not true?

I have spent my life failing to appreciate a great many things God has done for me. I am not speaking of you now; I am speaking of myself. I have spent my life not appreciating, not even noticing, a whole host of things God has been doing for me. I have never thanked Him for them. I never even realized them. Does God not have the right to be a little upset with me? "You ingrate! Do you know how much I do for you, constantly? Do you think you make your own heart beat while you are sleeping? Do you think you make yourself breathe? Do you think you make the neurons in your brain fire? Do you think you are the one who keeps yourself from being paralyzed, blinded, sick, dead? Do you think you do that? Let me teach you a lesson. Oh, you love basketball? You love football? Let me teach you a lesson. Let me make you trip, fall, injure your spine, and then spend the rest of your life in a wheelchair. Oh, you love playing video games? Let me teach you a lesson. Let me take those eyes away. Let me take those fingers away."

Can God do that? Yes, of course. But does He do it? No. I am ungrateful, and I go on playing, and I go on enjoying life, and He keeps on giving. He keeps on giving, and He keeps on giving. Is that not true?

Now, the thing is that He is not merely giving you all these gifts and the things you enjoy—health, strength, money, clothes, your friends, all of it. There is another dimension to this. The next realization is this: if God is giving me everything, if God is giving me everything that I have, then what about myself?

Please stop and think for a moment. What about myself? Do I own my own self? Did I create myself? Did I decide what I would look like? Did I decide that? Did I decide what color my eyes would be? How large my nose would be? Did I decide any of that? Did I decide my own personality? I did not. Not only are all the things around me given by Allah—I myself have been created by Allah. Do you realize that? Do you know what that means? It means that I am property. I am property. I have an owner.

I want you to understand the logical progression here. The first realization is that everything around you is owned by Allah, and He gave it to you as a gift, so that you could be grateful and could appreciate it. Then you realize it is not only everything around me. It is also me, myself. I am not, in truth, a product of myself. I have been created by Him. He does not merely own the things around me; He owns me as well. And when someone owns someone—I will say that again—when someone owns someone, that person is called Rabb, which means master, owner, the one who has complete authority. And after I realize that, I understand that He is not only my Rabb. He is the Rabb of whom? Of every human being. Rabbil alameen, of all nations, all cultures, all ethnicities, all generations, because all human beings have been given the gifts I have been given, more or less. They have all been given these gifts that come from the same source. He is the Rabb of them all. This is the realization we arrive at.

Now, when I reach this conclusion, it becomes even more frightening. If He is my owner, do I hold some notion of ownership myself? Do I own certain things? For example, I own an iPhone. I had it replaced a few months ago. Some of you know this. I accidentally washed my previous phone in the washing machine and then dried it in the dryer. Twice. Yes, it was that dirty. But then, oddly enough, it stopped working. This happened in the morning. Do you know what I did? I went straight to the Apple Store. I set the phone on the counter. I said, this thing is useless. It does nothing for me anymore. When you and I own something, and it does not do what we want, what do we do with it? We replace it. We toss it in the garbage. It is no good. Let me give you an example from long ago. Long ago, some man owns a goat, and he owns the goat only because he wants goat milk. One fine day the goat stops giving milk. That day he has goat biryani for lunch. Do you understand? When you own something, and it is useless and it does not do what you expect it to do, then, because you own it, you may do whatever you wish with it. Is that not logical?

Now, the relationship I had with Allah was that I was meant to praise Him and thank Him. As Allah's property, that was my original function. That is what I am meant to do. And if I am honest with myself, and I look back over my life, have I been doing that? Not really. Not really. And now I realize that He owns me. What does He have the right to do? Honestly, what does He have the right to do? Replace me with someone who will. Asif, why do you not simply die, and I will replace you with someone who will. Why do I not simply wipe you out, why do I not simply make you extinct? Does He have the power to do that, by the way? Can anyone question Him when He does it? Can anyone change His decision? Can you appeal His decision in a court? When He decides to grant someone death, can you go to a certain court, a certain doctor?

a certain procedure by which you can bring someone back again? I know that Allah has taken him, but is there anything you can do? Is that possible? No. He can take my life today, and there is nothing you or I can do about it. There is absolutely nothing that you or I, all of you together, all the people of the world together, all the people who are present now, who have ever existed, and who will ever exist in the future — all of them together — can do about it. I could weep over it. Well, I could not, for I would be dead; but you could weep over it, and others could complain of it. Even so, there is nothing anyone can do.

And does He have the right to do it? Yes. Would He be just in doing so? Absolutely. Now, if He has the right to do it, and the power to do it, and no one can stop Him, and yet He still does not do it, there are only two possibilities. If He has the right to do this to you and to me, because He owns us, because we are His property, and He does not do it, there are only two possibilities. The first is that we are doing a wonderful job, and this is why He is not eliminating us, or punishing us, or teaching us a lesson the hard way. That is one possibility. The other is that He is so loving, and so caring, and so patient with us, and so willing to give us chance after chance after chance, that His love is far beyond anything we can imagine.

For consider your mother: if you test her patience often enough, she will strike you. Consider your father: if you test his patience often enough, if you push him to his last nerve, he will turn you out of the house. There is no one else who loves you so much that you can disappoint them over and over and over again, and they still hold love for you, and they still wish to give you another chance. That does not happen in relationships. Between a husband and a wife, if the husband keeps making the wife angry and angry and angry, or the wife keeps making the husband angry and angry and angry, what happens in the end? They are divorced. They are separated. There is no other relationship in which, though your entire life you have ignored them, your entire life you have failed to appreciate them, your entire life they asked you to do a handful of things and you disobeyed them, you did not even care to ask or to consider what they might want from you, you did not even acknowledge their presence — indeed, you went so far as to deny their very existence — and yet all they have ever done is good for you, and all they are doing is good for you. They have the right to eliminate you. This can mean only one thing: that He must have a kind of love, a kind of care, that you and I have never seen before in all our lives. This kind of care and love is beyond our imagination, which is why the next words in the Fatiha are al-Rahman and al-Rahim. I translate the word rahma not as mercy but as loving and caring.

Some of us have never known any hardship in life, and so we do not see the value of what we have, for it is human nature to be ungrateful in times of blessing. وَإِذَا مَسَّكُمُ ٱلضُّرُّ فِى ٱلْبَحْرِ ضَلَّ مَن تَدْعُونَ إِلَّآ إِيَّاهُ ۖ فَلَمَّا نَجَّىٰكُمْ إِلَى ٱلْبَرِّ أَعْرَضْتُمْ ۚ — And when adversity touches you, you call upon Allah's help; and when He delivers you from it, you turn away from Him. وَكَانَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ كَفُورًا — Ah, human beings are so ungrateful!

As I said in the previous session, we live in the age of arrogance. We live in the age of ingratitude. We live in a time in which pride and arrogance are celebrated.

and humility and kindness are mocked and laughed at. For we are living in a time when Shaytan has taken the throne. Everything evil has been made to seem beautiful, and everything beautiful has been made to seem foolish. This has now created an even greater challenge for us. First, that we are ungrateful by our very nature. And to make matters worse, we live in an age in which being ungrateful, being obnoxious, and being disrespectful is the fashion of the day. It is considered admirable.

If any of you doubt me, consider the boy in your class whom everyone thinks is the most admirable of all — the one the whole class looks at and says, "He is so impressive!" Everyone wishes to be like him. I assure you, he is the greatest scoundrel among you. He is admired because he defies the rules; he is an outlaw. He is arrogant. He dresses in a manner that makes the homeless appear well kept. He has not cut his hair in six months. He carries about him an air that says, "Do not trouble me, or I will tear your head off." He curses so freely that he makes a sailor seem like a priest. He bullies the weak and delights in seeing them weep.

Or else he is the clown of the class. He makes everyone laugh, has the quickest retorts, and mocks everything and everyone he possibly can, with no respect for elders, parents, or teachers. So he is either the clown or the rebel — or he is both. That is the one all the girls are enthralled by. That is the one you wish to be like. This is the world in which we live today.

And, incidentally, I was not even describing anyone in your class. I was describing someone in my own class, when I was in school in 1847. And I assure you, things have only grown worse. On the other hand, there is the pleasant boy from a good family, always respectful, always kind, always striving to help his friends. In other words, a loser — is that not so?

So the harsh truth is this: we are, by our very nature, an ungrateful people, living in a time of ingratitude. In this day and age, if you wish to do what is right, I assure you it will not be easy. And the difficulty you will face is twofold. The first is your own desires, and the second is the environment around you, compelling you to act upon those desires. For we are the slaves of our desires.

What I want you to understand — the harsh truth I want us all to awaken to, myself included, you children included, your parents included — is that we are all slaves. And the worst of it is that we are slave not to a single master, but to many masters. The proof of this is that a slave has no choice of his own. That is the very definition of a slave: one who has no choice of his own, who is entirely at the disposal of his master's will.

Our first master is our own desires, our own pleasures. When the master commands, we obey. If any of you smoke, you have a master, for when that craving arises, you are unable to refuse it. And if you do refuse it now and again, you cannot refuse it for long. Some people are slaves to their habits. Some are slaves to fashion, unable to refuse the latest trends. Some are slaves to films and television programs.

But the truth is, Islam is not about ease. Islam is—

Not only did He grant him existence, He also created this universe around him, that he might put those gifts to use and delight in the creations around him. We see that Allah gave us eyes, and He gave us sight. But when we come into this world, there are in fact things for us to see. What if we had perfect—

And when someone does so much for you, all of it entirely undeserved.

And unearned. There can be only one possible response to that. We need only to cultivate it. And how do we cultivate it? How do we make it grow? By realizing that we are slaves. We are slaves who deserve nothing at all. And in spite of the fact that we are disobedient slaves — not even obedient, but disobedient — in spite of this, our gracious Rabb, our generous Rabb, constantly favors us with countless blessings, because He loves us, He cares for us, He is concerned for us, and He is merciful toward us. This is the first kind of gratitude: gratitude to Allah.

Now let us speak of gratitude again from another angle. When do you praise someone? When you appreciate or admire something, when you find it breathtaking. Just as you see a beautiful sunrise, a sunset, a snow-covered mountain, a beautiful car, and you praise it. The first thing you want to do is take out your camera and take a picture. Now you may say that if it is these intermediary arbaab doing all the work, then it is the intermediaries and not the Rabb who deserve the praise.

So now, if I ask you, to whom does the plant owe gratitude? It obviously owes gratitude to the farmer. But how? By being grateful to the intermediaries. By accepting and submitting to the rububiyyah — the training, the nurturing — of these elements, they are in fact expressing their gratitude to the farmer. Do you understand? Their gratitude to the farmer will be expressed in only one way: by their doing what they are supposed to do. For if they do not do that — let us say the roots refuse to absorb the water and the minerals, and the leaves refuse to absorb the sunlight — what will be the result? The plant is not going to grow and develop, which will waste the entire effort and the entire plan of the farmer, will it not?

Now, does the plant see the farmer? Does it know anything about the farmer? Does it know that the farmer is its true Rabb? No. Who is the Rabb from the plant's point of view? The soil, is it not? The soil, the water, the sunlight, the fertilizer, the minerals from the earth — all of these things are making it grow. The plant has absolutely no knowledge of the farmer. What farmer? To the plant, it is the natural elements, which are a series of causes and effects, that are making it grow. What the plant then fails to see is the design, the planning, and the control that are being carried out at each and every stage of its nourishment.

So now the question is, to whom does the plant owe gratitude? Obviously it owes gratitude to the natural elements — soil, water, sunlight, and so on — because they are the immediate benefactors of the plant. But to whom does the plant, in the truest sense, owe its gratitude? Obviously to the farmer. Why? Because even though the causes and their effects, such as soil, sunlight, and water — even though these intermediaries have the potential to make the plant grow — whose design and control, working behind the scenes, actually made it grow? The farmer's. If the farmer put the seeds in the ground and simply walked away, the soil would still be there, the water would still be present in the world, the sunlight would still be available to the world. But would all these things make the plant grow? Of course not. Even though they all have the potential, the capacity, to make plants grow, without the farmer none of these causes would have mattered. Correct? So the plant owes two kinds of gratitude. First, to the immediate causes, the intermediaries in the seen realm.

The next point is that slavery is always for the benefit of the master. Is it not? Throughout history, human beings have been enslaved — but for whose benefit? For the master's benefit, or the slave's? Always for the master's benefit. Is that not true? Yet is our servitude for the benefit of Allah? Does he have any need of us? Does he actually need our prayers, our efforts, our gratitude? No.

وَمَن يَشْكُرْ فَإِنَّمَا يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ

Whoever is grateful is truly being grateful only for his own sake. He benefits no one but himself.

وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌۭ

And whoever is ungrateful — then surely Allah is free of all need, and he is praised in and of himself. This master has absolutely no need of servants. He does not need our servitude. We accept him as our master, but for whose benefit? For our own. Servitude to Allah benefits us, and us alone. It does not benefit him in any way whatsoever. Indeed, it is out of his mercy, his rahma, that he accepts us and allows us to become his servants. Only consider the difference between us and him. How wretched and lowly we are before his glory and majesty. The very best efforts we have ever made in our lives — the best salah we ever prayed, the best fast we ever kept, the best zakat we ever gave — are they equal to his standards? Are they worthy of his rank? Of course not. And yet does he still accept them? Is he still pleased with our wretched efforts? Does he store up an immense reward for us in return? He does. And this too is unheard of when you think about what slavery is.

Then again, every other form of slavery we know of — is it voluntary or involuntary? Throughout history, have you ever heard of anyone regarding slavery as a profession? You know, I am not really sure what I want to become in life. I could go into medicine, I could become an engineer, or I could try slavery — that sounds like a noble profession, something I might explore. Does anyone ever think in this way? No. People are captured and forcibly sold into slavery, with no choice of their own.

Is this not so? But what of Allah? Does He force us into becoming His slaves? Consider first: could He force us? Does He have the power to compel us into submission? The One who has forced the galaxies into submission — does He not possess the ability to force us as well? And yet, does He?

And who is it that pays money to buy a slave? Every slave has a price, does he not? Even in former times, a master would have to go to the local store — Slaves R Us — and purchase a slave. There was always a price involved. But in this case, who pays the price? The slave does. We do. We are the ones who pay the price to enter into Allah's servitude. It is incredible. In every other slavery in the world, the master purchases the slave. But this عبودیۃ to Allah (Azza Wa Jal) — we desire it, we labor for it, we strive for it. We pay the price to become His slave. He does not hold a gun to our head.

لَآ إِكْرَاهَ فِى ٱلدِّينِ ۖ قَد تَّبَيَّنَ ٱلرُّشْدُ مِنَ ٱلْغَىِّ

There is absolutely no compulsion in religion. True guidance has been made clearly distinct from falsehood. The choice now rests with you. It is free will. If you wish to become My obedient slave, of your own free will — فَضَّل, you are most welcome. If you do not wish to become My obedient slave, if you would rather remain a slave of your nafs, then go right ahead. It is truly amazing when you reflect upon it.

Then consider: for every other slave, in the worldly sense, the title of "slave" is an insult. It is a dishonor. But to a believer, being Allah's slave is the greatest honor there is. What is the title bestowed upon the greatest man who ever walked the earth? اشھد ان محمد عبد و رسولہ. The Messenger of Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) devoted his entire life to earning this very title: "Abd," slave. It is the greatest honor that is humanly possible.

You tell me — not even as a Muslim, but simply as an objective individual — did the slavery of the Messenger of Allah honor him in this world, or dishonor him? He is the most honored individual in the Islamic world, and he is respected everywhere, even by non-Muslims. Why did he receive this honor? Because he became the slave of Allah. Indeed, this slavery to Allah honored him so greatly that it elevated him to become such a master himself that Maulana Ali said: انا عبدٌ من عبید محمد. I am a slave from among the slaves of Muhammad (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). Only imagine that.

The Messenger of Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) is the slave of Allah, and of him Maulana Ali proudly says: I am one of the many slaves of Muhammad (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). Maulana Ali considers himself honored to be called one of his slaves. Only think what a beautiful slavery this must be. Do not confuse this slavery with the slavery of the world. This is a slavery that people have begged and pleaded for. Consider Maulatina Fizza. She was an actual princess, the daughter of a king, true royalty. She gave up her palace and all her riches to become the slave of Maulatina Fatima (salawaatullah Alayha). Consider Maulana Qambar. He gave himself over to the slavery and service of Maulana Ali. So many times Maulana Ali set him free, yet he would not leave his side. He would not give up his slavery, because Hazrat Qambar knew that he was not the slave of just anyone. He knew who his master was. He was the slave of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he took great pride in it. In fact, there is this one incident — I am straying a little from my subject.

but I suppose it is relevant to what we are discussing. It is narrated that one day one of those people in Kufa who held Maulana Ali in contempt saw Hazrat Qambar walking down the street. He knew that Qambar was a slave of Maulana Ali, and he thought to himself, "Let me humiliate Qambar in public today." So he called out to Maulana Qambar in the marketplace, in front of everyone, and said, "O Qambar! انت عبداً؟ O Qambar! Are you not a slave?" For slavery is considered a disgrace, an insult. And so he said to Qambar, "Are you not a slave?"

Maulana Qambar turned to this man and answered, "Indeed I am a slave. But do you not know whose slave I am?" And then he began to recite this praise of Maulana Ali. It is beyond words. The sheer beauty of it is something one cannot fully take in. He goes on and on:

أنا مُوَلِّى من ضرب بسیفین . و طعن برمحین . وصلى القبلتین . وبایع البیعتین . وهاجر الهجرتین . ولم یکفر بالله طرفة عین. أنا مُوَلِّى صالح المؤمنین . ووارث النبیین . وخیر الوصیین . وأکبر المسلمین . ویعسوب المؤمنین . ونور المجاهدین . ورئیس البکائین . وزَین العابدین. وسراج الماضین . وضوء القائمین . وأفضل القانتین . ولسانِ رسولُ رَّبِّ العالمین . وأَوَّلُ الوصیین من آل یس . والمؤید بجبرئیل الامین . و المنصور بمیکائیل المتین . المحمود عند أهل السماء أجمعین . والمحامی عن حُرُمِ المسلمین . والمجاهدُ أعدائُہُ النَّاصبین . وأمینِهِ على المخلوقین . وخلیفةُ مَن بعث إلیها أجمعین . سید السابقین . وقاتل الناکثینَ والقاسطین . ومَبیَدِ المشرکین . وسَهمُ مِن مَرامِ اللهِ على المنافقین

And he goes on and on. This is only a small portion of what I remember. He continues for something like fifteen minutes, and every word is so perfect and so wondrous. SubhanAllah! And then, at the end of it all, he looked at the crowd and proudly said, "Which of you has a master like the one I have!" And everyone stood there, utterly dumbfounded and struck with awe.

This is the honor of عبدیۃ, the slavery of a magnificent master. So my point is this: even though the word for abd is slavery, and we are indeed becoming slaves of Allah, this is a completely different kind of slavery. It is unlike any other slavery we will ever come to know. It is an honor above and beyond all honors to become the slave of Allah. And so I thought, in order to keep this distinction in mind going forward, I am going to try no longer to use the word "slave." When I speak of this special kind of slavery, I will try to use the word abd. So when you hear this word abd, I want you to make this separation between the derogatory sense and the honorable sense that I have just explained.

The world operates by rububiyyah. Now let us return to hamd, which means gratitude and praise. I told you there are two kinds of hamd. There is gratitude to Allah, which we spoke about last time. And there is gratitude to the intermediaries of Allah, which I want to speak about today.

If you look at how our physical world operates, you will find every single thing in nature operating beneath the blanket of rububiyyah. If you keep those six definitions of the word Rabb in mind, you will see rububiyyah at work all around you. The heavens have been made a Rabb over the earth. They nurture it and provide it with rain. They bring the dead earth back to life.

ٱعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحْىِ ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا

Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death.

So the sky, the heavens, is a Rabb over the earth, which is to say the solar system. We know that this earth is surviving.

because of the rububiyyah of the solar system. If anything goes wrong with their rububiyyah, it is over for us. Is that not so? Then the earth is a Rabb for all living things. It provides them with food and water. It provides the nourishment that every species needs to survive.

Then, in our everyday lives, you will find rububiyyah in every organized system there is. Take your schooling, for instance. There is a board of education that is a Rabb over these various levels: primary education, middle school, high school, college. Is that not so? Then each one of these acts as a Rabb in its own right over the teachers. Teachers are a Rabb over their students. Parents are a Rabb over their children. Doctors are a Rabb over their patients. Governments are a Rabb over their country. The CEO and the board members are a Rabb over their corporations. Is that not so? So we see that this world operates under the canopy of rububiyyah.

That is the first thing. The next thing to understand is that rububiyyah works through intermediaries, which are the causes and effects required to get the task done. So there are two things to understand. First, rububiyyah is a process designed to provide a systematic and progressive benefit to the marboob. And the second is that the process of rububiyyah is carried out through various intermediaries in order to get the task done.

Gratitude to intermediaries

Let us look at the example of a farmer to understand this better. A farmer, in classical Arabic, is a perfect example of a Rabb, because he is responsible for cultivating his land and growing crops. So he holds ownership of that land and has authority over it. He nurtures the plants, tends them, and waters them. He protects them from insects and animals. He does everything implied by the definitions of the word Rabb. So the farmer is the Rabb of his crops. But does he actually grow the plant? Does he make the plant break out of the seed? Does he actually pull out its roots and spread them in the ground? Does he thrust his hand into the dirt, grab the plant by its neck, and stretch it into a tree? No! He does none of those things.

The way he carries out his rububiyyah is by delegating these responsibilities to certain intermediaries, which are the elements of nature: the soil, the water, the sunlight, the darkness. He controls them, and they in turn fulfill their tasks of raising the plant. Does that make sense? The farmer makes sure the soil has the right temperature. He makes sure water is provided in the right amounts and at the right time. He makes sure enough sunlight is provided, but not so much that it burns and kills the plant. He makes sure he uses the right fertilizer for the right kind of plant. Do you understand? So the farmer, as the ultimate Rabb, carries out his rububiyyah not directly but through these intermediaries. He does not interact with the plant at all. Who does he interact with? Whom does he influence? Whom does he work upon? The intermediaries, which are the soil, the water, the sunlight, the minerals. They are the ones doing all the work, under his guidance. But in terms of intention, whom is it that the farmer wants to benefit? The plant, right? His goal is the development of the plant. He is working on everything else so that the plant may receive the benefit.

Now the question is, these plants, these crops, whom should they be grateful to? Should they be grateful to the farmer? Or should they be grateful to the intermediaries?

Let us think about it. Granted, these intermediaries — soil, sunlight, water, minerals, fertilizer — no doubt they hold the potential and the ability to make the plant grow. But was that potential enough without the farmer's design and control? Suppose the farmer simply dumped the seeds into the ground, stamped on them a few times, and walked away. The soil is still there, the water is still there, the sunlight is still available. Would all these things, on their own, make the plant grow? No. Of course not. They all hold the potential, the capacity to make plants grow; but without the design and the control of the farmer, none of these intermediaries would be able to benefit the plant. Correct? Very well. Fair enough. The plant owes its gratitude to the farmer for its growth and survival.

But then, would that growth have been possible if the intermediaries had not done all the hard work they did for the plant? Had they not labored for the plant day in and day out, week after week, month after month, would the plant have been able to grow? Absolutely not. And so the plot thickens. To whom is the plant to be grateful now?

What we are learning here is this: even though the plant owes its gratitude, its hamd, ultimately to the farmer, justice dictates that it is not possible to be grateful to the farmer without first being grateful to the intermediaries, the asbaab, the wasaayel, that the farmer put in place for the plant. Because it is the intermediaries the plant deals with, not the farmer directly. So it must first be grateful to the intermediaries. And what does that mean? What would the plant's gratitude be? To accept and submit to the intermediaries, so that they may benefit it. There is a relationship here, is there not? The intermediaries are now the master, and a master needs an abd to complete the relationship. So the plant must complete the relationship by submitting to these intermediaries, allowing them to benefit it. That would be the plant's gratitude to the intermediaries, and that would be the plant's gratitude to the farmer.

Listen to this carefully. In this plant metaphor, the plant can only be grateful to the farmer by being grateful to the intermediaries. The plant's gratitude to the intermediaries — the plant submitting to the intermediaries, allowing the farmer to do what he intends to do — is its gratitude to the farmer.

Be grateful to the intermediaries, in order to be grateful to the Rabb.

Chain of gratitude

Now let us look at an example closer to home. For us human beings, when it comes to Rububiyyah, the closest thing we have in the seen realm, right in front of us, is our parents. So now, as decent human beings, we recognize that our parents, and especially our mothers, have done an enormous amount of good for us. Basic human decency dictates that we be grateful to our mothers — not as a Muslim, but simply as a decent human being. Why? Because she almost died giving you birth. She nearly killed herself so that you and I could be alive. That is no small thing. You and I would not be breathing right now if our mothers had not bled for us. That is simply a fact. So basic decency dictates that we be grateful to our parents, and especially to our mothers.

Now when I say I truly want to thank my mother, I truly want to be grateful to my mother, I realize.

that my mother was not opening up her stomach and placing spoons of food into my mouth. Something automatic was happening inside her, so that when she ate, I was fed. It was all being taken care of automatically, for me, within her. There was a predictable, systematic design of cause and effect unfolding inside my mother's womb, and it was feeding me, developing me, and allowing me to grow. All of that came from the nourishment reaching me through my mother. Which means that if my mother had not eaten, I would not have been fed. Is that not so?

This means that in order to be truly grateful, I must now also be grateful to the one who was feeding her, so that I could be fed. Perhaps she did not have the means to earn money at that time. Perhaps it was my father who earned the money that bought the groceries, which fed her, which in turn fed me. So perhaps I should thank my father, who was providing food for us both. So now I do not wish to thank only my mother, but my father as well, for earning that living. But then I consider my father and my mother, and I realize that my father would not have earned this living had he not received a good education, which my grandparents most likely arranged for him. Because it was that education that led him to earn a living, so that my mother could eat, so that I could receive food. Do you see what I am doing here?

So now I realize that I must be grateful to my grandparents as well, on both sides, for the food I am receiving in my mother's womb. Do you understand? But then I realize that my grandparents exist only because their parents existed and raised them, who then raised my parents, and so on. So now perhaps I should thank not only my parents, but also my grandparents, and their parents, and their parents, and so on. Because if all of that had not happened, I would not be having this meal in my mother's womb. Do you understand?

When you truly begin to think about thanking someone — and I mean truly feeling grateful for someone — does it end with the person you are about to thank? For they could not have done what they did for you if someone else had not done something for them. And if you go further back, whoever did something for them, someone else must have done something for them. And you keep going back. And if you are truly, truly grateful, then you realize: this all had to begin somewhere. It all had to begin somewhere. And that is how you reach whom? You reach Allah!

I am grateful for being born of my parents, who are grateful for being born of their parents, who are then grateful for being born of their parents. And it keeps going back until you arrive at the first parents, who are Adam and Hawwa (Alayhim AlSalaam), who were grateful for being created by Allah. So it all goes back to Allah.

When I was inside the womb, which was my entire world, my entire universe, within that world I was cared for by a process of rububiyyah, working through causes and effects, which was designed by Allah. Now that I am outside the womb, in the real world, I am still cared for by the same design, by the same process of rububiyyah, working through causes and effects. So when you think about true gratitude, it is not merely gratitude toward the person right in front of you; it is also gratitude for all the causes and effects set in place, so that this benefit could reach you. And when you truly reflect and trace that chain back, the one you find.

HOLDING this rope is Allah, Azza wa Jal. This is in the physical sense — physical rububiyyah. Now let us talk about spiritual rububiyyah. I am grateful to my teacher, my spiritual Rabb, Javeed bhai, who taught me everything I know today. I am truly grateful to him, because I owe my spiritual existence to him. But I cannot be truly grateful to him until I am grateful to his teachers, who taught him. Why? Because had they not taught him, I would have remained ignorant.
