Another gift is that Allah made it obligatory upon the Muslims to remember the Prophet and to send praises upon him (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). So a believer is forever looking for occasions to do so. But that is not all. Allah himself sent his praises and blessings upon his beloved Prophet: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ وَمَلَٓئِكَتَهُۥ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِىِّ. Without doubt, even Allah and his angels send praises upon his messenger without ceasing. يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ صَلُّوا۟ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمُوا۟ تَسْلِيمًا. So you who have believed, you must understand this, and you too must send praise and blessings upon my beloved messenger.

And there is something truly remarkable about this verse. There are so very many verses in the Qur'an in which Allah begins with يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟. But in this verse he did not begin that way. Allah did not begin by saying, "O you who have believed." He began by first speaking of himself and his angels, and then he said, يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟. Why? Because he is saying, I want you to understand that what I am commanding you to do is something I do myself, and my angels do it too. How, then, could the mention of this magnificent messenger fail to be raised up? And this is why we never say his name, Muhammad, without saying (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). For Allah curses the one who says the name of his beloved without praising him.

Then Allah swears by the city in which he lives: لا اقسم بھذا البلد. He swears by the city in which the messenger is born. He honors the city of Mecca. Why? وأنت حلٌّ بھذا البلد. For no reason but you, my beloved messenger, because you are living in it.

Then another gift from al-Kausar. Allah says, الم نشرح لک صدرک. Did we not open your chest for you? And what a magnificent opening, that the entire Qur'an can fit within it — the same Qur'an that would have shattered and split apart the mountains had it been revealed upon them. لَوْ أَنزَلْنَا هَذَا ٱلْقُرْآنَ عَلَىٰ جَبَلٍۢ لَّرَأَيْتَهُۥ خَشِعًۭا مُّتَصَدِّعًۭا مِّنْ خَشْيَةِ ٱللَّهِ. Yet this same Qur'an fits within the heart of the messenger.

Another wondrous gift to the messenger of Allah is an obedient servant like Maulana Ali. When the messenger of Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) had to migrate to Madina, he needed a decoy.

He needed someone to sleep in his bed while he himself escaped to Madina, and Maulana Ali alone agreed to do it. This was the very night on which the kuffar were plotting to assassinate the messenger of Allah. Maulana Ali knew this, and even so he chose to sleep in his bed that night. Long afterward he confessed it. He said: I swear, never in my entire life did I sleep as peacefully as I slept that night of the Hijra upon the bed of the messenger of Allah. Consider that. Men were coming to kill him, and he says that he never slept more peacefully than on that night — that it was the finest sleep of his whole life. What a gift, to have a servant like Maulana Ali.

My grandfather, Mulla Shafaqat Hussain, refers to this event in one of his poems. He says:

شب حجرت شجاعت کی، علی کی دیکھئے منظر
نڈر ہو کر باطمینان سوئے تان کر چادر
گواہی دے رہا تھا یہ رسول اللہ کا بستر
علی حیدر، علی صفدر، علی داور، علی یاور
علی ایماں ، علی قرآں، علی سلطاں ، علی آقا

Then another gift is the unbroken chain of the Imamat that will come from the progeny of Maulana Ali and Maulatina Fatima. The messenger of Allah compared these Imams to the ark of Noah:

مثل اهل بيتى فيكم . كمثل سفينه نوح
The likeness of my household among you is as the likeness of the ark of Noah.

من ركبها نجا . ومن تخلف عنها . غرق وهوى
Whoever boards it is saved, and whoever holds back from it drowns in this ocean of ignorance and is destroyed.

And the door to that ark is the Ahad Shareef. Through the Ahad Shareef we come aboard this ship of the Imamat. The Imamat is the guarantee of salvation for his Ummah — another remarkable gift.

There are thousands upon thousands of such gifts recounted in the Qur'an and the hadith. They are beyond counting and beyond price — gifts that Allah bestowed upon His beloved messenger, and in most cases without his even asking.

Consider how many prayers Ibraheem AS made concerning the qibla. Day and night he prayed to Allah to make Bait al-Maqdis the qibla for the believers, to turn the hearts of the people toward it, and to make it a place full of virtue and a place of peace:

وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَهِۦمُ رَبِّ ٱجْعَلْ هَذَا بَلَدًا آمِنًۭا وَٱرْزُقْ أَهْلَهُۥ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَتِ مَنْ آمَنَ مِنْهُم بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْآخِرِ

He made so many prayers, and after all those requests Allah made Masjid al-Aqsa the qibla for Ibraheem AS and his followers.

But when Allah changed the direction of the qibla from al-Aqsa to the Masjid al-Haraam, do you know why He did it? He explained His reason in the Qur'an, and that reason was this. Listen to it:

قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
My beloved messenger, We have seen your face turning toward the sky,

فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةًۭ . تَرْضَىٰهَا
and so We are turning you toward a qibla that will please you. There is no doubt about it.

فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ — We swear that We will surely turn the qibla toward you. Why? Simply because you looked at Me with that longing in your heart. Subhan Allah! He did not ask Allah. He did not pray to Allah. He made no dua. He only had a sorrowful look in his eyes, and he looked toward the sky, and in that very instant the ayah came down: See, We are changing the qibla. تَرْضَهَا — to make you happy. تَرْضَهَا — so that you would be pleased. Subhan Allah!

This single act — that the messenger of Allah looked toward the sky with a longing for the qibla to be changed to the Bait al-Haraam — changed the whole history of the world. Billions of people today pray in a different direction for one reason alone: تَرْضَهَا.

So that a smile might rest upon the face of the messenger. (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam.) This is a remarkable thing to appreciate: the love that the Creator holds for His beloved messenger.

Prayer is an expression of gratitude

Now, when Allah bestows such gifts upon His beloved messenger, how do you imagine the Messenger of Allah must have felt? What did we say is the natural response of any decent human being to a blessing, however small it may be? Praise and gratitude. Is that not so? Then what would you imagine the response of one like the Messenger of Allah would be for something like al-Kausar? Immense praise. Immense gratitude. Is that not so?

But how is he to express that gratitude? How can a humble, incapable servant — an ‘abd, a slave — express his gratitude to so benevolent, so merciful, so self-sufficient, so loving a Lord? For the gratitude must be acceptable to the benefactor, must it not? When someone does something extraordinary for you, what is your reaction toward that person? Tell me what I can do for you in return. You tell me what will make you happy, for there is no way I can conceive of repaying you for this. Please tell me if there is anything at all in the world that I can do for you. Does that not happen?

In history we learn that when people were granted an audience with the king, they would bring costly gifts — jewels and precious stones, or something of great historic worth — to win his pleasure. Why was that? It was to show appreciation and gratitude for that audience, for the chance to stand before the king. And plainly the gift, the gratitude, had to reflect the rank, the standing, the position of the king.

So how are we, as servants, as slaves, to express our gratitude to the King of all kings, to the Lord of all lords? And now the Messenger of Allah must show gratitude not for just any gift; he must show gratitude for al-Kausar — for uncountable, priceless blessings, each one better than the last. So who can possibly dictate the terms of that gratitude? Who is to tell him what measure of gratitude will be acceptable to Him? Plainly, Allah must set those terms. O Allah, with all that You have done for me, what can I now do to express my gratitude to You? A praise and a gratitude that would be acceptable in Your eyes? And Allah answers that very question in the next verse, as the surah continues.

فصل لربک ونحر

We have given you al-Kausar. We have given you gifts more precious than all the treasures and sovereignty of this world combined, with all its assets and all its wealth. So now, what do you do to express your gratitude? You establish salaah for your Master. You present your appreciation and your gratitude to your Lord. How? فصل لربک ونحر. Establish salaah for your Lord, and sacrifice — sacrifice being a reference to Hajj, when we must sacrifice an animal.

Once again, Allah joins two ends together. Remember, I explained to you before, He said: اشکر لی ولوالدیک — be grateful to Me and to your parents. He joined two ends together. Allah is at the furthest end for us; parents are at the nearest end for us. So He mentions the two intermediaries, but the implication is: and all the intermediaries in between. This is a characteristic style of classical Arabic. Here too He says: فصل لربک ونحر — prayer, which is obligatory every single day, five times a day, and Hajj, which is obligatory only once in a lifetime. You wish to praise Me and to be grateful to Me?

Then establish the prayer, which is due every single day, and the Hajj, which comes once in a lifetime, and everything that lies between them. So the seven دعائم are the form that the Messenger of Allah set for us in which to express our gratitude to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, and it begins with the prayer. FA is a connective particle in Arabic. It is used to show a response: I did this for you, so you do this for Me. إِنَّآ أَعْطَيْنَكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ — We gave you al-Kausar. ف — so — صل لربک ونحر — pray to your Lord and sacrifice.

And we know that anything the Messenger of Allah is taught in the Qur'an, that teaching applies to us automatically, because he is the intermediary through whom Allah speaks to us. He did not only give the Messenger of Allah al-Kausar; He gave us al-Kausar as well. What greater blessing could there be for us than the Messenger of Allah himself, sallallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam? Through this man we received the Qur'an; we received the means of our salvation, the recognition of our Master, his love, his mercy, protection from the fire, and the promise of paradise. And then the gift of Maulana Ali, and the panjatan, and the Imams and the duaat, and the manaseeb, teachers, parents. And so, even when we look into our own lives, we find within us countless, priceless gifts. This is why Allah mentioned the rule in Surah al-Kausar. You feel grateful? Then the prayer, and the Hajj, and everything between them.

Heart, tongue, limbs

With this understanding, I now want to take a more detailed look at Hamd and explain its various forms of manifestation within us as human beings. All of human activity is divided into three parts, or three components. First is the heart, which is where intention (نیت), will (ارادہ), and belief (ایمان) reside. Then we have the tongue, which is called ترجمان القلب, the interpreter of the heart, because it articulates what the heart feels. In other words, the tongue puts forward a claim based on an intention. And then, finally, we have the limbs, which are the tools for action. Action for what? To prove the claim that the tongue made, based on the intention of the heart. I will say it again. The action of the limbs is the physical proof of the claim that the tongue makes about the intention of the heart.

Intention is unseen; it is invisible. It is spiritual in nature. If I am feeling thirsty and I want to drink water, that feeling is something within my heart. There is no way for you to know it, because there is no hard evidence for that intention. But then that unseen intention is given life through a claim, which is speech. So I articulate that feeling to you by saying the words: I am thirsty. Now, through my claim, you have come to know of my intention. But the trouble with a claim is that it can be true, or it can also be false. And that is why the claim then needs to be followed by an action, which serves as solid, substantial proof of what the speech claimed about the intention of the heart. So now, if I am thirsty and I claim that I am thirsty, and then I back that up by drinking a glass of water, my act of drinking water becomes proof that my claim was true and that I really was feeling thirsty. Not only do you become a witness to my act; I myself become a witness to it.

This is why one of the attributes of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is الشھید. And Shahada means two things. It means witness, and it also means testimony. Now, you cannot testify until you have actually witnessed something, correct? So, when it comes to this entire universe, it is divided into two parts.

عالَم الغیب و الشہادۃ. The world that is unseen, الغیب. And the world that is seen, الشہادۃ. Allah exists in a realm that lies beyond both the spiritual and the physical worlds, because He is the creator of both. From that unseen realm He puts forth certain claims about Himself, about His essence and His attributes. How? Through the Qur'an. Through this revelation.

Why is it called revelation? Because it reveals to us what is hidden from us. And so Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is making claims about Himself. I am Rahman. I am Rahim. I am Azim. I am Ghafur. There is a reward for good deeds. There is a punishment for bad deeds. I will reward you. I will punish you. He is revealing Himself and His intentions to us through this Qur'an, which serves the purpose of a tongue. Because that is what the Qur'an is. It is speech. It is a لسان. A language.

وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ ‏وَإِنَّهُۥ لَتَنزِيلُ رَبِّ ٱلْعَلَمِينَ نَزَلَ بِهِ ٱلرُّوحُ ٱلْأَمِينُ عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ لِتَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُنذِرِينَ بِلِسَانٍ عَرَبِىٍّۢ مُّبِينٍۢ

So Allah is making all of these claims, revealing all of these things about the unseen world. Where is the proof? What is the evidence for all of these claims? This physical world. The Rabb al-Alameen created this عالَم as a witness and a testimony to His attributes and His existence. And this is what we learned in the session on Alameen. He created the عالَم so that the عالِم could witness the attributes of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, manifesting through His creation, and could testify that whatever Allah is saying through the Qur'an is in fact true. And that truly there is no ilah except Allah. لا الہ الا اللہ.

Allah Himself gave us physical evidence for all of His claims, to set an example for us: that ultimately it is action, and not words or intentions, that holds value. And this is why, if you look at the famous hadith of Rasul Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa aalihi wa sallam, on intentions, what does it say?

انما الاعمال بالنیات

No doubt, actions are based on intentions. There are several meanings of this hadith given by Imam Jafar as-Sadiq, alayhi as-salam. I will explain only one meaning today, the one that is in line with the context of our conversation. انما الاعمال بالنیات. No doubt, if you truly intended something, your actions will prove it.

And what is really interesting is the sequence of the words in this hadith. Which word comes first? Amal, or niyyah? انما الاعمال بالنیات. Amal comes first. But we know that intention happens first, so why is it stated this way? He could have said انما النیت محرک العمل — no doubt intentions drive action. No. He brought action first. Because this physical world is a world of action. It is دار العمل, the house of actions. The akhirah is دار النیۃ, the house of intentions. So anything that will be proven in this world will be proven through action. Therefore, no doubt, action is based on intention. If there is no action, then you have no evidence for your intention, and your claims about your intention are false.

In fact, notice that claim is not even mentioned in the hadith. There is only action and intention. Because those are the two things that truly matter. Claim is merely the middleman, connecting the two. Now, of course, there are cases when we intend to do something and are then unable to act upon it because of certain circumstances. But those are exceptions. The general rule is this: if you truly intend something.

you WILL prove it through your action. So these are the three components of a moral agent. Of any moral agent. The heart (قلب). The tongue, or the claim (لسان). And finally the limbs (جوارح). And in the final analysis, it is the physical act that becomes the clear evidence for a claim that was based on an intention. Just as this physical world manifests and testifies to the realities and truths of a spiritual universe, physical actions testify to the realities and truths of the soul.

The distribution of Hamd across the three components.

So now let us look at Hamd, and how it applies to these three parts of human activity. Hamd begins with the appreciation of a blessing. إِنَّآ أَعْطَيْنَكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ‎. We have granted you innumerable, invaluable blessings, all of which are good. The servant, recognizing these blessings from his Lord, develops an appreciation for them. Where? In his heart. He then articulates that appreciation through his tongue. He says, subhanAllah! What an amazing gift. And then his limbs come into action, in order to receive the benefit of that blessing. This is the process of praise that occurs through these three components: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

So this is how praise takes place before the benefit is received, which motivates us toward the benefit.

Now, once the benefit is received, what is generated in the heart is gratitude for the benefactor. That feeling of gratitude is then articulated by the tongue with words of gratitude. And then the limbs come into action, to take advantage of that blessing, to put that blessing to its proper use. This is very important to understand. Gratitude of the heart is the recognition of a blessing, that someone did something nice for us. Gratitude of the tongue is verbalizing that feeling by saying "thank you." But gratitude of the limbs is actually using the benefit for its intended purpose.

In the last session, we examined *hamd* in fine detail. I explained how appreciating a blessing—praise—makes us desire the benefit it offers. Then, when we benefit from the blessing, we feel the need to be grateful to the one who bestowed it. And true gratitude for a blessing is to use it for the purpose for which it was given. I then explained how *hamd* is divided among the three components of human activity: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. In today's session, I want to step back and speak about how we actually arrive at appreciation. For if we are unable to appreciate something, we cannot praise it, which means we will be unable to benefit from it, and therefore we will never be grateful for it.

The scholars say that the recognition of a blessing begins with knowledge, العلم. And knowledge is defined as understanding the true reality of something, معرفتُ الحقیقۃ. To be aware of the true reality of something is knowledge. Now, appreciation begins with the knowledge of two things: the knowledge of a need, and the knowledge of that which fulfills the need. When these two pieces come together, we develop what is called a true appreciation for that thing.

The scholars then draw a further distinction between superficial appreciation and true appreciation. For example, we know that hunger indicates a need of the body. And we also know that food will satisfy that hunger. That is why we appreciate food as a blessing. Yet, despite that knowledge, why do we waste food? Because we are certain that there will be more food tomorrow. So what if I throw away half of what is on my plate today? I know that I can buy more tomorrow. But if you go to one of these starving countries, I assure you that they do not think in this way. Why? Because, although they have the same need that I have, their resources are very limited. If I skip meals, it is because I am dieting. When they skip meals, it is because they are starving. So to them, hunger is very real, and that is why food is a true blessing to them. But for me, hunger is not a great matter. Therefore food is not a great matter either.

So you can see how need drives appreciation. And you can apply this to every aspect of your life. It holds true for anything in life. You go to school to learn. If that need to learn is real, if you possess that thirst for knowledge, you will naturally appreciate your teachers, and you will appreciate your education, because they are the instruments that can fulfill your need. The same applies to work, to friends, to parents, and it certainly holds true for Allah and His religion.

And so this reality has been placed within the very verse we are studying, الحمد للہ رب العالمین. For whom is the *hamd*? It is for Allah. Why? Because He is *Rabb*. *Rabb* of what? العالمین. Because a *marboob* needs his *Rabb*. Remember our conversation about relationships? Children need parents in order for parenting to take place. Students need teachers in order for learning to take place. A slave needs a master for direction. Every effect needs its cause. So in this verse, *Alameen* is the effect that necessitates the existence of a *Rabb*, a cause. And this is why the *Aleem* created the *Aalam*: to manifest and reflect His attributes, so that we could become aware of the reality that He is our *Rabb*. And this is why, if you look at these three words—*Alam*, *Alim*, and *Aleem*—they all share the same root word, علم.

Now, just as all human activity is divided into three components—the heart, the tongue, and the limbs—knowledge, too, has three levels.

The knowledge of operation, or function. How does a THING operate? How does it function? Then the second level is knowledge of structure. What are the different components involved in the function of this entity, and how do they all come together, in a very particular order, to accomplish its function? And then, finally, there is knowledge of INTENT. WHY? WHY are all these components designed this way? What were the factors that led to the creation of this entity? Why this material? Why this shape? These are all questions related to essential knowledge. INTENT.

From the standpoint of Islamic theology, these three levels are called Islam, Iman, and Ehsaan. But I do not want to get technical. I want to keep things really simple. We will call them Functional Knowledge (which is Islam), Structural Knowledge (which is Eman), and Essential Knowledge (which is Ehsaan).

Let us look at a very simple example to understand this. Let us use my usual example of a phone. It all has to begin with a NEED. So I realize this NEED to communicate with my friends and family. I walk into Best Buy and I explain my need to the salesman. I tell him, You know, I do not know what it is, but I have this strong urge to talk to my friends across the world. And this need is keeping me up at nights. I do not know what to do. Please help me. And so he takes me to the phone section, hands me this rectangular device, and says, THIS is what you need. It is called a PHONE. And I am like, huh? Really? This THING is what will help me communicate with my friends? How do I use it?

Now when I say, How do I use it?, what level of knowledge am I seeking? That is operational knowledge, right?

So he turns the phone on, and he starts demonstrating how this device works. Now when he is teaching me how to use this phone, if we simplify things, what are the broad categories his teachings fall under? The Requisites, the How-Tos, and the Dos and Don'ts. That is it, right?

What are the Requisites? You are absolutely required to charge your phone before you can use it. In order to do that, you have to have a power outlet that uses a specific type of socket, that outputs a certain amount of voltage. You HAVE to have that to use this phone.

Now, once you have gained an understanding of the Shareeah, once you have gained the knowledge of the need to render Hamd, and the knowledge of that which will fulfill your need, which is the Shareeah, you are on the road that will lead you to water. You have a direction. You know what you yourself require, and you know how to interact with others. Once you have perfected the outward form, the next level of knowledge is علم التاویل, the knowledge of Taveel.

This is the knowledge of the components and of what they represent: the Misaal and the Mamsool, the symbol and the one it symbolizes. So, for example, in wudu, why are there certain parts I must wash, and then others upon which I need only perform masah? What does washing symbolize? What does masah symbolize? When I wash my face, why should I place water in my eyes? In Salaah, what does the Rukoo symbolize? What does the Sajda symbolize? What does the Qayaam symbolize? And how are they all connected together? Why does Qayaam come first, then rukoo, then sajda? Why is there one rukoo and two sajda? Why is it that I spread my fingers upon my knee when I am in Rukoo, but bring them together when I am in sajda? All of this falls under the knowledge of Taveel.

The word Taveel means رجع الی الاول, returning to the beginning: how it all started. And how do you do that? How do you reach the beginning? By tracing the symbols back to the ones they symbolize. By decoding the external, physical form in order to understand what it represents in its counterpart, its inner, spiritual form. The external forms are all signs, ayaats, Misaal. They point to the Mamsoolaat. You trace one sign after another, and that is how you arrive at where it all began: the awwal. It is literally a bridge that connects the Shareeah to its purpose. التاویل جَسَرَ الحقائق — Taveel is the bridge that leads to realities.

But if you have not practiced and mastered the external form, how are you going to understand the internal representations? If you do not know the symbols, how are you going to reach the symbolized? You cannot do calculus without first learning algebra, can you? You cannot run until you have learned how to walk; you will fall.

So Taveel connects you to this third level of knowledge, which is the knowledge of the essence, or the intent. It is the knowledge of how it all began and how it will all end. It is the knowledge of pre-existence and of eternity.

What came before this physical universe existed. What the factors were that led to the creation of this physical order. Why all of this came into being. Where it came from. Where it is going. How it will all end. When it will all end. What the realities are of these oceans, these trees, the celestial bodies. All of that is covered by the knowledge of the origin and the return, Mabda and Maad. The Shariah gave us knowledge of the form. Taveel helped us return to the beginning by tracing the components back to their design. Mabda and Maad is how and why these components came into being, why they were made in this way, why they have this form, this shape, and how all of this will return to where it came from.

And then, just as in the study of matter today we can examine things at the molecular level, at the atomic level, at the sub-atomic level, there are also realms of knowledge that explain each composition at an exceedingly minute level. So you have Haqaiq. After that you have Daqaiq. After that you have Haqaiq Alyia. After that you have Daqaiqul Daqaia. After that you have Ifaadaat. So you can see that there is no end to knowledge.

And, by the way, how do you verify all three of these levels of knowledge? How do you prove to yourself that these concepts are not invented, fictitious things? For you cannot use the physical universe to prove them. Mabda and Maad is a realm of knowledge from before physicality even existed. So how do you know for certain that all of this is true? The Quran. Every single thing can be proven from the Quran. Hazrat Zia Ali Sahab used to say: the ignorant man thinks the Quran is merely a book of stories, but the Aalim knows that it is a book of Haqaiq and Daqaiq.

I hope I have given you some clarity on how all of this is organized, and on the importance of a systematic, progressive study. I know many people who have studied a little of this and a little of that, and ultimately a great deal of nothing. This is because they study at random: a little from here, a little from there. So that is what they end up with: random knowledge and confusion. You have to study systematically, but that takes a great deal of patience.

And, by the way, where do these sessions fit into all of this? All I hope to do in these sessions is to show you the way, to bring you from the scorching sands of the desert to the road that will lead you to water. I hope and pray that I am bringing you to the شارع. But there is a long, long road ahead of you. You have to learn the Shariah before you learn Taveel, before you learn Mabda and Maad. It is a long journey. But I can tell you from personal experience, wallahi, it is an amazing journey. Yet I can only bring you to the road. You are the one who has to walk upon it. We all have our own walking to do. And walking is a physical act. It is not a verbal claim, and it is not a good intention. It is physical work.

For those of you who have the time, I want to share four things that have truly helped me improve my salaah. And I hope that, God willing, it does the same for you. The first and foremost is this: remember why you are praying, remember the purpose of this instrument. We appreciate Allah's blessings, and we need to express our gratitude to Him, and the tool given to us to satisfy that need of Hamd is salaah. That is the only reason to pray. But then, while we are perfecting our prayers through daily practice, we also need to make an effort to study Taveel and Mabda and Maad, because what these uloom do is

they increase our conviction in Hamd. They raise the intensity of Hamd in our hearts. They make us more appreciative, more grateful for Allah's blessings. Consider this: from Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) to Maulana Ali, to the Imams, to the Duaat, to the manaseeb, down to us — we are all performing the exact same salaah. But the quality of conviction differs at each level. And what gives strength to that conviction is these higher realms of knowledge. The more you know, the thirstier you will be for Hamd, and the more you will wish to drink from this fountain of salaah. So that is my first recommendation. Study. Make that effort. I promise you it will be a rewarding one.

Begin by studying the Shareeah, and by perfecting the outward. The Shareeah, though it is the most precious thing we possess, is the most undervalued thing in our lives. It teaches us discipline, love, patience, courage, manners, hierarchy, adab. It teaches us all the divine attributes. It was designed and formulated by Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam). He witnessed the spiritual world, and he designed the Shareeah upon that same pattern for us.

The next thing is to understand what you say in salaah. You do not have to be a master of Arabic for that. All the translations are available. I have translated nearly all of the duas for you. Make an effort to understand them sentence by sentence. And to start, begin with your rukoo and your sujood. Slow them down. Some of you pray so fast that I am certain it sets off a hurricane somewhere. No wonder Texas gets so many hurricanes. It is because of your rukoo and sujood. When you go down into rukoo, the person standing beside you is struck by a gust of wind — swoosh. Slow down. At the very least, slow down your rukoo and your sujood. Start there.

Visualize your Hamd while you are in rukoo. Subhana Rabbi alazeem wabihamdih — my Rabb is so perfect and wondrous, and He is worthy of all praise and gratitude. Subhana Rabbiyal Aala wataala — my Rabb is so lofty and so mighty. Reflect on these words. Do this just for your farz; forget the rest. Only farz. That is not much to ask, is it? But reflect on these words. These are extremely powerful words: SubhanAllah and AlHamdulillah. They are the most beloved words to Allah (Subhanahu Wa Ta'ala). Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) said in a hadees:

کلِمَتَینْ. خَفِیفَتَینِ عَلی الِّسَانْ. ثَقِیلَتَینِ فِی المِیزَانْ. حَبِیبَتَینِ اِلَی الرَّحمٰنْ

Two words — کلِمَتَینْ — SubhanAllah and AlHamdulillah. خَفِیفَتَینِ عَلی الِّسَانْ — extremely light on the tongue. ثَقِیلَتَینِ فِی المِیزَانْ — extremely heavy on the scales on the Day of Judgment. حَبِیبَتَینِ اِلَی الرَّحمٰنْ — extremely beloved to the Rehman. And we are constantly repeating these words in our tasbeehaat. So start there, and slowly make an effort to expand outward. Understand the surahs, then the tashahhud, and then expand further. It will help a great deal with your focus. This is the reason we lose focus: because we do not know what we are saying. If I were to begin conducting these sessions in Urdu right now, how long would it take before those of you who do not understand Urdu passed out? A few minutes, right? That is exactly what happens in salaah. We begin with enthusiasm, and then we drift off, because we do not know what we are saying. So that is my second suggestion.

The next thing is to make salaah an event in your life. Salaah, and all forms of worship, are not meant to be an activity.

they are meant to be an experience. We have to learn to experience our salaah. Prepare for it. Think about it in advance. When you wake up in the morning to go to school, do you simply roll out of bed and head out the door? I know that some of you do. But I hope that some of you actually prepare for school. And parents, when you get ready to go to work, you do not simply get up and walk out, do you? You shower, you dress, and then you leave. Because work is a truly important thing, is it not?

Well, consider this: salaah is a far more important thing. Allah, our Rabb, is a most important One. Prepare for Him. Dress for Him. A person who prays in his T-shirt and pajamas clearly does not understand what he is doing. If you do that, especially for Fajr, you have absolutely no idea before whom you are standing and what you are doing. For I promise you, you would not turn up to work and stand before your employer in that outfit — the very outfit you are standing in before Allah.

Some say, "Oh, it is not haraam. It is pure, one hundred percent cotton, so technically I may pray in it." Well, technically it is not against the law for you to turn up to work in your bathrobe and slippers, is it? If technicality is all that matters, then turn up to work like that. You will not be arrested. Why do you not do it? Because you know your employer would not like it; it is disrespectful to him. Now, salaah is not a meeting with your employer, and it is not a meeting with your teacher. It is a meeting with your Creator, your Rabb. Be mindful of that. It will completely change your experience of salaah.

Begin to think about salaah, and begin to prepare for it in advance. Before you start your day, check the timings for all of the prayers, and plan your day accordingly. Make it a priority in your life. It is like anything else in life: if you make it important, it will become important. It is entirely up to you.

And try not to pray late. Pray in the earlier portion of the time. Understand that it is our Rabb who is calling us. What will happen if I turn up to work forty-five minutes late every day and tell my employer, "Oh, you know, the moment I want to leave, my son wraps himself around my leg and starts to cry. That is why I come in late every day. It is so adorable — I will show you a video next time." I do not think my employer will find that adorable. If it makes sense not to keep my employer waiting, then how can it make sense to keep my Master, my Rabb, waiting? So try your best to pray at the earliest possible time. I promise you, it will change your experience of salaah. I understand that it is not always easy to do that, given our work and our ways of living. But at the very least, try to do the best you can.

I always remind myself of this fact: a dog is chewing on a bone. What is the most pleasurable delight in the world to a dog? A bone. Yet when its master calls, it drops the bone and comes running to its master. So how is it, then, that my glorious Master, Rabb al-'Alameen, calls me — حی علی الصلوۃ. حی علی الفلاح — and I simply carry on with what I am doing, ignoring Him completely? May Allah protect me from sinking to a level that would make a dog look better than me.

And finally, measure your salaah by the time you spend when you are not in salaah. This is the hardest part, for all of us. Make an effort to be obedient to Allah. And this is where you will see the effects of your salaah. Every instrument in the world has a definitive result, does it not?

How do I know your knife is working properly? Because it cuts. A microwave is working properly if the food comes out hot. My phone is working properly if I am able to communicate with people. Every instrument has a definitive result. What is the result of salaah? How do you know your salaah is working? Is it some special tingling feeling in your chest while you are in prayer? No, that is heartburn.

Where do the effects of salaah show up? When you are not in salaah. Taqwaa. Consciousness of the presence of Allah in your life. If you are thinking more and more about your Rabb while you are in school, while you are at work; if your sins and your evil actions are constantly eating at you, if they disgust you; if your good actions for the sake of Allah are beginning to please you, then know that your salaah is working. But if, even after praying five times a day, all you are doing is lying, cheating, gossiping, backbiting, hurting people's feelings, using foul language, and watching filth on the internet, then you are not really praying. Even if you are going through the motions, something is very wrong there.

If the power outlet in the wall is working, and the charger is working fine, but the phone is still not charging, where is the problem? The phone battery, is it not? The battery is dead. You cannot show up to salaah with a dead heart and expect salaah to charge it for you. Evil acts and sins, they kill the heart. Allah says: وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ ۖ إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ Establish prayer. There is no doubt about it: salaah prevents you from evil and lewdness. And the word inna is used there, which means definitely, absolutely, without any doubt. Salaah prevents you from evils and shamelessness. So if someone is praying and is still engaged in shameful acts, then they are not really praying.

Second, this is how you use it. This is how you turn it on. This is how you turn it off. This is how you dial a number. This is how you download an app.

Finally, these are the things you do and these are the things you do not do. Keep the phone dry, do not take it swimming with you. It is delicate, so do not use it as a doorstop, do not try to hammer a nail into the wall with it. Keep the phone clean, do not use it as a dinner plate, especially if it is PLUS size. If it gets dirty, wipe it with a clean cloth. You do not have to put it in the washing machine and then the dryer, twice. So that is dos and don'ts.

That is it. Those are the three categories of operational knowledge. The Requisites, how to use it, and the Dos and Don'ts. If you do these things, this instrument will satisfy your need to communicate with your friends and family.

Now we know that, internally, every phone is made up of certain components that are structurally placed a certain way. There is a battery, a circuit board, a camera, a microphone, memory, a CPU. Now these are all completely different, completely independent components. Yet they are arranged in a VERY specific manner, to accomplish one single goal.

Consider how I use the phone. If I change anything in that structure, the phone will no longer work, correct? So all of this is structural knowledge, or knowledge at the level of the components. Now, do I need to know any of this in order to operate the phone? No. I need only the operational knowledge: how to turn it on, how to dial a number, and how to speak. I do not need to know the technical details of how things are working beneath the surface.

Who needs to know details of that kind? The phone-repair man. A technician needs to know them, so that when the phone stops working, he can fix it. That is the level of need at which he operates. He needs to possess the knowledge of the structure: what goes where, and how each individual component works. But you and I do not, because we are operating at the level of the consumer. The repairman, on the other hand, is operating at a higher level of knowledge.

Yet when he makes his calls, in spite of his additional knowledge, does he use the phone in exactly the same way as I do? Absolutely. And at the same time, does he have a far greater appreciation of how the phone works? Of course. He has a far greater awareness of it, and a far greater appreciation for it. Where I will say something like, "Look how beautiful the icons appear on this phone," he will say something like, "These are actually twenty-four-bit pixels being illuminated from a light source at the back, and each pixel is capable of showing ten million colors." Completely different levels of appreciation. My point is this: even though he and I will use the phone in exactly the same way, because of his knowledge of its structure and its components, he can appreciate things about this very same phone that I cannot.

And then there is the designer, the one who actually designed each and every component of this phone. This is the one who designed the circuit board, the camera, the microphone, and the screen, and who then assembled all of these things together in this particular order. Now this one is operating at a completely different level. He has an appreciation of the phone that you and I cannot even imagine. If I say, "Look how beautiful the icons appear on this phone," and the technician says, "These are twenty-four-bit pixels being illuminated," this one says, "Let me tell you why I designed it this way. Why I used twenty-four-bit colors and not thirty-two-bit colors. Let me tell you why I used copper here and plastic there. Let me show you everything I put into place simply to get this one component working. Let me tell you how this technology evolved from where it began, and what I am planning to do ten years from now."

This is the level of intent, where the designer is actually allowing you to enter his mind. And when we understand his thought process, we now have an appreciation such as we have never had before. And who is it that we truly appreciate through our appreciation of the phone? The designer himself, correct? "You are a genius. This is such perfect design. It is astonishing."

But now, when it comes to using this phone, does the designer also use it in exactly the same way as the technician does, and as we do? Absolutely.

So you see, at the operational level, at the level of Islam, in terms of function, we are all the same. We all do exactly the same things. From Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) to Maulana Ali, to the Imams, to the Duaat, to the Manaseeb, we all perform salaah in exactly the same way. At the level of function, we are all the same. But when it comes to the inner realms of knowledge, at the level of structure and of design,

What we are given are ranks, or *maratib*. One technician will know more than another. Yet no matter who knows how much, every level of knowledge exists to serve one purpose, and one purpose alone: the operation of the instrument. Think about it. What was the intent of the designer when he set out to design the phone? Was it merely the design of the phone, or was it its use? It was its use. If he assembled an amazing, mind-blowing design, chose the finest possible material for the components, and arranged them in the best possible way, but no one ever used it, would any of that matter? It would not. So intent and structure are both directed toward a single purpose: use. For it is only the actual use of the device that brings about the benefit. Only by using the phone will I satisfy my need to communicate with friends and family. Do you understand? So if I possess all the knowledge that exists about the phone but never actually use it, I gain nothing from it. On the other hand, if I have only the operational knowledge of the phone and know nothing beyond that, I will still benefit from it, provided I put it to use. In the end, then, it all comes down to action.

Is this not what we said about our own existence? There is the heart, which holds the intent, the highest level of knowledge. Then there is the tongue, which gives the intent its structure. How? Consider a thought, a desire, or an intention. These are all merely mental images; they have no particular structure of their own. But when we speak, we give that intent the structure of words. Is this not what speech is? It is structured words, arranged in a particular sequence according to the rules of grammar. Break that structure, and you can no longer deliver the intent. And finally there are the limbs, which are the tools of operation. They are the dos and don'ts of the intent; they are the prerequisites for executing it. They carry out the intent physically. In the final analysis, it is action, and not words or intent, that is counted as evidence. It is action, and not words or intent, that provides benefit. Is that not so? It is the ability to communicate through the phone, and not its structure or its design, that matters. And yet intent and speech contribute to the strength and the quality of my action. The stronger my intention and the stronger my belief, the more eloquent and the more powerful my speech will be, and that will translate into far greater effort in the quality of my action. So you see, though these are three different things, in essence they are one and the same. When all three combine, when the heart believes, and the tongue articulates what the heart believes, and the limbs act upon what the tongue claimed about the heart's belief, that is when you attain perfection in action. This is why a true believer is defined as the one who unites all three things:

تصدیقٌ بالجنان. قولٌ بالسان. و عملٌ بالارکان

A perfect believer is the one who believes in his heart, articulates that belief with his tongue, and acts upon that belief with his limbs. In other words, there is absolutely no contradiction, no conflict, between his belief, his speech, and his actions. They are all the same.

Now, having understood these levels of knowledge, when we look at the alam, the whole endeavor becomes one of reverse-engineering it. For when we study the alam, what we see is how it works, how it functions. So we study how it operates in order to understand its structure, so that we may understand the intent of the Creator.

Because every thing — شئی — has within it the مشیئا and the منشاء, the WILL and the INTENT of its creator. Think about our phones. We all use them in this particular way because that was the مشیئا and the منشاء, the WILL and the INTENT of their designer. If we reverse-engineer the phone, connecting its operation to the structure of its components, we can determine the will of its designer. The reason everything is structured this way is that this is how the designer intended for me to use it. And then the user manual confirms it.

So the idea is this: study the operations and the structure of this ALAM through the manual of the Quran, in order to understand the INTENT of the رب. Now, when we look at this universe — just like a phone or any other device — this AALAM is made up of many different components. Yet despite these completely disparate components, it acts as a single entity, with one UNIFIED purpose: to serve human beings. And if PRAISE is understanding the purpose, and gratitude is ACTING FOR that intended purpose, then EVERYTHING in nature is in a state of HAMD. Because everything understands its purpose, and it does EXACTLY what it is supposed to do, which is to serve me, to make life possible for me. This is what I learn from my study of how this world operates.

Which then forces me to think: I TOO am a creation, just like them. Therefore I must ALSO have a purpose. I must also have a HAMD. What is my HAMD? What is MY praise? What is MY gratitude? Because I am a fully functioning, fully operational unit, made up of all these independent components. I have not only been given the gift of sight through my eyes; I have ALSO been given the gift of scenery — all the things around me that I can see. I have ALSO been given light, the medium that enables me to SEE things. Again, three things: the ability to see, the objects that CAN be seen, and the medium through which I can see them. Likewise, I have not only been given the gift of hearing; I have also been given the gift of sounds in this world, and the medium of AIR, which enables me to hear those sounds.

I know I did not work for any of these things. Therefore, by definition, they are all gifts. And I realize that all these GIFTS have a very specific structure to them. My eyes sit in the upper part of my face. What if they were in my belly? Would I be able to see the world the way I do today? What if I had one eye on my forehead — would that limit my vision? Because of how they are placed, my eyes give me a linear line of sight with some peripheral vision, but my ears give me access to sounds in a complete circle, 360 degrees, because they are placed on the sides of my head. What if they were placed on my feet, or anywhere other than where they are right now? How would that have worked out for me? And then, why has everything been placed in such perfect balance? EVERYTHING that exists on the sides, inside and outside my body, exists in pairs. And EVERYTHING that exists in the center stands alone. We have one brain, one nose, one mouth, one neck, one heart, one belly button, one genital, because they are all in the center. And everything on the sides exists in pairs, whether internal or external: eyes, lungs, kidneys, arms, feet. Anything on the side — if one side fails, I can still survive using the other. If anything in the center fails, that is it for me. This is INCREDIBLE structure.

Can my eyes see all the way to the horizon? Then why can my ears not hear sounds as far as my eyes can see things? Why can my nose not smell things as far as my ears can hear sounds? Why can my tongue not taste as far as my nose can smell? Why is there this gradual falling away within my senses? Are these faculties placed within me to benefit me or to harm me? There is a book in which Imam Jaffar as-Saadiq explains the design of the human being to his Dai, Hazrat Mufaddal. All of his arguments prove one thing: every creature on this planet has been given exactly what it needed — no less and no more. Any less, and it would have been harmed; any more, and it would have been harmed. There is so much wisdom in this design. I see that everything has been set in place methodically, perfectly, for my benefit.

So now that I realize I have been given so many gifts — gifts that are uncountable, invaluable, and all of them good — انا اعطیناک الکوثر. There is no doubt about it: we have given you Kausar. Why is this Kausar for me? Because I now possess the knowledge of how greatly I need these gifts, and what a disaster it would be if I were to lose even one of them. Forget losing them: how much would I suffer if any of these gifts were merely to deteriorate. Therefore, Allahu Akbar. It is plainly beyond my ability to praise Allah for these astonishing gifts. He is beyond my ability to thank Him for these incredible gifts. So what am I to do now? فصل لربک والنحر. Establish Salaah for your Rabb, and sacrifice.

For the one who realizes the need to praise Allah, for the one who realizes that he has a need to be grateful to Allah — for such a person, these forms of worship are a true blessing, because they help him satisfy that need, that hunger, to be grateful to Allah, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala. But for the one who is ungrateful, for the one who is stuck in the filth of this Duniya, who is stuck at the level of the physics and chemistry and biology of things and cannot see anything beyond that, all he knows is to use these gifts to pursue vain pleasures and chase empty desires.

For the one entirely obsessed with himself — his money, his youth, his beauty, his cars, his business, his children — who believes that he is the author of his own destiny, who believes that he is his own Ilaah, for such a person worship means absolutely nothing. Salaah means nothing to such a person. It is as valuable to him as a phone is valuable to a monkey. Because he has no knowledge. He has no knowledge of his need, and so he will not even bother to look for that instrument which could satisfy his need.

I was speaking with one of the children the other day, and she told me that she is studying at school how nerve endings work, and how these signals are carried to the brain when we touch something. And she said that she turned to her friends and asked: How can this be without design? How can this be evolution? And I felt so happy. I remembered at once that this had come down to us in the hadees of Rasul Allah, Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam, that a disbeliever is bewildered by the creation, but a believer is bewildered by his Creator. الکافر حائرٌ فی المخلوق، والمؤمن حائرٌ فی الخالق. Another child in her class, of the same intellect, the same maturity, receiving the exact same knowledge of design, would stop at the level of the creation; but she saw Allah behind it. SubhanAllah! Because this is what the Rabb al-Alameen wants: for us to study and decode this physical Alam, and to see the Rabb working behind it. So in essence, what Yasu said in her own way is this.

La ilaha illa Allah. How can this be from anyone other than Allah? You know, it is so incredible: how these Arabs, in their eloquence, did not call human beings الحیوان العاقل, the intellectual beings. Instead they called them الحیوان الناطق, the articulating animal, or the animal of reason. Because نطق is also the root word for منطق, which means reason or logic, and we need language in order to reason. We cannot think without language. If you ever catch yourself thinking, you will notice you are using your native language to think in. So they called human beings الحیوان الناطق because of their ability to articulate. Why? Because Allah, Subhanhu wa Ta'ala, granted this ability to speak only to human beings, as a sign. Because if you look at speech, what is speech? It is encoding and decoding. I am encoding my intent. I am taking a meaning, which is spiritual or metaphysical in nature, and I am encoding it into a structure of physical words. You are then listening to those physical words, decoding them, and extracting the meaning from them. SubhanAllah! And this language, this ability to encode and decode, is what we have at the most basic level. Why? Because that is the very nature of this Aalam. It is the Word of Allah. It is encoded in the physical, so that we can decode it, to extract the meaning, the metaphysical, from it, which is the purpose of its creation. Talk about clear signs.

So now if we look at salaah, or any other form of worship for that matter, it is also a physical thing. It is شئی. It belongs to the world of worship. It is from عالم العبادۃ. It is an instrument, and instruments satisfy needs. What is that need it was built for? Hamd. Salaah is the food for the hunger and thirst of Hamd. Our internal need for Hamd is what drives us toward salaah. I cannot emphasize this enough. People ask, why do I need to pray? It is very simple. Are you grateful to your Rabb? Do you feel the need to express your gratitude to him in a way that would make him happy? Then salaah is your answer. It is really that simple.

This is how a believer judges his own gratitude. If you want to know whether you are grateful or not, measure yourself against salaah. Look, whether I want to talk to you or not is determined by whether I use my phone or not, correct? If I really want to talk to you, I will pick up the phone and I will call you. If I am hungry, I will eat. If I am thirsty, I will drink. That is how I know I was thirsty, because I enjoyed the drink. I know I was really hungry, because I enjoyed the food. I know I really wanted to talk to you, because I enjoyed the conversation. If you want to know whether you are grateful to Allah for Kausar or not, see if you enjoy salaah.

I personally feel this is such a blessing from Allah, Subhanhu wa Ta'ala, that he gave us these tools to measure ourselves against. Because we are delusional creatures. We think we love. We think we are just. We think we believe. How do we know for sure? These are the standards that Allah set for us. These are like symptoms for us. How does a doctor diagnose a physical problem? Through symptoms, right? If I have a fever, along with a sore throat and a runny nose, I clearly have diabetes. LOL. Good thing I did not go into medicine. Knowledge of symptoms is such an enormous blessing from Allah. Because if we did not have these symptoms, how would we ever fix the problem, right?

So if I feel this aversion to Salaah, something is wrong with my HAMD. That is what I must work on. This is where people go astray. When someone lacks the motivation to pray, they begin to force the prayer upon him with وعید, with threats of hellfire, with punishment, with pressure, with beating. But does this truly work? It does not, because it does not address the root cause, which is HAMD. The question to ask is why this person is not in NEED of HAMD. What is he missing? For HAMD is the most natural thing for a human being. One need only bring him to it. Once that thirst develops, Salaah becomes nothing more than his natural response to it.

Now let us examine the three levels of knowledge in the context of religion. The first is شریعۃ, which is the knowledge of operation and function, and it is entirely about Huqooq, or Rights. It begins with Huqooq Allah, the Rights of Allah. These are all the forms of worship and the matters that concern the dealings between the ABD and his Rabb.

Then there is Huqooq al-Nafs, the Rights of the soul. These cover such subjects as personal hygiene and the etiquettes of daily life: how to eat, how to sleep, how to speak, what to say and what not to say, how to use the bathroom, what to look upon and what not to look upon, what to listen to and what not to listen to. In short, all the rules that pertain to the body and the soul.

Then there is Huqooq al-Ibaad, Human Rights. These all concern one's dealings and interactions with others. They cover the laws of marriage, inheritance, politics, contracts, trade, economics, judicial affairs, and the like.

It is interesting that this word Shareeah comes from شارع, which means road. But شریعۃ is not merely any road. It is a particular road that leads to water. Imagine the Arabian desert, the scorching heat, the blazing sun, the extremely dry air. What could possibly be the greatest of all blessings for an Arab in the desert? Water. So to them this life, this world, was like a hot, scorching desert, which in their case it literally was. And the Aakhira, or jannah, was like a body of cool water.

Now when you drive along any road, there are laws to be obeyed, for example the speed limits and the right of way. These laws are set by a governing body, and they are all covered by Huqooq Allah. Then you are the one who actually undertakes the journey, so you must apply certain rules to yourself, for example fastening your seat belt, checking your side mirrors and your rearview mirror, making certain your car is clean, well serviced, and well maintained, and that you have filled it with fuel. These are all covered by Huqooq al-Nafs. And then there are all these people traveling beside you on the road. There are rules for interacting with them: the right of way, the slow lane, the fast lane, signaling when you turn. These are all covered by Huqooq al-Ibaad, Human Rights. So to the Arabs, if they followed the Shareeah, if they abided by these three rights, the Rights of Allah, the Rights of the Self, and the Rights of others, it would guarantee that they would all successfully reach the water.

Now everything dictated by Shareeah consists of physical actions. No matter which category of Huqooq you take, they are all physical actions, instruments. This means that they all have prerequisites, they all have their dos and don'ts, and they all have their methods. So if you take Salaah as an example, its operational knowledge would be the understanding of its prerequisites. Taharah is the first prerequisite. Then a complete wudu. These are absolutely required things. If you wish to charge the phone's battery, you must plug the charger into the wall.

You may not understand how or why the charger charges the phone, but you know that it certainly will. Wudu creates that very connection. It plugs you into the spiritual socket. Now, wudu is a thing in its own right, which means that it has its own set of prerequisites, its own methods, and its own dos and don'ts. Then there are the dos and don'ts of Salaah. There are certain things you may do, and certain things you may not. You must recite Surah Fateha, but after that you are free to recite whichever surah you like. You must perform the ruku with its tasbeeh, but then you may extend the ruku with as much further tasbeeh as you wish. You may not look away during the sajda; you may not speak with anyone; you may not read anything. These are all the methods of Salaah. This is how the instrument works. Does that make sense?

Why must I perform Salaah? To express my Hamd. How do I operate this instrument called Salaah? By meeting the prerequisites and following the dos and don'ts. Keep your hands within the janemaaz at all times. It is that simple.

Let us review briefly before we move on to the next verse. Allah says:

إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَآيَتٍۢ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَبِ

No doubt, in the creation of the heavens and the earth — in the creation of the AALAM — and in the conflict between the night and the day, there are signs, Ayaats, for the Ulil Albaab, the people of sound essence, those who possess a sound heart and a sound mind. We have studied that an ayah is something that has a purpose, that has meaning, that has value, and that it is a sign distinct from every other sign. So when such a person reflects on the universe outside himself, and on the universe within himself, what he finds is purpose, and what he discovers is meaning and value.

And how do they see these ayats?

ٱلَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ ٱللَّهَ قِيَمًۭا وَقُعُودًۭا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ

These are the ones who remember Allah constantly, in every state.

وَيَتَفَكَّرُونَ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ

And they reflect constantly upon the creation of the heavens and the earth. This word FIKAR, deep reflection, is an interesting word. It is made up of three letters: FA, KAAF, and RA. These are the very same letters that form KUFR. Rearrange the letters and you get KUFR, which is disbelief, or ingratitude. And we know that words sharing the same letters are connected in their meanings. So in essence, the one who does not engage in FIKR ends up in KUFR, in disbelief; he ends up being ungrateful. The same holds for SHUKR, which means gratitude. It has three letters: SHEEN, KAAF, and RA. Rearrange these letters and you get SHIRK, association of partners with Allah. For if you are not going to be grateful to Allah, you are going to be grateful to some other person or thing. If you are not going to see the MUSABBIB, the cause, you will end up being grateful to the SABAB, the medium through which Allah helped you. And you will end up partnering the SABAAB with Allah in your gratitude. This is one of the six types of SHIRK: ربطُ عَدِیَّاً. This is what western philosophy calls occasionalism: mistaking coincidental occurrences for cause and effect. So if you think it was the medicine that cured you, or the doctor who cured you, that belongs to the principles of KUFR. It was Allah who cured you, using the doctor and the medicine as a means. They are the SABAB.

So these people of essence reflect deeply upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, and they conclude that all of this is not without purpose.

رَبَّنَا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَذَا بَطِلًۭا

Our master, you did not create all of this without purpose. So he arrives at this conclusion by means of his sound heart and his sound intellect, entirely on his own. And then he hears the revelation calling to the very things he has already believed in:

رَّبَّنَآ إِنَّنَا سَمِعْنَا مُنَادِيًۭا يُنَادِى لِلْإِيمَنِ أَنْ آمِنُوا۟ بِرَبِّكُمْ

Master, no doubt we have heard your messenger calling us to Emaan, saying, believe in your master.

فَـَٔامَنَّا

We have already believed.

And then comes revelation, which is the commandments of Allah, and he hears them. The first is to seek Allah's protection from the cursed shaytaan.

To cut out ..... to eliminate the bad so that the good can begin ..... to eliminate the disease so that healing can take place ..... اعوذ باللہ من الشیطان الرجیم ..... In this verse is the explanation of who Shaytan is ..... his story ..... what he did to our parents Adam and Hawwa (سلامٌ علیھم) ..... and what he plans to do to us ..... and how it is ONLY Allah who can protect us from his attacks and from his constant and unrelenting whisperings ..... It includes the lesson of humility ..... of obedience ..... the acceptance of the fact that Shaytan IS in fact a powerful enemy, and therefore we have NO choice but to seek the protection of the سمیع العلیم ..... the all hearer and the all knower, against him ..... Once we are protected ..... once we have submitted ourselves to the protection of Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala) ..... the next thing is to begin our journey toward the recognition of Allah ..... معرفُ اللہ ..... And so the Fateha begins with ..... بسم اللہ الرحمن الرحیم ..... With the NAME of Allah ..... Allah is the name of his essence ..... and of his infinite beautiful attributes ..... which he refracted into this ALAM ..... so that we could recognize him ..... and gain some knowledge about who he is ..... And every attribute that is refracted by the creations of this ALAM he made shared and limited ..... to indicate that he alone is unique and absolute in them ..... From those attributes he separated out Rehman and Raheem ..... The number 1 giving strength to zeros KUFR and FIKAR SHUKR and SHIRK

In the Semitic languages, Arabic among them, all words derive from three-letter roots. Two is the first number in Arabic. Out of two came countless forms. Out of one came two (1+1), and three is the beginning of multiplicity. This is why language, which by its nature is inexhaustible, is built upon three. A whole constellation of meanings arises out of primitive root structures made of three letters.

The word Quran comes from ق ر ی, which means city. And a city creates civilization. The Quran is the image of civilization. The image is this: within the walls of the city there is civilization, and outside there is jungle. It civilized a barbaric people.

Civilizations are normally built upon books. It is worth noticing that the Arabs, ancient as their civilization was, had no concept of the book until the Quran. They had only oral poetry. The Quran was therefore a radical departure from the earlier ideas of knowledge.

Without an oral tradition there can be no written tradition. Orality is the process of becoming human. The Quran is oral before it is a book. QARAA means to recite as well as to read.

Book, KITAAB, comes from the root KATABA, which means to join together.

The Arabs would send their children to the bedouins for training in eloquence. Of the life of the Messenger of Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) up to his fortieth year we know little. He was kind to orphans and to the poor. He was reflective and contemplative. He was a very quiet person. He was sadiq and ameen. He belonged to an aristocratic clan that had fallen on hard times.

He used to go to جبل النور, the Mountain of Lights. There he was engaged in تَحَنُّث, which means to keep away from idols, that is, from polytheism.

In his fortieth year, in the month of Ramadan, he had an angelic experience. An angel came in human form and said اقرأ three times. He answered that he did not know how to read or recite: ما أنا بقاری. So Jibraeel pressed him until he thought his sides would burst.

The angel said: Read in the name of your master who created you from a clinging tissue; taught you with the pen; taught you that which you did not know.

When this revelation came upon the Prophet (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam), he grew troubled that he might have been possessed. So he went to his wife, Hazrat Khadeeja Kubra, who was older than he, and told her what had happened. She then went and spoke with her uncle Warqa bin Naufal, who was familiar with revelation. Having heard the words, he said that this is NAMOOS, which comes from the Greek word Nomus, meaning "LAW." He said that this is like what was given to Moosa AS. And he warned the Prophet (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) that once he began to deliver this message, the people would become his enemies.

After that, the revelations began to come fairly regularly. He described the experience as being like the vibrations of a ringing bell. If you read the مقطعات, such as ALIF LAAAM MEEM, you find that they carry a vibration. This is because revelation was moving into physical form from another realm. Divine meanings were being given a body in words.

The Quran is the uncreated speech of God. It consists of His eternal meanings, which move into the vehicle of language.

body.text_en:
The next revelation was یا ایھا المزمل, O you who are wrapped, for the Messenger of Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) would wrap himself in a blanket when he meditated.

The Messenger of Allah was asked to invite his family to the word of Allah.

Maulatina Khadeeja was the first to accept Islam, and Maulana Ali followed her. After that the Messenger of Allah invited the members of his family, who were of the Quraish. He asked them, "What if I told you that there is an army on the other side of this mountain, Qubais (جبل القبیس)? Would you believe me?" They all answered that they would believe him, because he was SAADIQ and AMEEN. So he said, "What if I tell you that I have been chosen as a messenger of God?" They said, "We do not believe you." They rejected him, and they began to oppose him. When he began to preach his message, one of the complaints the Quraish made was this: یُسَفِّہُ اَحلامَنا — he makes us look stupid. For he would say, "You worship these pieces of wood and stone. How can they benefit you?"

This was remarkably similar to the way Ibraheem AS took apart the idea of idolatry. When he was thirteen years old, there was a wedding in the neighboring village. The whole village left to attend it. He went into the main temple there and smashed all the idols with his axe. Then he hung the axe on the shoulder of the biggest idol. When the people returned and saw the state of their idols, they were very upset, and they began to investigate who could have done such a thing. Someone said, "We heard Ibraheem speak of such things." So they summoned him, and he said, "Why do you not ask this big idol, since he is the one holding the axe?" They said, "Do you think we are stupid? How can this idol speak?" He replied, "Then why do you worship him?"

The purpose of the Qur'an is to reflect on the throne-ness, and to ask why we are doing certain things. We do not reflect on the actions we perform. We do not question them. We simply do them because of culture, which is imposed upon us. Why are we burying our daughters? The Qur'an came to question things. This is why Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) faced so much opposition, because he began to say, "This is wrong."

The Qur'an is classified as having two major parts:

Meccan Qur'an — Madani Qur'an
85 Surahs — 39 Surahs
11 Para — 19 Para
Smaller — Larger

The main topic of the Meccan Qur'an was TAWHEED, which linguistically means "to make one" or "making one." It means to worship Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala) without associations. There is no anthropomorphism in Islam. There is no associating of God with His creations: لیس کمثلہ شئی — there is no THING (creation) like Him. Therefore, whatever occurs to the intellect, Allah (Subhanhu Wa Ta'ala) is not like that. Maulana Ali said: العجز عن درک ادراکہ اداک. The inability to comprehend God is the comprehension of God.

The Christian solution to the unknowability of God is Christ, in whom God becomes man, so that God can understand man. Incarnation means "becoming of flesh." But for Muslims, the knowability of God is ONLY through creation. We explore creation in order to understand God, because creation is the theater of divine manifestation. Muslims do not believe that God can become a thing. There is no embodiment.

body.text_en:
The Qur'an is not a linear book. The book asks its reader to surrender the desire for linearity. If someone cannot do that, he will have a great deal of trouble following the Qur'an, because it does not begin at the beginning and it does not end at the end.

The Qur'an speaks of the concept of AAKHIRA, which means the end, or the hereafter.

The Arabs did not believe in the concept of a hereafter. Their world was made up of manhood, chivalry, poetry, wine, and women. Most of their poems were about wine and women. They loved those two things. The Qur'an radically challenged that view of the world. They asked the Messenger, "How can decayed bones be brought back to life after they have become dust?" The Qur'an answers that the One who brought you the first time is able to do it again, because anything done a second time is easier than the first. The Qur'an speaks of a ساعۃ, which means the end of time. Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) was the first sign of the beginning of the end. On an individual level, it is the last moment of our lives, which is imminent death. All the previous traditions — Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism — indicate that at some point the human experience will come to an end. They all have a concept of an apocalyptic vision.

The descriptions of the afterlife in the Qur'an are highly detailed on both sides, heaven as well as hell, and these descriptions are sensual in nature. Of paradise it speaks of gardens with flowing rivers, fruits, beautiful maidens, and youths. But according to a hadith, when Rasul Allah (Salallahu alayhi wa aalihee wa sallam) was asked about heaven, he said: ما لا عین رأت ولا اذن سمعت ولا قطر علی قلب بشر. It is something no eye has seen, whose sounds no ear has heard, and which has not occurred to any heart. So the concepts of heaven and hell are described so that we can form some imagination of what they are, because after death there is no body. All that exists is the soul, and so it is a sensual experience rather than a physical one. For example, Aristotle asked his student, who was thirsty and reaching out for a drink: is it the drink that you seek, or the quenching of your thirst that you find pleasurable? The student replied, the quenching of the thirst. It is that human experience which has been described for jannah, and the physicality is only a symbol pointing to the underlying experience.

The Meccan surahs carry verses that address "O humanity" or "O mankind," whereas the Medinan surahs begin with "O you who have believed." The Meccan Qur'an was geared more toward the individual, while the Medinan Qur'an was about social interactions and behavior. So if you believe in Allah, how does that change your behavior toward His other creations? The Meccan Qur'an aimed at building individual personalities, whereas the Medinan Qur'an aimed at building a society. It was creating an environment in which the Qur'anic teachings would appear at the level of society, and not simply at the level of the individual.

How the Qur'an Was Compiled
